docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 5 — "Indra's Search: The Self in the Upaniṣads"
docs.text:
← Ep 4

Ep 6 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:44 In brief: The gods are everywhere in the Upaniṣads yet do surprisingly little philosophical work; the episode reads the Chāndogya story of the god Indra's century-long apprenticeship under Prajāpati as a parable about the self (ātman) — something so close to us that it can never be an object of perception, knowable only obliquely in the very act of perceiving and thinking. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Canary"; Prajāpati ≈ "Prachapati / Prachabati / Prajabati"; Virocana ≈ "Virochana"; Yājñavalkya ≈ "Yajnavakya / Yajnyalvakya / Yajnial Valkya"; Maitreyī ≈ "Maitra Yi"; Chāndogya ≈ "Chandogya"; Bṛhadāraṇyaka ≈ "great forest Upanishad"; Bimal Krishna Matilal ≈ "Bimal Krishna Matilal").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The Chāndogya Upaniṣad — source of the Indra/Prajāpati "search for the self" story that anchors the episode [00:05:21].
  • Indra — the most prominent god of the Ṛgveda, here cast not as creator-king but as a student searching for his true self [00:04:38].
  • Prajāpati — the reluctant teacher-creator who feeds Indra one false account of the self after another [00:06:04].
  • Yājñavalkya — Upaniṣadic sage of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka ("great forest") Upaniṣad, whose dialogue with his wife Maitreyī supplies the "not, not" and salt-mass images [00:13:20].
  • Bimal Krishna Matilal — modern scholar quoted to the effect that, in Indian philosophy, the gods are "window dressing" [00:03:48].

docs.title: The gods in the texts — and the contrast with Europe
docs.text:
• [00:00:38] One way to mark Indian philosophy off from European: it "first emerged and was always pursued in a religious context." We think of Buddhism, Jainism and Hinduism primarily as religions, not schools of philosophy — even though they produced rich philosophical argument.
  • [00:00:59] But the contrast can be challenged from both sides. Religious ideas were rarely far from European thinkers either — from ancient pagans to medieval theologians and beyond. And it is "notoriously difficult" to say whether, or in what sense, Buddhism is even a religion. Conveniently, this is a podcast on the history of philosophy, not of religion, so the issue can be set aside [00:01:23].
  • [00:01:28] Still, the religious elements in these ancient Indian texts have to be noticed. The most striking is the sheer presence of gods, who appear as characters in the Upaniṣads and the Mahābhārata. Even the Buddhists, who rejected much of Brahmanic ritual and doctrine, kept recognizing and talking about the gods [00:01:46].

docs.title: What philosophical work do the gods do? — natural theology and creation
docs.text:
• [00:01:56] The live question: what philosophical relevance do the gods carry? Can we speak of a "natural theology" in Buddhism or in Hindu sacred texts? Only, Adamson says, if we drop some of the expectations that phrase usually brings.
  • [00:02:11] A striking absence matches the striking presence of gods: there is little interest in creation of the world in the strong sense — bringing the universe into being out of nothing, at a distinct point in time. Instead the standard picture is one of world cycles, each lasting a vast period and followed by another equally long one.
  • [00:02:35] There are partial exceptions, flagged back in episode 3: in the Ṛgveda the gods extract the species of animals from Puruṣa, and one god, Prajāpati, is briefly a creator. He returns in the Mahābhārata, first fashioning a body for himself, then the underlying matter of the whole universe, from which he makes everything else [00:02:47].
  • [00:02:58] The Upaniṣads too sometimes convey that all things are caused by or depend on something — there brahman is the fundamental support of all reality. Indeed the word brahman means "that which bears up all things" [00:03:11].
  • [00:03:18] Yet if brahman is divine, it is a markedly impersonal divinity: rarely said to create, reward or punish. Already in the earlier Vedas the universe has a moral order independent of any theological force. That continues with karma, where a god's role is at most a kind of "cosmic bookkeeping" — invoked only to guarantee that our good and bad deeds actually shape our future fates [00:03:31].

docs.title: Matilal: the gods as "window dressing"
docs.text:
• [00:03:48] For these reasons the great scholar Bimal Krishna Matilal wrote that in Indian philosophy the gods are essentially "window dressing" — more a part of India's cultural heritage than anything load-bearing.
  • [00:04:01] And yet the gods are still there. We may find no creation from nothing and no divine-command theory of ethics, but gods populate the philosophical texts — and even take part in the philosophical discussions [00:04:07].
  • [00:04:14] Examples: the teacher at the centre of the Bhagavad-Gītā is Kṛṣṇa, an avatar of Viṣṇu; and gods appear as sage-like interlocutors in the Upaniṣads, perhaps as a strategy for lending authority to the teachings [00:04:27].

docs.title: Indra, the searching god (Chāndogya Upaniṣad)
docs.text:
• [00:04:38] One of the most famous of all Upaniṣadic stories has Indra as its lead. He is instantly familiar to anyone who has paged through the Ṛgveda — though hardly its only god. Natural phenomena (wind, sun, heaven, dawn) count as deities, as do ritual elements like Agni (the ritual fire) and Soma (the sacrificial plant) [00:04:50].
  • [00:05:04] Because the Ṛgveda centres on the sacrifice of Soma, and Soma is offered up to Indra, Indra is its most prominent god — far more so than Viṣṇu, who plays only a minor part there.
  • [00:05:21] All the more noteworthy, then, that in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad Indra appears not as almighty creator or priestly king but as a figure searching after wisdom — taking to heart the ubiquitous Upaniṣadic exhortation to go in search of your true self.
  • [00:05:46] As the previous episode showed, that search ends in realizing a hidden correspondence between oneself and the cosmos, and between both and the space of the Vedic ritual. The twist: you'd expect a god to be explaining this to a human — instead Indra is the one on the journey of self-discovery [00:05:57].
  • [00:06:04] The gods and demons have heard that Prajāpati speaks of "a self by discovering which one obtains all the worlds, and all one's desires are fulfilled." This fits the Ṛgveda's Prajāpati, exalted as creator and credited with knowledge surpassing the other gods [00:06:18].

docs.title: The apprenticeship: 101 years of being fobbed off
docs.text:
• [00:06:29] Indra, together with a demon named Virocana, goes to live as a celibate in Prajāpati's āśrama to learn the secret of the self. The first lesson is patience: Prajāpati says nothing for 32 years, then only asks them what they want [00:06:36].
  • [00:06:49] Up to here, Adamson jokes, the story resembles trying to renew your driver's license — but no government bureaucrat would deliver the conversation that follows. When Prajāpati hears their quest, he "fobs them off with an answer he knows to be false."
  • [00:07:12] First false answer — the mirror-image self. Look into a pan of water, he says; what you see is the self. They dress up, look again, and report seeing themselves "beautifully adorned, well dressed, all spruced up." "That is the self, that is the immortal, that is the one free from fear, that is brahman," Prajāpati tells them — and the two leave with contented hearts [00:07:59].
  • [00:08:05] Watching them go, Prajāpati remarks: "there they go, without learning about the self." Virocana is satisfied; Indra is not. He reasons that the reflected self cannot be the true self, for if the body can be made beautiful it can equally be made lame and crippled. He turns back for more instruction [00:08:19].
  • [00:08:32] Another 32-year wait (Indra now has the patience of "a major city hospital"), and a second fobbing-off. Second false answer — the dreaming self: "the one who goes happily about in a dream, that is the self… that is brahman." Indra falls for it, then on reflection sees that the dreaming self still suffers anxiety and disappointment [00:08:49].
  • [00:09:01] Back again, another 32 years, and a third false answer — the dreamless-sleep self: "when one is fast asleep, totally collected and serene, and sees no dreams, that is the self." Again Indra leaves happy, again the doubts return.
  • [00:09:26] This time he waits only five more years — a total of 101 years, which (Adamson notes) "by an amazing coincidence" is roughly how long it'll take to cover the whole history of philosophy in podcast form. Now Indra is finally given the true answer — and we, mercifully, only wait a few minutes for it [00:09:38].

docs.title: How knowledge works: the do-it-yourself self
docs.text:
• [00:09:51] Before the payoff, dwell on the manner of the story. Prajāpati shows astonishing reluctance and a willingness to deceive — not just the demon Virocana but a fellow god — and insists on long stretches of harsh living as the price of instruction [00:09:57].
  • [00:10:10] Crucially, Indra only improves by going away content with an answer and then beginning to question it. The ever-more-sophisticated accounts come as the grudging concessions of a teacher reluctant to share his wisdom even with another divinity [00:10:22].
  • [00:10:34] There's an implied theory of learning here, at least for the central Upaniṣadic topic of the self: one cannot leap straight to an adequate grasp. Before each new stage, Indra must first understand what was inadequate about the previous one. One must see why each idea of the self is false even to speculate on the truth of the next [00:11:06]. Had Indra not seen that the self is no reflection, he couldn't appreciate the subtler doctrine that the true self is met in dreams.
  • [00:11:23] And Prajāpati lets Indra discover each flaw for himself. Indra must not merely be told he is not a reflection — he must come to see the flaw "as the result of his own personal investigation." So Prajāpati could neither hand over the final doctrine nor announce that the earlier ones were false; he could only feed Indra each doctrine and wait to see if Indra would find it wanting [00:11:40].

docs.title: Why the self is so hard to find
docs.text:
• [00:11:53] Why does discovering the self demand this do-it-yourself approach — taking even a god over a century? The answer: the self is, ironically, "so close that it is nearly impossible to find" [00:12:12].
  • [00:12:20] Things outside us are possible objects of sensation: to perceive the Eiffel Tower you fly to Paris. But "no plane ticket" brings you to a vantage point from which to behold the self. Nor can it be reached by deduction or by another person's testimony — as later Indian philosophers would put it, there is no pramāṇa (means of knowledge) that leads to knowledge of the self [00:12:36].
  • [00:12:50] As the last episode suggested, brahman and the self make knowledge possible without themselves being knowable. Our natural instinct is to hunt the self among the objects of consciousness, because that strategy works for everything else — but in this one case it is exactly wrong [00:13:01].

docs.title: Yājñavalkya: "not, not" — the self that can't be objectified
docs.text:
• [00:13:09] Other Upaniṣadic passages confirm it: the self is not within reach of the senses and mind precisely because it is what makes sensing and thinking possible — "too close to be seen." This is voiced in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka ("great forest") Upaniṣad by the sage Yājñavalkya in dialogue with his wife Maitreyī [00:13:20].
  • [00:13:34] His argument: where there is a duality, one thing can smell, see, hear, greet, think of and perceive another. But when "the whole has become one's very self," there is no longer any other to smell or see, and nothing by which to do so. "By what means can one perceive the perceiver?" [00:14:04].
  • [00:14:12] Hence of the self one can only say "not, not" (neti neti): it is ungraspable (cannot be grasped), undecaying (not subject to decay), with nothing sticking to it; not bound, neither trembling in fear nor suffering injury. The self is "not even a possible target of language" [00:14:42]. As another passage puts it: you can't see the seer who sees, hear the hearer who hears, think the thinker who thinks, perceive the perceiver who perceives — "the self within all is this self of yours" [00:15:03].

docs.title: Re-reading Indra's three false answers
docs.text:
• [00:15:10] The framework now makes sense of Indra's education. The first two bogus answers tried to make the self a possible object of consciousness — first an object of sensory awareness (the reflected image), then an object of dream consciousness. Each fails because the self is the subject of sensation, not something sensed [00:15:24].
  • [00:15:34] The third answer moves to the idea that the self is no object of consciousness at all, but simply whatever undergoes dreamless, contentless sleep. Indra rejects even this — because that self "is in fact nothing at all." As he observes, in dreamless sleep the self "does not even know any of these beings here, it has become completely annihilated" [00:15:52].

docs.title: The true answer: the self as that-which-is-aware
docs.text:
• [00:16:03] Having diagnosed every false proposal — and shown himself, Adamson quips, "more expert" a waiter than any restaurant employs — Indra is ready for the truth [00:16:05].
  • [00:16:11] The answer: "the one who is aware, 'let me smell this' — that is the self," the faculty of smell merely enabling him to smell; likewise for speech, hearing and thought. The self is that which underlies thought, speech and sensation [00:16:44].
  • [00:16:55] The chariot analogy (from another Upaniṣad): intellect is the charioteer, the mind the reins, the body the chariot, the senses the horses. But that risks suggesting too active a self. Strictly, Prajāpati's self "is the source of neither action nor will." It stands still, observing itself as it sees, hears and thinks — not merely the one who sees, nor the one who decides to look, but the one aware of seeing and looking [00:17:19].
  • [00:17:31] Even so it is not a detached, impassive self disengaged from its own desires and actions, because it is aware of itself even as it pursues them. The self is "that in virtue of which the subject of consciousness is self-conscious," while never itself being an object of consciousness [00:17:44].

docs.title: Self-discovery without an object: catching the self in its activity
docs.text:
• [00:17:50] The remaining puzzle: in what can self-discovery consist if the self is not something we can discover? A hint from Yājñavalkya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka [00:17:57]: when a drum is beaten, you cannot catch the external sounds on their own — you catch them only "by getting hold of the drum or the men beating the drum."
  • [00:18:13] So too: we catch the sensing self only by getting hold of the sensing; we catch the thinker only by getting hold of the thinking. We reach the self "not directly, but by catching it in its activity" — found "in the shadowy edges of experience" [00:18:33].
  • [00:18:38] A modern gloss: the self is known only through the phenomenal quality of thinking — "the flavor of the experience of what it is like to think." There is something it feels like, from within, to be thinking; focusing on that, rather than on the thought one is thinking, makes one obliquely aware of the self [00:18:49].
  • [00:18:55] So we should abandon the instinctive assumption that the self is a core or centre of consciousness. Rather it "pervades all of consciousness" and can be extracted from it [00:19:00].
  • [00:19:07] Yājñavalkya's image (preferred even over Prajāpati's): "as a mass of salt has no distinctive core and surface, the whole thing is a single mass of flavor, so… this self has no distinctive core and surface — the whole thing is a compact mass of cognition" [00:19:20]. The self is hard to find precisely because it is always present: the phenomenal character of experience is barely noticeable, hidden behind the false desires of our worldly concerns [00:19:34].

docs.title: Is this religion? — and where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:19:44] Though the message passes from one god to another, it is "not necessarily religious in character." The self-knowledge here does resemble a mystic's awareness of God — graspable only indirectly, barely sayable [00:19:57]. But identifying that experience with a mystical awareness of the divine is a further step, taken only in the more theistic, later Upaniṣads [00:20:02].
  • [00:20:15] Besides, when most people think "religion and the Upaniṣads," it isn't self-knowledge that comes to mind — it's the cycle of rebirth, and above all the law of karma governing each individual's fate in the next life [00:20:20]. How distinctive of the Upaniṣads is that idea really, and how can karma be understood philosophically? "You won't have to wait 101 years to find out" — it's the next topic [00:20:39].

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Chāndogya Upaniṣad — Upaniṣad containing the central story of Indra's 101-year search for the self under Prajāpati.
  • Bṛhadāraṇyaka ("great forest") Upaniṣad — source of Yājñavalkya's "not, not" teaching and the salt-mass and drum images.
  • Indra — the Ṛgveda's most prominent god (recipient of the Soma sacrifice); cast here as a student of the self rather than creator-king.
  • Prajāpati — creator-figure and reluctant teacher who offers Indra three deliberately false accounts of the self before the true one.
  • Virocana — the demon who studies alongside Indra but leaves satisfied with the first (mirror-image) answer.
  • Yājñavalkya — Upaniṣadic sage; in dialogue with his wife Maitreyī he denies the self can be an object of perception or language.
  • Bimal Krishna Matilal — modern scholar who called the gods "window dressing" in Indian philosophy.
  • ātman / the self — that which underlies and is aware of all thinking, speech and sensation; the subject, never an object, of consciousness; "so close it is nearly impossible to find."
  • brahman — "that which bears up all things"; the impersonal divine support of reality, which makes knowledge possible without itself being knowable.
  • pramāṇa — a means/source of knowledge; the point being that no pramāṇa yields knowledge of the self.
  • karma — the law governing each individual's fate in the next life; the god's role in it is mere "cosmic bookkeeping."
  • neti neti ("not, not") — Yājñavalkya's formula: the self can only be characterized by negation, being ungraspable and beyond language.
  • Puruṣa / Prajāpati / world-cycles — the limited creation motifs of Indian texts, set against the absence of creation-from-nothing.
  • Ṛgveda · Agni · Soma · Viṣṇu · Kṛṣṇa — the Vedic ritual backdrop: ritual fire, sacrificial plant, and gods who appear (Kṛṣṇa as Viṣṇu's avatar) as philosophical interlocutors.

docs.text:
← Ep 5

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:18:46 In brief: Karma is not mere moral book-keeping or a prop for caste inequality; introduced as a secret doctrine in the earliest Upaniṣads, it is best read as a way to affirm human freedom and motivate good action — staked out against Ājīvika fatalism and Cārvāka materialism, then tested by objections about self-interest and the prospering of the wicked, and finally reframed by the Bhagavad-Gītā's call to act without desire for the fruits. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Gannery"; Ājīvika ≈ "Ajifaka/Ajivacus"; Gosāla ≈ "Goshala"; Cārvāka ≈ "Chavaka/Chadavaka/Charvaca"; Chāndogya Upaniṣad ≈ "Chandogyo Panishad"; Yājñavalkya ≈ "Yajnadhyakya"; Bṛhadāraṇyaka ≈ "great forest Upanishad"; Kṣatriya ≈ "Kshatria"; Vaiśya ≈ "Vaishya"; kartṛ ≈ "Kartri"; bhoktṛ ≈ "Bhaktri"; svadharma ≈ "swadharma").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The Bṛhadāraṇyaka ("Great Forest") Upaniṣad — source of the secret teaching of karma; the Yājñavalkya dialogue [00:04:32].
  • The Chāndogya Upaniṣad — the "pleasant womb / foul womb" passage used to read karma as caste-justification [00:06:32].
  • Gosāla — leader of the Ājīvikas, the fatalist ascetic whose views survive in the Buddha's dialogues [00:07:09].
  • The Cārvāka — materialist philosophers reported in the Buddhist canon as moral skeptics [00:09:00].
  • The Bhagavad-Gītā — the Arjuna–Kṛṣṇa dialogue inside the Mahābhārata; the "act without desire for the fruit" reply to karma [00:15:03].

docs.title: Karma even inspires dance music
docs.text:
• [00:00:32] Today's episode: "You Are What You Do — Karma." Adamson opens with a joke: it's the rare philosophical concept that inspires dance music. You won't find Kool & the Gang meditating on determinism, or Madonna setting a reductionist theory of mind to a disco beat.
  • [00:00:54] The exception is Culture Club's 1983 hit Karma Chameleon — but it may be the exception that proves the rule, since a close reading of the lyrics betrays a shaky grasp of the concept. Boy George complains, "When you go, you're gone forever," which is exactly missing the point.
  • [00:01:14] The ancient Indian notion of karma turns precisely on the idea that when we go, we are not gone forever. We will be reborn, and the actions we performed in this life will shape our fate in the next. The consequences of this idea for Indian philosophy and religion can hardly be exaggerated.

docs.title: Rebirth as re-death, and the project of eliminating karma
docs.text:
• [00:01:30] Rebirth sounds optimistic — surely we all fear death and would welcome living forever, even in another form. But that's not how many ancient Indians saw it. Their goal was to escape the cycle of rebirth, which is, after all, just as much a cycle of re-death.
  • [00:01:55] Since karma is the factor that ties one to the next incarnation, the only route to liberation seemed to be to eliminate all karma from oneself.
  • [00:02:05] Extreme measures followed. The early Jainas devised a practice that has been called immobility asceticism: after years of training they would try to stay completely still until they died of thirst, hunger, or exposure. The point was to avoid any action whatsoever — since all action, good or bad, produces karma — and the suffering of this agonizing death would cleanse the karma acquired earlier in life.
  • [00:02:37] Another dissenting group, the Ājīvikas, were more pessimistic: the cycle of rebirth simply cannot be escaped, and there is no point trying to affect one's karma. Each individual just has to wait until the cycle of incarnations runs out — which the Ājīvikas expected to take millions of years. "And you thought Indra showed patience."

docs.title: Where did karma come from? The rice-trail argument
docs.text:
• [00:03:00] Karma and rebirth already appear in the earliest Upaniṣads, so it's natural to tie the idea to the Brahmanic tradition rather than these dissident groups. But the origins are debated.
  • [00:03:14] The doctrine is not found in the Vedas themselves — the even earlier texts the Upaniṣads are reacting to. Some scholars assume a Vedic background anyway; others think karma is an "interloper" into Brahmanic culture.
  • [00:03:31] On the interloper view, the notion of karma already existed in the northeastern region around the valley of the Ganges. When the upholders of Brahmanism migrated in from their homelands in the Indus Valley, they fell under the influence of this older tradition and absorbed karma into their teachings.
  • [00:03:50] The debate has turned on surprising details — for instance the prevalence of rice metaphors for the cycle of rebirth, and the use of rice in rituals meant to manipulate karma. Rice is not a crop of the Indus region (where farmers grew wheat); it is characteristic of agriculture in the Ganges. This fine-grained historical analysis could support karma being an indigenous eastern idea rather than a Brahmanic one.
  • [00:04:26] Wherever it was born, karma was — fittingly — reborn in the Upaniṣads.

docs.title: The secret doctrine: Yājñavalkya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka
docs.text:
• [00:04:32] Adamson quotes again from the Bṛhadāraṇyaka ("Great Forest") Upaniṣad. A man dies and his parts disperse — speech into fire, breath into the wind, sight into the sun, mind into the moon, hearing into the quarters, body into the earth, soul into space, blood and seed into water. The question: what happens to that person?
  • [00:05:02] Yājñavalkya replies, "My friend, we cannot talk about this in public. Take my hand, let's discuss it in private." They leave and talk — and they talk about nothing but karma, and praise nothing but karma: "A man turns into something good by good action, and into something bad by bad action."
  • [00:05:28] This is one of the hidden teachings that give the Upaniṣads their name. The secret doctrine, not fit for public consumption, was karma: we are made into what we are by what we do, and in particular it is the moral quality of what we do that shapes the life we will enjoy or suffer.
  • [00:05:50] So here, in an early Upaniṣad, is the core idea most people (other than Boy George) associate with karma: be good, or else. Your moral decisions now will bring reward or punishment down the line — in the next life if not in this one.

docs.title: Is karma just moral retribution — or a prop for caste?
docs.text:
• [00:06:02] But is the theory merely an account of moral retribution? That doesn't sound very appealing — or very philosophical. And it gets worse.
  • [00:06:15] It's tempting to read karma as a justification for the inequality of Brahmanic culture: the Brahmans rewarded for good deeds in a former life, while members of the lower castes — and all women — are being punished for crimes they must have committed in past lives.
  • [00:06:32] The Chāndogya Upaniṣad supplies the material: those of pleasant conduct enter a pleasant womb, "like that of a Brahman, Kṣatriya, or Vaiśya," whereas those of foul behavior enter the foul womb of "a dog, a pig, or an outcast."
  • [00:06:51] But, Adamson insists, this would be a reductive and inadequate understanding. Properly grasped, the doctrine is a way to affirm human freedom and to give us a motivation for acting well. To see why, it helps to set karma against two rival theories.

docs.title: Rival one: Ājīvika fatalism (Gosāla)
docs.text:
• [00:07:04] The first rival is held by the unorthodox ascetic Gosāla, leader of the Ājīvikas, who denied the cycle of rebirth can be escaped. Gosāla held that everything happens exactly as fate predestines it — so human action is ineffective and inconsequential.
  • [00:07:29] The Ājīvika tradition did not survive past antiquity (unlike the other schools discussed), but Gosāla's views are recorded in the dialogues of the Buddha: "There is no deed performed by oneself or by others, no human action, no strength, no courage, no endurance or prowess. All beings are developed by destiny, chance, and nature." The cycle of birth and rebirth is "measured as with a bushel," fixed in length — it "can neither be lessened nor increased." Just as a thrown ball of thread unwinds to its full length, "so fool and wise alike will take their course and make an end of sorrow."
  • [00:08:10] So the Ājīvikas denied that we bear any responsibility for our actions — indeed they could be read as denying that action is possible at all, if acting involves making rational choices.
  • [00:08:24] How then should one live, if reason as a guide to action is a myth? Gosāla's answer is asceticism: withdraw as far as possible from the pretense of action, and live as a renunciate and forest-dweller. This was embraced especially by Ājīvikas who claimed their eons of waiting were finally over and they were living their last incarnation.

docs.title: Rival two: Cārvāka materialism
docs.text:
• [00:08:54] The opposite conclusion was drawn by the materialist philosophers known as the Cārvāka. Their ideas too are reported in the Buddhist canon, where they insist there is no good or evil in the world and that a human is nothing more than flesh and blood.
  • [00:09:11] "Man is formed of the four elements. When he dies, earth returns to earth, water to water, fire to fire, air to air, and the senses vanish into space." Four pallbearers carry the corpse to the burning ground, gossiping about the dead man, "where his bones turn the color of a dove's wing, and his sacrifices end in ashes." Those who preach almsgiving, and those who maintain the existence of immaterial categories, "speak vain and lying nonsense."
  • [00:09:45] So for the Cārvāka there are no reasons to act morally, because there are no moral reasons for action at all. As later episodes will show, this lent itself to a hedonist ethic: deliberative action is possible, but only one thing can guide our deliberations. Like Madonna, the Cārvāka were living in a material world, setting their sights on no goal more exalted than pleasure.

docs.title: Karma as the middle path: deliberative, moral action
docs.text:
• [00:10:13] What is the alternative to Ājīvika fatalism and Cārvāka moral skepticism? First, to hold that there is such a thing as deliberative action — action governed by reason and reflection. Second, to believe that moral considerations should play a role in that deliberation.
  • [00:10:32] To counter fate and chance, one must show there are moral motivations for action. That is why karma was taught as "a simple and effective solution to a tricky problem": the doctrine requires that a person's own character be his own destiny, and that each action has its appropriate consequences. Good actions — springing from a clear-sighted mind and a virtuous disposition — yield future happiness; bad actions — from ignorance, greed, and malice — produce only suffering.
  • [00:11:12] Crucially, for these consequences to bear on my choices, I must believe the results will affect me, not someone else. In Sanskrit terms, the kartṛ (the agent of an action) is the same person as the bhoktṛ (the enjoyer of its result).
  • [00:11:35] So karma implies — or perhaps just assumes — that the world is governed by justice: each person is guaranteed to reap what he or she sows.
  • [00:11:48] This may look like a religious conviction, but as the last episode showed, divine oversight was invoked only gradually. In the Upaniṣads it appears to be a brute fact that there is a moral order built into the universe; only later are divinities made responsible for dispensing justice by karmic merit and demerit. Early on, the world is simply a just place — "the law of karma is one that needs no lawgiver."

docs.title: Objection one: is this just naked self-interest?
docs.text:
• [00:12:24] But is this really morality on firm foundations, or just a naked appeal to self-interest? Each of us is told: behave well, since you and you alone will suffer the consequences of misbehaving — or, more cheerfully, if you want to flourish, behave well. The goal set before me is my own long-term happiness; virtue is a mere instrument for getting it.
  • [00:12:54] It's welcome news that the world rewards the good and punishes the bad — the vicious winding up as dogs and pigs while the virtuous get "a womb with a view upon happiness." But the doctrine seems to give us no reason to exercise genuine altruism, no moral concern for others' interests. If I am only optimizing my own future well-being, I make no effort to further anyone else's.
  • [00:13:17] The Buddha had a simple and brilliant answer: he denied there is any metaphysical distinction between self and others. Concern for others and concern for oneself are therefore one and the same. (The Buddhist theory of no-self gets fuller treatment later.) For now: it reconciles karma with altruism by extending the scope of self-interest.

docs.title: Objection two: but the wicked prosper
docs.text:
• [00:13:49] A more straightforward objection: it just isn't true that good conduct is the best route to happiness. We regularly see the good suffer and the wicked flourish; obviously I can advance my own interests by cheating and lying. Things would go badly if everyone did so, but in a world where people generally behave well, the clever and wicked prosper at the expense of the upright.
  • [00:14:15] Here the apparently religious side of the doctrine — rebirth / transmigration — earns its ethical keep. If I worry not only about this life but the next, my calculations of what is truly advantageous change. It's hardly a winning strategy to secure riches and pleasure by devious means now, if it means being born as a dog next time.
  • [00:14:47] But this postpones the problem rather than solving it. How can we be sure justice will be meted out in the next life for sins committed now? We still need a guaranteed connection between good action and what is good for the individual.

docs.title: The Bhagavad-Gītā: act, but desire no fruit
docs.text:
• [00:15:03] That guaranteed connection is forged in one of the most famous writings of ancient India, the Bhagavad-Gītā — the dialogue between Arjuna and Kṛṣṇa embedded in the Mahābhārata.
  • [00:15:09] On the eve of a great battle, the warrior prince Arjuna is racked with doubt: across the field are not nameless enemies but his own kinsfolk and elders. They are guilty of heinous crimes, and both duty and social convention favor fighting — yet he cannot persuade himself it is right to kill his own family, preferring "the life of a beggar and a mendicant."
  • [00:15:41] Kṛṣṇa intervenes to convince him he must fight, and in doing so rejects the instrumental reasoning bound up with the karma theory. Any action undertaken out of desire for a result only leads to further desires; whatever the outcome, this way of thinking ends only in suffering — one can never satisfy all one's desires, and the more one acts hoping for rewards, the more one is liable to disappointment. As Kṛṣṇa puts it: "From attachment springs desire; from desire is anger born."
  • [00:16:18] The karma theory's goal was to guide deliberation by moral considerations in order to achieve long-term benefit. Kṛṣṇa now argues that none of this matters: whatever goal you choose to desire, you will find only further discontent.
  • [00:16:36] How then should one be motivated to act, if not by desire for results? Kṛṣṇa's answer: the truly virtuous action does not aim at any objective, in this life or another — it is action free from any desire for any result. "Action alone is your proper business, never the fruits it may produce. Let not your motive be the fruit of action."
  • [00:17:02] But how do I know which action to perform, if not by consulting a cosmic system of reward and punishment? Simple: one must do what is natural or proper to oneself — one's svadharma. "Here is just how a man perfects himself, by doing and rejoicing in his proper work."
  • [00:17:24] So the Gītā tells us we must act, but without forming a desire to be fulfilled by acting. Arjuna is to act according to his duty and nature while remaining detached from any self-interest in the results. To act in a way true to one's character is to act well. The karmic consequences may still turn out good — but one should not be motivated by them.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:17:58] With this discussion of karma and the responses it provoked, the series has begun to touch the figures and texts of coming episodes: the Buddha, Jainism, and the Mahābhārata. Varied as they are, they share a reaction to the worldview of the earliest Upaniṣads — sometimes adapting the older ideas, often rejecting them. Many were "born of doubt and resistance directed against the Brahmanic Culture Club."
  • [00:18:33] Before moving on to those dissident groups, though, we're "not ready to let the Upaniṣads go and be gone forever." Next time Adamson is joined by an expert on these texts, Brian Black, for the first of the occasional interviews that will be a running feature of the series.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• karma — action and its moral fruits; "you are what you do." The moral quality of one's deeds shapes the life one will enjoy or suffer, in this incarnation or the next.
  • rebirth / transmigration — the cycle in which one is reborn; experienced as a cycle of re-death to be escaped, not an optimistic immortality.
  • kartṛ / bhoktṛ — the agent of an action and the enjoyer of its result; karma assumes they are the same person, so consequences fall on the one who acts.
  • Bṛhadāraṇyaka ("Great Forest") Upaniṣad — gives the "secret" doctrine of karma in the Yājñavalkya dialogue: a man becomes good by good action, bad by bad.
  • Yājñavalkya — the sage who insists the teaching on what survives death must be discussed privately — and it turns out to be karma.
  • Chāndogya Upaniṣad — source of the "pleasant womb / foul womb" passage (Brahman, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya vs. dog, pig, outcast), used — Adamson argues, reductively — to cast karma as caste-justification.
  • Jainas — practitioners of "immobility asceticism": staying motionless until death to perform no action and so burn off all karma.
  • Ājīvikas — fatalist school holding rebirth is inescapable and karma cannot be affected; one simply waits out millions of years of incarnations.
  • Gosāla — leader of the Ājīvikas; preached that all is fixed by destiny, chance, and nature, so action is inconsequential — recorded in the Buddha's dialogues.
  • Cārvāka — materialists who reduce the human to the four elements, deny good and evil, and (later) embrace a pleasure-seeking, hedonist ethic.
  • Buddha — answers the altruism objection by denying any metaphysical self/other distinction, so self-interest and concern for others coincide (the no-self theory, treated later).
  • Bhagavad-Gītā — the Arjuna–Kṛṣṇa dialogue in the Mahābhārata; reframes karma by urging action with no desire for its fruits.
  • svadharma — one's own proper duty/nature; the Gītā's guide to which action to perform once results are no longer the motive.
  • Mahābhārata — the great epic containing the Bhagavad-Gītā; one of the foundational texts the dissident schools react to.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 7 — "Brian Black on the Upaniṣads"
docs.text:
← Ep 6

Ep 8 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Brian Black 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Brian Black · Runtime: 00:36:00 In brief: An interview with Brian Black (Lancaster University) on how the Upaniṣads relate to earlier Vedic literature, who wrote them and for whom, whether "religious" and "philosophical" are useful labels, and what their dialogue form — including its women characters — tells us about reading them as philosophy. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Canary / Janard"; Brian Black ≈ "Brian Black"; Bṛhadāraṇyaka ≈ "Brihadaranyaku / Great Forest"; Chāndogya ≈ "Chandogia"; Kauṣītaki ≈ "Kashi-Taki"; Praśna ≈ "Prashna"; Maitrī ≈ "Mait"; Kaṭha ≈ "Kata"; Yājñavalkya ≈ "Yajnavalchia / Yagnyavalkya / Yagni Valkya"; Uddālaka Āruṇi ≈ "Udalaika Aruni"; Śāṇḍilya ≈ "Shandiliya"; Gārgī ≈ "Gargi"; Ājīvika ≈ "Ajivaka"; Brāhmaṇas ≈ "Brahmina's"; Purāṇas ≈ "piranhas"; Aśoka ≈ "Ashoka"; Vārāṇasī ≈ "Baranasi").

docs.title: Setting the scene: who's talking
docs.text:
• [00:00:17] Adamson opens with the usual credits — the History of Philosophy in India with Jonardon Ganeri and Peter Adamson, supported by King's College London and the LMU in Munich — then introduces the guest: Brian Black, a lecturer in religious studies at Lancaster University. Today is an interview about the Upaniṣads, the texts discussed over the last few episodes.
  • [00:00:50] Adamson sets up the central puzzle: the Upaniṣads are "routinely described as a kind of commentary on earlier Vedic texts," yet when you actually read them they don't read like commentaries at all — they're remarkably heterogeneous in their material. He asks Black to explain how exactly they relate to the earlier Vedic literature.

docs.title: How the Upaniṣads relate to the Vedas
docs.text:
• [00:01:11] Black agrees they are not, technically, commentaries — they say a lot about earlier Vedic texts, but that's different. He breaks Adamson's question into two: their heterogeneity and their relation to the Vedas more broadly.
  • [00:01:41] On heterogeneity: the Upaniṣads were composed over a long stretch of time. None of the dates for ancient Indian texts are anywhere near exact, but the scholarly consensus puts their composition between roughly 700 BCE and 200 BCE. Anything written across five centuries won't carry a single systematic position.
  • [00:02:22] They were also composed by members of different Vedic schools, often in direct competition with one another. Many Upaniṣads talk about the self (ātman) or ultimate reality (brahman) and share basic concerns, but individual Upaniṣads — or even different sections of the same one — can differ in interpretation or emphasis, precisely because their authors were vying over who had the best teaching of the self or of ultimate reality.
  • [00:03:09] On their relation to the Vedas: the Upaniṣads are part of the Vedas — the fourth and final section. So they can't be "commentaries on" the Vedas because they themselves are Veda. But the relationship to the earlier sections is complex. By claiming Vedic status they claim authority for themselves, and like the Vedas they privilege the Brahmin caste, the Vedic ritual, and the Vedas themselves.
  • [00:03:53] Yet at the same time they criticize earlier Vedic material. Some sections attack Brahmin ritualists for paying too much attention to ritual and not enough to the new philosophical ideas about the self, ultimate reality, the breath, and so on — or they criticize Brahmins for being Brahmin in name only, without really understanding the teachings. So the Upaniṣads are simultaneously part of the Vedas and critical of earlier Vedic material.
  • [00:04:43] Adamson finds this combination striking — presenting yourself as sacred literature while reflecting critically on an earlier text. It may happen in other religious traditions, but it's an unusual structure within Vedic literature: a layered series of texts, the last of which (the Upaniṣads) reflects on the others. Black confirms there are four layers in all, the Upaniṣads being the last.

docs.title: Who wrote them, and for whom
docs.text:
• [00:05:12] Adamson asks about authors and intended audience: the authors claim religious insight and the power to deliver a revealed or sacred discourse — who were they, and who were they talking to? Or, given the long span of composition, is that even a single question?
  • [00:05:48] Black: we don't really know who wrote them, but the internal evidence strongly suggests the authors were male Brahmins. Many of the earlier Upaniṣads also claim to be secret or esoteric — you can only learn an Upaniṣad in the proper way, from the proper teacher, after proper initiation. That tells us something important: they do not claim universal status.
  • [00:06:28] He contrasts this with later Hindu texts like the Bhagavad-Gītā, which present themselves as teachings available to everybody. The Upaniṣads — though Black thinks their subject matter is in fact relevant to everybody and worth reading today — do not claim that status for themselves. So the primary authors were Brahmins and the primary audience was Brahmins.
  • [00:07:10] But there's a second audience. Especially in the earlier Upaniṣads — the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, the Chāndogya, the Kauṣītaki — there seems to be an attempt to address a royal / kingly community as well. Black gives reasons.
  • [00:07:35] First, several passages claim that the knowledge in them originally came from outside Brahmin circles — from kings, the kingly class, or even a god or goddess.
  • [00:07:55] Some of these claims look mostly rhetorical. In the Chāndogya, a king claims to deliver a teaching never before known by Brahmins — but what he then teaches is almost verbatim material already found in older grammatical texts. So it reads more as a rhetorical device than a statement of historical fact. Still, the very fact that the text wants to bring a kingly audience into the conversation, sometimes crediting the knowledge to them, is significant.
  • [00:08:49] Adamson recalls passages where the kingly character tells the Brahmin, "Actually, I'll explain the teaching to you, rather than you to me" — and one passage (perhaps in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka / Great Forest Upaniṣad) where it's expressly noted that this reversal is unusual but will be allowed anyway.
  • [00:09:10] Black reads these passages — admitting interpretation here is speculative — as a way of reinforcing Brahmanical knowledge: making the king the mouthpiece of the teaching the Brahmins are promoting, to bolster the Brahmins' own status.
  • [00:09:38] A second way kings appear as audience is in the benefit-statements that often follow a teaching. Upaniṣadic passages frequently end by stating what the knowledge enables. Many promise things like immortality or a long life — but some promise rewards aimed squarely at royalty: that you will defeat all your enemies, expand your territory, even (in one case) "smash all your enemies to bits." That kind of payoff strongly suggests the teachings were directed outward toward the royal class, not Brahmins alone.
  • [00:10:53] Adamson jokes that "smash your enemies" is not a benefit a Buddhist would advertise. Black agrees Buddhists don't make those claims exactly — but notes that Buddhist sources do, in some cases, seem to have had a royal audience in mind too. (Adamson previews a later episode on Aśoka the Great, whose inscriptions seem influenced by Buddhism.)

docs.title: "Religious," "sacred," "philosophical" — competing labels?
docs.text:
• [00:11:19] Adamson raises a worry some listeners may have: the Upaniṣads are sacred texts and foundational texts for a religion (Hinduism). Is that consistent with calling them philosophical? Are the two roles in competition?
  • [00:11:51] Black: words like sacred, religious, and philosophical are our very modern categories. The Upaniṣads themselves don't draw those lines between the kinds of material they discuss. So things that look contradictory to us — what we'd expect from a "religious" versus a "philosophical" text — wouldn't have been contradictions at all to the composers and early listening communities (or, he adds, to most other ancient texts).
  • [00:12:41] His comparison: Plato is taught in philosophy departments, but one could argue Plato was also a deeply religious thinker in whom religion plays an important role — we just don't tend to read him that way. Go back to the ancient world, in Greece or India, and our own distinctions often don't quite work.
  • [00:13:12] Black is candid that he himself often approaches the Upaniṣads as philosophy — not the only way he reads them, but a frequent one — and that this is a hermeneutic / interpretive choice on his part as a modern reader and teacher. He thinks it's an important choice: if we labeled the Upaniṣads as merely religious, then made the further assumption that they are therefore "Hindu texts" specific to Hinduism, many readers who aren't from India or don't have a Hindu background would miss out on the insights and questions the texts raise — questions relevant to everyone's life but potentially "closed off" by an overly religious framing.
  • [00:14:30] So none of these labels — sacred, philosophical — works completely, but each has its place in a series on world philosophy. Reading the Upaniṣads as philosophy reveals overlaps in questions, themes, and methods of inquiry, both with other ancient texts and with our own philosophical inquiries today.
  • [00:15:04] Adamson sharpens the point into a two-way claim: approaching the Upaniṣads as philosophy says something about the Upaniṣads (there's philosophy there) and something about philosophy (a text like an Upaniṣad can count as a philosophical text). Black agrees emphatically: reading them as philosophy lets us notice things we'd miss through a purely religious lens, and at the same time prompts us to reflect on — and perhaps expand — our own category of philosophy.

docs.title: The dialogue form: what "dialogue" means
docs.text:
• [00:15:58] Adamson flags the feature most likely to be cited as evidence the Upaniṣads are philosophical: they are intensely dialogical — exchanges between teacher and student, between two sages, between competing sages, between sages and kings. This inevitably evokes Plato and his philosophical dialogues from antiquity. Black has edited a book on dialogue in the Upaniṣads and ancient Indian traditions; Adamson asks what he means by "dialogue" and why it matters for how we read these texts.
  • [00:16:49] Black's primary use of "dialogue" is descriptive and literary: portions of the Upaniṣads are presented as a conversation between named (and sometimes unnamed) speakers, often with emphasis on the speakers' interaction with one another.
  • [00:17:25] Dialogue is a crucial literary mechanism in ancient Indian religious and philosophical texts, used to frame whole works. Some Upaniṣads open as a dialogue and present their entire content as one — he names the Praśna, the Maitrī, and the Kaṭha Upaniṣads as texts literally organized as dialogues. These are thought to be later Upaniṣads.
  • [00:18:11] Interestingly, the earlier Upaniṣads — the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the Chāndogya — which contain some of the liveliest and most engaging dialogues, don't necessarily have as many dialogues overall as the later ones. So the technique of using dialogue to structure an entire text seems to have developed over time; it isn't there from the very beginning.
  • [00:18:49] After the Upaniṣads, later texts — the Mahābhārata, the Rāmāyaṇa, and throughout the Purāṇas — are likewise organized as dialogue, the whole text framed as a conversation. So the book's starting point is simply to notice how important and recurring dialogue is in organizing textual material.

docs.title: What dialogue does
docs.text:
• [00:19:24] But dialogue isn't always doing the same job; it has several different uses, and on any given occasion may do some and not others.
  • [00:19:46] In the Upaniṣads, one main function is to mimic or demonstrate the text's orality. There is heavy emphasis on the lineage of teachings — almost every Upaniṣad includes a long list of teachers and students across several generations. Any given dialogue can be read as a snapshot of one point in a lineage, re-emphasizing that the Vedas were originally composed and transmitted orally.
  • [00:20:35] A second function: dialogue confers authority by telling us who the teacher is. The Upaniṣads see the emergence of important philosophical personalities — Yājñavalkya, Uddālaka Āruṇi, Śāṇḍilya — who recur not only in the Upaniṣads but in earlier texts like the Brāhmaṇas. So when the Bṛhadāraṇyaka delivers famous teachings about the self, karma, or rebirth, the teaching carries weight not only from its content but because Yājñavalkya said it — much as Buddhist teachings gain authority as the words of the Buddha.
  • [00:21:44] A third function: dialogue puts philosophical or religious teaching in a social context. Black says this interested him while writing his book on the Upaniṣads, because Indian philosophy has a reputation for being conducted by solitary figures — the image that springs to mind is someone going off alone into the forest to practice yoga. Yet in some of the very oldest philosophical texts we don't see that: the main philosophical content unfolds in social situations, with people interacting. Even where a scene isn't a debate — sometimes it's just a teacher telling a student how it is, and the student listening attentively — there's still a sense that the ideas are placed in a setting where they could be contested.

docs.title: Are the dialogues actually philosophical? (Adamson plays devil's advocate)
docs.text:
• [00:22:58] Adamson pushes back: any honest reader admits the Upaniṣadic dialogues are not obviously philosophical in the Platonic sense. In Plato you get Socrates walking an interlocutor through a sequence of argument; in the Upaniṣads you often get riddling or mysterious pronouncements, with the interlocutor only saying "yes," "no," or "try again" — so you don't seem to have two genuine partners in an argument. Is that a reason to deny the Upaniṣads are genuinely philosophical, or is our job as readers to reconstruct the underlying arguments behind the riddling remarks?
  • [00:24:02] Black: first, the Upaniṣads "don't care whether we call them philosophy or not." Some dialogues are more philosophical than others, but yes — it is our job to look closely, at all the material (not only the dialogues), to uncover whatever philosophical methods are there.
  • [00:24:33] He makes two moves. First, although the dialogues are what draw attention to the Upaniṣads as possibly philosophical, he'd argue the dialogues are only one of several sections in the text that count as philosophical: the Upaniṣads also engage in introspection, observation, and experimentation, none of which require a dialogue.
  • [00:25:18] Second, even among dialogues, some are frankly not very philosophical, but others very much are. In a recent paper he's examined how some dialogues carry a dialectical structure — the same kind of dialectical structure visible later in Indian philosophy. So even a dialogue that doesn't look like a contested exchange can still set up the structure of an argument, even if the characters themselves aren't visibly arguing.
  • [00:26:07] His example of that structure: one character presents a thesis, the next offers a counter-argument, and a third section either tries to bring the two together or accepts a lingering tension between them. So the Upaniṣads aren't explicit, as a Platonic dialogue is, about how they're being philosophical — but read closely enough, a good case can be made that they are.

docs.title: Women characters in the Upaniṣads
docs.text:
• [00:26:49] Adamson notes Black mentioned recurring characters, and turns to the women who occasionally appear among the male sages — adding that there will be a whole later episode on the role of women in classical Indian texts, but since Black has written on this, he asks for his view.
  • [00:27:24] Black finds it "really refreshing" to see them. The texts are still primarily about men, but the female characters appear in positive ways — and, tellingly, the text doesn't make a big deal of their presence, as if the authors would expect to see women, at least on some occasions, included in public philosophy.
  • [00:28:09] He reads this on two levels. It may reflect a historical reality in which some women did participate in philosophy in ancient India — we can't know for sure, but he sees no reason to rule it out. But many female characters also have a symbolic function in the text.
  • [00:28:40] The symbolic point ties back to the Upaniṣads' critique of earlier Vedic ritual. To be a full participant in the Vedic ritual you had to be not only a Brahmin man but a man with sons — the sons would carry on your ritual duties after death. Yājñavalkya, the main character of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and the figure most critical of former Vedic practices, also claims that you don't need sons in order to be enlightened and to teach about the self.
  • [00:29:53] And Yājñavalkya turns out to be the character most likely to converse with women: he has a long conversation about the self with his wife in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, and he's involved in a debate in which Gārgī, a female character, takes part. So we both see women appear (possibly reflecting a real history of women in philosophy) and learn something about Yājñavalkya: his engaging women in philosophical discussion is, Black argues, part of his larger critique of early Vedic ritual practice.

docs.title: The Upaniṣads, Buddhism and Jainism: who influenced whom?
docs.text:
• [00:30:44] As a wrap-up — the podcast is about to move on to Buddhism — Adamson asks Black to situate the Upaniṣads relative to the other developments of roughly the same period: to what extent do we see influence, even mutual influence, between some Upaniṣads and early Buddhist texts?
  • [00:31:12] Black calls it a hotly contested question with two main positions in current scholarship.
  • [00:31:26] Position one: the Upaniṣads were composed before the rise of Buddhism and exerted a large influence on it — and on other movements of the time like Jainism and Ājīvikism.
  • [00:31:49] Position two: Buddhism, Jainism and Ājīvikism emerged in a region further east than where the Upaniṣads were composed. The Upaniṣads come from around what's now Delhi and Vārāṇasī, whereas Buddhism arose in roughly what is now Bihar — so in that eastern region the Upaniṣads may not have been well known, and these new movements shouldn't be read as reactionary teachings against them.
  • [00:32:42] Black places himself in the middle. On one hand, to understand early Buddhism you can't treat everything as a reaction to the Vedas; the old analogy that "Buddhism is to Vedic religion as Protestantism is to Catholicism" simply doesn't work. On the other hand, he finds it hard to believe the Upaniṣads had no influence on at least some early Buddhist and Jain teachings.
  • [00:33:28] His example: even though some Buddhist scholars deny that the doctrine of not-self (anattā) was a response to the Upaniṣadic ideal of the self, Black finds it hard not to see a relationship between the two — and notes that other Buddhist material reveals at least a shared philosophical and literary world that both traditions emerged from.
  • [00:34:10] More concretely: some dialogues in our earliest Buddhist texts are the same dialogues found in the Upaniṣads, just with the characters renamed and the closing teaching a little different. He also points to the well-known motif of one's head shattering apart if one loses a philosophical debate — its oldest references are in earlier Vedic material (the Brāhmaṇas), it appears prominently in the Upaniṣads, and it recurs in early Buddhist literature. So some contact is clearly going on.
  • [00:35:00] Black's own hunch: the Upaniṣads probably predate the earliest Buddhist material by at least a generation or two. But even if not, he sees the Upaniṣads, early Buddhism and early Jainism as emerging from a shared world in which these people knew of each other's teachings and were constantly articulating their own positions in response to their rivals.
  • [00:35:32] Adamson closes: next they'll look ahead to Buddhism in a couple of episodes, but first — before leaving Vedic material — the next episode turns to the grammatical analysis of Vedic language and the "astounding work" of the grammarian Pāṇini. He thanks Brian Black for coming on, and invites listeners to rejoin him and Jonardon Ganeri next time.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Brian Black — lecturer in religious studies at Lancaster University; the episode's guest, author of a book on the Upaniṣads and editor of a volume on dialogue in ancient Indian traditions.
  • Upaniṣads — the fourth and final layer of the Vedas; heterogeneous texts composed c. 700–200 BCE by male Brahmins of competing Vedic schools; claim Vedic authority yet criticize earlier Vedic ritualism.
  • Veda / Vedic layers — a layered series of four sections, the last of which (the Upaniṣads) reflects critically on the earlier ones; an unusual self-reflexive structure.
  • brahman / ātman — ultimate reality and the self; the recurring subjects the Upaniṣads' rival schools competed to teach best.
  • Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad ("Great Forest") — an early Upaniṣad with the liveliest dialogues; home of Yājñavalkya and famous teachings on the self, karma and rebirth.
  • Chāndogya Upaniṣad — early Upaniṣad; contains a king's (rhetorical) claim to teach knowledge unknown to Brahmins.
  • Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad — early Upaniṣad addressing, in part, a royal audience.
  • Praśna / Maitrī / Kaṭha Upaniṣads — later Upaniṣads literally organized as a single framing dialogue.
  • Yājñavalkya — major Upaniṣadic sage, fiercest critic of old Vedic ritual; claims one needs no sons for enlightenment; converses with women (his wife; and Gārgī).
  • Uddālaka Āruṇi / Śāṇḍilya — recurring Upaniṣadic philosophical personalities, also found in the Brāhmaṇas.
  • Gārgī — female character who takes part in a debate with Yājñavalkya; evidence (real and symbolic) for women in public philosophy.
  • dialogue — a literary mechanism that mimics the texts' orality, confers authority by naming the teacher, sets teachings in a social context, and can carry a dialectical thesis–counter-argument–synthesis structure.
  • Brāhmaṇas — earlier Vedic texts; source of the "head-shattering" debate motif later seen in Upaniṣads and Buddhism.
  • Bhagavad-Gītā — later Hindu text that, unlike the secret/esoteric Upaniṣads, claims to be a teaching available to everybody.
  • Buddhism / Jainism / Ājīvikism — roughly contemporaneous movements; debated whether they were influenced by the Upaniṣads or arose independently further east (Bihar vs. Delhi–Vārāṇasī).
  • not-self (anattā) — Buddhist doctrine Black suspects stands in some relationship to the Upaniṣadic ideal of the self.
  • Aśoka the Great — later king whose inscriptions seem influenced by Buddhism; cited as evidence Buddhists too had royal audiences in mind.
