docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 8 — "Case Worker: Pāṇini's Grammar"
docs.text:
← Ep 7

Ep 9 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:24 In brief: Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī analyses the whole of Sanskrit through thousands of aphoristic rules — making action (not subject/predicate) the core of a sentence and assigning nouns "thematic roles" (kārakas) — and in doing so the grammarians hand later Indian philosophy a toolbox: the use–mention distinction, double negation, the excluded middle, and an early, oblique version of the problem of universals. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Pāṇini ≈ "Ponanese / panani / Ponini / Pannony / Ponony"; Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari"; Aṣṭādhyāyī ≈ "Ashtad Yahy"; Patañjali ≈ "Patanjali"; Mahābhāṣya ≈ "Mahabashia"; vārttika ≈ "vartica"; bhāṣya ≈ "basya"; kāraka ≈ "caraca / caracca"; Devadatta ≈ "Devadata / De Vedata / divadata"; Bṛhaspati ≈ "Brihaspati"; Naiyāyikas ≈ "Nayayakas"; śiṣṭa ≈ "shishda"; Mīmāṃsā ≈ "Mimamsa").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Pāṇini — the great Sanskrit grammarian; author of the Aṣṭādhyāyī [00:01:45].
  • The Aṣṭādhyāyī ("Book in Eight Chapters") — his dense, technical grammar of Sanskrit in thousands of aphorisms [00:01:56].
  • Patañjali — author of the Mahābhāṣya, the most important commentary in the grammatical tradition, 2nd century BC [00:03:51].
  • The Naiyāyikas (logicians) — who clash with the grammarians over whether a pot can be an "agent" [00:13:49].
  • The Mīmāṃsā school — foreshadowed at the close: built on the idea that sacred Sanskrit is fixed for all time [00:19:35].

docs.title: Language, ritual, and Brahmanic power
docs.text:
• [00:00:41] The power of the Brahmins of ancient India came "not from armies or wealth, but from knowledge" — and was expressed not in wars or building projects but in words and ritual deeds: animal and plant sacrifice, the uttering of chants and formulas.
  • [00:01:02] So intimate was the bond between Brahmanic authority and language that they produced some of the world's oldest literature — literature that constantly refers to language, especially spoken language. The Vedas and Upaniṣads were transmitted orally for many generations before being written down.
  • [00:01:18] Speech is a running theme in the Upaniṣads: the self is said to consist of speech, mind, and breath, and the purifying sacrifice to be enacted through two things, mind and speech. The ritual succeeds only when both are correct — "as a cart cannot roll on only one wheel."
  • [00:01:38] No wonder, then, that ancient India produced one of the great feats in the history of linguistics: the grammar of Pāṇini.

docs.title: Pāṇini and the Aṣṭādhyāyī
docs.text:
• [00:01:49] As so often, his dates are uncertain, but he seems to have lived from the 6th to the 5th century BC. His fame rests on the Aṣṭādhyāyī, or "Book in Eight Chapters" — a dense, technical work describing the grammatical structure of Sanskrit through thousands of aphoristic remarks. An astounding achievement, even though it draws on earlier grammarians.
  • [00:02:26] The whole endeavour presupposes a religious context: it is the sacredness of the Sanskrit language that makes it worth analysing in such minute detail, and Pāṇini's most obvious precursors are works discussing Vedic verses word by word.
  • [00:02:44] But you needn't be a historian of religion to appreciate the results. Most scholarship on Pāṇini is by linguists who say nothing about his cultural or religious setting; he is taken seriously as a figure comparable to modern linguists like Noam Chomsky.

docs.title: The layers of commentary: sūtra, vārttika, bhāṣya
docs.text:
• [00:03:08] The reception of Pāṇini's work followed a pattern recurring throughout the series: like the philosophers of the various schools, the Pāṇinian grammarians produced layers of commentary on an authoritative source text — here, the Eight Chapters.
  • [00:03:20] Pāṇini's aphorisms were called sūtras — brief remarks to be memorized and passed on orally. Later grammarians added comments called vārttikas, meant to supplement Pāṇini (e.g. by making additional points absent from the original sūtras).
  • [00:03:39] There was also a detailed form of exegesis called bhāṣya, which unfolded the teaching and added illustrative examples. The most important such text was the Mahābhāṣya of Patañjali, written in the 2nd century BC.
  • [00:04:00] Such exegesis generally aimed to explain and expand the founder's remarks — but a bhāṣya could also challenge or correct them.
  • [00:04:11] Patañjali confirms the religious imperative behind the grammar: he writes at the start of his commentary that "grammar should be studied for the sake of the preservation of the Vedas."

docs.title: Why a philosopher should care
docs.text:
• [00:04:25] Yet Pāṇini's grammar is no Vedic commentary — it studies the entire Sanskrit language. The grammarians don't necessarily analyse Vedic verses; they attend to everyday examples like "Devadatta is cooking rice."
  • [00:04:44] So why should a philosopher care? Not in hopes of a vision of the universe and the individual's place in it, as in the Upaniṣads. Rather, the grammar is a reflection on the structure and, implicitly, the nature of language.
  • [00:04:54] Patañjali says grammar offers instruction about words — but not the sort children get from parents learning to talk, nor what you'd get in a Sanskrit class. It explains the formation of individual words, yet obviously cannot proceed word by word: that would be never-ending.
  • [00:05:21] Captured by a nice story: the god Bṛhaspati taught the patient Indra about language "for 1,000 years one word at a time," and by then they still hadn't finished. Grammar must instead deploy generalization and abstraction.

docs.title: Stand-in abbreviations: variables for language
docs.text:
• [00:05:35] One of Pāṇini's most important breakthroughs is to use stand-in abbreviations to represent a range of possible cases — comparable to how logicians use variables to expose the form of an argument. This lets him state a single rule covering an indefinite number of expressions.
  • [00:05:59] An English analogy: "take any verb and call it V; then V followed by the ending -ED is its past tense" — deriving walked from walk, cooked from cook. This is pretty much how Pāṇini's grammar works: he builds words out of basic roots with add-ons marking features like the case of a noun.
  • [00:06:26] The procedure will be familiar to anyone who has studied a language with declinable nouns — Greek or Latin, which are related to Sanskrit and share many of the same grammatical features.

docs.title: Action at the centre: agent, patient, and the kārakas
docs.text:
• [00:06:41] Even so, some of Pāṇini's proposals are surprising. We're usually taught a sentence's basic components are subject and predicate; Pāṇini instead makes action the core notion. That is why the Eight Chapters are supplemented with a list of all the verbal roots in Sanskrit — the basis of the whole language.
  • [00:07:06] What we'd call the subject is for him the agent of the action. Alongside agent and action, the other key part is the patient of an action — which (for those who know that "declining a noun" doesn't mean refusing to look it up) goes in the accusative case. In "Devadatta is cooking rice," the rice — our "object" — is the patient of cooking.
  • [00:07:42] Further components can be added: the place where the action happens, the instrument used, and so on — "Devadatta is cooking rice in the pot with fire." In Sanskrit one simply marks each noun's function with case endings, where English uses prepositions like in and with.
  • [00:08:09] Insofar as they play different functions, nouns become what Pāṇini calls kārakas — "contributory factors" for some action. Patañjali: "A thing becomes a kāraka with respect to the accomplishment of an action in which it participates." In the example, Devadatta is the kāraka of agent, which is primary and presupposed by all the others, since no action can occur without an agent.
  • [00:08:35] Pāṇini names six such thematic case-roles: agent, patient (or recipient), instrument, donor, target, and locus.
  • "The leaf falls from the tree to the ground": the leaf is the agent (it functions independently), the tree the donor, the ground the locus.
  • "The king gives wealth to the brahman by his own hand": the king is agent, the wealth the object given, the brahman the recipient, and the hand the instrument.
  • [00:09:18] The centrality of action shows in what's excluded: the relation expressed by "of" — the genitive case, as in "the brahman's money" — is not a kāraka. It denotes a relationship between two nouns, not between a verb and a contributory factor.
  • [00:09:42] Hence Pāṇini's kārakas are not simply the grammatical cases of Greek or Latin; they're more like thematic roles that words can play.

docs.title: More rules, and rules that override rules
docs.text:
• [00:09:49] Sentences get more complicated. What if the verb is passive ("the rice is being cooked")? What about indeclinable words that take no case endings, or compound words? This is why Pāṇini gives so many rules — guidelines for these and many other circumstances.
  • [00:10:18] In a much-discussed feature, Pāṇini sees that some rules are exceptions to others. There are the most general rules covering all words — which the grammarians compared to "the rain that falls on all alike" — and then more specific rules that trump them.
  • [00:10:37] English parallel: a verb already ending in E adds only D, not ED, for the past tense — liked, shared — "without which no one could describe what they've been doing on Facebook."
  • [00:10:54] To capture this, Pāṇini deliberately places the more general rules earlier in his list of sūtras and specifies that a later entry overrules an earlier one with which it conflicts.

docs.title: Descriptive vs. normative: how we talk vs. how we ought to
docs.text:
• [00:11:08] So far it sounds as if Pāṇini merely describes how Sanskrit works — but that isn't the only way to think about grammar. If a friend says "do you want to come with?" — or worse, "do you want to come with Jonardon, Peter, and I?" — a right-thinking person wouldn't just log these as English constructions, even though they're frequent. You'd correct the friend: "come with me," because "with" takes an object.
  • [00:11:44] The ancient Indian grammarians were likewise sticklers, treating their rules as marking correct vs. incorrect language. Their mission was not merely descriptive but prescriptive — philosophers would say normative: not how we do talk, but how we ought to.
  • [00:12:08] Yet they weren't free to decide arbitrarily what counts as correct Sanskrit. As Patañjali said: "If you want pots, go to a potter; but if you want words, don't go to a grammarian" — i.e. go to actual language users and see how they form sentences.

docs.title: The śiṣṭa: grammar of the well-educated
docs.text:
• [00:12:26] What's needed is a compromise between the descriptive and the normative: the Pāṇinians describe how people speak, but only when they speak correctly. So they defined a class called the śiṣṭa — the "well-educated" or "learned."
  • [00:12:46] Grammar describes the speech of these people, "not that of the riff-raff on the street." Strikingly, the Pāṇinians held that such elite speakers are distinguished by their upright moral character — not merely their class or level of education.

docs.title: Can a pot be an agent? Grammarians vs. logicians
docs.text:
• [00:13:03] A telling case. Pāṇini made agents and actions central — so what about "the pot cooks the rice"? One option: rule it incorrect, since it's Devadatta who cooks rice in the pot. But that is not what the grammarians say.
  • [00:13:20] Sanskrit users routinely treat inanimate things as agents — happily saying pots cook rice. We do too: told to get the rice cooker from the cupboard, you don't expect Devadatta stashed inside, but an appliance. The grammarians allowed this and laid down no rule forbidding a pot the kāraka of agent.
  • [00:13:49] This produced a disagreement with the Naiyāyikas (logicians), who insisted that only a living thing deserves the word "agent." Pāṇini's approach was more pragmatic, giving due weight to actual usage: it is correct to say either "Devadatta is cutting the tree" or "the axe is cutting the tree," so the axe must be allowed as an agent — even though we know it is really the instrument of cutting.

docs.title: Syntax vs. semantics: the deepest question
docs.text:
• [00:14:22] Here lies what may be the deepest philosophical question the Pāṇinians raise: does grammar expose the structure of underlying reality, or is it merely the study of linguistic usage that may tell us nothing about the world?
  • [00:14:42] Pāṇini himself doesn't address it — he restricts himself to the rules for forming sentences. But some scholars think he presupposes something deeper beneath surface grammar: the semantic level (meaning), as opposed to the level of syntax (grammatical form).
  • [00:15:08] With this distinction, the pot dispute may be a case of the two sides talking past one another: it is proper to use "pot" in the syntactic role of agent (the grammarians' concern); whether "pot" can actually mean an agent is a different, semantic matter.
  • [00:15:30] Scholars disagree on how much semantics matters in Pāṇini. On one reading, he asks us to look at a word's semantic role to fix its syntactic role: you don't generate a passive just by mechanically tweaking the active form — you go back to square one, see that a passive meaning is wanted, then consult the rulebook for the right ending.
  • [00:15:56] Against this, others argue Pāṇini cares only about constructing words, and out of words sentences, with no interest in semantics. Syntax can be indifferent to meaning — you can form perfectly grammatical sentences that mean nothing.
  • [00:16:20] The grammarians' wonderful example: "There goes the son of a barren woman, with his hair-top bedecked with sky-flower, bathed in the milk of a tortoise, carrying a bow made of the horn of a rabbit."

docs.title: Words, meanings, and the lurking problem of universals
docs.text:
• [00:16:32] Later grammarians did attend to how words relate to meanings, if only to stake out grammar's boundaries. Patañjali's example of a cow: the grammarian is not interested in the actual animal "with a tail and hooves" — it is the word that grammar discusses. The word is "that which, when uttered, causes one to think of the cow," the sound by which meaning is understood.
  • [00:17:05] This meaning is permanently linked to the word "cow," and what's meant could be cows in general or some particular cow. Difficult issues lurk: if the meaning is general, must we posit a universal nature of "cowness" for the word to latch onto?
  • [00:17:28] So European philosophers had no monopoly on the problem of universals. The grammarians raised it obliquely, via the function of words; it will be tackled head-on by the Nyāya school, who use the very same cow-and-milk example "for all its worth."

docs.title: The grammarians' gift to the philosopher's toolbox
docs.text:
• [00:17:46] We can't credit the grammarians with elaborate reflections on universals, but they forged conceptual instruments that went straight into the Indian philosopher's toolbox.
  • [00:18:03] One, closely connected, is the use–mention distinction: it's one thing to refer to the word cow, another to use the word to refer to cows — the difference between "cow has three letters" / "cow as a noun" and "I see a cow in the field." We mark it today with quotation marks; the ancient grammarians had no such device, yet Pāṇini has nonetheless been credited with drawing the distinction.
  • [00:18:41] Nor were the grammarians blind to logic. Patañjali formulated two basic laws of reasoning: that double negation equals affirmation ("if something is not not a cow, then it is a cow") and that there is no third option between an assertion and its denial — the law of the excluded middle.
  • [00:19:06] That grammarians and logicians could disagree (as over the agency of pots) shows they were "plowing different furrows" in closely adjacent fields.

docs.title: Where this leads: looking back to ritual, forward to its critics
docs.text:
• [00:19:23] All this gives the historian of philosophy good reason to take the Pāṇinians seriously — both for their own ideas and as foreshadowing later schools.
  • [00:19:35] For instance, the Mīmāṃsā school will be predicated on the idea that the sacred language of Sanskrit is fixed for all time — a reminder of the religious context that first gave rise to Pāṇini's project, and a reassertion of the grammatical tradition's value, hand in hand with devotion to Brahmanism.
  • [00:19:58] But, as promised repeatedly, the earliest phase of Indian thought was not marked by monolithic agreement on that culture's value. Fittingly, Pāṇini has been "sandwiched" between the Upaniṣads and the critics of Brahmanism. Next time: the greatest of those critics — the legend, legacy, and ideas of the Buddha.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Pāṇini — the great Sanskrit grammarian (6th–5th c. BC?); author of the Aṣṭādhyāyī; makes action the core of grammar and uses variable-like abbreviations to state general rules.
  • Aṣṭādhyāyī ("Eight Chapters") — Pāṇini's grammar of all Sanskrit, in thousands of aphoristic sūtras, supplemented by a list of every verbal root.
  • sūtra — a brief aphoristic rule, memorized and passed on orally; the form of Pāṇini's grammar.
  • vārttika — supplementary comments by later grammarians, adding points absent from the original sūtras.
  • bhāṣya — detailed exegesis that unfolds the teaching with examples, and may even challenge or correct the source.
  • Patañjali — author of the Mahābhāṣya (2nd c. BC), the tradition's most important bhāṣya; ties grammar to "preservation of the Vedas," yet formulates logical laws.
  • Mahābhāṣya — Patañjali's great commentary on Pāṇini.
  • kāraka — a noun's "contributory factor" / thematic role in an action; six in all: agent, patient (recipient), instrument, donor, target, locus. Not the same as Greek/Latin grammatical cases.
  • Devadatta — the stock everyman of the grammarians' examples ("Devadatta is cooking rice").
  • śiṣṭa — the "well-educated/learned," marked by upright moral character; grammar describes their correct speech, not the street's.
  • Naiyāyikas (logicians) — the Nyāya thinkers who, unlike the grammarians, insist only a living thing can be an "agent."
  • syntax vs. semantics — form vs. meaning; the unresolved question of whether grammar exposes reality or only usage.
  • use–mention distinction — referring to a word vs. using it to refer; credited (in seed form) to Pāṇini.
  • double negation / excluded middle — basic laws of reasoning formulated by Patañjali.
  • Mīmāṃsā — school predicated on Sanskrit being fixed for all time; continues the grammar-and-ritual tradition.
  • Bṛhaspati & Indra — the god who taught Indra language "one word at a time" for 1,000 years without finishing — illustrating why grammar needs abstraction.

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:21:49 In brief: The Buddha's diagnosis of the human condition — the Four Noble Truths — built on the claim that suffering is universal, that its cause is craving rooted in ignorance, and that escape requires the radical realization that there is no self to be liberated; with the chariot and the five skandhas as the classic illustrations of how a "person" is only a convenient name for an aggregate. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit/Pali terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari"; duḥkha ≈ "Dukka/Dukkah"; taṇhā ≈ "Tana"; Ājīvakas ≈ "Ajivacus/Ajivakas/Ajifakas/Ajivokas"; Tripiṭaka ≈ "Tripitaka"; Vinaya Piṭaka ≈ "Vinaya pittaka"; Abhidharma ≈ "Abidharma"; Milindapañha ≈ "Melinda Panya"; Nāgasena ≈ "Nagasena"; skandhas ≈ "scandas/scantas"; Pudgala/Pudgalavāda ≈ "Pugala/Pugalavada"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagajuna").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The Buddha — 5th-c. BCE royal prince of the kṣatriya class who renounced his comfort, found enlightenment under a tree, and taught the Four Noble Truths [00:00:28].
  • The Pali canon — earliest writings on the Buddha, in the Pali language; its three "baskets" are the Tripiṭaka [00:03:16].
  • The Nikāyas — collections of the Buddha's sayings and conversations, part of the canon [00:03:32].
  • The Milindapañha ("Questions of Menander") — early Buddhist text staging the sage Nāgasena with the Hellenistic king Menander of Bactria (2nd c. BCE) [00:13:47].

docs.title: The first step: admitting the problem
docs.text:
• [00:00:43] "The first step is admitting you have a problem" — advice aimed at addicts, but for the Buddha it applies to all of us. His teaching centres on the Four Noble Truths, and the first is that everyone has a problem so pervasive and so hard to escape that we usually fail even to perceive it as a problem.
  • [00:01:03] The problem is that we are alive, and life is suffering. That is the bad news. The worse news: death is no escape. In keeping with the doctrine of rebirth and karmic retribution, death frees us only from our current portion of suffering and delivers us directly into another.
  • [00:01:20] How can we possibly free ourselves? Only by understanding the predicament better — which crucially includes coming to understand that we have no selves that need to be set free in the first place. With this, the Buddha signalled his disagreement with the Brahminical tradition of the Upaniṣads, which made ātman (the self) its central preoccupation.

docs.title: A royal life renounced — the legend of the Buddha
docs.text:
• [00:01:50] The Buddha was no Brahmin. The elaborate legend of his former lives and final incarnation says he chose to be born into the kṣatriya class as a royal prince. His mother dreamed of a white elephant entering the side of her body and conceived the child who would become the Buddha.
  • [00:02:10] At birth he could already speak and walk. His first deed: he took seven steps and proclaimed that life is full of sorrow and that, after innumerable life-cycles, he had come to free both gods and men from this misery.
  • [00:02:21] Despite this precocious declaration, he spent his youth and early adulthood oblivious of his mission, growing up in comfort and luxury. He was set on the path to enlightenment only when, as a young man, he ventured beyond the palace walls and was confronted for the first time by the elderly, the sick, and the dead.
  • [00:02:42] He retreated to the forest and took up the extreme ascetic practices associated with the Ājīvakas, only to find them ineffective. Rejecting that path, he sat beneath a tree and began to meditate. When enlightenment came, he did not keep his new wisdom to himself but gathered students — the first Buddhists, and far from the last.

docs.title: The sources: Pali canon, Nikāyas, the three baskets
docs.text:
• [00:03:10] These details and far more are contained in the earliest writings about the Buddha, the Pali canon, so called because written in the Pali language. As with the Upaniṣads, this is an originally oral tradition, set down in writing only centuries after the Buddha's lifetime — probably the 5th century BCE.
  • [00:03:32] His sayings and conversations are collected in the Nikāyas, themselves only one of three bodies of early Buddhist literature, the Tripiṭaka ("three baskets"). The other two: the Vinaya Piṭaka, giving instructions for monks, and the most philosophical, the Abhidharma ("higher teaching").
  • [00:03:58] The Pali canon is the most obvious source but not the only one: there are Chinese biographies of the Buddha from the 2nd–4th centuries CE, and important architectural and iconographical material — notably the ancient burial mounds called stupas, surrounded by decorative railings and statues.
  • [00:04:23] You probably don't need an archaeologist to conjure the familiar image: the Buddha sitting cross-legged, eyes half-shut, smiling beatifically. Which raises the question — what's with the smiling? Why so serene when your message is that life is suffering? It turns out there's good news: three more Noble Truths, concerning the cause of suffering, what escape would mean, and the path to that escape.

docs.title: Is the first truth even plausible?
docs.text:
• [00:04:58] Before the solution, examine the problem. Is the Buddha's bleak assessment plausible? Life does involve disease and (if you're lucky) old age, with death as the inevitable conclusion — but in the meantime there's plenty to enjoy: the silent films of Buster Keaton, the occasional almond croissant, philosophy podcasts. The Buddha had none of these, but presumably antique India offered things almost equally worthwhile.
  • [00:05:30] More seriously, set the first truth in its historical setting. Life in pre-modern societies (and less affluent places today) is precarious and often unpleasant — the story of the Buddha shocked by what lay beyond the palace is telling. And other spiritual movements of his time were equally pessimistic: the Jains and Ājīvakas sought to escape the cycle of rebirth entirely rather than aim for the best rebirth.
  • [00:06:12] Some propose a less dramatic translation of the central term duḥkha — not "suffering" but "dissatisfaction." Unfortunately that wouldn't make the teaching more plausible: the problem must be not only inevitable but severe — severe enough to warrant restructuring one's entire life around the Buddhist path. "Into each life some rain must fall, but that doesn't mean we should think of nothing but finding an umbrella."

docs.title: The second truth: desire as the cause
docs.text:
• [00:06:49] The second Noble Truth reveals the cause of suffering: in a word, desire — lusting for pleasure, coveting possessions, wanting to avoid death. Both our longing for some things and our aversion to others fall under taṇhā, the general term for attached desire or craving.
  • [00:07:20] Tellingly, the counterproductive goals include the very goods that Brahminical ritual was meant to achieve, such as a large family. For the Buddhist these guarantee duḥkha: before you have them you suffer from unfulfilled craving (and the stronger the desire, the worse), and once you have them you suffer too, fearing their loss. In the longer term a desire-driven life keeps us stuck in the cycle of reincarnation, each rebirth merely another chance to suffer.
  • [00:07:57] This is why the Buddha gave up his life as a prince and, more importantly, the values it entailed — however cosseted, he would still face illness, age, and death. Following him, many Buddhists abandoned the life of the householder (a man devoted to family and material prosperity) to become renouncers living monastically — though Buddhism is also followed by laypeople who support the monks.

docs.title: The middle way
docs.text:
• [00:08:32] But "renouncer" can mislead. Recall that the Buddha tried extreme asceticism and found it did not bring enlightenment. He taught instead a middle way between the householding life and the self-abnegation of some anti-Brahminical traditions.
  • [00:08:50] This is highlighted at the very start of his first sermon, which urges students to avoid two extremes: on one side a life devoted to passion, on the other deliberate self-torment and pain. Both, says the Buddha, are ignoble and useless.

docs.title: Salvation through knowledge — the chain from ignorance
docs.text:
• [00:09:10] Though rejecting the Brahmins' ideas and values, the Buddha shared one thing with them: the belief that salvation comes through knowledge. The cause of suffering is desire, but desire has a further cause — ignorance.
  • [00:09:28] A chapter of the same Nikāya that transmits the first sermon explains the chain: ignorance gives rise to karma, karma to consciousness, which leads to sensation and therefore to desire; desire in turn leads to rebirth, and once born you are subject to death, age, and grief. The only way off this "train of tears" is to avoid boarding at the first station — by replacing ignorance with understanding.
  • [00:09:59] This understanding has nothing to do with propitiating the gods. Vedic sacrifices are no more effective than the asceticism of other dissident groups. The Buddhists accepted that the gods are real, but the gods too are subject to rebirth — so even the gods need liberation.
  • [00:10:25] Another difference: where the Upaniṣads claim to expose hidden truths and correspondences underlying everyday reality, early Buddhism seeks to unmask reality as merely conventional. This brings us to the third and fourth truths — how life would need to be to escape suffering, and how to get there.

docs.title: The third and fourth truths: no-self and nirvāṇa
docs.text:
• [00:10:50] The Buddha's recommendation is as simple as it is radical: you can stop being attached to things that falsely seem to benefit you, now and in the future, if you give up the idea that you have a self that can be benefited. Through embracing and acting on this theory of no-self we reach nirvāṇa, liberation from all suffering.
  • [00:11:15] An apparent contradiction: we're told to give up all desire — but what about the desire for liberation? Couldn't that be just another craving, replacing one desire with another, "as if he told us we could stay dry by coming in out of the rain to take a shower"?
  • [00:11:45] The project need not be self-defeating. The whole teaching is predicated on the desire to avoid suffering. Once we learn that suffering comes from cravings and fears, that initial desire should be transformed into a more useful one: we should desire to lose all desire. This new desire is vital to reaching the goal but may fall away once all other desires are eliminated — when liberation comes, the desire for it no longer serves any purpose. As one scholar put it, "craving is a stepping stone to getting rid of craving altogether."

docs.title: The trap of wanting annihilation
docs.text:
• [00:12:26] It looks as if there's at least one other desire the Buddha would approve: the desire to annihilate ourselves, since, like the Jains and Ājīvakas, he wants to help us escape the karmic cycle. But that would be a mistake.
  • [00:12:46] In the first sermon the Buddha lists among the desires that lead to suffering not only the longing to continue existing but also the longing to cease existing. The Buddhist way is instead to realize there is no self to annihilate.
  • [00:13:04] This is diametrically opposed to Brahminism. The Buddhists reject the idea of some unseen, unchanging centre of identity underlying all cognition and awareness. That still leaves room for less metaphysically ambitious notions of self: you needn't accept a permanent self to believe there's some sense in which you're the same person who started listening a few minutes ago, or that you can be aware of yourself listening. Still, the Buddhists clearly wanted to critique and revise our everyday assumptions about the reality of persons and things.

docs.title: The chariot and the fist: persons as conventional aggregates
docs.text:
• [00:13:47] A classic text on the issue is the Milindapañha, which depicts the sage Nāgasena in conversation with the Hellenistic king Menander, ruler of Bactria in the 2nd century BCE. The setting recalls the Upaniṣads, but the doctrine does not.
  • [00:14:07] Nāgasena tries to persuade the king that familiar objects are whole substances only by convention. His example: a chariot. There is nothing more to it than its parts — axle, yoke, wheels, reins, and so on. This doesn't mean we can't truthfully say "here is a chariot"; it means "chariot" is a conventional word, a term we find convenient for the whole aggregate of parts.
  • [00:14:40] Another nice example from the Buddhist literature: a fist, evidently nothing more than the hand and fingers temporarily clenched. And so with people too — people are aggregates that can lose and gain parts over time.

docs.title: What the parts are: dharmas and the five skandhas
docs.text:
• [00:14:52] A Brahminical sage might respond that every aggregate is made of constituents, those of further constituents — a paragraph of sentences, sentences of words — but in the end we reach fundamental parts, like the letters of the words. So if we seek the fundamental realities making up a person, why not identify the self as one such reality?
  • [00:15:24] Because the Buddhist has a rival answer. The Buddhists applied the name dharma to the simple components of any aggregate. In the case of the person there are five types of dharma. To stress their merely aggregative nature, these are called skandhas ("heaps").
  • [00:15:43] The five skandhas cover all aspects of our being: physical form, bodily feelings, emotions/perceptions, thinking, and consciousness itself. The list sounds familiar because in the Upaniṣads these are precisely the phenomena that conceal the more fundamental self hidden within. But for the Buddhists there is nothing to a person over and above the conglomeration of momentary skandhas — each present only for a fleeting moment before being replaced by others of the same type.
  • [00:16:20] Nor would it be right to identify yourself with any skandha, individually or in aggregate — that would again be attachment to the self. There are just the skandhas, and that is it. So we arrive at perhaps the most notorious doctrine of Buddhism: we are nothing more than flowing streams, with no firm identity from moment to moment. This will later be defended, and the Brahminical unchanging self attacked, with great virtuosity by Nāgārjuna — but it already emerges in the Pali canon, often when discussing reincarnation.

docs.title: The puzzle of rebirth without a self
docs.text:
• [00:17:03] Given that they rejected an enduring self, you might expect the Buddhists to drop the cycle of rebirth altogether — but no chance. It was core teaching that desire leads to suffering partly because it triggers rebirth, and a fundamental part of the Buddha's own journey was that he could remember his past lives.
  • [00:17:34] In previous incarnations he had already become a bodhisattva ("enlightened one"), but in an act of extraordinary generosity — the act that makes him not just a sage but the saviour of humans and gods — he determined to return again and again until he could help others reach enlightenment, not only himself.
  • [00:17:56] The rest of us are reborn to less purpose. One Nikāya compares the person going through reincarnation to a dog tied to a stake, fruitlessly running in circles. Even the idea that caste membership reflects one's deeds in former lives appears in early Buddhist literature — the Brahmins had no monopoly on it.
  • [00:18:21] But with their no-self doctrine the Buddhists had an obvious difficulty explaining reincarnation. Their solution seems paradoxical or no answer at all: reflecting on the belief that we'll be requited for our actions in the next life, they denied that he who experiences the fruit of a deed is the same as the one who performed it — yet also denied that the two are different.

docs.title: The giraffe: sameness in a weaker sense
docs.text:
• [00:18:50] Is this just embracing a contradiction? No — think more carefully about an aggregate changing over time. Take a giraffe: every day, through its digestive cycle, it loses and gains matter. Strictly, today's giraffe consists of different parts than yesterday's. Yet it's equally obvious that today's giraffe is not completely different — it retains some earlier parts, which is why we can truthfully say the giraffe gambolling in the field now is the same one that slept in the stable last night.
  • [00:19:29] Remember the Buddhists reject the Brahminical idea that the self is completely the same across time, an unchanging foundation enduring through changes of perception and even from one life-cycle to the next. If a person is just an aggregate of changing skandhas, it falls well short of that kind of sameness — yet may be the same in a weaker sense, e.g. because the stream of skandhas is causally interconnected.

docs.title: Rival answers and the Buddha's silence
docs.text:
• [00:19:57] Buddhist philosophy was itself a changing agglomeration, with thinkers holding rival views across the centuries — including on this question of what (if any) weaker persistence carries a person from one incarnation to another. A minimal view follows Nāgasena's chariot: calling one person "the same" across time is merely a useful convention.
  • [00:20:28] At the other end, some Buddhists endorsed an underlying subject that overlies or emerges from the skandhas and can undergo rebirth — they called it the Pudgala, and their school the Pudgalavāda. Other Buddhists felt this was tantamount to conceding the Brahminical self.
  • [00:20:54] Similar tensions appear over how exactly actions determine one's fate: sometimes the Buddha mocks the Jain idea that actions cause karma to adhere to us across lives; at other times he insists, like the Ājīvakas, that the right course is to avoid action entirely, precisely because it brings karma.
  • [00:21:15] Perhaps the inevitability of such tensions explains why, when once asked whether there is really a self, the Buddha simply refused to answer — a favourite strategy. Like many great thinkers he had not only original proposals in metaphysics, epistemology, and ethics, but an interesting view about the status of those very proposals — the subject of the next episode, on the philosophical method of early Buddhism, where "the sound of silence can speak louder than words."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• The Buddha — 5th-c. BCE kṣatriya prince who renounced palace life, attained enlightenment under a tree, and taught the Four Noble Truths; depicted serenely smiling despite teaching that life is suffering.
  • Four Noble Truths — (1) life is suffering; (2) its cause is desire/craving; (3) escape is possible (nirvāṇa); (4) there is a path to that escape.
  • duḥkha — "suffering," perhaps better "dissatisfaction"; the universal predicament — but it must be severe enough to justify restructuring one's whole life.
  • taṇhā — attached desire or craving (both longing and aversion); the cause of suffering named in the second truth.
  • nirvāṇa — liberation from all suffering, reached by acting on the no-self theory.
  • no-self (theory of no-self) — there is no unchanging centre of identity; a person is only an aggregate, so there is no self to be liberated or annihilated.
  • karma / rebirth — actions bear fruit across lives; death merely delivers one to another portion of suffering. The Buddhists keep rebirth despite denying a persisting self.
  • householder vs. renouncer — the family/prosperity life vs. the monastic life; the Buddha taught a middle way between passion and extreme asceticism.
  • Ājīvakas & Jains — contemporary movements seeking to escape the rebirth cycle entirely (the Ājīvakas' extreme asceticism the Buddha tried and rejected).
  • Pali canon / Nikāyas / Tripiṭaka — earliest Buddhist writings in Pali; the Nikāyas (the Buddha's sayings) sit alongside the Vinaya Piṭaka (monastic rules) and the Abhidharma (higher/philosophical teaching) in the "three baskets."
  • stupas — ancient burial mounds with railings and statues; non-textual source for early Buddhism.
  • dharma — here, the simple/fundamental component of any aggregate.
  • skandhas ("heaps") — the five types of dharma making up a person: physical form, feelings, emotions/perceptions, thinking, consciousness; momentary and the only constituents of a "self."
  • Milindapañha ("Questions of Menander") — text staging Nāgasena and king Menander of Bactria (2nd c. BCE); source of the chariot argument that the person is a conventional aggregate.
  • chariot / fist / giraffe — illustrations that wholes are conventional names for changing parts, yet retain a weaker, causally-connected sameness over time.
  • Pudgala / Pudgalavāda — a posited underlying subject that emerges from the skandhas and can be reborn, and the Buddhist school that affirmed it; criticized by others as conceding the Brahminical self.
  • bodhisattva — an "enlightened one"; the Buddha became one in past lives but chose to return repeatedly to save others.
  • Nāgārjuna — later Buddhist who would defend the no-self doctrine and attack the Brahminical self "with great virtuosity."

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 10 — "Crossover Appeal: The Nature of the Buddha's Teaching"
docs.text:
← Ep 9

Ep 11 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:56 In brief: What kind of thing is the Buddha's teaching? Through the Buddha's own images of the raft and the poisonous snake, the episode probes whether his dharma is only instrumentally valuable (and so indifferent to truth), how this bears on lying, silence, and compassion, and why the value of both teaching and virtue depends on how far along the path one has travelled. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannari"; dharma ≈ "dama"; nirvāṇa ≈ "Nirvana"; Prince Abhaya ≈ "Prince Abaya"; K. N. Jayatilleke ≈ "K. N. Jayatilike"; Pāli ≈ "Pali"; attha ≈ "Atta"; Lotus Sūtra ≈ "Lotus Sutra"; Śāriputra ≈ "Shari Putra"; Milinda-pañha ≈ "Melinda Panya"; Nāgasena ≈ "Nagasena"; puṇya ≈ "punya"; Arhat ≈ "Arachat/Arahat"; Aśoka ≈ "Ashoka"; Mauryan ≈ "Maorian"; Arthaśāstra ≈ "Arta Shastra").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The raft and the snake analogies — the Buddha's two images for the status of his own teaching [00:01:37].
  • Prince Abhaya dialogue — the conversation in which the Buddha lists the kinds of speech, with a telling omission [00:04:16].
  • K. N. Jayatilleke — Sri Lankan Buddhist scholar whose reading rules out the "white lie" [00:05:27].
  • The Lotus Sūtra — later Buddhist text with the parable of the burning house, where the tradition flirts with compassionate lying [00:06:21].
  • The Milinda-pañha (Questions of Menander) — early dialogue where Nāgasena explains the four kinds of question and the Buddha's silence [00:12:45].

docs.title: Recap: a journey without a traveller, but a journey nonetheless
docs.text:
• [00:00:36] Last time covered what the Buddha bequeathed to later Indian philosophy. With his doctrine of no self, the Buddha rejected the Upaniṣadic search for the self as misguided — the century-and-more the god Indra spent on that search was a waste of time, since what he sought never existed.
  • [00:01:01] Yet with the four noble truths the Buddha implicitly affirmed the Upaniṣadic conception of philosophy as being about path and purpose. There may be no journey of self-discovery, but there is a journey nonetheless. Its destination is nirvāṇa, the extinction of attachment and desire.
  • [00:01:25] So the function of the Buddha's teaching is much like that of the Upaniṣads: to help the student along a path of inner conceptual development. The Buddha was at pains to make his disciples grasp this, which is why he offered two analogies for the nature of his own philosophy — a raft and a poisonous snake.

docs.title: The raft: teaching you cross over on, then leave behind
docs.text:
• [00:01:43] A man builds a raft to get from a dangerous place to a place of safety. Having crossed, he thinks: this raft was so helpful, suppose I hoist it on my head and carry it wherever I go. The Buddha's point: the dharma is like the raft — for the purpose of crossing over, not for holding onto once you are on the other side.
  • [00:02:14] Hence the startling instruction: "when you know the dharma to be similar to a raft, you should abandon even the teachings. How much more so things contrary to the teachings?" Rafts are great — but only while crossing a river; once that condition is no longer met, the value disappears and the raft becomes an encumbrance. Attachment in any shape is a cause of suffering, and that applies even to being attached to the truth.

docs.title: The problem: is the teaching only instrumentally valuable?
docs.text:
• [00:03:04] Charming as it is, the analogy brings a problem. It appears to make the Buddha's teachings merely instrumentally valuable — useful because they get us where we want to go, and for that reason only, which would mean it makes no difference whether they are even true.
  • [00:03:21] After all, beliefs don't have to be true to be useful — which is why it is the rare parent who never misleads their children (Santa's lump of coal; "everything will be all right" when sadly it won't). On this reading the Brahminical theory of the unchanging self might even be true after all; it's just that believing it brings suffering, so we are better off convinced it is false.
  • [00:03:52] Worse: does the Buddha know his teachings could be untrue? If so, he isn't merely embroidering a useful story — he is telling a lie, albeit a helpful one. Surely that is not the lesson of the raft.

docs.title: The Abhaya dialogue and the missing "white lie"
docs.text:
• [00:04:16] To clarify the status of the teachings, turn to the dialogue with Prince Abhaya, who asks whether it is proper to utter speech that would be unwelcome or disagreeable to others. The Buddha says he can give no straightforward answer.
  • [00:04:35] He asks Abhaya what he would do if he saw a child put a pebble in its mouth; the prince says he would remove it even at the cost of hurting the child. The Buddha then lists the kinds of speech: he would not say what is untrue, unbeneficial, and unpleasant; nor what is true but not beneficial; but out of compassion he would speak what is truthful, beneficial, and agreeable — and would know the right time to say it.
  • [00:05:03] There is a glaring omission: speech that is beneficial without being true. This is no oversight — the case is awkward. The Buddha clearly doesn't think lying is always wrong (else why mention the unbeneficial lie but not the beneficial one?).
  • [00:05:27] The Sri Lankan scholar K. N. Jayatilleke speculates that for the Buddha there simply are no such cases. The Pāli term for "beneficial," attha, means what is morally good in the sense of being useful for attaining nirvāṇa; and since asserting a falsehood was held to be a moral evil, it would be logically or causally impossible for something false (i.e. morally evil) to produce something morally advantageous. On this reading there are no white lies, no beneficial untruths — and indeed the Buddha is said to have discouraged his disciples from lying without exception for expedient cases.

docs.title: The tradition flirts back: the burning house
docs.text:
• [00:06:15] Nonetheless the Buddhist tradition kept flirting with compassionate lying. In the later Lotus Sūtra, a father gets his children to leave a burning house by promising there are toys outside. Afterward the Buddha asks his interlocutor Śāriputra: was the father guilty of falsehood?
  • [00:06:40] Śāriputra answers no — the rich man simply made it possible for his sons to escape the fire and preserve their lives; since they survived, they had already obtained "a plaything of sorts," and all the more so since by expedient means they were rescued. And the Buddha agrees. So in yet another sign of the tradition's diversity, we find conflicting messages about the well-intentioned lie.

docs.title: The other end of the raft: looking back from enlightenment
docs.text:
• [00:07:13] A further issue: so far we have asked about the teaching's status for someone mid-crossing. But pose the same question from the standpoint of someone who has already crossed over. As with the paradoxical desire to lose all desire (which can be resolved by supposing that desire drops away once nirvāṇa is reached), the raft seems to say the teaching itself can be set aside once it has served its purpose.
  • [00:07:55] This recalls Wittgenstein, who told us to see the propositions of his Tractatus as a ladder to throw away once we have understood. Another Buddhist image: instruction is like a medicine that purges our ignorance but is then expelled along with whatever it purged. This seems inevitable once we accept that philosophy's purpose is to bring us to happiness, or release from suffering — for what guarantee is there that the beliefs that make you happy are the ones that are true?
  • [00:08:39] But remember: the Buddha traces suffering to attachment, attachment to desire, and desire to ignorance. He presupposes that we are freed from our predicament precisely by understanding that predicament more fully. To this extent the Buddha is a bringer of truth, even if not of straightforward doctrine. The process of enlightenment is therapeutic, and may eventually render the teaching otiose — but it begins by dispelling falsehood.
  • [00:09:21] So the Buddha may, after all, hold that the truth will set you free — but not all at once. If you heard last episode you already know the four noble truths and should be within "touching distance" of enlightenment; yet it takes lengthy, perhaps lifelong training to give up desire and attachment. Understanding the four truths is the easy part (we did it in one episode); living accordingly is the hard part.

docs.title: The snake: take the teaching by the head, not the tail
docs.text:
• [00:10:01] The second analogy makes this point. To catch a poisonous snake you must take it carefully by the head, not the tail — so too the Buddha's words must be grasped the right way. "This is a philosophy that bites."
  • [00:10:24] Some misguided men learn the dharma but do not inquire into its meaning; they learn it only to criticize others and win debates, and so do not experience the good for which it was meant. Wrongly grasped, the teachings conduce to their harm and suffering — just as a man seeking a snake who grabs its coils or tail gets bitten and may die "because of his wrong grasp of the snake."
  • [00:11:19] The Buddha's warning echoes Jack Nicholson in A Few Good Men: "you can't handle the truth." These students expect the wrong thing — they think learning exists to make you seem learned, that knowledge is shown by winning arguments. They treat the teaching as instrumental too, but as an instrument toward the wrong goal: victory and esteem — ironically the very desires the teaching tells them to abandon.
  • [00:12:00] To approach it rightly, we must be open to its power to change our goals and desires, not hope it will satisfy the goals and desires we already have.

docs.title: When to stay silent: the four kinds of question
docs.text:
• [00:12:11] What should a good teacher do with students who aren't ready? Lying is problematic; another option is to remain silent — an option the Buddha often chose. Not because he was bested in argument (as happens in the Upaniṣads, where a character often falls silent in defeat), but because he knows when speaking the truth will be beneficial and when it won't.
  • [00:12:45] In the Milinda-pañha (Questions of Menander), King Menander points to an apparent contradiction: the Buddha is said to keep nothing hidden (unlike teachers who keep things "hidden in their fists"), yet he habitually refused to answer questions. So did he teach openly or not?
  • [00:13:13] Nāgasena replies that there are four sorts of question: some call for a straightforward response, some for further clarification, some should elicit a counter-question, and some should be met with silence. This makes sense — if asked whether the colour blue is heavier than the number four, you couldn't reasonably give a simple answer; you might respond with another question ("what makes you think colours and numbers have weight?").
  • [00:13:47] When is it right to refuse to respond at all? Nāgasena says "there is no utterance or speech of the Buddhas that is without reason, without cause." So it is up to the interlocutor to deserve an answer — to be in a position where some answer would be productive. Confronted by someone who only wants to win debates or boast of his enlightenment, the Buddha offers stony silence rather than pearls of wisdom.

docs.title: Compassion: the Buddha's hallmark — and a puzzle
docs.text:
• [00:14:17] This carefully calibrated strategy may look like extreme tough love, but it is love nonetheless. Compassion is not just part of the Buddha's teaching, it is his hallmark — it is what distinguished him from others who achieved enlightenment, for he was not content to be liberated himself but laid down a teaching by which all humankind can be freed from suffering.
  • [00:14:46] But here is a puzzle: the Buddha says we escape suffering by giving up attachment — why should that have anything to do with compassion? A person who abandons desire would refrain from much wrongdoing (why kill out of vengeance, or steal, if you crave neither?). But compassion is not merely avoiding misdeeds; it means actively pursuing the welfare of others. Is the Buddhist like someone who confuses medicine's first rule, "do no harm," with the whole of medicine?
  • [00:15:20] Certainly not. Buddhist ethics emphasizes skillful action — action born of a proper understanding of things — and claims it will be morally upright and compassionate. This is enshrined in the eightfold path, which begins with right understanding but does not end there: one must pursue right speech, right action, and so on up to right mindfulness and concentration. Taking the right view (rejecting a stable unchanging self, seeing that attachment leads to suffering) is only the first step; living by it takes long training — which is why monasticism, searching self-criticism, and strict discipline are so central.

docs.title: Why behave well? Reincarnation, motive, and the wrong kind of reason
docs.text:
• [00:16:21] So good behaviour is crucial — but why, and how does it free us from suffering? One prominent answer: bad deeds doom you to a worse next life. Great stress falls on action that is puṇya, karmically fruitful; a good next life, rather than total liberation, is the goal of ordinary Buddhists — a feasible goal that gives them a reason to behave well.
  • [00:16:50] But that looks like the wrong sort of reason. I should not show compassion for my own (or my future self's) sake — not just because there is no self, but because compassion should be directed at the good of those for whom I feel it. Indeed the Buddha warns that a truly good action must spring from the right motive, and that desire for a favourable reincarnation, like all desire, would inevitably lead to suffering. If promises and threats about the next life play a role, it may again be like the raft: useful for those still making progress, not for those who have arrived.

docs.title: Is compassion itself a raft to discard?
docs.text:
• [00:17:34] A disquieting thought: might compassion itself be a raft or ladder discarded on arrival? Surely benevolence should characterize the perfect sage, not be left behind. Yet Buddhist texts sometimes suggest exactly this — the Arhat, one who has achieved full enlightenment, is said to have moved beyond puṇya and to be "no longer concerned with virtue."
  • [00:18:04] On its face this clashes with the Buddha's own zeal to help others. But perhaps such passages mean only that the Arhat is no longer concerned with action insofar as it bears on favourable reincarnation (since he desires nothing). Or that he need not deliberate, having reached a state where he just naturally acts well. Or that virtues like compassion take a different shape depending on how far along the path one is.

docs.title: Attachment's positive flip side, and the conditional value of truth
docs.text:
• [00:18:38] To see why the Arhat would in fact act well, return to giving up attachment — which we have been treating purely negatively. To abandon greed would mean never acting from greed. But the opposite of greed is not the mere absence of greed; it is generosity. The Buddhist rejection of envy, hostility, and greed is meant to bring about positive states of mind opposed to these sources of suffering. Someone with no desires, not even committed to the permanence of his own self, will be far more inclined to share whatever he has.
  • [00:19:20] This is the moral counterpart of the Buddha's gift of insight: banishing ignorance is not only giving up false beliefs but replacing them with positive true beliefs. And just as the Arhat is ultimately freed even from the exertion the rest of us put into being good, so the significance and value of the Buddha's teachings depend on what stage of the path one has reached.
  • [00:19:50] Denying that the value of truth is unconditional should not be taken to mean the truth has value only if some condition is met and otherwise none. Rather, what value the truth has is dependent on what condition is met — the truth has different values in different conditions.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:20:08] One may still object that this ethics is too centered on the individual — the Buddha tells us much about how each person should and shouldn't live. But does Buddhism also say how we should live together — does it offer any political ideas beyond the rules of monastic life? The answer is yes.
  • [00:20:38] Next time turns to a figure who can fairly be called a philosopher king — the legendary Mauryan emperor Aśoka — examining his attempt to rule as a Buddhist and comparing his ideas to the ancient Indian political treatise, the Arthaśāstra.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• dharma — the Buddha's teaching; likened to a raft and a snake, its value tied to the purpose it serves.
  • the raft analogy — teaching is for crossing over to safety, not to carry afterward; raises the worry that the teaching is only instrumentally valuable, indifferent to truth.
  • the poisonous snake analogy — the teaching must be grasped "by the head"; those who learn it only to win debates "grasp it by the tail" and are bitten.
  • nirvāṇa — the destination of the Buddhist path; the extinction of attachment and desire. The four noble truths are easy to understand but hard to live: understanding is the first step, lifelong training the rest.
  • Prince Abhaya dialogue — the Buddha lists kinds of speech but pointedly omits speech that is beneficial-yet-untrue.
  • K. N. Jayatilleke — scholar who argues the omission is principled: since attha (beneficial) means useful for nirvāṇa and falsehood is a moral evil, a beneficial untruth is impossible — no white lies.
  • attha (Pāli) — "beneficial," i.e. morally good in the sense of conducive to attaining nirvāṇa.
  • Lotus Sūtra / burning house — later text where a father lures children from a burning house with a promised toy; Śāriputra and the Buddha excuse it as expedient means — the tradition flirting with compassionate lying.
  • Milinda-pañha (Questions of Menander) — King Menander asks how the Buddha can both hide nothing and refuse to answer; Nāgasena replies with the four kinds of question, the fourth answered by silence (his response to those who don't deserve or can't benefit from an answer — unlike the Upaniṣadic silence of one defeated in debate).
  • compassion — the Buddha's hallmark, distinguishing him from other enlightened beings; not mere avoidance of harm but active pursuit of others' welfare, expressed through skillful action born of proper understanding.
  • eightfold path — begins with right understanding and proceeds through right speech, action, mindfulness, and concentration; right view is only the first step.
  • puṇya — karmically fruitful action earning a better rebirth; the ordinary Buddhist's goal, but the "wrong sort of reason" for genuine compassion.
  • Arhat — one fully enlightened, said to have moved beyond puṇya and concern with virtue; the puzzle of whether compassion is itself a "raft" left behind.
  • conditional value of truth — the truth's value is not unconditional but varies with one's condition; it has different values at different stages of the path.
