docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 11 — "Carry a Big Stick: Ancient Indian Political Thought"
docs.text:
← Ep 10

Ep 12 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:21:30 In brief: Ancient India did have political philosophy. The Arthaśāstra attributed to Kauṭilya — a vast manual of statecraft for the Mauryan court — oscillates between high-minded moralism (duty, justice, the king's virtue) and cold Machiavellian pragmatism (spies, deception, the "stick" of punishment); the same tension is dramatized in the legend and the edicts of the emperor Aśoka, who turns from tyrant to Buddhist moral exemplar yet rules by Dharma rather than abandoning power. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannari"; Arthaśāstra ≈ "Atta Shastra / Atashastra / Atha Shastra"; Kauṭilya ≈ "Cautilia / Kautilia"; Chandragupta ≈ "Chandra Gupta"; kṣatriya ≈ "Kashatria"; Ājīvika ≈ "Ajivaka"; daṇḍanīti ≈ "Dandaniti"; Dharmaśāstra ≈ "Dharma Shastras"; Manu-Smṛti ≈ "Manu Suruti"; Cārvāka ≈ "Charvaca"; Megasthenes ≈ "Magasthenes"; Aśoka ≈ "Ashoka / Asherka"; Caṇḍāśoka ≈ "Chandasoka"; Kaliṅga ≈ "Kalinga"; Upagupta ≈ "Uba Gupta"; Prākrit ≈ "Prachrit"; Rupert Gethin ≈ "Rupert Ghetten").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The Arthaśāstra — a long, elaborate treatise on statecraft attributed to Kauṭilya; the central text of the episode [00:01:19].
  • Kauṭilya — the supposed author, chief minister to Chandragupta Maurya; reports rival opinions and stakes out moderate middle positions [00:05:02].
  • The Dharmaśāstras / Manu-Smṛti — Brahminical law-books of roughly the same period, foil to the Arthaśāstra [00:07:59].
  • Chandragupta Maurya — founder of the Mauryan Empire, contemporary of Alexander, who supposedly ended his life as a Jain ascetic [00:05:08].
  • Aśoka — Chandragupta's grandson; the most famous ancient Indian ruler, whose legend and edicts embody the choice between brute force and moral rule [00:14:22].

docs.title: What was daily life like? — and why the Arthaśāstra helps
docs.text:
• [00:00:41] A thought experiment: if you'd been born — or reborn — in ancient India, the series so far might tempt you to imagine yourself a learned Brahmin schooled in the Vedas and ritual, a noble kṣatriya warrior, a Buddhist monk or nun, or a radical renouncer of the Ājīvika or Jaina schools. But far more likely you'd have been a farmer or a cowherd.
  • [00:01:12] Texts like the Upaniṣads or the Buddhist Pāli canon give only occasional, indirect glimpses of such ordinary lives. For the everyday, then, "good thing for the Arthaśāstra."
  • [00:01:26] This lengthy treatise on affairs of state lays down detailed regulations for all ancient Indians, "from the king to the slave, from the Brahmin to the ascetic." Its trivia is delightful: ancient Indian cows wore bells so they could be found; cattle were at risk from crocodiles and tigers; buffalo milk yields slightly more butter than cow's milk; and a cowherd who milked his animals twice daily in the dry season would have his thumb cut off.
  • [00:02:06] Beyond milk and butter, even a brief skim shows the text presents "the cream of classical Indian thought" on warfare, law, gender relations, slavery, and economics. Its interest for the historian is not in doubt.

docs.title: Is it philosophy? — Weber's challenge
docs.text:
• [00:02:36] The harder question: what is its interest for the historian of philosophy? Is the Arthaśāstra a pioneering work of political thought? Is its philosophical significance real but implicit — like Pāṇini's grammar for the philosophy of language? Or does its practical orientation mean we'd be mistaken to read it philosophically at all?
  • [00:02:55] After all, the Indian tradition is famous for its philosophy of the self, its metaphysics and epistemology — not for political thought. Max Weber, founder of modern sociology, claimed Buddhism in particular was "too otherworldly to bother with politics," and one might assume the same of ancient Indian philosophy as a whole.
  • [00:03:23] That assumption is overturned by the opening sections of the Arthaśāstra.

docs.title: Statecraft for rulers: the seven elements and the "stick"
docs.text:
• [00:03:31] However much it tells us about cowherds and farmers, the text is clearly written for the ruling elite — part of its aim is to instruct rulers (and would-be rulers) in the principles of governance.
  • [00:03:49] The reader learns of the seven elements of a well-run state: the ruler himself, his officials, the territory, the fortifications, the treasury, allied states, and — last but not least — daṇḍa, which literally means "stick" and here denotes both the army and the punishments imposed by the state.
  • [00:04:14] The stick is even the subject of a whole branch of knowledge, daṇḍanīti, variously translated "government," "science of punishment," and "rule of law." Future kings should be educated in this art from a young age, and Daṇḍanīti may even have been the work's original title.
  • [00:04:39] But the surviving title fits better: artha means advantage or success, so Arthaśāstra might be rendered "the Art of the Advantageous" — apt for a treatise whose fifteen books tell the ruler how to wield the stick of punishment and the military "to best advantage."

docs.title: Who wrote it? — the problem of Kauṭilya
docs.text:
• [00:05:02] Who wrote the Arthaśāstra? "If only it were that easy." The treatise presents itself as the work of Kauṭilya, chief minister to Chandragupta, founder of the Mauryan Empire in the northwest of the subcontinent. Chandragupta lived in the later 4th century BCE, a contemporary of Alexander the Great — and legend even has the two mighty rulers meeting face to face. So at first glance the text looks like a powerful official's advice to his even more powerful monarch.
  • [00:05:33] The problems start with the second and third glances. Since the manuscript came to light in the early 20th century, scholars have disagreed over its dating and over the historical Kauṭilya's role in its composition. Worse, the text appears to have been later reorganized, so we read a much-altered work; and its original version itself drew on earlier writings.
  • [00:06:07] Like Pāṇini compiling and building on earlier grammarians, "Kauṭilya — as we may as well call the author" — reports the political ideas of others even as he advances his own.

docs.title: The method of moderate opinion — Kauṭilya as Aristotle
docs.text:
• [00:06:20] This shows most clearly in passages juxtaposing a range of views on a question, where Kauṭilya's own opinion appears as the final, correct word — often because it adopts a reasonable middle ground between others' extremes.
  • [00:06:38] Example: how should a good ruler seek advice? One view — keep his own counsel; another — be open to ideas from absolutely everyone (even a child might offer a good suggestion); a third — consult a circle of experts. Kauṭilya compromises: the king should discuss each matter with a small handful of ministers (like Kauṭilya himself, "though tactful enough not to say so"). Likewise on the council's size: where others insisted on a precise ideal number, Kauṭilya says it depends on circumstances.
  • [00:07:22] This "ostentatious display of moderate opinion," set against the extremes of predecessors, "may remind you of Aristotle — if so, it might be because you've been listening to the right podcast."
  • [00:07:35] Rival opinions aren't just mentioned but assigned to specific, named individuals, making these passages reminiscent of the dialogues of the Upaniṣads — and they may reflect actual debates at court. The impression is of lively discussion of political matters among ancient Indian intellectuals.

docs.title: The Dharmaśāstras and the meaning of dharma
docs.text:
• [00:07:59] That impression is confirmed by other writings of roughly the same period, collectively the Dharmaśāstras, including the Manu-Smṛti or Laws of Manu. These Brahminical treatises will be an important inspiration in the Hindu tradition — for instance among thinkers of the Mīmāṃsā school — and scholars trace resonances between them and the Arthaśāstra to argue which influenced which.
  • [00:08:33] Philosophically, note the term dharma itself — "upright conduct or duty in the widest sense, moral, social, and religious." How much should we read into the contrasting titles? Is the Arthaśāstra really about expediency rather than morality, "about taking advantage rather than taking heed of one's duty"?

docs.title: The moralistic Arthaśāstra — Plato in India
docs.text:
• [00:09:00] At the start of the work, that's "certainly not the impression given." In a chapter describing India's stratified society, the Arthaśāstra defines the four classes — Brahmin, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra — in terms of their distinctive duties, and likewise such groups as householders and ascetics. The state flourishes so long as each group carries out its proper duty. "And if that reminds you of Plato, you've definitely been listening to the right podcast."
  • [00:09:32] Great emphasis falls on the ruler's character, with warnings about past kings who came to grief through wrathfulness, susceptibility to pleasure, and vanity; later, we're told the king's happiness is bound up with that of his subjects.
  • [00:09:49] A similarly moralistic note sounds on law. Kauṭilya makes justice a crucial royal responsibility, and many provisions weigh not just what is expedient but what is most just. He adopts the principle that punishment should fit the crime — sometimes attractively (people are excused for an accident if they took reasonable precautions), sometimes less so (the fine for violating a slave's rights is smaller than for wronging a free citizen).

docs.title: The Machiavellian Arthaśāstra — spies, thorns, and counterfeit coin
docs.text:
• [00:10:41] Yet for long stretches Kauṭilya takes a "purely pragmatic, if not cynical" approach. Religion in particular features chiefly as a social phenomenon the king should use to manage his subjects — leading some to see the Arthaśāstra as an early instance of the materialist, even atheistic attitude later espoused by the Cārvāka school.
  • [00:11:10] Kauṭilya has reason for his hard-headedness: he conceives political life largely as a struggle against threats to stability and prosperity. Internal and natural threats he calls "thorns," to be removed by precautions against floods and calamities, "to say nothing of attacks by tigers and demons."
  • [00:11:36] Of greater interest to him is the external threat of enemy kings. He offers ample advice on defeating them in war and on manipulating and deceiving them: how best to use spies, how to encourage subversive factions within a rival state, how an enemy king can be tricked into letting himself be captured.
  • [00:12:02] On finance he is "not above" underhanded techniques for filling the treasury — such as planting counterfeit money on an enemy of the state as a pretext to confiscate his property. Such passages call to mind not Plato but Machiavelli.

docs.title: Reconciling the two faces
docs.text:
• [00:12:25] The tension between moralistic and Machiavellian strands could be explained by the text's composite nature — different authors with different mindsets. Alternatively, Kauṭilya may be a moralist realistic enough to know that building a just society sometimes requires the ruler to get his hands dirty. Or one could argue the reverse: the talk of dharma, of the king's admirable character, of legal justice, all serves his practical aims — moderate punishments and dutiful subjects are means to the stability of the community and his continued rule, not ends in themselves.
  • [00:13:15] This oscillation, between the king as stick-wielding enforcer and the king as moral paragon, was embodied by Chandragupta himself: his empire was built on conquest (perhaps aided by the power vacuum Alexander left in northwestern India), yet at the end of his life he supposedly became devoted to the spiritual path of the Jainas. His death is even reported as a consequence of radical Jain ascetic practices — though it's also said he was poisoned by Kauṭilya, whose Arthaśāstra "just happens to mention" a debate over whether a minister should seize power on the monarch's death.

docs.title: Succession, election, and the rise of Aśoka
docs.text:
• [00:13:57] In the absence of an heir, the Indian tradition did recognize the possibility of the aristocracy electing a new leader — a custom reported by the Greek historian Megasthenes, perhaps mirrored in the story of Indra being chosen as king by the other gods. But when a son was available, power passed to him, as in the Mauryan dynasty.
  • [00:14:22] Which brings us to "the most famous political ruler of ancient India," Aśoka — Chandragupta's grandson, who inherited and further expanded the Mauryan Empire. He presents an even more acute case of the paradigmatic choice facing the ruler: brutal pragmatism or pious virtue.

docs.title: Aśoka the cruel — and the conversion
docs.text:
• [00:14:46] The many legends have Aśoka making the former choice early. Known as Caṇḍāśoka, "Aśoka the cruel," he had 99 of his brothers killed to eliminate rivals for the throne; when he learned the 500 women of his harem mocked his ugliness, he had them all burnt alive; he built a horrific prison and torture house known as "Aśoka's Hell."
  • [00:15:13] Then came a dramatic transformation — from merciless tyrant to a moral exemplar who so despised violence that he disliked even the killing and eating of animals, "a conversion, if you will, from stick to carrot." The cause, "in a word": Buddhism.
  • [00:15:33] It was especially the Buddhist tradition that passed down and elaborated his legends. Since it was chronologically implausible that Aśoka could have met the Buddha, the biographers settled for claiming that in a previous life he was a humble child who offered the passing Buddha the only gift he could manage — a handful of dirt.
  • [00:15:55] In his new life as king, after being converted by a Buddhist monk named Samudra, he turned from cruelty with the same enthusiasm he had reserved for tyranny, building 84,000 stūpas (burial mounds) in honor of the Buddha — a number that may reflect the traditional figure for the atoms in the human body. Over his ministers' protests he gave away all his wealth, with only half a piece of fruit left on his deathbed to donate to the monks. Other tales show him physically serving the saṅgha, the Buddhist monastic community.

docs.title: Why the legends mattered — and the duty of kings to defer
docs.text: • [00:16:36] Such stories encouraged the generosity of later monarchs and aristocrats, invited to follow Aśoka's example. But there was a deeper point: Buddhists retained the Brahminical conviction that rulers should not only respect wise sages but defer to them — prostrating at their feet, as Aśoka supposedly did before a Buddhist arhat named Upagupta.

docs.title: The edicts — a more ecumenical Aśoka
docs.text:
• [00:17:06] In modern times the Buddhist picture of Aśoka has been complemented and challenged by his inscriptions scattered across the former empire — edicts written to promulgate his policies. Composed in Prākrit, they became incomprehensible to later generations and were only deciphered in the 19th century.
  • [00:17:30] To an extent the edicts confirm the legends: some lay down rules for Buddhist monks, and Aśoka clearly did identify as a Buddhist. But he is far more ecumenical than the legends suggest, insisting in several edicts on harmony between different schools rather than urging all to adopt Buddhism — sometimes seeming to stand beyond sectarian divisions entirely in his role as king. His personal conversion, too, may have been gradual.
  • [00:18:10] There is nonetheless a "road to Damascus" moment implied: an inscription recording his shock and remorse at the slaughter in his war against the Kaliṅga kingdom — the very conflict that expanded his empire to cover most of the subcontinent.

docs.title: Aśoka as teacher, not ascetic
docs.text:
• [00:18:29] The Aśoka of the edicts is a moral paragon but not the humble ascetic of legend. Instead he is a teacher who exhorts his subjects to observe Dharma, or a wise father responsible for the moral education of his "children" — all who fall under his rule. He promotes Dharma by appointing special ministers to travel the realm as moral educators — and these are government officials, not Buddhist monks, again suggesting a moral authority above all sects.
  • [00:19:13] The actual ethical doctrines are "nothing too spectacular": honor your parents, respect life, speak the truth, show kindness to animals and slaves. More interesting is the implication that political authority should be wielded with an ethical purpose. Aśoka innovates by giving traditional kingly practices a moral dimension — styling himself as one who still seeks conquest, but now through Dharma rather than war, and touring his lands to promote Dharma rather than to enjoy the pleasures of the realm.

docs.title: Aśoka, the Buddha, and rule by persuasion
docs.text:
• [00:19:49] In all this we may compare Aśoka with the Buddha himself — also from the kṣatriya ruling class, and likewise not content merely to achieve his own enlightenment but seeking to liberate others. Aśoka, however, pursues that goal within political life rather than abandoning it as the Buddha did: he is the king whose own merit and Dharma consist in encouraging merit and Dharma among his subjects. This echoes the most idealistic passages of Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra — such as the one binding the king's happiness inextricably to his subjects'.
  • [00:20:31] A more cynical reading is available: Aśoka was among the first world emperors to use moral teaching to secure unity and obedience — and "certainly not the last" (compare the program of public morality under Caesar Augustus in Rome). But even the most jaundiced eye must grant that Aśoka at least bases his rule on the consent of the people rather than violent coercion — as he puts it in an edict placed, "significantly enough," in the conquered land of Kaliṅga, he wishes to rule by persuasion, not fear.
  • [00:21:13] As podcasters, Adamson notes, "we're more or less forced to follow his example" — persuading you to keep listening not by carrying a big stick but by talking softly, enticing you with the carrot of a fascinating interview next time. The guest will be Rupert Gethin, helping to wrap up the look at ancient Buddhism.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Arthaśāstra — a long treatise on statecraft (15 books) attributed to Kauṭilya; "the Art of the Advantageous," ranging from cow-herding regulations to warfare, law, and economics; the episode's central text and ancient India's chief work of political thought.
  • Kauṭilya — its supposed author and chief minister to Chandragupta; reports rivals' political views and settles on moderate middle positions (compared to Aristotle); the historical author's identity and date are disputed.
  • daṇḍa / daṇḍanīti — the "stick": the army and state punishments; daṇḍanīti, the "science of the stick," is the royal art of government and may have been the work's original title.
  • artha — advantage, success; gives the Arthaśāstra its name.
  • the seven elements of a state — ruler, officials, territory, fortifications, treasury, allied states, and the army/punishment (daṇḍa).
  • four classes (varṇa) — Brahmin, kṣatriya, vaiśya, śūdra; the Arthaśāstra defines them by their distinctive duties, the state flourishing when each fulfills its own (compared to Plato).
  • dharma — upright conduct or duty in the widest moral, social, and religious sense.
  • Dharmaśāstras / Manu-Smṛti (Laws of Manu) — Brahminical law-books of the same era; foundational for the Hindu tradition and for the Mīmāṃsā school.
  • Cārvāka — the materialist/atheist school; some see the Arthaśāstra's treatment of religion as social tool in this spirit.
  • Chandragupta Maurya — founder of the Mauryan Empire, contemporary of Alexander, served by Kauṭilya; supposedly died as a Jain ascetic (or poisoned by Kauṭilya).
  • Aśoka (Caṇḍāśoka) — Chandragupta's grandson; in legend a cruel tyrant converted by Buddhism into a moral exemplar building 84,000 stūpas; in his edicts an ecumenical teacher-king ruling by Dharma and "persuasion, not fear."
  • Kaliṅga — the kingdom whose conquest, with its slaughter, prompted Aśoka's remorse and is recorded in his edicts.
  • the edicts — Aśoka's inscriptions in Prākrit, deciphered only in the 19th century; show a more ecumenical, less ascetic ruler than the Buddhist legends.
  • Megasthenes — Greek historian who reports the Indian custom of electing a leader when there is no heir.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 12 — "Rupert Gethin on Buddhism and the Self"
docs.text:
← Ep 11

Ep 13 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Rupert Gethin 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Rupert Gethin · Runtime: 00:32:38 In brief: An interview with Rupert Gethin (Professor of Buddhist Studies, University of Bristol) on Buddhism's most counterintuitive thesis — the no-self (anātman) theory — what "self" it denies, how it answers objections about the unity of experience and moral responsibility, and how meditation fits a tradition that says there is no self to find. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Rupert Gethin ≈ "Rupert Getton/Geffen"; Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennary"; ātman ≈ "artman"; duḥkha ≈ "ducca"; skandhas ≈ "scandas"; suttas ≈ "Siddhas of the Pali canon"). Note: this episode's transcript carries no spoken title; the H1 above is editorial and should be reconciled against the show's canonical title.

docs.title: Setting up the no-self theory
docs.text:
• [00:00:32] Adamson introduces the guest: Rupert Gethin, Professor of Buddhist Studies at the University of Bristol, here for an interview on Buddhism. (The standard series credit names Jonardon Ganeri and Peter Adamson, but this is a solo-host interview episode.)
  • [00:00:47] Adamson goes "straight to the most philosophically challenging and counterintuitive contribution of Buddhism" — for his money, the no-self theory: we don't have any selves. He flags that how counterintuitive this is depends on what we mean by "self," and asks Gethin to start with what the Buddhists thought they were denying, and why.
  • [00:01:15] Gethin: the no-self doctrine is best read as a reaction to a particular idea of the self from early Indian thought — above all the Upaniṣads and their notion of the ātman. Ātman is just the ordinary Sanskrit word for "self," but in the Upaniṣads it acquires a special sense.
  • [00:01:56] The argument the Upaniṣads are answering: at one level we are obviously a flux — a set of changing experiences, feelings, thoughts. So they ask: what underlies all these? What ties them together? What is constant? Their answer is the self. The ātman is what is constant, contrasted with the changing flux as that which does not change.
  • [00:02:30] That, says Gethin, is the starting point of the Buddhist critique. Buddhism throws out a challenge: yes, there is a changing flow of experience; yes, we seem able to refer it back to a constant subject; but when we introspect, what we actually find is never the self — only a specific experience, feeling, and so forth.

docs.title: The Humean challenge: where is the self?
docs.text:
• [00:03:21] The Buddhist move is to challenge us to locate the unchanging constant that supposedly underlies our experiences — and to find that we can't. Gethin notes this is "a kind of precursor" to David Hume, who lays down a very similar challenge about the self.
  • [00:03:51] Adamson spells out the upshot for the listener: reflect on your own experience right now and you find the experiencing — hearing our voices — but not some further thing, a subject who does the hearing. He adds that the Upaniṣads to some extent concede this: in places the self is admitted to be a hidden, underlying subject that is hard to access.

docs.title: The Vedic reply: unity at a time and over time
docs.text:
• [00:04:24] Adamson plays devil's advocate for the Upaniṣadic / Vedic side and presses Gethin two ways:
  • Unity at a moment: I can experience more than one thing at once — listening to the podcast while running through a park, seeing trees and hearing voices. What binds these into one experience?
  • Identity over time: I want to be the same person who hears the end of the episode and who heard the beginning. Don't Buddhists struggle to explain both the unity of experience at a moment and the persistence of one agent who starts and finishes an action?
  • [00:05:26] Gethin's first reply: Buddhists do not deny an experiencing subject — there genuinely is that quality to experience, the sense of being a subject. What they deny is that this experiencing subject is a constant thing persisting through time.
  • [00:05:58] The subject is "a simple quality of experience," and when you abstract it from the experiences it is "a kind of nothing." It is part of the fact of the flow of experience but is not itself a thing; it needs the objects of experience to be there. Without them it is blank, contentless.
  • [00:06:31] So the Buddhist challenge to the Upaniṣadic thinkers: you are using this sense of subject but can tell us nothing about it. You project onto it that it is a constant, separate, independent thing persisting through time — but it is really just a particular quality of experiencing, not a continuing thing in itself.

docs.title: Aggregates and causal connection: the photograph analogy
docs.text:
• [00:07:11] Adamson pushes: if all we have is particular experiences, "aggregated" (as the Buddhists like to say), don't we still need to distinguish one aggregate from another? His example — my seeing of your face is bound up with my sensation of sitting in this chair, while your seeing of my face goes with a different chair-sensation. How do the Buddhists explain different aggregates of experience, at a time and over time, without selves?
  • [00:07:54] Gethin: they appeal to a theory of causality — causal connection between phenomena. You and I are each a collection of mental and physical events occurring in a causally connected cluster. The word "I" refers to a particular aggregate / cluster / pattern of mental and physical events that is arising and falling continuously from moment to moment — a constant state of flux.
  • [00:08:56] The pattern is not random: it follows certain laws of causality. It is the causal connection between the events that produces the appearance of unity when we experience things.
  • [00:09:11] His analogy: a colour photograph in a magazine. From a distance you see people, a mountain, a scene; under a magnifying glass you see only dots of colour (four colours making the whole range). The picture is just dots that come together, and we project the image onto them. We are like that: when we think of ourselves and others we don't see the flux, the pattern of events — we see people as solid and constant, but that's "not really what is there."

docs.title: Did the Buddha actually teach no-self?
docs.text:
• [00:10:25] Adamson asks whether this is one of those cases where the Buddha "wasn't a Buddhist" (like Marx allegedly wasn't a Marxist): did the Buddha himself teach the no-self theory, and why associate it with him in particular?
  • [00:10:57] Gethin: there is genuine discussion here. In the earliest sources — the suttas of the Pāli canon — there is no passage where the Buddha categorically says "there is no self." What he characteristically says is "this is not the self, this is not the self" — whatever you can point to, you can't take it as a self.
  • [00:11:22] Some infer that the earliest tradition (even the Buddha) leaves it open whether there is some kind of self. Gethin thinks this misunderstands what is going on, and connects it to what he calls the greater problem of the self.

docs.title: Two problems of the self: the intellectual and the attachment problem
docs.text:
• [00:11:57] Buddhism approaches the self two ways:
  • the intellectual problem — examining the notion of self through logic and reason, asking whether it makes sense (this is what the conversation has covered so far);
  • the bigger problem — the self bound up with attachment. To say "I have a self / this is my self" is in effect to try to mark off a part of the universe and say "this is mine and mine only."
  • [00:12:58] That, Gethin argues, is why the texts repeat "this is not myself": there is no single bit of the universe you can point to and say "that's mine, I control it, it will be mine forever." This is again a response to the Upaniṣadic use of "self."
  • [00:13:24] An aside: a modern Thai school of Buddhism is willing to call nirvāṇa "the self" in a sense. But for mainstream Buddhism there is almost a critique of the very word "self": to call something that cannot be individuated, made personal, and owned a "self" is to stretch the meaning of the word beyond ordinary use. Buddhism wants to deny that "self" can have any ultimate, meaningful referent in the universe.

docs.title: Self and selfishness; letting go of both self and not-self
docs.text:
• [00:14:26] Adamson, half-joking: "you can't be selfish if you don't have a self." Gethin: "that is precisely it." To have a self is inherently to be selfish, so the goal is to let go of self.
  • [00:14:40] Subtle point: sometimes you must let go of both self and not-self. Becoming too attached to the doctrine that there is no self is itself a form of attachment — you remain "preoccupied and caught up" in the question do I have a self?
  • [00:15:13] Adamson recalls a Pāli passage where the Buddha says you can be attached to continuing to survive or attached to being annihilated — perhaps a dig at rival ascetic traditions seeking liberation by self-obliteration. Gethin agrees: both the wish to last forever and the wish to blot oneself out are premised on the same concept — attachment to the self.

docs.title: The ethical objection: moral responsibility over time
docs.text:
• [00:15:48] Adamson grants the no-self theory has clearly ethical payoff, then raises an unwanted ethical worry. Morality leans heavily on moral responsibility: if you wrong me, I may hold you responsible tomorrow or next week. But on the Buddhist picture, all that links the skandhas (experiences) constituting me now and those constituting me next week is a causal relationship. Is that enough? It seems you can only say "me" (in scare quotes) next week has some relationship to me now — but don't I need to be genuinely the same agent to be held responsible later, or in a next life after reincarnation (which Buddhists accept)?
  • [00:17:21] Gethin concedes Buddhism "has a problem there." He frames two models of personal continuity — two kinds of "glue" holding a person together:
  • a substance theory — a constant, underlying, unchanging self that simply remains;
  • a process / causal theory — the causal connections that hold something together.
  • [00:18:16] Buddhism is committed to continuity and must preserve some sense of it; the question is whether causal connections are sufficient. At one level Buddhism can only insist that yes, they are, and then articulate in detail how those causal connections work.
  • [00:18:57] One way Buddhism develops is to throw the challenge back at its critics. Already in the Pāli canon people accuse the Buddha: "you teach the destruction of the self, you're a nihilist." The Buddha replies that this misunderstands him.
  • [00:19:33] The reply uses the middle way between two extremes:
  • eternalism — one and the same person acts and experiences the result (one way to ground moral responsibility);
  • annihilationism — one person acts and a different person experiences the result.
  • [00:20:29] Buddhism claims to be the middle between these, explained by reference to the causal connections that hold things together — traditionally dependent origination (the links between events). By that route Buddhism claims to avoid the annihilationist extreme: the causal continuity is enough to say it is, in some sense, the same person who experiences the results — just not in the full-blooded sense the Upaniṣadic thinkers want.

docs.title: Why would a no-self tradition meditate?
docs.text:
• [00:21:17] Adamson turns to meditation, something Gethin has worked on extensively, and notes an apparent paradox. Naïvely, meditation — e.g. closely attending to your breath — looks like concentrating on yourself, "getting in touch with yourself." People even say they meditate to "find myself." How can Buddhists be so invested in meditation while denying the self?
  • [00:22:05] Gethin starts from the Buddhist starting point: suffering — duḥkha. We try to be at peace, to be comfortable in the world, yet this proves elusive; something is wrong. Why?
  • [00:22:40] The basic premise: our problems arise because we don't see the world as it is. Not seeing what is really going on, we seek ways of being happy that are inappropriate — that don't fit how things actually work. So meditation is about looking again at what's going on, examining it.
  • [00:23:20] This examining ties back to the two aspects of the no-self theory:
  • We can criticize the self intellectually — even modern psychologists say we construct our personal identities, become possessive of them, feel threatened. We are emotionally attached to a notion of ourselves.
  • The intellectual grasp is not enough. I can read a book on Buddhist no-self, think "yeah, that makes sense," put it down — and the moment someone criticizes me I feel threatened and undermined. The idea "hasn't really affected me or changed me in any deep way."
  • [00:24:27] So meditation is looking inside to deconstruct ourselves emotionally and psychologically, not just intellectually. Yes, it can look like "navel-gazing," turning inward — but for Buddhism it is a necessary exercise, because we build our sense of self not over one lifetime but over many, many lifetimes; dismantling that requires work.

docs.title: Calm and insight meditation; mindfulness
docs.text:
• [00:25:22] Adamson asks whether meditation has been central throughout Buddhism's history, back to the Pāli canon. Gethin: it depends what you count — contemplative techniques of various sorts have always played a role, though not always literally sitting cross-legged on the floor; meditative technique is broader than that.
  • [00:26:03] Adamson notes the contrast with familiar European traditions: you don't picture David Hume meditating, even though he reaches some of the same conclusions about the self. Gethin agrees — Hume comes to similar conclusions, then "shrugs his shoulders" and carries on living as before.
  • [00:26:32] Gethin: these meditative techniques aren't peculiar to Buddhism — they are common to the Indian tradition generally, where philosophy is tied to the idea that you must do and practise something to realize the ideas. You search for liberating knowledge: you can get an idea of what it might be like, but that is quite different from realizing it, which requires practice.
  • [00:27:23] Adamson reframes: there's a distance between understanding the arguments and living out their conclusions, and meditation is meant to bridge that gap.
  • [00:27:34] Gethin lays out two aspects of meditation, traditionally calm meditation and insight meditation:
  • Calm meditation [00:28:09]: ordinarily our minds are scattered, jumbled, chaotic. As common sense says, when we're stirred up we don't see clearly ("calm down, tomorrow things will look better"). The technique is to take a simple object and focus on it to the exclusion of others, so the mind gradually stills. The image: impurities / mud stirred up in water gradually sink to the bottom and the water — the mind — becomes clear [00:29:25].
  • Insight meditation [00:29:44]: once the mind is clear you examine your physical and emotional experiences and try to see them for what they are.
  • [00:30:08] Mindfulness is described as the link between the two — a clarity of mind that holds and looks at what's going on.

docs.title: The detrimental side of meditation, and secularized mindfulness
docs.text:
• [00:30:28] Gethin raises the less-discussed detrimental effects of meditation: people who walk in off the street for ten-day intensive retreats with no prior experience sometimes come out feeling worse, even traumatized.
  • [00:31:04] What's interesting is that this is what you'd expect: intensive mindfulness is precisely about deconstructing the self, and deconstructing your sense of self is bound to be challenging.
  • [00:31:33] Hence traditional Buddhism's heavy emphasis on an ethical and religious framework: the symbols of the Buddha and keeping the ethical precepts help ground the practitioner and give confidence they are heading somewhere desirable. When you secularize mindfulness and strip away that support system, it's "not surprising" the experience can become more traumatic than expected.

docs.title: Close
docs.text:
• [00:32:17] On that "sobering note," Adamson thanks Rupert Gethin for the interview on Buddhism.
  • [00:32:25] Next time: the great Hindu epic the Mahābhārata, which contains the famous Bhagavad-Gītā, "a real high point of antique Indian philosophy."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• ātman — the Sanskrit word for "self"; in the Upaniṣads, the constant that underlies and ties together the changing flux of experience. The target of the Buddhist critique.
  • no-self / anātman theory — Buddhism's claim that we have no self; on introspection we find only particular experiences, never an unchanging subject.
  • Upaniṣads — early Indian texts that posit the constant ātman as what underlies the flux; Gethin notes some passages concede the self is a "hidden, hard-to-access" subject.
  • the Buddha — the suttas never have him say flatly "there is no self," only "this is not the self"; for Gethin this reflects the self-as-attachment problem, not agnosticism.
  • suttas / Pāli canon — the earliest Buddhist sources; site of the "this is not the self" formula and of early nihilism objections answered by the middle way.
  • skandhas (aggregates) — the bundle of causally connected mental and physical events that "I" names; arising and falling moment to moment.
  • causal connection / process view — the Buddhist alternative "glue" of personal continuity, opposed to a substance self; analogy of a photograph that is really just dots of colour.
  • David Hume — Western precursor who reaches a similar no-self conclusion by the same introspective challenge, but then "shrugs" and carries on living.
  • duḥkha (suffering) — the Buddhist starting point: our discomfort arises because we don't see the world as it is.
  • dependent origination — the doctrine of causal links that grounds the middle way between eternalism and annihilationism, preserving continuity (and moral responsibility) without a permanent self.
  • eternalism vs annihilationism — the two extremes on moral responsibility (same person acts and reaps / different person reaps); Buddhism claims the middle via causal continuity.
  • nirvāṇa — liberation; a modern Thai school will even call it "the self," though mainstream Buddhism resists applying the word "self" to it.
  • calm meditation (śamatha) — stilling the scattered mind by focusing on a simple object; the mud-settling-in-water image.
  • insight meditation (vipaśyanā) — examining one's physical and emotional experiences clearly, to see them as they are.
  • mindfulness — the clarity-of-mind link between calm and insight meditation; when secularized and stripped of its ethical/religious framework, can become destabilizing.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 13 — "Grand Illusion: Dharma and Deception in the Mahābhārata"
docs.text:
← Ep 12

Ep 14 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:25 In brief: The Mahābhārata as a great work of ethics done through storytelling: an epic of trickery and "grand illusion" that uses moral dilemmas about lying — above all the truth-teller Yudhiṣṭhira's fatal half-lie that kills Droṇa — to show that dharma operates on different levels, that genuine moral dilemmas can be tragic, and that the best thing to do may sometimes be something wrong. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari"; Kṛṣṇa ≈ "Krishna"; Yudhiṣṭhira ≈ "Yutistira/Yudistira/Yudishtira/Udistora"; Duryodhana ≈ "Doriodana"; Droṇa ≈ "Drona"; Bhīma ≈ "Bima"; Pāṇḍavas ≈ "Pandavas"; Vyāsa ≈ "Vyasa"; kāma ≈ "karma"/"pleasure"; mokṣa ≈ "moxha"; svadharma ≈ "swadharma"; kṣatriya ≈ "Kashatria"; Nicomachean ≈ "Nikamakian"; Arthaśāstra ≈ "Atta Shastra").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The Mahābhārata — the vast Indian epic, "great tale of the Bharata"; eight times the size of both Homeric epics combined, and a monument of Indian literature with religious meaning [00:00:33].
  • Kṛṣṇa — God incarnate as Arjuna's charioteer; teller of the truth-telling parable and instigator of the war's key deceptions [00:01:38].
  • Vyāsa — the single bard to whom the epic is ascribed (cf. Homer), who is also a character inside his own narrative [00:03:07].
  • Yudhiṣṭhira — eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, famed for never lying; his floating chariot and his fall are the episode's moral test case [00:06:35].
  • dharma — duty / law / morality / religion; the moral code whose ambiguity drives the whole discussion [00:07:35].
  • Bimal Matilal — modern interpreter who reads Kṛṣṇa as a "moral innovator" [00:17:05].

docs.title: A dilemma older than Kant: the truth-teller and the murderers
docs.text:
• [00:00:33] Today's episode: "Grand Illusion — Dharma and Deception in the Mahābhārata." It opens with a thought-experiment. A group of strangers rushes up begging for help: they're being pursued by murderous thieves who want to rob and kill them — don't tell them which way we ran. A minute later the cruel-looking pursuers arrive and ask which way the first group went.
  • [00:01:00] You're now in a dilemma. Stay silent and the robbers may torture the information out of you; lie and send them the wrong way; or tell the truth and send murderers after their victims.
  • [00:01:16] Philosophy students will recognize the puzzle: Immanuel Kant raised it as a challenge to his own teaching that one should never lie. But the example is much, much older than Kant — it features in the eighth of the 18 books of the Mahābhārata, told by none other than God himself, incarnated as the charioteer Kṛṣṇa.
  • [00:01:50] In Kṛṣṇa's version the dilemma falls to a priest who has vowed always to tell the truth. He duly tells the murderers which way to find their victims. Good though his intentions are, the priest is later sent to hell for the decision.

docs.title: A great work of ethics — done through stories
docs.text:
• [00:02:01] The Mahābhārata has plenty to teach about ethics, and it is certainly great — so it can be considered a great work of ethics. But it does not pursue the subject abstractly, the way Kant's Critique of Practical Reason does. This is ethics performed through the telling of stories.
  • [00:02:24] The product of generations of orally transmitted narratives, it is a monument in the landscape of Indian literature — a text that "holds within it a whole culture" and has, since antiquity, carried religious meaning for its readers. The epic even refers to itself as a fifth Veda.
  • [00:02:44] It is one of a pair of ancient epics, the other being the Rāmāyaṇa — which makes the comparison to the Greek Iliad and Odyssey almost irresistible, and to some extent genuinely illuminating. All four epics feature superhuman heroes who endure warfare while being manipulated by the gods; and like Homer's poems, the Mahābhārata is ascribed to a single bard, named Vyāsa.
  • [00:03:14] But "great" is meant in the most literal sense too: the epic is enormously long — eight times the size of both Homeric epics combined. And it is of more direct importance to the historian of philosophy, because embedded within it is a section called the Song of the Lord, the Bhagavad-Gītā, which (like the Iliad) centres on a great warrior's reluctance to fight but is a classic philosophical text. The Gītā is for next time.
  • [00:03:44] This episode looks at a few scenes from the rest of the epic that bear on one question: can deception ever be morally justified? It is just one of countless themes the text contains — the Mahābhārata boasts of its own comprehensiveness: "what is not here does not exist anywhere." But it is an especially apt theme, because the epic also flaunts its own status as a made narrative, a myth whose making is constantly thrust before the reader.

docs.title: Grand illusion: a self-aware myth of tricksters
docs.text:
• [00:04:21] The epic is presented through multiple frames. The whole is purportedly Vyāsa's work, but we hear it at several removes: he recited it to his son and disciples; one of them recited it again from memory; another bard repeated that, and his recitation is supposedly the basis of the 18-book version we have.
  • [00:04:48] This version is not just full but "stuffed to bursting," often with seemingly extraneous sub-tales — stories and digressions. They likely show that the epic narrative was treated as a framework, with generations of storytellers adding material relevant to their own times. The result is a text "invented and reinvented" that keeps making us aware of its own inventedness.
  • [00:05:15] Vyāsa, Kṛṣṇa and others both act within the narrative and tell stories inside it. This device — the myth-maker entering the plot of his own myth — reveals what the Mahābhārata is about: the elusiveness of truth and the ambiguity of moral rightness. Within the narrative too, the heroes deal constantly in deception, the plot driven forward by lies, tricks and subterfuge. This is "epic as grand illusion, featuring characters who are themselves illusionists."

docs.title: The central story: Pāṇḍavas vs. Kauravas
docs.text:
• [00:05:53] A brief summary makes the point. Two families within the same lineage, the Bharata line — which is also the name of the geographical territory of India (hence Mahā-bhārata, "Great Tale of the Bharata," with "great" again pointing to its scope).
  • [00:06:17] A first story tells how the text was literally weighed in scales against the four Vedas and found heavier. Pitted against each other are two sets of brothers. The Pāṇḍavas are the heroes, led — with some reluctance — by their eldest brother Yudhiṣṭhira, famed always for telling the truth; their number includes the great archer Arjuna, whose reluctance to fight his own kin will prompt Kṛṣṇa to preach the Gītā to him.
  • [00:06:59] On the other side, the Kauravas are a hundred brothers led by the anti-hero Duryodhana, who cheats the Pāṇḍavas of their birthright by duping Yudhiṣṭhira in two games of dice. The rest of the story tells of the Pāṇḍavas' wanderings, their return, and their victorious 18-day war against the Kauravas, at the cost of massive bloodshed on both sides. As in Homer, set-pieces detail the deaths of central heroes — and the most prominent deaths again involve deception and lies.

docs.title: What is dharma? From cosmic support to universal code
docs.text:
• [00:07:35] To grasp what moral code is being violated in such treachery, we need to think about dharma. We've met the word (and its Pali equivalent dhamma) before: it was used in early Buddhism for the Buddha's teaching and appears repeatedly in the moralizing inscriptions of the Buddhist king Aśoka.
  • [00:07:59] Translators render it across a "disconcertingly wide range" — from law to morality to religion. In modern India it can simply mean religion (philosophy of religion becomes dharma-darśana). But in the ancient context, dharma captures only the part of religion that bears on moral conduct. Living in accordance with dharma was sometimes said to be necessary but not sufficient for liberation from the cycle of reincarnation. In general, one's dharma is all one's various duties — as a particular individual, as a member of a family and society, and simply as a human being.
  • [00:08:50] But in the earliest surviving literature, dharma did not mean a general moral code. It hewed closer to its etymological root, a verb meaning "preserve" or "support." The first Vedas use dharma for supporting the cosmos — as when Indra holds the rivers apart from the plants. The same usage appears in ancient Iran: Zoroastrian texts use a linguistically cognate word for God holding up the heavens so they don't fall.
  • [00:09:27] Dharma then plays little role in later Vedic literature; where it appears, it is in social and legal contexts — the king's role of upholding order and justice, contrasted with the "law of the fish," where, absent royal protection, the bigger devour the smaller.
  • [00:09:55] This suggests a down-to-earth test for which actions accord with dharma: just look at existing social practice. Praiseworthy behaviour is dharma; behaviour that earns rebuke is its opposite, adharma. There's a parallel with linguistic correctness as the Sanskrit grammarians saw it: Patañjali remarked that if you want words, don't go to a grammarian but to a competent language-user — likewise, if you want ethics, don't ask a philosopher but find people agreed to be ethical. This socially-embedded picture recalls the idea of virtue in Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics.
  • [00:10:40] But dharma ultimately took on the more ambitious sense of an abstract, general set of moral requirements — and this seems to have happened especially, perhaps specifically, with the advent of Buddhism. The Buddha's dhamma was aimed at everyone regardless of social role or caste, the same universalism voiced in Aśoka's inscriptions.
  • [00:11:08] This sense then pervades later Indian literature, not least the Dharma-Sūtras (contrasted with Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra back in episode 11). At this stage dharma is named one of the main goals of life, alongside artha (practical advantage) and kāma (pleasure); movements like the Buddhists and Jains add a fourth, greater goal — mokṣa, liberation.
  • [00:11:29] The catch: this grander, absolute conception of dharma makes it much harder to know how to obey it. As one Dharma-Sūtra puts it, "Dharma and adharma do not go about saying, 'Here we are.'"

docs.title: Yudhiṣṭhira's fall: the floating chariot and the death of Droṇa
docs.text:
• [00:11:49] And this returns us to the Mahābhārata. The parable of the truth-telling priest shows it is no easy matter to say where dharma leads — even those who seek to live well may get it wrong, especially in moral dilemmas where no choice seems right.
  • [00:12:13] It's no accident that Kṛṣṇa's tale is about truth-telling, a recurrent theme of the epic. The Pāṇḍavas' leader Yudhiṣṭhira is so committed to honesty that his chariot floats a little above the ground as he rides. He comes crashing back to earth — literally — when he finally tells a falsehood.
  • [00:12:31] He does so out of desperation: there is no other way to slay the Kaurava hero Droṇa. Astonishingly, it is the divine Kṛṣṇa himself who proposes the base stratagem: Droṇa cannot be beaten by force, so "casting aside virtue," the Pāṇḍavas should resort to a winning method — Droṇa will stop fighting if he believes his son has been killed; "let some man say that he has been slain in battle."
  • [00:13:09] Reactions are mixed: Arjuna disagrees at once; the warlike Bhīma thinks it splendid. Yudhiṣṭhira is torn — he absolutely wants to win (it's said he is addicted to victory) but is loath to spoil his spotless moral record.
  • [00:13:33] The subterfuge they hit on: kill an elephant that happens to share the name of Droṇa's son, then report "the death" while thinking of the elephant but letting Droṇa assume the son is meant. As Arjuna puts it, this "covers a lie with a truth, as if with armour."
  • [00:13:51] Bhīma, untroubled, delivers the misleading news, but the suspicious Droṇa demands confirmation from Yudhiṣṭhira — who confirms the fateful lie, muttering under his breath that it is only an elephant who has died, too quietly for Droṇa to hear. The ruse works: Droṇa drops his weapons, ready to die in grief, and is killed.
  • [00:14:16] But success is short-lived. Droṇa's son will wreak great destruction on the Pāṇḍavas, and Yudhiṣṭhira has lost his spotless reputation — later forced to witness his brothers' suffering in hell, a vision then revealed to be an illusion, payback for his part in deceiving Droṇa.

docs.title: The epic's ambivalence: do the ends justify the means?
docs.text:
• [00:14:34] Despite the bitter fruit Yudhiṣṭhira reaps, the Mahābhārata's attitude to such deceptions is ambivalent. Elsewhere Kṛṣṇa warns that the Kaurava leader Duryodhana can only be killed by trickery — and here Kṛṣṇa is given a speech justifying (or perhaps just rationalizing) it: when enemies grow too numerous and powerful, "they should be slain by deceit and stratagems. This is the path formerly trodden by the gods to slay the demons, and a path trodden by the virtuous may be trodden by all."
  • [00:15:12] This reverses a slogan found elsewhere — "where dharma is, there is Kṛṣṇa" — into, roughly, if it's good enough for the gods, it's good enough for us. The idea seems to be that the end justifies the means: if the end is right, the necessary means are themselves right.
  • [00:15:35] Kṛṣṇa insists that only by deception can the Pāṇḍavas win, and remarks, "where dharma is, there is victory." On this reading the Pāṇḍavas' tricks are excused because they bring about the correct result — defeating enemies who are themselves tricksters. (Recall the whole war traces back to Duryodhana's double-dealing in the dice game that stripped the Pāṇḍavas of their kingdom.)

docs.title: Why the disapproving passages? Multiple imperatives and the moral innovator
docs.text:
• [00:16:05] But if the end justifies the means, why do other passages disapprove of the Pāṇḍavas — and especially Yudhiṣṭhira — for their ignoble tactics? A banal answer: the Mahābhārata was composed over generations by many hands, so the occasional self-contradiction is no surprise (as was said of the Arthaśāstra).
  • [00:16:36] But perhaps the epic doesn't want things to be so simple — that the way of dharma is either tell the truth and lose or win by lying, and we just need to pick the right one. It has been aptly said that "the Mahābhārata never wants to resolve itself." There are multiple ethical imperatives at work: it's good to tell the truth, but it's also good to defeat wicked enemies and secure victory for your clan — especially when a god urges you to.
  • [00:17:05] As Bimal Matilal argued, Kṛṣṇa's role in these passages could be that of a moral innovator, teaching the Pāṇḍavas to shake off the rigid code Yudhiṣṭhira had cherished — that one must tell the truth in all circumstances, the very code followed by the priest who led murderers to their victims. On this reading Kṛṣṇa is a moral agent who gave up moral integrity to avoid a total miscarriage of justice.
  • [00:17:37] Yet even if the duty to tell the truth is trumped by other concerns, it may remain a duty nonetheless. That is why it makes sense for the epic to show the consequences of Yudhiṣṭhira's act — the grounded chariot, the vision of hell. For him, and for all of us at times, the best thing to do may involve doing something wrong, something against dharma.

docs.title: Svadharma: the dharma of one person is not another's
docs.text:
• [00:18:00] To this the epic adds that the dharma of one group or person may differ from another's. Truth-telling is Yudhiṣṭhira's calling card; it is, in the deepest sense, out of character for him to collude in a lie. He thereby violates what may be called his svadharma — the duty or code relevant to him specifically.
  • [00:18:25] For a man like Bhīma, whose character revolves wholly around the kṣatriya (warrior) code of victory, the dilemma would hardly arise at all. No wonder Yudhiṣṭhira tried to have it both ways, muttering under his breath: his dharma as a truth-teller clashed with his dharma as a kṣatriya leader.
  • [00:18:48] In other passages Yudhiṣṭhira tries to escape by questioning the very validity of the warrior's dharma — the kṣatriya code, he suggests, is no better than the "law of the fish" where the strong prevail; better to give it up, even if that means retreating into the life of an ascetic: "the peaceful man sleeps happily, as he has given up both victory and defeat."

docs.title: The central insight: tragic dilemmas, but not "anything goes"
docs.text:
• [00:19:14] Here is the central insight emerging from the epic's moral dilemmas: it recognizes that such dilemmas may be genuinely tragic — that not all duties can be satisfied at once. This does not mean there's no right response at all: in Kṛṣṇa's story it seems clear the priest should not have told the murderers the truth.
  • [00:19:36] What it means is that dharma may operate on different levels, if only because we as moral agents are complex beings with different sorts of duty and responsibility. Yudhiṣṭhira is a truth-teller by character and inclination, a warrior by circumstance — a combination that leads to a conflict resolvable only by betraying himself or his responsibilities.
  • [00:19:55] The same kind of dilemma is the catalyst for the epic's most famous section: it begins when Yudhiṣṭhira's younger brother Arjuna hesitates over whether to act as a warrior and ride out against his enemies, or as a kinsman who should not slay members of his own family.
  • [00:20:14] "Fortunately, you face no such conflict" — joining us next time, as we turn to the Bhagavad-Gītā, should be an easy decision.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Mahābhārata — the vast Indian epic, "Great Tale of the Bharata"; eight times the length of both Homeric epics, calls itself a fifth Veda, and does ethics through storytelling rather than abstract argument.
  • Bhagavad-Gītā — the Song of the Lord, a classic philosophical text embedded in the epic; subject of the next episode (Kṛṣṇa persuading Arjuna to fight).
  • Rāmāyaṇa — the other of the two ancient Indian epics, paired with the Mahābhārata as Greece's Iliad and Odyssey are paired.
  • Vyāsa — the single bard to whom the epic is ascribed; also appears as a character inside the multiply-framed narrative.
  • Kṛṣṇa — God incarnate as Arjuna's charioteer; tells the truth-teller parable, yet proposes the deceptions that kill Droṇa and Duryodhana; "where dharma is, there is Kṛṣṇa / victory."
  • Yudhiṣṭhira — eldest Pāṇḍava, never lies; his chariot floats above the ground until his half-truth about Droṇa's "death" brings it crashing down.
  • Arjuna — great archer among the Pāṇḍavas; objects to the deception of Droṇa; his refusal to fight kin sets up the Gītā.
  • Bhīma — warlike Pāṇḍava for whom only the kṣatriya code of victory matters; happily delivers the lie that fells Droṇa.
  • Duryodhana — anti-hero leading the hundred Kaurava brothers; cheats the Pāṇḍavas of their kingdom in the rigged dice game.
  • Droṇa — Kaurava hero, undefeatable by force, killed once tricked into believing his son is dead (an identically-named elephant is slain instead).
  • dharma — duty / law / morality / religion; from a root meaning "support/preserve" (cosmic order) it grows into a universal moral code, especially via Buddhism. Hard to apply: "Dharma and adharma do not go about saying, 'Here we are.'"
  • adharma — the opposite of dharma; behaviour that earns rebuke.
  • svadharma — the dharma specific to one's own role/character; Yudhiṣṭhira violates his (truth-telling) when forced into a warrior's lie.
  • artha / kāma / mokṣa — the goals of life named alongside dharma: practical advantage, pleasure, and (added by Buddhists and Jains) liberation.
  • "law of the fish" — the state of nature without royal protection, where the bigger devour the smaller; the foil to dharma as order/justice.
  • Bimal Matilal — modern interpreter who reads Kṛṣṇa as a moral innovator, sacrificing integrity to prevent a miscarriage of justice.
  • Kant — raised the truth-teller-and-murderer dilemma to challenge his own absolute ban on lying; the Mahābhārata posed it millennia earlier.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 14 — "World on a String: The Bhagavad-Gītā"
docs.text:
← Ep 13

Ep 15 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:19:55 In brief: The Bhagavad-Gītā — Kṛṣṇa's battlefield counsel to the doubting warrior Arjuna — is read as a many-voiced philosophical text that answers "why act at all?" with its signature doctrine of unattached action: do your own duty (svadharma) without craving the fruits, as devotion to the highest god and as imitation of the god who keeps the cosmic wheel turning. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Gannery"; Bhagavad-Gītā ≈ "Bhagavad Gita"; Kṛṣṇa ≈ "Krishna"; Arjuna ≈ "Adjuna/Ajuna"; Mahābhārata ≈ "Barata"; kṣatriya ≈ "Kashatria"; Yudhiṣṭhira ≈ "Yudhistira"; Bimal Matilal ≈ "Bimal Matilal"; Gosāla / Ājīvaka ≈ "Gosala / Ajivaka"; Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad ≈ "Shvetashvattara"; Sāṃkhya ≈ "Samkhya"; prakṛti ≈ "Prakriti"; puruṣa ≈ "Purusha"; Īśvarakṛṣṇa / Sāṃkhya-kārikā ≈ "Ishvara Krishna / Samkhaakarika"; yogin ≈ "Jogin"; Rāja-Vidyā ≈ "Raja Vidya"; Aśoka ≈ "Ashoka"; Duryodhana ≈ "Duryodana"; Aldous Huxley ≈ "Elvis Huxley"; Oppenheimer ≈ "Opdheimer/Oppenheimer").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The Bhagavad-Gītā — "Song of the Lord," the section of the Mahābhārata in which Kṛṣṇa counsels Arjuna; a many-authored text read here as philosophy, not mere plot device [00:00:32].
  • Arjuna & Kṛṣṇa — the doubting warrior-prince and his charioteer, secretly the supreme god [00:02:25].
  • Sāṃkhya philosophy — the nature/observer (prakṛti / puruṣa) framework whose anticipations the Gītā contains; its central text is Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya-kārikā [00:14:09].
  • Yoga — spiritual discipline already intertwined with Sāṃkhya in the Gītā, made another name for the path of unattached action [00:16:05].

docs.title: A text for all time — and its political charge
docs.text:
• [00:00:40] The episode opens with the words of BJP Minister Sushma Swaraj, who urged everyone to read two couplets of the Gītā daily (700 couplets, finishable in a year) and proposed declaring it India's national book. Adamson notes this was "not an entirely innocuous suggestion": officially enshrining a Hindu classic sends a "none too subtle message" to non-Hindus.
  • [00:01:18] But you needn't be a Hindu nationalist to admire it. Gandhi memorized parts and drew from it inspiration for non-violent resistance; Aldous Huxley found in it a source for his "perennial philosophy"; the American writers Thoreau and Emerson admired it greatly.
  • [00:01:40] At the other end of the spectrum, Nazi-era Indologists in Germany read the Gītā as evidence of a "pure monotheism untainted by supposedly Semitic ideas," and Robert Oppenheimer quoted its line "Now I am become death, the destroyer of worlds" about his work on the atomic bomb. As Adamson quips, when it comes to a sentiment for any occasion, "no greeting card company can compete with the Gītā."

docs.title: Arjuna's dilemma: a genuinely philosophical doubt
docs.text:
• [00:02:12] The universal feeling that this is a text "for all time and all people" is surprising, given how few of us must decide whether to "unleash devastating war against several dozen siblings." That is the choice facing the hero Arjuna in the Mahābhārata.
  • [00:02:31] The action — "or perhaps we should say the inaction" — opens on the brink of the final battle between the Pāṇḍavas and Kauravas. Arjuna, the greatest Pāṇḍava warrior, brings both his chariot and the entire epic's narrative "to a grinding halt because he is beset by doubt."
  • [00:02:52] His dilemma is a conflict of dharma. As a kṣatriya (elite warrior) — a prince, son of the god Indra, a fabled archer whose bow has its own name — his birth was greeted not with cuddly toys but with the prediction that "the fire god will be fully sated with the fat of all the creatures in the Khāṇḍava forest." Yet he is reluctant to kill his own kinsmen. He feels two pulls: the kṣatriya-dharma (law of the warrior) and the kula-dharma (law of kinship).
  • [00:03:44] His proposed answer: do nothing — give up the warrior's life entirely and become a renouncer, the same temptation voiced last episode by his elder brother Yudhiṣṭhira.
  • [00:04:02] Crucially, Arjuna's problem is "distinctively philosophical": it is not weakness of will (knowing the right thing but lacking courage) but genuine puzzlement about his duty. Fortunately he has a resource unavailable to the average moral philosopher — "God is, quite literally, his co-pilot." His charioteer Kṛṣṇa is an incarnation of the highest divinity, creator of the universe, and the speaker of most of what follows; hence the title Bhagavad-Gītā, "Song of the Lord."

docs.title: Svadharma and "many authors, one chorus"
docs.text:
• [00:04:31] Kṛṣṇa sets out an argument urging Arjuna to follow his true path, his svadharma — the dharma uniquely appropriate to him. "It is even better to carry out one's own path badly than another's path well," and Arjuna "was born for this occasion." As Bimal Matilal puts it, "the entire Bhārata war was for Arjuna. It was his game and he should play."
  • [00:05:04] Is the Gītā then just a plot device to restart the stalled narrative after letting Arjuna air his scruples? "Hardly." Its authors seize the chance to explore the deeper question of why any of us should ever undertake any action at all.
  • [00:05:17] "Authors, not author, advisedly": scholars hold that the Gītā, like the whole Mahābhārata, was composed by numerous authors with varying agendas, situating Arjuna's choice within several different philosophical and religious contexts. The result is that Kṛṣṇa becomes a kind of chorus — a single voice expressing numerous viewpoints that may or may not finally fit together into one unified basis for action.

docs.title: First moves: shame, reincarnation, and the indifference to outcomes
docs.text:
• [00:06:01] Kṛṣṇa begins with the most obvious tactic: he tells Arjuna to stop being a wimp — "actually, to stop acting like a eunuch." Refusing to fight will earn only shame. This is a direct appeal to kṣatriya-dharma, but it cannot suffice, since it ignores his worry about kula-dharma.
  • [00:06:26] So Kṛṣṇa appeals to reincarnation: the relatives Arjuna may kill — and Arjuna himself, if slain — will all be reborn. Discarding bodies is "no more dramatic than changing our clothes." The true self is invulnerable: "swords do not cut him, fire does not burn him, water does not wet him, wind does not parch him."
  • [00:06:53] Having lowered the stakes, Kṛṣṇa adds that the outcome of fighting should be irrelevant to a true kṣatriya, who must fight bravely regardless of result. Here he plants the seed that blossoms across the rest of the Gītā: no one, warrior or peasant, should act with an eye to the fruits of their action.

docs.title: The core problem: why act at all? — unattached action vs. renunciation
docs.text:
• [00:07:13] This idea of unattached action was touched on in episode six on karma, but it raises Arjuna's own objection: if the fruits of action are nothing to me, why act at all? Why not "disengage entirely and become a renouncer"?
  • [00:07:37] That solution was adopted "in spectacular style" by ascetics like Gosāla and his Ājīvaka movement, and by the early Jainas. But Kṛṣṇa gives it short shrift: complete inaction is simply impossible — "no one lives even a moment without doing some act, for the forces of nature cause everyone to act." And "no one who has a body can renounce all acts completely; he is the true renouncer who renounces the fruits of his acts."
  • [00:08:08] Kṛṣṇa adds that inaction too has fruits — our "sins of omission." If you watch a child be hit by a truck and do nothing, it's no defense to tell the parents you're "in the action-renouncing business."
  • [00:08:37] Other passages, though, concede that deliberate inaction is at least a stage on the right path — just a less advanced one than unattached action. Kṛṣṇa distinguishes the simple-minded strategy of mere relinquishment from the genuine renunciation that consists in acting without regard to results.
  • [00:09:01] Here the Gītā offers a real innovation (also found in some presumably contemporary Upaniṣads), and like the Upaniṣads it coins striking metaphors: the true renouncer is like a tortoise — "as the tortoise draws in its limbs, so the renouncer withdraws even from his senses and focuses on his interior insight."

docs.title: "All this is strung on me": devotional theism
docs.text:
• [00:09:33] But Arjuna might still ask: toward what should interior insight be directed? Kṛṣṇa's answer is simple — "Think of me." "I am the origin of this entire universe and its dissolution… all this is strung on me, as strings of pearls are strung on a string." (The episode's title image.)
  • [00:09:56] This is the core teaching of the Gītā — "or at least of some of its authors." It justifies action through a devotional theism that does not abandon a plurality of gods but insists one highest god is the true object of all worship — close to later Upaniṣads like the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, which likewise makes a single god the cause of all things.
  • [00:10:27] Also Upaniṣadic is the Gītā's interest in sacrifice, which it frequently approves ("the world is not of him who fails to sacrifice"). The authors had reason to be nervous: the Brahmins "offered more fruits than a greengrocer," promising that correct sacrifices bring wealth, family, cattle and a good rebirth. Like the Buddhists and other dissidents, the Gītā distances itself from this "cash cow" view of ritual — yet urges us to keep sacrificing anyway, since ritual sacrifice becomes the paradigmatic approved action, one we must undertake "with our minds set upon God."

docs.title: War as sacrifice, devotion open to all, and keeping the wheel rolling
docs.text:
• [00:11:17] So Kṛṣṇa's exhortation is not merely to fight but to wage war as a kind of sacrifice — an action expressing nothing but devotion to him. It may be this idea of devotion that has made the text so meaningful across the centuries.
  • [00:11:35] You need not be a mighty warrior to devote your life to God: the Gītā explicitly upends the stratifications of Vedic culture, with Kṛṣṇa promising that even women and the low-born śūdras can be liberated through sincere devotion to him.
  • [00:11:47] The point is not just to direct our thoughts to Kṛṣṇa as we act, but to take him as our model: as he created the world and continues to hold it together, so we should act to maintain cosmic harmony — to "keep the wheel rolling." It is this, not any fruits accruing to us, that motivates the true renouncer.

docs.title: Fatalism: "I am time, grown old to destroy the world"
docs.text:
• [00:12:22] One could hardly blame Arjuna for wondering how his going to war helps hold the world together. Here the narrative context merges with the philosophical thrust: Arjuna is simply there to fight, and the story can only resume once he resolves to do so. The war — "spoiler alert, it's going to be very destructive indeed" — is destined to take place.
  • [00:12:55] The Gītā thus fits the Mahābhārata's recurring suggestion that its events were foreordained. The theistic setting deepens this fatalism: part of Kṛṣṇa's divine role is to ensure things unfold as they should; from his lofty vantage the future is already present — he knows the events "will, and indeed must, occur."
  • [00:13:18] This is perhaps the sense of Kṛṣṇa's saying that he is "time, grown old to destroy the world" — an alternative translation of the line Oppenheimer quoted. One might say Kṛṣṇa is not so much persuading Arjuna to fight as informing him that he is going to fight, so he may as well get on with it: "fettered by your own task which springs from your nature, you will inevitably do what you in your folly do not want to do."

docs.title: The Sāṃkhya strand: prakṛti and puruṣa
docs.text:
• [00:14:00] The religious teachings — divine plan, sacrifice — can make the Gītā seem "like an Upaniṣad inserted into the epic." But scholars detect another strand on which its pearls are strung: Sāṃkhya philosophy.
  • [00:14:16] Dating is uncertain — "educated guesses" place the Gītā's composition in stages between the 4th century BC and the 4th century AD — but it must predate the central Sāṃkhya text, Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya-kārikā, which itself predates its 6th-century Chinese translation.
  • [00:14:50] The most striking anticipation is the fundamental contrast between two principles, prakṛti and puruṣa — roughly nature and observer mind. Non-attached action can be restated in these terms: like the tortoise, the renouncer withdraws from prakṛti (nature) and focuses on his true self, his puruṣa (observer mind).
  • [00:15:22] The Gītā describes how the two interrelate: both are beginningless; prakṛti is a cause "as the agency and production of products," puruṣa a cause "in that he experiences happiness and unhappiness." The puruṣa is the purely observing self, unchanging despite its connection with body and, through body, with all of nature.
  • [00:15:52] So the Gītā can be seen responding to Buddhism by reasserting an enduring self — a notion already present in earlier Upaniṣads.

docs.title: Yoga: the discipline of the unattached self
docs.text:
• [00:16:05] But "all-seeing Kṛṣṇa" looks forward too. The later Sāṃkhya movement will intertwine with the tradition of yoga, and that intertwining is already in the Gītā (and elsewhere in the Mahābhārata). The Gītā frequently treats yoga as a path toward enlightenment, implying the would-be sage needs training and spiritual discipline, not just knowledge of the nature/self contrast.
  • [00:16:36] Yoga thus becomes another word for the path of unattached action, and the yogin is synonymous with Kṛṣṇa's true renouncer — superior to those who merely embrace asceticism and refuse to act. Through Sāṃkhya's insight Arjuna learns about his puruṣa / brahman, a true self transcending nature; through the practice of yoga he learns to see the world solely from that self's vantage. Since actions and consequences unfold in the realm of nature (prakṛti), they cannot touch him.

docs.title: Royal wisdom — and the abiding theme of violence
docs.text:
• [00:17:14] One final implication, not lost on original readers: though the Gītā's message is for everyone, Arjuna is a kṣatriya prince, and the text has a special message for elite readers. Kṛṣṇa calls his teaching a Rāja-Vidyā — "royal wisdom" or "knowledge of kings." The king is "uniquely appropriate" for imitating the divine king through his actions.
  • [00:17:57] Arjuna emerges as an ideal ruler who acts "because he ought to, and out of devotion to the highest lord, rather than in pursuit of his own advantage." One can imagine the real-life king Aśoka nodding in approval.
  • [00:18:13] The epic supplies a negative example: the Kaurava leader Duryodhana, whose most heinous sin is putting himself and his own interests above all else "rather than submitting to the divine rule of Kṛṣṇa."
  • [00:18:33] Few of us face Arjuna's (or Duryodhana's) exact situation, but "in a broader sense we all do." Warfare is a common human experience, and commoner still is the opportunity to do violence to humans and animals.
  • [00:18:52] Violence is an abiding theme of the Mahābhārata, which depicts both Arjuna's hesitation and the "horrendous devastation" of the battle. It may seem strange that Kṛṣṇa urges him on — but consider that Kṛṣṇa also endorses animal sacrifice: apparently "some blood must be spilled if the wheel of the world is to keep turning."
  • [00:19:14] Yet other ancient movements opposed such sacrifice — notably the Jainas, who sought to avoid all violence, intentional or unintentional. This commitment to non-violence is a legacy carried from antiquity to modern times, in India (Gandhi) and across the world; many non-Indian vegetarians take inspiration — "and recipes" — from Indian culture. Next time, Adamson signs off, "we give peace a chance."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Bhagavad-Gītā ("Song of the Lord") — the Mahābhārata section of Kṛṣṇa's counsel to Arjuna; a many-authored text reading Arjuna's dilemma through several philosophical and religious lenses.
  • Arjuna — greatest Pāṇḍava warrior, kṣatriya prince and son of Indra; halts the epic in doubt over killing his kinsmen.
  • Kṛṣṇa — Arjuna's charioteer, incarnation of the supreme creator-god; speaks the Gītā as a "chorus" of many viewpoints.
  • dharma (kṣatriya- vs. kula-dharma) — duty/law; Arjuna's conflict is between the warrior's law and the law of kinship.
  • svadharma — one's own uniquely appropriate duty; better done badly than another's done well.
  • renouncer / renunciation — the one who gives up not action (impossible) but the fruits of action; distinguished from "mere relinquishment."
  • unattached action — the Gītā's central doctrine: act without craving the results; restated via prakṛti/puruṣa and as yoga.
  • tortoise image — the renouncer withdrawing his senses as a tortoise draws in its limbs.
  • devotion (bhakti) / "all strung on me" — devotional theism making one highest god the object of worship and the motive for action.
  • sacrifice — approved as the paradigmatic action done "with minds set on God," even as the Gītā rejects the Brahmins' "cash cow" ritual bargain.
  • Rāja-Vidyā — "royal wisdom / knowledge of kings"; the Gītā's special message to elite rulers who imitate the divine king.
  • prakṛti / puruṣa — Sāṃkhya's "nature" and "observer mind"; the renouncer withdraws from prakṛti into his unchanging puruṣa (true self).
  • Sāṃkhya / Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya-kārikā — the nature/self philosophy anticipated by the Gītā; its central text (pre-6th c.), covered in a future episode.
  • yoga / yogin — spiritual discipline equated with the path of unattached action; the yogin is the true renouncer.
  • fatalism / "I am time" — the foreordained war and Kṛṣṇa's knowledge of the necessary future ("time, grown old to destroy the world").
  • Jainas / non-violence — opponents of sacrifice who sought to avoid all violence; antiquity's legacy of ahiṃsā down to Gandhi.
