docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 15 — "Mostly Harmless: Non-Violence"
docs.text:
← Ep 14

Ep 16 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:23:49 In brief: Indian non-violence (ahiṃsā) is broader and stranger than vegetarianism — a doctrine that may have grown out of Vedic ritual anxiety rather than ethical critique, that reaches its extreme in Jainism's reverence for all life, and that, across Buddhists, Jainas and Hindus, comes to hinge on the intention behind an act rather than the act itself. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Jonardin Gennary"; ahiṃsā ≈ "Ahimsa"; hiṃsā ≈ "Hymsa"; Mahāvīra ≈ "Mahavira"; kaṣāya ≈ "Kashaya"; kevalin ≈ "Kevalin"; sallekhanā ≈ "Salikana"; Padmanabh Jaini ≈ "Padmanab Jaini"; Yaśodhara ≈ "Yashodara"; Devadatta ≈ "Devadata"; Śvetāmbara ≈ "Shvetambara"; Digambara ≈ "digambara"; Mauryan ≈ "Morian"; Aśoka ≈ "Ashoka").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Ahiṃsā — "non-violence" or "non-injury"; the episode's central concept, broader than vegetarianism [00:03:01].
  • Mahāvīra and the ford-makers — last of the 24 tīrthaṅkaras ("ford-makers"); Jainism is named for his honorific Jina ("conqueror") [00:07:30].
  • The Laws of Manu — Hindu text that both laments meat-eating and licenses ritual killing as non-violence [00:03:54, 00:19:40].
  • The Mahābhārata / Bhagavad-Gītā — Hindu epic that contains exhortations to non-violence yet stages a dialogue urging Arjuna into war [00:04:00].
  • Padmanabh Jaini — modern scholar of Jainism quoted on food as the root cause of all hiṃsā [00:11:46].

docs.title: Philosophy is inevitable — and the steak on your plate
docs.text:
• [00:00:40] Of all the university disciplines, philosophy is the hardest to avoid in real life. You can skip literature, dodge physics and geology, even (if you play your cards right) get away without much maths — "though not if you actually play cards." Philosophy, by contrast, is inevitable: we all wrestle with philosophical problems whether or not we call them that, and never more so than with ethical dilemmas.
  • [00:01:13] The most obvious example: is it morally defensible to eat animals? Rich or poor, anyone can live as a vegetarian, so the choice faces everyone. If you eat meat it's either because you think there's nothing wrong with it, or because its wrongness "doesn't weigh heavily enough" to keep you from a juicy steak now and again.
  • [00:01:41] Yet despite being a textbook case of everyday philosophy, the ethics of killing animals only recently became much-debated by philosophers. Today there are figures like the utilitarian Peter Singer, famous for arguing for vegetarianism. This contrasts sharply with European antiquity and the Middle Ages: apart from a few exceptions — notably the late ancient thinkers Plutarch and Porphyry — philosophers there rarely argued at length about meat at all.
  • [00:02:15] In ancient India it was utterly different. Non-violence was one of the key themes of religious and philosophical culture. Buddhists, and especially Jainas, defined themselves by their reluctance or refusal to eat meat. Animal sacrifice was central to the Vedic culture they criticized — yet even texts growing out of that culture often urge us to avoid harming animals. And this is no museum piece: one of the most famous features of Indian society today is widespread vegetarianism. So the topic, Adamson notes, gives us "something to sink our teeth into."

docs.title: The real topic is ahiṃsā, not vegetarianism
docs.text:
• [00:02:55] First clarification: the subject is not vegetarianism as such, but what the traditions call ahiṃsā — "non-violence" or "non-injury."
  • [00:03:10] Avoiding violence may seem to imply vegetarianism, but some Vedic texts denied this, claiming the sacrifice of animals could be consistent with ahiṃsā. Conversely, those who did think non-violence required a vegetarian diet never thought it meant only that. Ahiṃsā obviously also covers avoiding violence toward humans — and, as the Jainas hold, one can even inflict hiṃsā on plants, or commit violence by lighting a fire or drinking water straight from a well.
  • [00:03:43] The breadth of ahiṃsā's implications is matched by the breadth of its acceptance. It is most prominent in the dissident traditions of Buddhism and Jainism, but exhortations against violence also appear in Hindu texts like the Laws of Manu and even the Mahābhārata — despite the fact that its most famous section, the Bhagavad-Gītā, is a dialogue urging participation in war.

docs.title: Where did ahiṃsā come from? Ritual anxiety, not first a critique
docs.text:
• [00:04:11] Strikingly, ahiṃsā has more often been studied by historians of religion than of philosophy. It's controversial how and why ancient Indians began thinking in these terms, but scholars usually trace it to religious practice: its origins may lie in the fear that ritualized violence could bring retribution.
  • [00:04:37] That fear could have produced taboos and devices designed to deflect blame from the sacrificer — reciting a formula to secure expiation for slaying an animal, or laying a blade of dry grass between the axe and a tree being felled for a sacrificial post. (Note the second case: it's a plant, not an animal, treated as the potentially injured party.)
  • [00:05:06] The upshot for the history of the idea: ahiṃsā did not first emerge as Buddhists and Jainas accusing the priests of violence from the outside. Those external accusations were preceded by an anxiety or embarrassment about sacrificial violence from within the Vedic tradition itself.

docs.title: Is non-violence moral, or merely self-interested?
docs.text:
• [00:05:27] A related controversy bears on whether ahiṃsā is even philosophically interesting: was non-violence pursued for moral reasons, or only religious ones? If the worry is purely about avoiding retribution, then the sacrificer is anxious about himself, not the interests of the animal he kills. The Laws of Manu sounds this self-interested note "with what sounds like a tone of wistful regret": we can't eat meat without injuring the living, and that injury blocks a blessed afterlife — so we must do without meat.
  • [00:06:01] But a fear of vengeance already implies that the animal (or plant) has interests of its own — the very interests the sacrificer risks violating. And ahiṃsā wasn't justified only by self-interest. One Buddhist work offers a reflection "strikingly reminiscent of the biblical golden rule": since I want to live, I would find it disagreeable for someone to take my life; another, too, wants to live and would find it disagreeable for me to take his; what is unpleasant to me is unpleasant to him — so how could I inflict on another what I find unpleasant myself? Similar ideas appear in Hindu texts, including the Mahābhārata.

docs.title: Jainism, the religion of non-violence
docs.text:
• [00:06:55] More than Buddhism or Hinduism, it was Jainism that was marked by an "unswerving devotion" to ahiṃsā — it has been called a religion of non-violence. If you know one thing about Jaina practice, it's probably the extreme measures: monks wearing masks to avoid inhaling insects and gently sweeping the ground before them as they walk, lest they tread on unseen life.
  • [00:07:30] Jainism takes its name from the honorific Jina ("conqueror"), bestowed on Mahāvīra, a contemporary of the Buddha. He is often called the founder of Jainism, but — by the Jainas' own belief — that's wrong: he was the last of 24 "ford-makers," whose title refers to providing a ford, a way out, of the unending flow of reincarnation. The Jainas regard Mahāvīra and his predecessors as divine saviours, all teaching the same lesson about escaping the cycle of rebirth.
  • [00:08:08] As seen in episode six, the Jainas held that escape comes only through the total elimination of karma. Even good karma ties you to rebirth (though it at least secures a more favourable one). This presupposes a dualist view of the person: the soul is an immaterial entity that enters into relation with the physical world and a series of individual bodies.

docs.title: Karma as a sticky substance — and what makes it stick
docs.text:
• [00:08:43] Karma itself is described as if it were a physical substance, like dust that clings to the soul more easily when we give in to passion or bad intention. The Jaina texts capture this nicely by calling passion kaṣāya, which literally means glue or resin.
  • [00:09:02] And it isn't only barbecue ribs that make you sticky: consuming any meat builds bad karma, since it inevitably involves the death of a being that desires to live.
  • [00:09:15] But Jaina asceticism is "more than observing ahiṃsā, and observing ahiṃsā is more than abstaining from meat." Jainism is the most ascetic of the world's organized religions, perhaps in all history. Renouncers and laity alike look to the ford-makers, and especially Mahāvīra, whose self-restraint "reached superhuman levels" — he and the others are said to have gone weeks, even a year, without eating anything at all.
  • [00:09:49] Through extreme practice the ascetic can shed all karma and become a kevalin — "someone who is alone," i.e. without the accretion of karma. The notorious practice of sallekhanā, in which a renouncer adopts total immobility until death by thirst, exposure and hunger, has been criticized as religiously inspired suicide. The Jainas insist those who take this path do not desire death (legend includes Chandragupta, founder of the Mauryan dynasty and grandfather of Aśoka); rather, they are avoiding the acquisition of new karma that might doom them to another rebirth.

docs.title: The elephant and the rabbit
docs.text: • [00:10:39] For ahiṃsā, vegetarianism is only the beginning. A "delightful story" brings home what's expected of the perfectly non-violent renouncer. A forest fire breaks out, and all the animals crowd around a lake to escape, packed shoulder to shoulder. An elephant lifts its foot briefly — and a rabbit darts into the spot beneath it. Rather than crush the rabbit, the elephant holds its foot aloft for three days, before finally collapsing and dying of fatigue. The happy ending: the elephant is reborn as a human and later reincarnated as an associate of Mahāvīra himself.

docs.title: "You don't have a leg to stand on" — and the lay community's help
docs.text:
• [00:11:25] You might object that, in pursuing absolute non-violence, the Jainas "likewise don't have a leg to stand on": you cannot get through life without harming a living thing, because we need to eat, and plants are alive too. As the aptly named scholar Padmanabh Jaini put it, the desire for food is the prime cause of all hiṃsā, since food cannot be consumed without destroying another life form.
  • [00:11:57] Far from denying this, the Jainas avoid many fruits and vegetables they believe to be aggregates of large numbers of life forms, and even restrict water, which a Jaina ascetic should drink only when strained or boiled to remove tiny organisms.
  • [00:12:21] But even so, avoiding all violence is impossible for the renouncer without assistance — and help is at hand in the Jaina layperson. As in Buddhism, the monastic life is supported by lay followers who live by less rigorous precepts. A renouncer forbidden to handle fire (which would kill creatures caught in the flames) instead takes water already boiled by a layperson; monks likewise subsist on alms of donated food.

docs.title: The rich-uncle robbery — and why leftovers are the answer
docs.text:
• [00:13:21] Is this a coherent way to handle the dilemma? Consider an analogy: I need money fast, and the only way is to rob my rich uncle — but my moral scruples forbid it. So I get my less fastidious friend to rob the house and split the cash. I didn't commit the robbery, but surely I'm morally culpable. By the same logic, the Jaina renouncer would seem to shoulder the hiṃsā committed in preparing his food, even if he didn't do the preparing.
  • [00:13:57] But there's more to the story. The renouncer may only take food and drink prepared without him in mind, and he verifies this before accepting it: he should live on leftovers, things that just happened to be available. Back to the analogy: this is more like accepting a charitable donation from a thief after confirming the money was not stolen for your sake.

docs.title: Intention is the heart of it — the innocent bystander
docs.text:
• [00:14:32] A critic still won't be satisfied: doesn't knowingly benefiting from a dubious act make your situation dubious? The deeper Jaina response invokes the centrality of intention. It is passion, desire, or intention that makes karma stick. By avoiding violence himself and eating only food not intended for him, the renouncer neither intends violence nor benefits from an intention to do violence on his behalf — he is "quite literally an innocent bystander."
  • [00:15:11] The same goes for unintentionally stepping on an insect or plant: the renouncer's conscience stays clean so long as he took every precaution. Hence the further precautions — not travelling in the rainy season, when more life is underfoot, and not eating after dark, since before electricity eating after sundown risked swallowing a bug. ("Maybe no one should eat after dark.")

docs.title: King Yaśodhara and the flour rooster
docs.text:
• [00:15:53] Intention's importance is dramatized by the story of King Yaśodhara. He has shed blood in war, but since death was never his goal he remains pure. Then, for complicated reasons, he resolves to perform an animal sacrifice — and, to avoid killing anything real, has a fake rooster made out of flour (a practice attested in other texts too). No real rooster dies, yet "the Jaina storyteller cries foul": Yaśodhara is elaborately punished in the afterlife, simply because his intention was violent.
  • [00:16:37] Notice, too, that the tale implies a Jaina king could pursue military aims; Jaina laypersons have frequently served as soldiers. It's even been proposed that the heroic ethic of Jaina asceticism was seen as continuous with the warrior heroism of the great Hindu epics. Still, only laypersons fight — the way of the renouncer would be to die rather than do violence.

docs.title: Against utilitarianism: an individualist goal
docs.text:
• [00:17:08] How does this stack up against modern views? There's an easy contrast with utilitarianism, which tries to minimize total harm and suffering, animals included. Jainas do try to persuade others toward non-violence, but their ancient approach to ahiṃsā aims at a different, more individualist goal: not simply reducing the overall amount of violence (though that follows too), but not being personally implicated in any act of violence.
  • [00:17:53] There's an irony here. The Jaina renouncer is sometimes accused of inflicting violence on himself, his asceticism is so severe — yet from a utilitarian standpoint he can look as though he's concentrating only on his own self-interest. That's why he needn't worry that his lifestyle depends on some hiṃsā committed by the laity: like other ancient ethical traditions in and beyond India, Jainism was about shaping and perfecting the self. The renouncer leaves the world better than he found it, but the main thing is to leave it and not come back — purifying the soul into a karma-free kevalin.

docs.title: The Buddhist challenge: the middle way
docs.text:
• [00:18:36] Jaina teaching was challenged by rivals of its own time. The Buddhists complained Jaina asceticism was excessive. The Buddha himself began his quest with Mahāvīra-like discipline and self-denial, including a starvation diet — but came to adopt a middle way between the extreme ascetic and the comfortable householder.
  • [00:19:00] He even parted ways with a follower, Devadatta, who wanted the community to adopt more rigorous rules, including strict vegetarianism. Instead, Buddhist writings suggest meat might be allowed for the monk on the same basis Jainas used for their vegetarian diet: it is permissible provided the meat was not prepared with the monk in mind. This rule may even have been absorbed into Buddhism from Jaina practice.

docs.title: Hindu intention: how sacrifice becomes non-violence
docs.text:
• [00:19:34] Hindu authors could exploit the same idea of intention to legitimate "that most un-Jaina of practices," the animal sacrifice. The Laws of Manu say slaying animals in a ritual context is in fact ahiṃsā and doesn't count as real killing. As the Bhagavad-Gītā suggests, sacrifice is needed to hold the world together.
  • [00:19:53] This was likewise the basis on which Arjuna was urged into battle: so long as the fight is undertaken with Kṛṣṇa in mind and not from the intention of achieving any result for himself. The upshot is a shared philosophical rationale for ahiṃsā across these traditions, despite huge variation in which practices counted as consistent with it.

docs.title: Agreement buried under insult
docs.text:
• [00:20:13] Given the competition between rival groups, disagreement got more emphasis than agreement. For centuries Hindus would sneer at the "squalid lifestyle" of the dissident sects, Buddhists would snipe at Jainas for "absurdly excessive self-punishment," and Jainas would proudly claim to be the only ones who really take non-violence seriously.
  • [00:20:43] One Jaina text mocks the Buddhist willingness to eat animals that died of old age: this, the author remarks, is like seducing a widow after her husband has died — the underlying desire is the same as a man's who would slaughter an animal for meat, or murder a husband to steal his wife.

docs.title: A split within Jainism: white-clad vs. sky-clad
docs.text:
• [00:21:03] Disputes over the demands of ahiṃsā and asceticism even erupted within the Jaina community. Early on it split into two branches: the Śvetāmbara ("white-clad") and the Digambara ("sky-clad") — referring respectively to the Śvetāmbara's white clothing and the nudity of the Digambaras, itself a form of rigorous asceticism.
  • [00:21:28] The Digambaras' stringent reading surfaced in debates about diet: they insisted a perfect kevalin like Mahāvīra — and any liberated renouncer — would no longer need to eat at all, freeing them even from indirect contact with hiṃsā. The Śvetāmbaras endorsed the more common-sense view that the need for food, unlike that for sex or comfort, is an inevitable, if regrettable, part of embodied life.

docs.title: Philosophy or religion? A blurry line
docs.text:
• [00:22:01] A recurring question about these traditions is whether they are really philosophical or religious. The case of non-violence shows the line is "at best a blurry one." Ahiṃsā may seem simple — it boils down to doing no harm — yet it has taken the form of both a religious taboo and an ethical precept, advanced by means ranging from doctrinaire assertion to subtle debate to crude insult.
  • [00:22:43] That mix is "going to stay with us" — especially the subtle debate, though also the occasional crude insult. Nothing typifies the next period, the Age of the Sūtra, so much as disagreement and debate, between and within schools: traditions will split (as the Jainas did), the disputatious climate will spur new reflection on argumentative method, and some groups — the Jainas included — will be led to ask whether any viewpoint is really better off than its rivals.
  • [00:23:20] But before the sūtras, the next episode turns to a less-celebrated feature of ancient Indian thought: the participation of women in philosophy — already glimpsed in the women who appeared as interlocutors in the Upaniṣads. "And by the way, no animals were harmed in the making of this podcast."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• ahiṃsā — "non-violence" / "non-injury"; broader than vegetarianism, covering humans, animals, plants, even harm via fire or unstrained water.
  • hiṃsā — violence / injury; the harm ahiṃsā seeks to avoid.
  • kaṣāya — "glue" or "resin"; the Jaina word for passion, which makes karma (likened to dust) stick to the soul.
  • kevalin — "one who is alone"; a soul that has shed all karma and attained liberation.
  • sallekhanā — the Jaina practice of fasting/immobility unto death; defended as avoiding new karma, not as suicide; legendarily including Chandragupta.
  • ford-makers (tīrthaṅkaras) — the 24 Jaina saviours who provide a "ford" out of reincarnation; Mahāvīra was the last, hence the honorific Jina ("conqueror") that names Jainism.
  • Mahāvīra — contemporary of the Buddha; exemplar of superhuman self-restraint and devotion to ahiṃsā.
  • Laws of Manu — Hindu text that laments meat-eating yet rules that ritual animal sacrifice counts as ahiṃsā, not real killing.
  • Mahābhārata / Bhagavad-Gītā — Hindu epic containing both non-violence teaching and the dialogue urging Arjuna into battle with Kṛṣṇa in mind, not self-interest.
  • Padmanabh Jaini — scholar of Jainism: "the desire for food is the prime cause for all forms of hiṃsā."
  • Yaśodhara — king punished in the afterlife for sacrificing a flour rooster, because his intention was violent — illustrating intention's centrality.
  • Devadatta — Buddhist follower who wanted stricter rules (incl. vegetarianism); the Buddha instead chose the middle way and a "not-prepared-for-me" meat allowance.
  • Śvetāmbara / Digambara — the "white-clad" and "sky-clad" (nude) branches of Jainism; split partly over whether a liberated kevalin still needs to eat.
  • Peter Singer / Plutarch / Porphyry — modern utilitarian (pro-vegetarian) and the rare ancient European thinkers who argued about meat — a foil for India's early, central engagement with the question.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 16 — "Better Half: Women in Ancient India"
docs.text:
← Ep 15

Ep 17 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:21:09 In brief: Ancient Indian texts were written mostly by men for men, and from misogynist law-codes to gendered notions of the self they treat women as inferior — yet renunciation was open to women, and a handful of remarkable female sages (Gārgī, Maitreyī, Sulabhā) hold their own with men in philosophical debate, even as their voices remain "filtered through the agency of men." Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannery"; Arthaśāstra ≈ "Atashastra"; Kauṭilya ≈ "Cautilia"; mokṣa ≈ "moxha"; Yājñavalkya ≈ "Yajnavakya/Yadnyavakia/Yajnyadha"; Gārgī Vācaknavī ≈ "Gargi Vachaknavi"; Maitreyī ≈ "Maitreye/Maitreji"; Sulabhā ≈ "Sulaba/Sulabah"; Janaka ≈ "Janika/Janica"; Bhīṣma ≈ "Bishma"; Yudhiṣṭhira ≈ "Yudistira"; Draupadī ≈ "Daraupadi"; Therīgāthā ≈ "Terigata/Tarigata"; Theragāthā ≈ "Teragata"; Śvetāmbara ≈ "Shetambara"; Prajāpati ≈ "Prajabati"; Sāṃkhya ≈ "Samkhya").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The Laws of Manu — Brahminical law-code; quoted both for stark misogyny and (later) for passages leaning the other way [00:01:06].
  • The Arthaśāstra of Kauṭilya — the political treatise, whose third book regulates marriage, divorce, and sexual offences [00:02:50].
  • The Therīgāthā / Theragāthā — paired anthologies in the Buddhist Pāli canon, of poems by nuns and by monks respectively [00:09:09].
  • Gārgī Vācaknavī & Maitreyī — female interlocutors of the sage Yājñavalkya in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka ("Great Forest") Upaniṣad [00:11:16].
  • Sulabhā — wandering female ascetic of the Mahābhārata who out-argues King Janaka; "the most astonishing example of a female philosopher in antique India" [00:14:55].

docs.title: Half the population, "not the better half"
docs.text:
• [00:00:36] A few episodes back we imagined ourselves in ancient India and weighed the social roles on offer — Brahmin, warrior, monk, farmer. But there was a roughly 50% chance you'd have been a woman. As in other pre-modern literary traditions, Indian writings were composed mostly by men and for men; from the authors' point of view, the half of the population that was female was "not the better half."
  • [00:01:06] A classic statement of misogyny is in the Laws of Manu: "A wife should do nothing independently even in her own house. Though her husband be uncouth and prone to pleasure, though he has no good points at all, the virtuous wife should ever worship her lord as a god."
  • [00:01:24] Many other texts in the series so far share the attitude. Discussions of reincarnation took for granted that it is worse to be reborn a woman than a man; political treatises excluded women from leading the state; and philosophical wisdom was usually a male privilege. It was men who taught other men to win liberation through renunciation, knowledge, and self-discipline — even when the men in question were gods like Indra or Kṛṣṇa.
  • [00:01:54] And yet the life of renunciation was open to women too. There were nuns in both the Buddhist and Jaina communities — though, as we'll see, this was controversial, and nuns never held the status of monks. Occasionally both Hindu and dissident literature concedes that women can reach mokṣa, liberation.
  • [00:02:19] More remarkable still are the female thinkers and sages who appear in the Upaniṣads and the Mahābhārata, depicted holding their own with men — even defeating them in argument. Still, these texts rarely if ever challenge the assumption that women are generally inferior. The verdict: the female thinkers of Indian literature are "not separate, but neither are they equal."

docs.title: The Arthaśāstra: women under the ideal king
docs.text:
• [00:02:50] To gauge the general status of women, turn again to the Arthaśāstra of Kauṭilya, the political treatise that reveals so much about the society the ideal king would rule. Its third book has much to say about women — and it "makes for rather grim reading."
  • [00:03:09] It lays out rules on the beating of wives, fines for women who flirt, and a scale of punishment for rapists — with those who rape slaves treated more leniently than those who assault free women. Kauṭilya even recognizes a kind of marriage that is effectively just abduction (though, "on the bright side," in that case the wife's property is not transferred to the new husband).
  • [00:03:31] Divorce is mostly the husband's to initiate, though a wife can sometimes leave — e.g. if he goes abroad for a prolonged period. In general the text's interest in women is confined to regulating sexual activity and the transfer of property within families.

docs.title: A full half of oneself: the wife in Vedic ritual
docs.text:
• [00:03:54] What of the religious side of Brahminical culture? An important role was reserved for the wife of a sacrificer. Only men could sacrifice, but the ritual was effective only if the wife was present. One text: "A full half of oneself is one's wife. As long as one does not obtain a wife, one can never be reborn, for he then remains incomplete."
  • [00:04:19] Even so, the wife is not the husband's better half — her role is above all to enable the husband to achieve his sacrificial purposes. When women appear in ritual symbolism, it is usually as comparisons between ritual objects and her sexual organs. Sex itself carries ritual overtones: the Upaniṣads say a man can use knowledge to acquire the merits of a woman through intercourse. Women can acquire men's merit too — "but without the part about knowledge."
  • [00:04:54] The virtue of women is all-important — not because we should care about women being virtuous, but because a wife's virtue brings karmic benefit to her husband.

docs.title: Reproducing oneself: marriage, sons, and the gendered self
docs.text:
• [00:05:04] Along the same lines, the Upaniṣads present marriage's chief purpose as providing a man with children — or rather with sons. Through the wife the husband "literally reproduces himself," so that seeing his son is like seeing his own face in a mirror: "the father is the same as the son, and the son is the same as the father."
  • [00:05:30] This finds its ultimate expression in the so-called right of transfer — a ritual in which a man and his son lie one atop the other to pass on karma and vital functions across the generations.
  • [00:05:43] The Vedic tradition even seems to assume that the ātman, the self belonging to each of us, has a gender — "and you'll never guess which one." The self is associated with male gods like Puruṣa and Prajāpati; we hear of the ātman producing a female body from his own and then immediately having intercourse with her.
  • [00:06:04] The Upaniṣads do recognize that women — and animals, perhaps even plants — have an inner self. So the message seems to be that at the core "we are all men," even those "unfortunate enough" to be living a current life in a female body.

docs.title: Why asceticism was so radical
docs.text:
• [00:06:21] Here, incidentally, is one reason asceticism was such a radical development. Renouncing the householder life, as Buddhist and Jaina monks did, meant renouncing sex and procreation. Their vow of chastity was not merely self-discipline but a departure from deeply held ideas about transferring karma — and even the self — from parent to child.
  • [00:06:46] If chastity was a dramatic gesture for men, it was "downright shocking" when women renounced family life. A householding-class woman who became a nun was defying her dharma twice over, rejecting the duties of both class and gender.
  • [00:07:04] The warrior kṣatriya's task is to fight; the humble śūdra's is to serve his betters; likewise woman has a special dharma — to be a devoted wife and bear children. Monasticism offered an escape from these expectations. Much as ancient Christian women turned to asceticism to avoid the constrictions of family life, so Buddhist and Jaina nuns may have taken vows to live a life that was, in a sense, less cloistered and held out greater prospects of individual fulfilment.

docs.title: Jain disagreement: can a woman reach liberation?
docs.text:
• [00:07:38] Unsurprisingly this was seen as problematic even within the Buddhist and Jaina movements. The Digambara branch of Jainism includes nudity among its severe ascetic practices. Since it was thought women could not decently or safely follow the lead of their "sky-clad" brethren, they were effectively barred from the perfect renunciation that leads to liberation.
  • [00:08:04] The Śvetāmbara Jainas, by contrast, hold that women can achieve this goal. They have even claimed that one of the ford-makers — the line of ancient teachers up to Mahāvīra who taught the way to liberation — was a woman.

docs.title: The Buddha and his nuns
docs.text:
• [00:08:18] As for the Buddha, no stranger to radical ideas, even he reportedly struggled to accept that women should join his community of renouncers. Nuns were admitted to his Saṅgha only a few years after he began accepting men as monks, and when he relented — ordaining his own aunt — it was "with misgivings."
  • [00:08:40] He is quoted as saying a monastic community that includes women is like a field afflicted by mildew, and that with this change in the rules the lifespan of his teaching would be halved from 1,000 to 500 years. Once admitted, nuns were made subservient to the monks and required to submit to their authority.
  • [00:08:57] Even so this could seem preferable to staying home as a good wife. One Buddhist nun "rejoiced in her freedom from three things: mortar, pestle, and my crooked husband."

docs.title: The Therīgāthā: poems of the nuns
docs.text:
• [00:09:09] That quotation is from a work in the Buddhist Pāli canon devoted entirely to women — an anthology of poems called the Therīgāthā. Though its women have refused to live as men's consorts, the text is a companion to a second work about Buddhist monks, the Theragāthā; some passages appear in both, with small changes.
  • [00:09:34] For example, both include a story of a chaste hero who rebuffs a seduction. In the female version, a nun approached by a sexual predator tries to dissuade him by discoursing on the decaying nature of bodily things — describing her own body as a corpse and a "painted puppet." When that fails, she removes one of her eyes and hands it to him, which does the trick. (A note to Oedipus: better to tear out your eyes before getting into an unwise sexual relationship.)
  • [00:10:09] The passage is typical of the Therīgāthā, full of meditations on decay, illness, and death in aid of suppressing bodily desire — a theme even more prominent here than in the partner text for monks, perhaps suggesting the authors (who may themselves have been male) believed women more prone to the lure of bodily pleasure. Sexist assumptions notwithstanding, the Therīgāthā is remarkable for its assumption that women can indeed achieve liberation.

docs.title: Hindu literature: appalling attitudes, and the other direction
docs.text:
• [00:10:40] What about Hindu literature? The Upaniṣads and Laws of Manu can be mined for appalling attitudes — but that isn't the whole story. As so often, the Laws of Manu also contain passages leaning the other way, including one that allows women to pursue the life of a wandering ascetic.
  • [00:11:09] And the Upaniṣads give women a role not only in ritual but in philosophical debate. Back in episode four we met, in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka ("Great Forest") Upaniṣad, a female sage named Gārgī Vācaknavī, who goes "toe to toe" with the philosophical hero Yājñavalkya.
  • [00:11:29] Admittedly she is silenced: told she goes "too far" when she repeatedly asks what underlies each in a successive series of cosmic principles — "keep this up and your head will explode," Yājñavalkya warns. Still, Gārgī outdoes the other male Brahmins present: she acknowledges Yājñavalkya's pre-eminence when they do not, and — head-shattering threats aside — she is ready to question him a second time after his first answers leave her unsatisfied.

docs.title: Maitreyī: love of the self, and of a husband
docs.text:
• [00:11:57] Nor is that Yājñavalkya's only female interlocutor. Elsewhere in the Great Forest Upaniṣad he discusses the self with his wife Maitreyī. The scene begins with Maitreyī asking how she can attain immortality — note that she asks this for herself, not how to help her husband live forever.
  • [00:12:31] Given the context this might seem presumptuous, but Yājñavalkya is "far from affronted." He favours Maitreyī over his second wife precisely for her philosophical keenness, contrasted with the other wife's interest in "nothing but womanly matters." He even seems to see the spousal relation in unusually equal terms: it's no surprise to hear "it is out of love for oneself that one holds a wife dear" — but very surprising to also hear "it is out of love for oneself that one holds a husband dear."

docs.title: The Mahābhārata's powerful women: Draupadī
docs.text:
• [00:13:06] True to its claim to contain all things, the Mahābhārata features several powerful female characters. The most obvious is Draupadī, wife of all five Pāṇḍava brothers and thus a major figure. Like Arjuna and other male heroes, she receives portentous predictions at birth: she will lead the kṣatriyas to their doom — and she does, urging warlike behaviour and castigating her husband Yudhiṣṭhira for failing to follow the warrior dharma.
  • [00:13:43] She has good reason: she was staked in a game of dice and treated with great disrespect at the fateful gambling match that launches the family conflict.
  • [00:13:53] Draupadī also counters the notion that these texts were aimed solely at men. Within the epic's framing devices, she and other women often serve as the audience for stories and lessons, making claims to knowledge and figuring as potential learners.
  • [00:14:18] This fits a tradition about the whole Mahābhārata: that it was composed for women and śūdras — a "fifth Veda," a Veda for everyone, whereas the other Vedas are for the priestly and ruling classes. The idea sits awkwardly with the epic's obsessive interest in warrior dharma, but it echoes in the Bhagavad-Gītā, where Kṛṣṇa teaches that even women and śūdras can attain liberation through devotion to him.

docs.title: Sulabhā: the most astonishing female philosopher
docs.text:
• [00:14:55] Another section of the Mahābhārata offers "the most astonishing example of a female philosopher in antique India" — Sulabhā. Her story comes where Bhīṣma, on his deathbed, explains techniques of liberation to Yudhiṣṭhira. He tells of a king named Janaka, who claims to have achieved liberation while still carrying out his royal duties.
  • [00:15:19] Sulabhā, who won liberation the old-fashioned way — rejecting the householder life and wandering as a rootless ascetic — finds it hard to believe Janaka has really attained freedom while living as a king. So she does "the obvious thing": uses her yoga power to transform into a stunningly beautiful woman, teleport to his court, and implant her mind into his body, so the two can hold an internal dialogue within Janaka's soul.
  • [00:15:55] King Janaka speaks first, in "arrogant and disdainful" terms, boasting that he reached freedom without asceticism, through knowledge alone, which lets him resist all attachment — "for him it is the same whether someone anoints his right arm or cuts off his left." This ethic of unattached action is the very teaching Kṛṣṇa offers in the Bhagavad-Gītā, so we might expect his claims to be vindicated.
  • [00:16:20] But Janaka grows less appealing as he rails against Sulabhā — who is this upstart young woman who dares enter his royal presence, and his very body?

docs.title: A perfect speech that exposes the king
docs.text:
• [00:16:39] Now Sulabhā responds. She first instructs Janaka on the qualities of good speech and promises to exemplify them: her remarks will be pleasing, neither too long nor too short, adapted to her audience, and free of emotion. (A characteristic feature of ancient Indian writing: the form of speech is inextricably bound up with the truth it teaches.)
  • [00:17:03] Her perfect discourse then exposes the king's hypocrisy. Using ideas reminiscent of the Sāṃkhya tradition, she argues that the true self is more fundamental than, and underlies, all other features of a person. Janaka's very demand to know who she is — his interest in her gender and class — shows he does not understand this basic truth.
  • [00:17:26] Furthermore, the life of a king is incompatible with liberation: he must constantly cope with the demands of other political actors and follow the kṣatriya dharma, rather than devoting himself solely to spiritual concerns as Sulabhā has.

docs.title: Undoing gender: the genderless true self
docs.text:
• [00:17:46] The narrator praises Sulabhā for her appropriate and convincing words. She does better even than Gārgī: she bests her rival philosophically and successfully challenges ideas actually defended elsewhere in the Mahābhārata. Along the way she defies and undermines traditional ideas about gender — for, according to her, the true self is neither male nor female, but the underlying source of this and all other differences.
  • [00:18:15] And the very depiction of such a character is itself an affront to those traditional ideas. It was often believed women could not attain liberation — either through "fundamental inferiority," or because they could not undertake rigorous asceticism, being "too vulnerable without men to protect them." But Sulabhā wanders free: she has refused to act as a woman is expected to, and "knows exactly what she is not doing."

docs.title: Do these prove real female sages? Maybe the question is backwards
docs.text:
• [00:18:43] Do Sulabhā, and figures like Gārgī and Maitreyī, prove there really were female Hindu sages in antiquity? "It's hard to say." We've mostly been asking what the texts tell us about how women were seen, assuming they reflect historical reality. But "perhaps this is backwards" — we could instead ask what the inclusion of such women tells us about the texts.
  • [00:19:14] Notably, the strong female philosophers of the Great Forest Upaniṣad are both associated with the even stronger male philosopher, Yājñavalkya. His willingness to debate women on a roughly equal footing is "unusual, if not unique" — so the point may be to mark him as an innovative, idiosyncratic figure, rather than to insist women can do philosophy, much less to record that real female philosophers existed.
  • [00:19:41] It's also striking that figures like Gārgī and Sulabhā are presented in various ways as masculine: Gārgī refers to herself as a warrior (using a grammatically male-gendered word); Maitreyī is pointedly contrasted with Yājñavalkya's "more feminine" other wife; and Sulabhā delivers her speech from within the body of a man. Nothing could more powerfully symbolize "the fundamental fact" that when these ancient women — whether fictional or real — speak to us, their speech is always filtered through the agency of men.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:20:18] With this look at the role of women in the early texts, the hosts have "just about said everything we wanted to say" before moving on to the proliferation of philosophical schools that defines the Age of the Sūtra.
  • [00:20:36] But first — following Yājñavalkya's example of letting someone else have her say — and because one of the most striking features of texts like the Upaniṣads, the Gītā, and the Buddhist canon is the interweaving of philosophical and religious themes, the next episode is an interview with an expert on the religious themes of Indian philosophy, Jessica Frazier, bringing the Origins series to a close.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Laws of Manu — Brahminical law-code; quoted for stark misogyny ("the virtuous wife should ever worship her lord as a god") but also for passages allowing a woman to become a wandering ascetic.
  • Arthaśāstra (of Kauṭilya) — political treatise whose third book regulates wife-beating, divorce, property transfer, and rape; its interest in women is largely confined to sex and property.
  • ātman — the self; the Vedic tradition seems to assume it is male (associated with Puruṣa, Prajāpati), so that "at core we are all men."
  • right of transfer — ritual in which father and son lie one atop the other to pass on karma and vital functions across generations.
  • dharma (of women) — a woman's prescribed duty: to be a devoted wife and bear children; a nun defies the dharma of both class and gender.
  • mokṣa — liberation; debated as to whether women can attain it.
  • Digambara vs Śvetāmbara — Jain branches: the "sky-clad" Digambaras effectively bar women from perfect (naked) renunciation; the Śvetāmbaras hold women can reach liberation, even claiming a female ford-maker.
  • ford-makers — the line of ancient Jaina teachers, up to Mahāvīra, who taught the way to liberation.
  • Saṅgha — the Buddha's monastic community; he admitted nuns reluctantly ("a field afflicted by mildew"; the teaching's lifespan halved from 1,000 to 500 years), making them subservient to monks.
  • Therīgāthā / Theragāthā — paired Pāli-canon anthologies of poems by nuns / by monks; the nuns' poems dwell heavily on bodily decay and assume women can achieve liberation.
  • Gārgī Vācaknavī — female sage of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad who out-argues the male Brahmins and questions Yājñavalkya twice, until warned her "head will explode"; refers to herself as a warrior.
  • Maitreyī — Yājñavalkya's philosophically keen wife, who asks how she may attain immortality; in their dialogue he says one holds a husband dear out of love for oneself.
  • Yājñavalkya — the Upaniṣadic "philosophical hero" whose unusual willingness to debate women may mark him as an idiosyncratic individual rather than evidence of real female sages.
  • Draupadī — wife of the five Pāṇḍava brothers; given a portentous birth-prophecy, staked at the fateful dice game, urges warrior dharma on Yudhiṣṭhira.
  • Mahābhārata as "fifth Veda" — tradition that the epic was composed for women and śūdras — a Veda for everyone — echoed by the Gītā's claim that women and śūdras can reach liberation through devotion to Kṛṣṇa.
  • Sulabhā — wandering female ascetic who uses yoga power to enter King Janaka's body and, in a "perfect speech" drawing on Sāṃkhya, exposes his hypocrisy and argues the true self is neither male nor female.
  • Janaka — king who claims liberation through knowledge while still ruling; bested by Sulabhā, who shows the royal life is incompatible with liberation.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 17 — "Jessica Frazier on Hinduism and Philosophy"
docs.text:
← Ep 16

Ep 18 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Jessica Frazier 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Jessica Frazier · Runtime: 00:34:41 In brief: An interview on how the Hindu traditions do philosophy of religion: Brahman arises not as a worshipped person but as a fundamental ontology — the ground that lets being and non-being be at all — and the tradition's signature problem is not the problem of evil but how an unchanging divine can underlie a plural, changing world. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari / Janard and Gennary"; Nāsadīya Sūkta ≈ "Nasadiyya Sukta"; Chāndogya ≈ "Chandogio"; Māṇḍūkya ≈ "Mandukyu"; Kena ≈ "Cano"; Bhartṛhari ≈ "Bartraharie"; Rāmānuja ≈ "Ramana"; Raphson ≈ "Rafson"; panhylism ≈ "panhealism"; Brahmins ≈ "the Romans").

docs.title: The guest and the frame
docs.text:
• [00:00:17] Adamson introduces an interview "about Hinduism and philosophy" with Jessica Frazier, lecturer in religious studies at the University of Kent and a fellow at the Oxford Centre for Hindu Studies. The natural starting point: since Hinduism is a religion, what conception(s) of God or the divine show up in the classic texts?
  • [00:01:01] Adamson's opening gambit: the obvious move is Brahman (found in the Upaniṣads) — isn't Brahman just "basically like the god of the Abrahamic religions," one all-powerful force pervading everything? Is that a good way in?

docs.title: Brahman as fundamental ontology, not a person
docs.text:
• [00:01:33] Frazier resists the parallel. Brahman is a "really unusual and distinctive" route to the divine because it arises out of reasoning — out of early philosophy around 500 BCE trying to make sense of the world. Personal deities like Yahweh, and personalism generally, do appear in the earliest texts, but that's not where the distinctive concept of Brahman comes from. It comes from an attempt to form something like a fundamental ontology.
  • [00:02:16] Her key example: the Nāsadīya Sūkta, a creation hymn in the Ṛg Veda — a very old text. Where you'd expect it to call on a god for help, it instead says that at the beginning "there was being and there was non-being" (notice it names both) — and then asks: what framed that? Where was it located? What gave the place for both being and non-being?
  • [00:02:53] The hymn even says the gods must know — but the gods can't know, because they are merely beings; they cannot know what the framework for everything is. Frazier calls this a crucial philosophical moment: the search is not for a person who made stuff, not for any contingent particular being, but for "what is the frame for anything to exist or not exist at all."
  • [00:03:16] Adamson sharpens it: a metaphysical grounding of everything, even the things that don't exist. Frazier agrees — what is the very principle of the possibility of being? She adds a polemical aside: the 20th-century complaint that "the West forgets the question of being" doesn't apply to India, which kept hold of ontology precisely because it was central to its concept of God.
  • [00:03:53] This generates rich accounts of the divine and of reality. The Upaniṣads give perhaps the first philosophical treatment of divine attributes: eternity / eternal infinity, simplicity (God is undivided), sovereignty or soleness — advaita, "without a second" — and self-existence, svayambhū, self-existence or ipseity in the classical vocabulary.

docs.title: Turning the ontological argument on its head — and the puzzle of worship
docs.text:
• [00:04:28] Adamson presses a tension: the "ground of all being and non-being" sounds transcendent, but it's not clear it's something you'd worship. Yet Frazier just said it has the traits we associate with the Abrahamic God. Does that make it an object of religious worship as well as a ground of ontology, or is there pressure between the two?
  • [00:05:14] Frazier's answer: the Indian approach generates the concept of the divine out of what is most fundamental to reality — "turning the ontological argument on its head." Rather than starting with a God and asking what makes him godly, it asks: what are the godly attributes — self-existent, eternal, infinite, immutable? Whatever has those, that is what we'll call God.
  • [00:05:54] The twist: Hindus have not, historically, tended to worship Brahman. You don't offer it things; you don't talk to it — "you can't talk to being in that way." So the West's idea that worship is central to religion may need revising. For something more like "the God of the philosophers," the fountain of religious thought and experience is not worship but awe or reflection.

docs.title: Brahman and the many gods — the cosmological move
docs.text:
• [00:06:26] Adamson raises the obvious counter: most listeners picture Hinduism as all those images and statues of gods. How does the ground of all things relate to that polytheistic framework?
  • [00:07:00] India has both models: personal beings descending from early Vedic deity-worship (animism is rife in early India — spirits and deities everywhere) and the philosophical concept of an ultimate ground. They ultimately combine — just as "Aristotle and the Bible finally get together" to generate scholastic thought.
  • [00:07:31] So India does produce proofs of the existence of God (here a personal creator), but that's not the focus of the Vedāntic tradition. When a text praises Kṛṣṇa, Śiva, or Durgā, it typically jumps in to say this is the deity who is the source of all. The personal beings get aligned with the cosmological argument: look beyond the anthropomorphic face and you see the material and efficient cause of the universe — that from which everything comes.
  • [00:08:30] For any religious tradition to become a philosophical culture, "the divine idea has to become philosophized." In India the gods come to signify not only the source but the very material of the universe — the divine is literally a kind of stuff out of which everything is made, with very concrete passages on this in the Vedic literature.

docs.title: Pantheism, and the stuff of the world: clay vs. consciousness
docs.text:
• [00:08:55] Adamson: doesn't that make everything — him, the microphone, Frazier, the listener, the device — literally made of God? That sounds like pantheism: one divine entity pervading everything. Is that the right reading, or is it more metaphorical?
  • [00:09:28] Frazier: the West's idea of pantheism is "quite a crude and undeveloped idea." Going back to Raphson, who coined the word, pantheism (everything is God) was set against panhylism (everything is mere unconscious substance). The Indian tradition lives in the space between — asking whether there is something divine, something extraordinary, about the eternal stratum that is the basis of everything.
  • [00:10:14] Crucially, India doesn't stop at "it's all made of God" — it gives the idea incredible nuance. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad says the divine material is like clay. But the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad says the divine is the consciousness of which all perceptions are made — "an ocean of consciousness" taking different forms. And the Kena Upaniṣad arguably presents a process ontology: God is "that by which events happen," the constant impeller of phenomena.
  • [00:10:59] The payoff: the substratum of existence — the hyle, the theos, the thing it's made of — is not simply matter, not simply stuff, not substantialism. The West, Frazier argues, "got stuck on the idea of substance," which doesn't answer the subtler questions about the fabric of being.
  • [00:11:31] Adamson: if the stuff of everything is consciousness, then you're describing the universe as a single self-aware mind grasping itself — which changes what "pantheism" means. But how does that square with the clay idea? Is clay just a metaphor for consciousness?
  • [00:12:11] Frazier: there's a whole tradition asking what kinds of thing can be the material of something. The Chāndogya offers a "raw materialism" — clay is insensate, unconscious stuff that takes on different names and forms (nāma-rūpa); you shape matter into the bookshelf, the book, you, me. But the Upaniṣads also take a phenomenological turn, perhaps inspired by the early yoga tradition of people examining their own thought: is the material of the world really matter? Isn't it all perception, concept, experience? From that the answer flips — it's consciousness we're all made of — and a whole separate tradition of thinking about "formedness" follows.

docs.title: The Upaniṣads as a plurality — questions, not treatises
docs.text:
• [00:13:34] Adamson notes this illustrates a recurring point: even within the Upaniṣads, and certainly within Hinduism, you find a variety of views and stages of thought.
  • [00:13:48] Frazier's image: the Upaniṣads are "as if you got together all the pre-Socratic philosophers, took their writing, and turned it into one scripture" — mixing myth, cosmology, early science, even mathematics, and channeling it into multiple philosophical suggestions (written by different families of priests and intelligentsia), laid out for you to explore and combine.
  • [00:14:21] And the Upaniṣads — like most later Indian texts — proceed less by treatise than by question: not telling you what's the case but asking what might be, then opening the field to a range of answers. A "proliferating, open tradition that welcomes multiple possible solutions."

docs.title: Proofs of God: the design and cosmological arguments
docs.text:
• [00:14:47] Adamson: we do nonetheless find positive arguments in the Hindu tradition. To what extent do they map onto modern philosophy of religion — proofs of God's existence, the nature of God, the afterlife, miracles? Do real proofs of God's existence appear in the texts?
  • [00:15:23] A few schools do try to prove the divine, often a personal god: Nyāya (the school of logic) and Vaiśeṣika (the atomists), "going hand in hand" — e.g. the Nyāyamañjarī of Jayanta. Their argument resembles Descartes: look at everything the world is made of — what causes it to function together as a unity? Why is there coherence in the world? There must be a unity-maker, a designer. Just as Descartes says God makes mind and world align, they argue the divine gets atoms, concepts, universals, even the metaphysical categories to generate a coherent world together.
  • [00:16:30] But the cosmological argument is the more common case. Throughout the Upaniṣads and the later Vedāntic tradition, thinkers barely have to argue there's a god — they simply say that which is the source is the thing we're talking about.
  • [00:16:53] A deep contrast: the West is preoccupied with creedal assent (assent to a religious belief or a philosophical proposition). By saying "the thing that exists is the thing we mean," the Upaniṣadic tradition bypasses that problem altogether.

docs.title: The real Indian question: immutability vs. change
docs.text:
• [00:17:12] Frazier thinks a different set of questions interests India most. Where the West worries about omnipotence vs. omnibenevolence (the problem of evil), India is gripped by immutability vs. plurality: God is one unchanging identity, yet the world shows change and multiplicity — how can both hold? This is the debate that generates a whole spread of answers.
  • [00:17:42] The menu of solutions:
  • Schools holding God changes only in non-essential attributes — an aupādhika change; only the contingent elements change.
  • Schools holding God does intrinsically change, but the underlying material stays the same.
  • Most interesting, schools seeking forms of plural identity — kinds of oneness that are intrinsically plural, so there's no loss of integrity. Bhartṛhari points to meaning: one meaning can be made of complex, subtle internal elements (a dialectical account). Rāmānuja, a medieval philosopher, points to agency: to act is to actualize multiple possibilities, which is to change — yet because that just is what agency is, in changing you remain an agent. Identity that incorporates an internal transformational element.
  • [00:18:49] The shared aim: find something that allows plurality within unity.

docs.title: God as the ground of consciousness = the self
docs.text:
• [00:18:57] Adamson connects two threads: God as the ground of consciousness sounds exactly like the debates about the self — is the self one unchanging thing, a plurality, or even an illusion? Maybe it's the same debate in two vocabularies: if God is the ground of consciousness, then God may be the self — and indeed there's the idea that Brahman is the self (ātman).
  • [00:19:48] Frazier: there's a real correlation, with a subtle difference. You could drop the word "God" — it's such a Western, person-presupposing idea — whereas Brahman literally means the foundation, that which bears up, and must be the foundation of everything. In both cases you must "account for a continuity that underlies change and a coherence that underlies plurality."

docs.title: The Buddhist straw man
docs.text:
• [00:20:34] In both debates (self and divine), "the silent voice, the straw man, is always the Buddhists." Present throughout India, they make the ultimate critique: there is nothing substantial, foundational, or permanent — no essence. If you define the divine (or what has intrinsic value) as that which is permanent and essential, the Buddhists have denied there's anything of intrinsic value at all. So Buddhists — constantly reminding everyone that change appears to destroy identity — are the opponents Hindus must answer about both the self and the divine. They want to go far enough to explain plurality, "but not so far that it becomes just plurality."
  • [00:21:22] Frazier admits she once agonized — "are the Buddhists right or the Hindus right?" — but thinks the Hindus land a good point. The Buddhists say you must specify what stuff is made of, and answer that everything is made of dharmas: tiny points of existence with no duration and no spatial extension. She finds this incoherent — an extensionless, durationless point with no intrinsic existence doesn't explain what these existence-points are themselves made of.
  • [00:22:16] So she returns to the Nāsadīya Sūkta: we still have to account for that which allows both existence and non-existence to be — and, extending it, that which allows change, phenomena, even insubstantial phenomena in consciousness, even illusions and misperceptions, to have an ontological basis. India keeps reminding us to go beyond substantialism toward a bigger fundamental ontology: "the being which grounds beings," ontology rather than ontic concepts.

docs.title: Does scripture fence in philosophy?
docs.text:
• [00:23:06] Adamson plays devil's advocate: this is a religious tradition built on scripture. Doesn't that limit the arguments and positions available, since you can't contradict the Vedic texts — a "fence around the possibility of philosophy"?
  • [00:23:59] Frazier turns it around: that's a standard "we haven't been holding Western philosophy to." Most Western philosophy from the rise of Christianity into the 20th century was religious in some sense — Kant, Descartes, Hegel. And the Indian scriptures are already quite philosophical in character: "it's like taking Plato as your Bible," whereas the actual Bible is light on metaphysics. So Hindu thinkers work with material that is already reasoned.
  • [00:24:53] More than that, text is an enabler, not a restriction. India commits early to the Vedic Śruti and then expands the canon again and again — to epics like the Bhagavad-Gītā, to philosophical texts like the Brahma-Sūtra, to diverse later texts like the Purāṇas — so the range of what counts as scripture keeps growing, facilitating creativity.
  • [00:25:34] And interpretation is central to their reasoning. You don't, like Descartes, sit alone deriving first postulates; you work with suggestions already there. One of the pramāṇas (sources of good reason) is anumāna, inference — a well-developed account of using analogies and examples to build new models. Philosophizing through commentary means you constantly develop and even change the ideas you draw out. There's "plenty written on how someone uses a text that says one thing and cleverly makes it say the opposite" — so the text ends up serving reason.
  • [00:26:23] Adamson, who's also covering medieval European philosophy, agrees: scholastic philosophy offers plenty of examples of taking a text that seems to say one thing and making it say the other.

docs.title: Ritual vs. philosophy — a false dichotomy
docs.text:
• [00:26:34] Adamson raises ritual as distinctive of the Vedāntic world — ritual act, ritual speech, manipulated objects. Doesn't ritual give an alternative route to your goal, maybe making philosophy unnecessary — two paths to God rather than one?
  • [00:27:13] Frazier: in some traditions it works that way, but the two aren't necessarily aiming at the same goal. Ritual is method — the means to certain ends. In Hindu culture rituals do many things: transubstantiational rituals, interactive rituals contacting spirits or deities, and many that celebrate natural law (Vedic rituals meant to "concretize" the laws of nature and society that already exist). They're modes, means, tools.
  • [00:27:57] But reason never loses its place as the thing by which you explain the world — "ritual can't explain anything." The Upaniṣads repeatedly show the son coming to the father, the king to the Brahmin, the priest to the king, even a god to another god: explain it to me, be my teacher. Whatever your place in the hierarchy, you want to know the meaning and, crucially, the purpose. Ritual is the method but doesn't tell you the goal of the method.
  • [00:28:43] So it's a false dichotomy to set ritual ("lighting fires and burning stuff") against philosophy ("debates at court"): philosophy is partly there to help you understand what the ritual is for, and the ritual is there to carry out the philosophical insight.

docs.title: Seers, and reason's independent life
docs.text:
• [00:29:02] Adamson agrees, and Frazier deepens it: India's original intelligentsia were the Brahmins, the priests — not a sideline but their very nature. The authors of the scriptures, the ṛṣis, are seers: not prophets reporting what God said, but seers who see the nature of reality.
  • [00:29:33] So the dichotomy "religion gets you magical salvation, reason is some extraneous activity" is wrong. Frazier notes that Jonardon Ganeri has reminded us reason often functioned independently of religion and could even challenge it — India's sciences were rich and widely respected. Reason and philosophy have their own life, "but it was never necessarily in contrast to religion." And the project of religion isn't just "some juicy reward": it is metaphysical — understanding, not merely a happy end.

docs.title: The caste critique — and Sulabhā's lesson
docs.text:
• [00:30:11] Adamson presses a social critique: the Brahmins make unique claims to knowledge and power — the ability to get the gods to deliver health, wealth, political success. Isn't the whole system of ritual-and-philosophy built to explain why they should be a caste above the others, with even kings prostrating at their feet?
  • [00:30:59] Frazier grants much of it. Brahmins are an intelligentsia, and intelligentsias are often class-based; the hard part in India is that it's explicitly endogamous, by birth — what was an informal class division in Europe becomes a formal caste division. So the de facto truth of the West (the philosophical elite is always an elite) was de jure true in India.
  • [00:31:38] But she argues that can only last so long. Her example: the Mahābhārata, a huge epic that gives voice to marginal characters — women, lower-caste figures — who suddenly speak out in philosophical language, calling everyone to witness the quality of their reasoning and defending themselves against higher castes.
  • [00:32:13] The story of Sulabhā: an independent woman yogi, a renouncer/ascetic. A king thinks it unreasonable that a woman should wander alone seeking knowledge. Having both philosophical and supernatural powers, she possesses him — enters his mind — and from within delivers a lecture whose key point is: look how reasonable I am, look at my well-grounded premises and the systematic formulation of my arguments; my rationality grounds me as your equal. Having shamed him and shown herself his equal "at the rational level," she finds his mind "terribly empty," declines to stay, and leaves.
  • [00:33:35] The moral Frazier draws: reason overcomes inequality. What reason does when it persuades is enter your mind and show you, from within, that something is true — so you are changed, made into someone who must respect the mind of the other. What began as something elite (philosophical practice) becomes the underpinning by which people throughout Indian history assert equality in the face of inequality.
  • [00:34:04] Adamson: "a beautiful example" of how philosophy and reason create a level playing field across religions, classes, and genders.

docs.title: Closing
docs.text: • [00:34:20] Adamson thanks Jessica Frazier, and previews the next big section of the series — the Age of the Sūtras — to be taken up again with Jonardon Ganeri.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Brahman — the foundation, "that which bears up"; reached through reasoning as the ground of being (and non-being), not a worshipped person; close to the self (ātman). Classical attributes: eternity, infinity, simplicity, advaita ("without a second"), svayambhū (self-existence).
  • Nāsadīya Sūkta — creation hymn in the Ṛg Veda; asks what frames both being and non-being — the gods can't know, being mere beings; Frazier's paradigm of fundamental ontology.
  • Upaniṣads — first philosophical treatments of the divine and reality; "like the pre-Socratics turned into one scripture"; proceed by question, not treatise. The Chāndogya makes the divine material clay (shaped into nāma-rūpa, name-and-form); the Māṇḍūkya makes it consciousness ("an ocean of consciousness"); the Kena gives a process ontology (God as "that by which events happen").
  • Nyāya & Vaiśeṣika — the logic school and the atomist school; offer a Descartes-like design argument for a personal god as the "unity-maker" of a coherent world (e.g. Jayanta's Nyāyamañjarī).
  • cosmological argument — the more common Indian proof: "that which is the source is the thing we're talking about," bypassing creedal assent.
  • aupādhika — change in non-essential / contingent attributes only; one proposed solution to immutability-vs-change.
  • Bhartṛhari — locates plural-in-one identity in meaning (one meaning made of subtle internal elements); a dialectical account.
  • Rāmānuja — medieval philosopher; locates plural-in-one identity in agency (to act is to change, yet remain an agent).
  • dharmas (Buddhist) — tiny points of existence with no duration or spatial extension; the Buddhist anti-substantialist answer Frazier finds incoherent — the straw man behind both the self and the divine debates.
  • Śruti — the Vedic canon Hinduism commits to, then expands (to the Bhagavad-Gītā, Brahma-Sūtra, Purāṇas) — text as enabler, not fence.
  • pramāṇa / anumāna — sources of valid knowledge / inference; the well-developed Indian art of reasoning by analogy and example, often via commentary.
  • ṛṣis — the "seers" who authored the scriptures; not prophets reporting God's words but seers of the nature of reality.
  • Mahābhārata / Sulabhā — epic giving philosophical voice to marginal figures; Sulabhā is the woman yogi who possesses a dismissive king and proves, from within his mind, her rational equality — Frazier's emblem of reason overcoming inequality.
