docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 18 — "A Tangled Web: The Age of the Sūtra"
docs.text:
← Ep 17

Ep 19 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:23:54 In brief: A road-map episode for the next stretch of the series. Adamson rejects the tidy "orthodox vs. heterodox / six Hindu systems vs. Buddhists & Jains" scheme and proposes a more neutral organising principle: the age of the sūtra — centuries when philosophy crystallised around terse, thread-like aphorisms (sūtra) that demanded commentaries (bhāṣya) to unpack them. It closes with a whistle-stop tour of all six systems. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennary"; sūtra ≈ "sutra"; bhāṣya ≈ "basya/Batya"; Nyāya ≈ "Naya/Niyaya"; Vaiśeṣika ≈ "Vaishaika/Vichesha/Vysheysheishika"; Mīmāṃsā ≈ "Mimansa/Mimamsa"; tantra ≈ "warp/tantra"; Vātsyāyana ≈ "Butz Yayana"; Pāṇini ≈ "ponenie/Panani"; Patañjali ≈ "Patanjali"; Pāyāsi ≈ "Paiasi"; Bṛhaspati ≈ "Prihaspati"; Cārvāka ≈ "Charvaca/Chavaka"; Gautama / Akṣapāda ≈ "Akhapada"; pramāṇa ≈ "pramana"; Pūrvapakṣa & Siddhānta ≈ "Purva Paksha and Sidanta"; Śramaṇa ≈ "Shramana"; Ājīvika ≈ "Ajivaka"; Aśoka ≈ "Ashoka/Aschaka"; Ikṣvāku ≈ "Ichvacu"; Rudradāman ≈ "Rudradaman"; Prākrit ≈ "Prachrit/Prachrit"; Kaṇāda ≈ "Kanada"; Jaimini ≈ "Jaimani/Jiamini"; Śabara ≈ "Shavara"; Kumārila Bhaṭṭa ≈ "Kumarela Bhata"; Prabhākara ≈ "Prabhakara"; Bādarāyaṇa ≈ "Badarayana"; Vyāsa ≈ "Vyasa"; Īśvarakṛṣṇa ≈ "Ishvara Krishna"; Sāṃkhya-kārikā ≈ "Samkhya Karika"; Madhyamaka ≈ "Madyamika"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagajuna").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The six systems (darśanas) — Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta, the so-called "orthodox" schools, here re-described as the sūtra-writing traditions [00:01:21].
  • sūtra & bhāṣya — the "thread"-like aphorism and the commentary that unfolds it; the organising literary form of the whole period [00:03:35].
  • Pāṇini & Patañjali — the grammarian's Aṣṭādhyāyī (sūtras) and the 2nd-c. CE Mahābhāṣya (commentary) supply the model for every later school [00:03:58].
  • Cārvāka / Bṛhaspati's Cārvāka-Sūtra — a sūtra-based tradition outside the supposed orthodox mainstream, materialist heir to the older naturalist Pāyāsi [00:08:06].
  • Rudradāman's inscription (c. 150 CE) — the marker for Sanskrit's rise to dominance as the language of philosophy [00:11:15].
  • Gautama, Kaṇāda, Jaimini, Bādarāyaṇa, Patañjali, Īśvarakṛṣṇa — the founding (or attributed) authors of the six systems, surveyed in the closing roll-call [00:16:40].

docs.title: It's at this point that things get complicated
docs.text:
• [00:00:36] The episode is titled "A Tangled Web." Up to now Indian intellectual life has been lively; from here on we face such a proliferation of texts, movements, schools and rivalries that it may be hard to keep them all straight. Historians have stepped in with ways of organising the mass of material.
  • [00:00:59] The standard scheme is a basic split between orthodox and heterodox movements, the orthodox ones growing out of the Brahminic culture of the Vedas. On the orthodox side historians count six systems that took up ideas from the Upaniṣads, parts of the epics, the Dharma-Sūtras and the Laws of Manu.
  • [00:01:21] The six: Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, and Vedānta. Collectively they are made to stand for "the Hindu perspective," which is then challenged by the sceptical, relativist heterodox thinkers — basically the Buddhists and Jains, who opposed orthodox theories of ritual, metaphysics and epistemology.

docs.title: Why the orthodox/heterodox scheme fails
docs.text:
• [00:01:45] The series already voiced dissatisfaction with this neat account. The most obvious problem: it reflects the Hindu point of view itself. "Orthodox" literally means right-believing — so framing it this way is almost like saying there were two kinds of Indian philosophers, "the good guys and the other guys."
  • [00:02:08] It's also problematic to call the six schools Hindu at all. The series has loosely used "Hindu" for works expressing traditional Brahminic and Kṣatriya values (e.g. calling the Mahābhārata a Hindu epic), but applying the label to such early texts is a contentious bit of retrospective labelling.
  • [00:02:28] "Orthodoxy" also implies an unrealistic agreement among the six. True, some movements eventually grow together: in the 11th or 12th century Vaiśeṣika and Nyāya effectively merge, so scholars can speak of a single Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosophy, and there's an intimate association of Sāṃkhya with Yoga. But it would hardly be worth distinguishing six systems if they all coalesced into one Hindu outlook.
  • [00:03:05] In fact there were prolonged disputes between the so-called orthodox schools, and even within individual schools, which split into sub-traditions — much as the Jains divided into the white-clad and sky-clad factions. So the picture of a unified orthodoxy doesn't hold.

docs.title: A more neutral contrast: the age of the sūtra
docs.text:
• [00:03:29] Instead, Adamson proposes a more ideologically neutral distinction, based on how the texts were actually written. The coming episodes cover what he calls the age of the sūtra — a period stretching over the first several centuries CE, when philosophy centred on interpreting compressed, lapidary statements called sūtras, literally "threads."
  • [00:03:52] These sūtras were so pregnant with meaning that commentary was needed to deliver it fully. The explanatory texts are called bhāṣyas. We've already met this with Pāṇini's Sanskrit grammar, written as sūtras, which received an influential bhāṣya from the 2nd-century CE grammarian Patañjali.
  • [00:04:15] The age of the sūtra is also the age in which Sanskrit, the language of the Vedas, becomes dominant across philosophical writing. So it's apt — and presumably no coincidence — that Pāṇini's eight chapters provided the model for how texts would be written: each school traced its ideas to a founding text in sūtra form, made the subject of authoritative commentary in a bhāṣya.
  • [00:04:45] The pairing of sūtra with bhāṣya was so ingrained that in some cases a single author wrote both the aphorisms and his own commentary on them.

docs.title: Form shapes content
docs.text:
• [00:05:00] It may seem perverse to stress the format: isn't content more important than form? But we shouldn't underestimate how the form of the text shapes the content and how readers understand it. Philosophy in this period is moving away from the exhortations and evocations of the earlier "philosophies of path and purpose" toward systematic inquiry — and this goes hand in hand with writing bhāṣya commentaries.
  • [00:05:35] A good bhāṣya uncovered the principles and arguments implicit in the sūtras: exposing their coherence and completeness, and showing how the ideas could be justified and defended against rivals' criticisms.
  • [00:05:51] The commentator's job is to weave the threads into a unified conceptual web — which the commentators themselves called a tantra, literally "warp" (the weaving kind, "not the kind involved in Star Trek"). Vātsyāyana, author of a major commentary on the Nyāya-Sūtra, explained that a tantra is "a system consisting in the statement of a collection of interrelated ideas."
  • [00:06:18] Commentators also describe their task as amplification or expansion of the sūtra. In a more Star Trek-friendly metaphor: a sūtra is like an uncompressed (i.e. compressed) data file that needs decompressing — its meaning unfolded by the commentator who adds the bhāṣya.
  • [00:06:42] This was no easy task. From Pāṇini's eight chapters on, sūtras typically look like nothing more than lists — a series of isolated statements with no organising principle. It was the commentator's job to impose — or, as he'd say, reveal — an intelligible structure: identify the chief overall theme, then divide the sūtras by sub-theme into groups, turning a mere list into a network of ideas and arguments with clear interrelationships.
  • [00:07:11] The goal was not to provide an easier-to-follow replacement for the sūtra, but to guide the reader through the original. Like the Greek commentaries on Plato and Aristotle in the same historical period, the bhāṣyas have a fundamentally pedagogical purpose.

docs.title: The fault line: almost, but not quite, the old one
docs.text:
• [00:07:35] This focus on the sūtra form almost divides the terrain along the same fault line as the old orthodox/heterodox contrast: the six systems all used the sūtra-bhāṣya style, whereas the Buddhists did not.
  • [00:07:57] But the division isn't exactly the same, because there were other sūtra-based movements outside the supposed orthodox Hindu mainstream — in particular Cārvāka philosophy. Cārvāka is not one of the six, yet it has its own foundational document, Bṛhaspati's Cārvāka-Sūtra.
  • [00:08:19] A warning: Bṛhaspati did not emerge from nowhere ("boldly going where no one had gone before"). He continued an older tradition of naturalism begun by Pāyāsi, probably a contemporary of the Buddha. And that's typical: each founding text is ascribed to a founding father — Gautama initiating Nyāya with his Nyāya-Sūtra, Patañjali beginning Yoga with his Yoga-Sūtra, and so on.
  • [00:08:55] We must reckon that these supposed foundations were themselves built out of found materials. We usually think of sūtras as the oldest canonical texts of a tradition, but it's safer to call them the oldest surviving texts that came to be recognised as canonical — sūtras may in part be compilations based on still older, now-lost literature.

docs.title: Why "orthodox" and "heterodox" leak into each other
docs.text:
• [00:09:20] This also explains a feature that doesn't fit the orthodox/heterodox antithesis: the agenda and terminology of the "unorthodox" traditions keep turning up in orthodox literature. Turn to the Yoga-Sūtra and you find the idea of escaping the cycle of rebirth by eliminating all desire — obviously an echo of Buddhism.
  • [00:09:48] This is unsurprising. Earlier, a gap had opened between Brahminic culture and the Śramaṇa movements — the renouncers who stressed an ascetic path to liberation: Buddhists, Jains, and Ājīvikas. But, "as in a good history of philosophy," that gap was also being closed: motifs like non-attached action and non-violence appeared on both sides.
  • [00:10:16] At the political level, rulers paid respect to sages of both persuasions. The standout is Aśoka, best known for his attraction to Buddhism but who seems to have seen himself as transcending sectarian division — the exception that proved the rule. Later rulers kept bestowing favour on both Brahminic and dissident groups: toward the end of this age, the southern Ikṣvāku dynasty had female members giving gifts to Buddhists while the male kings carried out Vedic sacrifices.

docs.title: Sanskrit takes over — the Rudradāman inscription
docs.text:
• [00:10:59] Archaeologists are grateful that later rulers followed Aśoka in another respect: putting up stone inscriptions to communicate with their subjects. There are even cases where a king added his own inscriptions alongside Aśoka's words.
  • [00:11:17] This was done around 150 CE for the king Rudradāman, and what he carved is telling. It shows a continued alliance of royalty and philosophy: Rudradāman boasts that, on top of martial prowess and good looks, he has "knowledge and practice of grammar, music, logic, and other great sciences."
  • [00:11:41] More interesting than what he says is the language: namely Sanskrit, whereas Aśoka's inscriptions are mostly in Prākrit. This is the stage at which Sanskrit establishes itself as the main language you need to read the primary sources of Indian philosophy. The Buddha himself spoke Prākrit, and the Buddhist canon was composed in Pali — but going forward, almost all philosophical literature is in Sanskrit.
  • [00:12:09] For Brahminic authors, Sanskrit — the language of revelation and of Pāṇini's grammar — has a unique status: it alone is eternal. Buddhists never accept this exceptionalist story, but they nonetheless begin to write in the language of their Brahminic adversaries.

docs.title: Adversarial structure: Pūrvapakṣa and Siddhānta
docs.text:
• [00:12:33] Adversarial relationships are crucial to philosophy in this age. From the description of sūtra-plus-bhāṣya as a self-contained web, you might imagine these texts resemble the Elements of Euclid more than the dialectical exchanges of Plato's dialogues or Aristotle's treatises. But because the authors are sensitive to challenges from other schools, they constantly raise potential objections and supply reasoned answers.
  • [00:13:02] In Sanskrit these are Pūrvapakṣa (the prior view / objection) and Siddhānta (the established conclusion / reply). In this respect the literature keeps something of the dialogue structure that marked the Upaniṣads, the philosophical sections of the Mahābhārata, and many stories of the Buddha in the Pali canon.

docs.title: Not all six are equally "systematic"
docs.text:
• [00:13:33] A final caution about the "six systems": they are not equally systematic. The label fits Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika well, but Sāṃkhya and Yoga less so — these are not so much philosophical systems as bodies of philosophical method, recalling the "philosophies of path and purpose" of the earlier period.
  • [00:13:57] Though Sāṃkhya and Yoga do have canonical sūtras, those were composed retrospectively, to give the traditions the same air of authority and lineage other schools claimed. The Sāṃkhya-Sūtra in fact dates from as late as the 14th century.

docs.title: The main topics of debate
docs.text:
• [00:14:14] What are the sūtras and commentaries actually arguing about? Again there's continuity with the earlier period. One dominant question: is there a self underlying all cognition and experience? The Buddhist denies it, Brahminic culture asserts it.
  • [00:14:34] But beware oversimplification. Within Buddhism there are disagreements about how to account for the survival of one and the same person across time and even across incarnations. And on the "orthodox" side there are major differences: the Mīmāṃsā school develops the self as an empirically engaged agent, while other traditions hold the self to be a pure consciousness that remains aloof from cognition and agency.
  • [00:15:03] The means by which the self comes to know the world and its own nature is much debated, with the Nyāya school making especially powerful contributions to epistemology. Against such positive accounts, a more sceptical note is struck within Buddhism and Jainism — the Jains developing the remarkable idea that truth depends on one's standpoint, what we'd call a perspectivist approach.
  • [00:15:34] In metaphysics too there are fundamental disagreements: the Vaiśeṣika school tries to establish six fundamental categories of reality, against rival views including the naturalism of the Cārvākas.
  • [00:15:52] Much action is in philosophy of mind, epistemology and metaphysics, but thinkers don't drop the earlier concern with ethics and salvation. The brilliant Nāgārjuna, founder of the Madhyamaka school within Buddhism, is the example: best known for the radical doctrine of emptiness, he never loses sight that the goal of accepting this doctrine (or "non-doctrine") is freedom from suffering.

docs.title: Roll-call of the schools — Nyāya
docs.text:
• [00:16:28] The episode closes with a quick rundown — "probably too much to take in all at once," but useful to refer back to. Nyāya first: its foundational Nyāya-Sūtra was probably compiled in the first or second century CE. The traditional compiler is Gautama, sometimes called Akṣapāda — "one whose eyes are in his feet" — apparently a reference to the foundationalism and empiricism of his system.
  • [00:16:58] Gautama forcefully advocates the pramāṇa method for rational inquiry, a pramāṇa being a way of gaining knowledge or a principle of justification. For him all knowledge rests on three main sources — perception, inference, and testimony — plus a fourth, comparison, whose exact meaning is unclear.
  • [00:17:22] The first and fifth chapters of the Nyāya-Sūtra concentrate on debate techniques, and may originally have been a separate text. So Nyāya's main issues: the nature of philosophical inquiry, the epistemology of the sources of knowledge, and the theory of debate.

docs.title: Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā
docs.text:
• [00:17:47] The allied Vaiśeṣika system has as its canonical text Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra, which may have been composed as early as 100 BCE. Its main claim to fame is a six-category metaphysics that influenced thinkers across the spectrum of Indian philosophy.
  • [00:18:07] Mīmāṃsā was in the first instance a system of Vedic hermeneutics — concerned with interpreting and clarifying the Vedas, defending Vedic authority, and analysing the meaning of ritual injunctions. Its foundational text is the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra, hard to date: perhaps it existed in some form around 400 BCE, with compilation of the version we have over the following centuries.
  • [00:18:42] The Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra is traditionally attributed to Jaimini, while the bhāṣya was written by Śabara around 400 CE. Though focused on Vedic interpretation, this led Mīmāṃsā to a much wider range of issues; it shared a broadly realist epistemology with Nyāya and contributed especially to the theory of perception. In the 7th century the school split into two sub-schools, following Kumārila Bhaṭṭa and Prabhākara respectively.

docs.title: Vedānta
docs.text:
• [00:19:15] Jaimini's Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra has a twin in Bādarāyaṇa's Vedānta-Sūtra, also called the Brahma-Sūtra. The two authors were contemporaries, with a suggestion of some collaboration.
  • [00:19:33] The division of labour: Jaimini focuses on the ritual formulations of the Vedas and the concept of dharma (duty, the actions one ought to perform) — hence the school's name, mīmāṃsā meaning "investigation," the investigation that illuminates ritual prescriptions.
  • [00:19:53] Bādarāyaṇa's motivation is also in the name: Vedānta means "what comes after the Vedas" — that is, the Upaniṣads. So the school's themes are the Upaniṣadic ones: cosmic unity, brahman, and the quest to discover brahman within one's own self.
  • [00:20:18] The Vedānta-Sūtra also illustrates inter-school rivalry: its four chapters defend the view that brahman is the central concern of scripture and that there is only one consistent interpretation of it — set against the Vaiśeṣika school, and with Buddhist and Jain views subjected to refutation. It also gives an extended description of the spiritual exercises leading one to comprehend one's identity with brahman.

docs.title: Yoga and Sāṃkhya
docs.text:
• [00:20:54] That reference to spiritual exercises leads to the Yoga-Sūtra, attributed to the mythical Vyāsa — though more likely both it and the Yoga-bhāṣya were written by a Patañjali, probably not the grammarian who commented on Pāṇini.
  • [00:21:13] This Patañjali itemises the elements needed to subdue mental disturbance: restraint and observance (restraint from injuring others, stealing, lying, greed; observance of cleanliness, purification, study), then posture, breath-regulation, abstraction of the senses, concentration, meditation, and trance. Backing this is a detailed theory of mind distinguishing the unchanging self from the states that make up a mental life. The Yoga school became theistic, with God entering as a self of this kind — unaffected by suffering or actions.
  • [00:21:55] Providing further theoretical backbone to spiritual discipline, yet without any obvious initial theism, is Sāṃkhya — whose sūtra, as noted, came only much later. Its real foundational document is Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya-kārikā ("verses on Sāṃkhya").
  • [00:22:13] Īśvarakṛṣṇa insists on a strict dualism between the self and nature/matter. Out of original matter the material world evolves, on the principle that an effect pre-exists in its cause. Strikingly, what evolves first is what we'd call mental phenomena: first intellect, then sense of self, then mind, then the five domains of sense experience and the senses, and finally the five material elements — air, light, water, earth, and ether. All this is part of nature, with the true self transcending all natural evolution.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:22:53] Along with the Cārvāka naturalists, these six schools will occupy the next ~20 episodes. After surveying them, it will be time to turn to the critical voices among the Buddhists and Jains.
  • [00:23:18] But since sceptical worries form such an important part of the context, the series will begin by exploring the emergence of philosophical doubts about the efficacy of action — especially Vedic ritual — and the possibility of knowledge. Sceptical arguments were put forward both against and within the schools. Next time: picking up the threads in the age of the sūtra.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• sūtra — a compressed, lapidary aphorism; literally a "thread." Each school traces itself to a founding text in this form; sūtras often look like bare lists.
  • bhāṣya — the authoritative commentary that "unfolds" a sūtra's meaning, weaving it into a structured, defensible system; pedagogical in purpose, like Greek commentaries on Plato and Aristotle.
  • tantra — the unified "web" of interrelated ideas a commentator weaves from the sūtra-threads; literally the "warp" of weaving (per Vātsyāyana on the Nyāya-Sūtra).
  • Pūrvapakṣa / Siddhānta — the objection (prior view) and the established reply; the built-in adversarial, dialogue structure of sūtra-age texts.
  • orthodox / heterodox — the rejected scheme: six "right-believing" Hindu systems vs. Buddhists and Jains. Faulted as Hindu-biased, anachronistic, and overstating agreement.
  • the six systems (darśanas) — Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta; re-described here as the sūtra-bhāṣya-writing traditions (though not all equally "systematic").
  • Cārvāka — materialist/naturalist tradition outside the six, with Bṛhaspati's Cārvāka-Sūtra, heir to the earlier naturalist Pāyāsi (a contemporary of the Buddha).
  • Śramaṇa movements — the renouncer traditions (Buddhists, Jains, Ājīvikas) stressing asceticism and liberation; their motifs (non-attachment, non-violence) leak into Brahminic texts.
  • Sanskrit vs. Prākrit/Pali — Sanskrit becomes the dominant philosophical language (Rudradāman's c. 150 CE inscription is the marker); for Brahmins it "alone is eternal," whereas the Buddha spoke Prākrit and the canon was in Pali.
  • Nyāya — Gautama (Akṣapāda)'s Nyāya-Sūtra (1st–2nd c. CE); epistemology of the pramāṇas (perception, inference, testimony, + comparison) and theory of debate.
  • Vaiśeṣika — Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra (perhaps c. 100 BCE); a six-category metaphysics; later merges with Nyāya (11th–12th c.).
  • Mīmāṃsā — "investigation"; Jaimini's Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra (bhāṣya by Śabara, c. 400 CE); Vedic hermeneutics, ritual, dharma, theory of perception; splits into Kumārila Bhaṭṭa and Prabhākara sub-schools (7th c.).
  • Vedānta — "what comes after the Vedas" (the Upaniṣads); Bādarāyaṇa's Vedānta-Sūtra / Brahma-Sūtra; brahman, cosmic unity, identity of self with brahman; polemical against rivals.
  • Yoga — Yoga-Sūtra attributed to Vyāsa, more likely a Patañjali (not the grammarian); discipline to arrest mental disturbance + a theory of the unchanging self; became theistic.
  • Sāṃkhya — Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya-kārikā; strict self/matter dualism; the world evolves from primal matter (effect pre-exists in cause), mental phenomena evolving before the five elements.
  • Nāgārjuna / Madhyamaka — founder of the Madhyamaka school; the doctrine (or "non-doctrine") of emptiness, whose aim remains freedom from suffering.
  • pramāṇa — a means of gaining knowledge / principle of justification; central to Nyāya's program.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 19 — "When in Doubt: The Rise of Skepticism"
docs.text:
← Ep 18

Ep 20 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:22:59 In brief: Indian philosophy splits into realist movements that presuppose knowledge can be had and skeptical ones that doubt it — and the systematic schools meet the skeptic head-on, from the ancient "paradox of inquiry" (how can you investigate what you don't yet know?) to the regress of the pramāṇas (how can a means of knowing certify itself?). Śabara, Kumārila, and Śaṅkara answer the first; Nāgārjuna, Jayarāśi, and Śrīharṣa press the second. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannery"; Śabara ≈ "Shabara"; Kumārila Bhaṭṭa ≈ "Kumaraara/Kumarira Bata"; Jayarāśi ≈ "Jayaashi"; Śrīharṣa ≈ "Shriharsha/Shri Hasha"; Madhyamaka ≈ "Madiamaka"; jijñāsā ≈ "Jijnasa"; vyutpatti ≈ "Vyutpati"; nirvacana ≈ "Nirvachana"; Sañjaya ≈ "Sanjaya"; Kena Upaniṣad ≈ "Kena Upanishad"; Cārvāka ≈ "Chattvaka").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Śabara — Mīmāṃsā commentator who raises (and answers) the paradox of inquiry on the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra [00:03:56].
  • Kumārila Bhaṭṭa — later Mīmāṃsā writer who sharpens the same paradox [00:04:40].
  • Śaṅkara — 8th-century Vedānta thinker whose Brahma-Sūtra commentary fields the skeptical challenge with three replies [00:05:10].
  • Nāgārjuna — 2nd-century CE Buddhist, founder of the Madhyamaka school; presses the regress of the means of knowing [00:15:19].
  • Jayarāśi — 9th-century skeptic who denies knowledge can even be defined [00:15:27].
  • Śrīharṣa — 12th-century skeptic who turns the regress against counterfactual reasoning [00:15:27].
  • Udayana — 11th-century Vaiśeṣika who proposed counterfactual reasoning as a route to knowledge [00:20:31].

docs.title: Recap: realist systems versus skeptical movements
docs.text:
• [00:00:35] Last time began the age of the sūtra with a fundamental clash in Indian philosophy. Rather than the tendentious "orthodox vs. heterodox" framing, the series prefers a cleaner contrast: on one side, systematic works of inquiry written as aphorisms-with-commentary (sūtra and bhāṣya); on the other, traditions that challenge the very terms of those systems.
  • [00:01:02] The clash had political consequences — there are stories of rulers persecuting Buddhists to uphold Brahminical teaching (for the history, Adamson plugs Kit Patrick's History of India podcast). But for this series the rift matters philosophically: broadly, realist movements versus skeptical ones.
  • [00:01:35] Buddhist and Jaina thinkers attacked the core notions of the other schools — language, mind, the self, action, the efficacy of ritual — and went further, doubting the very possibility of systematic inquiry. That worry haunted the commentators who expounded the sūtras.

docs.title: The sūtras presuppose that knowledge is possible
docs.text:
• [00:01:59] The sūtras plainly assume knowledge can be had and promise to deliver it through inquiry — you only have to read their first sentences.
  • [00:02:12] The Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra and the Brahma-Sūtra (the founding texts of Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta) are complementary — one aimed at the duties of Vedic ritual, the other at knowledge of the unifying cosmic principle brahman already found in the Upaniṣads — so their openings are nearly identical: "Now then, an inquiry into dharma," and "Now then, an inquiry into brahman." (Adamson's aside to undergraduates: in your essays, cut to the chase like this.)
  • [00:02:57] The Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra and Yoga-Sūtra open not with a promise of inquiry but with an exposition: the Yoga-Sūtra begins "Now an exposition of yoga" — yoga meaning psychophysical discipline — so, as in a well-run yoga class, you know where you stand. Even the lost founding text of the naturalist Cārvāka school began with still greater confidence: "Now then, we will explain reality."
  • [00:03:37] All of which the skeptic threatens to dissolve: if inquiry and explanation are impossible, we could stop reading every one of these sūtras on the spot.

docs.title: The paradox of inquiry — Śabara and Kumārila
docs.text:
• [00:03:45] Knowing the best defence is a good offence, the commentators raise the worry themselves. Expounding the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra, Śabara ventriloquizes a critic: what dharma is must be either commonly known or not. If it's commonly known, there's no need for inquiry; if it isn't commonly known, then inquiry into it is pointless.
  • [00:04:20] The word for inquiry is jijñāsā, literally "desire to know." Śabara's point: a desire to obtain something presupposes you already know what you want — so a desire to know something would require that you already know it. A paradox.
  • [00:04:40] Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, a later Mīmāṃsā writer, restates it: what is commonly known can be known, but being already known there's no desire to know it; what is not commonly known is impossible to know, and so is no possible object of a desire to know either.
  • [00:05:02] The same worry crosses into Vedānta. Because the Brahma-Sūtra opens with that promise to inquire into brahman, Śaṅkara (8th c.) begins his commentary with the identical challenge: if we don't already know what brahman is, how could we search for it? — but if we do, there's nothing left to discover.

docs.title: Nyāya shrugs it off — and Plato's parallel
docs.text:
• [00:05:27] Curiously, the realists most invested in epistemology, the Nyāya, never confront the paradox head-on. They simply take for granted that there's a way to investigate and reach knowledge. Their interest is in the method for ordinary questions — "is that thing over there a man or a tree stump?" — not the more abstract question of whether such a method could exist at all.
  • [00:06:05] For Nyāya, doubt is not epistemic paralysis but a state in which one has already partially grasped an object, so that it can be a target for further questioning. On their picture the puzzle of inquiry never even arises.
  • [00:06:22] Faithful listeners of the main podcast will recognize the puzzle from elsewhere: Plato's Meno, where Socrates faces the identical problem — you'd need knowledge of a thing in order to inquire into it. Plato's radical fix is recollection: we already know everything knowable, having learned it before birth, and merely need reminding.
  • [00:06:56] But that isn't the only or most obvious solution. Inquiry into something you already know perfectly is fruitless; inquiry into something of which you haven't the foggiest clue is impossible (you couldn't even get started). The natural thought is that our starting point lies in the middle: inquiry begins not from a blank slate or from mastery, but from partial understanding or uncertain belief.

docs.title: Śabara's real answer: too many beliefs, not too few
docs.text:
• [00:07:33] That middle-ground move is exactly Śabara's reply to the skeptic. Inquiry into dharma arises not because we know nothing but because we have too many beliefs — there is conflict between rival conceptions of duty, the very sort of conflict dramatized in the Mahābhārata. We investigate in order to decide between them.
  • [00:07:59] A good account of how moral philosophy avoids starting from scratch — but it has a gap. It gives no reason to think two people who disagree about dharma (or brahman) are even disagreeing about the same thing. Is a Vedāntin's clash with a Buddhist critic resolvable on common assumptions, or are they just talking past one another, using the same words in different senses?

docs.title: Śaṅkara's three replies: common idea, etymology, direct self-knowledge
docs.text:
• [00:08:22] Śaṅkara's commentary anticipates that further worry. He grants people disagree about brahman's qualities, but insists we all share a common idea of it that gives partial knowledge.
  • [00:08:41] His first proof is an etymology. It was widely held that linguistic analysis — vyutpatti or nirvacana — explains why we use a given word for a given thing (so dharma, from its verbal root, means "that which upholds"). Śaṅkara derives brahman from a root meaning "to grow," showing brahman is maximally great — "all grown up." Another reminder of how central Sanskrit grammar is for Indian philosophers.
  • [00:09:47] That looks flimsy, so Śaṅkara has a stronger, more European-sounding move: the paradox poses no threat here because brahman is a case of direct knowledge. "Everyone knows of the existence of his own self and does not think, 'I am not.'" If one's own self weren't perfectly well known, anyone could doubt his own existence — and no one does.
  • [00:10:16] The parallel with Augustine and Descartes is almost too obvious to mention — but unlike Descartes' "I think therefore I am," Śaṅkara isn't refuting global skepticism. He only wants to show the inquiry into brahman is possible. He invokes the Upaniṣadic "you are that," read as "this self is brahman": since the self can't be doubted, and the self is brahman, brahman can't be doubted either — so there is something there to investigate.
  • [00:11:00] But possibility isn't enough; he must show inquiry is also needed. If we already have immediate knowledge of self/brahman, why inquire? Because our intimate awareness of brahman does not include its true nature. Witness the disputes about the self: materialists and common folk think it's the body; Buddhists that it's just the flow of cognitions; Nyāya that it's an agent and subject of experience distinct from the body; Sāṃkhya that it differs from the body but is not an agent — and so on. Plenty of dispute, hence plenty of reason to investigate.

docs.title: Skepticism is as old as Indian philosophy itself
docs.text:
• [00:11:59] These weren't merely hypothetical foes. The history of skepticism in India is at least as old as the history of philosophy in India. The ancient Ṛg Veda's hymn of creation asks: "Who knows for certain... whence came this creation? The gods were born after this creation, then who can know whence it has arisen?... He who surveys it in the highest heaven, he only knows — or perhaps he does not." The secrets of creation may elude even the gods; mere humans certainly won't do better.
  • [00:12:54] Skeptical thoughts surface in the Upaniṣads too, some suggesting mystical insight is the only way past the limits of human knowledge. The Kena Upaniṣad: "If you think 'I know it well,' perhaps you know ever so little... I do not think that I know it well, but I know not that I do not know."

docs.title: The challenge from outside: the Śramaṇa movements
docs.text:
• [00:13:31] The skepticism that really worried Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta wasn't in their own sacred texts. From the moment they arose, the dissident Śramaṇa movements used philosophical arguments to undermine Vedic authority — enough to rattle even the epic poets.
  • [00:13:48] In the Mahābhārata, the god Indra ruefully confesses: "I used to be... a reasoner, a scorner of the Veda. I was pointlessly fond of critical inquiry and the science of argument... I was an unbeliever, skeptical about everything, and, though stupid, I thought myself wise."
  • [00:14:19] The Buddhists, who would soon adopt the skeptic's role themselves, nonetheless preserved condemnations of skeptics. The Buddhist Nikāya describes one Sañjaya who, "by reason of his dullness," resorts to verbal eel-wriggling: "I do not say so. I do not say thus. I do not say otherwise. I do not say no. I deny the denials." Unlike Nancy Reagan's "just say no," Sañjaya's policy was to disavow even the naysaying.

docs.title: Three great skeptics and the regress of the pramāṇas
docs.text:
• [00:15:06] Alongside the rise of systematic philosophy in the age of the sūtra came rival forms of skepticism. Three great critical thinkers span the periods: Nāgārjuna (2nd c. CE), Jayarāśi (9th c.), and Śrīharṣa (12th c.).
  • [00:15:31] Strictly, only Jayarāśi is a skeptic in the full sense of withholding all belief. Nāgārjuna was a Buddhist — founder of the Madhyamaka branch — and Śrīharṣa seems to have had underlying metaphysical commitments. But all three deploy skeptical arguments against a cherished idea of their opponents: that we can not only know things but also know that we know them.
  • [00:15:58] It seems obvious that knowledge is "reflective" — if I know there's a giraffe in the room, surely I know that I know it. The three skeptics deny it's obvious at all. Suppose you know there's a giraffe in the room only on a zookeeper friend's say-so; pressed, you'd admit testimony can mislead, so you might still believe it while conceding you aren't sure you know it.
  • [00:16:43] Go in and look for yourself, and the only puzzle left seems to be how they got the giraffe through the front door. But not so fast: how do you know your sense experience gives you knowledge? Eyesight, an Indian philosopher would explain, is a pramāṇa — a way of knowing — and there are others (inference, sometimes testimony); which count depends on your school.
  • [00:17:33] And here comes "the elephant in the room": the viability of the whole idea of a pramāṇa. The skeptic asks how any pramāṇa can be trusted unless we first establish it is reliable. As Nāgārjuna puts it: "If just such objects are established for you by way of a means of knowing, tell me how you establish those means of knowing themselves" — for if they are established by other means of knowing, there is an infinite regress.
  • [00:18:06] Saying "my eyes work, I'm not dreaming" won't satisfy Nāgārjuna — you don't know your eyes work or that you aren't hallucinating; perception can't ratify its own trustworthiness. Appeal instead to inference (my eyes proved dependable before) and you've merely invoked another pramāṇa, whose reliability is no better established than your eyes'. "You can already see why skeptics in India were regarded as very irritating people."

docs.title: Jayarāśi: you can't even define knowledge
docs.text:
• [00:19:08] And it gets worse. Jayarāśi challenges the realist epistemologists to define knowledge itself and argues it can't be done: the means of knowing depend on their true definition, and the things known depend on the means of knowing; when the one is absent, how can you talk of the other two as real? Otherwise you might as well talk of "color in the soul" or "pleasure in a pot."
  • [00:19:39] His point isn't quite that you can't know that you're knowing; it's the deeper worry that you can't even know what knowledge is. Before claiming to know anything you must define knowledge — but how could you be satisfied that any definition counts as knowledge unless you already know what knowledge is?
  • [00:20:01] Like Nāgārjuna, Jayarāśi aims at an abstract, highly philosophical target — the epistemologists, not the person with pressing practical concerns about clearing giraffes from her front room. He cheerfully grants that ordinary people have an everyday knowledge that makes life possible: "the worldly path should be followed; with respect to everyday practice, the wise resembles the fool."

docs.title: Śrīharṣa against Udayana's counterfactual reasoning
docs.text:
• [00:20:31] A few centuries on, Śrīharṣa (12th c.) responds to a new proposal from the 11th-century Vaiśeṣika Udayana: that knowledge can be reached through what we'd now call counterfactual reasoning. In doubt whether a giraffe is in the next room, I reason: "If there were a giraffe in there, I would smell it; no giraffe-fragrance hangs in the air; therefore the room is giraffe-free." Eminently reasonable — indeed a big part of what reasoning is.
  • [00:21:14] But Śrīharṣa is, predictably, skeptical: counterfactual inferences themselves need justification. I rule out the giraffe only by invoking the rule "if there were a giraffe there, I'd smell it" — and what makes me so certain of that? The regress looms again: every inference seems to call for a further inference to ground it, each no more secure than the last.

docs.title: Skepticism that bites: ritual and the supernatural
docs.text:
• [00:21:43] These paralyzing challenges are, in real life, not paralyzing at all. Jayarāśi expected his arguments to leave ordinary everyday knowledge standing; in the European tradition too the skeptics got cheerfully on with life — Sextus Empiricus acted as if he held the beliefs his arguments undercut, and Hume famously dropped his skeptical worries when he left his study.
  • [00:22:14] But the Śramaṇa traditions pressed other skeptical challenges with real practical bite: they questioned the efficacy of Vedic ritual and the reality of the supernatural entities those rituals presuppose. This was no abstract musing about knowledge-in-general but a gauntlet thrown down against the elite of the Brahminical tradition.
  • [00:22:40] The Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya schools rose to it — Mīmāṃsā especially insisting that the Vedas are an indispensable source of vital truths attainable in no other way. The next episode turns to those debates over ritual and the supernatural.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• sūtra and bhāṣya — aphorism-text plus commentary; the form of the systematic schools, contrasted with traditions that challenge the systems' terms.
  • paradox of inquiry — if you already know X there's nothing to inquire into; if you don't know X at all, you can't inquire into it; so inquiry seems impossible.
  • jijñāsā — "desire to know," the word for inquiry; desiring to know presupposes already knowing what you want, hence the paradox.
  • Śabara — Mīmāṃsā commentator; raises the paradox, then answers that inquiry arises from too many conflicting beliefs about dharma, not too few.
  • Kumārila Bhaṭṭa — later Mīmāṃsā writer who restates the paradox in sharpened form.
  • Śaṅkara — 8th-c. Vedāntin; answers the paradox with a common idea of brahman, an etymology ("to grow" → maximally great), and the indubitable direct knowledge of one's own self ("you are that").
  • Nyāya — realist epistemologists who never confront the paradox; for them doubt is partial grasp of an object, a target for further questioning, not paralysis.
  • vyutpatti / nirvacana — semantic/etymological analysis; held to explain why a word fits its thing (e.g. dharma = "that which upholds").
  • pramāṇa — a means or way of knowing (perception, inference, sometimes testimony); which ones count depends on your school.
  • regress of the means of knowing — Nāgārjuna's argument that a pramāṇa can't certify its own reliability, and certifying it by another pramāṇa launches an infinite regress.
  • Nāgārjuna — 2nd-c. CE Buddhist, founder of Madhyamaka; presses the pramāṇa regress against realist epistemology.
  • Jayarāśi — 9th-c. thoroughgoing skeptic; argues knowledge cannot even be defined, yet grants ordinary everyday knowledge.
  • Śrīharṣa — 12th-c. skeptic; turns the regress against Udayana's counterfactual reasoning.
  • Udayana — 11th-c. Vaiśeṣika; proposed counterfactual ("if there were a giraffe I'd smell it") reasoning as a route to knowledge.
  • Sañjaya — skeptic condemned in the Buddhist Nikāya for "eel-wriggling": "I deny the denials."
  • Śramaṇa movements — dissident (Buddhist/Jaina) traditions whose practical skepticism targeted the efficacy of Vedic ritual and the reality of the supernatural, challenging Brahminical authority directly.

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:26 In brief: The Mīmāṃsā school set out to systematize and defend Vedic ritual, but in doing so it produced a general theory of practical action: Jaimini's Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra grounds all duty (dharma) in the authorless, eternal Veda, makes every action — ritual included — a rule applied in virtue of a desire, and ends by subordinating the human agent to the intrinsic value of the ritual and the text itself. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennary"; Jaimini ≈ "Jiamini"; Mīmāṃsā ≈ "Mimamsa"; Nyāya / Naiyāyikas ≈ "Niyaya/Neaiacus"; Vātsyāyana ≈ "Vatsyaana"; Maitrāyaṇa Upaniṣad ≈ "Maitrayana Paneshad"; Bādarāyaṇa ≈ "Bararyana"; Śabara ≈ "Shabbara"; Kumārila Bhaṭṭa ≈ "Kumarira Bata"; Prabhākara Miśra ≈ "Prabhakara Misha"; pūrvapakṣin ≈ "Purva Paxin"; siddhāntin ≈ "Siddhantin"; śruti ≈ "Shruti"; ṛṣis ≈ "Rishis").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Mīmāṃsā — the school whose mission is to expound and interpret the Veda so as to establish proper ritual conduct; its generalizable ideas amount to a theory of practical action [00:06:01].
  • Jaimini — author (at least nominally) of the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra, the school's core text [00:08:42].
  • The Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra — longest of the sūtra collections, 2,745 sūtras; founds Pūrva ("prior") Mīmāṃsā [00:08:08].
  • Śabara — the authoritative commentator, centuries later, without whom the obscure sūtra is barely readable [00:12:14].
  • Bādarāyaṇa — named inside the sūtra; also the author of the Vedānta-Sūtra, hinting the two schools are intertwined [00:10:41].

docs.title: Ritual as the heart of Brahminical culture — and the target of critics
docs.text:
• [00:00:37] In the Brahminical culture that spawned the coming philosophical schools, nothing was more central than ritual: from a king's spectacular year-long horse sacrifice to everyday offerings of plants or milk into a fire, rituals were how householders propitiated the gods — and the key to the high status of the Brahmin priests.
  • [00:01:02] So it was inevitable that the validity of ritual, and the authority of the Vedic texts on which it rested, would be the central point of dispute between the Brahminical tradition and its critics. For the Buddhists, rituals were nothing special — just another set of actions undertaken to pursue desires we'd be better off without.
  • [00:01:23] Adherents of the Veda called these texts śruti — "what is heard" — a revelatory source of knowledge about the duties laid upon humanity.

docs.title: The opponent's three charges: false, inconsistent, repetitive
docs.text:
• [00:01:41] Brahminical texts often record the critics' challenges. The Nyāya-Sūtra, founding text of the logic-minded Nyāya school, sums up the attack: the Vedas cannot command assent because they suffer three epistemological defects — falsity, inconsistency, and repetition.
  • [00:02:12] Falsity: the promises of Vedic ritual aren't always fulfilled. A householder wanting wealth might adapt a boiled-rice ritual by instead boiling 100 gold coins in the water (Adamson notes that someone with 100 gold coins is already doing fine — but set that aside). The sacrificer follows a rule — if you want riches, boil gold coins and offer them — yet may perform it and stay poor, or do a fertility ritual and remain childless.
  • [00:02:53] A possible escape: like the Buddhists and other śramaṇa movements, redirect attention away from concrete goals toward spiritual ones, where the ritual reliably delivers — "or at least where it is harder to tell whether the ritual delivers or not." The Maitrāyaṇa Upaniṣad supplies just such an injunction: one who desires heaven should perform the fire ritual.
  • [00:03:25] But Vātsyāyana, a commentator on the Nyāya-Sūtra, admits the dodge may not be enough: a skeptic can reply that if any ritual injunction in the Veda is false, that brings the Veda's authority as a whole into disrepute. "If you can't rely on the Vedas to get kids and gold, why think they'll get you into heaven?"
  • [00:03:48] Inconsistency and repetition seem less damning, and they worry the Naiyāyikas just as much. The Veda says both after sunrise, perform the sacrifice and the sacrifice performed after sunrise goes to the dogs. And it says the same thing again and again — "the rambling of a drunkard." Implicitly the critic invokes rules of rational, trustworthy discourse — fit the facts, be consistent, say what's needed and no more — and charges that the Vedas violate them.
  • [00:04:24] Tellingly, this line of attack appears most sharply in the logic- and rationality-obsessed Nyāya tradition, raised as an objection against their own position. Actual Buddhist critique of ritual focused more on the violence of animal sacrifices; the Naiyāyikas may even have invented this objection themselves.

docs.title: The Naiyāyikas' replies
docs.text:
• [00:04:53] Defending the rationality of their sacred text, the Naiyāyikas answer each charge. Failure: rituals sometimes fail, but when they do it's because of faulty execution by the sacrificer, not a defect in the rules governing the ritual.
  • [00:05:10] Inconsistency: apparently conflicting rules simply apply to different situations. The after-sunrise sacrifice "goes to the dogs" only if you had previously resolved to perform it before sunrise.
  • [00:05:21] Repetition: it's sometimes useful — like reminding a mother in labour, repeatedly, to breathe and push (Adamson leaves it to mothers to judge how helpful that is).

docs.title: Why a school was needed: Mīmāṃsā's mission
docs.text:
• [00:05:38] Even the staunchest defender had to admit the Veda is a problematic text: beyond the three difficulties, rituals are often described in insufficient detail. Some rational method was needed to systematize the Vedic injunctions and to proceed in the face of incomplete information.
  • [00:06:01] This was the ambition of the Mīmāṃsā, a school whose mission was to expound and interpret the Veda in hopes of establishing proper ritual conduct. What has this to do with philosophy? Its ideas can be generalized from the ritual context into a general theory of practical action.

docs.title: Reasoning by analogy: transfer, adaptation, "rice in the pan"
docs.text:
• [00:06:25] Mīmāṃsā deals with gaps in the Veda by reasoning from one case to analogous cases. When a ritual is under-described, the remedy is transfer, adaptation, and annulment of details: borrow the details of a similar "model" ritual for the one you must perform. Adamson's analogy — replacing a car battery for the first time: you know what to do because you've done it on other cars and can adapt to this design. (The gold-for-rice swap was already an example.)
  • [00:07:13] The logicians called this golden rule of Vedic interpretation "rice in the pan" reasoning: like tasting one grain to judge whether all are cooked, you transfer a property from one thing (the tasted grain) to others (the rest).
  • [00:07:33] Strikingly, Mīmāṃsā applies "rice in the pan" reasoning to duties — dharma in the ritual context. Since dharma has a broader moral connotation too, we can extrapolate to ethical reasoning as a whole: we know the right thing to do in a new situation because, for all its specificity, it resembles other situations where we knew what to do — and the Indian tradition encourages exactly this extrapolation.

docs.title: Dharma depends on the Veda — the only guide we have
docs.text:
• [00:08:09] The core text, the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra, declares: dharma depends upon the Veda, so whatever is not Veda is not to be trusted. But how, if the Veda is at best an incomplete guide? Because incomplete or not, it is the only guide we have: most knowledge comes (directly or indirectly) from sense experience, but our senses tell us nothing about morality and ritual — there, the Veda is our sole source.
  • [00:08:42] Jaimini frames the opening sentence of his sūtra by casting the inquiry into Vedic exegesis as an inquiry into dharma.
  • [00:08:52] To this conviction Mīmāṃsā adds another: the world has always been as we see it now. The Veda has always existed and always governed ritual, so we can trust that the rituals handed down to us have a basis in the Veda even when that basis is obscure.
  • [00:09:12] And this authority isn't parochial: the Veda's authority in matters of dharma is not just unchallenged but universal. When the sūtra asks whether a ritual described as applying in one region should be restricted to it, the answer is no — by its very nature, dharma applies in all places and all times.

docs.title: The dialogue form: pūrvapakṣin vs. siddhāntin
docs.text:
• [00:09:42] This is typical of the sūtra's structure, which becomes a model for many later texts. It often reads as a dialogue between two voices: the pūrvapakṣin, who states a prima facie view, and the siddhāntin, who overrules him with the decisive, considered position.
  • [00:10:06] The siddhāntin's view coincides with the sūtra's own — tempting to call him the voice of Jaimini, though (as usual) the authorship is historically uncertain. The date is already problematic: perhaps composed c. 4th–2nd century BC, possibly in stages and by more than one author.

docs.title: Two branches of Mīmāṃsā: Jaimini and Bādarāyaṇa
docs.text:
• [00:10:35] The sūtra explicitly names earlier and contemporary thinkers, including Bādarāyaṇa — also the name of the author of the Vedānta-Sūtra. So at the very outset we see the Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta schools intertwined; they're sometimes called two branches of Mīmāṃsā.
  • [00:10:53] Jaimini's sūtra founds prior, or Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā; Bādarāyaṇa's Vedānta is posterior, or Uttara-Mīmāṃsā. Jaimini and his followers focus on the original Vedas and their ritual prescriptions; Vedānta means "at the end of the Veda," an allusion to the more obviously philosophical material in the Upaniṣads. Either way, the school stages an inquiry into the underlying principles of its texts — which is what "mīmāṃsā" means: an inquiry into the doubtful or difficult aspects of the Vedic tradition.

docs.title: A formidable text and its commentators
docs.text:
• [00:11:36] The Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra is the longest of the sūtra collections of this age — a massive 2,745 sūtras, against (for instance) only 555 in the Vedānta-Sūtra. And it's not just the size: crack it open and you immediately need help. Like other sūtra collections it's difficult and obscure, "perhaps not even meant to be read without an accompanying commentary."
  • [00:12:14] Thank goodness, then, for Śabara, who lived several centuries after the sūtra's composition; his commentary is authoritative for all Mīmāṃsakas. Around the 7th century AD the school split into two rival factions named for two further interpreters, Kumārila Bhaṭṭa and Prabhākara Miśra. As the layers of text and commentary accumulate, things grow more sophisticated and philosophical — partly from the need to answer rival schools — but there's already plenty of interest in Jaimini, best understood with Śabara's help.

docs.title: Rules about rules: the analysis of action
docs.text:
• [00:12:54] Unlike earlier works of Vedic exegesis, Jaimini operates at an abstract, general level. He's interested in the rules governing rituals, but expresses that interest above all by considering the rules that govern those rules (as with transferring rules between rituals). When he mentions specific practices, it's usually only to illustrate his overall theory.
  • [00:13:20] At the theory's heart is an analysis of human action. Rituals are special actions, but actions nonetheless, so to understand them we explore the mechanisms of action generally. Whenever you do something, you are at least implicitly following a rule or injunction, which applies to you because of some desire you have. In the mood for risotto, you apply the rule: if you want rice for dinner, cook the rice in boiling water.
  • [00:13:56] In general the causal situation involves four elements: an agent with a desire, the object/advantage desired, the instrument by which it's achieved, and the procedure. For risotto: you (agent), the rice (object), cooking (instrument), and the whole sequence — gathering firewood, drawing water, and so on (procedure). For one who desires riches should boil gold coins: the sacrificer (agent), wealth (object/goal), the ritual sacrifice (instrument), and the sacrificial steps (procedure).

docs.title: No desire, no duty — the controversial consequences
docs.text:
• [00:14:35] This looks straightforward, but recalling the discussions of Buddhism and the Bhagavad-Gītā shows it's philosophically controversial: Jaimini claims that any action presupposes desire in the one who performs it. Instead of giving up all desire, or detaching from the outcome, you should act by following the rules that apply to you in virtue of your desires.
  • [00:15:01] It seems surprising that Jaimini makes participation in Vedic ritual so contingent on the sacrificer's goals. Don't we have a standing obligation to perform the rites? The answer is no: there is no pure duty to perform the Vedic rites, for without desire the injunction to perform a ritual simply does not apply.
  • [00:15:27] Jaimini goes so far as to say that if a sacrificer loses interest in the outcome partway through, he should just stop, leaving the ritual incomplete.
  • [00:15:38] To the counter that some Vedic rituals specify no intended outcome, Jaimini replies that in such cases heaven serves as the default object of desire — for heaven is happiness, and happiness is desired by all.
  • [00:15:54] Another consequence: women are invited to participate, and not merely as their husbands' living instruments — their involvement is justified on the basis that they too have desires.

docs.title: The twist: ritual uses the agent, not the reverse
docs.text:
• [00:16:08] You might think ritual is being subordinated to human whims — but in fact the reverse is true. For Jaimini, what has ultimate, intrinsic value is the ritual itself. One might say the ritual uses the human agent, rather than the other way around: the sacrificer and his desire merely provide the occasion for the ritual. Without human goals no ritual would occur — but the ritual's value isn't exhausted by fulfilling those goals; it exists for its own sake.
  • [00:16:38] A dramatic illustration: it was laid down that if a sacrificer dies partway through, his bones could be placed inside an antelope skin, and this "posthumous puppet" made to carry out the remaining steps.
  • [00:16:55] Francis Clooney sums up Jaimini's view: by seeing himself as only one element in the web of relationships, the sacrificer transcends his self-centeredness even as he admits it, letting it lead him to the sacrifice; he learns to play his part without worrying about ridding himself of the desires that integrate him into the larger whole.

docs.title: Mīmāṃsā vs. Buddhism — and the quiet absorption of its rival
docs.text:
• [00:17:20] The Mīmāṃsā viewpoint is diametrically opposed to Buddhism in its total commitment to the value of ritual, the authority of the Veda, and its endorsement of human desire. Yet it also captures something of Buddhism's spirit, and may be responding to the Buddhist challenge by absorbing some of its ideas:
  • a shift away from concrete goals (money, family) toward heaven as a universal aim;
  • not the elimination of desire, but the humbling of the individual's desire to a mere contributing factor in the ritual;
  • most strikingly, an elimination of the supernatural — the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra does not tell us to sacrifice to please the gods or out of absolute religious obligation. Ritual is treated as parallel to humdrum everyday action: if the goal is risotto, consult a cookbook; if the goal has to do with dharma, consult the Veda.

docs.title: The boldest claim: the Veda has no author
docs.text:
• [00:18:26] Though scholars often call the Veda revealed, Mīmāṃsā insists it was not revealed by anyone. The Veda has no author, and the seers (ṛṣis) who expounded it are not prophets like those of the Old Testament — they simply transmit an authoritative Veda that existed before them and has always existed.
  • [00:18:50] Again human agency is sidelined, subordinated to the intrinsic value of the Veda just as it is to the ritual. The forefathers who passed on wisdom and reliable practices were admirable and trustworthy, but they did not invent or compose what they handed on. The most a human can do is be a conduit from the past to the future — never a conduit between the divine and humanity, as the Hebrew prophets or Muhammad were. No such conduit is needed: the Veda has always been here, "a permanent source of knowledge set down by neither God nor man."
  • [00:19:32] With this bold claim Mīmāṃsā makes the strongest possible case for Vedic authority: far from false, the Veda is a truth both unimpeachable and originary. But the bolder the claim, the greater the pressure to defend it — and Jaimini already draws the astounding conclusion that if the Veda is authorless and permanent, then language too must be permanent.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text: • [00:20:03] Jaimini's commentators provide a further defense of language's permanence and a sophisticated theory of knowledge meant to explain exactly why the Veda's authority is beyond challenge. Those are the next topics — the school justifying religious ritual by philosophical argument rather than divine authority.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Mīmāṃsā — school dedicated to expounding and interpreting the Veda to fix proper ritual conduct; the word means "inquiry into the doubtful/difficult aspects" of the Vedic tradition; its method generalizes into a theory of practical action.
  • Jaimini — author (nominally) of the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra; frames the inquiry into Vedic exegesis as an inquiry into dharma, and analyzes ritual as a species of desire-driven action.
  • Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra — the school's core text; longest of the sūtra collections (2,745 sūtras vs. 555 in the Vedānta-Sūtra); obscure, requiring commentary; structured as a dialogue, datable perhaps c. 4th–2nd century BC.
  • dharma — duty/moral law; depends entirely on the Veda, which is our only source of knowledge about it; applies in all places and all times.
  • śruti — "what is heard"; the Veda as revelatory knowledge of duty (though Mīmāṃsā denies it had any revealer).
  • "rice in the pan" reasoning — the logicians' name for Vedic interpretation by analogy: transfer a property from one case (a tasted grain) to others (the rest of the rice); applied even to duties.
  • transfer / adaptation / annulment — Mīmāṃsā's procedures for filling gaps in under-described rituals by borrowing details from a model ritual.
  • pūrvapakṣin / siddhāntin — the two voices of the sūtra: the one who states the prima facie view and the one who delivers the decisive verdict (the latter speaking for the text itself).
  • Pūrva- vs. Uttara-Mīmāṃsā — "prior" Mīmāṃsā (Jaimini, on Vedic ritual) vs. "posterior" Mīmāṃsā = Vedānta (Bādarāyaṇa, on the Upaniṣads, "the end of the Veda"); two branches of one inquiry.
  • Bādarāyaṇa — named within Jaimini's sūtra; author of the Vedānta-Sūtra; evidence the two schools are intertwined.
  • Śabara — the authoritative commentator (centuries later) without whom the sūtra is barely intelligible to all Mīmāṃsakas.
  • Kumārila Bhaṭṭa & Prabhākara Miśra — interpreters for whom the two rival Mīmāṃsā factions are named after the school split around the 7th century AD.
  • Nyāya-Sūtra / Naiyāyikas — the logic-obsessed school whose founding text records (perhaps invents) the three charges against the Veda — falsity, inconsistency, repetition — and answers them; Vātsyāyana is its commentator.
  • theory of action — Jaimini's claim that every action implicitly follows a rule applying to you in virtue of a desire; its four elements are agent, object, instrument, procedure; hence no desire, no duty (no standing obligation to perform the rites), with heaven as the default desired object.
  • authorless, eternal Veda — Mīmāṃsā's boldest doctrine: the Veda was composed by neither God nor man and has always existed; the ṛṣis only transmit it — implying language too is permanent.

docs.text:
