🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:00 In brief: How the Mīmāṃsā school defends the absolute authority of the Veda — not by appealing to a divine author but by denying the Veda has any author at all — and underpins this with a hard-nosed, empiricist epistemology ("cognitions are innocent until proven guilty") and a theory that language itself is beginningless. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannery"; Mīmāṃsā ≈ "Mimamsa"; Mīmāṃsaka(s) ≈ "Mimamsakas"; Jaimini ≈ "Jiamini"; pramāṇa ≈ "Pramana/promana"; Veda ≈ "Vedah"; Śabara ≈ "Shabara/Shavarazya"; Kumārila Bhaṭṭa ≈ "Kumara-Bata/Kumaraela/Kumadela"; svataḥ prāmāṇya ≈ "svata pramagna"; Prabhākara ≈ "Prabakara"; Nyāya ≈ "Niyaya"; Pāṇini ≈ "Panani"; dharma ≈ "Dharma"; Dārā Shukōh ≈ "Dada Shiku"; Elisa Freschi ≈ "Eliza Fresci").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The Veda(s) — Mīmāṃsā's holy books, held to be authorless and beginningless, the unique source of knowledge about dharma [00:01:15].
  • Jaimini — author of the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra, source of the school's empiricist account of perception [00:02:52].
  • Śabara — author of the authoritative early commentary on Jaimini [00:04:27].
  • Kumārila Bhaṭṭa — commentator who develops the "intrinsic validity" (svataḥ prāmāṇya) doctrine [00:05:08].
  • Prabhākara — the rival commentator; the Mīmāṃsā split follows him vs. Kumārila on words and sentences [00:14:18].
  • Elisa Freschi — the scholar who will be next episode's guest on Mīmāṃsā [00:19:54].

docs.title: Revelation vs. an authorless scripture
docs.text:
• [00:00:37] The episode opens with the Islamic idea that God sends different revelations to different peoples — the Torah for the Jews, the Gospels for the Christians, and finally and definitively the Quran for the Muslims. This was extended to India: Buddhists and Hindus, too, were treated as "peoples of the book," and the Muslim prince Dārā Shukōh, living in India in the 17th century, even claimed to detect an allusion to the Upaniṣads inside the Quran itself.
  • [00:01:08] But Mīmāṃsā would reject this well-meaning analogy. Where Torah, Gospels and Quran are thought to be sent to humankind by God through divine revelation, the Mīmāṃsakas held that their holy books, the Vedas, have no author at all. The Veda did not come from the gods or from any prophet, and it was not sent. It is permanent — in the sense of having always existed, or having no beginning.
  • [00:01:37] Since the Veda consists of words and sentences, this implies that language itself is permanent — a consequence the Mīmāṃsakas were more than happy to embrace.

docs.title: Why deny the Veda an author?
docs.text:
• [00:01:50] This idea (raised already last time) is part of the Mīmāṃsā attempt to establish unimpeachable authority for the Veda. But why adopt such a radical proposal — one rejected even by other Brahminical schools like Nyāya?
  • [00:02:06] The short answer: if the Veda is permanent and has no author, then it cannot contain any errors. Errors only arise where there is someone — an author — in a position to make a mistake. With no author, the Veda must be entirely trustworthy.
  • [00:02:24] The long answer is the rest of the episode: it requires looking at Mīmāṃsā's ideas about knowledge and language.

docs.title: The empiricist foundation: perception as a pramāṇa
docs.text:
• [00:02:32] The Mīmāṃsakas ground their account of the Veda in an empiricist and naturalist account of human knowledge. Roughly, their reasons for accepting the truth of the Veda are the same kind of reasons you have for accepting that you are hearing this voice right now, and that the objects around you are what they seem to be.
  • [00:02:52] The roots lie in a passage of the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra where Jaimini writes: "Perception is the knowledge which one has by the senses coming into contact with something existent." He straightforwardly endorses that sense perception gives accurate information about things. In later terms, sensation is a pramāṇa — a source of knowledge or justification.
  • [00:03:20] But (as we know from earlier discussion of skepticism in ancient India) such claims won't go unchallenged — and the skeptic looks especially well placed against this pramāṇa. She need only point out that sensation is often misleading: the stuff cooking in the pan looks like rice but is actually tapioca; that man looks like Jim Rice who played baseball for the Red Sox, but it's actually his twin brother.

docs.title: "Rice-in-the-pan" reasoning and the skeptic's leverage
docs.text:
• [00:03:48] The empiricist can reply that sensation is very rarely misleading, so we can generally depend on it. But the Mīmāṃsakas seem badly placed to say this, because they themselves are happy to use so-called "rice-in-the-pan" reasoning in other contexts: they say all the rice is cooked if one grain is soft, and that the details of one ritual can be transferred to another.
  • [00:04:12] So how can they stop the skeptic from arguing in the same way — from the misleading nature of one sense experience to the doubtfulness of sensation as a whole?

docs.title: Innocent until proven guilty
docs.text:
• [00:04:22] The Mīmāṃsā answer: sensations are innocent until proven guilty. The idea enters the commentary tradition early, before Śabara's authoritative commentary on Jaimini. We should take every cognition to be true unless it is trumped by another cognition that overturns it.
  • [00:04:39] The commentators, including Śabara, readily admit many factors can undermine a sensation: you might taste the stuff in the pan and find it too sweet to be rice, or you might be drunk or deranged (which undermines belief generally). Today philosophers would call such things defeaters. In the absence of any defeater, the perception should be taken as true.

docs.title: Kumārila and intrinsic validity (svataḥ prāmāṇya)
docs.text:
• [00:05:08] Developing this, Kumārila Bhaṭṭa states in his commentary on Śabara that sensations possess svataḥ prāmāṇya — intrinsic validity. Later Mīmāṃsakas couldn't agree on what this meant.
  • [00:05:23] A minority read it as: a sensation is valid so long as it arose in a reliable way — provided you're not in fact deranged or drunk, your cognitions are reliable. It's then up to each of us to check whether a cognition arose trustworthily, and if so, to trust it.
  • [00:05:45] Others took Kumārila to mean valid sensations simply present themselves as true. If you see rice in a bowl in normal conditions, you have no hesitation in taking yourself to know there's rice there; only a warning sign — a strange taste, an awareness of being drunk — would even prompt doubt.
  • [00:06:08] This second reading is "exactly right," per Kumārila: "That cognition which is unshaken and does not conflict with cognitions occurring at other times and places is a pramāṇa — a source of knowledge." In normal conditions we should not fret about possible falsehood, and certainly not surrender to the skeptic's worry that all cognitions may be unreliable.

docs.title: Turning the skeptic's regress against her
docs.text:
• [00:06:34] But isn't this just an unjustified leap of faith? It's no good for Kumārila to insist dogmatically that we can trust perception — that's precisely what the skeptic denies, and she has reason, since perceptions are occasionally misleading.
  • [00:06:51] The Mīmāṃsakas have another move: borrow a weapon from the skeptic's own arsenal. If we demand confirmation for every cognition, a regress looms — each cognition needs another to confirm it. If I double-check the bowl is rice by tasting it, how do I know I'm tasting accurately? I could ask you to taste it too, but your agreement is also open to challenge.
  • [00:07:28] The skeptic draws the moral that no pramāṇa is reliable. Mīmāṃsā draws the reverse: there must be some foundational cognitions, since otherwise we could never be confident of knowing anything — yet of course we are confident in having knowledge.

docs.title: Back to the authorless Veda
docs.text:
• [00:07:44] Now return to the Veda having no author. Though this became a distinctive Mīmāṃsā claim, it doesn't appear explicitly in Jaimini, who says only that words are always prior to their speakers — which can be taken to imply that the Veda, and language in general, are permanent.
  • [00:08:03] The Veda's absolute authority can only be challenged on the basis of some defeater. Had it been authored, we could always fear the author — even a divine one — made a mistake. We trust sensation unless we have reason to think it arose defectively; we trust the Veda in exactly the same way, except that here there can be no worry it arose defectively, because it did not arise at all.
  • [00:08:37] It may seem this buys the Veda's authority too cheaply — its validity is supreme simply because it has no competition, so it wins by default. But put yourself in Jaimini's or Kumārila's position. The Vedic tradition was under fire from Buddhists, Jainas and others, so the Mīmāṃsakas were not oblivious to religious pluralism — yet Kumārila was confident the alternatives could be exposed as invalid. The critics of Vedic ritual had given no good reasons to doubt the ritual's efficacy (or none the Mīmāṃsakas rated). And if there were good reasons to doubt, we would know about them.
  • [00:09:24] Kumārila is so confident in the sources of knowledge that for him the absence of a cognition is itself a reason to reject a thing, given favorable conditions: if you're positioned to know a pan's contents yet have no evidence of rice there, that is reason to believe there's no rice. Likewise, there is no cognition — nor even the possibility of one — that could overturn Vedic authority. With no defeaters in sight, Mīmāṃsā declares victory.

docs.title: Against the Buddhists: an enduring self
docs.text:
• [00:09:58] The stance has other implications, including renewed conflict with the Buddhists. Where Buddhism denies an enduring self, Mīmāṃsā insists on it. We recognize automatically that there's an "I" who experienced the things we remember and feel that this is still who we are: just as I see a dirty pan in the sink waiting to be washed, so I remember myself eating the rice prepared in that pan.
  • [00:10:28] Making short shrift of the Buddhists' nuanced critique, Mīmāṃsā simply assumes we are right to take ourselves as enduring subjects of experience, since there is nothing to defeat that impression — and indeed nothing could overturn the impression that one has a self.

docs.title: Language has no beginning
docs.text:
• [00:10:46] The most far-reaching and celebrated part of the view on the beginninglessness of the Veda is the inference that language itself must have no beginning.
  • [00:10:58] One argument: children learn language by watching adults use language. We have no evidence things were ever otherwise, so — basing ourselves on experience — we may assume language, like the Veda, has always been passed down from generation to generation.
  • [00:11:21] A second argument that things cannot be otherwise. Take the word "cow," Sanskrit go. (Aside: you can tell a lot about a culture by what it means by the syllable "go" — for ancient Indians, cow; in Japan, a board game of almost infinite complexity; for Americans, where you start when building a monopoly.) The word "cow" refers not to any particular cow but to cows universally, and when I say it on many occasions I'm using the same word over and over, not a new word each time. Or, appealing to Mīmāṃsā epistemology: it seems I'm using the same word repeatedly, and there's no reason to doubt it, so we take it as true.

docs.title: The "no way to introduce language as such" argument
docs.text:
• [00:12:10] The argument may seem unconvincing, since it assumes "cow" has either always existed or is a new word every utterance. There's a third possibility: each word is introduced at some point, then used with a stable meaning by convention and agreement.
  • [00:12:32] Against this, Mīmāṃsā argues that even if one can learn the meaning of individual new words, there is no way to introduce language as such. It's impossible to learn to speak or understand speech without already engaging in and observing linguistic activity. Children learning to talk must discover each word's meaning by watching their elders; once competent, we can learn new words by hearing them explained in other words — but it's inconceivable the whole process could have begun from a situation with no language at all.

docs.title: Universal meaning vs. "bring the cow"
docs.text:
• [00:13:11] A critic resists: on the theory, words have universal meaning, yet if I tell my ritual assistant "bring the cow" (a standard Mīmāṃsā example), I mean a specific cow. How, if "cow" refers universally?
  • [00:13:38] The answer: a word on its own cannot refer to anything particular. For that you need context — at least the rest of the sentence, and probably surrounding sentences and circumstances. By putting "bring the" in front of "cow," as I'm erecting a sacrificial post, I get my assistant to fetch the particular cow about to be tied to the post and sacrificed.

docs.title: Kumārila vs. Prabhākara: words and sentences
docs.text:
• [00:14:05] That satisfies the critic but not the Mīmāṃsakas themselves. As the tradition developed, a dispute arose over the relation between words and sentences — one aspect of a split following the commentators Kumārila and Prabhākara.
  • [00:14:24] Kumārila accepts that words have a general meaning standing alone — the utterance "cow" does signify something — but that meaning is affected by being placed in a complete sentence, connecting words to produce a new composite meaning. His view is the "theory of the connection of what has been expressed."
  • [00:14:48] Prabhākara holds that words must appear within a sentence to have any meaning at all — the "theory of expression through what has been connected." This seems implausible (surely "cow" alone calls something to mind), but shouldn't be dismissed: many words lack fixed meaning apart from context. Consider "at" across "the cow is at the sacrificial post," "we will sacrifice her at sunrise," "the cow looked at me with her big brown eyes, and all at once I decided I couldn't go through with it."

docs.title: Ritual injunctions and the centrality of the verb
docs.text:
• [00:15:36] Prabhākara's view fits Mīmāṃsā's overall aim: inquiry into ritual injunctions like "one who desires heaven should perform the fire ritual." The injunction is the most important of the four kinds of statement in the Veda — the others being the mantra (formula spoken during the ritual), the statement that indicates a name, and the explanation of a goal pursued in ritual.
  • [00:16:04] Jaimini stated that a ritual injunction is a meaningful unity composed of its words — and not just any string will do. Here Mīmāṃsā draws on Sanskrit grammar, carrying forward Pāṇini's idea that the action expressed by the verb is central to a sentence's meaning. The distinctions can be subtle — e.g., verbs go in the middle voice when the action is performed by the sacrificer (for himself) and not by the attending priest.

docs.title: Injunctions point to an unobservable future — to dharma
docs.text:
• [00:16:40] A more basic point returns to Mīmāṃsā's core mission, inquiry into Vedic language. Where everyday language typically describes the world we see, an injunction inevitably refers to something not yet present — the goal sought in the ritual. Because ritual injunctions are directed to the future, their validity is not grounded in sense perception. When the Veda tells you how to sacrifice to have children, get rich, or reach heaven, it looks to an unobservable future reward — distinctive, even definitive, of the language that reveals dharma.
  • [00:17:27] This gives another reason the Veda can't be overturned: how could sensation conflict with the Veda, when sensation tells us nothing about the questions at stake in ritual — questions of dharma?

docs.title: Ordinary words, no supernaturalism
docs.text:
• [00:17:44] Despite this, Mīmāṃsā insists the Veda's words are used in their normal sense: "tie a cow to a post" is not allegorical or extended — it calls a cow a cow and a post a post. Still, the Veda is a unique source of knowledge, one that could only be delivered as language, since we need language to articulate goals not yet present and explain how to reach them.
  • [00:18:20] This is typical Mīmāṃsā: a theory devoted to interpreting the sacred Veda, yet offering an epistemology grounded in sense experience and an analysis of language that applies just as well to sentences uttered by cowherds (assuming the cowherds speak Sanskrit). It makes no appeal to supernatural knowledge and impatiently rejects such claims by others — dismissing that the Buddha was omniscient, and that yoga confers special insight. Such supposed cognitions have no basis in normal experience, and it's normal experience we should follow, along with testimony in the form of language — unless we have good reason not to.

docs.title: A scriptural empiricism: Augustine meets Hume
docs.text:
• [00:19:05] Mīmāṃsā exemplifies Indian philosophy's potential to overturn assumptions natural to European traditions. We may suppose that devotion to scriptural authority must come bundled with belief in higher supernatural cognition and in a revelation that erupts into history, dividing an ignorant past from a new age graced with previously inaccessible truth.
  • [00:19:30] But no European thinker beats Mīmāṃsā for respect for scriptural authority, yet its adherents vehemently rejected the rest of that supernaturalist picture — fusing a hermeneutics worthy of Augustine with an empiricism so hard-nosed it might impress David Hume.
  • [00:19:47] Reason enough to give the tradition one more episode: next time the guest is Elisa Freschi, "an outstanding interpreter of this school of interpretation."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Mīmāṃsā / Mīmāṃsakas — the school devoted to interpreting the Veda; defends its supreme authority via empiricist epistemology and the doctrine that the Veda (and language) is authorless and beginningless.
  • Veda — Mīmāṃsā's holy books; held to have no author and no beginning, hence to contain no errors and to be the unique source of knowledge about dharma.
  • Jaimini — author of the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra; defines perception as knowledge from the senses contacting "something existent," and says words are prior to their speakers.
  • Śabara — author of the authoritative early commentary on Jaimini; admits factors (defeaters) can undermine sensation.
  • Kumārila Bhaṭṭa — commentator; champions svataḥ prāmāṇya (intrinsic validity) and holds that words have meaning alone but combine into a composite sentence-meaning ("connection of what has been expressed").
  • Prabhākara — rival commentator; holds words have meaning only within a sentence ("expression through what has been connected").
  • pramāṇa — a source of knowledge/justification; for Mīmāṃsā, perception is one, valid unless defeated.
  • svataḥ prāmāṇya — "intrinsic validity"; a cognition is valid in itself (because reliably produced, or because it presents itself as true) absent a defeater.
  • defeater — modern term the episode uses for anything (odd taste, drunkenness, derangement) that overturns a cognition; the Veda is uniquely immune since it never "arose."
  • "innocent until proven guilty" — Mīmāṃsā's epistemic principle: take every cognition as true unless trumped by another cognition.
  • dharma — the subject of Vedic injunctions; directed to an unobservable future reward, so beyond the reach of sense perception (which therefore can never contradict the Veda).
  • ritual injunction — most important of the Veda's four statement-types (with mantra, name-indicating statement, goal-explanation); a meaningful unity of words centered, after Pāṇini, on the action of the verb.
  • go ("cow") — the worked example: a word referring to cows universally, needing sentential context to pick out a particular cow ("bring the cow").
  • Pāṇini — grammarian whose principle that the verb's action is central to sentence-meaning is carried into Mīmāṃsā's analysis of injunctions.
  • Elisa Freschi — Mīmāṃsā scholar, the next episode's guest.

docs.text:

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Elisa Freschi 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Elisa Freschi · Runtime: 00:35:29 In brief: An interview with Elisa Freschi (Austrian Academy of Sciences, Vienna; University of Vienna) on the Mīmāṃsā school — how an exegetical tradition built around Vedic sacrificial injunctions became a serious philosophy of language, action, and the self, and how the rival Bhāṭṭa (Kumārila) and Prābhākara (Prabhākara) sub-schools split over whether its conclusions extend beyond the Veda. Topic order, not strict narration; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennari"; Elisa Freschi ≈ "Elisa Freschie/Eliza Feski"; Mīmāṃsā ≈ "Mimansa/Mianza/Riemansa/muonza"; Kumārila Bhaṭṭa ≈ "Kumara/Kumala/Komal/Khamarabhara"; Prabhākara Miśra ≈ "Prabhaka/Pramagara/Parabaga"; Śabara ≈ "Shabara"; Jaimini ≈ "Jiamini/Jamini"; Bādarāyaṇa ≈ "Baddharayana"; Śrautasūtra ≈ "Shraudashu/Shratasudra"; Vṛttikāra ≈ "Vritikara"; Asko Parpola ≈ "Asco Parpola/Ascovarvara"; Johannes Bronkhorst ≈ "Johannes Brankhurst"; Francis Clooney ≈ "Francis Clooney"; Kiyotaka Yoshimizu ≈ "Kiyodaka Yoshimitsu"; śyena ≈ "Shiena"; Pāṇini ≈ "punanee").

docs.title: Who the Mīmāṃsā are: exegesis of the Veda
docs.text:
• [00:00:28] Adamson introduces the guest: Elisa Freschi, a researcher at the Austrian Academy of Sciences in Vienna and lecturer at the University of Vienna. The topic: philosophical ideas in Mīmāṃsā, "a school that's associated with the exegesis of the sacred Vedic literature."
  • [00:01:01] Freschi: Mīmāṃsā originated from a school of exegesis of the Veda. The Veda spans many genres — from the hymns of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā through the Upaniṣads — but Mīmāṃsā scholars care specifically about the Brāhmaṇas, the parts containing sacrificial injunctions. Not the mythical or mystical portions: just the parts that say "if you want rain, sacrifice with the X sacrifice."
  • [00:01:42] Adamson notes wryly that this is "the part of the Vedas we discussed least" — almost not at all.

docs.title: Where the philosophy comes from
docs.text:
• [00:01:48] Adamson presses: why is any of this philosophical? Freschi concedes there's "nothing philosophical in this part of the Veda" itself — "you can find physics everywhere" too. What's philosophical is the way Mīmāṃsā approaches it.
  • [00:02:08] Contrast case: the Śrautasūtra tradition also does exegesis of these texts, but only to "make a ritual out of the ritual prescriptions" — how many spoons of butter to use, etc. Purely technical, nothing philosophical.
  • [00:02:25] Mīmāṃsā instead thinks systematically about the prescriptions, which forces deep questions: how is the Veda valid cognition, and how sure can we be? Who is eligible to sacrifice (→ the concept of the subject)? The nature of language; the form of action.
  • [00:03:21] Were they self-aware about this? Yes — and here's the key difference from the Śrautasūtra. The Śrautasūtras just systematize Vedic texts to enable sacrifice (technical). Mīmāṃsā describes itself as concerned with the itikartavyatā of the Veda — its "procedure," a reflective element the thinkers were conscious of. This self-awareness increases over time, from Jaimini → Śabara → Kumārila.

docs.title: The three textual layers (and the lost texts behind each)
docs.text:
• [00:04:19] Mīmāṃsā, like most schools of the period, is not monolithic — it subdivides and develops historically. Freschi gives the outline:
  • [00:04:25] The oldest extant text (not necessarily the oldest that existed), recognized as foundational by all later authors, is the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra, attributed to Jaimini. But the Sūtra itself names other authors alongside Jaimini — e.g. "thus says Jaimini, as well as Bādarāyaṇa," or "Bādari says." Jaimini appears as just one of many authorities within his own text. (Bādarāyaṇa is credited with the Brahma-Sūtra — coming up in a later episode.)
  • [00:05:11] Despite this, the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra has strong inner consistency — not a random collection of aphorisms by earlier authors, but (as Francis Clooney and others have shown) arguably a unitary product.
  • [00:05:29] Second layer: after Jaimini comes Śabara, who wrote a Bhāṣya (commentary). But Śabara constantly refers to earlier commentators whose work is lost — so a major development happened between Jaimini and Śabara that we can't directly see. Śabara has far more that looks philosophically relevant.
  • [00:06:18] Adamson systematizes: a Sūtra level (an intelligent compilation of many people's ideas) and a Bhāṣya / commentary level. Freschi refines it: Śabara isn't engaging a vague crowd — he has a "pet opponent," the Vṛttikāra (author of a lost Vṛtti), deeply into epistemology (which instruments of knowledge are reliable). A specific dialectical context, not a mess of voices.
  • [00:06:45] Third layer — the split into two schools, after the Bhāṣya. Kumārila Bhaṭṭa founds the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā; Prabhākara Miśra founds the Prābhākara school. Both commented on the Śabara-Bhāṣya and accepted the authority of both the Sūtra and the Bhāṣya — but their interpretations diverge sharply.
  • [00:07:30] Even before the split there were divergent traditions: Kumārila refers to someone who can't be Prabhākara (since, following Kiyotaka Yoshimizu's arguments, Prabhākara was a slightly younger contemporary of Kumārila) yet cites ideas later found in the Prābhākara school. So at least two distinct Mīmāṃsā traditions predate the named split.
  • [00:08:09] Adamson's takeaway: at all three levels — Sūtra, Bhāṣya, two-school split — there are lost texts in the background, represented only through the earliest surviving texts. "Quite typical for this whole period" — a good warning.

docs.title: The standard injunction: "one who desires heaven should sacrifice"
docs.text:
• [00:08:37] To show why this is philosophically interesting, Adamson asks for the stock example. Freschi gives it: darśa-pūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta — "the one who desires heaven should sacrifice with the darśa and pūrṇamāsa," the new-moon and full-moon sacrifices. (Adamson: "I think it's good that you said that and not me.")
  • [00:09:19] First philosophical wrinkle: this exact sentence isn't found in the Veda. It might sit in a lost portion, but more typically it is an abstraction made by Mīmāṃsā authors — characteristic of their method. They treat the disorderly Brāhmaṇas (full of mythical digressions) as if they were orderly procedural texts, then rationalize them into main prescriptions, auxiliaries, etc.
  • [00:10:00] To do this they invented a large body of exegetical rules (e.g. for deciding whether a passage forms a single unitary statement). These spread through Indian thought — rhetoric, Dharmaśāstra, Vedānta — as rational rules for connecting sentences and determining meaning. Mīmāṃsā were "the first ones who decided how we can define what a sentence is."

docs.title: Authorless words and the force of a prescription
docs.text:
• [00:10:49] So one part of the analysis is strictly exegetical/linguistic, and another concerns what a Vedic prescription is really doing. Crucially, for Mīmāṃsā the Veda is authorless (apauruṣeya). They can't say the injunction is telling you God's will — "our normal Christian-influenced answer." So they ask: is there a prescriptive force in the injunction itself? How is it communicated — through your understanding of it, or through the force of the optative/injunctive suffix?
  • [00:11:36] What does "authorless" even mean — where do the words come from? Freschi: language for Mīmāṃsā is anādi, beginningless. Unless you can prove otherwise — "a photo of the Big Bang" — there's no reason to assume language was ever different than it is now. The Veda has always been part of the intellectual landscape; looking for its origin is "an unwarranted move."
  • [00:12:27] So a Vedic prescription is more like a moral prescription — it comes from nowhere, it's just a rule to obey. Freschi: yes, Kumārila argues much like this, treating them as "eternal moral thoughts."

docs.title: Desire as the trigger — and as the root of all action
docs.text:
• [00:12:44] The injunction is conditional on desiring heaven — so if I don't desire heaven, I'm off the hook? Freschi: the sixth chapter of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra says everyone desires heaven, because heaven is happiness and everyone desires happiness.
  • [00:13:14] For Kumārila, this generalizes into a universal theory of action: "no one undertakes an action unless he desires its result." Not just Vedic injunctions — every action whatsoever is driven by desire.
  • [00:13:44] But the schools diverge. Prabhākara stays focused on the Veda and treats ordinary language as an exception to it, whereas Kumārila centers ordinary life. So for Prabhākara desire is merely the identifier of who is eligible to sacrifice — with no guarantee of the result. It picks you out as the right performer, even if the fruit never comes.
  • [00:14:44] Concretely: everyone must perform the darśa-pūrṇamāsa (everyone desires heaven), but more specific sacrifices — for rain, for conquering a village — apply only to those with that particular desire. Adamson: if there's already too much rain, the "desire rain" injunction simply doesn't apply to me.

docs.title: Who is eligible: women, lower classes, the "open-minded" sixth chapter
docs.text:
• [00:15:15] Adamson: don't a lot of these injunctions apply only to the Brahmin class? Freschi calls the sixth chapter (on desire) strikingly open-minded by contemporary standards: it speaks of the omnipresence of desire across all human beings and even animals. Women can desire things, so in principle they'd be entitled to sacrifice; so would lower classes.
  • [00:15:55] The limitations imposed are contingent, not a priori. Women would be entitled to sacrifice but don't own property — so they lack cows to offer the priests. That's different from declaring them irrational or excluded by nature. Similarly, mute people can't perform sacrifices because they can't utter the mantras — an instrumental lack, not a deficit of reason. "They have the desire, but not the instrument."

docs.title: Against the Buddhists: can there be desireless action?
docs.text:
• [00:16:31] Adamson: this all sounds uncontroversial — I want X, the rule tells me how to get X. But in India it is controversial, because the Buddhists (and even the Bhagavad-Gītā's ideal of unattached action) say we shouldn't act from desire. Do the Mīmāṃsakas have good arguments for desire's centrality?
  • [00:17:26] Yes — Kumārila is "quite rude" against the Buddhists, mocking the idea that action without desire is possible. His argument: if the Buddha truly reached nirvāṇa and is desireless, why did he start teaching? Teaching requires wanting to communicate. So either he reached nirvāṇa and stays silent, or he teaches — which means he still has desire and is "just a fake."
  • [00:18:05] A Buddhist opponent in Kumārila's text replies: the Buddha doesn't really utter words; they come out of him "naturally," without his meaning them. Kumārila: then you're just a blind believer. Freschi relishes the irony — Westerners reading Mīmāṃsā assume they are the blind believers in the Veda, when in fact the Mīmāṃsakas saw themselves as rational, empiricist, down-to-earth people following common sense, and ridiculed the Buddhists for the "bizarre" notion of desireless action.
  • [00:18:48] Adamson finds the example plausible. But what about the Gītā's unattached action: Arjuna must fight, yet without attachment to the outcome, perhaps dedicating the act to God? Couldn't I have reasons to act while staying open to the action failing?
  • [00:19:46] Freschi: back to the Kumārila/Prabhākara split. Kumārila would say even then there is desire — the desire to comply with a moral law you believe in, to please God, to be a good person. Without some desire you'd never begin acting at all. (Adamson: so the desire is devotion to God rather than winning the battle — yes.)
  • [00:20:18] Prabhākara's answer: the result merely identifies the agent. It picks you out of all possible individuals as the one who must act — but there's no guarantee you'll get the result, and you needn't be attached to getting it. You'd like to win the battle, and that's what brings you onto the battlefield, but you act without knowing you'll succeed.
  • [00:21:01] Freschi notes that later Vedāntin authors (working in a theistic setting the podcast won't reach) used Prabhākara-style arguments about non-attachment to results — dovetailing with the idea that you sacrifice because the Veda commands it, not for the result. The Veda is truthful so it will work, but the reason to sacrifice is the command, not the payoff.

docs.title: The self as an agent: Kumārila vs. everyone
docs.text:
• [00:21:41] Lurking behind the theory of action is a self / agent who forms the desire and performs the act — commonsensical, but denied by other traditions. What does Mīmāṃsā say to prove there's a self?
  • [00:22:18] Freschi: the argument again starts from common sense. Without an agent, you couldn't ensure that the karma you accumulate accrues to you and not to someone else. The whole karma framework — shared by almost everyone in Indian philosophy — collapses without an enduring agent. And we know the Buddhists struggled to justify karma without a persisting self.
  • [00:22:50] But the Nyāya / Sāṃkhya / Vedānta opponents are different: they admit there is a self, but it's changeless — aloof from action and cognition, hence useless for explaining everyday acts. Kumārila argues this changeless self is no help at all — it's "very much akin to the Buddhist self" in being useless for explaining how the world works.
  • [00:23:33] In the Ātmavāda ("doctrine of the self") portion of his Ślokavārttika — a main work — Kumārila is even willing to give up the self's nityatva (eternality/permanence) if permanence is taken to mean it can't change. He'd rather keep a permanent self that is no longer changeless, because his self must be a person who engages in actions.
  • [00:24:13] This is genuinely controversial: most schools posit either no self (Buddhists) or a self devoid of action (Nyāya, Sāṃkhya, Vedānta — action belongs to lower, accidental faculties). For Kumārila the self is intrinsically an agent, intrinsically able to cognize, hence able to acquire new cognitions — i.e. to change. His analogy: a baby becomes a child, then an adult, while remaining the same person. A self can change yet stay identical; it needn't be static to be the same person.

docs.title: Is this all just exegesis dressed up? And: is it even "religious"?
docs.text:
• [00:25:21] Adamson presses the deep worry: how much of this is just an effort to make the Vedic sentences come out true? There's a nice irony that a "highly religious exegetical project" ends up defending the deliverances of common sense ("yes, I do have a self that acts and knows"). And how much rides on grammatical analysis — going back to Pāṇini's grammar (the nominative-case agent, the action, the instrument, the outcome)? Is Mīmāṃsā essentially claiming the grammar of Vedic sentences mirrors the structure of the world?
  • [00:26:25] Freschi unpacks several tangled things. First, she resists calling Mīmāṃsā "religious": "religion" is hard to define, and in the Christian-influenced West we tie it to God — but Mīmāṃsā is basically an atheist school, so the label would mislead listeners.
  • [00:26:59] On whether the conclusions hold outside the Veda: it depends on which school. Kumārila is "really a philosopher" in the philosophical arena — he wants to debate and, if possible, demolish the Buddhist epistemologists and the Nyāya views, so his ideas are meant to apply beyond Vedic validity.
  • [00:27:31] Prabhākara, by contrast, is Veda-focused and treats ordinary language as an exception. He defends the controversial, counter-commonsensical thesis that language is inherently prescriptive: any sentence is either meaningless or has meaning only insofar as it is subsidiary to a prescription.
  • [00:27:55] Freschi's teaching example: telling a young boy "it's nine o'clock" really means "go to bed, brush your teeth" — language only makes sense as an addition to a prescription. Even her own descriptive sentences would, on this view, be part of the overarching prescription "believe what I'm telling you."
  • [00:28:39] So the answer to Adamson's question depends on the branch: one associates the theory of action with language generally (Kumārila), the other with a specific use of language (Prabhākara). Freschi qualifies: for Prabhākara, Vedic language is the paradigmatic case — not a special kind of language but the main thing; you understand language best by starting with Vedic language and generalizing. From the outside it looks like he's focused on a narrow case; he'd say he's focused on the paradigm.

docs.title: Contradictions in the Veda: the śyena sacrifice
docs.text:
• [00:29:15] Another problem: the Veda is a huge corpus, so it can contradict itself — telling you to do one thing here, another there. Do they worry? Very much — it's a hot topic.
  • [00:29:46] The standard case: the general injunction "na hiṃsyāt sarvabhūtāni" — "you should not harm any living being" — versus the śyena sacrifice, which says that if you want to harm your enemy, sacrifice with the śyena and your enemy will die. All Mīmāṃsakas agree you ought not perform the śyena, but disagree why.
  • [00:30:21] The bind: saying "it's immoral, so don't" puts an authority above the Veda, which no Mīmāṃsaka will accept. So they need another solution. One option: a hierarchy of prescriptions — some (typically prohibitions, like the ban on violence) apply more generally than others.
  • [00:30:58] A "quite nice" alternative: the Veda simply states everything, and your desire identifies which injunctions apply to you. If you want to harm your enemy, then yes, you should perform the śyena — but you shouldn't have gotten that far. By desiring to harm your enemy you've already violated the prohibition on harming any living being, which includes harming with your thoughts. So again, desire determines when you fall under an injunction's scope.

docs.title: Action as effort, not physical motion
docs.text: • [00:31:40] An aside Freschi adds: for Mīmāṃsā (unlike Vaiśeṣika), action is the undertaking of the action — the effort toward it — not the physical realization. Adamson: so it's forming the intention and commanding your limbs to move that is the action, not the limbs actually moving. Yes.

docs.title: Why no God, afterlife, or rebirth — and the link to Vedānta
docs.text:
• [00:32:02] Final question: Freschi called Mīmāṃsā atheist, and indeed it sounds so focused on parsing the rules that much of even the Vedic worldview goes missing — nothing about afterlife, rebirth, or God (later Mīmāṃsā gets more theistic). Why is that all absent?
  • [00:33:01] One answer (from Asko Parpola): the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra and the Brahma-Sūtra (Vedānta's foundational text) were originally a single text — plausibly, since both cite the same authors and share a structure. On that view the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra is one part of a whole whose latter part handled the self, God, immortality, etc.
  • [00:33:53] But the thesis "might be wrong": Johannes Bronkhorst argues the Brahma-Sūtra is just a later imitation of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra's style. Freschi can't subscribe to Parpola's reading, attractive as it is.
  • [00:34:13] Either way, the two were eventually made to complement each other — Mīmāṃsā analyzing the rules, Vedānta supplying the context of salvation. Historically, Vedāntin authors did adopt Mīmāṃsā as a preliminary stage of their own school — most clearly in the theistic Vedāntas.
  • [00:34:45] The exception is Śaṅkara's Advaita Vedānta (likely the only Vedānta the podcast will cover), which is much more against Mīmāṃsā: being anti-realist and anti-commonsensical, defending a changeless self, Śaṅkara is far less willing to treat Kumārila as preliminary. But the theistic Vedāntas see Mīmāṃsā as the first step in a continuous development.
  • [00:35:11] Adamson: a perfect transition, since the podcast now moves to Vedānta — "almost as if we planned that in advance." He thanks Elisa Freschi; she thanks him; on to Vedānta next time.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Mīmāṃsā — school of Vedic exegesis turned philosophy; atheist, realist, common-sensical; focuses on the Brāhmaṇas' sacrificial injunctions, not the myth or mysticism.
  • Veda / Brāhmaṇas — the sacred corpus; Mīmāṃsā mines the Brāhmaṇas' ritual injunctions ("if you want rain, sacrifice with X").
  • Śrautasūtra — rival exegetical tradition that systematizes ritual only technically (how many spoons of butter), with no philosophy.
  • itikartavyatā — the Veda's "procedure"; Mīmāṃsā's reflective, self-aware concern with it (vs. the Śrautasūtras' bare systematizing).
  • Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra — oldest extant Mīmāṃsā text, attributed to Jaimini but citing other authorities; argued (Clooney) to be a consistent unitary work.
  • Jaimini — named author of the foundational Sūtra, himself one of several authorities it cites.
  • Bādarāyaṇa — authority cited in the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra; credited with the Brahma-Sūtra (Vedānta's foundational text).
  • Śabara / Śabara-Bhāṣya — author of the foundational Bhāṣya (commentary); engages the lost epistemologist Vṛttikāra as his pet opponent.
  • Kumārila Bhaṭṭa — founder of Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā; brought Mīmāṃsā into the philosophical arena; universal desire-theory of action; self as intrinsically an agent; Ślokavārttika.
  • Prabhākara Miśra — founder of the Prābhākara school; Veda-centric; desire merely identifies the eligible agent with no guarantee of result; language is inherently prescriptive.
  • Ślokavārttika — Kumārila's major work; its Ātmavāda section argues the self can change yet remain the same person.
  • apauruṣeya / anādi — the Veda is authorless and language beginningless; no origin to seek, so no God's-will reading of injunctions.
  • darśa-pūrṇamāsa — the new-moon/full-moon sacrifices in the stock injunction "one who desires heaven should sacrifice"; the injunction is itself a Mīmāṃsā abstraction.
  • svarga-kāma — "desirous of heaven"; everyone desires heaven (= happiness), so the conditional injunction binds all.
  • karma — accruing fruits of action; needs an enduring agent to ensure your karma accrues to you (a problem for Buddhists).
  • śyena — the harm-your-enemy sacrifice; its clash with "harm no living being" is the test case for Vedic self-contradiction; resolved via desire/prohibition-hierarchy.
  • na hiṃsyāt sarvabhūtāni — "you should not harm any living being"; the general prohibition trumping the śyena.
  • unattached action (Bhagavad-Gītā / Arjuna) — acting without attachment to results; Kumārila reads even this as desire (to please God), Prabhākara as desire merely identifying the agent.
  • Asko Parpola — argues the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra and Brahma-Sūtra were originally one text.
  • Johannes Bronkhorst — counter-argues the Brahma-Sūtra merely imitates the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra's style.
  • Śaṅkara / Advaita Vedānta — anti-realist, changeless-self Vedānta most hostile to Mīmāṃsā; theistic Vedāntas instead treat Mīmāṃsā as a preliminary stage.

docs.text:

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:18:17 In brief: The founding text of Vedānta — Bādarāyaṇa's Vedānta-Sūtra (a.k.a. Brahma-Sūtra / Uttara-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra) — read on its own terms, before Śaṅkara: a cryptic, code-like work of scriptural exegesis whose single mission is to show that brahman is the one source of all things, the intimate ground of the individual self, and the knowledge of which brings liberation. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennary"; Bādarāyaṇa ≈ "Bararayana/Barareana/Barterayana/Barraena"; Vedānta ≈ "Vedanta"; Mīmāṃsā ≈ "mimamsa"; Śaṅkara ≈ "Shankara"; Śabara ≈ "Shabara"; Kumārila ≈ "Kumara"; Prabhākara ≈ "Prabakara"; Chāndogya ≈ "Chandogya"; Yājñavalkya ≈ "Yajnavukya/Yajnalvika"; Gārgī ≈ "Gargi"; Sāṃkhya ≈ "Samkhya"; pradhāna ≈ "Pradana"; śārīraka ≈ "Sharidaka"; pūrva-pakṣa ≈ "Purva Paksha"; siddhānta ≈ "Sidanta").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The Vedānta-Sūtra (Brahma-Sūtra / Uttara-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra / Śārīraka-Sūtra) — the founding text of Vedānta, composed in current form likely in the 5th century CE [00:02:20].
  • Bādarāyaṇa — the putative author whose "decisive view" the sūtra endorses [00:07:18].
  • Śaṅkara — the 8th-century non-dualist (Advaita) Vedāntin whose commentary dominates how the text is read [00:01:35].
  • Jaimini — the prior-Mīmāṃsā master, here cast as the foil whose ritual-focused view gets corrected [00:07:21].
  • The early Upaniṣads — especially the Chāndogya and the Great Forest (Bṛhadāraṇyaka) Upaniṣad — the texts the sūtra interprets [00:04:24].
  • The Sāṃkhya school — the rival Brahmanical system, with its unintelligent material principle pradhāna, made the target of sustained critique [00:13:43].

docs.title: From Mīmāṃsā to Vedānta: prior vs. posterior exegesis
docs.text:
• [00:00:30] Following on from the Mīmāṃsā episodes: even if you weren't persuaded that Vedic ritual brings its promised fruits, the intellectual harvest of Jaimini and his successors should convince you that a tradition devoted to exegesis of sacred texts can be philosophically fruitful. And if you're still the stubborn type, there's more to come, because we aren't done with Mīmāṃsā in the broader sense.
  • [00:01:08] Jaimini, Śabara, Kumārila and Prabhākara represent Pūrva ("prior") Mīmāṃsā. But it was Uttara ("posterior") Mīmāṃsā that gave rise to one of the most famous branches of Indian philosophy. Uttara-Mīmāṃsā is also called Vedānta, and like Mīmāṃsā it eventually subdivided into rival approaches.
  • [00:01:35] The most famous approach is that of the most famous Vedāntin, the 8th-century thinker Śaṅkara — his system is non-dualist or Advaita Vedānta, a name many listeners will have met before finding the podcast.

docs.title: Reading the founding text before Śaṅkara
docs.text:
• [00:01:50] Just as it was hard to excavate Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā without being guided (and sometimes misled) by the commentator Śabara, so it is with Śaṅkara's reading of Uttara-Mīmāṃsā (which from here on is simply called Vedānta). The power of Śaṅkara's philosophy makes it tempting to equate Vedānta with that philosophy.
  • [00:02:08] But just as the series tried to recover Jaimini's Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra in its own right, it now devotes an episode to the founding text of Vedānta, composed in its current form several centuries before Śaṅkara — likely in the 5th century CE.

docs.title: A book of many names — one source in many guises
docs.text:
• [00:02:25] Predictably the book is called the Vedānta-Sūtra, also the Uttara-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra. But it has yet more titles. Its primary subject, announced in its very first line, is brahman — so it is sometimes the Brahma-Sūtra. And because it speaks of the nature of a self that possesses a bodily form (śārīraka), it has been called the Śārīraka-Sūtra.
  • [00:02:52] This welter of titles could hardly be more appropriate: the core mission of the Vedānta-Sūtra is to investigate a single source of all things, presenting itself in many guises — and that source is, of course, brahman.
  • [00:03:08] The sūtra doesn't merely argue that brahman is the source of all things; it also explores the relationship between our individual selves and this transcendent principle, tells us how we can come to know brahman, and promises liberation from the snares and karmic consequences of bodily existence to whoever attains that knowledge.

docs.title: A text written in code
docs.text:
• [00:03:25] Described that way it sounds like a systematic work of philosophical cosmology — but if so, the system is hard to extract. Like the sūtra texts at the origins of other Indian traditions, the Vedānta-Sūtra at times "seems almost to be written in code." Śaṅkara's authority looms partly because we need his help and that of other commentators to understand it.
  • [00:03:56] The sūtra form is partly to blame, but another reason is that the Vedānta-Sūtra is a philosophical treatise that doubles as a work of exegesis, devoted to the texts at the end of the Veda — hence Vedānta — namely the Upaniṣads.
  • [00:04:13] To be more specific: texts called Upaniṣads kept being produced alongside and long after the sūtra (later Upaniṣads are themselves an expression of the Vedānta tradition). But the Vedānta-Sūtra interprets a select group of early Upaniṣads — especially the Chāndogya, but also the Great Forest Upaniṣad and others. It thus revisits passages discussed earlier in the series, such as the dialogues featuring Yājñavalkya. Such key passages came to be known as the "great sayings," receiving especially focused treatment from later Vedāntins.

docs.title: "Because of abiding and eating": the two birds
docs.text:
• [00:04:57] The sūtra is hard to read because it rarely identifies the passage it interprets. You must know the Upaniṣads so well that even a single key word reveals which text is at stake — or you fall back on the commentators.
  • [00:05:15] Example: one sūtra says simply, "because of abiding and eating." The context shows it is meant to convince us that brahman holds of all things, but the remark stays incomprehensible until you realize it alludes to a passage describing two birds — one eating, the other sitting quietly. The eating bird symbolizes the individual soul engaged in worldly action; the quiet bird is brahman, which simply abides unchanging.
  • [00:05:50] This is the interpretive project that dominates the text: it reads the sacred writings as putting forward a single coherent doctrine centred on brahman. For later Vedāntins the sūtra itself, and for good measure the Bhagavad-Gītā, joined the Upaniṣads as fundamental sources — which is why Śaṅkara commented on the Gītā as well as on the sūtra and several early Upaniṣads.

docs.title: Exegesis as the battlefield
docs.text:
• [00:06:19] This brahman-centric approach was controversial and rejected by other Brahmanical schools. When the Vedānta-Sūtra refutes those schools, it typically concentrates on showing that the Vedānta reading is better grounded in the sacred texts.
  • [00:06:35] This is not faith triumphing over reason; it shows the opponents are themselves committed to the truth of the Upaniṣads. Exegesis is the ground the sūtra chooses on which to wage its philosophical battles.

docs.title: Bādarāyaṇa vs. Jaimini — and the technique of the sūtra
docs.text:
• [00:06:46] Though it shares the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra's interpretive aims, the Vedānta-Sūtra is not just a "second installment" that moves on to the Upaniṣads. The difference shows in the men credited with the two texts.
  • [00:07:05] The Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra was supposedly written (or compiled) by Jaimini, yet he is mentioned there in the third person. The same happens in the Vedānta-Sūtra, which names and reports the ideas of its own putative author, Bādarāyaṇa.
  • [00:07:22] At several points Bādarāyaṇa's ideas are contrasted with Jaimini's. In the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra it is Jaimini who usually gets the last decisive word; in the Vedānta-Sūtra it is Bādarāyaṇa whose view is allowed to triumph — presumably why tradition credits him with authorship.
  • [00:07:43] Safer to use the technical terms of sūtra literature: Jaimini's opinion is treated as the initial or prima facie view, the pūrva-pakṣa, only to be corrected by the more adequate view, the siddhānta, of Bādarāyaṇa.

docs.title: The shift of emphasis: from ritual to liberation
docs.text:
• [00:08:02] Bādarāyaṇa's authoritative position has consequences. Where Jaimini placed all his focus on Vedic ritual, Bādarāyaṇa is more interested in the prospect of liberation through the knowledge of brahman. At one point we're told a person with such knowledge can dispense with things like lighting ritual fires.
  • [00:08:20] In keeping with this, Bādarāyaṇa is less attached to the life of the householder and tends to emphasize the superiority of the ascetic life of renouncers. The knowledge of brahman imparted in the Upaniṣads is valued for its own sake — not, as Jaimini would have it, as a supplement helping us grasp the purpose of ritual.
  • [00:08:50] There are other disagreements. Bādarāyaṇa thinks even the gods can achieve liberation by knowing brahman, whereas Jaimini restricts liberation to humans and even denies the existence of gods. A core Mīmāṃsā doctrine is that the Veda had no origin but has always existed; that idea appears in the Vedānta-Sūtra too, but so does the idea that the Veda has its source in brahman.

docs.title: Brahman as cause — objections answered
docs.text:
• [00:09:16] It is typical of the Age of the Sūtra that the theory develops through dialectical argument: Bādarāyaṇa (or whoever was finally responsible for the text) constantly raises objections against himself, then refutes them. The weightiest concern the nature of brahman as a cause.
  • [00:09:37] Objection: how can all things be produced by brahman, given that brahman is transcendent above those things? It seems impossible that a cause give rise to things utterly unlike it. Reply: such things are simply known to happen. Bādarāyaṇa doesn't supply an example, but Śaṅkara's commentary offers cases where the living emerges from the dead (a scorpion "spontaneously generated" from a pile of manure) and the inanimate comes from the living (we grow hair and fingernails).
  • [00:10:15] Objection: why would brahman bother to produce the world at all? For no real reason — out of mere sport or play that brahman does so.
  • [00:10:22] Objection: but wouldn't brahman have had good reason not to cause a world so full of suffering and unjust inequality? True, concedes Bādarāyaṇa, but this is not brahman's fault: all suffering is punishment for wicked deeds, perhaps committed in past lives. Since the cycle of rebirth has gone on endlessly, any particular suffering can always be referred back to earlier actions that justify it. (Here Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta agree the world has always existed much as now — though Bādarāyaṇa insists this eternal world has a source in brahman, a notion foreign to Jaimini.)

docs.title: The conceptual sequence of creation
docs.text:
• [00:11:12] The world caused by brahman may be permanent, but it has a kind of conceptual sequence that recalls the Upaniṣads. When Yājñavalkya was challenged by his female interlocutor Gārgī to name the fundamental principle on which all things are "woven," he eventually satisfied her by saying it might be space.
  • [00:11:40] Naturally Bādarāyaṇa accepts this and infers that space is the very first effect of brahman — or, at another point, that space is even identical to brahman. From space emerge further principles reminiscent of ancient Greek cosmology: the sequence air, fire, water, earth, produced one after another with brahman as ultimate source. When the world cycle finally ends, they return to brahman, dissolving in the reverse order of their generation.

docs.title: Brahman as efficient and material cause
docs.text:
• [00:12:16] So the universe is like an effective stand-up comedian: it has great material — the best possible material, namely brahman itself, which is both the moving (efficient) cause of all things and in some way the stuff out of which things are made. Taking a leaf from Aristotle, brahman is both the efficient and material cause of the world — captured in the dictum that brahman is "the support of heaven, earth, and all other things."
  • [00:12:52] Though it takes on the forms of other things, brahman is in itself formless. The Upaniṣads characterize it variously (freely admitted in the sūtra), but many characterizations are metaphors — a favorite being that brahman is like the sun or single light whose rays fall on and illuminate many things. The sacred text may even mislead, as when it suggests brahman has size. In fact it does not: nothing other than it exists, so it is everywhere, pervading all things rather than occupying any particular dimensions.

docs.title: The quarrel with Sāṃkhya — milk from grass
docs.text:
• [00:13:33] This brings a fine example of the "orthodox" Hindu schools entering heated disputes with one another. Bādarāyaṇa's insistence that brahman is the material cause of all things brings him into direct conflict with the Sāṃkhya school, which is named explicitly and made the target of a sustained critique.
  • [00:13:55] Sāṃkhya sees the world as evolving naturally from an underlying material stuff called pradhāna. Though Sāṃkhya too positions itself within the Brahmanical tradition, here it seems diametrically opposed to Vedānta: far from recognizing an intelligent, divine creator mind manifesting as all things, it has everything generated from pradhāna, an unintelligent stuff.
  • [00:14:29] Against this Bādarāyaṇa invokes the most familiar proof of a guiding intelligence in the universe — its striking, apparently providential order. He appeals "not so much to a stock example as a livestock example": getting the world we see out of pradhāna without brahman would be like getting milk out of grass without the involvement of a living cause, namely a cow.
  • [00:14:57] But the dispute is not only philosophical. Bādarāyaṇa wants us to see not just that the Sāṃkhya theory makes no sense, but that it cannot make sense of key Upaniṣadic texts — a point that emerges especially in Śaṅkara's commentary, which delves into extensive exegesis to show Sāṃkhya misreads the background passages.

docs.title: Against materialism — and the self that is not the body
docs.text: • [00:15:19] The sūtra also sets its face against more radical materialism and naturalism. Not only do the Vedas reject such attitudes, but if we relied on sensation and material causes alone we could never attain the liberation so dear to Bādarāyaṇa. Materialist explanations fail for the world as a whole and also for the human individual: the individual's self cannot be reduced to the body but is in fact independent of it.

docs.title: Brahman and the individual self: identity held in tension
docs.text:
• [00:15:54] Here comes what may be the single most famous teaching of the Vedānta-Sūtra, famous partly for its central role in Śaṅkara: that brahman has a very intimate relationship to the individual self. What sort of relationship exactly is not an easy question.
  • [00:16:09] Śaṅkara's Advaita Vedānta insists nothing is real apart from brahman — including every individual self. So the apparent fact that each of us is distinct from other things and from the ground of all existence is actually an illusion.
  • [00:16:33] Śaṅkara can draw on compelling evidence: Bādarāyaṇa suggests there is ultimately no difference between brahman as cause and the things it creates; on the self, he says brahman is identical with our vital breath, and instructs us to grasp brahman by meditating on it as our own self.
  • [00:16:56] Yet other passages seem to draw a firm distinction between the individual self and the highest self that is brahman. We glimpse here a debate already raging before the sūtra was written: earlier scholars who commented on the Upaniṣads held differing views — e.g. that brahman is simply the material constituent of the individual self, or that the individual self is distinct from brahman but becomes identical to it once liberated from the body.
  • [00:17:37] Perhaps the best conclusion on the basis of the sūtra itself is that the relation between brahman and the individual self is held in tension between sheer identity and difference. One's impression depends on which passage one reads — and certain passages "want to have it both ways," as when brahman is said to relate to individual selves like a snake to its coils.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text: • [00:17:59] As Vedānta develops, we'll meet someone who definitely doesn't want to have it both ways. After a short summer break the podcast returns in September with "only one way forward" — the non-dualism of Śaṅkara and Advaita Vedānta.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Vedānta-Sūtra — the founding text of Vedānta (Uttara-Mīmāṃsā), composed in current form likely 5th c. CE; cryptic, code-like, both philosophy and Upaniṣadic exegesis. Also called the Brahma-Sūtra (its first line is on brahman), the Uttara-Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra, and the Śārīraka-Sūtra (treating the embodied self).
  • Bādarāyaṇa — putative author; the sūtra's siddhānta (settled view) is given to him, triumphing over Jaimini's.
  • Pūrva- vs. Uttara-Mīmāṃsā — "prior" Mīmāṃsā (Jaimini, Śabara, Kumārila, Prabhākara; ritual exegesis) vs. "posterior" Mīmāṃsā = Vedānta (exegesis of the Upaniṣads, focused on brahman).
  • Jaimini — the Mīmāṃsā master here cast as the pūrva-pakṣa (initial view); ritual-focused, householder-oriented, restricts liberation to humans and denies gods.
  • Śaṅkara — 8th-c. non-dualist whose commentary dominates the reading of the sūtra; founder of Advaita Vedānta.
  • brahman — the single formless source of all things; both efficient and material cause of the world (Aristotle's terms), pervading everything, intimately related to the individual self.
  • the early Upaniṣads — esp. the Chāndogya and Great Forest (Bṛhadāraṇyaka); the texts the sūtra interprets, often by a single key word (the "great sayings").
  • "because of abiding and eating" — a one-line sūtra alluding to the two birds: the eating bird = the individual soul in worldly action; the quiet bird = brahman abiding unchanged.
  • liberation through knowledge of brahman — Bādarāyaṇa's central goal; valued for its own sake, lets one dispense with ritual fires, available even to the gods, favoring the ascetic over the householder.
  • brahman's "sport or play" — brahman creates the world for no real reason but mere play; the world's suffering is not brahman's fault but karmic punishment across endless rebirths.
  • the creation sequence — space (first effect, even identified with brahman, after Yājñavalkya's answer to Gārgī) → air → fire → water → earth, dissolving back into brahman in reverse at the cycle's end.
  • Sāṃkhya / pradhāna — rival Brahmanical school deriving the world from an unintelligent material principle (pradhāna); refuted via the world's providential order — "milk from grass without a cow."
  • identity-vs-difference of self and brahman — the sūtra's most famous, unresolved teaching; held "in tension," brahman relating to individual selves "like a snake to its coils."
