🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:21:43 In brief: Śaṅkara's radical "non-dual" Vedānta holds that the everyday world is an illusion (māyā/avidyā) masking the single, formless reality of brahman, and that liberation comes from knowing one's self (ātman) to be identical with it. The episode lays out his scriptural method, his attack on the Buddhists, the charge of inconsistency levelled by his critic Bhāskara, and a sympathetic reading that turns his apparent self-contradictions into stages on the path. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennari"; Śaṅkara ≈ "Shankara"; Śabara ≈ "Shabara"; Pūrva Mīmāṃsā ≈ "Purva Memamsa"; Mīmāṃsākas ≈ "mimamsukas"; brahman ≈ "Brahmann"; avidyā ≈ "avidya"; ātman ≈ "Atman"; Kumārila ≈ "Kumara"; bhāṣya ≈ "basya"; Bādarāyaṇa ≈ "Badarayana"; Upadeśasāhasrī ≈ "Upadehsha Sahastri"; Dvaita ≈ "Dwighta"; Bhāskara ≈ "Baskara"; Gauḍapāda ≈ "Gaudapada/Gautapada/Gautopada"; śruti ≈ "Shruti"; Sāṃkhya ≈ "Samkya"; jīva ≈ "Jiva"; skandhas ≈ "Scandhas/Skandas"; Mahāyāna ≈ "Mahayana"; Vijñānavāda ≈ "Lijnianavada"; Śūdras ≈ "Shudras"; Śṛṅgeri ≈ "Shringeri"; Bhartṛhari ≈ "Batsri Hari").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Śaṅkara — 8th-c. CE commentator, founder of Advaita (non-dual) Vedānta; the world is illusion, brahman alone is real [00:01:06].
  • Śabara — the great commentator on Pūrva Mīmāṃsā, defender of common sense, set up as Śaṅkara's foil [00:01:06].
  • The Vedānta-Sūtra of Bādarāyaṇa — the text on which Śaṅkara wrote his most celebrated commentary (bhāṣya) [00:04:05].
  • Gauḍapāda — Śaṅkara's "Paramaguru," precursor who already held many Advaita ideas and analogies [00:06:49].
  • Bhāskara — rival Vedānta commentator, Śaṅkara's near-contemporary critic, who charged him with hypocrisy [00:06:10].

docs.title: Two temperaments: leave the world alone, or overturn it
docs.text:
• [00:00:37] Some philosophers want to "leave the world pretty much as they find it," seeking a deeper understanding of reality as it seems, trusting everyday experience. Others want to overturn common sense, believing reality is very different from how it appears.
  • [00:00:56] These two approaches are usually ascribed to Aristotle and Plato among the Greeks — but the contrast fits, with at least as much accuracy, the Indian commentators Śabara and Śaṅkara, the authoritative interpreters of Pūrva Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta.
  • [00:01:14] On the face of it the two belong to a single tradition, devoted to interpreting the earlier and later parts of the Veda. But Śabara and the Mīmāṃsākas who followed him were "implacable defenders of common sense": the world is as we see it, and always has been. Śaṅkara "couldn't agree less."

docs.title: Śaṅkara's astonishing thesis: the world is an illusion
docs.text:
• [00:01:36] For Śaṅkara, the world is an illusion that masks the single underlying reality of brahman. To accept the reality of the everyday world is ignorance (avidyā). To know the sole reality of brahman, and the identity of the self (ātman) with brahman, is to achieve liberation.
  • [00:01:53] What led him to this view? "Nothing but the authority of Vedānta" — the later parts of the Veda, i.e. the Upaniṣads. Śaṅkara never tires of insisting his doctrine is stated plainly in numerous Upaniṣadic passages [00:02:08]: "Brahman is without a before and an after, without an inner and an outer"; "Brahman is this self here, which perceives everything"; "the finest essence here, that constitutes the self of this whole world… that is the truth, that is the self"; "it is brahman alone that extends over this whole universe."
  • [00:02:40] Other Vedic thinkers knew these passages too, but it was Śaṅkara who put them at the heart of Vedānta. Before and after him, other Vedāntins accepted that brahman is the single source of all things yet also that the world we see is real — for them everyday reality is a modification of brahman, which has taken on the forms of the things around us.
  • [00:03:04] Śaṅkara denied there could be two levels of reality, one apparent and one fundamental. Brahman "is not two": it is single and supreme, unchanging and ineffable. Hence the name of his tradition — Advaita, or non-dual Vedānta.

docs.title: Who Śaṅkara was, and how he wrote
docs.text:
• [00:03:30] One thing about him is utterly familiar: we don't know exactly when he lived. The traditional birth date is 788 AD, probably a bit late, but he was safely active in the 8th century — making him a rough contemporary of Kumārila, the great exponent of Pūrva Mīmāṃsā.
  • [00:03:46] He wrote commentaries on several Upaniṣads and on the Bhagavad-Gītā, which he held to encapsulate the essence of the whole Veda. His most celebrated work is his lengthy commentary, or bhāṣya, on the Vedānta-Sūtra ascribed to Bādarāyaṇa.
  • [00:04:12] Adamson's joke: you may feel cheated, wading through so much material only to learn it is all unreal except brahman. A shortcut exists — a far briefer introductory work, the Upadeśasāhasrī, which encapsulates his teaching. Still, it's worth reading as much Śaṅkara as you can, because he is "great philosophical reading."
  • [00:04:35] Unlike the compressed, elliptical Vedānta-Sūtra, Śaṅkara mounts elaborate arguments, often while refuting rival schools. He also has a good line in analogies [00:04:47]: the apparent reality of life is like the foam on the sea, like a seashell that seems to be silver, like a snake that turns out to be a coil of rope. To the puzzle of how a single brahman manifests as an illusory world, he answers that the single moon can appear as two to someone with double vision. The soul that finally gives up ignorance and accepts brahman is like a weary carpenter laying down his tools, or a tired falcon alighting to rest.
  • [00:05:27] Śaṅkara is also credited with founding four major centres of Hindu worship, taking a leaf from Buddhist monastic practice; the most famous is at Śṛṅgeri, where a temple still stands. All this earned him a leading place in the history of Indian religion and philosophy.

docs.title: Advaita as only one strand — and early critics
docs.text:
• [00:05:48] We should remember Advaita was only one sub-school within the larger Vedānta tradition. Centuries later a rival approach emerged, pointedly called Dvaita ("dual," as opposed to non-dual) Vedānta.
  • [00:06:05] Already within a generation or two, Śaṅkara was heavily criticized by other Vedāntins, including a major commentator on the Vedānta-Sūtra named Bhāskara. Bhāskara was appalled by Śaṅkara's tendency to abandon the ritual side of the Vedic tradition — the inevitable consequence, it seemed to him, of deeming the world of actions and fruits a mere illusion.
  • [00:06:32] Yet modern scholars find that, despite Bhāskara's disdain, the two commentaries share much common material — suggesting both drew on a rich earlier Vedānta tradition, now largely lost.
  • [00:06:49] We do know of a precursor, Gauḍapāda. Many of Śaṅkara's key ideas, and some of those nice analogies, are already in Gauḍapāda. Śaṅkara speaks of him with admiration, calling him Paramaguru — possibly "the teacher of Śaṅkara's teacher." But Adamson sets aside the question of how much credit belongs to each; the real questions are what the doctrine amounts to and whether there is any reason to believe it.

docs.title: The method: scripture, not argument
docs.text:
• [00:07:26] On whether there is reason to believe it, Śaṅkara is clear. Just as Pūrva Mīmāṃsā taught that matters of dharma are known only from the Veda, so Śaṅkara holds we could never come to know the truth of brahman if left to our own devices. Advaita is grounded in the interpretation of the sacred texts — śruti — not in philosophical arguments.
  • [00:07:45] Since many rivals (like the Sāṃkhya school) also accept Vedic authority, Śaṅkara often refutes them simply by quoting scriptures that fit his view better than theirs. He even complains that Sāṃkhya makes inferences from experience of the world when it should appeal to śruti: their empirical approach is wrong-headed, because the world is precisely an illusion masking brahman, so we cannot learn about brahman by observing it.
  • [00:08:22] In itself brahman is formless, so even with revelation it eludes both thought and speech. The closest we can come to experiencing it is an experience that is empty, utterly devoid of form — what happens in deep, dreamless sleep.

docs.title: Liberation through knowledge alone
docs.text:
• [00:08:41] This may sound mystical and anti-rationalist, but in another sense Śaṅkara is "a philosopher's philosopher." Most ancient Indian thinkers held that even the deepest understanding had to be combined with long practice. For Śaṅkara, meditation and ritual may be useful steps toward liberation, but ultimately liberation is secured through knowledge alone.
  • [00:09:04] If you truly understand that your individual self is identical to brahman, you are immediately freed from all suffering — and, for that matter, from all pleasure. This is because brahman is unchanging, unaffected by the processes the individual self undergoes through its ignorance.
  • [00:09:27] We reach liberation by being slowly weaned from the individual self, giving up identifying features such as caste, family affiliation, and even the desire to perform ritual — since brahman can never acquire the fruits of rituals. (You can see why a Vedic traditionalist like Bhāskara was annoyed.)

docs.title: Is Advaita just nihilism? The pure consciousness reply
docs.text:
• [00:09:55] Our own worry: doesn't Advaita amount to a kind of nihilism? If brahman is formless and ineffable, then saying "brahman alone is real" may seem to say the only reality is nothing at all.
  • [00:10:12] Not quite. Though brahman is not to be confused with the individual self — which Śaṅkara calls the jīva — ātman is still recognizably a kind of self: it is, for lack of better terms, consciousness or awareness. But a special, pure consciousness that is not aware of anything in particular.
  • [00:10:34] Back to deep sleep: when asleep there is not pure emptiness, but rather "an act of seeing without any visible object." Consciousness is evident to itself even when there is nothing of which it is conscious — the way the sun is luminous in itself before it illuminates anything else.
  • [00:10:58] A fine distinction — does it matter whether there is nothing at all or nothing but a conscious self conscious of nothing in particular? To Śaṅkara it makes all the difference, as emerges from his critique of Buddhism.

docs.title: The critique of Buddhism — and Śaṅkara's debts to it
docs.text:
• [00:11:09] The critique is remarkable partly because Śaṅkara seems deeply influenced by Buddhism, likely absorbing its ideas indirectly via Gauḍapāda. The Advaita rejection of everyday reality looks very Buddhist, as does its faith that liberation follows a proper understanding of the self, and its admission that Vedic ritual becomes irrelevant for the liberated.
  • [00:11:39] With his dismissal of caste and family as features of the illusory self, Śaṅkara also seems to hold out liberation to all people, as the Buddhists did. This is problematic for the lowest class, the Śūdras, since his own authoritative text, the Vedānta-Sūtra, seems to exclude them. Śaṅkara admits they cannot study the Vedas, but offers the prospect of other forms of learning.
  • [00:12:10] An aside: a legend tells that Śaṅkara once shied from touching a man of mixed caste as impure, and the man castigated him — pointing out that Śaṅkara's own Advaita implies such distinctions are irrelevant to the true self.
  • [00:12:26] These borrowings did not stop Śaṅkara attacking the Buddhists. He complains the Buddha taught several inconsistent theories, all false, perhaps because he was such a spiteful character that he deliberately wanted to confuse people. This "breathtakingly rude" remark shows Śaṅkara felt no sympathy — and that he didn't realize, or didn't care, that the supposedly inconsistent teachings actually belonged to different rival strands within Buddhism. Impolite and lacking historical nuance, the critique is nonetheless philosophically astute.

docs.title: Against the no-self doctrine: causation and memory
docs.text:
• [00:13:15] Śaṅkara aims at the Buddhist theory that there is no enduring self — only momentary features and acts of consciousness, the skandhas, which cause one another across time and aggregate into the illusion of a coherent, enduring individual.
  • [00:13:33] First argument: it's hard to see how a skandha existing only fleetingly at one moment can cause another skandha at the next — for by the time it should be causing the new one, it is already gone. (Śaṅkara here invokes his own, non-Buddhist, assumption that effects depend on causes that exist simultaneously with them.)
  • [00:14:02] Second, memory shows the same individual survives over time: part of what I remember in recalling a past experience is precisely that it was me who had it. Remembering an almond croissant eaten this morning, I am in no doubt that the person who enjoyed it is the same person I am now.
  • [00:14:25] By itself the memory argument isn't sufficient — the Buddhist can reply that the former aggregate only seems identical to the present one because of the causal links between them. But Śaṅkara has already blocked that move by denying that momentary aggregates can form causal chains at all.

docs.title: Against Vijñānavāda — and the charge of hypocrisy
docs.text:
• [00:14:53] A more surprising diatribe targets a Mahāyāna teaching called Vijñānavāda, which rejects everyday reality as illusion. Śaṅkara dismisses it scornfully: it is futile to deny that external things cause our experiences, since this is patently obvious. Experience clearly involves both a subject and an object, yet these Buddhists deny both — doubting both the enduring self and the real things we perceive.
  • [00:15:30] But hang on: how can Śaṅkara of all people insist on the reality of the world? Doesn't he, like his Mahāyāna opponent, take the world to be mere illusion? This is exactly the objection made by Bhāskara, who accused Śaṅkara of rank hypocrisy — insisting on realism against the Buddhists, only to lapse into anti-realism in setting out his own Advaita.
  • [00:16:00] The suspicion deepens elsewhere in the commentary. For every passage stressing the illusory nature of all but brahman, there is another suggesting brahman really does produce the world by taking on form: brahman makes things without any instrument or pre-existing material, like the spider spinning its web from itself; brahman is both the stuff things are made of and the agent that makes them; and there is a distinction between a higher brahman (formless) and a lower brahman (which takes on forms available to experience, or plays the role of the embodied self). What is the point of all this if the things made, and the individual self, are nothing but illusions?

docs.title: Resolving the contradiction: stages on the path
docs.text:
• [00:17:08] A sympathetic reader might take refuge in history: perhaps Śaṅkara includes contradictory material because he is reproducing earlier commentators, many more realist than Gauḍapāda or himself — so his bhāṣya would be a "microcosm of the Vedānta tradition." One historian wrote that, since Vedānta itself split and absorbed ideas from other schools, its history is "a miniature copy or reflection of the entire history of Indian philosophy."
  • [00:17:45] But is Śaṅkara really so thoughtless as to compile disparate material without trying for consistency — especially in the very section where he insults the Buddha for inconsistency? Some scholars think his own ideas developed over his career, moving from Gauḍapāda's radicalism toward a more realist understanding.
  • [00:18:13] A more satisfying solution extracts a defensible position from the text. Remember: we cannot reason our way to brahman; that truth is found only in śruti, which the Buddhists reject. So it is entirely consistent for Śaṅkara to say the Buddhist has no basis for rejecting everyday experience, even though he himself ultimately will — on the authority of śruti, not argument.
  • [00:18:43] Moreover, even once śruti is accepted, abandoning everyday experience is not the first move in his philosophy but the last. Along the way it is a useful step to think of brahman as the underlying cause of all things, then to realize that effects are implicitly present in their causes. An effect is not wholly non-existent before it appears — not like "the son of a barren woman," Śaṅkara's example of something that cannot exist at all. If effects were not somehow pre-contained in causes, anything could come from anything — clay pots from milk.
  • [00:19:28] This account of causation improves on the Buddhist one, but it is "like an unfired clay pot, not yet finished." The next realization: effects are really nothing other than their causes — pots are just clay in a certain shape. On that basis the forms imposed on the cause can be seen as unreal. Śaṅkara calls this superimposition: the guise brahman wears is a kind of mask, and it is sheer ignorance to mistake the mask for what lies beneath — to confuse a real thing with a property falsely ascribed to it, like the seashell that looks like silver.
  • [00:20:21] Only after this "arduous and challenging" chain of thought are we ready for the radical conclusions of Advaita. And — crucially — without the prompting of śruti we would have no warrant to follow the argument to its end. For all his sophistication, Śaṅkara looks ultimately to the Upaniṣads as the sole source of our knowledge of the unchanging consciousness that is brahman.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:20:56] Having examined the Vedānta-Sūtra and its most famous commentary, we are nearly ready to move to other schools — but first, another body of literature from the context of Vedic exegesis. As we saw with Pāṇini, the study of Sanskrit grammar often yielded philosophical insight, and in the age of the sūtra grammarians went on producing ever more nuanced linguistic analysis, even as all schools adopted Sanskrit as the language of discourse.
  • [00:21:31] One of the most important of these grammarians, Bhartṛhari, was apparently also an important member of the Vedānta tradition. Next time: "grammar school" — bring an apple for the teacher.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Śaṅkara — 8th-c. CE commentator, founder of Advaita Vedānta; the everyday world is illusion, brahman alone is real, and liberation comes from knowing ātman = brahman.
  • Advaita Vedānta — "non-dual" Vedānta; denies two levels of reality, holding brahman to be single, unchanging, ineffable.
  • brahman — the sole ultimate reality; formless, eludes thought and speech; both higher (formless) and lower (form-taking) aspects appear in Śaṅkara's text.
  • ātman / jīva — ātman is the self, identical with brahman; pure consciousness aware of nothing in particular. The jīva is the individual embodied self we must be weaned from.
  • avidyā — ignorance; accepting the reality of the everyday world.
  • māyā / illusion — the everyday world as a mask over brahman; illustrated by foam on the sea, a snake that is a coil of rope, a seashell that looks like silver, two moons in double vision.
  • śruti — the sacred revealed texts (esp. the Upaniṣads); for Śaṅkara the sole source of knowledge of brahman, since reason alone cannot reach it.
  • Vedānta-Sūtra — the text ascribed to Bādarāyaṇa on which Śaṅkara wrote his great commentary; compressed and elliptical.
  • bhāṣya — a commentary; Śaṅkara's bhāṣya on the Vedānta-Sūtra is his most celebrated work.
  • Upadeśasāhasrī — a brief introductory work encapsulating Śaṅkara's teaching; the "shortcut."
  • Śabara / Pūrva Mīmāṃsā / Mīmāṃsākas — the commentator and school of common-sense realism, treated as Śaṅkara's foil; the world is as we see it.
  • Gauḍapāda — Śaṅkara's "Paramaguru" and precursor, source of many Advaita ideas and analogies, more radical than later realist Vedāntins.
  • Bhāskara — rival Vedānta commentator who attacked Śaṅkara for abandoning ritual and for hypocrisy (realism against Buddhists, anti-realism in his own view).
  • Dvaita — the later "dual" Vedānta, named in contrast to Advaita.
  • skandhas — the Buddhist momentary aggregates of consciousness that supposedly create the illusion of an enduring self; Śaṅkara refutes them via causation and memory.
  • Vijñānavāda — the Mahāyāna teaching rejecting external reality, which Śaṅkara attacks for denying both subject and object.
  • superimposition — Śaṅkara's term for mistaking the form (mask) for the underlying real cause; confusing a thing with a property falsely ascribed to it.
  • Bhartṛhari — Sanskrit grammarian, also said to belong to the Vedānta tradition; subject of the next episode.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 25 — "Communication Breakdown: Bhartṛhari on Language"
docs.text:
← Ep 24

Ep 26 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:19:03 In brief: The grammarian Bhartṛhari makes the study of language "the door to liberation," arguing that meaning (sphoṭa) is a single, partless, timeless reality that whole sentences merely make manifest — and that this indivisible meaning ultimately points back to Brahman, making his linguistics a distinctively grammatical version of Vedānta. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Bhartṛhari ≈ "Batri Hari/Barzrihari/Barthihari/Bhatrihari/Batrijari/Patsri-Hari"; Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janard and Gannery"; Pāṇini ≈ "Panani/Pannoni"; Patañjali ≈ "Patanjali"; Mahābhāṣya ≈ "Mahabashya"; Vākyapadīya ≈ "vaciapadilla/Vakia Padilla"; sphoṭa ≈ "Svota"; śabda ≈ "Shabda"; jāti ≈ "Jiva"; Vṛtti ≈ "Vriti"; Ṭīkā/Dīpikā ≈ "Tika/Dipika"; Brahman ≈ "Brahmann"; Porphyry ≈ "Porfurian"; Dignāga ≈ "Dignaga"; Śaṅkara ≈ "Shankara").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Bhartṛhari — 5th-c. CE grammarian-philosopher who treats the analysis of language as the path to liberation [00:01:01].
  • Pāṇini (6th/5th c. BCE) and his commentator Patañjali (2nd c. CE, the Mahābhāṣya) — the grammatical lineage Bhartṛhari inherits [00:01:20].
  • The Vākyapadīya — Bhartṛhari's "treatise on words and sentences," with its possibly self-authored explanatory Vṛtti [00:02:12].
  • The Mīmāṃsā school — the rival theory of meaning Bhartṛhari argues against [00:06:36].
  • Dignāga — the Buddhist thinker who later reacted to Bhartṛhari and drew out his skeptical implications [00:18:16].

docs.title: The grammarian's boast: language is the door to liberation
docs.text:
• [00:00:36] Intellectuals tend to think their own discipline is the most important: historians warn that those who forget the past are doomed to repeat it, mathematicians prize the certainty of their proofs, and philosophers call their field "the queen of the sciences," with everything else a mere "subject."
  • [00:01:01] So it's par for the course that Bhartṛhari, one of the greatest figures in classical Sanskrit grammar, tells us that the study of language constitutes the door to liberation. He's modest enough, though, to credit others with opening that door.
  • [00:01:20] He belongs to the tradition founded by the great Pāṇini (episode 8), but responds directly to the later Patañjali, whose great commentary on Pāṇini — the Mahābhāṣya — inspires Bhartṛhari's own treatises.
  • [00:01:39] The dates span a millennium: Pāṇini worked in the 6th or 5th centuries BCE, his commentator Patañjali in the 2nd century CE, both drawing on shadowier predecessors; Bhartṛhari then arrives in the 5th century CE, a full thousand years after Pāṇini.

docs.title: Bhartṛhari's works
docs.text:
• [00:02:00] He was apparently the first to write a super-commentary — a Ṭīkā or Dīpikā — on Patañjali's commentary. But his fame rests on another work based on Patañjali: the Vākyapadīya, the treatise on words and sentences.
  • [00:02:14] Its style is by now familiar — terse, aphoristic remarks that presuppose knowledge of the texts being alluded to. True to Indian habit, the Vākyapadīya itself acquired further commentary: an accompanying explanatory work, the Vṛtti, may even have been written by Bhartṛhari himself. Whether or not it was, the Vṛtti is a helpful guide to the much more compressed Vākyapadīya.

docs.title: Grammar is philosophy — and it leads to Brahman
docs.text:
• [00:02:51] More than Pāṇini or Patañjali, Bhartṛhari shows the philosophical importance of the Sanskrit grammatical tradition. His boast that grammar is the door to liberation suggests that for him the study of language simply is philosophy. Where other Indian thinkers saw meditation or ethical discipline as the route to liberation, Bhartṛhari takes a far more intellectualist stance: it is knowledge that sets us free.
  • [00:03:21] Not knowledge of grammatical minutiae — case endings, singular versus plural — though the Vākyapadīya covers those at length. Rather, the analysis of language is a step toward a higher understanding in which we grasp the reality that underlies and gives rise to language. That reality is Brahman.
  • [00:03:48] This is why Bhartṛhari is covered here alongside Vedānta. Like the Vedāntins, he is convinced that Brahman is the single fundamental principle of all things, known to us only because of the Veda. Bhartṛhari offers a distinctively linguistic version of this idea: grammar is worth studying simply to interpret the Sanskrit of the Veda, but more fundamentally, it is language that accounts for the division of the single Brahman into the multiple reality we experience.

docs.title: sphoṭa and śabda: meaning and its representation
docs.text:
• [00:04:26] To see how, we must ask what Bhartṛhari takes language to be — not an easy question, since the Vākyapadīya summarizes and refutes many rival views while sometimes leaving his own position unclear, and uses technical terms whose sense isn't obvious. The two most important here are sphoṭa and śabda.
  • [00:04:57] Roughly: sphoṭa is the inner meaning of language, while śabda is the language used to represent that meaning. Straightforward enough — except that śabda (linguistic representation) can occur either in the mind or in actual verbal speech.
  • [00:05:14] Bhartṛhari says language in the mind gives rise to expressed language "like one fire kindling another." When you hear an utterance you depend on your own mental representations to understand it, and so gain access to the inner meaning (sphoṭa) the speaker was trying to express.
  • [00:05:38] So far this sounds commonsensical. Suppose I want to warn you that there's a giraffe in your kitchen: I formulate the sentence in my mind, utter it aloud, and trigger comprehension in your mind (along with the hope the giraffe will clean up last night's dishes). The verbal utterance and the two mental acts all point toward a single shared meaning.

docs.title: The partless, timeless meaning
docs.text: • [00:06:03] It's here that things get controversial. The meaning (sphoṭa) is in a sense the core of language, since capturing meaning is the whole point of the linguistic enterprise. Yet sphoṭa is also non-linguistic: according to Bhartṛhari, meaning in itself has no parts and is not subject to time. Only actual verbal utterances are affected by time, because we must speak one word after another — whereas a meaning can be represented in the mind all at once.

docs.title: Against Mīmāṃsā: words don't build meaning, they manifest it
docs.text:
• [00:06:36] This is diametrically opposed to a rival view Bhartṛhari associates with the Mīmāṃsā school. For the Mīmāṃsakas, meaning is not prior to linguistic expression; rather, it is constituted by the verbal utterance, whose parts work together to give rise to the intended meaning. Words like "giraffe" and "kitchen" get fitted into a grammatical structure, and the result is a meaningful sentence.
  • [00:07:05] For Bhartṛhari this gets things backward. Individual words have no meaning in their own right; they signify only in the context of a sentence — just as the sounds making up a word ("jir," "a," "f") are not themselves meaningful. Two arguments:
  • [00:07:25] The words pass away as they are uttered. By the time I reach "kitchen," "giraffe" has already come and gone, so the words cannot literally combine to produce a single united meaning, because they never coexist.
  • [00:07:47] Some words have no referent. In "there is not a giraffe in the kitchen," the word "giraffe" signifies no actual giraffe; it is meaningful only as part of the whole sentence.
  • [00:08:06] So Bhartṛhari concludes that the words in a sentence make an inner meaning manifest, rather than actually constituting it.
  • [00:08:13] The same holds from the listener's side: rather than grasping each word's meaning in sequence, one comprehends the meaning of the whole sentence at once, in a "flash of understanding" that arrives when the sentence reaches its conclusion.

docs.title: The objection from contradiction
docs.text:
• [00:08:31] Bhartṛhari anticipates a Mīmāṃsā objection: part-by-part composition would better explain logical relations between sentences, such as contradiction. "There is a giraffe in the kitchen" and "there is not a giraffe in the kitchen" look like the same sentence with one part — the word "not" — added to generate a contradictory meaning.
  • [00:09:06] His reply: relations between sentences, contradiction included, simply have to do with the degree of overall resemblance between the indivisible meanings of the sentences in question. No part-composition required.
  • [00:09:17] Despite this holism, Bhartṛhari still has much to say about the grammatical features of individual words — case, gender of nouns. But ultimately grammar is the study of the way communication breaks down meaning: the grammarian analyzes the parts of speech that let us express meaning, while realizing that the meaning is unified and prior to that expression. The Mīmāṃsā approach, by contrast, is "like trying to understand a pot by starting from broken shards rather than the whole vessel."

docs.title: From language to reality: the latent seed of speech
docs.text:
• [00:09:55] Now comes a flash of understanding of our own, noting the affinity between Bhartṛhari's theory of language and the Vedānta theory of reality. Just as Vedānta sees the multiplicity of phenomenal experience as an expression of the single source, Brahman, so Bhartṛhari thinks divisible speech expresses indivisible meaning.
  • [00:10:13] But there's more than analogy here: for Bhartṛhari, language is the very means by which we have experience and come to know the world. Even the most rudimentary perceptions — like those of small children — contain what he calls a "latent seed of language," which cannot yet be communicated. Full-blown cognition, though, is always linguistic, so that our knowledge is permeated by words.
  • [00:10:44] This too looks like common sense: we grasp things only by filing them under descriptions or concepts. Perceiving the alarmingly tall animal in the kitchen as a giraffe arguably depends on my having the word "giraffe" in my vocabulary.

docs.title: Universals (jāti) and the primacy of the general
docs.text:
• [00:11:09] These classifying concepts are what philosophers today call universals, and Bhartṛhari uses the same notion; his Sanskrit term is jāti. He's deeply interested in universals, partly because they're so critical to grammar. Some grammarians held that language refers first to individual things — the particular giraffe in your kitchen — but for Bhartṛhari meanings are primarily universal. The universal, indeed, is what we really mean by sphoṭa.
  • [00:11:51] This shows in how words work, especially in a language like Sanskrit where you start with a basic noun and add endings for gender and number. His English-friendly example: actor, actors, actress, actresses — a single universal meaning ("someone who acts on stage") licenses us to apply the related words to many objects.
  • [00:12:23] He again uses resemblance: we call every giraffe "giraffe" because they resemble one another in the relevant way while differing otherwise (this one doing dishes in the kitchen, that one reading philosophy in the study). Even the same individual resembles itself at other times — which is why we can say "you are like yourself," the remark you might make at a school reunion after thirty years.

docs.title: From universal meaning to a universe of universals
docs.text:
• [00:12:52] Most Indian thinkers believed language reveals the structure of reality, and as a language expert Bhartṛhari was hardly going to disagree. So the primacy of the universal at the level of meaning shows that reality itself is first universal and only then particular: individual things reveal the universal just as individual words reveal the meaning of a whole sentence.
  • [00:13:24] Why trust that language captures the way things are? Because Bhartṛhari adheres to a belief first met in Mīmāṃsā: the Veda — and hence language itself — is unoriginated. He takes this to imply a primary classification of reality in terms of universals, the eternal meanings revealed in the language of scripture.
  • [00:13:55] That makes him sound a bit like Plato: universals, like Platonic Forms, give significance to our words and serve as the fundamental principles of all things.

docs.title: How do the universals relate to Brahman?
docs.text:
• [00:14:06] But for Bhartṛhari the truly fundamental principle is Brahman — so how do his universals relate to that single source? Scholars don't agree.
  • [00:14:20] Reading one: Brahman is effectively the most general universal, identical with being — the class of all things that exist. Other universals add differentiation, progressively narrowing it down: some beings are alive, some living things are animals, some animals are giraffes, and some giraffes (though not many) are in kitchens. On this reading Bhartṛhari sounds less like Plato and more like a Neoplatonist using Aristotelian logic — specifically like Porphyry, whose famous "Porphyrian tree" is just such a hierarchy of genera and species.
  • [00:15:09] Reading two (which has challenged the first fairly persuasively): what we really find in the Vākyapadīya is that the universals are all identical with Brahman, constituting various means of expressing its fundamental reality. This yields a neat parallel: just as the universals divide Brahman while being identical with it, so individual giraffes both divide and yet are somehow identical with the universal giraffe.
  • [00:15:44] Either way, for Bhartṛhari the universals form a second layer of principles that manifest and differentiate the most fundamental reality, Brahman — and the universals are in turn made manifest, on the metaphysical side by individuals, on the linguistic side by mental representation and speech.

docs.title: Dualism or non-dualism? Is grammar a ladder to throw away?
docs.text:
• [00:16:12] Less clear is whether this amounts to the radical proposal found last time in Śaṅkara's Advaita Vedānta. Is Bhartṛhari saying that the language and universal meaning he devoted himself to is, in the end, a falsification of the single reality of Brahman — our world of experience, structured by language, just an illusion? If so, grammar would be less a door to liberation than a ladder to be thrown away once Brahman is grasped directly.
  • [00:16:49] As with the Brahma-Sūtra, the Vākyapadīya contains passages supporting both readings:
  • [00:17:01] For dualism (the world of experience is real, but a secondary, lesser reality than Brahman): Brahman is said to possess powers for producing other things and to take on forms when they're produced. Bhartṛhari's celebrated image fits here — Brahman is like a peacock's egg, which reveals a welter of brilliant colors once it hatches into the bird and its plumage.
  • [00:17:30] For non-dualism: passages connecting language with unreality. Words can express non-existent things — compared to the circle we see when looking at a whirling firebrand — and elsewhere Bhartṛhari says the study of language is a path to truth even though it deals with what is unreal. Comments at the start of the Vākyapadīya in the explanatory Vṛtti also tend non-dualist.
  • [00:18:04] This side of Bhartṛhari brings him close not only to the later Śaṅkara but also to contemporary Buddhists, who were more forthright in condemning the world of experience as illusion.

docs.title: Dignāga's reaction, and where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:18:16] In fact one thinker who reacted to Bhartṛhari was the great Buddhist Dignāga, quick to point out the skeptical implications lurking in the theory: language may distort reality by dividing it, pulling it apart into an infinity of fragments. Much more on Dignāga, but much later.
  • [00:18:39] For now there are more Vedic schools to consider — soon moving on from Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta to the Sāṃkhya and Yoga schools. But before closing the door on Vedānta, the next episode features a guest, the indologist Francis Clooney, for one more attempt to liberate listeners from confusion about the tradition.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Bhartṛhari — 5th-c. CE Sanskrit grammarian; holds that the study of language is "the door to liberation" and that knowledge of language's underlying reality (Brahman) sets us free.
  • Pāṇini — founder of the grammatical tradition (6th/5th c. BCE), covered in episode 8.
  • Patañjali — Pāṇini's 2nd-c. CE commentator; his Mahābhāṣya inspired Bhartṛhari's treatises.
  • Vākyapadīya — Bhartṛhari's terse, aphoristic "treatise on words and sentences," his main philosophical work.
  • Vṛtti — an explanatory commentary on the Vākyapadīya, possibly by Bhartṛhari himself; tends in a non-dualist direction.
  • Ṭīkā / Dīpikā — Bhartṛhari's super-commentary on Patañjali's commentary.
  • sphoṭa — the inner meaning of language; partless, timeless, non-linguistic, grasped "all at once"; identified with the universal.
  • śabda — the linguistic representation of meaning, occurring either in the mind or in spoken utterance; mental language kindles spoken language "like one fire kindling another."
  • jāti — the universal; for Bhartṛhari, meaning is primarily universal, and universals (revealed eternally in scripture) classify reality.
  • Mīmāṃsā — rival school holding that meaning is constituted by the verbal utterance's parts, not (as Bhartṛhari says) merely manifested by them.
  • Brahman — the single fundamental principle; either the most general universal (being) or the reality with which all universals are identical.
  • Veda — held to be unoriginated; the warrant that language reflects the eternal structure of reality.
  • Dignāga — Buddhist thinker who reacted to Bhartṛhari, exposing the skeptical implication that language distorts reality by fragmenting it.
  • Śaṅkara — Advaita Vedāntin (previous episode); the non-dualist reading brings Bhartṛhari close to him.
  • peacock's egg — Bhartṛhari's image for (dualist) Brahman producing the colorful manifold world.
  • whirling firebrand — image for how words can express non-existent things, illustrating the non-dualist/unreality strand.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 26 — "Francis Clooney on Vedānta"
docs.text:
← Ep 25

Ep 27 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Francis Clooney 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Francis Clooney · Runtime: 00:34:07 In brief: An interview with Francis Clooney (Parkman Professor of Divinity, Harvard) on Vedānta as the "later Mīmāṃsā" — its layered texts (Veda → sūtra → commentary), why exegesis of scripture still counts as philosophy, whether it's better called theology, and how Śaṅkara's radical non-dualism sits within (and strains against) a tradition that submits to the Veda. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannery"; Mīmāṃsā ≈ "me-mamsa / Memomsa / Mamma'sa"; Jaimini ≈ "Jiamini"; Bādarāyaṇa ≈ "Badryana / Badurayana / Bahayayana"; Śabara ≈ "Shabura / Shavara / Shubara"; Śaṅkara ≈ "chakra / chancra / Shankar"; Rāmānuja ≈ "Ramanaja / Ramanages"; Madhva ≈ "mudva"; Bhartṛhari ≈ "Batrari"; Pierre Hadot ≈ "Pierre Adou"; Chāndogya ≈ "Chandogia"; Bṛhadāraṇyaka ≈ "Brihadaranyika").

docs.title: Two halves of one tradition: Mīmāṃsā and Vedānta
docs.text:
• [00:00:13] Adamson introduces the guest: Francis Clooney, Parkman Professor of Divinity, Professor of Comparative Theology, and Director of the Center for the Study of World Religions at Harvard, here to discuss Vedānta.
  • [00:00:43] Vedānta is also known as Uttara-Mīmāṃsā ("later Mīmāṃsā"), as opposed to Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā ("prior Mīmāṃsā"). Adamson asks how the two relate and whether they form one united tradition.
  • [00:01:10] Clooney starts from the source material, very different on each side. Mīmāṃsā works on the Vedic ritual texts — those uttered in ritual plus the directives for performing it — and its job, at every stage, is to "understand and show the coherence" between what the text says and the actual performance.
  • [00:01:49] Vedānta is traced instead to the Upaniṣads, the "so-called late Vedic texts." Sharing the same ritual heritage, they are nonetheless "rather more philosophical" — concerned with the nature of reality, the self, what happens after death, "what is true or undeniable in reality." So at one level the two schools differ simply by their starting material.
  • [00:02:26] But they are also alike: both have sūtra texts — short aphorisms that combine, organize, and clarify each body of material. On the Mīmāṃsā side, the ~2,700 sūtras of Jaimini organize a vast ritual literature, raising the hard problems and resolving them economically. On the Vedānta side, the many Upaniṣads say many different things about the self, brahman, the world, and human destiny, and the sūtra attributed to Bādarāyaṇa aims to show "there is a coherent teaching across the Upaniṣads and not a multiplicity of meanings." Both share a "scholastic intent to show the harmony" of their texts.
  • [00:03:38] Adamson notes the Mīmāṃsakas and Vedāntins themselves think of earlier and later Veda as one united body — "the Veda broadly considered." Clooney agrees [00:03:51]: any scholar sees these as stages, chronologically earlier and later, in "a singular development over time." The later isn't necessarily better, "but the later does seem to presume the earlier," so both sides treat early and late Veda as "integrally connected" and "together for some purpose."

docs.title: Layers of text: Veda, sūtra, commentary
docs.text:
• [00:04:45] Adamson reframes it as a layering of texts: (1) the original Vedic texts, including the Upaniṣads; (2) the sūtras that systematize them; (3) the commentary on those sūtras. Some of the most important figures in both schools are commentators — Śaṅkara, for example.
  • [00:05:11] Adamson recalls that in his early Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā work, Clooney stressed "excavating the meaning" of Jaimini's sūtra — appreciating it for its own sake, if not stripping away the later commentary. How far is that possible for Bādarāyaṇa's Vedānta-Sūtra?
  • [00:05:39] Clooney calls it a necessary question. Both sūtra texts — Jaimini's ~2,700, Bādarāyaṇa's ~500 — are "as it were, floating in space." No author simply "sat down one day and composed these vast sūtra texts without any context"; they bear the marks of teaching traditions, likely reminders to teachers and students of the topics to consider — tools "in the lively context of debating" ritual problems on one side and philosophical problems on the other.
  • [00:06:35] Over time the texts detach from those contexts. We're left with the settled sūtras, which — if they were reminders of an ongoing discussion — "can seem rather more obscure" once the discussions stop, or to readers who were never part of them. Being memory-prompts, they're "often extremely brief," rarely full sentences, "often just a word or two" [00:07:12] — so problems of interpretation come to the fore.
  • [00:07:35] And the commentators may be separated by centuries from the sūtras: Śabara two to four centuries after Jaimini, Śaṅkara two or three after Bādarāyaṇa. One must trust that "something coherent and continuous went on in the teaching tradition," but the gap raises the real question: "do we actually understand what the original text was intending?"

docs.title: Lost debates preserved inside the commentaries
docs.text:
• [00:08:12] Adamson observes that Śabara and Śaṅkara reveal intervening debates: just as the sūtras allude to other views, the commentators allude to people who lived between the sūtra and themselves. So even though those intermediate works are lost, "those other ideas are kind of preserved in the commentaries themselves."
  • [00:08:34] Clooney confirms it. Both sūtra texts name older teachers prior to themselves, and the commentators — Śabara on one side, Śaṅkara ("the first commentator of Vedānta whose written work has come down to us") on the other — refer to other opinions, occasionally a named teacher but often vaguely, "there are some who say this... some who say that." These intervening arguments are "further developed" forms of arguments already in the (argumentative) sūtras, and the commentators are "trying to encapsulate and then take a strong opinion regarding debates that have happened before their time."

docs.title: Philosophy or theology? Exegesis as a way of thinking
docs.text:
• [00:09:25] Adamson presses the framing. Clooney called Mīmāṃsā "more about ritual" and Vedānta "more about philosophy," and the series treats Vedānta as philosophy. But Clooney is a professor of comparative theology — so is it legitimate, or more legitimate, to think of Vedānta texts as theological rather than philosophical works?
  • [00:10:01] Clooney backs up. In both schools there's a distinction between the ritual and meditative practice and the authors' and commentators' efforts to understand, contextualize, "read according to tradition," and find claims about reality in the texts — moving into "an entire religious context" where intellectual, performative, and ethical questions interconnect.
  • [00:10:52] Crucially, the structure of "having the sūtras and then having the commentary is an allegiance to the older texts which are considered to be sacred scripture." There is material "we are beholden to. We submit ourselves to it and work within its frame," then think "as vigorously and robustly as we can."
  • [00:11:22] On the modern Western philosophy/theology distinction: though both schools have strong philosophical elements, there's "a certain boundary within which their deliberation takes place." These thinkers will not question the authority of scripture; they take it as presenting the problems we must deal with. That "deference to scripture" "could easily be called theological thinking, rather than a philosophical thinking where independence of thought" is at issue. Where there is sacred scripture and expectations of religious performance, "theology seems to be a very good word to use."
  • [00:12:23] Adamson quotes Clooney back to himself: Vedānta is "an exegesis of texts and a philosophy of response to texts." That raises the worry whether exegesis on sacred texts can be philosophy at all — since many think philosophy must be a "disinterested, dispassionate, non-authority-laden search for truth," whereas these thinkers look like they're "just trying to tell us what a text means."
  • [00:13:11] Clooney answers via the structure of Bādarāyaṇa's Vedānta-Sūtra: he organizes the problems and insights of the Upaniṣads to stress taking them to heart, believing the scriptures are coherent and non-contradictory, that their positions are preferable to rival schools (Jains, Buddhists, others), and that properly understanding the Upaniṣads on self, world, and brahman "prepares one for the arduous work of meditation" — pursued both on the texts and within "a certain way of life." The last part of the sūtras describes the result: a transformation of one's life and "an ascent to a higher reality and ultimately to union with brahman."
  • [00:14:24] So given "the intensity of the debates," one can call it philosophical "if one has a rich sense of philosophy" — Clooney invokes Pierre Hadot's philosophy as a way of life: thought transformative of the thinker, "following the right ideas through to a coherent conclusion." Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, and Madhva disagree on what ultimate reality is like, "but they agree that this is a transformative philosophy." Clarifying understanding and removing errors transform you now and prepare you for a life that "passes beyond this world," as the Chāndogya Upaniṣad says, not returning to ordinary existence.

docs.title: Brahman: a philosophical and a theological idea at once
docs.text:
• [00:15:35] Adamson notes that brahman seems "simultaneously a philosophical and theological idea." There's a metaphysical question — what is brahman, how does the phenomenal world relate to it? — and Śaṅkara's "very radical answer" that the world is an illusion, or just how brahman presents itself, sounds like a philosophical proposal "with a kind of skeptical" edge. Yet brahman is also an object of worship; people often think of brahman in Vedānta as God. So this is "either both theological and philosophical, or maybe the distinction breaks down here."
  • [00:16:26] Clooney agrees that real philosophical questions arise — the one and the many, how time relates to a timeless reality, sense-knowledge versus knowledge beyond the senses, "a kind of idealism" about a pure self or ultimate reality — debated over centuries, in India "but not only in India."
  • [00:17:06] What is distinctive to Vedānta is "a certain skepticism about the ability of the human mind on its own" to speculate usefully here. With so many possibilities — is brahman the same as the world or greater, is the world real or illusory, is our ordinary identity true or a falsehood — "there are as many opinions as there are teachers."
  • [00:17:43] So the shared view (cutting across Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, and the rest) is that the Upaniṣads, clarified by the sūtras, give "a correct approach to this higher knowledge." Human questioning is valuable, "but at a certain point one must submit one's understanding... to the frame of knowledge given in the Upaniṣads as read through the sūtras" — a transition from independent philosophizing to one that pays due deference to tradition in all Vedānta schools.

docs.title: Is Śaṅkara even faithful to the Veda? The ritual problem
docs.text:
• [00:18:30] Adamson raises a tension specific to Advaita Vedānta. Has "philosophical speculation led [Śaṅkara] to sacrifice" what should be incumbent on him as a Vedic exegete? Rival commentators say exactly that: he has effectively dispensed with ritual, and perhaps there's no longer a coherent notion of karma or dharma, since all of that is phenomenal. If he "condemns all of that as illusory" (maybe too strong, Adamson allows), how can he make sense of "these very fundamental aspects of Vedic tradition?"
  • [00:19:29] Clooney sorts it into levels. First, rhetoric: rival schools — the "different / non-different" schools and the "kind of dualist" school of Madhva — can be "quite polemical and quite devastating," attacking Śaṅkara as "unfaithful to the Vedas," "dismissive of tradition," "tantamount to being a Buddhist." This is "part of the either game or the serious project" of arguing about these materials.
  • [00:20:20] Second, when one separates the philosophy from the exegesis — especially reading Śaṅkara through later teachers and modern textbooks — he can look like a system-builder "not really deferential to the Upaniṣads." But "if one actually reads his work" — the Brahma-Sūtra commentary, where he "arduously" struggles both to establish the non-dualism of brahman and self and "to still find a place for ritual performance," for the teacher, for scripture, "even... a sense of karma" — one sees "the struggle of an intellectual who's chosen not to leave the Vedic tradition behind."
  • [00:21:23] Finally, beyond the "classic statement" in the Brahma-Sūtra commentary, one must read his commentaries on the individual Upaniṣads — "most notably" his "brilliant and greatest" commentary on the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. There he works out brahman as self with "very careful gradations" of how that higher consciousness becomes accessible to people who begin as committed ritualists — how their "dharmic practice" enables them "to move beyond dharma to a higher kind of knowledge." So he is "not simply offering an alternative philosophy divorced from the Upaniṣads," but showing "how this philosophy and liberative theory grows out of the text he's commenting on."

docs.title: Ritual as preparation for knowledge — and the Buddhist comparison
docs.text:
• [00:22:46] Adamson asks whether Śaṅkara could treat dharmic ritual as an initial / preparatory stage transcended once you achieve "identifying your consciousness with brahman." Clooney points to the third book of the Brahma-Sūtra, where Bādarāyaṇa's sūtras hold that "there can be no guarantee that ritual action causes knowledge" — many ritualists never pass "from the cause, the ritual practice, to the effect, the higher knowledge."
  • [00:23:40] Yet ritual is necessary to prepare the person for higher knowledge. As Śaṅkara puts it: "dharmic action does not cause knowledge, but it prepares the way for the arising of knowledge." By rooting out bad ideas, ego, stray desires, and worldly interests, the difficult discipline of ritual makes one disciplined and attentive — and, "because it is so difficult, wants something more," and so ready to read the Upaniṣads and rise to higher knowledge. Śaṅkara, like most Vedānta teachers, would be skeptical [00:24:35] of someone who "with no ritual background, with no discipline" expects to just read the Upaniṣads and have something happen: the background is "only background, but it's the background one needs."
  • [00:24:51] Adamson notes this is also Śaṅkara's critique of the Buddhists — even though "the end result sounds so Buddhist." Clooney agrees, granting it "may be quite unfair": Śaṅkara charges that the Buddhists' wrong ideas and practices "not prepare one for higher knowledge but distract one" — being "rooted in the ego of the individual" — whereas ritual's point is "to purify that ego and detach one's higher knowledge from the ego." Adamson calls it "a very ironic accusation to level at the Buddhists of all people," but sees why: without "subordinating your own self to a ritual," you might find no way to eliminate ego-based desire.
  • [00:26:13] Clooney closes the thread: there's real "common ground between Śaṅkara and the Buddhists" — moving away from ritual, cultivating a better self, realizing a transformative higher reality — but what is determinative of Śaṅkara, who stays "within the brahminical and Vedānta fold," is that the background "has to be gone through first." Only the rare individual (perhaps carrying "karmic residues from a previous life") enters ready; otherwise the claim that "the Veda is not necessary, the ritual is not necessary" could be "simply the ego... putting aside the difficult, necessary work." For Śaṅkara, unlike the Buddhists, "the narrow path runs through Vedic performance."

docs.title: Beyond Śaṅkara: the other Vedāntas and the theistic schools
docs.text:
• [00:27:10] Adamson worries the series may mislead by concentrating on Śaṅkara (they've covered the Vedānta-Sūtra, Śaṅkara, and grammar-and-Vedānta in Bhartṛhari). Is it a "distortion" to dwell on him? Are other Vedāntins "much more interested in retaining a final place for ritual," so that Mīmāṃsā as a whole stays a deeply ritual-based tradition with Śaṅkara as "a kind of outlier or exception"?
  • [00:28:05] Clooney returns to the starting point: for all these thinkers the Veda, ritual, sūtras, Upaniṣads, and meditation are "all connected." That forces "a very hard question about the Śaṅkara tradition" — whether, for the sake of "a purity of higher knowledge" and "an absolute transition which leaves the world and practice behind," he offered "a very fine narrative of a higher knowledge that is irreversible" but in fact oversimplifying — and (though he'd never say so) "improving on the Upaniṣads and on Bādarāyaṇa's sūtras." Go back to any great Upaniṣad [00:28:54] and one finds "quite a diversity of claims"; "deities appear, deities are sometimes very central," and the Upaniṣads seem "quite comfortable with the diversity of narratives" about reality.
  • [00:29:18] Most scholars reading Bādarāyaṇa "in himself" find a compromised position — "not so much ultimate non-duality, but a kind of duality-non-duality in conjunction": a higher knowledge that "does not entirely obliterate a world of difference," still requiring ritual, leaving "some sense of distinction between self and brahman" even after liberation.
  • [00:29:54] In the theistic schools this follows easily — e.g. Rāmānuja, "a few centuries after Śaṅkara," where realizing the Upaniṣads' teaching happens "in a world where there is still some differentiation," above all brahman "now as the Lord, whom one worships, to whom one offers pūjā, sacrifices, and the like."
  • [00:30:18] A historiographical point: the great Western interest in Śaṅkara over two centuries owes something to "the brilliance of his thinking," but also to scholars "trained in traditions of idealism" who took his system for "the highest form of Indian thought." Those who know the Upaniṣadic heritage well may concede that "the other schools of Vedānta may actually gain insights... that Śaṅkara, for the sake of his zealous clarification, may have put aside."

docs.title: What Vedānta brings to comparative theology
docs.text:
• [00:31:01] Adamson asks: if idealism isn't the best lens, what does Vedānta as a whole bring to comparative theology — something distinctive, in Śaṅkara and the others, for comparative work?
  • [00:31:32] Clooney answers that the "incredibly rich traditions of Vedānta" — "doubly rich" set beside Mīmāṃsā ritual theory and the whole world of the Veda — give "an extraordinarily developed, sophisticated, multi-generational tradition of interpretation," "multidimensional and very insightful about the nature of the world and reality." If one is open to calling this theological learning — "deferential to tradition and scripture" and open to "transformative practice" — then in Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, or other versions, "these are magnificent theological systems": not just "doctrines of God," but "the entire apparatus of thinking through the nature of reality, taking words seriously, taking experience seriously, taking practice seriously, and believing that in the end there is an ultimate truth one can reach." To see them whole is to see, "outside the West and outside... the Christian tradition, full-scale, developed theological understandings of the world."
  • [00:32:58] For comparative work, what matters is not treating other traditions as "raw material... as we perpetuate our own models of theology," but realizing that "the thinkers of these great traditions of the East... are our intellectual peers," doing "the same kind of work of understanding reality in a whole and complete, effective way as we are ourselves doing."
  • [00:33:46] Adamson agrees wholeheartedly, thanks Francis Clooney, and previews the next episode: the Sāṃkhya school, "which was criticized by the Vedāntins."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Vedānta / Uttara-Mīmāṃsā — the "later Mīmāṃsā"; traced to the Upaniṣads, concerned with the nature of reality, the self, and what is undeniably true; treated here as exegesis-and-philosophy-of-response to sacred texts.
  • Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā — the "prior Mīmāṃsā"; works on the Vedic ritual texts, showing the coherence between what scripture says and how ritual is performed.
  • brahman — ultimate reality; in Vedānta both a metaphysical question (how the phenomenal world relates to it) and an object of worship; for Śaṅkara, the phenomenal world is its illusory appearance.
  • sūtra — terse aphorisms (Jaimini's ~2,700; Bādarāyaṇa's ~500) that organize and harmonize a vast body of material; memory-prompts for larger oral teaching debates, hence brief and obscure once the debates ended.
  • Jaimini — author of the Mīmāṃsā-Sūtra (~2,700 sūtras).
  • Bādarāyaṇa — attributed author of the Vedānta-Sūtra (Brahma-Sūtra), arguing the Upaniṣads form one coherent teaching; read "in themselves," his sūtras suggest a duality-and-non-duality compromise rather than pure non-dualism.
  • Śabara — early Mīmāṃsā commentator on Jaimini, centuries after the sūtras.
  • Śaṅkara — first surviving Vedānta commentator; founder of Advaita (non-dual) Vedānta; radical illusionism about the world; charged by rivals with abandoning ritual/karma/dharma and "being a Buddhist," but in his Brahma-Sūtra and Upaniṣad commentaries struggles to keep a place for ritual.
  • Advaita Vedānta — Śaṅkara's non-dualism: identity of self and brahman, the phenomenal world as illusion.
  • Rāmānuja — theistic Vedāntin a few centuries after Śaṅkara; realization is possible in a world that retains differentiation, with brahman as the Lord one worships (pūjā).
  • Madhva — dualist Vedāntin; reality not the same as the self; polemical critic of Śaṅkara.
  • Bhartṛhari — figure linking grammar and Vedānta (covered earlier in the series).
  • Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad — subject of Śaṅkara's "brilliant and greatest" commentary, working out brahman-as-self in careful gradations.
  • Chāndogya Upaniṣad — cited for the claim that the liberated one "does not return again to ordinary existence."
  • karma / dharma — action and duty/law; located in the phenomenal realm, raising the worry of whether Śaṅkara can still accommodate them; for him, dharmic ritual prepares but does not cause higher knowledge.
  • philosophy as a way of life (Pierre Hadot) — the rich sense of philosophy as transformative of the thinker, by which Vedānta counts as philosophy and not just exegesis.
  • comparative theology — Clooney's project: treating Vedānta thinkers as intellectual peers doing full-scale theology, not raw material for Western models.
