docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 27 — "The Theory of Evolution: Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya-kārikā"
docs.text:
← Ep 26

Ep 28 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:24:06 In brief: Sāṃkhya — the "counting" system — explained through Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhya-kārikā: a dualism of inactive pure consciousness (puruṣa) and productive primordial matter (prakṛti), which spontaneously "evolves" into the 25 principles via three intertwined forces (the guṇas), with liberation coming from identifying with the passive witness and letting everything else go. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannari"; Sāṃkhya ≈ "Samkhya/Sanjia/Sankya"; Sāṃkhya-kārikā ≈ "Samkhya Karika/Kharika"; Īśvarakṛṣṇa ≈ "Ishvara Krishna/Ishvika/Ishverakrishna"; Kauṭilya ≈ "Cautilia"; Arthaśāstra ≈ "Ata Shastra"; puruṣa ≈ "Purusha/Porusha"; prakṛti ≈ "Prachriti/Procriti/Prokraty"; guṇa ≈ "guna"; sattva ≈ "Satva"; rajas ≈ "Rajas"; tamas ≈ "Tamas"; Kapila ≈ "Kapila"; Āsuri ≈ "Asuri"; Pañcaśikha ≈ "Panchashika/Panchachika"; Gauḍapāda ≈ "Gautapada/Gaudapada"; Patañjali ≈ "Patanjali"; Pāṇini ≈ "Panani"; Śaṅkara ≈ "Shankara"; Chāndogya ≈ "Chandogya"; buddhi ≈ "Budi"; ahaṃkāra ≈ "eye-making"; ākāśa ≈ "akasha"; Bhartṛhari ≈ "Batrihari").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Sāṃkhya — the "counting / enumeration" tradition; arguably the oldest of the Vedic schools, existing long before it was a school [00:01:31].
  • Īśvarakṛṣṇa — author of the Sāṃkhya-kārikā, the oldest surviving Sāṃkhya treatise; lived c. 350–450 CE, a late entry in the lineage [00:00:29].
  • Kapila, Āsuri, Pañcaśikha — the legendary earlier Sāṃkhya teachers, the "Great Sage" founder and his successors [00:02:56].
  • The Sāṃkhya-kārikā — the verse text itemizing the 25 principles, the 8 behavioural tendencies, and 50 types of result [00:01:52].

docs.title: What the Muppets would make of it — Sāṃkhya as counting
docs.text:
• [00:00:37] A "pivotal question": what would the Muppets make of Indian philosophy? Different Muppets, like the Indian thinkers, would differ — Miss Piggy would admire the Jaina ban on violence to animals, the self-abnegating Scooter is "practically a Buddhist already," Sam the Eagle would endorse the strict politics of Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra, and the Swedish Chef would feel kinship with the sūtra texts "since you usually can't tell what the heck they are saying either."
  • [00:01:20] The best fit is Count von Count from Sesame Street, the vampire who teaches children arithmetic. He'd want to get his teeth into Sāṃkhya, whose name "literally means counting or enumeration." Sāṃkhya loves numbers and offers "a whole system of itemizing lists."
  • [00:01:52] The catalogues include the 25 principles that constitute self and cosmos, the 8 tendencies guiding human behaviour, and the 50 types of result for humans — running from five basic misunderstandings of the world to nine kinds of contentment. These lists are mentioned (though usually not fully spelled out) in the oldest surviving treatise of the school, the Sāṃkhya-kārikā, ascribed to Īśvarakṛṣṇa, thought to have lived between 350 and 450 CE.

docs.title: An ancient school with a late spokesman
docs.text:
• [00:02:28] This sounds ancient — and is — but like other supposed "founding fathers" seen in earlier episodes, Īśvarakṛṣṇa was heir to a still older tradition. You can argue Sāṃkhya is the oldest of the Vedic schools, "especially if you add the caveat that it existed long before being a school."
  • [00:02:51] At the end of the Sāṃkhya-kārikā, Īśvarakṛṣṇa is revealed as a fairly late entry in a list of thinkers. The real founder — called simply "the Great Sage" — is identified by ancient commentators as Kapila, followed by two more teachers, Āsuri and Pañcaśikha, with Īśvarakṛṣṇa coming an unspecified number of generations later.
  • [00:03:15] Whatever the accuracy of the lineage, Sāṃkhya reaches deep into the past. Its characteristic ideas trace back to the earliest Vedas, and there are passages in the Upaniṣads and the Mahābhārata with unmistakable similarities to Īśvarakṛṣṇa's teaching. The enumeration of principles is anticipated in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, and the legendary figures appear in earlier texts — the Mahābhārata describes how Pañcaśikha defeated 100 other sages in debate.
  • [00:03:53] Sāṃkhya develops "in concert with the tradition of yoga," which gives a practical complement to Sāṃkhya's "enumerative system-mongering." The Mahābhārata says yoga and Sāṃkhya share a single teaching, though it also reports teachers identifying with one school or the other.
  • [00:04:20] In the Sāṃkhya-kārikā, Īśvarakṛṣṇa too was "reaching into the past," retrenching to a more conservative version of the system to challenge more recent innovations. As so often, the oldest surviving text drops us into the middle of an ongoing conversation — so we shouldn't assume his ideas are definitive of Sāṃkhya just because his is the work that survived rather than his rivals'.

docs.title: The commentators — and Śaṅkara's hostility
docs.text:
• [00:04:49] On the other hand, Īśvarakṛṣṇa's ideas did come to dominate. More counting: there are no fewer than eight early commentaries on the Sāṃkhya-kārikā. Two are by authors with familiar names — Gauḍapāda and Patañjali (this Patañjali not to be confused with the grammarian who wrote the authoritative commentary on Pāṇini). It's possible the Gauḍapāda who commented here is the same Vedāntin who anticipated Śaṅkara.
  • [00:05:26] What is certain is that Śaṅkara "really had it in for Sāṃkhya." As noted in his episode, he sternly criticized Īśvarakṛṣṇa's whole approach — taking exception to their cosmology, their conception of the self, and their epistemology.

docs.title: Dualism: puruṣa and prakṛti
docs.text:
• [00:05:53] Śaṅkara's Advaita ("non-dual") Vedānta sees the distinction between brahman and all else as illusory: only one principle is real. Sāṃkhya, by contrast, is dualist — "the Bert and Ernie of the system," two very different characters in close partnership: puruṣa and prakṛti.
  • [00:06:24] We met puruṣa back in episode three, in the Ṛg Veda cosmology where the gods cut it up in a world-forming sacrifice, fashioning its limbs into the groups of society — there it seemed an originary human complete with body. In the Sāṃkhya-kārikā, puruṣa is far more abstract: "that which witnesses all, yet remains inactive." This is pure consciousness, the subject underlying all objects of awareness — a thoroughly Upaniṣadic idea here used as the foundation of the whole system.
  • [00:07:12] The Vedāntins could agree so far, but would reject the next move: identifying pure consciousness as only one of two fundamental principles. The other, prakṛti, is translated "nature" or "primordial matter" — the principle that gives rise to all other things by undergoing a complex, step-by-step process of transformation, while puruṣa remains inactive, "maintaining an unending silent vigil" as it observes prakṛti develop.
  • [00:07:52] This is not dualism as in Gnosticism: Sāṃkhya shares the idea of two independent principles, neither the cause of the other, but there's no God acting on matter and no good principle in conflict with a counterbalancing source of evil. Rather, nature spontaneously turns itself into all things, while consciousness just bears witness.
  • [00:08:24] Yet puruṣa has a role in explaining the phenomena. Īśvarakṛṣṇa says prakṛti, though productive, is unintelligent — without puruṣa there could be no awareness within nature's products. The two are compared to a blind man cooperating with a lame man: nature is blind (lacking consciousness), consciousness is lame (without nature it stays inert).

docs.title: The 23 evolutes and effects pre-existing in causes
docs.text:
• [00:08:47] We've only counted to two; the remaining 23 principles are less fundamental — the phenomena that emerge from prakṛti as it undergoes what Īśvarakṛṣṇa calls modification. Scholars sometimes call these 23 results "the evolutes" — which "sounds more like a 1950s singing group" — but the term fits, since they evolve out of prakṛti in a gradual, stepwise process.
  • [00:09:31] In defence of this evolutionary theory, Īśvarakṛṣṇa appeals to the idea that effects pre-exist in their causes. The same assumption appeared in Vedānta, where Śaṅkara argued all things are virtually present in brahman, "as pots are already somehow in the clay." This explains why pots don't emerge from sheer non-being, and why a given material can only make certain things: "You can put a chicken in every pot, but you can't make a chicken out of a pot" — though Adamson admits it would be a great act for the Amazing Gonzo to attempt.

docs.title: Prakṛti the unmanifest, and the three sources of knowledge
docs.text:
• [00:10:09] Taking a closer look at prakṛti is difficult: the Sāṃkhya-kārikā calls it unmanifest and too subtle to perceive. Though it implicitly contains all things, in itself it is none of them, so we cannot grasp it directly — only as a postulate or hypothesis.
  • [00:10:46] To justify this, Īśvarakṛṣṇa touches on a theme explored later with the Nyāya school: the sources of knowledge. Sāṃkhya recognizes three — direct perception, inference, and valid testimony. For prakṛti it is inference that applies: we infer it must be real, without grasping it directly, because there must be a single principle to explain how there is order and limit in things.

docs.title: The three guṇas — cords of change
docs.text:
• [00:11:19] The mechanism of change is "one of the most intriguing yet elusive aspects" of the system: the three guṇas, a word literally meaning "cords or threads." At the metaphorical level, think of a rope of three intertwined strands; philosophically, the guṇas are the functional modes or interacting tendencies inherent in prakṛti by which nature transforms.
  • [00:11:53] The three are sattva, rajas, and tamas — terms hard to translate that "really take the cake," reaching deep into Vedic literary history. Originally they may have alluded to sun, sky, and earth (which together make growing food possible), and they're associated with white, red, and black, perhaps a traditional colour scheme for clothing. In the Sāṃkhya-kārikā they are the three forces of change driving the evolution of things from prakṛti:
  • sattva — connected to lightness and pleasure;
  • rajas — change, and the upheaval that causes suffering;
  • tamas — heavy, to do with resistance and despondency.
  • [00:12:49] So each guṇa carries a striking combination of cosmological and psychological traits — a hallmark of the whole system. Within the cosmos, different realms are dominated by the three forces, apparently explaining the difference between the divine/heavenly realm, humanity, and animals and plants; the guṇas govern all things "from Brahmā down to a blade of grass." Psychologically, sattva was historically linked to liberation: individual selves may be dominated by sattva or by tamas — that is, they may live wisely or not.
  • [00:13:40] In both cosmos and person, the central point is that the three guṇas operate together dynamically, each stage of evolution proceeding from the last. The rope metaphor helps — nature extending strands and developing in ever-increasing complexity — or the Mahābhārata's image of guṇas "created in regular order and dissolved in reverse order, like the waves of the sea." Īśvarakṛṣṇa offers his own analogy: the three forces are like a lamp — the commentators explain he means the oil, fire, and wick that together allow illumination.

docs.title: The first evolutes: an inner organ, not mere matter
docs.text:
• [00:14:22] Since prakṛti is often understood materially, it's tempting to read this as a purely physical process — but the first results cast doubt on that. The immediate product of prakṛti is buddhi, also called "the Great One." It is the first thing manifest (so we can grasp it directly) and is typically rendered intellect: a kind of impersonal, undirected thought or striving to create further stages.
  • [00:14:58] Next the emerging subject acquires a sense of its own identity, in a stage literally called "I-making" (ahaṃkāra) — i.e. self-awareness, the ability to take a first-person view. Only at the next stage does Īśvarakṛṣṇa introduce mind (manas), responsible for actual thinking and perceiving. Collectively these three powers — buddhi, I-making, and mind — are the interior organ, as opposed to the external sense organs.
  • [00:15:35] So Sāṃkhya's dualism is not that of Plato or Descartes, where a mental principle is contrasted with a physical one. True, one of the two principles is pure consciousness, recalling the Cartesian mind — but all other aspects of mental life sit on the side of the other principle, prakṛti. The capacities for thinking are even the first things generated, though none could be aware at all without "the lurking presence of consciousness," prakṛti's unoriginated partner puruṣa.

docs.title: Counting up to 25
docs.text:
• [00:16:15] We're still only at five — the two fundamental principles plus the three aspects of the interior organ. Now it speeds up: the mind generates the five sense faculties (vision, hearing, etc.) plus five anatomical powers to match (like speaking and moving). With this exterior organ added, we seem to have a well-rounded person — mental life, sensation, and abilities to interact with the world.
  • [00:16:48] The catch: there isn't really a world yet, only a person. So these 15 principles are complemented by the five sensible features of the world, which generate five bodily elements — the four familiar from Greek philosophy (air, earth, fire, water) plus ākāśa, meaning empty space or a kind of ether pervading the universe. Counting along, this finally reaches 25.

docs.title: Two loose ends: generic sensibles and a boundary-crossing puzzle
docs.text:
• [00:17:22] Following Īśvarakṛṣṇa's example, most philosophical issues are passed over, but two are flagged — one detail, one general puzzle.
  • [00:17:34] The detail: the sensible features generated near the end are very generic — the whole phenomena of taste, smell, sound, not particular flavours or noises. The generic sensibles supposedly give rise to the elements, and particular qualities (a given colour) arise only once we have the physical elements and their compounds. Some authors, including "our new favourite philosophizing grammarian" Bhartṛhari, claim that for Sāṃkhya everyday bodies are made of sensible qualities — so a pot would be nothing more than its colour, hardness, the metallic sound it makes falling on the Swedish Chef's head, and so on. But in the earlier tradition of Īśvarakṛṣṇa, the qualities likely belong to an underlying subject — namely prakṛti, the quasi-material principle ultimately transformed into everyday things.
  • [00:18:44] The broader puzzle: the disconcerting way the 25 principles cut across cosmological and human realms — sensation and the sensible, mental and material, private and public. In the initial stages we get human psychological powers; before long those powers are "acting like a record executive in the disco era and producing earth, wind, and fire."
  • [00:19:15] One suspicion: the physical aspects of the evolution are really an illusion, a show the mind puts on for itself when bound to nature. A late passage in the Sāṃkhya-kārikā says the phenomenal world is "like a dance watched by the audience that is puruṣa." This reading could head toward later commentators (after Śaṅkara) who tried to reconcile Sāṃkhya with Advaita Vedānta's skeptical view of the phenomenal world.
  • [00:19:52] But there may be other reasons the outer world is so closely tied to the world of mind. Vedic literature constantly compared the cosmos to an individual animal, person, or god, and the threefold-guṇa theory supports this boundary-crossing: the same forces that yield a person's mind and body also give rise to the physical universe.

docs.title: Why Sāṃkhya and Vedānta cannot fully agree
docs.text: • [00:20:18] There are major obstacles to reconciling Sāṃkhya with Vedānta. Sāṃkhya embraces two fundamental principles where Vedānta has one, and it resists the Vedāntic notion of a single true self (brahman). The fact that there are different courses of life and experiences proves, says Īśvarakṛṣṇa, that puruṣa is many — "you have one pure consciousness and I have another."

docs.title: Liberation: identifying with the passive witness
docs.text:
• [00:20:50] Yet there is deep agreement between the two Vedic schools: both are convinced that knowledge of their teachings brings liberation. The very first sentence of the Sāṃkhya-kārikā states the purpose of the teaching is the escape from suffering. The early thinker Pañcaśikha held this out for all comers, not just the priestly caste: a knower of the 25 principles, "in whatever order of life... whether he wears braided hair, a topknot, or is shaven, is liberated from existence."
  • [00:21:24] But why would counting to 25 help achieve this? One suspicion is that Īśvarakṛṣṇa is just keeping up with the Buddhists, who built their whole teaching around the pervasiveness of suffering and the path of escape. Still, Sāṃkhya is from its foundations built to pursue liberation. Positing puruṣa addresses philosophy of mind by making pure consciousness prior to all experience — but Īśvarakṛṣṇa insists that without puruṣa there can be no liberation: only a pure, contentless consciousness can stand outside the turmoil of the world that emerges from prakṛti. Consciousness can declare itself satisfied at having seen the evolved world, while nature is satisfied at having shown itself and been seen.
  • [00:22:25] So we know what must be given up to be liberated: everything. We must let go of all physical action, all sensation, all mental activity, even any sense of an individual self — saying "I do not exist, nothing is mine, I am not." This is what it means to identify with the passive witness, puruṣa.
  • [00:22:46] Īśvarakṛṣṇa calls this an escape from ignorance. Ignorance is not why the world evolved from prakṛti — that was a spontaneous natural process. Ignorance is rather what keeps us bound to the world once it has evolved. The bondage is unnecessary, because we can simply choose to cast ourselves as audience instead of performer. To take oneself to be puruṣa is to be liberated, simply because puruṣa stands outside the evolutionary process — it was never unfree.
  • [00:23:24] This is asking a lot. Īśvarakṛṣṇa would be content if you keep seeing yourself as "something more modest, the audience of this podcast." Next time: ancient Indian medicine, closely connected to both Sāṃkhya and its partner tradition yoga — complete with medical puns from the Muppet Show's veterinarian's hospital sketch ("Dr. Bob, how can you stand to wait until the next episode?" — "Easy. I have lots of patience.").

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Sāṃkhya — the "counting / enumeration" tradition; itemizes the 25 principles, 8 tendencies, and 50 results; arguably the oldest Vedic school, dualist and aimed at liberation.
  • Īśvarakṛṣṇa — author of the Sāṃkhya-kārikā (c. 350–450 CE), the oldest surviving Sāṃkhya treatise; a late figure whose version came to dominate.
  • Sāṃkhya-kārikā — the verse treatise; states its purpose is escape from suffering and lays out the 25-principle evolution.
  • Kapila / Āsuri / Pañcaśikha — the legendary earlier teachers: the "Great Sage" founder Kapila, his successors Āsuri and Pañcaśikha (who defeated 100 sages in debate and offered liberation to all castes).
  • puruṣa — pure consciousness; the inactive witness, the subject underlying all objects of awareness; shown to be many, one per person.
  • prakṛti — nature / primordial matter; productive but unintelligent and unmanifest; transforms step-by-step into all things while puruṣa watches.
  • the blind man and the lame man — image of puruṣa and prakṛti's cooperation: nature is blind (no consciousness), consciousness is lame (inert without nature).
  • effects pre-exist in causes — the doctrine justifying evolution; pots are "already in the clay," so things come from being, not nothing.
  • three sources of knowledge — perception, inference, valid testimony; prakṛti is known only by inference (from the order and limit in things).
  • guṇa — "cord/thread"; the functional mode or tendency in prakṛti driving change; three intertwined strands.
  • sattva / rajas / tamas — the three guṇas: lightness/pleasure (and liberation); change/upheaval/suffering; heaviness/resistance/despondency — each both cosmological and psychological.
  • buddhi — intellect, "the Great One"; first evolute, impersonal undirected thought.
  • ahaṃkāra ("I-making") — self-awareness, the first-person stance; second evolute.
  • manas (mind) — actual thinking and perceiving; with buddhi and ahaṃkāra forms the interior organ.
  • ākāśa — empty space or pervading ether; fifth element alongside air, earth, fire, water.
  • liberation — identifying with puruṣa, the audience not the performer; an escape from the ignorance that binds us to the evolved world.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 28 — "Who Wants to Live Forever: Early Āyurvedic Medicine"
docs.text:
← Ep 27

Ep 29 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:23:42 In brief: Early Āyurveda — "the knowledge of longevity" — treated through its oldest texts, the Caraka-Saṃhitā and Suśruta-Saṃhitā: its modest goal of prolonging life, its theory of the three disease-causing doṣas (wind, bile, phlegm), its blend of naturalist science with karma, demons and Vedic authority, and the open question of whether it grew from Vedic, Buddhist/śramaṇa, or even Greek roots. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennari"; Īśvarakṛṣṇa ≈ "Ishvara Krishna"; Sāṃkhya-kārikā ≈ "Samhya Karika"; Gauḍapāda ≈ "Gauda Pada/Gautopada"; Āyurveda ≈ "Ayurveda"; Caraka ≈ "Charaqa/Chara/Characca/Chattaca"; Caraka-Saṃhitā ≈ "Charakha Samhita/Shadaka"; Suśruta ≈ "Sushustra/So Schuster"; Suśruta-Saṃhitā ≈ "Sushustra Samita"; Kaniṣka ≈ "Kanisheka"; Aśvins ≈ "Ashvins"; Ātreya ≈ "Atreya"; doṣa ≈ "dosas"; pramāṇa ≈ "pramanas/Promanas"; rasa ≈ "rasa"; sannipātika ≈ "sanipatica"; śramaṇa ≈ "Shramana"; melaina cholē ≈ "Melaina-Hole"; colpo d'aria ≈ "culpodia").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• The Caraka-Saṃhitā — the oldest complete surviving Āyurvedic treatise, named for its compiler Caraka [00:02:23].
  • The Suśruta-Saṃhitā — an old treatise focused especially on surgery [00:03:19].
  • Caraka — physician, said to have been an advisor to King Kaniṣka; wrote c. 300 AD [00:02:36].
  • Ātreya — the sage quoted as a medical authority throughout the Caraka-Saṃhitā [00:03:01].
  • Īśvarakṛṣṇa & Gauḍapāda — the Sāṃkhya author and his commentator, used as the entry point [00:00:38].

docs.title: From Sāṃkhya's threefold suffering to bodily disease
docs.text:
• [00:00:38] At the start of his Sāṃkhya-kārikā, Īśvarakṛṣṇa speaks of a threefold suffering his teaching aims to dispel. Like "any self-respecting author of a foundational text," he doesn't explain what he means — and like any self-respecting commentator, Gauḍapāda rushes to fill the gap.
  • [00:00:57] Gauḍapāda: suffering is threefold because its cause may be internal, external, or divine. Internal suffering in turn has two forms, bodily and mental. After the Sāṃkhya episodes we understand mental suffering well — it is the anguish arising from ignorance of the true self.
  • [00:01:21] But bodily suffering, says Gauḍapāda, is caused by the disordering of three substances in the body: wind, bile, and phlegm. So we have a threefold enumeration illustrating one aspect of the first item of another threefold enumeration — "yes, this is Sāṃkhya all right." Yet this idea of disease from wind, bile and phlegm would be familiar to Gauḍapāda's readers from a different tradition: Āyurveda.

docs.title: Āyurveda: a living tradition with very old roots
docs.text:
• [00:01:54] Unlike Sāṃkhya, Āyurveda is "still the name to conjure with" — practised across the English-speaking world as "alternative medicine," and alive in India where ancient ideas blend with newer theory to make what's called modern Āyurveda. But this episode looks at a version that is "anything but modern."
  • [00:02:17] The oldest medical texts go back to the early centuries AD. The oldest complete surviving treatise is the Caraka-Saṃhitā, named for its author — or rather compiler — Caraka. Listeners to the History of India podcast may recall King Kaniṣka and his three close advisors; one was a doctor, none other than this Caraka.
  • [00:02:47] By the text's own testimony, Caraka passes on wisdom first handed down by the gods to the mythical Aśvins (also named in the Mahābhārata), whose teaching eventually passed to the sage Ātreya, frequently quoted in the Caraka-Saṃhitā. Caraka himself is thought to have written c. 300 AD, with the surviving redaction produced c. 500 AD.
  • [00:03:19] Besides the Caraka-Saṃhitā there are other very old treatises, including one focused especially on surgical technique, the Suśruta-Saṃhitā.

docs.title: The modest goal: prolonging life
docs.text:
• [00:03:31] After all the talk of fulfilling one's dharma, achieving liberation, and grasping identity with brahman, it's "somewhat refreshing" that Āyurveda has the more straightforward goal of prolonging your life — indeed that is what the word means: knowledge of longevity.
  • [00:03:50] Caraka makes no apologies for this modest aim. He admits a long life is not the only worthwhile thing — one may also seek wealth and a good fate after death — but to pursue any of these you must first stay healthy as long as possible. As he puts it, "when life is lost, everything is lost."
  • [00:04:15] This is not a quest for immortality. Āyurveda accepts each person has a proper, limited lifespan, which is why even the best doctor cannot prolong some patients' lives, and why trying may be pointless.

docs.title: Karma, fatalism, and the lazy argument
docs.text:
• [00:04:33] In the Indian context there was even reason to think doctors cannot extend lifespan at all: if you believe in karma, you might think everyone's lifespan is preordained at birth. This is the familiar problem facing any fatalist worldview.
  • [00:04:51] Compare the ancient Greek Stoics, thoroughgoing determinists who had to answer the so-called lazy argument: a Stoic seemingly has no reason to see a doctor, since if fated to die of the illness he will die regardless of treatment, and if fated to live, treatment is unnecessary.
  • [00:05:12] Confronting his own version, Caraka quotes Ātreya: lifespan is not simply fixed by karma but determined by several factors. There is more than one kind of karma — our fate is shaped by deeds in past lives and by what we do now — and sometimes even the combined karma exerts only a weak influence, so our actions can change the outcome.
  • [00:05:39] Therefore lifespan cannot be wholly predetermined: if it were, "never mind not going to the doctor, you wouldn't even bother to avoid stepping off cliffs." Still, the good physician isn't out to extend life indefinitely; he aims to bring you to the right time for death — much as a chariot axle is meant to wear out after a set time and no earlier.

docs.title: Naturalism versus inherited belief — tension or synthesis?
docs.text:
• [00:06:05] This illustrates a running theme in early Āyurveda: a tension between a naturalist, scientific outlook and older cultural beliefs retained in the texts. Examples abound: invasive diseases are caused by poor judgment and bad hygiene — including those brought on by demons; wind/breath is both a bodily constituent and a divine force causing all things.
  • [00:06:38] Speaking "as an identical twin," Adamson is fond of a passage explaining that differences between twins are caused by both karma and an unequal distribution of blood and generative seed.
  • [00:06:51] It's tempting to praise the authors' naturalism while deploring their clinging to religion — but we should grant them the courtesy of a well-thought-out synthesis, not merely a clash of old and new. In favour of this generous reading, an early passage in the Caraka-Saṃhitā entertains a skeptical objection to Caraka's third goal, the favourable afterlife.

docs.title: Four ways of knowing — the pramāṇas in medicine
docs.text:
• [00:07:26] To the doubter that we live on after death, Caraka invokes a characteristic Indian epistemology: four methods of knowing, or pramāṇas — authority, perception, inference, and reasoning — all four of which testify we may be reborn after past lives. Vedic authority says so; perception confirms it too, since people don't always take after their parents and so must have another source.
  • [00:08:02] These same ways of knowing are used in medicine itself. Great weight falls on authoritative testimony, given that the teaching supposedly comes from the gods; Caraka also uses premises clearly the fruit of inference and reasoning.
  • [00:08:25] But of the four pramāṇas, the most important may be perception. Āyurveda stresses the senses, especially in diagnostics: per Suśruta, examine a patient using all five senses and by asking questions — what we'd call taking a medical history.
  • [00:08:45] The Suśruta-Saṃhitā gives concrete advice to trainee surgeons: before cutting human bodies, practise on melons, gourds, and hunks of meat and other items resembling body parts. Practical experience lets physicians cope with the infinite variety of patients' conditions — "no one can teach you what to do in every case. You must learn by doing."
  • [00:09:08] Yet hands-on practice is combined with speculative reasoning about the body. Neither theory nor experience suffices alone — using only one would be "like a bird trying to fly with one wing." A good doctor must grasp the principles giving rise to the body and shaping each individual's constitution.

docs.title: Cosmology: five elements, six flavours, and rasa
docs.text:
• [00:09:39] The theoretical basis alludes to the cosmology of Sāṃkhya: five elements — ether, wind, earth, fire, and water — from which our bodies, and our food, are ultimately composed.
  • [00:09:59] Also Sāṃkhya-like, foods are classified by six flavours: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, and astringent. The doctor must know foods' characters, since a buildup of harmful humours can be combated by eating something of opposing nature — too much wind? eat something sweet, sour or salty (or all three, "like dill pickles with caramel coating" — which "might just make you sicker").
  • [00:10:33] Once digested, food becomes rasa, the nutritive juice, which passes into the heart and is circulated around the body.

docs.title: Why wind, bile and phlegm aren't quite "humours"
docs.text:
• [00:10:45] Alongside elemental composition runs the idea that wind/breath is a fundamental bodily principle — a point of agreement between the Āyurvedic texts and older works like the Upaniṣads. Summaries often list wind as merely one of three humours alongside bile and phlegm, but (taking Sāṃkhya's love of enumeration as inspiration) "let us count the ways" this is misleading.
  • [00:11:15] First: bile and phlegm are opposed to each other, with wind playing a more fundamental, leading role — perhaps because of its prominence in Vedic literature.
  • [00:11:27] Second: in some passages blood is treated as another humour. It is a chief product of nutrition; processed over a month it becomes menstrual blood in women and semen in men, and can cause disease when corrupted or in excess — hence bloodletting. Suśruta says "blood is life," a maxim "still endorsed today by cardiologists and vampires."
  • [00:11:58] Third, and most important: it's not clear wind, bile and phlegm are humours in the European sense. There the four humours (blood, black bile, yellow bile, phlegm) had to be in qualitative balance — a theory our language preserves when we call someone melancholic, literally "characterized by black bile" (Greek melaina cholē). In India, by contrast, these three substances — the doṣas — are conceived solely as sources of disease. In the earliest references there's no talk of balancing them, only of eliminating them or keeping them from being stirred up, since it's when riled that they cause illness.
  • [00:13:04] A better parallel than Greek science might be the folk medicine of modern Italy, where you may be afflicted by a colpo d'aria — "the dreaded blast of air" likely to earn a sick day off work.

docs.title: The working life and ethics of the ancient doctor
docs.text:
• [00:13:22] Working conditions aren't addressed head-on, but Caraka and Suśruta drop incidental detail. High-born doctors of the brahmin or kṣatriya castes may have practised charitably, whereas vaiśya doctors presumably took payment. Students attached themselves to masters through a formalized process and, once trained, adopted a distinctive outfit: Suśruta says the physician should dress in white and carry an umbrella and a stick.
  • [00:14:07] Both stress that moral probity is paramount: the patient must trust the doctor, and the doctor must earn it — though he need not be above the occasional deception, e.g. withholding news that a patient hasn't long to live, or hiding that a medicine contains meat of animals not usually eaten. Indeed the texts prescribe consuming meat and even drinking blood as treatment; the oldest texts take this for granted, but later commentators grow nervous about departing from non-violence, one excusing it on the grounds that in medicine "we are pursuing health, not dharma."
  • [00:14:55] On medical ethics the texts seem "remarkably uninterested." Caraka lists patients a wise doctor won't treat: those with an incurable terminal illness (though an incurable chronic ailment may be managed); and, shockingly, the poor — until you realize he may mean those who can't afford the medicines (Suśruta more admirably says fee-charging doctors should waive fees for poor patients). Finally, very wicked patients "who actively enjoy wrongdoing" shouldn't be treated — not as punishment, but like the untreatable: the undertaking is doomed to fail and would harm the doctor's reputation.

docs.title: Why character affects prognosis — and the problem of epidemics
docs.text:
• [00:15:51] Why should a patient's wickedness affect prognosis? Because diseases are caused by bad character and bad judgment: Caraka holds that diseases from external factors, including demons, are brought on by ethical failings.
  • [00:16:10] An apparent exception is epidemics — a plague. Given Āyurveda's stress on individual constitution, it's strange that great numbers fall ill at once; this can be put down to corruption of air or water where the victims live. But that doesn't fit a moralist outlook linking disease to bad character — are we to believe a whole plague-ridden city just ate the wrong foods? Not quite.
  • [00:17:00] Ātreya's answer: epidemics are brought on by wicked rulers, whose evil deeds cause the gods to abandon their lands, which are then afflicted by adverse weather. The moral cause is relocated from the patients to the sovereign.

docs.title: Where did Āyurveda come from? Vedic, Buddhist, or Greek?
docs.text:
• [00:17:12] The texts are "remarkably sophisticated" — covering good practice, explanations of disease at the moral, physical, and religious levels, and a theory of knowledge. But none of this came from nowhere; the saṃhitās quote earlier authorities. Can we trace the story further back?
  • [00:17:47] Caraka and Suśruta are "at pains" to associate themselves with Vedic authority — the story of the art descending from the gods, liberal use of Vedic terms; even the word Āyurveda first appears in the Mahābhārata. But is Vedic culture really the ultimate source? The Vedas don't develop medical theory with anything like this complexity: Suśruta's surgery shows a formidable anatomy, whereas Vedic anatomical references look like "chance observations" made during animal sacrifice, and Vedic cures tend to use magic and ritual, not diet, drugs, or surgery.
  • [00:18:43] An alternative: Āyurveda may have grown from a "very different part of Indian culture" — the ascetic śramaṇa movements that dissented from the Vedic mainstream, and in particular Buddhism. One clue: in classical brahminical culture, physicians were likely seen as impure through physical contact with all sorts of people, so doctors were probably itinerant healers rather than the respected aristocrats Caraka portrays.
  • [00:19:13] Tellingly, the name Caraka itself means "someone who wanders," and students are told to roam freely offering services after training — so early doctors may have had "a touch of the vagabond," natural bedfellows of the supreme social outsiders of the śramaṇa tradition, especially the Buddhists.
  • [00:19:44] This is speculative but may be backed by Buddhist texts. The Pāli canon says the Buddha had monks nurse one another and let them keep medicine; in one passage he says illnesses are caused by excess of wind, phlegm, or bile, and sometimes by sannipātika — a "harmful combination of several humours." That is "a highly technical term of medical art"; an expert says it's as if the Buddha "blamed illness on hemoglobin levels."
  • [00:20:21] It makes sense the Buddhists were medical pioneers: Buddhism is "all about the avoidance of suffering," and just as the middle way discouraged extreme asceticism it would have encouraged eliminating distracting, painful illness. Buddhists were also urged to reflect on the transience of the body and contemplate dying bodies — as in the Buddha's long enumeration of the body's parts ("Sāṃkhya, eat your heart out — and also your liver and spleen").
  • [00:21:23] The Āyurvedic authors themselves "give no sign of Buddhist allegiance" — on the contrary they stress their Vedic lineage — but this may be a "Hindu veneer laid over an originally non-Vedic body of thought."

docs.title: The Greek parallels — suggestive, but no smoking gun
docs.text:
• [00:21:36] As long as we're weighing non-Vedic sources, what of the Greek ideas? The comparisons are "almost irresistible." There's the theory of humours (the Indians had three, not four, and not even three of the four Greek ones, since they didn't include wind — and maybe they're really pathogens anyway, "but still").
  • [00:22:06] There's the centrality of breath, echoing Greek medical literature including the Hippocratic text On Breaths; the Hippocratics also appeal to local conditions — "airs, waters, and places" — to explain illness, including epidemics. Much later, Galen holds ideas Caraka would approve: the doctor must assess each individual patient and master both theory and practice.
  • [00:22:34] Yet there's room for doubt: the Sanskrit of the saṃhitās is "innocent of Greek loan words," and no scholar has found a "smoking gun" proving influence either way — "appropriately enough, given that smoking and guns are both bad for your health." The parallels are suggestive but that's all current research can say; keep them "in the back of our minds" for a future episode on Indian–Greek connections.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text: • [00:23:12] We've seen Sāṃkhya provides a good background for Āyurveda — elemental theory and a love of enumeration both echo in Caraka. But the tradition most closely tied to Sāṃkhya is "a very different one." Having learned to care for the body, "next time we'll look after the rest of you," moving on to the spiritual practices of yoga.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Āyurveda — "knowledge of longevity"; an Indian medical tradition whose modest goal is to prolong life ("when life is lost, everything is lost") to the body's natural span, not to win immortality.
  • Caraka-Saṃhitā — the oldest complete surviving Āyurvedic treatise, compiled by Caraka (written c. 300 AD, redacted c. 500 AD).
  • Caraka — its compiler-physician, said to have advised King Kaniṣka; the name means "one who wanders," a clue to doctors' itinerant origins.
  • Suśruta-Saṃhitā / Suśruta — an old treatise focused on surgery, urging practice on melons, gourds and meat, examination with all five senses, and the maxim "blood is life."
  • Ātreya — the sage and medical authority quoted by Caraka (on lifespan not being fixed by karma, and on epidemics caused by wicked rulers).
  • Aśvins — mythical figures to whom the gods first handed down the medical teaching.
  • doṣa — the three disease-causing substances, wind, bile, and phlegm; in early India conceived as pathogens to be eliminated/kept un-stirred, not (as in Greek medicine) humours to be balanced.
  • wind/breath — the leading doṣa and a fundamental bodily principle, also a divine cosmic force; bile and phlegm are opposed to each other beneath it.
  • rasa — the nutritive juice food becomes once digested, passing into the heart and circulating through the body.
  • pramāṇa — the four means of knowing (authority, perception, inference, reasoning) used both to defend rebirth and to practise medicine; perception is foremost in diagnosis.
  • five elements / six flavours — ether, wind, earth, fire, water (Sāṃkhya cosmology) compose body and food; foods classed as sweet, sour, salty, bitter, pungent, astringent, used to counter harmful buildup by opposing nature.
  • sannipātika — technical term for a harmful combination of several humours; found in the Buddhist Pāli canon, hinting at Āyurveda's link to Buddhism.
  • śramaṇa / Buddhism — the ascetic, dissenting movements from which Āyurveda may have grown, doctors being impure itinerant outsiders in brahminical eyes.
  • Sāṃkhya (Īśvarakṛṣṇa & Gauḍapāda) — the source-of-suffering framework (threefold suffering; bodily disease from wind/bile/phlegm) that frames the episode and supplies Āyurveda's elemental, enumerative background.
  • the lazy argument — the Stoic fatalist puzzle (why see a doctor if your fate is fixed?) that Caraka answers by making lifespan depend on multiple karmas plus present action.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 29 — "Practice Makes Perfect: Patañjali's Yoga-Sūtra"
docs.text:
← Ep 28

Ep 30 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:19:29 In brief: The Yoga-Sūtra of Patañjali is not the gym-class yoga of posture and breath but a practical "user's manual" built on Sāṃkhya metaphysics: through long, repetitive discipline (action yoga) the adept stills the mind, disengages from the fruits of action and karma, and aims at liberation — leaving open the deep question of whether the goal is total withdrawal from nature or a serene engagement with it. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennari"; Patañjali ≈ "Batanjali / Patangeli / but Tanghly"; Pāṇini ≈ "Panani"; Vyāsa ≈ "Vyasa"; bhāṣya ≈ "Basya/Basha"; Philipp Maas ≈ "Philip Mas"; Yogaśāstra ≈ "Yoga Shasra"; Īśvarakṛṣṇa ≈ "Ishvara Krishna"; citta ≈ "chita"; abhyāsa ≈ "Abyasa"; kriyā yoga ≈ "kria yoga"; Ājīvikas ≈ "Ajivakas"; Ian Whicher ≈ "Ian Witcher"; nirodha ≈ "Niroda"; kaivalya ≈ "Kaivalya").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Patañjali — author of the Yoga-Sūtra; sharing a name with the famous grammarian and said to be the incarnation of a serpent god, but a distinct figure [00:02:09].
  • The Yoga-Sūtra (and its bhāṣya commentary) — the foundational text of the yoga tradition, recently argued to be the work of a single author [00:01:53].
  • Vyāsa — the name attached to the commentary, probably a generic "commentator" name rather than the epic bard [00:02:42].
  • Īśvarakṛṣṇa & the Sāṃkhya-kārikā — the near-contemporary Sāṃkhya text whose metaphysics frames yoga [00:03:26].
  • Philipp Maas — modern philologist whose work re-dated and re-authored the text; the next episode's interview guest [00:02:54].
  • Ian Whicher — modern interpreter who reads yoga as anti-dualist [00:14:02].

docs.title: Yoga, Yoda, and the occult chapter
docs.text:
• [00:00:36] Enroll in a yoga class and you expect stretching, better posture, awareness of body and breath, focus, maybe meditation — but not the power to levitate, read minds, or foresee the future. For that you'd need a Jedi master: changing one letter from "yoga" to "Yoda" seems to make all the difference.
  • [00:01:02] Or does it? The third chapter of the foundational text promises that the adept yogin really does wield exactly such magical powers — recall of previous lives, the ability to speak other languages, heightened senses, supernatural stealth, and more.
  • [00:01:28] This occult portion is rarely highlighted in scholarly discussion, perhaps because interpreters find it embarrassing or irrelevant. But it shouldn't be discounted: the talk of supernatural powers fits yoga's overall message — that we are capable of mastering, and ultimately transcending, nature itself.

docs.title: Who wrote it — three figures, one author
docs.text:
• [00:01:53] Like the other foundational texts in the series, the Yoga-Sūtra is written in a compressed, elliptical style — though its author has less trouble with grammar than Master Yoda.
  • [00:02:09] The author shares the name Patañjali with a famous grammarian, author of the great commentary on Pāṇini, and Patañjali is also said to be the incarnation of a divine serpent named Ananta. We can be confident the grammarian Patañjali was not the Yoga-Sūtra Patañjali (whether either was a snake god is "a question for further research").
  • [00:02:30] The confusion continues with the authoritative commentary, the bhāṣya, ascribed to Vyāsa — the name of the bard who supposedly compiled the Mahābhārata, but here probably just a generic name for a commentator.
  • [00:02:54] Recent philological work by Philipp Maas suggests the sūtra and its bhāṣya were written by one and the same author: Patañjali set down his teaching in sūtra form and then immediately supplied his own exegesis, rather than waiting for later commentators.
  • [00:03:17] Maas dates the combined work — the Yogaśāstra — to between c. 325 and 425 CE, long after the grammarian Patañjali, but right around the time Īśvarakṛṣṇa wrote his Sāṃkhya-kārikā.

docs.title: Yoga's intimate relationship with Sāṃkhya
docs.text:
• [00:03:33] This is no coincidence. Yoga is so closely tied to Sāṃkhya that scholars sometimes speak of a combined Yoga-Sāṃkhya school — and not without reason.
  • [00:03:45] One sequence in the Yoga-Sūtra reads like a summary of Īśvarakṛṣṇa: when the seer is conjoined to that which is seen, suffering inevitably results — a clear allusion to the Sāṃkhya idea that suffering ends only when we free ourselves from nature (prakṛti) and identify with the pure consciousness that is puruṣa.
  • [00:04:09] Patañjali also invokes the dynamic forces called guṇas to explain how things evolve out of the unmanifest principle of prakṛti. In the commentary he goes even further toward Sāṃkhya, fitting its detailed cosmology and psychology into the simpler frame of the sūtra.
  • [00:04:35] If sūtra and commentary are by the same person, then the whole Sāṃkhya system provides the framework for both texts: the sūtra simply leaves a lot out, as befits its condensed form, reserving the technical details for the commentary.

docs.title: Theory vs. practice — why we still need yoga
docs.text:
• [00:04:56] So why bother with the Yoga-Sūtra if it just echoes the Sāṃkhya-kārikā? At the very least, the two differ in purpose and emphasis.
  • [00:05:09] The common observation is that Sāṃkhya offers theory, yoga concentrates on practice. It's not quite that neat — both stress that the goal is the higher insight that comes when we discriminate between nature and consciousness — but the Yoga-Sūtra is indeed more practical: where Īśvarakṛṣṇa provides a blueprint of the world and the person, Patañjali offers a user's manual.
  • [00:05:42] This tracks the earlier use of the terms in the Bhagavad-Gītā, which treats Sāṃkhya and yoga as complementary strands. We need yoga's practical advice because liberation cannot be achieved by merely understanding the difference between prakṛti and puruṣa intellectually — freeing oneself from nature takes long practice and steady effort.

docs.title: Action yoga — repetition, the three techniques, the eight limbs
docs.text:
• [00:06:00] The Sanskrit word translated as "practice" is abhyāsa, which literally means repetition. Patañjali makes it the focus of his second chapter, explaining the three techniques of what he calls action yoga (kriyā yoga):
  • First, impose ascetic disciplines on oneself — deliberately undergoing hunger and thirst, making vows of silence or celibacy.
  • Second, repeatedly recite certain words — an ancient Vedic practice that could involve memorized scripture or just the single syllable oṃ.
  • Third, religious devotion (more on this shortly).
  • [00:06:49] Together these eliminate the sources of affliction: desires, the fear of death, and the sense of one's own individual self.
  • [00:07:02] Later Patañjali adds the so-called eight limbs of yoga — "eight more limbs than you'd expect from a snake god" — including ethical guidelines, control over posture and breath, withdrawal from the senses, and three kinds of meditation. This is the part that corresponds to what we associate with yoga today.
  • [00:07:25] The central insight is ironic: following Sāṃkhya, we seek to wean ourselves away from mental and physical engagement, since engagement binds us to nature — yet we can only desist from action by undertaking other actions. Hence "action yoga." Through long discipline of mind and body, we teach the mind and body to be still, avoiding the tumult of fluctuations that arise as prakṛti is transformed by the guṇas.

docs.title: Citta — yoga as the cessation of mental activity
docs.text:
• [00:07:56] The stillness sought is mental, not merely physical. Where Sāṃkhya gives a complicated analysis of the mind as several powers forming an "interior organ," Patañjali speaks of one simple faculty, the citta.
  • [00:08:19] He goes so far as to define yoga as the cessation of activity within this mind. Again the Yoga-Sūtra takes the simpler route, but the two texts are in basic agreement.

docs.title: Devotion to Īśvara — a theistic turn?
docs.text:
• [00:08:35] On one point many scholars see a sharp contrast. The third recommended practice was devotion — but devotion to whom? The first chapter introduces Īśvara, i.e. God: instead of contemplating the self, we should contemplate God.
  • [00:09:06] We saw no such theistic component in Sāṃkhya — despite his name, Īśvarakṛṣṇa had nothing to say about a deity called Īśvara — so some read this as a fundamental divergence.
  • [00:09:20] But Sāṃkhya does speak of a divine realm, so it is at least open to divinities. A divine being could simply be a particularly pure version of consciousness, relatively untouched by the turbulence of nature — which is exactly what the Yoga-Sūtra says: Īśvara is a special sort of puruṣa, always already liberated from the suffering of attachment to nature.

docs.title: Why is it so hard to live like God? Habit and karma
docs.text:
• [00:09:52] If liberation is just identifying with puruṣa, why can't someone read the Sāṃkhya-kārikā, decide Īśvarakṛṣṇa is right, and be liberated on the spot? An intellectualist would say understanding a teaching is one thing, being sincerely convinced another — but that's not Patañjali's view.
  • [00:10:17] He thinks our bondage to prakṛti is perpetuated by powerful habits that must be gradually subdued. Adamson's example: his desire for almond croissants. Even if he's convinced that wanting them brings more suffering than pleasure — enjoying one, then immediately wondering when he'll get another, worrying the bakery will be closed — that conviction won't make the desire vanish. A deep-seated habit can't be abandoned by a decision; one has to train oneself, via the threefold regimen of action yoga.
  • [00:11:13] So far this looks like a commonsense point about the difficulty of rehabilitation. But Patañjali gives it an ancient Indian twist via the theory of karma: our actions build up karmic deposits that bear fruit in this or the next life, so each of us is born already burdened with karma from previous lives.

docs.title: Fight fire with fire — detachment from the fruits of action
docs.text:
• [00:11:42] A puzzle lurks: if action causes karma and karma prevents liberation, why does Patañjali prescribe more action to achieve liberation? That sounds like fighting fire with fire and getting a larger blaze.
  • [00:12:00] The resolution: perhaps it isn't the action as such that builds karma, but its immediate fruits. Eating the croissant isn't the problem; the resulting pleasure is what makes one crave more. The solution, then, is to train oneself to disengage from the results of one's actions — and the ascetic practices are tailor-made for this, since they aren't intended to yield enjoyable results, while recitation and devotion direct attention away from one's own urges and anxieties.
  • [00:12:46] On this reading Patañjali aligns with the Bhagavad-Gītā: the path to liberation is not complete withdrawal from action — the radical strategy of the Ājīvikas, who stood still until they starved to death — but detachment from the fruits of action. The yogin still gradually disengages from mental fluctuations through patient practice, without necessarily withdrawing from practical life entirely.

docs.title: Dualist or anti-dualist? The Whicher reading
docs.text:
• [00:13:24] This returns us to yoga's relationship with Sāṃkhya. Sāṃkhya is fundamentally dualist, offering a stark choice: engage with the phenomenal world evolved from prakṛti, or identify with the pure consciousness that is puruṣa. At first yoga looks equally dualist.
  • [00:13:42] But what if one could remain mentally aloof from action while still living fully in the world? Then the purpose of yoga would be not to escape nature, but to live within it without suffering for oneself or others.
  • [00:14:02] This anti-dualist reading is championed by the modern interpreter Ian Whicher. He notes that even Sāṃkhya speaks well of one of the three guṇas: turmoil and despondency come from rajas and tamas (the second and third), but the first, sattva, is light and connected to pleasant feelings.
  • [00:14:31] Whicher suggests yoga is a technique for eliminating the afflictions caused by ignorance, desire, and concern for the self — all traced to rajas and tamas — while leaving sattva intact, so the person engages with the world of prakṛti in a "non-conflicting and unselfish manner."

docs.title: Nirodha — what "cessation" really means
docs.text:
• [00:14:50] Not everyone agrees. Some scholars think yoga aims to eliminate all mental activity, even beneficial activity — after all, Patañjali defines yoga as cessation of such activity.
  • [00:15:10] The debate turns on what Patañjali means by cessation, nirodha. On Whicher's reading it does not mean eliminating or restraining the mind's activity; it means the mind remains unaffected even while involved in action. The adept achieves this so long as she does not confuse her real self with her phenomenal self.
  • [00:15:40] The goal, then, is not to sit motionless in a cave with an empty mind. One can keep living an engaged life so long as one shifts one's perspective on it, identifying with consciousness rather than with the objects of consciousness.
  • [00:15:58] Whicher's supporting point: if fulfillment required complete disengagement, it would be hard to explain why yoga gurus are actively teaching their disciples.

docs.title: Īśvara the timeless guru — and the smooth flow
docs.text:
• [00:16:10] Support also comes from the description of the divine Īśvara, who is pure puruṣa living outside of time. Yet his timelessness means he has always been there — able to instruct the first adepts of yoga in the distant past.
  • [00:16:30] This is puzzling: how can God be a teacher, and how can a timeless being relate to time-bound creatures? Patañjali doesn't say — but what little he says indicates Īśvara is simultaneously liberated and engaged in a form of selfless action that gives rise to no suffering. It only makes sense that we should aspire to the same.
  • [00:17:01] Another clue is in the commentary, where Vyāsa (probably Patañjali himself) discusses eliminating desire through constant practice, which is meant to yield a smooth flow in the mind: unconflicted, unattached mental activity untouched by fluctuations — significantly different from banishing activity entirely.

docs.title: Kaivalya and the unresolved tension
docs.text:
• [00:17:31] This is an alluring picture of the good life: the yoga adept can, as it were, have her almond croissant and eat it too, so long as she remains unaffected as she does so.
  • [00:17:45] But whether this is really Patañjali's meaning is debated. At the very end of the Yoga-Sūtra he sounds like he is recommending total withdrawal from the world of the guṇas, speaking of achieving kaivalya, meaning "aloneness." At this stage karma and change come to an end; everything in nature has served its purpose because puruṣa has returned to itself.
  • [00:18:14] This sounds like more than a shift in viewpoint — though it could just mean puruṣa is "alone" in the sense of seeing without being attached to what it sees.
  • [00:18:25] The same ambiguity haunts his account of the stages of meditative contemplation, samādhi: as we progress we may reach a contemplation that still involves some knowledge, but ultimately what we want is a pure contemplative state with no object, all karmic burdens eliminated and the mind at peace.
  • [00:18:46] Is the mind at peace because nothing is happening, or because the adept's mind is not changed by what is happening? No yoga instructor would end a class on an unresolved tension like this — but that, Adamson admits, is exactly what he is going to do.
  • [00:18:59] We're not done with this school, though: next time the series turns to Philipp Maas, who has done the most important recent work on the origins and composition of the Yoga-Sūtra and its bhāṣya. As Master Yoda might say, "A piece of his mind next time he will give us."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Patañjali — author of the Yoga-Sūtra; distinct from the grammarian of the same name, and (legendarily) an incarnation of the serpent Ananta; probably wrote both sūtra and commentary.
  • Yoga-Sūtra — the foundational, compressed text of the yoga tradition; defines yoga as the cessation of activity in the mind; its occult third chapter promises supernatural powers.
  • bhāṣya / Vyāsa — the authoritative commentary, ascribed to "Vyāsa" (a generic commentator-name), but likely Patañjali's own self-exegesis.
  • Yogaśāstra — Philipp Maas's name for the combined sūtra-plus-commentary work, dated to c. 325–425 CE.
  • Sāṃkhya / Sāṃkhya-kārikā / Īśvarakṛṣṇa — the near-contemporary dualist system whose metaphysics frames yoga; "Sāṃkhya is theory, yoga is practice."
  • prakṛti — nature, the unmanifest principle out of which things evolve; the source of bondage and suffering.
  • puruṣa — pure consciousness; liberation is to identify with it rather than nature. Īśvara is a special, always-liberated puruṣa.
  • guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas) — the dynamic forces driving cosmic and mental evolution; rajas and tamas cause affliction, sattva is light and pleasant.
  • abhyāsa — "practice," literally repetition; the core of yogic discipline.
  • kriyā yoga (action yoga) — the threefold regimen: ascetic discipline, recitation (e.g. oṃ), and devotion; the irony that we must act in order to cease acting.
  • eight limbs of yoga — ethics, posture, breath-control, sense-withdrawal, and three kinds of meditation.
  • citta — the single mental faculty whose cessation of activity is yoga.
  • Īśvara — God; a special liberated puruṣa, object of devotion and timeless first teacher of yoga.
  • karma — actions build "karmic deposits" bearing fruit across lives; the puzzle is escaping karma by further action, solved by detaching from the fruits of action.
  • Ājīvikas — ascetics who pursued total withdrawal by standing still until they starved; contrasted with the Bhagavad-Gītā's detachment-from-fruits.
  • nirodha — "cessation"; on Whicher's reading not the elimination of mental activity but the mind remaining unaffected within it.
  • Ian Whicher — modern interpreter reading yoga as anti-dualist: engaged, unselfish living with sattva intact rather than escape from nature.
  • kaivalya — "aloneness," the end-state where karma and change cease and puruṣa returns to itself; ambiguously total withdrawal or pure unattached awareness.
  • samādhi — meditative contemplation; its stages culminate in a pure objectless state with the mind at peace.
  • Philipp Maas — philologist who re-dated and re-authored the text; next episode's interview guest.

docs.text:
← Ep 29
