🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:19:41 In brief: Having defended perception, Nyāya turns to its second source of knowledge — inference (anumāna). The episode lays out the anatomy of an inference (sign, locus, thing-inferred), Gautama's three kinds of reliable sign and Vātsyāyana's competing readings of them, Nyāya's case-based "give an example" style of reasoning, and the five fallacies that mark out a bad inference — a body of logic so rigorous that "even the most determined skeptic" must concede it is philosophy. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari"; Nyāya ≈ "Niyaya/Niyya/Naya"; anumāna ≈ "unumana"; pramāṇa ≈ "pramana/promana"; Gautama ≈ "Gautima/Scoutima/Gautoma/Gautaum"; Vātsyāyana ≈ "Batsyayyayana/Vatsyayana/Zayena/Zayana/the Ayyana/Batsya Jaina"; Caraka Saṃhitā ≈ "Chara Samhita"; hetu/liṅga ≈ "hetu/linga"; pakṣa ≈ "pachshha"; sādhya ≈ "Sadiya"; pūrvavat ≈ "Purvavat"; śeṣavat ≈ "Sheshavat"; sāmānyatodṛṣṭa ≈ "Samay…"; jāti ≈ "Jati"; hetvābhāsa ≈ "Hedvabasa"; vyāpti ≈ "Vyapti"; Gaṅgeśa ≈ "Gungesha"; Śāntarakṣita ≈ "Shantarachita"; Dignāga ≈ "Dignaga"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagajuna"; probans/probandum ≈ "probands/probandum").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Gautama (Akṣapāda) — founder of Nyāya, who lists inference as a pramāṇa and classifies signs and fallacies [00:00:13].
  • Vātsyāyana — Gautama's commentator, who offers two rival interpretations of the three kinds of sign and supplies most of the worked examples [00:05:02].
  • The Nyāya-Sūtra — its final book, on genuine versus bogus resemblance, may be a separate work [00:10:50].
  • The Caraka Saṃhitā — an early medical text whose diagnostic reasoning shaped Gautama's theory of inference [00:02:10].
  • Gaṅgeśa — the 13th-century founder of "later Nyāya," celebrated for five definitions of vyāpti [00:03:38].

docs.title: Perception is not enough — we have to infer
docs.text:
• [00:00:13] Today's episode: "Standard Deductions — Nyāya on reasoning." According to the Nyāya school we can know the world simply by perceiving it; as the previous episode showed, Gautama and his commentators mounted a spirited defence of perception as a source of knowledge — our senses tell us about things, their properties, even about absences.
  • [00:00:45] But we cannot get through life on perceptions alone. Adamson's set-piece: you are an ancient Indian walking through a forest and you hear a distinctive low growl, unmistakably the sound of a tiger. The right response is to "run like hell" — but to apply that rule you must do more than perceive the sound. You need to make an inference: you flee not from the sound but from the unseen tiger whose presence you infer from the sound.
  • [00:01:26] Inference is therefore as crucial to survival as perception, and Gautama duly lists it alongside perception as a pramāṇa (source of knowledge). The close link is built into the very word for inference, anumāna — "that which follows after perception." Inference is what lets us go beyond the directly perceived to what we cannot perceive: hidden, like the tiger in the trees, or in principle imperceptible, like the illness inferred from the symptoms it produces in the body.
  • [00:02:04] The medical example is chosen advisedly. In framing his theory Gautama seems to have been influenced by early medical works like the Caraka Saṃhitā. Diagnosis is the paradigm case of inference: cough and fever are signs of pneumonia — "less dangerous than a tiger, but still nothing to sneeze at."

docs.title: The anatomy of an inference: sign, locus, and thing-inferred
docs.text:
• [00:02:27] The standard Indian example is the one already met: the mountain has fire because it has smoke. We perceive smoke on a distant hillside and from that sign arrive at knowledge of an unseen fire. Latin-showoffs would call the smoke the probans ("that which offers proof") and the fire the probandum ("that which is proven").
  • [00:02:58] The Nyāya thinkers, "not so strong on scholastic Latin," call the smoke a hetu or liṅga — a mark or sign. The technical vocabulary has three slots:
  • the sign (hetu/liṅga) — the smoke, the growl — which must always be present in the object the inference is about;
  • the pakṣa — that object, the locus: the mountain where smoke is seen, the trees from which the growl emanates;
  • the sādhya (sādhya-dharma) — the thing whose presence we infer from the sign: the fire on the mountain, the tiger in the trees.
  • [00:03:29] Nyāya logicians also gave great weight to the ability to cite an example — a second case where the same kind of sign revealed the same kind of signified thing, e.g. the smoke-producing fire in the kitchen. "When I tell you to get that cough checked out, I explain that I knew a guy with just these symptoms who died of pneumonia — or would have, if he hadn't first been eaten by a tiger because he was walking in the woods listening to a podcast with the volume turned up."

docs.title: Which signs are reliable? Gautama's three kinds
docs.text:
• [00:04:04] Giving one parallel example does not guarantee the inference yields knowledge. Suppose you see fire and infer there must be smoke — that is bad reasoning: fire sometimes makes smoke, but we have also seen fiery things with no smoke, so fire is not a dependable sign of smoke. And, come to think of it, tiger-sounds are not an absolutely reliable sign of tigers either — perhaps someone is doing an incredibly realistic tiger impression, or playing a tape recorder ("younger listeners may want to ask their parents what a tape recorder is").
  • [00:04:45] So if the Naiyāyikas want inferences to count as unimpeachable knowledge "in some cases," they owe us a story about which signs are reliable. We can piece one together from Gautama and his commentator Vātsyāyana. Gautama names three kinds of dependable sign: pūrvavat ("based on what is prior"), śeṣavat ("based on a remainder"), and a third, glossed as observation of a generality (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa (?)).
  • [00:05:16] The original meaning of these three terms is obscure — even the earliest commentators were unsure — and Vātsyāyana was uncertain enough to offer two alternative interpretations.

docs.title: Vātsyāyana's first reading — cause, effect, and generalization
docs.text:
• [00:05:30] On the first reading the three signs mean reasoning from cause to effect, from effect to cause, and from a generalization to a particular case:
  • cause→effect: it will rain because of the large black cloud;
  • effect→cause: it has been raining, because the river is swollen;
  • generalization→particular: the sun must be moving now, even though it doesn't look like it, because over a longer period it is observed to change position.
  • [00:06:00] Despite the humble examples, this credits Vātsyāyana with sketching an account of scientific inference and prediction — with obvious applications in medicine, and (the moving sun) in a field like astronomy.

docs.title: Vātsyāyana's second reading — three different sorts of reasoning
docs.text:
• [00:06:22] On the second reading the three terms name three different kinds of reasoning:
  • "based on what is prior" covers all causal inference (including everything in the first interpretation);
  • "based on a remainder" is reasoning by process of elimination — Vātsyāyana's example: sound is a substance, because it is not a universal, not a quality, not a motion, and so on. We fix a finite list of possibilities that exhausts the options and then eliminate all but one. Adamson likens this to doctors using tests to rule out diagnoses, and to Sherlock Holmes's maxim that "when you have eliminated the impossible, whatever remains, however improbable, must be the truth";
  • observation of a generality means assigning a property to something because of the class it belongs to — e.g. infer that tigers are predators from the fact that they are cats, since all cats are predators. Vātsyāyana's own example: mental states are qualities; qualities have subjects; therefore there is a subject of mental states, namely the self.
  • [00:07:47] That last example is a flag that this whole discussion matters for philosophical method, not just medical diagnosis and tiger-avoidance — Nyāya will use exactly this style of argument to establish the existence of the self.

docs.title: Positive and negative examples
docs.text:
• [00:08:00] The Naiyāyikas are keen on examples, and elsewhere in the Nyāya-Sūtra Gautama explains that there are two kinds that can motivate an inference:
  • positive examples, which turn on a similarity — smoke indicating fire on the mountainside, as it also does in the kitchen;
  • negative examples, which cite a case where the sign is absent and the signified is also absent — instead of the kitchen, the surface of a lake, where neither smoke nor fire is found. By disanalogy, the mountain, which does have smoke, should have fire too.
  • [00:08:49] Whether positive or negative, such reasoning moves straightforwardly from one case to another — kitchen or lake to mountainside — with no appeal to any law of nature or universal rule.

docs.title: In praise of case-based reasoning — and its limits
docs.text:
• [00:09:01] This may seem naïve, but there is much to be said for case-based reasoning. To persuade you it is about to rain: "Look at that large black cloud. Last time you saw a cloud like that, what happened? It rained. It's the same now, so it's definitely going to rain." The Nyāya-Sūtra offers a range of such cases: seeing ants carrying their eggs, one infers it will rain; seeing a full, swiftly-flowing river, one infers it has been raining; seeing smoke, one infers an unseen fire.
  • [00:09:43] One might dig deeper and ask why a sign is regularly linked to a thing — we have noticed ants carry their eggs before rain, while remaining "mystified as to how ants predict the weather." The same applies to inference by sampling: from the salty taste of one drop of seawater we infer the whole sea is salty; tasting one grain of rice, we infer all the rice is cooked. We tacitly assume a common underlying structure between sample and rest — this grain sat in the same pan, in the same water, for the same time.
  • [00:10:38] But case-based reasoning can go awry, so it becomes "a matter of cardinal importance" to distinguish genuine from bogus resemblance. This is the subject of the whole final book of the Nyāya-Sūtra — a section some modern scholars read as an independent work. Either way it shows Gautama was as interested in how things go wrong as in how we get them right.

docs.title: When resemblance is false: the jāti fallacy
docs.text: • [00:11:11] Argument from a false resemblance suffers the fallacy called jāti — a merely apparent commonality between an example and a locus. Recall inferring a tiger in the trees: in other cases that sound did accompany a real tiger, but in this case, "hopefully," it is only a tape recorder. The resemblance is superficial; the inference fails.

docs.title: Gautama's five fallacies (hetvābhāsa)
docs.text:
• [00:11:33] Gautama in fact identifies five kinds of fallacy that undermine arguments. The Sanskrit for fallacy is hetvābhāsa — literally "something that merely has the appearance of being a sign." Their importance is partly tied to Nyāya's interest in debate (spotting a fallacy in an opponent's argument is a sure way to win), but also to the dependability of scientific prediction and medical prognosis — and mapping how arguments go astray is "an indirect way of showing what a sound argument is." Avoid all five and you can be sure you are reasoning correctly. The five — "which, coincidentally, are also the five pitfalls faced by teenagers when they start dating":

  • [00:12:34] 1. The deviating. The sign is present but the inferred property is not. Vātsyāyana's example: sound is eternal because it is intangible — but we can name intangible things that are not eternal, e.g. pain (intangible, but thankfully it goes away). The lesson, turned around: a dependable sign must not deviate from the property — wherever the sign occurs, so must the signified. An analogy is not enough; there must be a universal rule connecting sign and signified. Only if tiger-noises always signify tigers can you confidently infer a tiger (though "you might want to run anyway, just to be safe").

  • [00:13:31] This universal rule, vyāpti (pervasion), became a major topic of later Nyāya, initiated in the 13th century by Gaṅgeśa with his celebrated five definitions of vyāpti.

  • [00:13:45] 2. The incoherent. A conclusion should not contradict your other well-established beliefs, even if it looks plausible out of context. This is not a purely formal defect inside a single inference; rather, we reason within a larger set of commitments, and if an inference clashes with firmly held beliefs it is rational to doubt your premises. The strained example: fire is cold, because it is a substance — more plausible than it sounds, since all substances other than fire and fiery things are indeed cold; but fire is the exception, and our wider net of beliefs raises a warning flag ("fire is in fact hot"), so the argument must have gone wrong.

  • [00:14:51] 3. The indecisive. Two equally strong arguments lead to opposite conclusions; though neither can be faulted on formal grounds, we should reserve judgment. Example: sound is eternal because it is eternal — formally valid (a tautology, like "Socrates is mortal and all mortals are mortal, therefore Socrates is mortal"), but useless, because one could equally argue sound is non-eternal because it is non-eternal. With no ground for preferring one tautology, neither can be accepted.

  • [00:15:34] This is "highly reminiscent" of Greek skeptics like Sextus Empiricus, who induced suspension of judgment by arguing both sides of an issue. But Gautama is not endorsing skepticism: he assumes such standoffs arise only occasionally, not pervasively throughout philosophical argument as Sextus claimed.

  • [00:16:15] 4. The same predicament. A sign "not distinguished from what is signified… because it itself needs to be proved." Vātsyāyana's example: a shadow is a substance because it moves. This looks fine, since movement is unique to substances — but the sign itself (that a shadow moves) has not been demonstrated. It is no good arguing for a doubtful proposition on the strength of another doubtful proposition; we must resolve the doubtful case by appeal to known facts.

  • [00:16:56] 5. The mis-timed. The most enigmatic — commentators could not agree on Gautama's meaning. The basic idea: sometimes merely formulating a thesis is enough to show it cannot be true, so offering a reason in support would be pointless, hence "mistimed." Later Naiyāyikas read it differently — as cases where the intended conclusion has already been shown false by other means, making argument redundant; but Adamson finds that implausible (it would just be a case of the incoherent — a redundancy the Buddhist Śāntarakṣita in fact pointed out). The better reading: a thesis that is just obviously false — self-contradictory, like "there is a tiger in the trees but no tiger in the trees," or patently absurd, like "there is a tiger in the trees, but don't worry, he's a vegetarian." Reasoning for such a thesis is a waste of time.

docs.title: Why this counts as philosophy — and where Nyāya goes next
docs.text:
• [00:18:10] Gautama's treatment of argument and its failures shows "a keen sensitivity to the nature of philosophical activity and to the demands of science." We have lingered on the logic because Nyāya is so notable for its analysis of method — and "even the most determined skeptic would have difficulty denying that this is philosophy." From a Western angle one may be puzzled by Nyāya's lack of a sharp line between the purely rational and the empirical — between (more Latin showing-off) the a priori and the a posteriori.
  • [00:18:46] Nyāya was not the only Indian contributor to logic. Nāgārjuna, "certainly a determined skeptic," subjected the theory of reasoning to a searching critique, and another Buddhist, Dignāga, would give a more precise definition of the good inferential sign — both to come later in the series.
  • [00:19:08] But the groundwork for the Nyāya–Buddhist contrast is not finished. The Buddhists were notorious for denying any stable self that persists through time as the locus of awareness; Nyāya, true to its optimism about reasoning, is optimistic here too — Gautama and his followers affirm that there is a self and investigate the faculties of thought and attention. Next time: from Nyāya epistemology and logic to Nyāya philosophy of mind.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• anumāna — inference; "that which follows after perception," the second pramāṇa, which takes us beyond the perceived to the unperceived (the hidden tiger, the imperceptible illness).
  • pramāṇa — a source/means of knowledge; Gautama lists inference alongside perception.
  • hetu / liṅga — the sign or mark from which we infer (the smoke, the growl); must always be present in the locus. Latin: probans.
  • pakṣa — the locus, the object the inference is about (the mountain, the trees).
  • sādhya (sādhya-dharma) — the thing inferred, whose presence the sign reveals (the fire, the tiger). Latin: probandum.
  • pūrvavat / śeṣavat / sāmānyatodṛṣṭa (?) — Gautama's three kinds of dependable sign ("based on what is prior," "based on a remainder," "observation of a generality"), given two rival readings by Vātsyāyana (cause/effect/generalization vs. causal inference / elimination / class-membership).
  • example (positive & negative) — a second corroborating case: positive turns on similarity (kitchen fire), negative on disanalogy (smokeless, fireless lake). Nyāya reasons case-to-case, with no appeal to a law of nature.
  • jāti — the fallacy of a merely apparent commonality between example and locus (false resemblance).
  • hetvābhāsa — "fallacy"; literally something that only appears to be a sign. Gautama lists five.
  • the five fallacies — the deviating (sign present, property absent), the incoherent (conclusion clashes with established beliefs), the indecisive (equal arguments both ways), the same predicament (the sign itself is unproven), and the mis-timed (reasoning for an obviously/self-evidently false thesis).
  • vyāpti — the universal "pervasion" rule connecting sign to signified; the central topic of later Nyāya.
  • Gautama (Akṣapāda) — founder of Nyāya; author of the Nyāya-Sūtra's theory of signs and fallacies.
  • Vātsyāyana — Gautama's commentator; offers the worked examples and the two interpretations of the three signs.
  • Caraka Saṃhitā — early medical text; its diagnostic reasoning influenced Gautama's theory of inference.
  • Gaṅgeśa — 13th-century founder of "later Nyāya," famed for five definitions of vyāpti.
  • Nāgārjuna / Dignāga — Buddhist thinkers who, respectively, critiqued the theory of reasoning and refined the definition of the good inferential sign.
  • Śāntarakṣita — Buddhist philosopher who noted the redundancy in one reading of the "mis-timed" fallacy.
  • Sextus Empiricus — Greek skeptic; the "indecisive" fallacy resembles his arguing-both-sides, but Gautama denies it leads to general skepticism.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 34 — "The Truth Shall Set You Free: Nyāya on the Mind"
docs.text:
← Ep 33

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:21:27 In brief: Having established how we know (perception, inference), Gautama's Nyāya now asks what we can know — above all the human subject. The self (ātman) is argued to be a distinct theoretical entity, separate from both body and mind (manas); the mind is demoted to a mere instrument and inner sense; and the whole apparatus is aimed at liberation, since true beliefs yield good desires, good actions, and the freedom from suffering that is the highest good. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari"; Nyāya ≈ "Neaya/Niyaya/Niae/Niyah/Niaya"; Gautama ≈ "Gautima/Gautoma/Gaurama"; Vaiśeṣika ≈ "Vaisheeshika/Bysheeshika"; Sāṃkhya ≈ "Samkhya"; Cārvāka ≈ "Chavaka"; Vātsyāyana ≈ "Vatsyayana/Batsyayana"; Bhartṛhari ≈ "Bautrihari"; Pāṇinian ≈ "Ponenese"; prameya ≈ "pramaya"; Ujjwala Jha ≈ "Ujjwalha Jha").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Gautama — founder of Nyāya, here laying out the objects of knowledge and his theory of self and mind [00:00:13].
  • Vātsyāyana — Gautama's commentator, who pulls scattered remarks into full demonstrations [00:07:08].
  • The Nyāya-Sūtra & Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra — paired sources for the claim that beliefs and desires are qualities needing a substrate [00:05:21].
  • The Buddhists & the Cārvāka — the two foils: the Buddhists deny an enduring self, the Cārvāka reduce the mental to the material [00:02:55].

docs.title: From knowing how to knowing what
docs.text:
• [00:00:13] We now have a good grip on Gautama's epistemology: against the skeptical arguments circulating in ancient India, he insists we really can have knowledge, gained through various means of knowing (pramāṇas) — most fundamentally sense perception, plus the argumentative inferences he and his fellow Naiyāyikas have rigorously analysed.
  • [00:00:59] What's been unclear is which things he thinks we can know. The endless talk of "fire on the mountainside" might seem relevant only to a forest ranger dodging tigers; the theory earns its keep when it turns to philosophical understanding — what the sources of knowledge tell us about the structure of the world and of ourselves.
  • [00:01:21] Nyāya does not outsource this to its more metaphysically-minded colleagues in Sāṃkhya and Vaiśeṣika. Gautama offers his own enumeration of the knowable things (the prameyas), but it bears his stamp: his primary interests are epistemic and soteriological (knowledge and liberation), not pure metaphysics.
  • [00:01:46] Of the twelve items he names, half concern psychology / the nature of human beings, the other half ethics and karma. The first group: the self, the mind, the body, the sense faculties, the objects of the senses, and the various mental states and events. Note that only one item — the objects of the senses — lies outside the human knower, and even it is defined by reference to human knowledge (a catch-all for what is available to the senses). The second group: motivation, evil (fault), rebirth, the fruits of action, suffering, and the destination the whole philosophy leads to — liberation. Adamson saves liberation for last, because "if we started with that, you might not bother listening to the rest of the episode."

docs.title: Why posit a self at all — the Buddhist and Cārvāka targets
docs.text:
• [00:02:45] As with knowledge, Gautama develops his account of self and mind with an eye to refuting rivals. The Buddhists are one target: they refuse to accept any enduring self. The Cārvāka are another: their reductionism holds that mental experiences emerge from an entirely material basis.
  • [00:03:13] Against both, Gautama argues for the reality of the "ingredients" of the human, insisting that the self is not to be identified with the bundle of body, sense faculties and mental processes — and, crucially, that there is a difference between ātman and manas, which we may translate as self and mind.
  • [00:03:38] So Gautama goes Descartes's mind–body dualism one better: we each have a self in addition to a mind and a body. Or is this going Descartes one worse? Most philosophers today are skeptical about positing a mind distinct from the body, never mind a further self distinct from the mind — and, by informal surveys, these skeptics aren't even Buddhists. Gautama therefore has a lot of arguing to do. Fortunately, arguments are what he does best.

docs.title: Arguments for the self
docs.text:
• [00:04:12] The self as subject of mental states. If there is a belief or desire, there must be someone doing the believing and desiring; where there's pleasure and pain, someone to enjoy the good times and suffer the bad. (We met this before as Vātsyāyana's example of arguing from generalities to particular instances, rather than cause-to-effect.)
  • [00:04:47] The self as a theoretical entity. The Buddhists doubted the self could be reached by causal inference, noting that the self never "shows up" when we go looking for it as one more thing in the world. Anticipating this, Gautama treats the self like a theoretical posit — not observed in itself, but hypothesised to explain what we do observe.
  • [00:05:09] Qualities need a substrate. Fitting a wider Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika pattern of proving the self without appeal to cause and effect: both the Nyāya-Sūtra and the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra classify beliefs and desires as qualities. They can't be substances in their own right, nor motions, nor universals — and qualities "don't float around free, like ontological balloons cut loose." So there must be a substrate to which they belong: the self. (This is argument by elimination — a belief is neither substance nor universal nor motion, so it can only be a quality of something.)
  • [00:06:12] The negative example. The strange-seeming Nyāya strategy of citing a case where both terms are absent — you support "smoke indicates fire" by pointing to a lake, where smoke and fire are alike absent. So too for the self: in inanimate objects mental events like beliefs and desires are absent because a self is absent; in us, the mental qualities and the self are found together, "like smoke and fire." (One reason Nyāya catalogued kinds of argument so carefully was precisely to forge tools for establishing the self — unsurprising for a school heir to the Vedic demand to seek self-knowledge above all.)
  • [00:07:08] The self as integrator across time (Vātsyāyana). The self doesn't just underlie individual states; it integrates states occurring at different times. I desire an almond croissant only because I've experienced croissants before — and without a self enduring over time, how could I recognise anew something experienced before? The same move drives Nyāya's karma theory: if I am rightly held accountable for past actions (eating too many croissants, punished by reincarnation as a Frenchman), the recipient of the karmic fruits must be the same self that performed the act.
  • [00:08:18] The self as integrator across senses (the crocodile). You can also run it with multiple events at one time — more effective against Buddhists, who can explain memory as a chain of sequential events causing one another with no enduring binder. So picture Jonardon's pet crocodile, Gina, basking in the mud; raised from birth, she's tame enough to pat. When you pat her you perceive one and the same object through both vision and touch — "I touch the crocodile that I see." That judgement is impossible unless there is a single judge comparing the deliverances of the different senses; and since it stands over sight, hearing and touch, this judge is distinct from all of them. It is nothing other than yourself — distinct from sensation.

docs.title: The mind (manas) — inner sense and faculty of attention
docs.text:
• [00:09:24] You are more than body-plus-self: you also have manas, the mind. The Nyāya-Sūtra gives it two roles — an internal sense and a faculty of attention.
  • [00:09:39] Why an internal sense? You have processes that are wholly interior — wondering whether fraternising with a crocodile is wise, or dreaming of being attacked by a tiger — plus an inner awareness of your own mental states by reflecting on what you're perceiving or desiring. This goes on "behind the stage," unobservable by others or by your own outer sense organs. So there must be an internal sense whose job is to perceive inner happenings: the mind, a faculty of introspection, an inner monitor.
  • [00:10:24] Why can't the self do this directly? It too is distinct from the senses and is the subject of mental life. Gautama replies that the mind is very much like a sense faculty, differing only in working inward rather than outward; the self is the underlying agent and subject, which uses the mind as an instrument.

docs.title: Agent vs instrument — the grammarian's point
docs.text:
• [00:10:55] The argument leans on an observation from Pāṇinian grammar: the agent of an action is distinct from the instrument with which it's performed. You needn't know Sanskrit — think of the Latin contrast between nominative and dative case endings. Sanskrit grammarians mark it by calling the agent an independent causal factor and the instrument dependent on the agent.
  • [00:11:20] "Jonardon leads Gina with a leash": Jonardon is not identical with the leash but is the agent using it. Likewise your self is the agent that thinks or dreams about a crocodile using your mind, just as it uses the outer senses to see or touch the crocodile.

docs.title: Private, but not transparent
docs.text:
• [00:11:38] Some philosophers think the self has immediate, transparent access to its own interior — no special faculty needed to know what you're thinking. That would make thinking-about-Gina quite unlike seeing-Gina, where it's obvious you use an instrument (the sense faculty) and need extra conditions (Gina has to be illuminated, not hiding in the river).
  • [00:12:21] But Gautama and other Naiyāyikas, while agreeing each person's mental life is private (available to that person alone), deny it is transparent to the self. The reason your access is privileged is simply that your internal monitor can monitor only your own mental life: Jonardon can't use his mind to be aware that Peter is thinking of a giraffe, nor can Peter use his to be aware that Jonardon is dreaming of crocodiles. Privacy comes from the instrument, not from any direct transparency.

docs.title: Attention — the bottleneck theory
docs.text:
• [00:12:49] The mind's second function marks a striking difference from external sensation. The senses can operate simultaneously (seeing and touching the same thing at once), but awareness cannot: there is only one successive flow of thought, directed to one object at a time. So an additional factor is needed in producing awareness — something working like a switch, selecting one stream of inner experience at a time for the self to appreciate. This makes Gautama perhaps the first figure in the history of philosophy to formulate what's now called the bottleneck or filter theory of attention.
  • [00:13:41] But is the self really limited to sequential experience? Don't two mental events often happen at once — remembering a crocodile while thinking of a giraffe? Gautama says no: apparent simultaneity is an illusion caused by the rapid succession of distinct awarenesses, just as a whirling fire on a rope looks like a single continuous circle of flame.
  • [00:14:13] Sometimes the illusion comes from subconscious processes, as when we grasp a sentence's meaning on hearing its words: we hear them one after another yet seem to understand the whole "in a flash." For Gautama this too is mere illusion — though, as we may remember, this very experience convinced the grammarian Bhartṛhari that such sudden grasping of a whole is how we comprehend language.

docs.title: A problem for selective attention — the leaping tiger
docs.text:
• [00:14:43] Selective awareness faces an objection. If I must use my mind to attend deliberately to my senses — e.g. deciding to listen — how could I ever become aware of anything without first choosing to? That can't be right: when a tiger leaps out of the jungle with a tremendous roar, my problem is certainly not that I fail to hear it; the sudden loud noise forces me to attend.
  • [00:15:16] The Nyāya-Sūtra notes the objection but doesn't answer it satisfactorily. A possible reply: the mind is constantly running a subconscious scan for sensory input — but then it must be doing so even while we sleep, since otherwise alarm clocks wouldn't work.

docs.title: Where consciousness lives — and a second karma argument
docs.text:
• [00:15:34] So where in this model does consciousness reside? Clearly in the self, the subject of conscious states like believing and perceiving. But why deny that the mind is also a conscious subject? Because if both self and mind were conscious, you'd have two centres of consciousness, your inner life split in half. Gautama avoids this by insisting the mind as such is not conscious: it is the instrument, not the agent, of thinking — dependent on the self that uses it, unable to act independently. The mind directs attention, but that falls short of full-blown consciousness, which can reside only in the ātman.
  • [00:16:32] A further argument from karma: a basic premise of traditional karma theory is that we each enjoy or suffer the results of our own actions — nothing I do can alter your karmic fruits. But if self and mind were two independent subjects, the mind's actions could carry moral consequences for the self — moral responsibility shuffled between two agents in one person. The absurdity is the point: the mind cannot be a morally responsible agent. And note the argument doesn't actually require belief in reincarnation — anyone who thinks we bear moral responsibility for our past actions wants that responsibility to belong to a single agent per person. (Gautama, though, certainly does believe in karma.)

docs.title: Liberation — truth as the road to freedom
docs.text:
• [00:17:43] This brings us to the final topic of the Nyāya-Sūtra: liberation. The whole Nyāya theory of knowledge — its pramāṇas, prameyas, its accounts of inference and debating procedure — is meant to yield the highest good. The second sūtra explains how studying philosophy leads there, and it all turns on the relation between beliefs and actions.
  • [00:18:12] Actions stem from beliefs together with desires. I succeed in fondly patting a crocodile's spiny back because I desire to and have true beliefs about what crocodiles look like, where to find them, and how best to pat them. But actions are not merely successful or unsuccessful — they're good or bad, and their moral quality depends on the desire behind them: malicious desire causes bad action.
  • [00:18:49] Beliefs aren't innocent either: they don't only guide actions, they give rise to the desires that motivate them. True beliefs cause benevolent desires, false beliefs malicious ones. (Believe wealth worth more than friendship, and you might steal a crocodile from your friend Jonardon to sell on the black market.) So having true beliefs is paramount — every reason to seek a proper understanding of Nyāya, which teaches the reliable sources of true belief and the difference between sound and spurious arguments. It is, effectively, a tool for avoiding false belief.
  • [00:19:26] The chain: no false beliefs → no wicked desires → no bad actions → no karmic punishment down the line. Here Gautama signals acceptance of the traditional idea that every action has a future effect on the agent — character is destiny: good acts bring pleasurable effects, wicked acts painful ones, in a broad sense; either way I reap what I have sowed.
  • [00:20:07] And it gets better: truth not only earns good karma, it sets you free. Gautama defines the highest good — liberation (mokṣa) — as the absence of suffering, the complete elimination of all distress. To reach it we must avoid bad actions, hence bad desires, hence false beliefs: in other words, study the Nyāya-Sūtra and implement it carefully. For Gautama there is a direct link between the rational aim (believe the truth and nothing but) and the moral imperative (do good, avoid evil). For all the technical sophistication of Nyāya logic and epistemology, the teaching of this school is, as so often in Indian philosophy, an answer to the question of how best to live.
  • [00:21:08] Next time: the series' first-ever interview — featuring a married couple, Ujjwala Jha and V.N. Jha, who have made huge contributions to the study of Nyāya philosophy in modern India.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Gautama — founder of Nyāya; here enumerates the twelve prameyas (knowable things) and argues for a self distinct from both body and mind, all aimed at liberation.
  • Nyāya-Sūtra — Gautama's text; assigns the mind two roles (inner sense + attention) and, in its second sūtra, derives liberation from the link between true belief and good action.
  • Vātsyāyana — Gautama's commentator; mounts the demonstration that the self integrates mental states across time, grounding recognition and karmic accountability.
  • Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra — paired with Nyāya in classifying beliefs and desires as qualities that require a substrate (the self).
  • ātman (self) — a theoretical entity hypothesised to explain experience; the single subject, judge across the senses, and sole locus of consciousness and moral responsibility.
  • manas (mind) — an internal sense (introspective "inner monitor") and faculty of attention; an instrument used by the self, not itself conscious and not a moral agent.
  • prameya — a knowable object; Gautama lists twelve, half psychological, half ethical/karmic.
  • pramāṇa — a reliable means of knowing (perception, inference); Nyāya's tool-kit for securing true belief.
  • bottleneck / filter theory of attention — Gautama's claim that awareness flows one object at a time, a "switch" selecting one stream; possibly the first such theory in philosophy.
  • the Buddhists — deny an enduring self, explaining memory as a causal chain of momentary events; Gautama's chief foil.
  • Cārvāka — materialist reductionists who derive the mental from a purely material basis; a second foil.
  • Bhartṛhari — grammarian who took the flash-grasp of a whole sentence's meaning as veridical (whereas Gautama treats such simultaneity as illusion, like a whirling firebrand).
  • Pāṇinian grammar — supplies the agent vs. instrument distinction (independent vs. dependent causal factor) underwriting the self–mind relation.
  • karma — the doctrine that each person reaps the fruits of their own actions; used both to require a single enduring self and to show the mind cannot be an independent agent.
  • mokṣa (liberation) — the highest good, defined as the complete absence of suffering, reached by true belief → good desire → good action.
  • Ujjwala Jha & V.N. Jha — Nyāya scholars in modern India, guests of the next (first-ever) interview episode.

docs.text:
← Ep 34

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Ujjwala Jha and V.N. Jha 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Ujjwala Jha and V.N. Jha · Runtime: 00:40:12 In brief: An interview on the early Nyāya school — its place among the six orthodox systems, why a school of logic and epistemology is ultimately after release from suffering, the famous five-member syllogism, Nyāya's "utter realism," its answer to the skeptic's regress of justification, and the long road through Udayana and Gaṅgeśa to the technical "new logic" (Navya-Nyāya) still spoken in Sanskrit debate today. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Jinnardin Ganari"; V.N. Jha & Ujjwala Jha ≈ "Ujjjjwala Jha / Ujwalaja"; Nyāya ≈ "Niyaya / Nyaa / Neai"; Vātsyāyana ≈ "Vatshyayana"; Uddyotakara ≈ "Udiyotakara"; Vācaspati Miśra ≈ "Vachaspati Mishra"; Udayana ≈ "Udainachari"; mithyā-jñāna ≈ "mythia gianna"; Praśastapāda ≈ "Prashastapada"; Gaṅgeśa ≈ "Gangesha"; Tattvacintāmaṇi ≈ "Tata Chintamani"; Śeṣadhara ≈ "Sheshadhara"; Jayanta Bhaṭṭa ≈ "Jayantabhattah"; Annaṃbhaṭṭa ≈ "Annambattah"; Viśvanātha ≈ "Vishwanathah").

The guests are V.N. Jha and Ujjwala Jha, both former directors of the Center of Advanced Study in Sanskrit at the University of Pune, where Ujjwala Jha is still Professor of Sanskrit [00:00:24]. As Adamson notes at the close [00:40:02], this is the show's first interview with a married couple — V.N. Jha takes the lead on epistemology, metaphysics and soteriology; Ujjwala Jha on logic and the syllogism.

docs.title: Nyāya among the six orthodox schools
docs.text:
• [00:01:04] V.N. Jha sets the frame: Nyāya is one of the six orthodox schools of Indian philosophy. The Sanskrit for an orthodox school is āstika (as against nāstika), and the word for philosophy itself is darśana.
  • [00:01:30] A caution about that word: darśana comes from the root dṛś, "to see." It implies that philosophy is meant to make us visualize, discover, realize — to actually see the reality, not merely theorize about it. That sense of "seeing the real" is how the whole enterprise should be understood.
  • [00:02:08] Gautama is the systematizer of Nyāya; he wrote the Nyāya-Sūtra, and from it flows "a history of a thousand years of dialogue through commentaries" — the Sūtra commented on by Vātsyāyana, then Uddyotakara, then Vācaspati Miśra, then Udayana ("Udayanācārya," 10th century CE).
  • [00:02:45] Why so many commentaries? Because each is a move in a debate: when Gautama puts forward a thesis, it is not acceptable "to one and all," so objections are raised, and commentaries are written to answer them. The result is a recorded history — "fortunately" preserved — of a thousand years of intense philosophical dialogue.
  • [00:03:32] Over that time Nyāya developed its characteristic tools, all in the service of communication: an epistemology, a logic, and "a universal model of inquiry." Out of this came "very deep epistemological results."

docs.title: Why a logic-school is really after the end of suffering
docs.text:
• [00:04:00] Adamson presses the puzzle: Nyāya is famous for epistemology and logic, yet it shares the Vedic schools' goal of ultimate happiness (like Vedānta or Yoga). How do the technical project and the soteriological one connect?
  • [00:04:30] V.N. Jha: philosophizing must have a purpose — the Indian tradition "did not believe that philosophy should be simply a mental exercise." Thought has to be put into practice; therefore philosophy must address human purpose.
  • [00:05:00] Adamson reframes it: so I have beliefs about how to live, and what Nyāya really cares about is whether such belief counts as knowledge. Jha points to Gautama's first sūtra, which lays out a "roadmap" for a person to arrive at reality and identify who he is — answering the old Upaniṣadic question, who am I?
  • [00:05:41] The first sūtra says that by the true cognition of 16 entities (padārthas) — beginning with pramāṇa (the process / means of knowing) and prameya (the knowable, the object) — one attains the ultimate goal of human life. Nyāya accepts four means of knowing.
  • [00:06:13] A careful point about prameya and the word padārtha: the Vaiśeṣikas also tried to understand the whole universe through language, and for them padārtha — "the referent of language," whatever language refers to — is the universe, a categorial term. Gautama borrows the same word but uses it differently: his 16 padārthas are not the whole universe but a chosen few entities, the ones "required for engaging yourself in arguments in order to understand who you are."
  • [00:07:07] The logic of the selection: to discover myself I must identify myself, and I am one entity among all. So I need to grasp "me and non-me" — unless I know what I am not, how can I identify what I am? Hence the inquiry must reach out into the whole universe (which is why the Vaiśeṣikas catalogue everything), but Gautama keeps only the entities useful for distinguishing the self from the not-self.
  • [00:08:17] The link to liberation is in sūtra 1.1.2, which gives the whole causal chain of bondage. We live in a "conditioned state" and therefore suffer. To be conditioned means precisely to have taken X to be Y — if the reality is X but we cognize it as Y. This is mithyā-jñāna, wrong cognition / misconception.
  • [00:09:02] From that misconception an attitude immediately arises; the attitude prompts behavior; behavior yields results, good and bad, which accumulate and ultimately drive the cycle of birth and rebirth. So the wheel of rebirth is produced, at root, by mithyā-jñāna.
  • [00:09:46] The cure: since the root cause has been diagnosed, it can be removed — only by tattva-jñāna (also yathārtha-jñāna), correct cognition, knowing X as X. Right knowledge dissolves the misconception; the corrected attitude corrects behavior, which then "leaves no residue" to fuel further suffering and rebirth. That is what knowledge has to do with the wider aims of Nyāya — already present in Gautama, and shared (Adamson adds) with schools Vedic and non-Vedic alike: the Buddhists too make knowledge the road out of suffering.

docs.title: The five-member syllogism
docs.text:
• [00:11:05] Adamson turns to Ujjwala Jha for the other face of early Nyāya — logic. If you care about knowledge you care about arguments, and early Nyāya develops a theory of the syllogism that can look "simplistic or ad hoc." Is there a defense of it?
  • [00:11:39] Ujjwala Jha: one should not call it ad hoc. The sūtra-kāra (Gautama) defined the syllogism with five members, each well-defined and then explained by the bhāṣya-kāra (Vātsyāyana). Had it been ad hoc, it would have been dropped once its purpose was served — but the same five-member form is defended right through the tradition: up to Viśvanātha's Nyāya-Siddhānta-Muktāvalī in the 17th century, and by Annaṃbhaṭṭa in his Tarka-saṃgraha. Vātsyāyana even weighed a rival view that the syllogism should have ten members, and rejected it: only five.
  • [00:13:16] The stock example, member by member:
  • Pratijñā (the proposition): parvato vahnimān — "the mountain has fire."
  • Hetu (the reason / probans): dhūmavat — "because it has smoke."
  • Udāharaṇa (the example, which is also the statement of the invariable relation): yatra yatra dhūmaḥ tatra tatra vahniḥ, yathā mahānasa — "wherever there is smoke there is fire, as in the kitchen."
  • Upanaya (the confirmatory recognition): tathā ca ayam — "and the same [smoke, invariably tied to fire] is on this mountain."
  • Nigamana (the conclusion): tasmāt tathā — "therefore [the mountain has fire]."
  • [00:13:52] The engine is the invariable relationship between smoke and fire: when one knows that X and Y are invariably related, then seeing X, "he invariably remembers Y."
  • [00:14:39] The Mīmāṃsakas keep objecting: why five? three are enough, because two of the steps seem to be mere repetition. Nyāya refutes this; but even the sūtra-kāra was aware of the apparent repetition.
  • [00:15:17] Which two steps repeat? The first member (parvato vahnimān — "there is fire on the mountain") and the conclusion ("therefore there is fire on the mountain") — i.e. I first state what I aim to prove, then conclude that it is proven. Nyāya answers this in its very definition of the conclusion: the term for conclusion is nigamana, defined as punar-vacana, the restatement of the proposition. (The opening proposition itself is pratijñā; the reason, hetu, glossed as "probans," the thing that proves.)
  • [00:16:26] Adamson and Jha tighten the logic of the third member: the example must assert an invariable relation between the thing to be proved and the basis for proving it — and the direction matters. "Wherever there is smoke, there is fire," not the reverse — because there can be fire without smoke. A lit candle, or (a traditional Nyāya case) "a hot iron ball," has fire but no smoke.
  • [00:17:48] Hence the terminology of pervader and pervaded: fire covers a larger area than smoke, so smoke (the pervaded) can be the basis for inferring fire (the pervader), but never the other way around.
  • [00:18:05] How general is the syllogism meant to be? Adamson asks whether it can prove any questionable conclusion at all. Exactly so — because, as Jha says, Nyāya is essentially developing "the methodology of dialectics," and in a dialectic you must be able to prove your own point. This five-step form is anumāna-prayoga, "the form of inference."
  • [00:18:56] A closing reminder on the fourth member, the confirmatory recognition: after recalling the invariable relation, you confirm that "the same type of smoke" — the kind invariably tied to fire — is present on the mountain, which is what licenses the conclusion. And all five are necessary; anything less does not complete the process. The five sentences together form one whole, the mahāvākya.

docs.title: Nyāya's "utter realism" and the status of perception
docs.text:
• [00:18:42] Adamson raises a tension: the proof is described linguistically, yet one of Nyāya's pramāṇas is perception (pratyakṣa). When I perceive smoke, do I already see it as smoke (the relation coming "for free" with perception), or do I get raw data that I then interpret with a concept?
  • [00:20:50] V.N. Jha redirects: that question belongs to another debate. The crucial thing is that Nyāya is "a system of utter realism." For Nyāya, the real is that which is knowable and namable.
  • [00:21:07] The realist argument from causation: knowing is a process, so there is a causal relationship between what I know and the knowledge that emerges. A cause must precede its effect — the world I know is the kāraṇa (cause), the perception of it the kārya (effect). Since the cause precedes the effect, the world must precede, and so be independent of, my mind. Therefore "the entire world is independent of mind."
  • [00:21:57] A second front: the idealists held that reality cannot be captured through language — a position that began in the Upaniṣadic period and was "concretized" by the Buddhist logicians. Against them, Nyāya consistently held that language too can refer to reality.
  • [00:22:29] On these two issues — establishing the self, and establishing God — Udayana (Udayanācārya of Mithilā, 10th century) wrote two texts: the Ātma-tattva-viveka (to establish the self) and the Nyāyakusumāñjali (to establish God / Īśvara).
  • [00:22:45] The pay-off of the realist criterion: be it a paramāṇu (an atom — so subtle our gross eyes cannot perceive it) or God himself, anything that exists is knowable and namable. By these two criteria alone Nyāya makes its claim about what is real — "a very optimistic epistemology."

docs.title: Answering the skeptic's regress
docs.text:
• [00:23:17] Adamson: an optimistic epistemology is "under an obligation" to face skeptical attack, which duly comes from the Buddhists. He poses one form — the regress of justification: whatever pramāṇa I rely on, I seem to need a further reason guaranteeing its reliability; that reason will be another pramāṇa, and so on forever.
  • [00:24:25] Ujjwala Jha: the accusation's own premise is faulty — namely that a pramāṇa must already be known before it can operate toward its object. Nyāya accepts two types of source of knowledge: one that is known first and then operates, and one that operates even without itself being known. (In Sanskrit: jñātaṃ sat pramāṇaṃ bhavati — something is a means of knowledge when it is itself already known — versus ajñātaṃ sat pramāṇaṃ bhavati — a means of knowledge that is not itself known.)
  • [00:25:23] The basic case is pratyakṣa (perception), whose pramāṇa is just the sense organ. For perceptual cognition you need not know your own sense organ first: the eye sees a color without the knower first "knowing the eye." So the regress never gets started for perception.
  • [00:26:03] But the other means — anumāna (inference), upamāna (analogy / comparison), śabda (verbal testimony) — do require prior knowledge. Inference requires knowing the invariable relation between X and Y (itself grasped by perception — "perception is the basis of all pramāṇas"). Upamāna rests on knowing a resemblance. Śabda requires knowing the language — the padārtha-sambandha-jñāna, the relation between word and meaning, must be known by the hearer prior to communication.
  • [00:27:49] Adamson maps this onto the modern externalist / internalist distinction in epistemology: externalists deny the knower must have access to the fact that they know (it is enough that their eyes work, the lighting is good, etc.); internalists insist you must somehow know that you know. Nyāya, he observes, looks externalist about perception but internalist about the other sources — for language you can know that your linguistic knowledge is accurate, a demand they do not make of perception. Jha confirms: "Yes."

docs.title: Yoga, transformation, and the road to the "new logic"
docs.text:
• [00:29:23] Adamson asks about Nyāya's links to the other Vedic schools — not just Vaiśeṣika (already discussed) but Yoga, with its practical, ethical orientation. Can such technical logic be brought together with yoga?
  • [00:29:52] V.N. Jha: Yoga is itself "a plan of a journey — an inner journey — from a conditioned state of man to a deconditioned state." He invokes Jayanta Bhaṭṭa, the Kashmiri logician ("a very fascinating man"): one can travel only so far by thought; "unless thought is put into action, transformation is not going to be that easy." So the methods Patañjali sets out in the Yoga-Sūtra need to be practiced even by Naiyāyikas, because Nyāya too is ultimately a system for transformation — and transformation must happen inside. Patañjali's roadmap "should be made available to one in all systems," and the Naiyāyikas "very happily accepted" it.
  • [00:31:09] Adamson: this combination of highly technical philosophy and ethical self-shaping in the same thinkers recalls ancient Greek philosophy. But how technical does it actually get — is there anything like formal logic?
  • [00:31:59] Ujjwala Jha: not formal logic in the contemporary sense, but something arrived at over centuries. From the start Nyāya pursued dialectics, and the dialectics kept failing on the ambiguity of ordinary language: what Vātsyāyana (the bhāṣya-kāra) meant was misread by the Buddhist logicians, who raised objections; Uddyotakara answered them, but his meaning too was misunderstood — a thousand years of dialogue in which "one term is taken to mean something else by the other."
  • [00:33:08] So the moment came when the medium of communication itself had to be reformed — a new, unambiguous language of discourse. The turn begins after Praśastapāda (6th century CE), who wrote a commentary on the very old Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra (roughly contemporary with the Nyāya-Sūtra, perhaps 100 BCE); his bhāṣya notably brings in Īśvara, so the two schools begin to merge. Udayana, commenting on Praśastapāda, warns that the same terminology should not be reused loosely, and starts coining precise terms so that "if you want to say X, the hearer will understand only X and nothing else."
  • [00:34:49] That terminology was developed further by Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya in the 13th century, by way of Śeṣadhara (whose Nyāya-Siddhānta-Dīpa was "a little compact," later expanded fully by Gaṅgeśa). Gaṅgeśa's Tattvacintāmaṇi became "the magnum opus of Navya-Nyāya" — the point at which "the things are formalized," all ambiguity driven out for the sake of precise communication. The resulting Navya-Nyāya language ("new logic") is, she stresses, best understood as the proper name of the language itself.

docs.title: A living tradition
docs.text:
• [00:36:34] Adamson asks whether Nyāya carried on through early modernity — through the coming of Islam in India and even to the present — a living tradition, with its five-step syllogism still defended in the 17th century "giving Aristotle a run for his money."
  • [00:37:11] V.N. Jha: yes. See Nyāya in two phases — up to the 10th century, then the new form (Navya-Nyāya) afterward — the hinge being Udayana, who "could have an overlook" of why the same questions kept recurring and located the problem in the medium of communication. Language thus became central. Just as the West had its linguistic turn only very late, "after Chomsky," India had Udayana making the same point about the importance of language in the 10th century: we can accept or reject only what we first understand, and natural language, the more we use it, "opens the gate for ambiguity."
  • [00:38:42] So a new language of discourse was needed — and once Vaiśeṣika and Nyāya had become one (sharing the same metaphysics), the other systems too — Mīmāṃsā, Yoga, Sāṃkhya, Dharmaśāstra, the eight varieties of Vedānta — all began conducting their philosophical discourse through the medium of Navya-Nyāya language. After the 13th century, anyone doing Vedānta, Mīmāṃsā, grammar or poetics adopted it.
  • [00:40:00] "To tell you the truth," Jha adds, in every traditional Sanskrit institution even today debate takes place only in Navya-Nyāya language — whatever school the debater belongs to, that is the shared medium of discourse. Adamson thanks both professors, notes the milestone of the show's first married-couple interview, and previews the next stretch: the tradition so often paired with Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Nyāya — one of the six āstika (orthodox) schools; a darśana (philosophy, from dṛś "to see") aimed at logic, epistemology and a universal method of inquiry.
  • Gautama — systematizer of Nyāya; author of the Nyāya-Sūtra, whose first sūtra lists 16 entities and whose sūtra 1.1.2 gives the causal chain of bondage and release.
  • Vātsyāyana / Uddyotakara / Vācaspati Miśra / Udayana — the chain of classical commentators that makes Nyāya a thousand-year recorded dialogue.
  • pramāṇa / prameya — the means of knowing (Nyāya accepts four) and the knowable object; the first two of Gautama's 16 padārthas.
  • padārtha — "referent of language"; for Vaiśeṣika it is the whole categorized universe, for Gautama a chosen few entities useful for telling self from not-self.
  • mithyā-jñāna — wrong cognition, "taking X to be Y"; the root cause of attitude, action, accumulation, and the cycle of rebirth.
  • tattva-jñāna / yathārtha-jñāna — correct cognition, "knowing X as X"; the cure that dissolves misconception and ends suffering.
  • The five-member syllogism (anumāna-prayoga) — pratijñā (proposition), hetu (reason/probans), udāharaṇa (example + invariable relation), upanaya (confirmation), nigamana (conclusion); the five sentences form one mahāvākya.
  • parvato vahnimān, dhūmavat — the stock inference: "the mountain has fire, because it has smoke."
  • invariable relation; pervader & pervaded — smoke (pervaded) invariably accompanies fire (pervader), so smoke proves fire but not vice versa (a candle / hot iron ball has fire without smoke).
  • pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, śabda — perception, inference, analogy/comparison, verbal testimony: Nyāya's four means of knowledge; perception is the basis of the rest.
  • jñātaṃ / ajñātaṃ sat pramāṇaṃ — the two kinds of source: one known before it operates, one that operates without being known; perception is the latter, which blocks the skeptic's regress.
  • utter realism — the real is what is knowable and namable (from atom, paramāṇu, to God, Īśvara); defended via cause (kāraṇa) preceding effect (kārya), so the world is mind-independent.
  • Udayana (10th c.) — author of the Ātma-tattva-viveka (to establish the self) and Nyāyakusumāñjali (to establish God); the hinge to the "new logic," who diagnosed language as the source of endless dispute.
  • Praśastapāda (6th c.) — commentator on the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra whose bhāṣya brings in Īśvara, beginning the merger of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika.
  • Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya (13th c.) & the Tattvacintāmaṇi — the magnum opus of Navya-Nyāya ("new logic"), where Nyāya discourse is formalized to remove ambiguity; built on Śeṣadhara's compact Nyāya-Siddhānta-Dīpa.
  • Navya-Nyāya language — the precise technical idiom adopted across all later Indian schools (Mīmāṃsā, Vedānta, grammar, poetics) and still the medium of traditional Sanskrit debate today.
  • Jayanta Bhaṭṭa — Kashmiri logician cited for the claim that thought must be put into action; hence even Naiyāyikas should practice Patañjali's Yoga-Sūtra, since Nyāya too aims at inner transformation.

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:19:05 In brief: Against the cliché that all Indian thought derives everything from one source, Vaiśeṣika is a thoroughgoing realist pluralism: Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra carves the world into six categories (substance, quality, motion, universals, individuators, inherence), builds bodies up from eternal atoms, and — allied with Nyāya — promises that knowing this structure of reality leads to the highest good, against the anti-realist "therapy" of the Buddhists. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Canary"; Vaiśeṣika ≈ "Vaichesika / Vysheeshika / Vichita"; Kaṇāda ≈ "Kananda"; al-Kindī ≈ "Akindi / Okindi"; Praśastapāda ≈ "Prasashtapada"; Wilhelm Halbfass ≈ "Wilhelm Halbfas"; Ulūka ≈ "Ulika / Uluca"; padārtha ≈ "padarta"; Ākāśa ≈ "Akasha"; aṇu ≈ "anu"; bhūta ≈ "Bhuta"; samavāya ≈ "Samavaya"; Śaṅkara ≈ "Shankara"; Nyāya ≈ "Niyaya").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Vaiśeṣika — the realist, pluralist "partner school" of Nyāya; heroes of metaphysical pluralism [00:01:44].
  • Kaṇāda (Ulūka, "the owl") — author of the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra, the founding document of the school [00:02:43].
  • Praśastapāda — 6th-c. CE author whose freestanding treatise (not a commentary) became the school's real touchstone [00:03:31].
  • al-Kindī — 9th-c. Muslim philosopher, used as the framing foil with his theory about why Indians play one-stringed instruments [00:00:37].

docs.title: A one-stringed instrument? The cliché of the single cause
docs.text:
• [00:00:37] The 9th-century Muslim philosopher al-Kindī had strange ideas about music: he reportedly once cured a young man's apoplexy by having tunes played on a lute, and held that music can affect the soul and expresses the character of the people who play it.
  • [00:00:57] On this theory, different cultures use different numbers of strings. The Greeks, who invented the theory of four elements, played four-stringed lutes; the Indians, al-Kindī claims, make do with a single-stringed instrument to represent their view that the whole world arises from only one cause.
  • [00:01:14] "But we know better." If the survey of the Vedic philosophical schools has taught anything, it is that Indian thinkers were not all singing from the same hymn sheet. True, Vedānta emphasized the derivation of all things from the one brahman — or even, in Advaita Vedānta, the identity of things with that source. But ancient India also had its fair share of pluralists.

docs.title: Vaiśeṣika: pluralist, realist, and accused of "semi-nihilism"
docs.text:
• [00:01:44] The heroes of metaphysical pluralism were the partner school of Nyāya, who went by the name Vaiśeṣika.
  • [00:01:50] Śaṅkara, founder of Advaita Vedānta, scornfully dismissed the Vaiśeṣikas as semi-nihilists, because they failed to ground all things in the one true reality of brahman.
  • [00:02:02] But Vaiśeṣika is in fact committed to thoroughgoing realism. Unlike Advaita, it assumes there is a structured world out there, independent of human conceptions and thought — yet a world we can understand, in the first instance by offering a classification or division of reality into its various types.

docs.title: The founding text and its owlish author
docs.text:
• [00:02:25] This classifying task is undertaken in the school's founding document, the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra, thought to have been compiled around the first century CE — though Vaiśeṣika ideas were certainly circulating much earlier.
  • [00:02:43] Its author is Kaṇāda, also known as Ulūka, "the owl." Several explanations are offered for the nickname: perhaps it just plays on "Kaṇāda," which means grain-eater (like an owl), though it can also be read as atom-eater, since Vaiśeṣika is committed to atomism. A more fabulous story has it that the whole system was revealed to Kaṇāda by a god who had assumed the form of an owl.
  • [00:03:14] Like other works in sūtra form, the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra is compressed and hard to understand. Since "no further explanation was forthcoming from divine owls," the tradition turned for clarification to a later work by Praśastapāda, who lived in the 6th century CE.
  • [00:03:35] In a departure from the usual procedure, Praśastapāda's work is not a formal commentary (bhāṣya) but a freestanding treatise, albeit one clearly inspired by Kaṇāda. It became the touchstone for later authors even more than the sūtra itself — modern scholar Wilhelm Halbfass calls Praśastapāda "the most authoritative representative, if not the creator, of classical Vaiśeṣika."
  • [00:04:02] Though both men are known above all for metaphysics, they keep a keen interest in ethics and liberation. The ethically loaded term dharma even opens the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra — though here it may carry the more metaphysical meaning it has in Buddhism rather than the ethical sense familiar from Mīmāṃsā, which fits better with the metaphysical analysis that immediately follows.

docs.title: The six categories (padārtha) — the world structured like language
docs.text:
• [00:04:36] Experience with Sāṃkhya would lead us to expect this analysis to come as a list, with items subdivided into further lists — and Kaṇāda does not disappoint.
  • [00:04:52] The initial analysis itemizes six categories, some broken down further: the first category, substance, has nine types; the second, quality, no fewer than 24 types; and so on.
  • [00:05:10] A clue to the project lies in the very word "category," in Sanskrit padārtha. Commentators tell us this combines pada and artha — "word" and "meaning." A category is thus a type of thing that can be signified by language: the noun "owl" refers to a substance (the first category), the adjective "white" to a quality (the second), and so on.
  • [00:05:40] In other words, the system of categories says the world is structured so as to correspond to our language — once again Indian philosophers take their cue from grammar.

docs.title: Substance, quality, motion — and the unobservable substances
docs.text:
• [00:05:53] The first three categories are substance, quality, and motion. An owl is a substance; it has qualities (the color of its feathers) and motions (its swoop down on an unsuspecting mouse).
  • [00:06:09] Crucially, for Vaiśeṣika a quality or motion is just as much a particular individual entity as the owl itself. The white of this owl belongs only to it, as does the particular swoop it performs to land on the shoulder of its wizard owner.
  • [00:06:24] Although the theory accommodates such familiar examples, the substances in Kaṇāda's first category are not necessarily observable. You can perceive an owl, but from the Vaiśeṣika point of view there are also substances unobservable in principle — and these are the most fundamental: atoms (paramāṇu), space, time, and a pervasive substance called Ākāśa, sometimes translated "ether."
  • [00:06:57] Observable beings like owls are composed from atoms, which (unlike owls) are indestructible and eternal. So too are ether and the more familiar elements — earth, water, fire, air. These five are called bhūta, or "physical substance," meaning they have sensible qualities.
  • [00:07:15] Originally the school may have correlated each of the five substances to one of the five sensible qualities — odor residing in earth, color in fire, and so on — so that a complex substance like an owl, combining all five elements, is perceptible to the full range of our senses. Perhaps the wish to match our five senses even motivated positing five substances. But the simple version is hard to credit (is earth really invisible until mixed with fire to give it color?), and by the time of the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra it had been abandoned; Kaṇāda still draws correlations, but makes them more complex.

docs.title: Why atoms? The argument from divisibility
docs.text:
• [00:08:15] Our most basic bodily substances, then, are atoms of the basic elements — atoms of earth, of water, and so on. They are too tiny to perceive and have a special minimal size simply called aṇu ("small"): the smallest any existing thing can be.
  • [00:08:33] But how do we know bodies are at bottom made of indivisible particles? The standard argument: it is an empirically established truth that whatever is perceived is composite. Even the smallest perceptible thing — a fleck of dust in a sunbeam — has parts; and those parts, being smaller than the smallest visible thing, are themselves invisible. Yet (says Vaiśeṣika) those invisible parts have further parts, just as visible cloth is made of threads and threads of smaller strands.
  • [00:09:08] More precisely: the invisible particle is a triad made of three subparts, each of which is a dyad of two parts, and those sub-sub-subparts are the atoms. Going the other way — small to large — pairs of atoms join, three pairs combine into an invisible particle, and these combine into things we can actually see.
  • [00:09:40] The obvious objection: how do we know division can't go on forever? Why not say the six bits of the invisible particle are each still divisible? One Vaiśeṣika answer: if indefinite division were possible, then a mountain and a mustard seed would be the same size, since each would have the same number of constituent parts — namely an infinite number.
  • [00:10:16] The implicit premise (made explicit by other Vaiśeṣikas) is that the size of a whole is a function of the size, number, and spatial arrangement of its parts. The argument looks question-begging: that premise is only true if atomism is already accepted. A non-atomist will say an object's size is fixed not by its constituents but by the spatial boundaries of the continuous stuff it is made of.

docs.title: Realism extended: even absences are real
docs.text:
• [00:10:39] Elsewhere in the history of philosophy, atomists have been tempted to think non-atomic substances and their qualities are somehow unreal — as in Democritus's line, "by convention sweet, by convention color, but in reality, atoms and void."
  • [00:11:05] Not so for Vaiśeṣika, with its strong commitment to realism: for Kaṇāda and his successors, the owl, the owl's color, and the atoms are all real.
  • [00:11:18] Later in the tradition, from about the 12th century, this realism was extended even to the absences of things, added as a seventh category. This is the metaphysical version of the thesis met in the sister school Nyāya — that you can perceive an absence, like Ferris Bueller missing from behind his desk. (Getting ahead of the list and of history.)

docs.title: Categories four and five: universals and individuators
docs.text:
• [00:11:48] The fourth category is universals — the general classes under which substances, qualities, and motions fall. There are not just individual owls like Hedwig but the whole species (snowy owl), which belongs to the more general class of owls, which belongs to the still-more-general class of animals.
  • [00:12:19] The chain does not go on indefinitely: in Vaiśeṣika, being is the highest, most general universal, since everything that exists is a being. There are universals for qualities and motions too — Hedwig's white belongs to her alone, but whiteness is found in many substances, so whiteness is a general class just as "owl" is.
  • [00:12:47] The fifth category answers: how does an individual owl become that individual? This was a major issue for medieval Europe too — Peter Abelard, Gilbert of Poitiers, Duns Scotus. Vaiśeṣika's answer strikingly anticipates Scotus (or rather Scotus echoes Vaiśeṣika, since Kaṇāda proposed it more than a millennium earlier): there must be a unique distinguisher, a principle of individuation for each particular.
  • [00:13:29] Kaṇāda's real need for this is less about owls than atoms. One snowy owl can be told from another (whiter feathers, more tired from delivering the post), but one fire atom is liable to be utterly indistinguishable from every other. The distinguishing principle explains why each individual atom is the atom it is. This matters all the more because owls and all bodies are atomic compounds, so the individuality of complex bodies ultimately stands or falls with the individuality of their atoms.

docs.title: Category six: inherence (samavāya)
docs.text:
• [00:14:14] The sixth and final category is inherence (samavāya) — again Kaṇāda anticipates a problem and solves it before anyone can complain (or perhaps someone had complained).
  • [00:14:33] The problem: on one side we have substances; on the other the qualities, motions, universals, and individuating distinguishers that belong to them. What connects these features to the substances that display them? What explains that this white belongs to Hedwig? Simply the fact that it inheres in her — and this connection of inherence is itself something real, deserving its place on the list.
  • [00:15:03] Inherence even explains why substances have a special place: they do not inhere in anything else, but rather have other things inhering in them. Our owl does not belong to anything the way her white color belongs to her.
  • [00:15:22] But that isn't quite right. The Vaiśeṣikas are intensely interested in how wholes relate to their parts, because Kaṇāda and his followers want to refute the Buddhists, who deny the reality and unity of wholes by decomposing them into parts — the chariot that is "nothing more than wheels, axle, and so on."
  • [00:15:52] The realist Vaiśeṣika instead recognizes wholes as perfectly respectable entities: Hedwig is real, even made of atoms. But a composite being differs from her atoms, and this difference is expressed via inherence: the whole inheres in its parts, much as white color inheres in Hedwig. So strictly, an owl has two kinds of inherence relations — white color inheres in her, and she inheres in her own parts (ultimately the atoms). Atoms alone inherit in nothing: they belong to nothing the way a quality or motion does, and they have no parts.

docs.title: Knowledge of the categories and the highest good
docs.text:
• [00:16:39] All this may seem far from the moral duty and liberation stressed by the other Vedic schools. What could ethical goals have to do with a list of six categories that merely "enumerates everything in this world that has the character of being"?
  • [00:17:03] Plenty, says Praśastapāda: knowing the truth about the six categories of being does help lead us to the highest good. No wonder Vaiśeṣika joins forces with Nyāya, since both promise that knowledge leads to this lofty goal — Nyāya supplying an account of what knowledge consists in, Vaiśeṣika the analysis of the world we grasp when knowledge is achieved. "Like the United States, Gautama has a friendly neighbor in the shape of Kaṇāda."

docs.title: The real rival: Buddhist anti-realism
docs.text:
• [00:17:33] But Gautama and Kaṇāda, and their followers in Nyāya–Vaiśeṣika, have a serious rival: the anti-realism of the Buddhists, who also promise to bring us to liberation and the highest good — but by unmasking the unreality of what seems real.
  • [00:17:47] For the Buddhist, the only therapy for human suffering is to undermine commitment to a world of enduring subjects and objects, because the belief that we and other things are real and endure through time inevitably provokes needs, cravings, and attachments.
  • [00:18:04] Some Hindu thinkers, inspired rather than appalled by this strategy, also embraced anti-realism — arguably the Advaita Vedānta thinkers, who keep the authority of the Upaniṣads but read them as pointing toward brahman, a single reality hidden behind appearances.
  • [00:18:29] For the Vaiśeṣikas, a better response is to demonstrate that realism is true — for if it is, then Buddhist therapy rests on a mistake. Nor is it their only mistake: the Vaiśeṣikas insist on the reality of wholes made of parts as well as partless atoms.
  • [00:18:50] What arguments could defeat the Buddhist view, and what more can be said about the whole–part relation beyond a "rather mysterious appeal to the idea of inherence"? That is the subject of the next part, devoted entirely to the Vaiśeṣika theory of material composition.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Vaiśeṣika — realist, pluralist school, partner of Nyāya; classifies reality into six (later seven) categories; dismissed by Śaṅkara as "semi-nihilist" for not grounding all things in brahman.
  • Kaṇāda (Ulūka, "the owl") — author of the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra; the name means "grain-eater" or "atom-eater," and one legend has the system revealed to him by an owl-shaped god.
  • Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra — the school's founding document, compiled c. 1st c. CE; compressed sūtra form, opening with the term dharma.
  • Praśastapāda — 6th-c. CE author of a freestanding treatise (not a bhāṣya) that became the school's true touchstone; called by Halbfass "the creator of classical Vaiśeṣika."
  • padārtha — "category"; etymologized as pada + artha ("word" + "meaning"), i.e. a type of thing that language can signify — so the categories mirror grammar.
  • the six categories — substance, quality, motion, universals, individuators (principle of individuation), and inherence (a seventh, absence, added c. 12th c.).
  • dravya (substance) — first category, nine types; includes both observable things (owls) and unobservable fundamentals (atoms, space, time, ether).
  • paramāṇu (atom) / aṇu — eternal, indestructible, indivisible particle of minimal size (aṇu = "small"); bodies are built from atom-pairs → dyads → triads (the smallest invisible particle).
  • bhūta — "physical substance"; the five elements (earth, water, fire, air, ether) that bear sensible qualities, perhaps matched to the five senses.
  • Ākāśa — ether; a pervasive, unobservable, eternal substance.
  • universals — general classes (snowy owl → owl → animal); being is the highest, since everything that exists is a being.
  • principle of individuation — the unique distinguisher that makes each particular itself; chiefly needed for otherwise-identical atoms; anticipates Duns Scotus.
  • samavāya (inherence) — the real connection binding qualities/motions/etc. to substances, and wholes to their parts; substances are special because they inhere in nothing else.
  • realism vs. Buddhist anti-realism — Vaiśeṣika defends the reality of owls, qualities, atoms, and wholes against Buddhists who dissolve wholes into parts (the chariot) as therapy against craving; allied with Nyāya, it holds that knowing reality's structure leads to the highest good.

docs.text:
← Ep 36
