🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:22:26 In brief: Vaiśeṣika is a realism about wholes (avayavin): a chariot, a book, a person is a single new thing over and above its parts, not just a heap. The episode runs the Buddhist anti-realist arguments against wholes — and Vaiśeṣika's increasingly subtle replies via the inherence relation (samavāya) — then widens out to causation, the running obsession of Indian philosophy. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Gannery"; Vaiśeṣika ≈ "Sheeshika / Vichesha / Vysheyshecica"; Kaṇāda ≈ "Kanada"; Kurukṣetra ≈ "Curuchetra"; Vātsyāyana ≈ "Vatsyayana"; Bimal Matilal ≈ "Bimal Matilal"; Pāṇini ≈ "Pannani"; kāraka ≈ "cataca"; pramāṇa ≈ "pramana"; Nyāya ≈ "Niaya / Niyaya"; Dharmakīrti ≈ "Dama Kirti"; David Lewis; Bertrand Russell).

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Kaṇāda — the Vaiśeṣika founder; a metaphysical realist about substances, properties, universals — and about complex wholes [00:02:44].
  • The Buddhist anti-realists — who treat chariots, books and persons as mental fabrications/constructions, not real wholes [00:03:55].
  • Bimal Matilal — modern scholar cited: Indian philosophy grew out of the cosmogonic speculations of the Vedas and Upaniṣads [00:11:55].
  • Dharmakīrti — late-6th-century Buddhist whose multicoloured-cloth argument attacks the reality of wholes [00:16:57].
  • Vātsyāyana — paired with Kaṇāda as defending common sense with highly theoretical tools [00:20:38].

docs.title: More than the sum of its parts
docs.text:
• [00:00:37] The hook: you sit through an incoherent film and tell a friend "that wasn't much more than the sum of its parts." Entertainment should be more than an unconnected series of celebrity cameos or action scenes. Chariots of Fire becomes a classic not just for a good theme song and the beach-running opening, but for a well-structured, coherent narrative and characters whose development we follow. Coherence and structure give rise to something new: they produce wholes that are genuinely more than the sum of their parts. (Quentin Tarantino is the running counter-joke — success without that kind of coherence.)
  • [00:01:29] If that's true of Chariots of Fire, it's true of plain old chariots. A chariot is more than a heap of axles, wheels and carriages lying around the chariot-making factory. Only once the parts are assembled into an organized structure does the chariot become a chariot — and thanks to that structure it can do what a mere heap cannot: carry Arjuna into war against his foes on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra.

docs.title: Wholes, and the self that says "I"
docs.text:
• [00:02:08] What goes for the chariot goes for the charioteer. A person is not a random sequence of individual thoughts and feelings but an organized unity of cognition and conception that persists over time. That is why a person can say "I" — "I saw Chariots of Fire last night, and I still can't get the theme song out of my head." Using "I" presupposes that experience is not a stream of disunited impressions (first the watching, later the remembering) but the experience of an enduring, united self.
  • [00:02:44] This is the view of the Vaiśeṣika philosopher Kaṇāda. As established last time, he's a metaphysical realist about substances, their properties, and the universals applying to them — and he's also a realist about complex things. Over and above an aggregate or collection of parts there is a further object: a whole (avayavin). Wholes include the middle-sized objects of ordinary experience — the book in your hands is more than pages, covers and spine; the chariot you ride is more than axles, wheels and carriage.
  • [00:03:26] Though he probably didn't know he was agreeing with Kaṇāda, Bertrand Russell put it nicely: a whole is "a new single term distinct from each of its parts and from all of them; it is one, not many, and it is related to the parts, but has a being distinct from theirs." Vaiśeṣika thus agrees with both Russell and common sense — "an unbeatable combination."

docs.title: The Buddhist opponent
docs.text:
• [00:03:55] But it faces a formidable opponent: Buddhist philosophers who take books and chariots — the objects of everyday experience — to be fabrications or constructions of our minds. They give two lines of argument. First, the concepts of things like chariots or books are built from nothing more than momentary sensory experiences; if so, there need be no persisting chariot, only a stream of fleeting impressions. Second, they doubt there's any single enduring person experiencing these impressions in sequence — a central Buddhist tenet is that there is no enduring self, and giving up the illusion of the self is a step on the road to liberation.
  • [00:04:49] Vaiśeṣika's obvious rejoinder: if a chariot is not really a whole but just a bunch of parts, what's the difference between the chariot and a random grab-bag — say, the collection whose members are Gina the crocodile, an old videotape of Chariots of Fire, and the moon? Three things that even more obviously than the latest Tarantino effort fail to form a single coherent whole. On the Buddhist view such a random assortment is no different from a chariot — which seems hard to believe — so Vaiśeṣika concludes there's a real metaphysical difference: the assortment is no true whole; the chariot (or charioteer) is one real thing made of parts.
  • [00:05:36] The Buddhists answer that we distinguish the two cases merely by convention. Human concerns and interests make it more useful to speak of a chariot than of a crocodile-plus-videotape-plus-moon, but neither "whole" is any more real than the other. Still, you don't have to beat Russell to feel Vaiśeṣika has the better of it so far: the Buddhists banish familiar objects and persons from reality, while Vaiśeṣika validates our everyday assumptions — so the burden of proof seems to lie with the Buddhists.

docs.title: Buddhist arguments for anti-realism
docs.text:
• [00:06:20] Realizing this, the Buddhists offer several arguments. At least some everyday objects really are mere sums of parts: a forest is nothing more than a bunch of trees, an army just a bunch of soldiers. And Chariots of Fire itself — however coherent its narrative — is actually just a series of images shown in rapid succession to produce the illusion of continuity; on a digital screen it's built from individual pixels of light that cohere into one image, like an Impressionist painting seen from a distance. Some apparent wholes are plainly assemblages whose unity is illusion or convention — so why not suspect the same in other cases?
  • [00:07:25] Vaiśeṣika is especially vulnerable here, because the school holds that familiar objects like crocodiles and chariots are actually collections of atoms (paramāṇu). So why not say the crocodile or chariot is just an illusion created by the conjunction of atoms? Reply: Vaiśeṣika is not the reductionist sort of atomist. Individual atoms are too small to be perceived, so when I look at a crocodile I am not seeing a vast number of atoms and combining my experience of them into one alarmingly large animal — I cannot see the atoms at all. Therefore the crocodile in front of me must be a real thing over and above the atoms; if the only real things present were atoms, there would be nothing I could perceive.

docs.title: The inherence dilemma
docs.text:
• [00:08:25] Another Buddhist argument targets the relation between whole and parts. Kaṇāda's school says a whole inheres in its parts (loosely: resides or occurs in them) — a book resides in its pages and cover. The Buddhist forces a dilemma: does the entire book reside in each page? That seems impossible — if the book is entirely in page 56 it can't also be entirely in page 57, or it'd be in two places at once. So the book must reside only partly in each page — but then the whole is divided into as many bits as it has parts, exactly contradicting the realist's claim that the whole is a unity over and above its parts.
  • [00:09:21] To escape, Vaiśeṣika must clarify what it means by inherence (samavāya). Take first the inherence of a universal in its particulars. Vaiśeṣika is convinced the universal nature crocodile is real — but its reality depends on there being actual particular crocodiles like Gina; remove her and all other crocodiles and the universal is gone too. The universal is inseparable from its instances — unlike the transcendent Forms of Plato, more like the immanent universals of the Aristotelians.
  • [00:10:01] The whole–part case is similar but not identical. The chariot is more than axle, wheels and carriage yet couldn't exist if those parts didn't. But universals are taken to be eternal and uncreated: they depend on particular instances, yet there are always some instances around, so the universal never vanishes — the nature crocodile is untroubled by individual crocodiles dying, as long as others are born. Not so for wholes: a book, a videotape, or sadly a crocodile, all break up and disappear. So Vaiśeṣika treats the parts of a whole as a special kind of cause — a substrate — the difference being that a universal can survive when its instances don't, whereas a whole cannot survive without its particular parts surviving. Despite this, both universals and wholes stand in a relation of inherence to their particulars/parts, and both are subject to a special kind of causation: instances cause the universal, parts cause the whole.

docs.title: Causation: the running theme of Indian philosophy
docs.text:
• [00:11:43] This idea of inherence feeds a long-running Indian debate about causation — present throughout the whole podcast series. The earliest cosmological speculations in Vedic literature were fundamentally an inquiry into causes. As Bimal Matilal pointed out, philosophical activity in India arose out of the cosmogonic speculations of the Vedas and Upaniṣads: the all-important business of philosophy was to find some simple unitary cause for the origin of this complex universe.
  • [00:12:13] The Sanskrit grammar tradition had causal reflection at its heart too: Pāṇini's system of kārakas, the relations between verb and noun, rests on a causal model in which the verb designates an event and the nouns contribute to bringing it about — as agent, as instrument, and so on.
  • [00:12:39] The same idea informs Indian epistemology and the theory of pramāṇas — the processes that cause an event of awareness and knowledge. In Nyāya epistemology four pramāṇas are recognized — perception, inference, comparison, testimony — each explained causally: what causes a perceptual experience? what distinguishes the causal factors of true vs. false perception? under what conditions does knowledge of an argument cause knowledge of its conclusion? Anyone reading ancient Indian philosophy quickly gets used to such causal accounts — and even faster, to the same examples recurring.

docs.title: The three standard examples
docs.text:
• [00:13:33] Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika almost always illustrate causation with one of three cases. (1) The ceramic pot: its causes include the obvious potter, but also the potter's wheel and stick, and less obviously the two halves the potter joins, the contact between the pot-halves, and the contact between them and the stick. (2) A cloth made of threads: among its causes are the threads, the weaver, the shuttle, the loom, and various instances of contact (e.g. between the woven threads that touch). (3) Chopping down a tree: the felling is caused by an axe, by its contact with the tree, by the lumberjack who wields it, and so on.
  • [00:14:30] Notice the parts are counted among the causes (the threads of the cloth): these are substrate (inherence) causes, contrasted with non-substrate (non-inherence) causes like the weaver or the contact between threads, and with instrumental causes like the weaver's shuttle. Notice too that the effect may be a thing (pot, cloth) or an event (a tree's being felled) — events too have substrates, here the tree.

docs.title: Substrate cause vs. Aristotle's material cause
docs.text: • [00:15:07] Tempting to spot a parallel with Aristotle's four causes — doesn't the substrate cause sound like the material cause? Perhaps, but not quite. The parts of an object aren't necessarily identical with the material it's made from — that would be clay for the pot, wood for the chariot (and obscure 1970s martial-arts flicks in the case of a Tarantino movie). Also, an immaterial substance can't be an Aristotelian material cause, but Vaiśeṣika admits it can be a substrate cause: the soul, for instance, is the substrate cause of mental events.

docs.title: The impenetrability objection
docs.text:
• [00:15:51] Another Buddhist argument: two distinct objects can't occupy the same region of space at the same time — you can stuff a cloth inside a pot only because the pot is hollow; matter is impenetrable. But if wholes were real over and above their parts, they'd break this rule: the two halves of the pot are in exactly the same place as the whole pot, so Vaiśeṣika has to allow more than one thing in the same location.
  • [00:16:27] Reply: the impenetrability rule needs qualifying. Material objects can't usually share a space — but this needn't hold when one inheres in the other as in a substrate. In fact the whole has to be in the same place as its parts, because whenever the parts move, the whole moves with them.

docs.title: Dharmakīrti's multicoloured cloth (and David Lewis)
docs.text:
• [00:16:57] Yet another unravelling, due to the late-6th-century Buddhist Dharmakīrti: a cloth woven from threads of different colours, some blue, some not. What colour is the whole cloth? Not blue (some parts aren't), not non-blue (some parts are), and "both blue and not blue" is a contradiction. So there's no colour the multicoloured cloth can be — suggesting the cloth as a whole isn't real.
  • [00:17:36] Strikingly similar to an argument by the contemporary philosopher David Lewis against the idea that things persisting over time are wholes made of temporal parts (time-slices): if so, whole objects would have contrary properties — dye a white cloth red and one and the same cloth is both white (before) and red (after), so a single persisting whole would bear contrary properties.
  • [00:18:17] Vaiśeṣika, "determined to weave genuine wholes into the fabric of reality," answers by defining terms. The Buddhist trades on the idea that a thing either just has a property or just doesn't. But there are two ways of having a property: pervasive and non-pervasive. A property occurs pervasively if it's in every part — the red of Little Red Riding Hood's cloak. It can occur non-pervasively — the red in a Scotsman's plaid tartan kilt: the kilt has colour pervasively (every part is coloured) but each particular colour only non-pervasively (no one colour appears in every part). With this distinction the Buddhist argument is like the kilt itself — impressive at first glance, but nothing underneath.

docs.title: Wholes may or may not share properties with their parts
docs.text: • [00:19:17] A lesson from the multicoloured cloth: wholes may or may not inherit features from their parts. It's tempting to think they must — recall the sampling inference met in earlier episodes: we infer the whole sea is salty because a randomly drawn drop is salty, valid because each drop's saltiness guarantees the sea's. But sometimes wholes lack properties their parts have: a thread may be entirely blue yet belong to a cloth that isn't; a thread weighs little but can be part of a heavy tapestry. And conversely a whole can have properties its parts lack: a pot is a suitable vessel for making stew, while half a pot is useless; a chariot can convey Arjuna into battle (once he finally decides to fight) where no axle, wheel or carriage can. And per Vaiśeṣika the pot, cloth and chariot all have the property of visibility despite being made of invisible atoms.

docs.title: Common sense defended by theory
docs.text: • [00:20:38] A curious upshot: Kaṇāda and Vātsyāyana apparently just wanted to defend common sense against the Buddhists, yet ended up adopting highly theoretical, speculative ideas. Distinguishing pervasive from non-pervasive properties, or classifying ways one thing adheres in another, doesn't fly in the face of intuition the way Buddhist teachings can — but it's hardly plain common sense either. Just as Nyāya makes sophisticated epistemological proposals to uphold the reliability of everyday inferences, Vaiśeṣika offers a sophisticated metaphysics to defend the reality of everyday things — pots, chariots, textiles. Under dialectical pressure the Vaiśeṣikas were provoked into ever subtler distinctions and into recognizing new real entities such as inherence and absences. Taken together the theory stays a single, admirably coherent system — "appropriately enough, more than the sum of its parts."

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text: • [00:21:48] So far the system has been treated under metaphysics, since Vaiśeṣika is above all an attempt to classify and understand reality. But many of its ideas really fall under physics — notably its atomism, which in ancient Greek thought (and still today) counts as physical science, not metaphysics — and Kaṇāda has ideas about other physical fundamentals like space and time. Until those are covered the whole story hasn't been told: next time, a final part of the series on the Vaiśeṣika school.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Vaiśeṣika — the school defended here; metaphysical realism about substances, properties, universals — and about complex wholes, validating everyday objects against Buddhist anti-realism.
  • Kaṇāda — Vaiśeṣika's founder; holds that a whole is a real new thing over and above its parts, and that the self is an enduring unity (what licenses saying "I").
  • avayavin (whole) — the real composite object — chariot, book, person — that is one thing, not a heap, and can do what no part can alone.
  • paramāṇu (atom) — the imperceptibly small constituents; Vaiśeṣika is an atomist but not a reductionist, since unperceivable atoms can't be what we see.
  • samavāya (inherence) — the special relation by which a whole resides in its parts (and a universal in its instances); clarified to escape the "entire book in each page" dilemma.
  • substrate cause — the parts of a whole, treated as a special cause; like an immanent universal's dependence on instances, but a whole (unlike an eternal universal) dies when its parts do.
  • pervasive vs. non-pervasive property — two ways of having a property: in every part (red cloak) vs. only in some parts (tartan kilt); defuses Dharmakīrti's colour argument.
  • the Buddhist anti-realists — treat wholes and the self as conventional mental constructions; deny any enduring self, as a step toward liberation.
  • Dharmakīrti — late-6th-century Buddhist; argues a multicoloured cloth can have no colour, so the whole isn't real.
  • causation — the running Indian theme; per Bimal Matilal, Indian philosophy grew from the cosmogonic search (in Vedas/Upaniṣads) for a unitary cause of the complex universe.
  • kāraka — Pāṇini's grammar of verb–noun relations, built on a causal model (agent, instrument, etc.).
  • pramāṇa — means of knowledge, understood causally; Nyāya recognizes four (perception, inference, comparison, testimony).
  • substrate / non-substrate / instrumental causes — the standard taxonomy illustrated by the three stock examples: the ceramic pot, the woven cloth, the felled tree.
  • Aristotle (parallel) — the substrate cause resembles but isn't the material cause: parts aren't always the material, and immaterial substances (the soul) can be substrate causes.
  • Vātsyāyana — paired with Kaṇāda as defending common sense with deeply theoretical metaphysics.

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:21:27 In brief: A survey of how Indian thinkers theorised kāla (time): from the awe-inspiring cosmic world-cycles of the Mahābhārata, through the Vedic tradition's tendency to demote time as unreal or merely mental (Bhartṛhari, Sāṃkhya, Yoga), to the lone realist holdout — Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣika — which treats both space and time as eternal substances and builds out Praśastapāda's "impetus" (vega) theory of motion. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannery"; King's College London ≈ "Coons College London"; Lagadha ≈ "Lagada/Ladaga"; Prajāpati ≈ "Prajabati"; Atharva-Veda ≈ "Atara-Veda"; Mahābhārata ≈ "Mahabharata"; Luis González Reimann ≈ "Luis Gonzales Riemann"; kāla ≈ "kala"; Bhartṛhari ≈ "Batriari/Batrihari"; Vākyapadīya ≈ "Vakya Padilla"; Vedānta ≈ "Vedanta"; brahman ≈ "Brahmann"; Sāṃkhya ≈ "Samkhya"; Yoga-Sūtra ≈ "Yoga Sutra"; Sāṃkhya-kārikā ≈ "Samkhya Karika"; Gauḍapāda ≈ "Gauta Pada"; Vaiśeṣika ≈ "Vaiseshika/Vysheeshika"; Kaṇāda ≈ "Kanada"; paramadīrgha ≈ "paramadirga"; Nyāya-Sūtra ≈ "Nyaya Sutra"; Gautama ≈ "Godama/Godima"; Praśastapāda ≈ "Prashashtapada/Roshastapada/Prahastapada"; John Philoponus ≈ "John Philopinus"; vega ≈ "Vega"; adṛṣṭa ≈ "adrista"; Cārvāka ≈ "Chavaka"; Pāyāsi ≈ "Paiasi").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Lagadha — 5th-c. BCE author who calls astrology "the science of time," the discipline by which "he who knows it knows all" [00:02:00].
  • The Mahābhārata — where the destructive cosmic world-cycle is thematised and time (kāla) becomes "practically synonymous with death" [00:03:55].
  • Bhartṛhari — grammarian-philosopher whose Vākyapadīya gives a broadly Vedāntic account of time as an instrument through which the one brahman manifests as the many [00:06:56].
  • Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣika — the lone realist on time and space; treats both as eternal, ubiquitous substances [00:09:48].
  • Praśastapāda — Vaiśeṣika thinker (6th c. AD) who develops the theory of vega (impetus) to explain motion [00:15:09].

docs.title: Astrology, the "science of time"
docs.text:
• [00:00:37] A historian "should never dismiss as unserious ideas that historical figures took seriously." Take astrology: now reduced to newspaper horoscopes printed beside the comic strips, but in former ages "serious business" — a way of legitimising political rule and an important discipline.
  • [00:00:59] We now sharply distinguish astronomy (a science) from astrology (a pseudoscience), but in ancient and medieval societies an expert in one was likely expert in the other — the 2nd-century AD scientist Ptolemy leading the way.
  • [00:01:15] Astrology is a star example of ideas travelling between cultures: Babylonian astronomical techniques for time-measurement reached Indian astrologers in the Mauryan period; Greek astrological writing was translated into Sanskrit in the 2nd century AD; and by the 4th–5th centuries Indians were even deploying the Greek theory of epicycles (planets seated on smaller rotating spheres carried by larger celestial ones).
  • [00:01:46] Beyond cultural exchange, astrology "embodies a particular view of the cosmos and our place in it" — it is, among other things, the study of time. The 5th-century BCE author Lagadha saw this: "The Vedas went forth for the sake of the sacrifices. The sacrifices were established as proceeding regularly in time. Therefore, he who knows astrology, this science of time, knows all."
  • [00:02:17] His point: astronomical measurements fixed the auspicious moment for Vedic rituals. It is by studying the motions of the stars that Indians — and we — divide time; the days and years of our lives are "astronomically defined."

docs.title: Cosmic world-cycles: kalpa, yuga, and a day in the life of Brahmā
docs.text:
• [00:02:40] The ancient Indian scientists didn't stop at days and years — they envisioned vastly larger spans: "the day in the life of God, or Brahmā." This brings us to a notorious feature of Indian thought, the cosmic world-cycle.
  • [00:02:57] Terms like kalpa or yuga carry the vague sense of "extremely long periods of time with which the Indians measure the age of the universe." Kalpa — a word already in Aśoka's inscriptions, meaning simply "a very long time" — became the name for one Brahmā-day.
  • [00:03:18] Indian deities had to be patient: recall Indra waiting 101 years for instruction from Prajāpati. But that is nothing beside Brahmā: his single day lasts the whole cosmic cycle, reckoned at 4.32 billion years, and he lives for 72,000 such days — "you're going to need a calculator with an extra-wide screen." Each of his days sees the cosmos created, endure, and finally be destroyed.

docs.title: Time as destroyer: kāla becomes death
docs.text:
• [00:03:55] The idea of a destructive world-cycle does not yet appear in the early Vedas but is thematised in the Mahābhārata. The expert Luis González Reimann notes that by the end of the Vedic period and the composition of the Mahābhārata, "the importance of time as a destructive force had reached new heights," and the word kāla ("time") "had practically become synonymous with death."
  • [00:04:28] Another pessimistic idea from the Mahābhārata: each world-cycle subdivides into four periods of unequal length, marked by gradual degradation and loss of dharma — shown, for instance, in ever-shorter human lifespans. The four sub-periods, or yugas, are named after four unequally valuable throws in a game of dice.
  • [00:04:51] Depressingly, we now live in the age of the least valuable throw — the Kali — which is why ours is the Kali Yuga, with an ideal lifespan of "a mere 100 years."
  • [00:05:04] How close is the end? Views varied. Astrologers dated the most recent great conjunction of the stars that began the Kali Yuga to 3102 BC, leaving us "hundreds of thousands of years" to go. But other texts predict a more imminent cosmic demise — perhaps reflecting the destabilising foreign invasions of India between the Mauryan and Gupta empires.
  • [00:05:41] This awe-inspiring conception of cosmic time forms the background to karmic retribution and reincarnation: "if you escape just punishment for your misdeeds, it won't be for lack of time." Even the gods are subject to time, living through daily cycles with cosmic genesis and destruction correlated to dawn and dusk.

docs.title: Is time itself a divine, creative principle?
docs.text:
• [00:06:08] That the gods themselves live by cosmic days might suggest time is a divine principle, "or even a principle beyond divinity." But that notion finds full expression only in one unusual passage of the Atharva-Veda, where all things — including the creator god Prajāpati — are originated by time itself.
  • [00:06:24] It is not a doctrine that caught on. One of the Upaniṣads explicitly rejects the claim that time is a creative principle, and the Vedic philosophical tradition goes further in this "metaphysical demotion of time" — by doubting whether it is real at all.

docs.title: Doubting time's reality: Bhartṛhari's Vākyapadīya
docs.text:
• [00:06:43] We might expect such doubt in Vedānta, especially its Advaita variety, where everything other than brahman is exposed as illusion. But one of the more interesting treatments, from a broadly Vedānta standpoint, doesn't go quite that far: a section of the Vākyapadīya by the grammarian-philosopher Bhartṛhari.
  • [00:07:06] Bhartṛhari introduces time at the very outset of his treatise, explaining that it conditions the appearance of the one brahman as many things subject to growth and decay. On this reckoning, time is "not exactly unreal," but a mere instrument or power through which brahman makes itself manifest as our changing, multifarious world. So all phenomenal things are "bound to time, like birds held captive by strings."
  • [00:07:40] Still, from the standpoint of brahman — and of the Vedānta philosopher — there is no real difference between past, present, and future. As usual in Sanskrit grammar, Bhartṛhari puts action at the centre: the three tenses are "nothing but an attitude we take towards actions." Past tense marks actions already performed, present tense actions mid-completion, future tense actions not yet undertaken.

docs.title: Time as a product of mind: Sāṃkhya and Yoga
docs.text:
• [00:08:16] Other Vedic thinkers are even more sceptical. Sāṃkhya and Yoga in particular claim time is "merely a product of our minds." The Yoga-Sūtra speaks obscurely of a knowledge arising "from our awareness of moments and succession."
  • [00:08:31] Fortunately the commentary explains: a moment (kṣaṇa) is the smallest part of time, "just as an atom is a smallest part of matter." We mentally combine moments into an impression of flowing, continuous time — but time is "nothing real out in the world." Most of us see only from the perspective of the present moment, and so fail to realise that past and future are also real, even if only present events are manifest.
  • [00:08:59] The Sāṃkhya commentators take their cue from a sūtra of the Sāṃkhya-kārikā: the external senses grasp only the present, whereas the mental organ can also grasp past and future. Gauḍapāda explains that the mind can infer past and future from present perceptions — the familiar examples: realising it must have rained because the river is swollen, or that it will rain because ants are carrying their eggs to safety.

docs.title: The realist holdout: Vaiśeṣika on space
docs.text:
• [00:09:34] So far the ancient Indians seem impressed by the immensity of time, "but not so impressed that they were willing to admit that time is actually real." But we haven't yet considered the Vedic school "most notable for its realist approach," Vaiśeṣika. Having defended controversial items like qualities, universals, and the self, Kaṇāda is "not likely to adopt an anti-realist theory of time."
  • [00:10:01] His strategy in the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra is previewed by how he handles space, which (no surprise) he also takes to be real. Space, like the self, cannot be apprehended directly; we infer its existence by observing things that are spatially arranged. And relative arrangement, Kaṇāda assumes, is best explained in terms of contact.
  • [00:10:33] The example: a young couple holding hands — the woman is to the man's left because he holds her right hand; their relative position is secured by direct physical contact. But picture them years later, now with their child in the middle: the mother is again to the father's left, yet she is no longer in contact with him (she holds the child's hand). What fixes their relative position now?
  • [00:11:03] Kaṇāda's answer is still contact — not between the parents, nor indirectly via the child, but the contact each parent has with space itself. Space provides the framework within which the woman can be to the left of the man. For this to work, space must be the sort of thing one can contact — which means it must be a substance: a unique, ubiquitous, and eternal substance, an instrumental cause of every physical effect, grounding the two spatial relations of nearness and farness. "It's thanks to the reality of space that we can say… the mother is to the father's left, or Germany is to the east of the United Kingdom."
  • [00:11:59] How big is space? Kaṇāda is not entirely clear. Since space is introduced to explain relations among physical objects, it might be enough for it to be just the size of the cosmos — that is where all the objects are. Yet Kaṇāda also says most bodies are "long or short," which only makes sense if they have parts bounding them at the edges; space has no parts and hence no boundary, so how can it have a determinate size? For this reason some later Vaiśeṣikas conclude space is limited in extent, while others grant it a spatial dimension they call paramadīrgha, "maximal length."

docs.title: Vaiśeṣika on time — and the problem of the present moment
docs.text:
• [00:12:59] Kaṇāda's view of time closely mirrors his view of space: time too is a substance — unique, eternal, ubiquitous, an instrumental cause of every effect. Just as space grounds relative judgments of position, time grounds relative judgments about past, present, and future: it is thanks to time that we can say "I lived in the United Kingdom before I lived in Germany."
  • [00:13:31] One difference, though: what is spatially near or far varies from person to person, but what is temporally near or far is the same for everyone. We are all "right now in contact with the same present moment," whereas each of us contacts a different region of space.
  • [00:13:49] Unfortunately the present moment turns out to be problematic. In the Nyāya-Sūtra, Gautama reports an argument against present time "strikingly reminiscent" of the paradox of the pre-Socratic Zeno. Imagine an object falling toward the ground: divide its path into the part already traversed and the part not yet traversed. Together these make up the whole path, measured out by past and future time — so there is no part of the trajectory left for the present moment. The present could only be an imaginary point dividing elapsed time from time not yet elapsed.
  • [00:14:32] Gautama replies that past and future are relative to the present, not to one another. He may mean that even if the present is only a boundary, it can still be real — "how could the present moment divide past from future if it were imaginary?" He also notes that if there were no present moment, nothing could be known through the senses, since the external senses grasp things only in the present.

docs.title: Motion and impetus: Praśastapāda's theory of vega
docs.text:
• [00:15:02] As the falling object shows, debates about time are "inextricably bound up" with debates about motion. Beginning with Praśastapāda, early Vaiśeṣika philosophers took a serious interest in projectiles and moving bodies — and again there's a striking parallel with Greek thought: his ideas are comparable to the celebrated theory of impetus in a near-contemporary, John Philoponus. Both lived in the 6th century AD ("unless, of course, time is unreal").
  • [00:15:41] For Praśastapāda, motion is the cause of conjunction and disjunction, and comes in varieties each explained by a quality of the moving body: heaviness causes downward motion, fluidity causes flowing motion, and so on. Insisting that motions are caused by qualities and not by prior motions avoids an infinite regress in which every motion needs a previous one.
  • [00:16:10] To explain why motion continues once started, Praśastapāda invokes a quality called vega — impetus or speed: a tendency or disposition of the body, comparable to elasticity. Impetus explains why falling things keep falling; elasticity, why bodies snap back to their original shape after being stretched.
  • [00:16:41] First illustration — a fruit falling from a tree. While on the branch the fruit has the quality of weight, but it is counteracted by contact with the tree via its stem. The stem breaks; no longer impeded, weight makes the fruit move to a new position — in Kaṇāda's terms, from contacting one part of the substance of space to contacting the part just below. But weight only initiates the fall. To explain what happens next, we say that at that same moment an impetus is produced in the fruit, causing further downward motion, and so on for every subsequent moment of the fall.
  • [00:17:38] This is why vega is best translated "impetus," not confused with inertia: the point is not that a moving body simply continues unless impeded, but that there is an internally impressed quality in the falling fruit — just like the internal elasticity that makes a rubber ball spring back after being squeezed.

docs.title: The javelin, and the limits of the theory
docs.text:
• [00:18:04] Praśastapāda's second example, the javelin, is interesting because it moves despite its weight (the fruit moved because of weight). The throw gives the javelin both an initial motion and an initial impetus; the impetus counteracts its weight so it can keep travelling upward. Eventually the impetus is exhausted through contact with the air, weight takes over and imparts a downward impetus, and the javelin falls — now "behaving like a particularly long, sharp piece of fruit."
  • [00:18:45] Thrown at an angle, it also moves horizontally; its continued flight is caused by the impetus imparted by the thrower, depleted by air contact. "The harder you throw, the more impetus you impart" — which determines how far it travels: enough impetus, and "you just might win an Olympic medal."
  • [00:19:10] Later Vaiśeṣikas extend the theory to other motions — an iron needle toward a magnet, the upward flickering of flames, the circulation of air — assuming in each case some quality that initiates motion. But weight, fluidity, and elasticity don't fit these, so they resort to adṛṣṭa, literally "the unseen," postulated to account for such movements.
  • [00:19:43] This "may look more like magical thinking than scientific explanation," but we could read it as "admirably open-minded": realist as ever, Vaiśeṣika assumes there is some genuine property in things making them behave as they do, even if we can't yet identify it — and empirical investigation may reveal more. The worry is that adṛṣṭa later assumes more speculative roles (explaining why atoms start moving at the creation of the universe, or our fate in the afterlife) — developments "the down-to-earth Praśastapāda would probably not have approved."

docs.title: A naturalistic school — and where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:20:27] Despite such developments, it's fair to call Vaiśeṣika in general down-to-earth, or better, naturalistic: it offers accounts of the physical world and the human place in it while "avoiding appeals to supernatural forces." God is given no significant explanatory role, at least in early Vaiśeṣika.
  • [00:20:49] But if you like naturalism, an even more appealing school is coming. The groups examined so far all gave some role to non-physical things — gods, brahman, the human self or mind. Next on the agenda is a group "who shocked their contemporaries by banning all supernatural, non-physical entities from their worldview": the Cārvāka school, who traced their philosophy to a figure from the time of the Buddha named Pāyāsi. "It's only natural that you should join us to hear all about him."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• kāla — time; in the Mahābhārata it becomes "practically synonymous with death," a destructive force.
  • kalpa — a "very long time" (word already in Aśoka's inscriptions); the length of one Brahmā-day, the full cosmic cycle (≈ 4.32 billion years).
  • yuga — one of four world-ages of unequal length, named after dice-throws; ours is the Kali Yuga, the worst, dated from 3102 BC.
  • Lagadha — 5th-c. BCE author who called astrology "the science of time" — knowing it, "he who knows… knows all."
  • Atharva-Veda — contains the unusual passage in which all things, including Prajāpati, are originated by time itself (a doctrine the Upaniṣads reject).
  • Bhartṛhari — grammarian-philosopher; in the Vākyapadīya time is not unreal but an instrument through which the one brahman manifests as the changing many; the three tenses are just attitudes toward action.
  • Sāṃkhya & Yoga — hold time is a product of the mind; the Yoga-Sūtra commentary defines a moment (kṣaṇa) as the smallest part of time, atom-like, combined mentally into apparent continuous flow.
  • Gauḍapāda — Sāṃkhya commentator: the senses grasp only the present, but the mind infers past and future (swollen river → it rained; ants moving eggs → it will rain).
  • Vaiśeṣika — the realist school: treats both space and time as unique, eternal, ubiquitous substances, instrumental causes of every effect.
  • Kaṇāda — author of the Vaiśeṣika-Sūtra; grounds spatial relations (left/right, near/far) in contact with space-as-substance (the couple-and-child example).
  • paramadīrgha — "maximal length," the spatial dimension some later Vaiśeṣikas attribute to space when debating its size.
  • Gautama — in the Nyāya-Sūtra reports (and answers) a Zeno-like argument that the present moment is merely an imaginary boundary between past and future.
  • Praśastapāda — Vaiśeṣika thinker (6th c. AD, contemporary of John Philoponus); explains continued motion by the quality vega (impetus), illustrated by the falling fruit and the thrown javelin.
  • vega — impetus: an internally impressed quality that keeps a body moving; distinct from inertia.
  • adṛṣṭa — "the unseen"; postulated to explain motions (magnet, flame, air) not covered by ordinary qualities — open-minded realism, or magical thinking.
  • Cārvāka / Pāyāsi — the materialist school (next episode) that bans all non-physical entities, traced to Pāyāsi, a figure from the time of the Buddha.

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:19:30 In brief: The materialist outsiders of classical India — the Cārvāka or Lokāyata school — rejected the Vedas, Buddhist and Jain asceticism, the afterlife and the soul, looking only to "the evident and immediate consequences" of action; the episode reconstructs their (poorly preserved) ethics and their sharp but puzzling epistemology, where everyday inference is fine but inference to the unseen is a wolf's footprint scratched in the dust. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari"; Cārvāka ≈ "Chardvaka/Chavaka/Chadvika/Chattvaca/Charbacca"; Lokāyata ≈ "locayata"; Bṛhaspati ≈ "Prihaspati/Rehaspati/Brihasviti/Brasbati"; Cārvāka-Sūtra ≈ "Charvaka Sutra"; śramaṇa ≈ "shramana"; Ajita Keśakambala ≈ "Ajita Kesa Kambala"; Ramkrishna Bhattacharya ≈ "Ramchrishna Batacharya"; Hemacandra ≈ "Hemachandra"; Nyāya ≈ "Niyaya/Niaya"; pramāṇa ≈ "pramana"; Purandara ≈ "Pondara"; Somatilaka ≈ "Somatilaka"; Akbar ≈ "Akbar").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Cārvāka / Lokāyata — the materialist, this-worldly school; the "true outsiders" of classical Indian thought, opposed to Vedic, Buddhist and Jain alike [00:01:37].
  • Bṛhaspati — the figure to whom the lost Cārvāka-Sūtra is ascribed; the school's blunt founding voice [00:01:55].
  • Ajita Keśakambala — a contemporary of the Buddha, credited as the originator of Indian materialism [00:04:35].
  • The Epicureans / Sextus Empiricus — Greek comparison-cases: hedonists who weren't debauched, and skeptics whose suspension of judgement the Cārvāka does not share [00:06:53], [00:16:45].
  • The wolf's-footprint parable — the school's signature anecdote about inference and gullible scholars [00:13:14].

docs.title: Why naturalism arose: over-insistence breeds dissent
docs.text:
• [00:00:13] When you try to persuade someone, being too insistent is usually a mistake — it makes people dig in their heels, since it is human nature to greet confident certainty with stubborn skepticism. So it was "all but guaranteed" that the Brahminical schools would provoke disagreement: by insisting so emphatically on the truth of the Vedas and their indispensability on the path to wisdom and liberation, those thinkers invited contradiction.
  • [00:01:07] Contradiction came above all from the Buddhists and Jains (covered soon). But first Adamson looks at an even more radical response.

docs.title: Cārvāka / Lokāyata: turning the sūtra form against itself
docs.text:
• [00:01:13] This school used the very sūtra-and-commentary form made familiar by the Brahminical schools — but used it to reject everything those schools held dear. It was equally hostile to Buddhists and Jains, making the Cārvākas "the true outsiders of classical Indian thought," champions of a philosophy and a way of life grounded firmly within this world.
  • [00:01:37] Called Cārvāka or Lokāyata, it took its cue from early materialist ideas already circulating around the time of the Buddha.

docs.title: The lost text, and a hearing at Akbar's court
docs.text:
• [00:01:55] The key text is ascribed to a man named Bṛhaspati — the Cārvāka-Sūtra. It is lost, but can be partly reconstructed from quotations preserved by angry rivals; later Cārvāka thinkers and the verses encapsulating their teaching also survive only indirectly. Of all the traditions examined so far, Cārvāka is "by far the least well-preserved" precisely because of its irreverence.
  • [00:02:28] Yet it was still known in 16th-century India, when it was explained to the Mughal Emperor Akbar that the Cārvākas regard paradise as a state in which a man lives as he chooses, free from another's control, and hell as the state in which he lives subject to another's rule. They admit only such disciplines as promote external order — knowledge of just administration and benevolent government.
  • [00:02:56] By sheer chance the same thought surfaced in the early-1970s soul group The Undisputed Truth, who sang "you make your own heaven and hell right here on earth."

docs.title: Against ritual and against asceticism alike
docs.text:
• [00:03:02] The Cārvākas disputed both Vedic ritual practice and the ascetic śramaṇa movements, which promised that good deeds bring good fruits — in this life, another world, or a future incarnation. Bṛhaspati dismisses all of it, stating bluntly in two consecutive sūtras that religious acts are not to be performed and that religion's instructions are not to be relied upon.
  • [00:03:34] The Cārvāka verses are blunter still: "There is no heaven, no final liberation, nor any soul in another world… nor do the actions of the [castes/orders] produce any real effect." Bṛhaspati: the fire ritual, the three Vedas, the ascetic's three staves, and smearing oneself with ashes are all "the livelihood of those destitute of knowledge and manliness."
  • [00:04:00] He is an equal-opportunity offender, ridiculing the Vedic believer and the Buddhist/Jain ascetic alike. Mocking the Brahmins: if beings in heaven are gratified by our offerings here, then why not feed those standing on the rooftop down below? And mocking the śramaṇas: "the Jain, the Buddhist, dimwit, given to practicing physical hardship — who has taught you this way of leading life?"

docs.title: Ajita Keśakambala, originator of Indian materialism
docs.text:
• [00:04:35] Bṛhaspati was not the first to say such unpopular things. Ajita Keśakambala, a rough contemporary of the Buddha, held that there is "no consequence to almsgiving, sacrifice, or oblation," and that a good or bad action produces no result. (Ajita also denied that a human being has any self or soul surviving bodily death — next episode.)
  • [00:04:56] On this basis the Cārvāka expert Ramkrishna Bhattacharya credits Ajita with originating materialism in India.
  • [00:05:06] In a typical case of rivals distorting a view, Ajita is also reported to have denied the reality of both this world and the other world — making him sound like a radical nihilist. More likely he said only that we are guaranteed no future fruits from our actions in either world. In place of the Vedas', the Buddha's, or Mahāvīra's unfounded promises, the advice of Ajita and the later Cārvākas is to look solely to the evident and immediate consequences of what we do.

docs.title: Were they crass hedonists? The Epicurean parallel
docs.text:
• [00:05:48] Having rejected both ritual and asceticism and given up on any afterlife, did the Cārvākas have nothing left but crass hedonism? Their rivals say so. The very name Cārvāka may relate to cāru, "pleasant" — though an alternative etymology connects it to a root meaning the Cārvāka thinker is one who "chews up" or destroys the self. The label Lokāyata ("this-worldly") points the same ethical way. A Cārvāka verse: "While life remains, let a man live happily; nothing is beyond death."
  • [00:06:33] The Jain author Hemacandra, a staunch enemy, captures their teaching with a picturesque jibe: abandoning pleasures in this world to strive for them in the next is "like licking the elbow" — leaving what is to be licked in your hand.
  • [00:06:48] But, "like someone looking up the last drops of a margarita," take this with a grain of salt. Compare the Greek Epicureans, likewise smeared as hedonists. The Epicureans were hedonists — pleasure is the highest good — but they did not favour debauched excess: Epicurus held that the highest pleasure is simply the absence of pain, best achieved by training oneself to have minimal desires.
  • [00:07:28] For the Cārvākas the hedonist reading may be even more misleading. The best collection of Cārvāka-Sūtra fragments makes no mention of pleasure, and other critics fail to confirm Hemacandra's portrait — they would hardly have missed such a "golden opportunity." In fact a standard complaint is that the Cārvākas had no positive teaching at all — not what you'd say of committed hedonists. More likely they simply didn't bother challenging ritualism's basic premise (that we want concrete rewards); their point was that rituals are no way to get them: if you want fruits, harvest them here and now.

docs.title: The other contribution: epistemology and inference
docs.text:
• [00:08:17] It would be misleading to think Cārvāka was only forthright rejection without argument. On at least two central topics they made real contributions: the theory of the self (next time) and epistemology, especially the reliability of inference.
  • [00:08:40] Recall that the Nyāya school recognized inference as a pramāṇa (source of knowledge) — e.g. inferring a tiger in the trees from its growl. Cārvāka responds critically, but because the evidence is so poor it is unclear how radical that response was. What is certain: they accepted Nyāya's first source of knowledge, sense perception. The trickier question is whether they reject inferences built on perception, or accept them in some circumstances.

docs.title: Bṛhaspati and "everyday inference"
docs.text:
• [00:09:27] Later commentators in the tradition accepted inference. One, named Purandara, is reported to say the Cārvākas accept inference but object to anyone using it beyond the limits of perceptual experience. Some scholars read this as a softening of an original extreme empiricism — only sense perception gives knowledge — perhaps to stay competitive with rival epistemologists.
  • [00:10:03] But the balance of evidence suggests Bṛhaspati himself already admitted everyday inference. His compressed sūtras say: perception is the means of right knowledge, since that means must be non-secondary; "it is difficult to ascertain an object by means of inference," and "there is no means of knowledge for determining the other world."
  • [00:10:28] One could read this as sensation alone being a pramāṇa — and indeed the Cārvākas were sometimes called pramāṇaikavādins, "those who accept only one pramāṇa." The implicit argument: perception alone is primary, whereas inference (or testimony) is secondary.

docs.title: Tiger and rice: perception double-checks
docs.text:
• [00:10:54] If you hear a tiger sound, you can be certain there's a tiger sound, because you are immediately aware of it; but inferring a real tiger from it, or trusting someone's testimony, falls below the standard of certainty.
  • [00:11:10] Nonetheless such belief-forming can be perfectly acceptable. Perhaps you don't much mind about certainty — or you can use perception to double-check the belief. This is everyday life: you believe eating rice will end hunger because it has before, and you can satisfy any doubt right along with the hunger, by eating some rice.

docs.title: The inferences Cārvāka refuses
docs.text:
• [00:11:37] The problem is whether such inferences extend to topics like the other world or an incorporeal self — precisely the inferences Nyāya and other Vedic schools wanted to make, in the service of arguing for the soul and liberation. These are exactly what Cārvāka is committed to refuting.
  • [00:12:06] Here the claims are controversial and there's no way to check them by perception — we can't visit the other world to see if it's there. So Cārvāka might even welcome the inferences of scientific explanation, since those are hypotheses checkable against empirical evidence. The Cārvāka verses make the point: "Who will deny the validity of inference when one infers fire from smoke? Even ordinary people ascertain what is to be proven by such inferences, though they may not be pestered by the logicians." But "inferences that seek to prove a self, God, an omniscient being, the other world… are not considered valid by those who know the real nature of things." Everyday people do fine so long as their minds are not vitiated by cunning logicians.

docs.title: The parable of the wolf's footprint
docs.text:
• [00:13:14] A beautiful anecdote makes the point better than any argument. A married couple: the husband a materialist, the wife a devout believer. Unable to convince her by argument, he tries another approach — when no one is watching, he uses his fingers to scratch marks in the dust of a crossroads, mimicking a wolf's footprints. When the marks are found, the local scholars solemnly agree they "can only be explained by a wolf that has come into the village out of the forest." The husband then triumphantly tells his wife: consider, too, the case of these footprints of the wolf.
  • [00:13:58] This version explains an otherwise incomprehensible Cārvāka verse comparing learned scholars' teachings to saying "look at the footprint of the wolf."
  • [00:14:10] It may look like a caution against everyday inference — wolves are perceptible, unlike the other world or an immaterial self, and inferring a wolf from its tracks is hardly exotic reasoning. The verse even prefaces the footprint line with "man consists of only as much as is within the scope of the senses."
  • [00:14:38] But a 14th-century author, Somatilaka, stresses that the dupes include the self-styled scholars who informed everyone else a wolf must be about. He says: "these people, knaves in the garb of the pious, deceive normal folk" by convincing them of the infallibility of certain inferences and testimonies, "enticing them away with the hope of enjoying pleasures to be attained after reaching heaven, and produce blind faith in pious acts." On this reading the parable is not a wide-ranging skepticism about all inference — it casts doubt on the misleading promises of the Vedic learned men.

docs.title: Not skeptics: the Sextus Empiricus contrast
docs.text:
• [00:15:29] The puzzle about the scope of Cārvāka's critique echoes Hellenistic skepticism — but Adamson hastens to add the Cārvākas are clearly not skeptics in the Greek sense, since they accept one authoritative pramāṇa, sense perception. In that respect their epistemology fits the Epicureans, who likewise grounded all knowledge in sensation.
  • [00:16:03] Just as it's controversial how to read Cārvāka's critique of inference, it's controversial how to read the Hellenistic skeptics: on one reading they withheld assent from all beliefs; on another, only from the abstruse, technical claims of the dogmatic schools. On the reading defended here, Cārvāka lines up with the second — happy with everyday inferences, hostile only to the ambitious inferences of their Vedic and śramaṇa rivals.

docs.title: The deeper error — and negative dogmatism
docs.text:
• [00:16:45] There is a more fundamental difference from Greek skepticism as defended by Sextus Empiricus, whose skepticism was a suspension of judgement about (at least) philosophical doctrines. But it's "abundantly clear" the Cārvākas did not suspend judgement about the fruits of ritual or a self independent of the body — they judged, and very harshly: it's all bunk.
  • [00:17:13] But on what basis? To say there is no watertight inference or testimony for these things is far from showing them false. That would be like seeing a mark that looks like a wolf's footprint, realizing a husband could have made it in a marital dispute, and leaping to the conclusion that no wolf made it. More abstractly: for the Cārvākas it seems that "if there is no definite proof of something, then it should be taken not to exist" — and that looks like a crass philosophical error.
  • [00:17:52] Two responses on their behalf. (1) For something like the other world or the independent self, proof is unavailable in principle — unlike the wolf, which perception could in fact track down and verify. A world reached only after death would be completely inaccessible to perception, the source of all knowledge; and it makes a certain sense to reject belief in things that are in principle unknowable, since there could not possibly be any evidence for them. A stringent skeptic like Sextus would still call this negative dogmatism — the truly skeptical move is to make no judgement either way — but the lack of even possible evidence may have been enough for Bṛhaspati, and "might be enough for us too."
  • [00:19:06] (2) The other response is to build a rival positive theory. In the case of the self, this is precisely what the Cārvākas do — not content with calling the immortal self unproven, they offer "an innovative theory of the mind, with startling similarity to ideas current in modern-day philosophy." If you're "hungry like the wolf" to hear it, you'll have to join the next episode.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Cārvāka / Lokāyata — India's materialist, this-worldly school; rejected Vedas, afterlife, soul and karmic fruits; the "true outsiders," opposed to Brahminical, Buddhist and Jain teaching alike.
  • Bṛhaspati — figure to whom the lost Cārvāka-Sūtra is ascribed; declared religious acts not to be performed and religion's instructions not to be relied upon.
  • Cārvāka-Sūtra — the school's lost key text, reconstructable only from quotations preserved by hostile rivals.
  • Akbar — 16th-c. Mughal emperor to whom the Cārvāka doctrine was explained (paradise = living free of another's control; hell = living under another's rule).
  • śramaṇa movements — the ascetic (Buddhist/Jain) traditions promising future fruits for good deeds; mocked by Bṛhaspati alongside the Brahmins.
  • Ajita Keśakambala — contemporary of the Buddha who denied any result from sacrifice or almsgiving and any self surviving death; credited (by Ramkrishna Bhattacharya) with originating Indian materialism.
  • Epicureans / Epicurus — Greek comparison: genuine hedonists, but who equated highest pleasure with absence of pain via minimal desire; grounded knowledge in sensation, like Cārvāka.
  • Hemacandra — Jain critic who caricatured Cārvāka ethics ("licking the elbow" instead of what's in your hand); his hedonist portrait is unconfirmed by other sources.
  • pramāṇa — a means/source of knowledge; Nyāya admitted perception and inference, Cārvākas were called pramāṇaikavādins ("accepting only one pramāṇa," sense perception).
  • inference (fire from smoke; tiger from growl) — accepted by Cārvāka for everyday, perception-checkable cases; rejected when used to reach the unverifiable (self, God, the other world).
  • Purandara — later Cārvāka commentator who accepted inference but barred its use beyond perceptual experience.
  • wolf's-footprint parable — a materialist husband fakes wolf tracks; the village scholars are fooled, showing the unreliability of the learned men's inferences and promises (fullest version by Somatilaka, 14th c.).
  • Sextus Empiricus — late-ancient Greek skeptic who suspended judgement; contrast-case showing Cārvāka is not skeptical — it judges harshly, risking what Sextus would call negative dogmatism.
  • negative dogmatism — Sextus's term for denying something's existence on the grounds that it can't be proven; the philosophical trap the Cārvāka critique may fall into.

docs.text:
← Ep 39
