🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:00 In brief: The Cārvāka (Lokāyata) materialists held that consciousness and the self are not immaterial principles that outlive the body but emerge from it — a "startling anticipation" of modern emergentism. Adamson traces the view from early naturalists (Ajita Keśakambala, prince Pāyāsi) through the Cārvāka-Sūtra of Bṛhaspati to the hostile reports of Prabhācandra and Jayanta, and distinguishes Cārvāka's enduring-but-bodily mind from the Buddhist no-self. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari"; Cārvāka ≈ "Chavaka/Chardbaka/Chattvaka/Chadvika"; Bṛhaspati ≈ "Brihaspati/Budhaspati/Brehaspati/Yhasbati"; Ajita Keśakambala ≈ "Ajita Kesa Kambala/Agita"; Pāyāsi ≈ "Paiasi/Payasi"; Kāśyapa ≈ "Kashyapa"; Keśi ≈ "Kessi/Kesi"; Prabhācandra ≈ "Prabha Chandra/Prabachandra"; Vaiśeṣika ≈ "Sheshika"; T. H. Huxley ≈ "T. Huxley"; Monima Chadha ≈ "Monima Chada").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Cārvāka / Lokāyata — the Indian materialists; their theory of mind anticipates modern emergentism [00:01:30].
  • Ajita Keśakambala — pioneering materialist, contemporary of the Buddha; the person is a compound of four elements [00:03:33].
  • Pāyāsi — a prince, "ancient Indian David Hume," who ran experiments to disprove a separable soul [00:03:58].
  • Bṛhaspati — reputed author of the Cārvāka-Sūtra, who states the materialist account of mind [00:07:42].
  • Prabhācandra (11th c.) & Jayanta (9th c.) — Jain and Nyāya opponents whose hostile reports preserve Cārvāka's view [00:12:40].

docs.title: Two ways to get philosophers interested in the past
docs.text:
• [00:00:36] There are basically two ways to get modern-day philosophers interested in the history of philosophy. First: point out that ideas from long-ago eras are excitingly different from our own. Adamson quotes Peter Geach: the usefulness of historical knowledge in philosophy is that "the prejudices of our own period may lose their grip on us if we imaginatively enter into another period when people's prejudices were different." Ancient Indian philosophy offers plenty of material for this — how many contemporary philosophers seriously engage with acting without desire (the central topic of the Bhagavad-Gītā), or with the consciousness-monism of Advaita Vedānta?
  • [00:01:20] But there's also a second, diametrically opposed strategy: pointing out startling anticipations of modern ideas in the historical record. Today's episode is dedicated to just such a case — the Cārvāka theory of mind, which is remarkably similar to a position defended by many philosophers nowadays called emergentism.

docs.title: Emergentism: mind out of matter
docs.text:
• [00:01:43] As the name implies, emergentism holds that the mind emerges from the body. This means, on the one hand, that physical properties — like chemical processes in the brain — somehow give rise to mental life (philosophers speak of the mental supervening on the physical). Yet, on the other hand, mental life cannot simply be reduced to bodily processes: the mind has its own causal powers, and even the most sophisticated science couldn't eliminate talk of the mental and replace it with talk of things happening in the brain.
  • [00:02:16] The nice thing about emergentism: consciousness and other features of the mind are generated by the body, but don't then just hang around as impotent byproducts with all the real causation happening at the physical level.
  • [00:02:33] A metaphor found in discussions of Cārvāka makes the point beautifully: a spark of flame is produced by rubbing two sticks together, and the resulting fire can then be a genuine cause of heat and burning, with the help of other materials. Similarly, the body's composition gives rise to mental phenomena — thoughts, desires — which can then cause further thoughts and desires.

docs.title: The opposing schools
docs.text: • [00:02:57] This view is powerfully opposed to what we've seen in other ancient Indian schools. The strongest contrast is with the Vedānta tendency to make brahman a mental principle, the cause of all physical phenomena — which may even be seen as unreal. But Sāṃkhya and Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika also insisted that humans have some immaterial psychological principle. More generally, there was widespread acceptance that the mind or self, if it exists at all, can survive on its own without the body.

docs.title: Early forerunner: Ajita Keśakambala
docs.text: • [00:03:27] Widespread though this idea was, it came under attack very early in Indian history. Last time we met the pioneering materialist Ajita Keśakambala. In support of his rejection of Vedic ritual and its fruits — whether in this life or the next — Ajita claimed that the human person is but a compound of the four great primary elements. After death the person is dissolved, with earth returning to earth, water to water, and so on.

docs.title: Prince Pāyāsi, the "Indian David Hume"
docs.text:
• [00:03:58] Another forerunner of the Cārvāka view of mind was a prince called Pāyāsi. Like Ajita, he seems to have lived around the time of the Buddha himself, and we have a report of his ideas in the Buddhist Nikāya. It tells us how Pāyāsi, like an ancient Indian version of David Hume, undertook experiments to show there is no self separable from the body.
  • [00:04:22] These experiments "would not pass muster with a modern-day scientific ethics committee." Pāyāsi suggested putting a person in a large sealed vessel and baking it until the person dies — then opening the jar and watching carefully to see if the soul escapes. (We see none.) Failing a jar that big, just beat the life out of the person and watch for a departing soul; or weigh someone before and after killing them to see if anything has escaped; or, "if you're feeling sadistic and curious in equal measure," peel the person layer by layer to see whether a soul is exposed at the core.

docs.title: Kāśyapa's reply: the silent trumpet
docs.text:
• [00:05:05] All of this is proposed in a dialogue with Kāśyapa, supposedly a companion of the Buddha. Kāśyapa can hardly insist the soul is detectable through Pāyāsi's gruesome experiments — but he denies their relevance, arguing that thrashing a person's body to find the soul is like thrashing a trumpet to get at the music it used to make. Just as a trumpet not being played by a musician is silent, the body without soul is inert: without life, heat and consciousness it is incapable of motion, sense-perception and thought.
  • [00:05:35] As a Buddhist, Kāśyapa has no interest in defending a self as an enduring simple entity. His objection is rather methodological: whatever our doctrine of the self, we should not suppose that the mental can be investigated using the same approach we take in studying the natural world.

docs.title: Pāyāsi in the Jain version: Keśi's lamp
docs.text:
• [00:05:53] The figure of Pāyāsi is also known from Jain literature, which again makes him an interlocutor in a dialogue about the soul — this time with a man named Keśi. Pāyāsi puts it to Keśi that an ant and an elephant should have souls of the same size — so why are an elephant's activities so much more impressive than an ant's?
  • [00:06:13] Keśi responds with a metaphor: imagine a windowless, doorless hall — no light can escape. A lamp is lit in the middle; it illuminates the entire hall but nothing outside. Cover the lamp with a bushel, and only the much smaller space inside the bushel is lit. In just the same way the soul is reborn into a body — small or large — as it is bound by the karma of its previous existence, and animates it accordingly. Therefore, Pāyāsi, the soul and the body are different, not identical.
  • [00:06:55] The story of Pāyāsi shows that naturalism was a strong undercurrent in Indian philosophy from the very beginning. Like its rivals it was a philosophy of path and purpose — but one that recommended living for the here and now rather than in pursuit of transcendental ideals. Ajita and Pāyāsi dismissed the pretensions of Vedic ritual as a means to satisfying desire, and rejected the idea that God exists and can intervene on earth. Their skepticism about the soul was part and parcel of a more general philosophy with the potential to challenge the Vedic tradition — and also Buddhism and Jainism — once it was systematized into a proper school.

docs.title: The Cārvāka-Sūtra of Bṛhaspati
docs.text:
• [00:07:42] As so often, systematization meant producing a canonical text in sūtra form — hence the Cārvāka-Sūtra, ascribed to Bṛhaspati. We saw last time that Bṛhaspati, and Cārvāka more generally, carried on the early naturalist project with an epistemology that privileged sense-perception over inference and testimony. But at least as much emphasis was placed on the naturalist account of mind — indeed this topic seems to have featured at the very beginning of the Cārvāka-Sūtra.
  • [00:08:18] The latest reconstruction has the text starting roughly: "Earth, fire, air and water are the reals. Their combination is called the body, senses and objects. Consciousness is formed out of these elements, as the power to intoxicate is formed out of fermenting ingredients. A human being is a body qualified by consciousness. Thinking is from the body alone, because of its presence when there is a body."
  • [00:08:48] This is a stunningly forthright affirmation of naturalism / physicalism: everything that exists, states Bṛhaspati, is identical to the elements or some combination of them. In case we wonder how our complex surroundings could arise from such simple ingredients, he adds: "The world is varied due to variations in origin, as the eye in the peacock's tail." Modern philosophers would speak of the causal history of different things — things are complicated because they arose from a complex process of combination and interaction between simpler materials.

docs.title: The intoxication analogy and the question of causal power
docs.text:
• [00:09:29] Bṛhaspati's account applies also — even especially — to the human mind. Tellingly, he does not speak of self (ātman), but only of the generation of the human being or person (Sanskrit puruṣa). He doesn't do his opponents the favour of assuming there is any such thing as a self that could be independent of body; instead the whole person, including the power of thought, is made from the four elements.
  • [00:10:00] Bṛhaspati compares the emergence of consciousness from matter to the way the capacity to intoxicate arises from mixing the ingredients of an alcoholic beverage. This analogy strongly suggests the mind that arises from matter would have its own causal powers, as emergentism requires: earth and water cannot think on their own, just as hops, barley and water cannot make you drunk on their own. The trick is all in the combination, from which arises a new power.

docs.title: The ablative ambiguity — three readings
docs.text: • [00:10:36] Unfortunately the surviving Cārvāka-Sūtra leaves doubt about the exact relationship between mind and its material basis. The problem centres on the noun for "elements," here apparently in the ablative case. As in Latin, the Sanskrit ablative can mean several things: Bṛhaspati might be saying that mind is made from the elements, that thinking is because of the elements, or that thought is produced out of the elements. This — plus the typically compressed style of the aphorisms — left commentators room for several interpretations.

docs.title: The reductive reading: Huxley's steam whistle
docs.text:
• [00:11:10] One idea: mind is only the manifestation of processes at the physical level, with those physical processes carrying all the explanatory weight. On this reading Bṛhaspati was simply identifying the mind with a combination of bodily elements; our mental life would just be the way we register the physical processes caused by elemental combination.
  • [00:11:38] This resonates with some modern ideas: in the late 19th century, T. H. Huxley proposed that mental phenomena could be a mere byproduct of physical phenomena, comparing the mind to the steam whistle of a locomotive (no role in running the train) or the bell of a clock (no help in keeping time). On this reading Bṛhaspati's mind is causally inert — it doesn't do anything in its own right, just manifests the elemental combination.
  • [00:12:09] Yet there are good reasons to doubt this reading. The intoxicating-beverage comparison seems designed to show the mind does do something distinctive of its own. Other Cārvākas duly held that the mind is a distinct power which emerges from the combination of material elements without being identical to them.

docs.title: The hostile witnesses: Prabhācandra and Jayanta
docs.text:
• [00:12:40] There is textual evidence of this disagreement among the Cārvākas. Prabhācandra, an 11th-century Jain philosopher, discusses their views with unprecedented detail. He explains that a "manifestation" puts together well — refines and perfects — what is already there, rather than bringing into being something that wasn't there before; so the manifestation is not a separate thing over and above the four elements.
  • [00:13:15] Prabhācandra lays out the options for explaining mind in terms of body. (1) The most radical: the mind or self simply is the body — an identity. (2) The physicalist need not go that far: she might say mind is one of the body's qualities or states — for which he uses the term guṇa (familiar from Sāṃkhya); this aligns with the train-whistle, mere-byproduct idea. (3) Finally — and, "for our money," the most plausible reading of the Cārvāka-Sūtra — mind is an effect of the body, well captured by the spark giving rise to flame. Again it is Prabhācandra who records this idea on behalf of his Cārvāka opponents.
  • [00:14:11] Another insightful opponent was the 9th-century Nyāya philosopher Jayanta, who explained the theory in order to refute it. He confirms Prabhācandra's observation that for Cārvāka the self is not a separate entity, and — befitting a Nyāya thinker — focuses on Cārvāka's epistemological arguments against an independent self.

docs.title: The self is not perceived, inferred, or testified
docs.text:
• [00:14:36] Since Cārvāka grounds all human knowledge in sense-perception, it makes sense for them to argue (as Jayanta reports) that the self is not given to us in perception: our external senses give no access to any self distinct from the body. "When was the last time you saw or heard a self?" Nor can introspection deliver it, since internal perception is always a perception of something like a particular pain or pleasure — not of a subject of consciousness.
  • [00:15:16] This is more convincing than it sounds, given the views Cārvāka is criticizing: recall how Nyāya carefully distinguished the internal perception enjoyed by the interior mental organ from the role played by the self.
  • [00:15:27] If the self can't be perceived directly, perhaps we could infer it. But Cārvāka doubted the possibility of inferences concerning things beyond the senses, and explicitly rejected arguments that inferred a separate self from its apparent function in our mental lives: we need posit no self to explain memory or the comparison of multiple sensory experiences — these are all things the body can do.
  • [00:16:01] No better is establishing the self by authoritative testimony such as the ancient scriptures. Cārvāka gives arguments from authority no credence anyway — but they also point out (per Jayanta) that one can just as well use the scriptures to support a naturalist view of mind, citing a passage stating that the self is "a single mass of cognition which has risen up out of these elements and is dissolved into them."

docs.title: Not the same as Buddhist no-self
docs.text:
• [00:16:47] It might be tempting to associate the materialists with the Buddhists, whose famous no-self theory posed a similar challenge to the Brahminical tradition. But we should not conflate the two. Admittedly Bṛhaspati avoids the word self — but the Cārvākas are not, like the Buddhists, questioning that the human mind persists over time. They are fully committed to the reality of such an enduring mind; it's just that they believe it emerges from and depends on the body.
  • [00:17:15] So Cārvāka could agree with the other sūtra-based traditions that we have persisting minds, while disagreeing by explaining those mental subjects in a bottom-up rather than top-down way. Cārvāka is like a mirror image of Vedānta: the mental arises out of the material world, rather than the material out of the mental.
  • [00:17:38] That language is slightly misleading, though. If Bṛhaspati really is an early forerunner of emergentism, then in a sense he does make room for top-down causation: once the mind is produced out of material composition, it can exert its own causal influence — thoughts are not inert but play a role in explaining the world. The real point is that for Cārvāka the thinking subject is not a fundamental explanatory principle (as so many Vedic philosophers insisted), but merely an effect of the body.

docs.title: Conclusion and what's next
docs.text:
• [00:18:15] It's a real shame the Cārvāka theory of mind is so poorly preserved — the school's works are lost, known only indirectly through hostile reports. But Bṛhaspati proposed that human beings are physical bodies which can be conscious, that consciousness emerges out of the organization of physical matter and disappears again when that organization is destroyed. His position resonates powerfully with most modern philosophers of mind, who likewise see an intimate relationship between mind and body, the physical somehow giving rise to the mental.
  • [00:18:48] Still, we shouldn't underestimate the first motivation for doing history of philosophy: the spectrum of Indian theories of mind is interesting precisely because it is so different from the spectrum current today. Before moving on to the Buddhists and their searching critique of the enduring self, the series will explore the ancient Indian psychological theories more deeply — in an upcoming conversation with Monima Chadha.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Cārvāka / Lokāyata — the Indian materialists; mind and self emerge from the body and perish with it. Known only through hostile reports.
  • emergentism — the modern view Cārvāka anticipates: mind is generated by the body (supervenes on the physical) yet has its own causal powers and can't be reduced to brain processes.
  • spark / fire analogy — emergentism's image: fire produced by rubbing sticks then genuinely causes heat; likewise the body produces mind, which then causes further mental events.
  • Ajita Keśakambala — early materialist, contemporary of the Buddha; the person is a compound of the four great elements and dissolves at death.
  • Pāyāsi — a prince, "ancient Indian David Hume," who proposed grisly experiments (baking, weighing, peeling a body) to show no soul departs at death.
  • Kāśyapa — Buddhist interlocutor who answers Pāyāsi: thrashing a body to find the soul is like thrashing a trumpet to get its music; a methodological, not a metaphysical, objection.
  • Keśi — Jain interlocutor who answers Pāyāsi's "ant and elephant have equal souls" with the lamp-and-bushel image: one soul animates bodies large or small per the karma of past lives.
  • Bṛhaspati — reputed author of the Cārvāka-Sūtra; states that the four elements are the reals, consciousness "is formed out of" them, and thinking is "from the body alone."
  • Cārvāka-Sūtra — the school's systematizing canonical text; its opening aphorisms give the naturalist account of mind (and the peacock's-tail line on variety).
  • intoxication analogy — consciousness arises from the elements as the power to intoxicate arises from fermenting ingredients; the combination yields a genuinely new power.
  • ablative ambiguity — the elements-noun's case allows three readings: mind made from / because of / produced out of the elements — hence the interpretive disputes.
  • Huxley's steam whistle / clock bell — T. H. Huxley's images for mind as a causally inert byproduct; the reductive reading of Bṛhaspati that the intoxication analogy argues against.
  • Prabhācandra — 11th-c. Jain reporter who lays out the options: mind = body (identity), mind as a guṇa/quality (byproduct), or mind as an effect of the body (the emergentist reading).
  • Jayanta — 9th-c. Nyāya reporter who details Cārvāka's epistemology: the self is given by neither perception, introspection, inference, nor scriptural testimony.
  • ātman / puruṣa — self vs. person; Bṛhaspati pointedly speaks of generating the person (puruṣa), not a self (ātman) independent of body.
  • guṇa — "quality/state" (term borrowed from Sāṃkhya); one option for relating mind to body.
  • top-down vs bottom-up — Vedānta derives matter from mind (top-down); Cārvāka derives mind from matter (bottom-up) — yet emergent mind can still exert top-down causation.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 41 — "Monima Chadha on Indian Philosophy of Mind"
docs.text:
← Ep 40

Ep 42 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Monima Chadha 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Monima Chadha · Runtime: 00:29:30 In brief: An interview on ancient Indian philosophy of mind, centred on the great self/no-self debate between the Vedic ("Hindu") schools and the Buddhists — why "mind" (manas) is not "self" (ātman), how the Buddhists argue that impermanent mental faculties can do all the work the Vedic self was meant to do (memory, the unity of consciousness, agency), and how these debates speak to contemporary, eliminativist philosophy of mind. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Monima Chadha ≈ "Monima Chalha / Moni Machada"; Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennary"; Vasubandhu ≈ "Basu Bandhu / Vazupandu"; Cārvāka ≈ "Chharvaka / Chavaka / Chalaka"; Nyāya ≈ "Niyya / Niyahi"; Abhidharma ≈ "Abidharma"; ālayavijñāna ≈ "Aleh Vidyan"; ahaṃkāra ≈ "ahamqar"; citta ≈ "chita"; buddhi ≈ "budi"; Philosophy East and West ≈ "philosophy Eastern West").

docs.title: Is there a Sanskrit word for "mind"?
docs.text:
• [00:00:28] The guest is Monima Chadha, senior lecturer in philosophy at Monash University; the episode is an interview on ancient Indian philosophy of mind.
  • [00:00:56] Adamson opens with terminology: is there a single Sanskrit word that means just what English means by "mind"? Chadha's answer is "yes and no, as you'd expect from a philosopher."
  • [00:01:04] There is manas, standardly translated "mind." But there are several other relevant terms naming distinct mental faculties — citta, ahaṃkāra (the "I-maker"/ego), buddhi (intellect). So when we say "mind" in Indian philosophy we are really talking about a cluster of mental faculties and conscious states. In Buddhist philosophy especially, mind is often spoken of as citta.
  • [00:01:50] So there's no clean one-to-one mapping: you can't pick one Sanskrit word and call it the equivalent of the English "mind."

docs.title: Mind belongs to the category of "not-self"
docs.text:
• [00:01:57] The crucial point for the whole episode: in the Indian tradition "mind" falls under the category of the not-self. The fundamental divide is not mind versus body (as in the West) but self versus not-self.
  • [00:02:24] What separates the two categories, in Chadha's view, is permanence. Mind — together with body, the sense organs, and the rest of the not-self — is impermanent. The self (ātman) is by contrast permanent, even eternal for some Vedic schools. So whenever we think about mind in this tradition we must think of it as an impermanent entity.
  • [00:02:53] She recalls a riddle from the mythological tradition: "what is swifter than the wind?" — the answer being the mind. But the deeper warning is terminological: in Western philosophy we freely use "mind," "self," and "person" interchangeably; in Indian philosophy that is a mistake, because mind belongs to an altogether different category from self.

docs.title: Is the self/no-self debate really about mind?
docs.text:
• [00:03:29] This sets up the central ancient Indian debate: the Buddhists deny a persistent self, the Vedic schools insist on one. Adamson presses a worry: since the Vedic tradition itself distinguishes mind from self, is this really a debate in the philosophy of mind at all?
  • [00:03:53] Chadha reframes it. The debate is officially about whether there is a self. But you can read it as a debate about mind, because the Buddhist move is to argue that the mind can do all the work of the self — so we don't need a self at all. Whatever the Hindu schools claim the self does, the Buddhist says the mind can do.
  • [00:04:36] Adamson adds the complication: the Buddhists deny that the mind persists over time either — indeed they deny that anything persists. Chadha agrees; this is precisely the challenge. If the mind is impermanent, how can it explain phenomena like memory? The Hindus postulate a self largely because otherwise memory has no good explanation. The Buddhist reply is: no, we can account for memory and the other mental functions the Hindus point to, using impermanent mental faculties.

docs.title: The argument from memory — and what the Nyāya-Sūtra actually says
docs.text:
• [00:05:32] The most prominent Vedic argument for a persisting self, from the Nyāya school: "I must persist over time because I can remember things I experienced yesterday." A powerful argument, Adamson grants.
  • [00:05:56] Chadha corrects a common assumption: the original argument in the Nyāya-Sūtra does not mention memory. The original argument is about the need to explain desire — how can I desire something unless I've had the relevant experiences before? Therefore there must be a persisting self. Memory enters only in the commentaries.
  • [00:06:29] And in the commentaries it's specifically episodic memory — not just remembering facts about the past, but remembering episodes: e.g. "I was the one singing at my 40th birthday," a vivid first-person recollection. That kind of memory, the Nyāya argue, cannot be explained without a permanent self.
  • [00:07:13] Adamson probes the timescale: is it only about long-ago events, or also ongoing memory (e.g. remembering you've been talking for several minutes)? Chadha finds the question interesting — how much time must pass before something counts as a memory? Even comprehending a single sentence requires holding the earlier words, but they treat sentence comprehension as happening "all at once," so that wouldn't count. Something from a few minutes ago, though, probably should count.
  • [00:08:03] And no, she says, they don't draw a short-term / long-term memory distinction in framing this argument for the self.

docs.title: The unity of consciousness
docs.text:
• [00:08:13] Adamson raises a second Vedic argument — not about persistence over time but about the unity of consciousness at a single moment, the first-person perspective. Right now he hears Chadha's voice and sees the room; there seems to need to be some mental principle (the mind? the self?) that gathers these impressions into a single "gestalt awareness."
  • [00:08:58] Chadha: the Nyāya and Hindu schools will indeed say only the self can unite experiences at a time. But the Buddhists answer that a mental faculty — the eighth consciousness or storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) — can account for this synchronic unity of experiences, without postulating a self.
  • [00:09:51] Adamson tries to locate the mind/self difference here: perhaps the Vedic side says the mind does certain jobs, but I also have sense perception, so I need a self to unify what's in the mind with what's in sense perception into one consciousness (e.g. recalling yesterday while looking at a painting). The Buddhists, on this reading, say you can get by with just whatever mind and sense perception do.
  • [00:10:30] Chadha refines it: the Buddhist doesn't actually distinguish sense perception from mind in that way. The Buddhist treats the various consciousnesses as all being kinds of minds. There is no single thing called "the mind"; mind just is a series of states, changing and causally connected over time. Sense perception is one kind of conscious awareness, self-awareness another, bodily awareness another — multiple simultaneous series that share a time-frame and causal interactions, and together they can do the work the Hindus assign to a self.

docs.title: How the Buddhist critique differs from the Cārvāka
docs.text:
• [00:11:38] Adamson links back to earlier episodes on the Cārvāka (materialist) position. The Cārvākas seem to accept at least a mind and maybe a self — though the Cārvāka-Sūtra avoids the word ātman, speaking of mental phenomena instead. The Buddhists are saying something very different.
  • [00:12:19] Chadha: the Cārvākas treat consciousness as an emergent property of the material elements. The Buddhists are not materialists — they distinguish mental atoms/elements from physical elements, speak of psychophysical complexes, and refuse to reduce mind to body.
  • [00:12:58] But the deeper difference is impermanence: for the Buddhist, mind is not a persisting thing but a series of conscious awarenesses (indeed many series). Their critique of persistence would apply to the emergent Cārvāka mind just as much as to Vedānta theories of self — because the Cārvākas do take the material elements to persist over time, combining to give rise to the new property of consciousness.
  • [00:13:36] So the debate between Cārvākas and Hindus is not about persistence; that's a different debate. The Buddhist/Hindu debate is specifically about whether we need persisting entities in our ontology to explain everything there is.

docs.title: From Occam's Razor to an argument against existence
docs.text:
• [00:13:53] Adamson notes that as described, the Buddhist argument sounds like Occam's Razor — we can explain the phenomena without a persisting self or mind, so we shouldn't posit one. (He's covering Ockham in the parallel medieval episodes.) Is it merely that, or do they also argue the self is incoherent?
  • [00:14:45] Different schools, different arguments. The economy argument Chadha has been describing belongs to the Abhidharma school. Vasubandhu sharpens it: for the Abhidharma, the criterion of reality is causal efficacy — "to be is to be causally efficacious." His claim is that the self is causally inefficacious; there's nothing for the self to do; therefore there is no self.
  • [00:17:36] Adamson observes this is how you turn a merely economical Occam-style argument into an aggressive one that shows something doesn't exist: you add the premise that to exist just is to be causally efficacious, and so bootstrap from "we don't need it" to "it doesn't exist."

docs.title: The "it will make you unhappy" argument — and aggression on both sides
docs.text:
• [00:15:42] A second, very different Buddhist argument: if you postulate a self, it will make you unhappy — because with a self comes self-interest. The self is not only doing no work, it is an illusion that causes misery, so we should be rid of it. (There is also a separate incoherence argument in the tradition.) All these are competing interpretations of what the Buddha meant by the denial of self.
  • [00:16:35] Adamson finds the "it'll make you unhappy" argument strange: philosophy of mind is supposed to be an abstract, theoretical branch, yet here is an argument from misery. Chadha pushes back firmly: the argument is not "don't believe in the mind," it's "don't believe in the self" — or more carefully, "don't believe in persisting things." Mind, as momentary mental awareness, is not a persisting thing; it exists only momentarily before giving rise to the next conscious state. So the unhappiness argument targets the persisting self, not mind.
  • [00:18:14] Aggression, she adds, runs on both sides. The Hindus are no gentler when debating Buddhists. She recalls an exchange in the journal Philosophy East and West: a Buddhist philosopher disagreed with her, and the Nyāya scholar Stephen Phillips (a professor in Texas) quipped, "Chadha might not be right, but against the Buddhists, everything is fair."

docs.title: Storehouse consciousness and the unity of consciousness, again
docs.text:
• [00:18:51] Adamson concedes memory is easy for the Buddhists — it just falls under their general account of apparent persistence (causal connections between fleeting momentary phenomena). Harder, he thinks, is the unity of consciousness: without a self, what centre of awareness directs attention across all the cognitions happening at one moment?
  • [00:19:55] Chadha (specifying the Abhidharma school and the philosopher Vasubandhu, a tradition of northern India) explains via the storehouse consciousness — which the later Vasubandhu takes over from the Yogācāra school. The storehouse consciousness acts as a base: there is a two-way interaction between it and the sensory consciousnesses (eye-consciousness, olfactory, taste, etc.). It helps the other consciousnesses, and they in turn feed their objects back into it. All the sensory consciousnesses thus share a common base.
  • [00:21:19] Crucially, this base is not a persisting thing: it is itself a changing consciousness like every other. So whatever a transcendent single self overseeing everything was supposed to do, the Buddhist does instead by appealing to the interrelationships between the components of the momentary person.

docs.title: "Am I my mind?" — eliminating the "I"
docs.text:
• [00:21:54] Since the Buddhists accept mind as momentary cognition, and (in Chadha's published work on Vasubandhu) this momentary mind does the work of a self or person — would Vasubandhu say "I am my mind"?
  • [00:22:25] No, she thinks the Buddhists would not be happy with that. They dislike the notion of "I" altogether: the "I" is a fiction, a conceptual imposition on what is really real, and this imposition causes great suffering — because with "I" comes "me" and "mine," ego and self-interest.
  • [00:22:54] So it's a reductionist / eliminativist account. Adamson contrasts the Cārvākas again: they say mental life emerges from the elements but is nonetheless real. The Buddhists, by contrast, want us to abandon all thought of the self / the "I" — because they think it brings nothing but pain.

docs.title: Contribution to contemporary philosophy of mind
docs.text:
• [00:23:38] Adamson closes by asking how all this bears on contemporary philosophy of mind — noting he's never been to a contemporary talk that opens with "liberation from suffering," so the motivation is clearly different.
  • [00:24:20] Chadha's first answer: moral responsibility and agency. If you give up persons and the self, you also seem to give up the agent of action — and the Buddhists embrace that. She gives Vasubandhu's worked example: you see a mango → a desire for the mango arises → that causes an intention → that causes bodily actions → you procure the mango and satisfy the desire. Where is the agent in all this? There is just an interaction of mental and physical states explaining the action; no agent is needed. Some Buddhists say the very sense of agency is an illusion: responsibility can be handled by the causal relations without positing agents as the bearers of moral responsibility.
  • [00:26:22] Adamson notes the fit: much contemporary philosophy of mind tends eliminativist or toward supervenience theories, trying to get away from Cartesian pictures of self and mind and reduce them to the material. So even though the Buddhists started from very different motivations, their drive to eliminate apparent mental phenomena slots into the modern debate neatly.
  • [00:27:04] A further contribution: degrees / levels of conscious awareness. For the Buddhists it's not simply "conscious state vs. unconscious"; there are degrees of awareness. Her example: one is not directly conscious of one's body, but the moment it's mentioned it comes into awareness. Contemporary philosophy and the sciences of mind could attend to this more carefully rather than treating consciousness as binary.
  • [00:28:02] And it isn't only the Buddhists: the Hindu / Vedic tradition offers a fine-grained taxonomy of conscious states — waking, dream states, and deep dreamless sleep (what happens to consciousness there?). These are exactly the questions entering contemporary philosophy and the science of mind — evidence suggesting degrees of consciousness even in sleep. So this is not merely history: it has potential to contribute to live debates.
  • [00:28:54] Adamson thanks Chadha; this whets the appetite for the forthcoming Buddhist episodes. But first, a change of tack: the next episode turns to ancient theories of aesthetics — drama, poetry, and music — before the series moves on to the Buddhists and Jains, alongside Jonardon Ganeri.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• manas — the term standardly translated "mind"; but only one of several Indian words for mental faculties.
  • citta — "mind" in the sense of conscious states/awareness, especially in Buddhist philosophy.
  • ahaṃkāra — the "I-maker," the ego-faculty; a mental faculty distinct from manas.
  • buddhi — the intellect; another of the mental faculties grouped under "mind."
  • ātman — the self; for the Vedic schools permanent, even eternal — the thing the Buddhists deny.
  • self vs. not-self — the fundamental Indian divide (not mind vs. body); mind, body, and sense organs all belong to the impermanent not-self.
  • Nyāya — Vedic school; argues for a persisting self — originally from the need to explain desire (the Nyāya-Sūtra), and, in the commentaries, episodic memory.
  • Cārvāka — materialist school; treats consciousness as an emergent property of persisting material elements; avoids the word ātman in its sūtra.
  • Buddhists (Abhidharma) — deny any persisting self; hold that impermanent mental faculties, a series of momentary conscious awarenesses, can do all the self's work.
  • Vasubandhu — Abhidharma philosopher of northern India; argues the self is causally inefficacious (and so unreal), and develops the storehouse-consciousness account of the unity of experience.
  • causal efficacy — the Abhidharma criterion of reality: "to be is to be causally efficacious"; since the self does nothing, it does not exist.
  • ālayavijñāna (storehouse / eighth consciousness) — a non-persisting "base" consciousness, taken from Yogācāra, that interacts two-way with the sensory consciousnesses to explain their synchronic unity without a self.
  • Yogācāra — Buddhist school from which the later Vasubandhu adopts the storehouse-consciousness idea.
  • episodic memory — vivid first-person recollection of past episodes; the Nyāya commentators argue it requires a permanent self.
  • unity of consciousness — the gathering of simultaneous cognitions into one awareness; the Vedic argument says only a self can do it, the Buddhists answer with the storehouse consciousness.
  • the "I" as fiction — for the Buddhists the "I" is a conceptual imposition that breeds "me," "mine," ego, and suffering, and should be abandoned (an eliminativist account).
  • agency / moral responsibility — Vasubandhu's mango example shows action explained by interacting mental and physical states with no agent; the sense of agency is, for some Buddhists, itself an illusion.
  • degrees of consciousness — both Buddhist and Vedic traditions offer fine-grained taxonomies of awareness (waking, dream, deep dreamless sleep), a contribution to contemporary philosophy and science of mind.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 42 — "In Good Taste: The Aesthetics of Rasa"
docs.text:
← Ep 41

Ep 43 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:40 In brief: Ancient India's theory of aesthetic emotion — how fiction stirs fear and longing without putting us in real danger or love. Built on Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra, the concept of rasa ("flavour") names the savoured aesthetic response a drama, poem, or piece of music is engineered to evoke; later theorists tie it to suggestion (dhvani), and finally to philosophical ideals of detachment and liberation. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Gennary"; Bharata ≈ "Barata"; Nāṭyaśāstra ≈ "Natcha Shastra/Natya Sastra"; rasa ≈ "Rasa"; Ānandavardhana ≈ "Ananda Vardana/Anandavardana/Ananda Vratana"; Abhinavagupta ≈ "Abina Vagukta/Abinava Gupta"; Mahima Bhaṭṭa ≈ "Maima Bata/Mahima Bata"; dhvani ≈ "Thvani/divani"; śleṣa ≈ "Schleza"; Bhartṛhari ≈ "Batrihari"; Vālmīki ≈ "Valmiki"; Rāmāyaṇa ≈ "Ramayana"; Dattilam ≈ "Tatilam"; jāti ≈ "jatis"; artha ≈ "arta").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra ("Treatise on Drama") — the key text of the Indian aesthetic tradition, probably compiled in the early centuries CE; source of the rasa theory [00:01:49].
  • rasa — "flavour/savour"; the aesthetic response a performance is built to evoke [00:03:01].
  • Ānandavardhana — 9th-century Kashmiri literary theorist who developed the theory of suggestion (dhvani) [00:07:17].
  • Mahima Bhaṭṭa — 11th-century aesthetician and critic of Ānandavardhana; closes the episode with the cleanest account of dramatic emotion [00:07:54].
  • Abhinavagupta — 10th-century commentator who reads rasa as a universal emotion linked to liberation [00:14:11].

docs.title: Horror movies, rom-coms, and the puzzle of fictional emotion
docs.text:
• [00:00:36] Horror movies are a puzzling form of entertainment. Many people don't enjoy them, and those who do would be hard-pressed to say why — in everyday life you wouldn't thrill to the sight of innocent teenagers chased by an axe-wielding psychopath. Why enjoy watching it on a screen?
  • [00:00:57] The obvious reply — "they know it isn't real" — only deepens the puzzle: if the audience is aware the danger is entirely fictional, why should it provoke any emotional response at all?
  • [00:01:10] The same goes for the romantic comedy. We know Jennifer Aniston and "that handsome actor whose name escapes us" aren't really falling in love, yet we're swept away by their flirtation. How do fictional representations solicit emotions like fear and romantic yearning — without generating exactly the responses we'd have if we were really being pursued by an axe-wielding psychopath (or by Jennifer Aniston)?
  • [00:01:44] These questions were central to ancient Indian writings on aesthetics.

docs.title: Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and the basics of rasa
docs.text:
• [00:01:49] The tradition's key text is the Nāṭyaśāstra ("Treatise on Drama"), ascribed to an author named Bharata and probably compiled in the early centuries CE. (Listeners of Kit Patrick's History of India podcast will have met it in his episode 3A.) It is a very lengthy work offering detailed instructions on theatrical performance — from the construction of the theatre space to the gestures of actors and the metrical features of the recited text.
  • [00:02:21] Because drama involves poetry and music, Bharata says much about those arts too, so later theorists of literary and musical aesthetics draw on him. For music there was also a roughly contemporaneous early work, the Dattilam.
  • [00:02:40] Unlike the modern horror movie, ancient Indian dramas were not out to surprise you with plot twists — the audience already knew the stories. The real art lay in the effective and affecting presentation of those familiar tales.
  • [00:03:01] The key idea is rasa: an aesthetic response elicited by the drama. Though intimately associated with emotion, rasa is not the same thing as an emotion — rather it derives from emotion.
  • [00:03:24] The chain: an emotion is originally felt by the poet who authored the piece; it is then represented by actors through good dramatic technique. Erotic love, for instance, is conveyed by sidelong glances and gestures the skilled actor must master.
  • [00:03:43] A poet may touch many emotions in passing for brief effects, but the most important are the eight "emotional dispositions" (bhāva) around which a whole drama can be built. Bharata says the transitory effects serve to heighten these eight, "like attendants surrounding a monarch."
  • [00:04:06] Corresponding to the eight dispositions are eight kinds of rasa: the erotic, the comic, the pathetic, the furious, the heroic, the terrible, the odious, and the marvellous.

docs.title: "Flavour": the food metaphor
docs.text:
• [00:04:18] Bharata compares the rasas to the overall taste of a mixed beverage, alluding to the literal meaning of rasa — the savour or nutritive juice in food. (We meet it with that sense in ancient Indian medical works.)
  • [00:04:38] Take a successful horror film like Hitchcock's Psycho. On Bharata's analysis, every aspect — the disturbing music, the smallest detail of Anthony Perkins' uncanny performance as the hotel owner — is designed to evoke a continuous feeling of dread. Moments of disgust or surprise, like the famous reveal of the owner's mother, only serve to build up that core feeling, achieving the rasa of the terrible, the goal of the whole piece. Hitchcock would have this in mind even in innocuous scenes, not just the famous moments of violence.
  • [00:05:24] Of course, ancient Indian dramas did not centre on murderous hotel owners. Even when aiming at the terrible, they sought to impart moral instruction, serving a social function not usually associated with Hollywood horror.
  • [00:05:42] Producing rasa is a matter of consummate artistry — compare the skilled chef who balances ingredients for the right overall savour. As the later aesthetician Kuntaka puts it, only when natural charm is imparted by beauty, "coruscating with the innate artistry of the poet" and enlivened by the full complement of aesthetic elements, can even a proper rasa convey its deepest beauty to the reader — "whose heart then overflows with rasa the way a moonstone is liquefied by moonbeams."

docs.title: The connoisseur: rasa needs a skilled audience
docs.text:
• [00:06:25] Even when conception and acting are top-notch, rasa results only for an audience member who is equally proficient. Extending the food analogy, Bharata says the skilled audience member is like the connoisseur with a fine appreciation of drama — quite literally "in the best possible taste."
  • [00:06:48] His commentators say the audience's goal is sympathy of the heart with the actors on stage, so as fully to experience the emotion that gives rise to rasa.
  • [00:06:57] The commentators disagree, however, on whether this is the only legitimate goal of drama or poetry. Some suggest rasa could be a mere bonus or ornament — e.g. in a poem whose main purpose is flattery.
  • [00:07:17] The 9th-century Kashmiri theorist Ānandavardhana uses this idea to explain why a piece might evoke two rival emotions (say, sadness and erotic longing), which would seem to block a single overall rasa: only when a single rasa predominates is it the ultimate aim of the poem as a whole. Others argue rasa can never be a mere ornament — all poetry worthy of the name must have rasa as its main purpose.

docs.title: What can spoil rasa: redundancy and bad puns
docs.text:
• [00:07:50] Attention also goes to factors that impede rasa. There's a long discussion in another aesthetician, a critic of Ānandavardhana named Mahima Bhaṭṭa. He complains about poets who use redundant expressions, citing: "he who cuts the necks of his evil enemies with the extremely fierce blow of the front end of the drawn sharpened sword held in his hand." Why not just say he who cuts the necks of his enemies with a sword?
  • [00:08:25] Another flaw is the pun that doesn't quite work. The pun (or double meaning) was "almost as important an element in Sanskrit literature as in this podcast series." This device, called śleṣa, exploits ambiguous meanings of words or whole sentences, and could be used to reveal the complexity of a literary character — not for cheap laughs like the play on "executed" a moment ago.

docs.title: Rasa in music — and the borrowed idea of suggestion
docs.text:
• [00:08:47] Rasa appears not only in commentaries on the Nāṭyaśāstra and works on poetics but also in treatises on music. The ancient music theorists don't discuss specific written-down compositions; they focus on melody types called jāti, associated with certain moods and emotions.
  • [00:09:19] One early theorist, Matanga, shows how literary ideas penetrated music: he borrowed the poetic concept of suggestion (dhvani) — the idea that a performance can evoke or express something without alluding to it explicitly.
  • [00:09:38] This makes sense. If you want the audience to appreciate sadness, it's counterproductive to have a character say "I'm sad now." Think how you're taken out of a film when the director picks a soundtrack song whose lyrics too obviously name the desired emotion.

docs.title: Ānandavardhana on dhvani (poetic suggestion)
docs.text:
• [00:10:01] It was especially Ānandavardhana who developed dhvani to explain how rasa is evoked by poetry. In doing so he appropriated a term from the grammatical tradition: the grammarian Bhartṛhari had said that uttered sounds are dhvani and "make manifest" linguistic meaning.
  • [00:10:26] Taking inspiration from this, Ānandavardhana argues dhvani / suggestion is a special function of poetic language: the poet's art avoids explicit reference to the emotion he wants to produce, and instead implicitly suggests it, thus eliciting the desired rasa.
  • [00:10:47] His example: "Wander confidently, monk — the dog that frightened you has been killed by a lion." The literal meaning is that the frightening dog is gone, and it still stands; but the point of the verse is that the monk should be more frightened than ever — now a lion is on the loose. That is the suggestion, the unstated meaning.
  • [00:11:12] Another example: saying a village is on the river Ganges — true literally, but its full significance (that the village is a holy place) is conveyed only to someone who knows the river's sanctity.
  • [00:11:25] For Ānandavardhana, suggestion is distinct from both the straightforward meaning of words and from metaphor. Poetic language can keep its normal meaning while evoking rasa, whereas metaphor requires giving up the normal meaning. His illustration: when we say a village is "on" the Ganges, we don't imagine a floating village; we transfer the word "on" and understand the village is arrayed on the bank. By contrast, poetic suggestion leaves the literal meaning intact — it is something additional, conveyed only implicitly, which "shines above the parts of the poem like a woman's charm." It's crucial the poet can work indirectly, since direct statement would ruin the effect.

docs.title: The poet as inspired creator
docs.text:
• [00:12:34] Ānandavardhana adds that the meaning conveyed (at least to the skilled audience member) is one originally experienced by the poet. He recalls a story about Vālmīki, supposed author of the great epic Rāmāyaṇa: while bathing, the poet witnessed a hunter killing one of a pair of birds and heard the mate's plaintive cry, then cried out in a spontaneous verse that came from divine inspiration.
  • [00:13:05] This fits older ideas of the poet as a kind of religious intermediary, like the seers who pass down the Vedas. Poets were thought to benefit from a special unbidden illumination, distinguished from other visionaries because they actually set their visions down in words.
  • [00:13:28] In an echo of this, Ānandavardhana says the poet may choose any primary meaning he likes in his quest to evoke rasa by suggestion: "In the boundless world of literature, the author is sole creator God. The whole universe takes on whatever form he wills." The resulting poem becomes a means of conveying to the listener the rasa the poet originally felt — "to taste what he tasted."

docs.title: Rasa as meaning — and Abhinavagupta's universal emotion
docs.text:
• [00:13:59] For Ānandavardhana, rasa is really an effect of language, like the meaning of words — so it is called an artha ("meaning").
  • [00:14:11] But for one of his most important commentators, the 10th-century author Abhinavagupta, the rasa experienced and conveyed by the poet is an emotion that is universal in character. In the Vālmīki story, the dead bird and its mourning mate are simply the occasion that inspired the poet to experience a generalized sorrow.
  • [00:14:29] Likewise the audience member who experiences rasa is not having the everyday emotion: you are not in love with the rom-com characters, nor afraid for your own safety while watching Psycho. Though you feel romance and fear, these feelings are not directed at any particular object.
  • [00:14:55] This recalls Indian ideas of detachment and liberation — and it seems to have reminded Abhinavagupta of the same. By this period the eight canonical rasas had been joined by a ninth, Tranquility (śānta). For Ānandavardhana this is the rasa intended by no less a work than the Mahābhārata, which (like any good poem) has the production of rasa as its sole aim.
  • [00:15:28] Abhinavagupta links this rasa of tranquility to liberation: "This enjoyment of rasa is like the bliss that comes from realizing one's identity with the highest brahman, for it consists of repose in the bliss which is the true nature of one's own self."

docs.title: The actor's problem: feeling without being
docs.text:
• [00:15:42] What about the performers? Consider Anthony Perkins in Psycho: we know he's an actor, not really a murderer, yet we respond with fear and revulsion. How does he provoke this without having murder in his heart?
  • [00:16:14] Bharata already stated the actor's role is to express a psychological state without actually being in that same state. Later commentators dug deeper.
  • [00:16:30] One view — imitation: the actor merely imitates the character at the surface level (gesture and so on), inviting the audience to make an inference about the intended emotion. The sidelong glance signifies love, and skilled viewers read it as such, though aware he is acting. As one text nicely puts it: we think the actor is the character, but not that the actor is really the character.
  • [00:16:58] The objection: this inference would be fallacious. Recall inferring fire from smoke on a mountain — a bad inference if what we see is not really smoke but merely looks like it (low-hanging mist). Likewise, if the sidelong glance is only an empty imitation of how a lover would look, it's mistaken to infer that real love is present. Besides, the actor isn't an empty vessel going through the motions — he has his own psychological states, which must somehow connect to the aesthetic effect.
  • [00:17:39] The contrary view — total identification: the actor identifies completely with the character, recreating the character's emotion on stage. But this met skepticism too: how could the actor keep performing while genuinely in the throes of such powerful emotions?

docs.title: Mahima Bhaṭṭa's solution: aesthetic emotion is its own kind
docs.text:
• [00:18:02] In the 11th century, Mahima Bhaṭṭa made a convincing proposal that avoids these problems. Referring back to Bharata's statement that rasa is manifested because of the aesthetic features of a theatrical performance, he points out that such aesthetic features simply do not exist in everyday life. You see the actor on stage as a representation of the character, not as the character truly undergoing the drama's events.
  • [00:18:33] As he puts it, "since aesthetic elements are fictitious, whereas cause and effect are real" — the former pertaining to literature, the latter to the world — the two differ in both their natures and their objects.
  • [00:18:50] So when we see a terrorized victim in a horror movie, we do not make an erroneous inference from a fake representation to a real fear (like inferring real fire from fake smoke). Rather, we experience it as a properly aesthetic representation, and the inference we make is to a properly aesthetic emotion — which is precisely the savouring of rasa.

docs.title: What the debate shows
docs.text:
• [00:19:07] We can infer something from the whole debate: the ideas of the philosophical schools were not confined to those schools. The wider intelligentsia of Indian society knew them and applied them in new contexts. Just as the philosophers appropriated the apparatus of the Sanskrit grammarians, these literary aestheticians appropriated philosophical terms and concepts.
  • [00:19:42] Discussion of rasa took its initial cue from Bharata and was sustained for the better part of a millennium (and could have gone further). It grew steadily more sophisticated, with later authors keeping the Nāṭyaśāstra as touchstone while connecting it to ideals of detachment and liberation and notions from the philosophy of language.
  • [00:20:05] Whatever we make of their aesthetic judgments, these scholars were right about one thing: the richness and fruitfulness of the theories put forth by the Vedic schools.
  • [00:20:23] But — as intimated many times — some other philosophers were not so impressed. These same schools were subjected to searching critiques by the Buddhists and Jains, critiques philosophically rich in their own right. Next time, the curtain goes up on the last stage of the series: the so-called unorthodox traditions.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• rasa — literally "savour/juice"; the aesthetic response a performance is engineered to evoke. Derived from emotion but not identical to it; there are eight canonical kinds (erotic, comic, pathetic, furious, heroic, terrible, odious, marvellous), later nine.
  • Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra — "Treatise on Drama" (early centuries CE); foundational text of Indian aesthetics, with detailed instructions on theatre, gesture, poetry, and music.
  • bhāva — the eight "emotional dispositions" around which a drama is built; transitory emotions heighten them "like attendants surrounding a monarch."
  • Dattilam — early treatise on music, roughly contemporaneous with the Nāṭyaśāstra.
  • Kuntaka — later aesthetician; quoted on how a poem's natural charm overflows the reader's heart with rasa "the way a moonstone is liquefied by moonbeams."
  • connoisseur — the skilled audience member; rasa arises only for one proficient enough to sympathize with the actors and savour the performance "in the best possible taste."
  • Ānandavardhana — 9th-century Kashmiri theorist; developed dhvani (suggestion); held that one rasa must predominate, and that rasa is an artha (meaning, effect of language).
  • dhvani — "suggestion"; poetic language's special function of conveying an emotion implicitly rather than naming it; borrowed from the grammarian Bhartṛhari's term for meaning-bearing sound.
  • Bhartṛhari — grammarian who said uttered sounds are dhvani that make manifest linguistic meaning; the source Ānandavardhana adapts.
  • artha — "meaning"; Ānandavardhana's classification of rasa as an effect of language.
  • śleṣa — the pun / deliberate double meaning, prized in Sanskrit literature; a poorly-working one is a flaw that impedes rasa.
  • Mahima Bhaṭṭa — 11th-century aesthetician and critic of Ānandavardhana; argued aesthetic emotion is its own fictitious kind, so we infer not real feeling but a properly aesthetic emotion — the savouring of rasa.
  • jāti — melody types in Indian music theory, associated with particular moods/emotions.
  • Matanga — early music theorist who imported the poetic idea of suggestion (dhvani) into music.
  • Vālmīki / Rāmāyaṇa — supposed author of the great epic; his spontaneous, divinely inspired verse on a slain bird models the poet as inspired religious intermediary.
  • Abhinavagupta — 10th-century commentator; reads rasa as a universal, object-less emotion, linking the ninth rasa of Tranquility to liberation and identity with brahman.
  • Tranquility (śānta) — the ninth rasa added after Bharata's eight; the rasa Ānandavardhana sees as the aim of the Mahābhārata, tied to detachment and liberation.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 43 — "We Beg to Differ: The Buddhists and Jains"
docs.text:
← Ep 42
