🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:28 In brief: A roadmap to the two great heterodox traditions and how each answers the "problem of philosophical diversity" — the Buddhists (above all Nāgārjuna) by a skeptical refusal of dogma, the Jains by a syncretist "non-one-sidedness" — surveying the branching Buddhist schools (Abhidharma, Sarvāstivāda, Theravāda, Mahāyāna, Madhyamaka, Yogācāra) and the founding Jain philosophers, all of whom turned anti-dogmatism into innovations in logic and epistemology. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Gannery"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagajuna / Nagarduna"; Abhidharma ≈ "Abidharma"; Cārvāka ≈ "Chattvaka / Chavaka"; Pāyāsi ≈ "Paiasi"; Pudgalavāda ≈ "Pugala Vada"; Sarvāstivāda ≈ "Sarvasta Vadens / Sabastivada"; Buddhaghosa ≈ "Buda Gosa"; Visuddhimagga ≈ "Visudimanga"; Vasubandhu ≈ "Vasubandu / Vazubandu"; Abhidharmakośa ≈ "Abidharma Kosha"; Saṃghabhadra ≈ "Samgabhadra"; Madhyamaka ≈ "Madyamaka"; Yogācāra ≈ "Yoga Chara"; Dignāga ≈ "Dignaga"; Dharmakīrti ≈ "Dharma Kirti / Dharma Kiyati"; Fa Xian ≈ "Fa Hecien"; Xuanzang ≈ "Suan Sang"; Nālandā ≈ "Naranda"; Kundakunda ≈ "Kunda Kunda"; Umāsvāti ≈ "Umaswati"; Siddhasena Divākara ≈ "Siddacena di Vakara"; Prabhācandra ≈ "Prabha Chandra"; Haribhadra Sūri ≈ "Haribadra Suri"; Prākrit ≈ "Pracrit").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Nāgārjuna — 2nd-c. CE Buddhist, founder of Madhyamaka ("Middle Way") and the skeptical response to diversity; "philosophy of emptiness" [00:01:46].
  • The Jain founders — Kundakunda, Umāsvāti, and Siddhasena Divākara, the syncretist response [00:17:08].
  • Vasubandhu — c. 400 CE; wrote the Abhidharmakośa, then converted to Mahāyāna [00:08:14].
  • The Abhidharma & the rival vādas — Pudgalavāda, Sarvāstivāda, Theravāda; systematic accounts of Buddhist doctrine [00:03:01].
  • Dignāga & Dharmakīrti — the Yogācāra logicians (c. 500 and c. 600 CE) who set the agenda for all later Buddhist philosophy [00:14:37].

docs.title: The problem of philosophical diversity — and two ways to answer it
docs.text:
• [00:00:35] We've now seen a variety of philosophical systems arise in ancient India, each built around a core text of aphoristic verses, or sūtras. This great plurality of doctrinal opinion is India's strength — but it is also a philosophical problem in its own right. For even though these systems emerged out of the same Vedic culture, they adopted contradictory positions on essentially every key issue: self, mind, and world; human aspiration and human ability.
  • [00:01:09] The two traditions of this chapter — Buddhists and Jains — each offer a response to this problem of diversity, i.e. to the bare availability of opposing standpoints. One response is the skeptic's: our chronic inability to agree on philosophical questions shows that no one answer is justified. The other is the syncretist's: every position contains at least a grain of truth, so we should accept all of them — but only conditionally.
  • [00:01:43] In India the skeptical road was taken by a school of Buddhism, most notably by Nāgārjuna; the syncretist road was the Jains' preferred option. Both ways of rejecting dogmatism drove innovations in epistemology and logic, as each tradition strained to avoid the trap of self-refutation.

docs.title: Setting the scene: Sanskrit, the śramaṇa movements, and intellectual context
docs.text:
• [00:02:01] Nāgārjuna lived in the 2nd century CE, a critical moment for both Buddhism and Jainism. In this period thinkers of both traditions began writing in Sanskrit, having previously used Pāli (the Buddhists) and Prākrit (the Jains). Adopting Sanskrit let the śramaṇa (renouncer) movements meet their Vedic opponents on the same linguistic ground — and at the same time argue with one another.
  • [00:02:32] Buddhist philosophy is often told as if it emerged in an intellectual vacuum. But just as the Brahminical schools refined their ideas in response to Buddhist critique, we must factor in the broader intellectual context to understand Buddhist or Jain thought. Having already surveyed the orthodox systems, we are well placed to do this.

docs.title: The branching of Buddhism: the vādas and the Abhidharma
docs.text:
• [00:02:55] We pick up the story after the death of Aśoka, the emperor who promoted Buddhist thought; he reigned in the 3rd century BCE, roughly when Buddhism underwent the first of several splits into rival intellectual schools called vādas. These set out systematic accounts of what they took to be Buddhist doctrine in seven canonical texts, each called an Abhidharma.
  • [00:03:25] Take the central Buddhist tenet that there is no eternal, unchanging self or soul. We readily associate "no self" with Buddhism — yet mental reality is in some sense affirmed, which is why Buddhist texts react critically against the frank materialism of the Cārvāka forerunner Pāyāsi. The truth about the self lies somewhere in between: we are neither identical to our bodies (as Cārvāka would have it), nor are we souls cut off from everything else (a view close to the Jain theory of the self).
  • [00:04:00] So the Buddha was at least as concerned to position himself relative to other dissident groups as to critique Brahminical hegemony. To convey his own view he used similes: a person is not like the single thread running through a necklace of pearls, but like the flowing of a river or the flickering of a candle flame.
  • [00:04:24] Pressing that last image: liberation from bodily existence is nirvāṇa, a "blowing out" of the flame. And there is a fuel that keeps the flame burning — in a human being that fuel is craving, attachment, and false desire.

docs.title: "Neither the same nor another": Nāgasena and King Menander
docs.text:
• [00:04:46] The Buddha's ideas about the self were avidly explored in later generations, as in one of the earliest works of philosophical Buddhism — a Pāli text describing the encounter between the Buddhist monk Nāgasena and the king Menander.
  • [00:05:03] Menander asks: he who is reborn, is he the same person or another? Nāgasena replies: "neither the same nor another." Asked for an illustration, he offers the milk that turns to curds, then butter, then ghee: it would be wrong to call the ghee, butter, and curds the same as the milk — yet they came from it, so neither is it right to call them something else.
  • [00:05:34] The rival vādas tried to work out the theory behind such metaphors. Back in episode nine we met the Pudgalavāda, distinguished by their willingness to admit there is in some sense an enduring person or self that changes over time. Another group, the Sarvāstivāda, rejected this — yet were themselves reluctant to say that nothing is real apart from the fleeting, momentary dharmas that make up an aggregate thing. Partly to explain how there can be karmic effects of past deeds, the Sarvāstivāda proposed that past and future things are real or existent ("Sarvāstivāda" = "the doctrine that everything exists").

docs.title: How the Buddhists wrote: sūtra vs. Abhidharma, and "skillful means"
docs.text:
• [00:06:14] With the Abhidharma writings we see the Buddhists adopting writing strategies different from the Brahminical schools. The Buddhists did not write sūtra texts — the compressed, difficult works needing explanatory commentary. Confusingly, the early Buddhists do use the term sūtra (Pāli sutta), but with a different meaning: the recorded sayings of the Buddha himself, set down in the Nikāyas.
  • [00:06:50] The schools tried to get beneath these explicit teachings to reveal the deep unity of philosophical truth within. One standard exegetical move: distinguish those utterances of the Buddha that directly express the deep truth from those whose meaning needs drawing out.
  • [00:07:11] This becomes a running theme in later Buddhism. The Mahāyāna especially deployed the notion of skillful means: as an ideal teacher, the Buddha often said things that are not strictly true in order to help listeners advance along the path to liberation.

docs.title: Theravāda and Sarvāstivāda: the Abhidharma's afterlives
docs.text:
• [00:07:29] The Abhidharma teachings had varying afterlives. Sarvāstivāda became dominant in northern India and Central Asia; Theravāda developed on the island of Ceylon (Sri Lanka).
  • [00:07:43] Theravāda's most remarkable ancient representative lived in the 5th century CE: Buddhaghosa, author of a definitive unified commentary on both the Nikāyas and the canonical Abhidharma treatises. His work, the Visuddhimagga ("Path to Purity"), still exercises great influence in Sri Lanka, Burma, and Thailand, where Theravāda is alive and well.
  • [00:08:11] The Sarvāstivāda branch had even wider influence. Its key philosopher was Vasubandhu (c. 400 CE), who wrote a pivotal digest of Abhidharma theory, the Abhidharmakośa, plus an important analysis of the five factors that, according to the Buddha, constitute the psychophysical "river" that is a human being.

docs.title: Vasubandhu's conversion and the rise of Mahāyāna
docs.text:
• [00:08:34] Vasubandhu also belongs to the next chapter: the spread of Mahāyāna ("Great Vehicle") Buddhism — so called because its proponents wished to distinguish it from what they considered less complete accounts of the Buddha's teaching, condescendingly tagging rivals (including the Theravāda) Hīnayāna, "Lesser Vehicle."
  • [00:08:56] Having begun as a Sarvāstivāda proponent, Vasubandhu was apparently persuaded by his brother Asaṅga to switch to Mahāyāna. He went on to write some of its fundamental texts — and even a self-commentary on his own Abhidharmakośa, now from the Mahāyāna perspective. That was enough to annoy another Abhidharma scholar, Saṃghabhadra, into writing a rival commentary defending Vasubandhu's old view against his new one. Among Vasubandhu's new Mahāyāna works, his Twenty Verses and Thirty Verses are works of immense philosophical accomplishment.
  • [00:09:37] Mahāyāna had in fact already emerged well before Vasubandhu's time — sometime around the last century BCE or first century CE. Its claimed superiority turned on pursuing a higher ethical goal. Where others were content to become enlightened and reach the status of an arhat, the Mahāyāna emphasized the more exalted role of the bodhisattva (their school was originally also called the Bodhisattvayāna).
  • [00:10:10] A bodhisattva is more than an arhat or even a Buddha, because he goes beyond his own perfect liberation and wisdom by seeking to bring others to that same state. So the Mahāyāna placed other-regarding ethics at the center of Buddhism — recognizing that great sacrifice and patience are required, and speaking of needing millions of world-cycles to reach the bodhisattva level.

docs.title: Mahāyāna's expanded canon and its many Buddhas
docs.text:
• [00:10:34] Mahāyāna is also distinguished by the texts it accepts as authoritative. It treats a number of new sūtras as genuine records of the Buddha's sayings, despite their becoming available only centuries after his death — they had been hidden in the meantime, or posthumously divulged by the Buddha in dreams.
  • [00:10:56] More generally, Mahāyāna thinks of the Buddha less as an individual person and more as a functional role: the Buddha teaches at all times and adopts many guises, and there has been more than one Buddha — indeed as many as the grains of sand in the Ganges.

docs.title: Two Mahāyāna sub-schools: Madhyamaka and Yogācāra
docs.text:
• [00:11:14] So far Buddhist history is less a single flowing river than a set of branching tributaries — and this continues with Mahāyāna, which itself split into two main sub-schools. One is Madhyamaka, the "philosophy of the Middle Way," founded by Nāgārjuna. Nāgārjuna's philosophy went on to great things in Tibet, China, and Japan, and is the ultimate source of Zen Buddhism.
  • [00:11:46] It is tempting to think of Buddhism as having a first Indian phase and a later phase where it gradually disappeared from India even as its ideas spread across Asia — but the waters are muddier than that. Sri Lanka hosted Theravāda from early on, and some of our earliest sources for various strands of Buddhism (including Madhyamaka) are in Chinese. We owe valuable information about Indian Buddhism to two Chinese travelers, Fa Xian in the 5th century and Xuanzang in the 7th — and there are even cases where Buddhist works were written in Chinese and translated into Sanskrit.
  • [00:12:21] Nāgārjuna lived around 150–200 CE, making him a contemporary of Gautama, author/compiler of the Nyāya-Sūtra. His most famous works are the Verses on the Middle Way and the Refutation of My Opponents, in which he tries to undermine the Nyāya theory of knowledge and answers Nyāya criticisms of his own work.
  • [00:12:47] His central thesis — though, as we'll see, even calling it a "thesis" is problematic — is that all human conceptual schemes and all philosophical systems are empty, or null. Hence his teaching is the philosophy of emptiness. He is a severe critic of the pramāṇa method of rational inquiry, urging instead the use of reason to expose inconsistencies within the fabric of one's own conceptions, never mind those of rivals.
  • [00:13:24] Why call this radical brand "Middle Way"? Because it neither embraces the permanence of things nor denies that anything is real. Just as Nāgasena told Menander that things are neither the same nor different over time, Nāgārjuna says things are neither simply independently existent nor non-existent — rather they are real insofar as they depend on other things. To be is to be relative. (If that sounds mysterious, a Buddhist would advise you not to let it worry you.)
  • [00:14:06] The other Mahāyāna sub-school is Yogācāra, first set out by the brothers Asaṅga and Vasubandhu. It is not so much opposed to Madhyamaka as complementary, focusing on psychological and spiritual issues. It is not to be confused with the Yoga branch of Brahminical thought; it is "Yogācāra" because it emphasizes spiritual practices, yoga, like meditation.
  • [00:14:30] Around 500 CE, about a century after Vasubandhu, Yogācāra found its most brilliant exponent in Dignāga, whose ideas in logic and epistemology — and their criticism and revision at the hands of Dharmakīrti (about 600 CE) — we'll examine later. That's about as far as this series goes, but these figures set the agenda for all subsequent Buddhist philosophy: later thinkers tend to write either commentaries on Dharmakīrti or manuals presenting his thought in more manageable form.

docs.title: Scholasticism and its institutions: stūpas, monasteries, and Nālandā
docs.text:
• [00:15:13] This bewildering multiplication of schools and textual traditions may recall the scholasticism of later Islamic or Latin medieval thought — all the more so since the social and institutional context was not dissimilar. Just as the Latin Church and secular princes fostered the European universities, and Muslim rulers and viziers built the madrasa system, so Buddhism received intermittent but often substantial support from various Indian rulers.
  • [00:15:42] Generous laypersons did more than put food in monks' begging bowls. Their lavish gifts made it possible to build spectacular stūpas (Buddhist shrines), to carve and decorate whole complexes of caves for monastic study, and to found such centers of learning as Nālandā, a huge monastery often described as playing the role of a university.
  • [00:16:11] You might have wondered how Buddhist scholars could spend decades studying there, given the relative simplicity of the Buddha's original teaching. But considering the mass of writings produced by all these groups — and the fact that a competent Buddhist philosopher needed a detailed understanding of the Brahminical schools too, in order to refute them — you begin to believe that "one or two reincarnations might be needed" to explain a truly accomplished thinker like Vasubandhu or Dharmakīrti.

docs.title: The Jains: inclusivism and the doctrine of non-one-sidedness
docs.text:
• [00:16:43] Happily, things are more straightforward with the Jains. As mentioned in episode 15, Jainism split into two branches — the Śvetāmbara and Digambara ("white-clad" and "sky-clad") — but we can ignore this, because the philosophers discussed would be read and accepted by both sides. The three founding figures of Jain philosophy are Kundakunda, Umāsvāti, and Siddhasena Divākara, who may have lived in the 3rd, 4th, and 5th centuries respectively, though their dates are uncertain.
  • [00:17:20] No less than the Buddhists, the Jains were deeply knowledgeable about other systems, and their descriptions tend to be faithful — which makes them a useful source for otherwise-lost ideas. We could not say nearly so much about Cārvāka without the later Jain philosopher Prabhācandra. They were also sophisticated doxographers: the 8th-century Haribhadra Sūri composed a Compendium of the Six Systems — which here means Buddhism and Jainism plus four Hindu systems, not the six Brahminical schools. The only thing Haribhadra regards as beyond the pale is Cārvāka naturalism.
  • [00:18:01] There's a good reason for the Jains' interest in others' ideas, and it is not merely "knowing one's enemy" — actually, Jains don't really have enemies. Their philosophy is justly celebrated for its inclusivism, codified in a theory of the non-one-sidedness of reality, and in the idea that truth is always approached from a specific point of view.
  • [00:18:27] Kundakunda sums up Jain pluralism in a dense remark: all substances are non-different from the substantial viewpoint, but again different from the modificational viewpoint, because of the individual modification pervading each for the time being; "according to some modification or other, it is stated that a substance exists, does not exist, is indescribable, is both, or otherwise." (The elements of this — especially the different metaphysical standpoints — get unpacked in later episodes.)
  • [00:19:04] Whereas Kundakunda wrote exclusively in Prākrit, Umāsvāti was the first Jain philosopher to compose in Sanskrit — calling his great treatise a sūtra, "the sūtra on what there is." Almost every significant later Jain philosopher would write a commentary on this book, using the chance to defend their own views and attack their foes'. So maybe Jains do have enemies after all — certainly they were willing to defend their perspectivalism against critics.
  • [00:19:40] We should bear this in mind in considering how Jain epistemology relates to the rest of their tradition. It's often assumed this epistemology is an intellectual version of ahiṃsā: just as the Jain observes strict non-violence in practical matters, so in theory the Jain embraces tolerance and harmony. That reading may not be wholly wrong, but it seems too simple — for the Jains were every bit as ready as the Brahminical thinkers and the Buddhists to engage in that quintessential ancient Indian practice, debate.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text: • [00:20:14] Next time we begin to look at Nāgārjuna — a thinker whose works are full of insight and dense argument, "which is pretty ironic given that his signature doctrine is that everything is empty."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• the problem of diversity — that India's many systems contradict one another on every key issue; the Buddhists answer it as skeptics ("no answer is justified"), the Jains as syncretists ("every view holds a conditional grain of truth").
  • vāda — an intellectual school/sect of Buddhism; the post-Aśoka splits produced rival vādas with their own canonical accounts of doctrine.
  • Abhidharma — the seven canonical texts giving systematic accounts of Buddhist doctrine; Buddhists wrote these instead of cryptic sūtras.
  • dharmas — the fleeting, momentary constituents that make up an aggregate thing (e.g. a person).
  • Pudgalavāda / Sarvāstivāda — rival vādas: the former admits an enduring "person/self"; the latter denies it but holds that past and future things are real, to ground karmic effects.
  • nirvāṇa — the "blowing out" of the flame of bodily existence; its fuel is craving, attachment, and false desire.
  • Nāgasena & Menander — Pāli dialogue: the reborn person is "neither the same nor another," illustrated by milk → curds → butter → ghee.
  • Theravāda / Buddhaghosa / Visuddhimagga — the Ceylon (Sri Lanka) school; Buddhaghosa (5th c. CE) wrote the Visuddhimagga ("Path to Purity"), still influential in Sri Lanka, Burma, Thailand.
  • Vasubandhu — c. 400 CE; wrote the Abhidharmakośa as a Sarvāstivādin, then converted to Mahāyāna (urged by his brother Asaṅga) and wrote the Twenty Verses and Thirty Verses.
  • Mahāyāna ("Great Vehicle") — emerged c. 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE; centers other-regarding ethics on the bodhisattva (who exceeds the arhat by bringing others to liberation); dismisses rivals as Hīnayāna; accepts a wider sūtra canon and treats the Buddha as a recurring functional role.
  • skillful means — the Mahāyāna idea that the Buddha, an ideal teacher, sometimes says things not strictly true to move listeners toward liberation.
  • Madhyamaka / emptiness — Nāgārjuna's "Middle Way": all conceptual schemes are empty/null; things are neither independently existent nor non-existent but real insofar as they depend on others — "to be is to be relative." Source of Zen.
  • Yogācāra — Mahāyāna sub-school of Asaṅga & Vasubandhu, complementary to Madhyamaka, stressing meditation (yoga); its logicians Dignāga (c. 500 CE) and Dharmakīrti (c. 600 CE) set the agenda for later Buddhist philosophy.
  • pramāṇa — means/method of rational inquiry; Nāgārjuna is its severe critic, preferring to expose internal inconsistencies.
  • Nālandā / stūpa — the great monastic "university" funded by rulers and lay donors; stūpas are Buddhist shrines.
  • Jain non-one-sidedness (perspectivalism) — reality has many aspects, truth is always approached from a viewpoint; expressed by Kundakunda's "substantial vs. modificational" standpoints.
  • Jain founders — Kundakunda (Prākrit), Umāsvāti (first to use Sanskrit; his sūtra drew commentary from nearly every later Jain), Siddhasena Divākara.
  • ahiṃsā — non-violence; often read as the practical analogue of Jain epistemic tolerance — though the Jains debated as fiercely as anyone.
  • Cārvāka doxography — Jain sources (e.g. Prabhācandra, and Haribhadra Sūri's Compendium of the Six Systems) preserve much of the otherwise-lost Cārvāka materialism they reject.

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:21:21 In brief: Nāgārjuna's doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā): nothing has svabhāva, an independent self-nature; everything exists only relative to other things ("dependent origination"). Adamson lays out the Madhyamaka "middle way" between eternalism and nihilism, the prasaṅga method of arguing by contradiction (causation, the four options for origination), the two-truths distinction, three rival interpretations of what Nāgārjuna is up to, and his defence against the charge that emptiness is self-refuting. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Gennary"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagadjuna/Nagajuna/Nagatrina/Nagadruna/Gagena"; Madhyamaka ≈ "Madyamaka"; śūnya/śūnyatā ≈ "Shunya"; svabhāva ≈ "swavava"; Abhidharma ≈ "Abidharma/Abidodama"; prasaṅga ≈ "prasanga"; Vaiśeṣika ≈ "Vaishika/Vaishishika"; Nyāya ≈ "Niaya"; Gautama ≈ "Kautima"; saṃvṛtisat ≈ "samvritisat"; paramārthasat ≈ "paramata sat"; Candrakīrti ≈ "Chandrakirti"; Jan Westerhoff ≈ "Jan Vestohof"; Bimal Matilal ≈ "Bimal Matel"; "Paint It Black" ≈ "Painted Black").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Nāgārjuna — 2nd-century CE Buddhist, founder of the Madhyamaka or "middle-way" philosophy; revered in Tibet as "the second Buddha" [00:01:28].
  • Verses on the Middle Way (Mūlamadhyamakakārikā) — his central work, where dependent origination is identified with emptiness [00:01:51].
  • Refutation of My Opponents — his second book, answering the charge that emptiness is self-refuting [00:17:48].
  • The Abhidharma school — fellow Buddhists, Nāgārjuna's main targets, who analyse experience into momentary dharmas [00:03:15].
  • Candrakīrti — his 6th-century commentator, source of the "conventionalist" reading carried on in Tibet [00:14:13].

docs.title: The red door: intrinsic vs. dependent properties
docs.text:
• [00:00:32] The episode opens with the Rolling Stones' "Paint It Black" — "I see a red door and I want it painted black." Mick Jagger's lyric reports his mental state, but it also tells us something about how things outside us relate to our mental states. He'd like the door black; it "stubbornly insists on being a jolly red."
  • [00:01:08] The commonsense view: the door and its properties are independent of us — of our desires and attitudes — and indeed independent of anything else. The door is red in itself, just as it is a door in itself, and our perception and knowledge must be true to those independent, intrinsic facts.
  • [00:01:24] The 2nd-century CE Buddhist Nāgārjuna would not say that. He challenges the very assumption that there are such independent, freestanding things and properties. Instead, all things are marked by dependent origination — which means that they are empty. This is the core teaching of Madhyamaka, the "middle-way" Buddhist philosophy.
  • [00:01:51] As he puts it in the Verses on the Middle Way: "whatever is dependently co-arisen, that is explained to be emptiness; that, being a dependent designation, is itself the middle way."

docs.title: A controversial teaching with an enormous afterlife
docs.text:
• [00:02:09] Nāgārjuna's emptiness teaching is one of the most intriguing — and controversial — developments in ancient Indian thought. It has been read as mystical and skeptical, as metaphysical and anti-metaphysical, as admirably consistent and deliberately contradictory, and compared to thinkers from the ancient skeptics to Kant, Heidegger and Wittgenstein.
  • [00:02:26] Its historical influence was enormous. Madhyamaka enjoyed only limited success in India but flourished elsewhere in East Asia, especially Tibet, where Nāgārjuna is revered as the "second Buddha."

docs.title: Who Nāgārjuna is really arguing with
docs.text:
• [00:02:45] His writings are powerfully opposed to the Vedic schools of recent episodes — he argues vociferously with Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika, among others. He seems to have been a contemporary of Gautama (the Nyāya founder): there are passages in the Nyāya-Sūtra that look as if they have Nāgārjuna in mind, and passages where Nāgārjuna seems to attack Gautama.
  • [00:03:07] Yet his principal opponents are actually other Buddhists, mainly the Abhidharma school. One way to see his project: he takes earlier Buddhist skeptical tendencies further than other Buddhists were willing to go — "about as far as anyone could imagine going."
  • [00:03:33] It was standard Buddhist fare to reject the reality of certain entities — especially selves, but also wholes, the classic example being the chariot that is nothing more than its parts. The Buddha sometimes seemed to admit such things exist (e.g. warning that persons survive into the next life to reap the karmic fruits of their actions), but most Buddhists treated this as a concession to conventional thinking, made to teach those who haven't yet grasped the deeper truths.
  • [00:04:01] Nāgārjuna makes no such concession. He convicts all apparent reality of being empty, or śūnya. And we'd better get the idea right, given his own warning: "emptiness wrongly conceived can ruin a slow-witted person" — like a mishandled snake or a poorly executed incantation.

docs.title: Emptiness = the denial of svabhāva (self-nature)
docs.text:
• [00:04:30] With emptiness, Nāgārjuna is clearly contributing to metaphysics. To say an object is empty means denying that it has what he calls svabhāva, or self-nature — and that, in turn, means denying that it is independent of other things.
  • [00:04:46] Back to the red door. It seems the redness is intrinsic to it: Jagger's viewing the door doesn't make it red, nor does anything else — it's just red in itself. By contrast, some properties arise only through a relation, e.g. the door's being six feet away from a depressed rock star.
  • [00:05:04] In the Verses on the Middle Way, Nāgārjuna works to undermine this contrast between intrinsic and relative properties. He runs through a wide range of phenomena — whole and part, cause and effect, sensation and the sensed, motion and the moved — and shows that in every case what seems to have a fixed essence is in fact relative.
  • [00:05:34] When Jagger sees the red door, he depends on the door in order to be someone who sees, and the red door depends on him in order to be seen. "Sensation is like a child, born of two parents." This is Nāgārjuna's reading of the Buddha's famous teaching that everything in the world is interdependent — and he sees rival Buddhist schools as insufficiently committed to it, insufficiently careful to avoid essentialism.

docs.title: Against the Abhidharma dharmas — and Vaiśeṣika substance
docs.text:
• [00:05:58] Contrast his view with Abhidharma Buddhist theories that invoked so-called dharmas — analysing all experience into fleeting individual processes. Where an Abhidharmika might say a dharma (e.g. a moment of conscious awareness) has the property of arising, Nāgārjuna says this makes no sense.
  • [00:06:22] Arising cannot have any intrinsic reality that would let it ground the occurrence of the moment of consciousness — because the arising of that moment would itself have to arise or be produced, leading to a regress. So insofar as some Abhidharma Buddhists describe dharmas as having independent self-nature, their theory falls prey to his battery of skeptical arguments.
  • [00:06:45] The same arguments also destroy a system like Vaiśeṣika, which envisions an independently existing substance bearing intrinsic properties.

docs.title: Not nihilism: the middle way between eternalism and annihilationism
docs.text:
• [00:06:55] What does the theory of emptiness leave behind? Some say, obviously, nothing — a few modern scholars and many ancient thinkers associated Nāgārjuna with nihilism, the view that nothing is real. But this looks more like polemical criticism than plausible interpretation: his philosophy styles itself a middle way, and as the Nāgārjuna expert Jan Westerhoff notes, "it's hard to imagine a more extreme and less moderate view than nihilism."
  • [00:07:33] Instead he charts a course between two extremes prevalent in his day (and the Buddha's): eternalism and annihilationism. The eternalist is an essentialist who says each object exists independently, with an immutable essence. The annihilationist says objects don't exist at all.
  • [00:07:56] Nāgārjuna's middle position: objects do exist, but not by subsisting in themselves. The nature and subsistence of each thing is determined by its relations to other objects. So redness is empty — not because there's no such thing as red, but because redness always depends on other things, e.g. the door that has the red colour.

docs.title: Śūnya = zero: a suggestive analogy
docs.text:
• [00:08:14] The Sanskrit word for empty, śūnya, has another technical sense: early Indian mathematicians used it as the name for zero. The point of zero in their counting system was to be a place marker — in 307, the zero shows the tens place is empty.
  • [00:08:44] There's probably no actual historical connection between this mathematical use and Nāgārjuna's philosophical one, but there is an analogy. As Bimal Matilal remarked, in Madhyamaka, objects are like zeros: they have a value — a claim to reality — only in relation to something else or to the position they occupy in a complex, and so have no absolute value.

docs.title: Words and concepts are empty too — the prasaṅga method
docs.text:
• [00:09:04] One might object: redness can't be like zero, because it needs an intrinsic essence to secure the meaning of the word "red," which we'd refer to whenever we use it. But Nāgārjuna insists that our words, concepts and philosophical theories have no independent meaning, any more than objects have independent metaphysical properties. The word "redness" plays a role in our language, but there's no distinct thing in the world to which it refers.
  • [00:09:45] To unmask the emptiness of words and concepts, he uses a style of argument called prasaṅga: showing that a given concept would imply a contradiction if it had independent reality or essence.
  • [00:09:56] His worked example is the round square. "This round square is round" obviously involves a contradiction (a square being round). But I can't deny "a round square is round" either — if anything is a round square, it's surely round. The upshot: the round square is not anything at all; the phrase has no reference and no real meaning, since granting its reality lands us in absurdity. Nāgārjuna is a master at applying this to apparently innocuous cases and showing they too are empty.

docs.title: Causation: cause vs. causal condition
docs.text:
• [00:10:34] A nice example is causation. He distinguishes a cause as such (that from which something originates) from a mere causal condition (that whose occurrence is necessary for something's existence).
  • [00:10:57] The causal-condition idea has an impeccable Buddhist pedigree, appearing in the four noble truths: there is suffering; suffering has a cause; removing the causes of suffering ends it; and there is an eightfold path for removing those causes.
  • [00:11:13] Here the cause of suffering — attachment — is a condition: something whose continuing presence is necessary for the continuing existence of its effect. So long as you stay attached to things, you continue to suffer.
  • [00:11:28] This gives another way to express emptiness: when Nāgārjuna says all things are empty, he means all things have causal conditions on which they depend. The existence of each thing depends on something else; nothing is self-sufficient.

docs.title: The four options for origination (the pot and the potter)
docs.text:
• [00:11:49] An opponent replies that this is obviously false: once a potter makes a pot, the pot is self-sufficient; many things originate from their causes and then have independent existence. The Verses on the Middle Way opens with a prasaṅga attack showing that the notion of origination itself leads to contradictions, via four options:
  • [00:12:13] (1) Self-causation — a thing originates spontaneously, causing itself. But it would have to exist first in order to bring itself into being. Absurd.
  • [00:12:29] (2) Other-causation — a thing is entirely originated by something else, as the potter makes the pot. But on reflection the pot's continued existence does not depend on the potter: the potter can die without the pot vanishing. So something else — e.g. the clay — must explain its persistence.
  • [00:12:56] (3) Both — caused by itself and by something else. No: then one part of the thing depends on itself and another on something else, and we just re-apply the previous arguments against self- and other-causation to those two parts.
  • [00:13:24] (4) Neither — things originate neither from themselves nor from others. No again: this amounts to admitting the thing is permanent or eternal rather than originated, giving up the idea that it was caused at all. (Adamson notes Nāgārjuna "is much better at saying no than at saying yes.")
  • [00:13:43] The upshot: there's no option on which causal origination makes sense; as a concept it fares no better than the round square.

docs.title: But everyday talk may survive — the two truths
docs.text:
• [00:13:55] It doesn't follow that Nāgārjuna wants to ban all talk of origination. A predominant interpretation — beginning with his 6th-century commentator Candrakīrti and carried on in the later Tibetan tradition — claims he's only showing that our concepts are conventional: fit for communication and practical purposes. The Madhyamaka critique only bites when these concepts are deployed in philosophical theories about how things really are in themselves. (Hence the Wittgenstein comparison: there's no problem saying "the potter makes the pot" — only when "making" is taken as an aspect of ultimate reality or a theory of causation do we run into trouble.)
  • [00:15:01] This is why Madhyamaka puts so much weight on a distinction between two truths: truth as it seems in the conventional world of everyday transaction (saṃvṛtisat), and truth as things are in reality, "how things really are in themselves quite apart from their utility to us" (paramārthasat).
  • [00:15:26] This distinction had roots in early attempts to dispel apparent contradictions within the Buddha's own teaching; here it is turned to a more ambitious philosophical — or better, anti-philosophical — purpose.

docs.title: Three ways to read Nāgārjuna
docs.text:
• [00:15:37] (a) The conventionalist reading: we cannot get at things in themselves — either because the very notion of an ultimate reality is incoherent, or because we simply lack the cognitive resources to reach things as they truly are.
  • [00:15:55] (b) The metaphysical reading (the one suggested earlier in the episode): Nāgārjuna does have a metaphysical view — that reality is always relative. Conventional concepts and language misrepresent things by treating them as independent and intrinsically propertied; the theory of emptiness lets us see things rightly by exposing their interdependence.
  • [00:16:23] (c) The thorough-going skeptic reading: like his near-contemporary the Greek skeptic Sextus Empiricus, his arguments are neither negative nor positive but dialectical and reactive — solely aimed at undermining other philosophers' concepts and theories, never advancing a position of his own. This fits his famous remark that his teaching involves the abandonment of all views.

docs.title: The self-refutation test and the Refutation of My Opponents
docs.text:
• [00:17:06] A good way to test these readings — and Nāgārjuna as a philosopher — is to ask whether Madhyamaka collapses into self-refutation. If all statements are empty of content or reference, the thesis seems to undermine itself: if "all statements are empty" is itself empty, it can be dismissed; if it's not empty, it's a counterexample to its own claim.
  • [00:17:42] Critics must have pressed this in his lifetime — whether Gautama, the Naiyāyika, or the Abhidharma Buddhists. To answer, he wrote a second book, "winningly entitled" the Refutation of My Opponents, defusing the charge that the middle way is self-defeating.
  • [00:17:59] To the accusation that his arguments achieve nothing if empty, he replies that the chariot too is empty, but it can still carry wood. And what would it mean for the emptiness thesis to be itself empty? His answer: he in fact has no thesis, no philosophical theory — at least not of the same type as his rivals' systems. He offers two analogies to show the difference between his empty statements and the statements that constitute a philosophical system.

docs.title: The silence analogy and the artificial-person analogy
docs.text:
• [00:18:30] The silence analogy. The opponent says the doctrine of emptiness is like someone who shouts "Silence!" — succeeding only in making a noise, defeating his own purpose. Nāgārjuna turns it around: if there is silence, we cannot announce it; the fact of silence can't be stated out loud. Likewise, if all the concepts we use to make the world intelligible are devoid of meaning, this cannot be announced without using those very empty concepts. But that it can't be announced doesn't mean it isn't true — just as there can be silence even though no one can observe it without falsifying the very observation they're making.
  • [00:19:22] The artificial-person analogy. The middle-way philosophy is like the action of one artificial person preventing the actions of another, or a magician doing magic to counter another magician's spell. The point: even though "all theses are empty" is itself empty and so cannot state anything, it can still show or reveal that this is the true state of affairs. Nāgārjuna doesn't fight fire with fire; he fights empty statements with more empty statements.

docs.title: Emptiness is not itself a thing
docs.text:
• [00:19:57] These statements do not urge us to make emptiness into a kind of metaphysical reality. To claim the door's redness is empty is not to say there is "emptiness" there instead of redness — it's to correct a mistake about the redness, namely the error of believing redness has independent existence.
  • [00:20:16] So the middle way is not self-refuting. Nāgārjuna's words imply something that cannot be stated — that the very words he is using are without foundation. This isn't just another move in the language game but an ironic intervention within it. Like the snake he warned about, he's "clearly a pretty slippery character."

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:20:34] To get a better hold on him, the next episode examines a specific application of his prasaṅga method: his critique of motion and change, showing that a person sprinting along a track is "in fact running on empty."
  • [00:20:53] These arguments have often been compared to the paradoxes of Zeno — and the discussion will be ready "just as soon as you're done waiting for half the time between this and the next episode to elapse, then half the remaining time," and so on. Maybe Jagger was right that you can't get no satisfaction — but if you try, you can get what you need: the next installment.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Nāgārjuna — 2nd-c. CE Buddhist; founder of Madhyamaka; argues that nothing has independent self-nature, so all things are empty; revered in Tibet as the "second Buddha."
  • śūnyatā / śūnya (emptiness / empty) — the thesis that nothing has independent existence; an object's nature is fixed only by its relations to other things. (Pun: śūnya is also the mathematicians' word for zero, a mere place-marker with value only relative to position.)
  • svabhāva (self-nature) — intrinsic, independent reality; to be empty is precisely to lack svabhāva.
  • dependent origination — the Buddha's teaching that everything is interdependent; Nāgārjuna identifies it with emptiness ("sensation is a child of two parents").
  • Madhyamaka (the middle way) — Nāgārjuna's school, steering between eternalism (essentialism: things have immutable independent essences) and annihilationism / nihilism (nothing exists at all).
  • Verses on the Middle Way — his central work; surveys whole/part, cause/effect, sensation/sensed, motion/moved, and opens with the four-options attack on origination.
  • Refutation of My Opponents — his second book, answering the self-refutation charge ("the chariot too is empty, but it can carry wood").
  • prasaṅga — his method of arguing by reductio: a concept implies a contradiction if it has independent reality (the round square; the four options for origination).
  • Abhidharma — rival Buddhist school analysing experience into momentary dharmas; Nāgārjuna's chief target, since treating a dharma's "arising" as real triggers a regress.
  • two truths — saṃvṛtisat & paramārthasat — conventional truth (everyday transaction) vs. ultimate truth (how things are in themselves); concepts are fine conventionally but misrepresent ultimate reality.
  • Candrakīrti — 6th-c. commentator behind the "conventionalist" reading later dominant in Tibet; concepts are conventional, the critique biting only when they enter philosophical theory (cf. Wittgenstein).
  • Sextus Empiricus — Greek skeptic, near-contemporary; cited for the reading on which Nāgārjuna is purely dialectical, advancing no view ("abandonment of all views").
  • Jan Westerhoff — modern Nāgārjuna expert; notes nihilism is the least moderate possible view, so a "middle way" can't be nihilist.
  • Bimal Matilal — scholar quoted on the zero analogy: in Madhyamaka, objects are like zeros, with value only relative to position.

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:22:59 In brief: Nāgārjuna turns his prasaṅga method on the everyday notion of motion, arguing — via the rules of Sanskrit grammar — that we cannot say where a movement is located or when it begins without lapsing into tautology, regress or incoherence; the same template then dismantles the very idea of a "means of knowledge," exposing motion and cognition alike as "empty." Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari/Janardin"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagadjana/Nagajuna/Nagajan/Regardjuna/Nagadrina/Nagatran/Nagavjana/Nagadrenah"; Zeno of Elea ≈ "Zeno of Alea/Zina"; Pāṇini ≈ "Panani"; Patañjali ≈ "Patanjali"; prasaṅga ≈ "pasanga"; Madhyamaka ≈ "Madyamaka/Matyamaka"; Candrakīrti ≈ "Chandrakyipti/Chandra Kirti/Shandra Kirti/Chandra Kiyoti"; Vaiśeṣika ≈ "Bysheishika"; Jan Westerhoff ≈ "Jan Vestohof"; Nyāya ≈ "Niaya"; pramāṇa ≈ "promana"; prameya ≈ "pramaya"; siddha-sādhana ≈ "Siddha sadana"; tetralemma ≈ "tetra lemma"; Mahābhārata ≈ "Mahabharata").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Nāgārjuna — his Verses on the Middle Way, chapter two on motion, plus his Refutation of My Opponents on the means of knowledge [00:01:46].
  • Zeno of Elea — the Greek inventor of the paradoxes of motion, the recurring comparison case [00:01:22].
  • Patañjali (the grammarian) — in his great commentary on Pāṇini, an earlier Indian denial of motion as objectively real [00:01:55].
  • Candrakīrti — the Madhyamaka commentator whose elaboration of Nāgārjuna's compressed verses guides the reading [00:02:47].
  • Jan Westerhoff — modern scholar cited for the view that the motion chapter is really an argumentative template [00:09:33].

docs.title: A race between a crocodile and a giraffe
docs.text:
• [00:00:36] Adamson and Ganeri agree about most things — that Indian philosophy is fascinating, that Buster Keaton's silent films are works of genius — but split over the relative merits of giraffes and crocodiles. To settle it they stage a race between Gina (a short-legged crocodile, given a head start) and Hiawatha (a giraffe).
  • [00:01:15] Ganeri is confident that, despite Hiawatha's "fleetness of hoof," she cannot overtake Gina. Adamson assumes Ganeri has been reading Zeno of Elea, who invented paradoxes denying the possibility of motion: Gina's lead can never be overcome because Hiawatha must first reach the point Gina just occupied, by which time Gina has moved further on.
  • [00:01:43] But Ganeri was not thinking of Zeno at all — he had been reading Nāgārjuna.

docs.title: An older Indian denial of motion
docs.text:
• [00:01:46] Nāgārjuna was not the first Indian thinker to deny motion. In his great commentary on Pāṇini, the grammarian Patañjali refers to a teaching that motion is not an objectively real thing — merely a conceptual construct used to explain that things arrive at a given place.
  • [00:02:07] Nāgārjuna maintains the same idea in the second chapter of his Verses on the Middle Way. He applies his prasaṅga (dialectical, reductio) method to two questions about motion, arguing that both are unanswerable: where are movements located? and when do they begin?
  • [00:02:26] His aim, as always, is to show that our concept of motion is empty. And as always, scholars disagree about why: is Nāgārjuna saying human cognition simply cannot conceive the world correctly, so we should stop trying — or that our conventional idea of motion must be replaced with a more refined theory that avoids postulating intrinsic essences (svabhāva) in things?
  • [00:02:47] Help comes from the Madhyamaka commentator Candrakīrti, who elaborates the discussion; the episode follows him, while noting his is only one possible reading of Nāgārjuna's verses.

docs.title: First question: where is a movement located?
docs.text:
• [00:03:12] Approach via the Sanskrit grammarians. Verbal roots refer to actions or events, which may be located either where the agent is or where the object of the verb is. "Enter" names an event located where the agent is (Ganeri entering the racetrack: the event is at the gate). "Hit" names an action located in the thing struck (the gong Peter strikes to start the race).
  • [00:03:54] Presupposing this, Nāgārjuna says that if someone is travelling, we can say the traveller travels the place that is being travelled. "Travel" marks an event located in the spot on the road where the travelling happens. In fact there are two things going on: the place of travelling is being travelled, and the traveller is travelling. So far, common sense.
  • [00:04:24] But Nāgārjuna uses common sense as a jumping-off point for a prasaṅga refutation. Take the path of a motion — Gina's slow progress along a 100-metre track — and divide it into three: the part already traversed, the part yet to be traversed, and the part currently being traversed. Which is the location of Gina's motion? Not the first or second, since the place being crossed now cannot be the place already crossed or the place not yet reached. So the motion must occur in the part just now being moved across.
  • [00:05:01] But that too is impossible. Candrakīrti's reasoning: every point on the path is either already traversed or yet to be traversed — there is no portion left over to accommodate the current motion. This recalls a sceptical argument about time seen before in Gautama's Nyāya-Sūtra: past and future do not currently exist, while the present has no duration, being merely the dividing line between them.

docs.title: A second argument: the redundancy of motion-talk
docs.text:
• [00:05:39] Another line. Consider "the place of travelling is being travelled" and "the place of movement is being traversed." Nāgārjuna points out these are redundant — like saying "I am where I am" (what Popeye would say if he were a GPS), or answering "where was the race held?" with "it happened where the race took place," or claiming to have solved a crime by saying it was committed by whoever perpetrated it. Such statements make no substantive claim at all.
  • [00:06:14] The same applies to "the mover moves." This is a tautology — guaranteed true but uninformative, like "the bachelor is unmarried." It is useless to point at sprinting Hiawatha and say "the running Hiawatha is running." Yet if Hiawatha is not running, it is false to say she is running. So there seems to be no way to truly and informatively say she is running.
  • [00:06:52] One escape: suppose there is a further motion — a second motion that makes Hiawatha be running. But if there are two motions, surely there should be two things moving, not one. Or perhaps not: can't a single giraffe be the subject of many actions at once — running, hearing the crowd, narrowing her eyes at Gina?

docs.title: Candrakīrti's reply: grammatical roles, and the axe
docs.text:
• [00:07:22] Candrakīrti's answer trades on a subtlety of Sanskrit grammatical theory. Of one and the same axe we can say many things: "the axe is made of metal" (agent), "he sees the axe" (direct object), "he cuts the tree with the axe" (instrument). The same object plays different grammatical roles relative to different verbs; each statement refers to the axe only insofar as it adopts that role.
  • [00:08:05] Likewise the running Hiawatha is not identical to the hearing Hiawatha or the seeing Hiawatha. Only the running Hiawatha is Hiawatha-insofar-as-she-runs. And the place she runs over, insofar as she traverses it, is not just a patch of ground but a spot being travelled over.
  • [00:08:29] This illuminates the compressed argument: the problem is not only that "the place travelled over is travelled over" and "the mover moves" are trivial — it is that this uninformative description is the only way to describe what is happening, for it is only the thing insofar as it is moving that moves.
  • [00:08:53] The template generalizes. Mick Jagger sees a red door and wants it painted black: he sees the door insofar as it is seen, wants it painted insofar as it is the object of his desire.

docs.title: Dependent origination, and the argumentative template
docs.text:
• [00:09:11] In tackling motion near the start of the Verses on the Middle Way, Nāgārjuna gives a first taste of dependent origination: the motion of running is dependent on — cannot exist without — running Hiawatha, and vice versa. The same style later shows an object of vision co-originated with the act of seeing, an object of desire co-originated with the desire.
  • [00:09:33] Jan Westerhoff has thus argued the movement chapter was not meant as a specific investigation of motion or the structure of time and place; rather it uses motion as an example to illustrate an argumentative template deployable in many contexts.

docs.title: Can the argument be escaped?
docs.text:
• [00:09:56] Is there a way out? Seemingly yes: just distinguish the various roles Hiawatha performs from Hiawatha herself. That she plays different grammatical functions in different sentences need not show — as Candrakīrti thinks — that we cannot form a notion of Hiawatha-in-herself; nor need we deny that one patch of ground could first be occupied by Gina and seconds later by Hiawatha.
  • [00:10:37] But this reply presupposes the very thing Madhyamaka attacks — that there are things-in-themselves (substances, like those of Vaiśeṣika, or of Aristotle) which take on and lose properties. As seen last time, Nāgārjuna's challenge is that any description of a so-called substance must invoke some property with which the substance, as so described, is mutually interdependent.
  • [00:11:10] And Sanskrit grammar agrees: if you cannot frame a sentence about Hiawatha or a patch of ground without tying it to a verb, you cannot refer to these things without treating them as playing a role marked by the grammar of the sentence.

docs.title: Second question: when does a motion begin?
docs.text:
• [00:11:28] A second line seems more specifically about motion itself, not just one instance of the general strategy. Nāgārjuna asks when do motions begin? — and means to show any answer is incoherent.
  • [00:11:49] Take the start of the race, when Gina begins to run — well, waddle. Threefold division again: a time at which her waddling has not yet occurred, a time while it is taking place, and a time at which she has already finished. In which does her motion begin?
  • [00:12:12] Not before she begins — she is still waiting for the starter's gong. Not after she has already moved. But neither while she is moving, since once underway she must already have started. The implication: she does not begin to move at all — which (Adamson quips) should give Hiawatha a good chance of catching her, if only Hiawatha could begin moving herself.

docs.title: Comparison with Zeno — and with Aristotle
docs.text:
• [00:12:40] Here we see why scholars compare Nāgārjuna with Zeno. Zeno's arrow can never reach its target, since at each moment it is, as Zeno says, "against something equal" — in a durational instant the arrow occupies a spatial extension identical to its own size, so cannot get from one region to the next; and if true at every instant, it cannot move at all. Hence, as Tom Stoppard observed, St. Sebastian died of fright.
  • [00:13:19] Nāgārjuna's argument is indeed reminiscent — it would similarly license the conclusion that all the warriors slain by Arjuna's bow in the Mahābhārata died of fright, and it turns on the same problem of motion and an unextended part of time. Yet the point differs: Nāgārjuna asks about the moment motion begins, not just any instant at which it occurs. A closer Greek parallel may be Aristotle's worry about the end of a change: at the instant a change is completed, the change is no longer going on.
  • [00:14:03] Stepping back over the whole battery of arguments, especially on Candrakīrti's reading, they are unlike Zeno's in being inspired by grammar. Nāgārjuna focuses not so much on whether motion is a coherent concept as on whether language can consistently and informatively describe it.
  • [00:14:26] Sentences about motion have the same logical form as sentences about actions and events, so Nāgārjuna takes motion to be located at a place and a time. But motion is precisely a displacement during a passage of time, so fixing one location or moment for it is doomed. We could adopt an artificial idiom (physicists' coordinate systems), but that just concedes his point that natural languages lack the resources to describe motion.

docs.title: The same template against knowledge
docs.text:
• [00:15:07] Nāgārjuna uses the same style to unmask the emptiness of things beyond motion — notably cognition, the bone of contention between him and his Nyāya critics. Sanskrit grammar forces us to treat verbs of thinking and knowing as acts that happen to an agent, just like motion.
  • [00:15:34] In his Refutation of My Opponents, Nāgārjuna attacks the concept of knowledge by attacking the notion of giving a proof. Recall Gautama's Nyāya epistemology: we are justified in our beliefs by a means of knowing (pramāṇa) — sensation, reason. The thing known by such a legitimate means is the prameya. So we have the instrument and direct object of a verb of knowing.
  • [00:16:06] Example: just as Ganeri restrains Gina with the instrument of a leash (so she won't bite Hiawatha after losing), so Ganeri knows Gina is dark green by the instrument of his eyesight. Ganeri is the knower, Gina the prameya (object known), his vision the pramāṇa.
  • [00:16:29] Then Nāgārjuna strikes. Everything we know is known through some instrument — but how do we know the instruments themselves are reliable? If Ganeri knows Gina is green by his eyesight, he must also know his eyesight can be trusted. If he appeals to a further instrument to reassure himself, he can worry about that one too — an infinite regress, each pramāṇa needing confirmation by another.

docs.title: Nāgārjuna classifies and eliminates the options
docs.text:
• [00:17:18] As usual, Nāgārjuna classifies all possible responses to his question — how can a pramāṇa be established as reliable?
  • [00:17:38] Intrinsic validation (without reference to things known), in three ways. (1) Validated by another source of knowledge — this is where the infinite regress bites. (2) Simply insist sources of knowledge need no validation (arguably the whole point of distinguishing prameya from pramāṇa: the object must be established, the means need not). Nāgārjuna rules this out on the starting assumption that whatever is known must be known through some means — if things can be known without a means, why need the pramāṇa at all? And what distinguishes the pramāṇa that needs no checking from the prameya that does, when any pramāṇa can become a prameya (an optician's chart tests whether your eyesight works)?
  • [00:18:49] (3) Each means is self-validating — establishing itself along with the objects it makes known, like a fire that illuminates both itself and other things. Nāgārjuna retorts that it is meaningless to say fire is illuminated: fire is the source of light, whereas the illuminated is what receives light. To suppose a pramāṇa makes itself known the way it makes other things known is like saying an axe cuts itself. Grammatically: if the source plays the role of instrument for the action of knowing, it cannot also be the object of that action.
  • [00:19:39] So much for intrinsic validation. Extrinsic validation (in relation to the objects), two options. (1) The source is validated by its own objects — vision is validated so long as it represents visible objects as they really are (corroborated by correspondence). But this assumes the very thing at issue: that the objects are already established — which was precisely the job of the pramāṇa. The opponent commits the fallacy of siddha-sādhana, "proving what is already proven."
  • [00:20:35] (2) Source and objects are mutually interdependent. This sounds congenial to Madhyamaka, but is hopeless as a theory of justification for the opponent — it is plainly circular.

docs.title: The self-refutation worry — and the escape
docs.text:
• [00:20:58] The upshot: apparently nothing can be known. Oops — another case where Nāgārjuna seems to refute himself. How can he know knowledge is impossible? How can a complex set of arguments be given for the conclusion that no conclusion can ever be established by reason?
  • [00:21:18] His reply: he is using his opponents' own methods against them. If the whole exercise is an internal critique of the justificatory system of philosophers like Gautama, it can establish that system's incoherence without any commitment on Nāgārjuna's part.
  • [00:21:45] This is familiar: an anti-democratic movement seeking power through a democratic election; a poem about the impossibility of writing poetry; or saying "I cannot recommend Buster Keaton films highly enough" precisely to recommend them emphatically. So Nāgārjuna can avoid being bitten by his own snake.

docs.title: The signature form — and where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:22:12] The arguments about motion and knowledge alike always lay out a set of options and eliminate them one by one — entirely characteristic of Nāgārjuna. We have met prasaṅga, the destructive argument that reduces empty concepts to absurdity.
  • [00:22:32] But not yet his most important contribution to logic: a negative proof with four options, each refuted — the form scholars call the tetralemma. With it, you should be able to prove anything — so long as what you want to prove is that someone else is talking nonsense. That logic is the subject of the next episode.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Nāgārjuna — Madhyamaka Buddhist; in the Verses on the Middle Way (ch. 2) he argues motion has no coherent location or beginning, and in the Refutation of My Opponents that no "means of knowledge" can be validated — both showing such concepts are "empty."
  • prasaṅga — Nāgārjuna's destructive/reductio method: lay out the options for a concept and eliminate each, reducing it to absurdity.
  • svabhāva — intrinsic essence / thing-in-itself; what Nāgārjuna's analysis aims to deny things have.
  • dependent origination — Nāgārjuna's positive lesson: e.g. the motion of running and the running Hiawatha mutually depend and "co-originate"; likewise object and act of seeing, object and desire.
  • Candrakīrti — Madhyamaka commentator who elaborates Nāgārjuna via Sanskrit grammar (the axe playing agent/object/instrument roles); the episode's main interpretive guide.
  • Patañjali (the grammarian) — in his commentary on Pāṇini reports an earlier teaching that motion is no objectively real thing, only a conceptual construct.
  • Pāṇini — the foundational Sanskrit grammarian on whom Patañjali comments.
  • Vaiśeṣika — the substance-recognizing school (with Aristotle) whose things-in-themselves taking on/losing properties Nāgārjuna's argument undermines.
  • pramāṇa — a means/instrument of knowing (e.g. vision, reason); Nāgārjuna argues none can be established as reliable without regress, circularity or incoherence.
  • prameya — the object known by a pramāṇa; Nāgārjuna notes any pramāṇa can itself become a prameya (e.g. an eye-test).
  • siddha-sādhana — the fallacy of "proving what is already proven"; committed if one validates a pramāṇa by assuming its objects are already established.
  • tetralemma — Nāgārjuna's four-option negative proof (each cornered option refuted); his key contribution to logic, deferred to the next episode.
  • Zeno of Elea — Greek author of the motion paradoxes (the arrow "against something equal"); the recurring comparison, though Nāgārjuna's grammar-driven worry about when motion begins differs from Zeno's.
  • Aristotle — invoked for the worry about the end of a change (at completion the change is no longer occurring), a closer parallel than Zeno to Nāgārjuna's "when does motion begin?"
  • Jan Westerhoff — scholar cited for reading the motion chapter as an argumentative template rather than a study of motion as such.

docs.text:
← Ep 45
