🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:23 In brief: Nāgārjuna's signature logical weapon, the four-cornered catuṣkoṭi or tetralemma, lays out every logically possible answer to a question — yes, no, both, neither — and refutes all four. The episode walks through four scholarly attempts to make sense of a method that seems to flout classical logic, and settles on reading Nāgārjuna's refusal of all four corners as a special, non-committal negation that empties the disputed concept of any grip on reality. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennarion"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagajuna/Nagadjana/Nagadrin"; catuṣkoṭi ≈ "Chachishkoti"; tetralemma ≈ "tetra lemma"; prasaṅga ≈ "Prasanga/presanga"; paryudāsa ≈ "Pariodasa"; prasajya ≈ "Prasagia/presagia/prosagia"; svabhāva ≈ "spavava"; Stanisław Schayer ≈ "Stanisval Shaya/Sheer"; Łukasiewicz ≈ "Wukasovitz"; K. N. Jayatilleke ≈ "Jayatileke/Geatilike"; Bimal Matilal ≈ "Bibal Matila"; Jan Westerhoff ≈ "Jan Vestahov"; Billie Holiday ≈ "Billy Holiday"; Sonny Corleone ≈ "Sonny Carleone").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Nāgārjuna — the Madhyamaka Buddhist whose tetralemma is the episode's subject; his verses on the middle way are quoted throughout [00:03:24].
  • catuṣkoṭi / tetralemma — the "doctrine of the four alternatives," Nāgārjuna's four-cornered logic [00:03:48].
  • Stanisław Schayer — Polish Indologist, first to treat the tetralemma as a logical problem [00:06:16].
  • Richard Robinson — proposed the tetralemma is about properties belonging to classes [00:08:45].
  • K. N. Jayatilleke — Sri Lankan scholar of early Buddhist logic; the reading the episode prefers [00:11:23].
  • Bimal Matilal & Jan Westerhoff — the two-kinds-of-negation interpretation; Westerhoff is next episode's interview guest [00:15:40].

docs.title: Yes, no — and two more answers
docs.text:
• [00:00:35] Life is full of yes-no questions: "Will you marry me?", "Do you want fries with that?" But sometimes things are more complicated. Asked whether the Godfather movies are worth seeing, you shouldn't just say yes or no but yes and no — the first two are essential, the third a disappointment.
  • [00:00:55] In other cases the answer is neither yes nor no: asked whether the fourth Godfather film is worth seeing, the right move is to challenge the question itself — no such film has been made.
  • [00:01:05] The same holds in philosophy. Often philosophers argue straightforwardly for a positive or negative answer ("Yes, we have free will"; "No, God doesn't exist"). But just as often they argue for something more nuanced. Thomas Aquinas' Summa Theologiae is a master class in saying both yes and no: the scholastic format poses questions that can be taken in more than one way, so that in one sense the answer is affirmative, in another negative.
  • [00:01:41] As for "neither yes nor no," a standard modern move is spotting a category mistake. Asked whether the soul is located in the brain, you might reply that the question is malformed — the soul is immaterial and has no spatial location at all.

docs.title: Classical logic and the law of the excluded middle
docs.text:
• [00:02:01] Despite these being standard philosophical moves, the formal study of logic has usually contented itself with the simpler yes-or-no situation. A fundamental rule of classical logic, beginning with Aristotle, is the law of the excluded middle: for any proposition, either it is true or its negation is true. Either the Godfather is worth seeing or it is not — no third option.
  • [00:02:32] How could Aristotle overlook the two more complex possibilities, given that he himself was fond of the yes-and-no answer and helped inspire Aquinas' tactic? His defence: the excluded middle applies only to meaningful propositions with clearly defined terms. It holds so long as we are not making a category mistake (assuming the soul has a location) and not speaking too imprecisely (asking about all the Godfather films collectively instead of one by one).
  • [00:03:07] That solution works by limiting the range of statements to which logic is applied. But there is another possibility: we could expand our logic to take in the more nuanced cases. This is what we find in Buddhism, and in particular in Nāgārjuna.

docs.title: The four alternatives — and refuting all of them
docs.text:
• [00:03:24] We have already seen Nāgārjuna use the prasaṅga technique to undermine dogmatic philosophical systems: he sets out an exhaustive and exclusive list of all the logically possible positions on a topic, then shows each is untenable. Typically his list has four possibilities, not two — his doctrine of the four alternatives, the catuṣkoṭi, usually translated tetralemma.
  • [00:03:55] Nāgārjuna takes the tetralemma to be definitive of the Buddha's philosophy: "Everything is such as it is, not such as it is, both such as it is and not such as it is, and neither such as it is nor not such as it is. That is the Buddha's teaching." He admits the schema is not original to him — it appears in earlier reports of the Buddha's teaching — but he deploys it with unprecedented rigour and relentlessness.
  • [00:04:33] That schema isn't the whole method, though. Typically Nāgārjuna gives the four options and then refutes all four. One can imagine Aristotle or Aquinas raising a quizzical eyebrow: it is one thing to say a question gets no clear yes-or-no because it is imprecise; quite another to rule out yes, no, both, and neither.
  • [00:04:58] A good example opens the verses on the middle way, as if Nāgārjuna is modelling how he will argue throughout: "At nowhere and at no time can entities ever exist by originating out of themselves, from others, from both themselves and others, or from the lack of causes."
  • [00:05:21] Later he applies the tetralemma to his own doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā): "Nothing could be asserted to be empty, not empty, both empty and not empty, and neither empty nor not empty. They are asserted only for the purpose of provisional understanding." He refuses to endorse any thesis that would stand on a par with rival doctrines, thereby avoiding self-refutation. If someone misunderstands and supposes Middle Way Buddhism is a philosophy to give their allegiance to, "the snake — that is, the prasaṅga method — will coil itself around them."

docs.title: Four interpretations: first, Schayer
docs.text:
• [00:06:11] Because the tetralemma is so central, and because it seems to flout the rules of logic, many scholars have tried to understand it. The episode discusses — appropriately — four such attempts.
  • [00:06:16] The Polish Indologist Stanisław Schayer was the first to see the tetralemma as a worthwhile logical problem. A student of Łukasiewicz — the Polish logician who revived medieval Aristotelian syllogistic using modern formal methods — Schayer wanted to do something similar for Nāgārjuna, reading the tetralemma within classical propositional logic. He took the four options to be that a disputed statement is either true, not true, both true and not true, or neither true nor not true: p, not-p, p and not-p, not-p and not-not-p.
  • [00:07:03] This reading is unsatisfactory for two reasons. First, the third option — both true and not true — is a straightforward contradiction, not a genuine alternative; Nāgārjuna would be wasting effort refuting it, like someone troubling to refute the claim that there both is and is not a fourth Godfather movie. Second, the fourth option collapses into the third, since two negations cancel out — a point overlooked by Sonny Corleone when he says the FBI "don't respect nothing." Saying Luca Brasi both sleeps with the fishes and does not, is the same as saying he does not sleep with the fishes and does not not sleep with the fishes.
  • [00:07:54] Some scholars nonetheless embrace this reading and triumphantly declare that Nāgārjuna rejects the law of non-contradiction — adding that this distinguishes Eastern from Western philosophy, and proves Eastern thought is essentially mystical. But that extravagant line falls at the first hurdle: Nāgārjuna explicitly endorses non-contradiction. Mid-refutation he says nobody can perform an action that is both existent and non-existent, "for they are contradictory; where can existence and non-existence coexist?"

docs.title: Second: Robinson on properties and classes
docs.text:
• [00:08:45] Richard Robinson proposed the tetralemma is not about whether propositions are true or false, but about whether a property belongs to a class of objects — bringing it closer to Aristotle, who cared about statements like "all humans are rational." Robinson could point to the lines summarizing the Buddha's teaching ("everything is such as it is, not such as it is…") and to "everything is self-caused, everything is caused by another," and so on.
  • [00:09:35] The advantage: the third option is no longer contradictory. Take having a colour. First, maybe everything is blue (unlikely but intelligible). Second, maybe nothing is blue (comprehensible, though it would thwart advice to brides). Third, "everything is blue and not blue" — this needn't be a contradiction; it could mean some things are blue and some not (when Billie Holiday asked "Am I blue?" she was wondering which category she fell into). Fourth, "everything is both blue and not blue" — more problematic, but Robinson thinks even this could be meaningful: if anything existed it would be both blue and not blue, which is impossible, so we infer nothing exists.
  • [00:10:42] But the reading doesn't fit the text well. Nāgārjuna gives no warning that the "everything" of the third option must be split into "some things blue, some not." And if the tetralemma deals only with classes, not individuals, Nāgārjuna couldn't apply his favourite tool to one-off dogmatic claims about particular objects — if someone said "Billie Holiday really is blue, just listen to her sing," he'd have to shrug and agree.

docs.title: Third: Jayatilleke on opposite properties and parts vs wholes
docs.text:
• [00:11:23] The episode prefers K. N. Jayatilleke, a Sri Lankan expert in early Buddhist logic, whose reading turns on two insights. First, the oppositions might involve opposite properties rather than sheer negations — black and white, rather than black and not-black. Second, Nāgārjuna might be exploiting the idea that a part of something can have a property the whole lacks.
  • [00:11:59] Jayatilleke's geometric example: A is east of B, or west of B, or both east and west of B, or neither east nor west of B. The third — "both east and west" — looks contradictory but isn't: if B is a point and A is an east-west line of latitude running through it, part of A is east of B and another part west. The fourth — "neither" — also works: a line of latitude wholly north of the point is neither east nor west of it (the line through Boston is neither east nor west of New York).
  • [00:12:52] You might object that Jayatilleke is cheating with the unusual properties of east and west — but the same applies to colour. First, some things are wholly white, like chalk. Second, others are wholly non-white, like a wholly black lump of coal. Third, however much it frustrates Mick Jagger, not everything is painted black: some things are white and non-white, like a zebra. Fourth, some things are neither white nor non-white — because it may be a category mistake to apply colour at all: the line of latitude through Boston is neither white, black, nor any colour.
  • [00:13:46] The reading is promising because it makes the tetralemma plainly applicable in philosophy. Take the opening question of whether things are self-caused. First, perhaps every object is wholly self-caused and spontaneous (some have thought this of God). Second, perhaps every object is caused by something else (a film made by director, actors, crew). Third, things may be caused both by themselves and by others (an animal generated by its parents that can then move its own limbs). Fourth, things may be neither, because causation may not apply to them (the number four might be like this). All are respectable positions on causation — so to show the concept of causation is empty, each must be refuted, which is exactly what Nāgārjuna does.

docs.title: The deeper puzzle: denying all four corners
docs.text: • [00:14:45] We are not out of the woods. Having made sense of the tetralemma, we must ask how Nāgārjuna can formulate an exhaustive list of four options and then deny all of them. Imagine someone denying a movie is good, denying it is bad, denying that parts are good and parts bad, and denying that it is a film for which good-and-bad don't arise (a cult film so bad it's good). Bizarre — yet this is exactly what the prasaṅga method does, rejecting even the negative options. The rejection involved must be a rather special one.

docs.title: Fourth: Matilal and Westerhoff on two kinds of negation
docs.text:
• [00:15:40] For help we turn to a fourth interpretation, put forward by Bimal Matilal and defended recently by Jan Westerhoff. It draws on an ancient Indian distinction, originally grammatical, between two kinds of negation: paryudāsa and prasajya.
  • [00:15:58] The first turns one noun into another, like adding "in-" to "vertebrate" to get "invertebrate." The second is the "not" in "I do not say I will come to your house." The key difference: negating a noun still makes a positive assertion ("the snail is an invertebrate"), whereas negating the verb does not — "I do not say I will come to your house" leaves open that I might come after all; I am just unwilling to commit until I know what movie you'll be showing.
  • [00:16:33] The distinction was used elsewhere, notably in the Mīmāṃsā theory of ritual: how to read a prohibition like "Don't slaughter a goat"? It might mean slaughter a non-goat — go ahead and sacrifice a cow or chicken, just not a goat (paryudāsa). Or it might tell you to refrain from any sacrificial act at all (prasajya).
  • [00:17:00] The prasajya (verb-negating) negation works nicely with category errors. When I deny that Godfather Four is a good movie, I am not asserting it is a non-good movie — it doesn't exist, so it isn't a movie at all. And there are non-category-error cases too: the leading question "Have you stopped beating your wife?" A married man would want to challenge the presupposition behind it, even though the question is no category mistake — he is indeed someone who could engage in domestic abuse.
  • [00:17:42] We can take Nāgārjuna to be using this non-committal negation when he rejects all four options. Since failing to assert a proposition differs from asserting its opposite, he can withhold assent from all four alternatives — showing that each involves a concept with no purchase on reality.

docs.title: The Buddha's silence — and the conclusion
docs.text:
• [00:18:06] This has a precedent in the Buddha's own practice: he sometimes fell silent when pressed. Asked whether the world is eternal, he did not answer; nor when asked if it is not eternal; likewise on whether the self is identical to the body or not. In one text he is silent before a series of four questions of the now-familiar structure: whether an enlightened being survives death, does not survive, both survives and does not, or neither survives nor does not.
  • [00:18:45] The Buddha's silence is not uncertainty but a rejection of the very line of questioning. Nāgārjuna's rejection of the four alternatives likewise wants us to dispel belief in the reality of the thing being talked about in all four options.
  • [00:19:03] Consider once more the opening of the verses on the middle way. The first three alternatives claim objects have some cause — internal, external, or mixed — while the fourth denies this. By refusing to agree to any of them, Nāgārjuna suggests the word "cause" does not refer to anything at all: it has no independent reality, no svabhāva. When the dogmatic philosopher offers a choice between self-causation and other-causation, "he is making us an offer we can and should refuse."
  • [00:19:40] This rounds off the look at Nāgārjuna, invoked at the very launch of the series to show some ancient Indian thinkers were obviously — and very interestingly — philosophers. Because he is so important and so difficult to interpret, he gets an interview episode for a further perspective: next time features one of the four interpreters discussed here, Jan Westerhoff. "Now that's an offer you can't refuse."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Nāgārjuna — Buddhist philosopher whose tetralemma method lists all four logical options on a topic and refutes every one, to show the concept at issue is empty.
  • catuṣkoṭi / tetralemma — the "four alternatives": a claim is asserted, denied, both, or neither; Nāgārjuna treats it as definitive of the Buddha's teaching.
  • prasaṅga — Nāgārjuna's method of laying out an exhaustive, exclusive list of positions and showing each is untenable; "the snake that coils around" anyone who treats Madhyamaka as a thesis.
  • law of the excluded middle — Aristotle's rule that for any proposition either it or its negation is true; defensible only for meaningful, precise statements free of category mistakes.
  • category mistake — a malformed question (e.g. asking where the immaterial soul is located); a standard ground for answering "neither yes nor no."
  • emptiness (śūnyatā) / svabhāva — Nāgārjuna denies anything has svabhāva (independent, intrinsic reality); even "empty" is asserted only "for provisional understanding," not as a thesis.
  • Stanisław Schayer — Polish Indologist (student of Łukasiewicz) who read the tetralemma in classical propositional logic; criticized because its third option is a contradiction and its fourth collapses into the third.
  • Richard Robinson — read the tetralemma as a property belonging to a class (the "blue" example); criticized for not fitting the text and for failing on individual objects.
  • K. N. Jayatilleke — Sri Lankan scholar; reads the corners as opposite properties plus part/whole distinctions (east-west line, white zebra), making the third and fourth options coherent. The episode's preferred reading.
  • Bimal Matilal & Jan Westerhoff — read Nāgārjuna's rejection via two ancient Indian negations.
  • paryudāsa vs prasajya — noun-negation that still makes a positive assertion ("invertebrate"; "slaughter a non-goat") versus verb-negation that commits to nothing; Nāgārjuna's denial of all four corners is the non-committal prasajya kind.
  • Mīmāṃsā — ritual theory that used the two-negation distinction to interpret prohibitions like "Don't slaughter a goat."
  • the Buddha's silence — precedent for Nāgārjuna: refusing to answer four-cornered questions (e.g. whether an enlightened being survives death) is rejection of the question, not uncertainty.
  • verses on the middle way — Nāgārjuna's text, opening with the tetralemma on origination (from self, other, both, or no cause) and supplying the episode's running examples.

docs.text:
← Ep 46

Ep 48 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Jan Westerhoff 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Jan Westerhoff · Runtime: 00:36:10 In brief: An interview revisiting Nāgārjuna's doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā) — what svabhāva is and why he rejects it, whether emptiness is skepticism or nihilism, how emptiness can be empty of itself, the status of conventional reality, the tetralemma, and Nāgārjuna's afterlife in India and Tibet. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jan Westerhoff ≈ "Jan Vestohov"; Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari / Janard and Canary"; Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ≈ "Mullah Madiamaka Karika"; prajñāpāramitā ≈ "pranja-paramita / Playa Parameter / Tranja Paramita"; Madhyamaka/Madhyamika ≈ "Madyamika"; svabhāva ≈ "Svava / Svababa / Subava"; Abhidharma ≈ "Abidharma / Abidama"; Candrakīrti ≈ "Chandra Kirti / Chandrakehate"; Bhāviveka ≈ "Babiwaker / Bavi Veka / Bobby Baker"; Prāsaṅgika ≈ "Prasangika").

docs.title: Who Nāgārjuna was, and his one great text
docs.text:
• [00:00:29] The episode is an interview about the Buddhist philosopher Nāgārjuna with Jan Westerhoff, introduced as Associate Professor in Religious Ethics at the University of Oxford and a fellow tutoring theology and religion at Lady Margaret Hall, Oxford [00:00:40].
  • [00:01:00] Dating: Nāgārjuna probably lived in the 2nd–3rd century CE, though traditional biographies inflate his lifespan to several hundred years. He was likely active somewhere in southern India (the exact place is unknown) and was most likely a Buddhist monk — that is about as far as the firm data go.
  • [00:01:32] His most famous work is the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ("Fundamental Stanzas / Fundamental Wisdom of the Middle Way"), a text of 450 verses, and most of the material discussed comes from it.
  • [00:01:47] The text is closely aligned with the perfection of wisdom sūtras (the prajñāpāramitā texts): it provides a systematic way of spelling out claims those sūtras make. Westerhoff stresses the link is also mythological [00:02:08] — the perfection-of-wisdom texts were said to have been taught by the historical Buddha, then entrusted to underwater serpent spirits called nāgas, who guarded them until the time was right to return them. Nāgārjuna's name carries "nāga" precisely because he is the one who brought these texts back from the nāgas to the human world and explicated them [00:02:38]. Adamson notes this is a "rather untraditional way of transmitting philosophical" texts.
  • [00:02:54] A concrete textual link: the praise of the Buddha at the very opening of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā is a close paraphrase of a passage in the Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra in 25,000 lines.

docs.title: Commentator or independent philosopher?
docs.text:
• [00:03:17] Adamson asks whether Nāgārjuna is essentially a commentator, traceable to root texts, or a freer thinker. Westerhoff: the kārikās are not a commentary — they don't gloss an earlier root text, and they name only one sūtra in the whole work [00:03:44].
  • [00:03:53] The better description is a philosophical explication of specific claims in the perfection of wisdom sūtras. Those sūtras are unusual: they make many philosophical claims but do not supply the arguments. So Nāgārjuna can be read as supplying the arguments — especially for the claims about emptiness that the prajñāpāramitā sūtras make [00:04:20].
  • [00:04:48] He is not a philosopher "doing his own thing": his stated aim, declared at the very start of the text, is to explicate the Buddha's message in the way the prajñāpāramitā sūtras state it. So it is "a commentary" only in the sense of explicating something present across many texts.

docs.title: Emptiness and what it rejects: svabhāva
docs.text:
• [00:05:18] His most prominent doctrine is emptiness (śūnyatā), and it is easier to grasp via what it rejects, which goes under the name svabhāva — roughly "stable reality."
  • [00:05:38] Etymology: svabhāva compounds sva ("own") and bhāva ("existence/being") — literally "own being," which by itself says little. Western translators have rendered it as substance, essence, or intrinsic nature; none captures the whole, but each gets fairly close.
  • [00:06:19] Westerhoff distinguishes three dimensions of svabhāva:
  • Ontological [00:06:25] — svabhāva as a ground of being (closest to "substance"). The Indian commentary literature spells this grounding out several ways: mereological grounding (the most fundamental parts, the atoms), causal grounding (a first cause), and grounding of our conceptualization of reality (some non-conceptual "stuff" our concepts are about). Reject svabhāva and all of this is rejected.
  • Semantic [00:07:09] — a view of language on which there is a "ready-made and structured world out there" and a language here, the two related by structural similarity. To work "with svabhāva" is for language to structurally match an objectively structured reality [00:07:40]. Example [00:07:56]: if you analyse sentences into agents, actions and objects — what grammarians do — and assume a one-to-one match between grammatical and ontological structure, that is a svabhāva reading of semantics. Westerhoff cites Sanskrit grammar's kāraka theory of sentence components [00:08:09].
  • Cognitive [00:08:33] — "in a way the most important" — svabhāva as a cognitive default we automatically project onto the world whenever we perceive anything. The aim of the Buddhist practice Nāgārjuna's philosophy supports is to train us out of this intuitive superimposition.
  • [00:09:08] So Nāgārjuna is a philosopher who treats philosophy as a kind of therapy — one dimension of the point, Westerhoff agrees.

docs.title: Is this skepticism? Selflessness extended to all dharmas
docs.text:
• [00:09:16] Adamson worries the position sounds extremely skeptical — nothing has essence (ontological), language doesn't mirror reality (semantic), thought doesn't latch onto reality (cognitive) — yet many of Nāgārjuna's opponents hold "ambitious metaphysical postulations" anyway, like the unchanging ātman of the Vedic tradition. So is Nāgārjuna telling us to abandon common sense, or merely not to be a Hindu philosopher [00:10:14]?
  • [00:10:23] Westerhoff resists the label "skepticism": the claims are not exclusively about how we know the world. Though Nāgārjuna has much to say about epistemology, the enterprise is "at least as ontological as it is epistemological."
  • [00:10:58] What Madhyamaka does is extend the Buddha's idea of selflessness: not only the selflessness of persons but the selflessness of all dharmas — the fundamental phenomena identified by early Buddhist philosophy. So emptiness is not just a rejection of the Hindu ātman [00:11:21].
  • [00:11:27] It is also a rejection of the entire Abhidharma metaphysics, which Westerhoff reads as a kind of trope theory: a fundamental level of reality consisting of momentary tropes that conglomerate into the "medium-sized dry goods" around us. A trope is a particular instance of a universal — this red, this sweet taste; a particular property [00:11:56].
  • [00:12:01] The ethical payoff: if I accept not only that I have no enduring self but that, say, chocolate cake has no enduring reality, it can help me lose my attachment to it. Westerhoff: that is one reading, though the link between Madhyamaka ontology and ethics is complicated [00:12:21] — rejecting even the conventionally real ātman raises hard questions about karmic causality, karmic responsibility, and who is reborn. But at some level this is indeed an attempt to combat attachment.

docs.title: Is there a positive ontology? Emptiness is empty of itself
docs.text:
• [00:13:01] Having covered the negative side — the critique of ātman and of svabhāva in general — Adamson asks whether there's a positive ontology, any positive description of the world.
  • [00:13:32] The "intriguing" claim: the theory of emptiness applies to itself — emptiness is itself empty. So Madhyamaka holds it is not possible to give any objective account of what the world is ultimately like. A materialist says "ultimately everything is material"; the Madhyamaka does not correspondingly say "ultimately everything is empty" as a master thesis [00:13:56].
  • [00:14:02] Method: a piecemeal approach — take specific concepts especially prone to being conceptualized in terms of svabhāva and take them apart, one by one. This is open-ended (you can't predict what svabhāva-like notion an opponent will produce next), which is why there is no master argument for Madhyamaka that settles everything for all comers [00:14:34]. You shoot down each positive ontological claim individually.
  • [00:14:50] What's unique: Madhyamaka applies its dissolving analysis to its own theory, yielding a theory that says there is no ultimately true account of the world — raising the question of whether that even counts as an ontological/philosophical theory, since such theories are usually meant to tell us what the world is ultimately like [00:15:18].
  • [00:15:33] The pressure comes from the self-refutation objection: opponents say "you refute yourself — you claim everything is empty, but that very claim can't be empty, or it couldn't be true." Nāgārjuna's reply [00:16:05]: yes, the theory of emptiness is empty too, but that doesn't stop it doing philosophical work, such as refuting other theories. His analogy: just as an empty chariot can still carry wood, an empty philosophical theory can still do many things without being an ultimate account of reality [00:16:16]. This returns us to the therapeutic reading [00:16:26].

docs.title: The status of conventional reality
docs.text:
• [00:16:33] If emptiness leaves us with conventional reality, is conventional reality simply left standing — we just drop the idea of a svabhāva behind it — or is conventional reality itself put in question?
  • [00:16:56] This becomes a huge issue in the post-Nāgārjuna commentary tradition, with two main positions:
  • Conventional reality is false [00:17:14]: it carries the superimpositions of svabhāva; we interact with it for practical purposes, but it can't tell us what the world is really like.
  • Stratified conventions [00:17:31]: there is no ultimately true theory, but that doesn't make every conventionally true theory as bad as every other. Conventional theories can be ranked better or worse even though none is best.
  • [00:17:56] Adamson presses: couldn't a brahmanical opponent then say "fine — if our theory of ātman and the gods is the best conventional reality, we'll settle for that"? Westerhoff: no — that concedes Brahman is not ultimately true, just a convenient fiction; you've pulled the metaphysical rug out from under it [00:18:20]. The brahmanical opponent won't settle for mere pragmatic utility, so the two schools can't be reconciled this way [00:18:37].

docs.title: Personal identity and rebirth
docs.text:
• [00:18:48] A doctrine that sounds positively ontological: that one and the same person is reincarnated — we're told that without liberation we'll be reborn, and that actions yield fruits in a next life. But if you take no-self seriously, it's hard to see how anyone could be reborn, or even be the same person as fifteen minutes ago [00:19:31].
  • [00:19:42] This problem is as old as the no-self doctrine (which goes back to the historical Buddha). The standard Abhidharma solution: treat the person as a causal complex of momentary phenomena — physical and mental — forming a stream unified by one moment causing the next [00:19:55]. For the Abhidharmikas this stream is the underlying reality on which "person" is superimposed, and it does all the work — explaining memory, karmic responsibility, and what is reborn.
  • [00:20:24] The candle analogy: light one candle from another and you can't say it's strictly the same flame, but there's a causal chain from the first to the second — which is how you differentiate persons.
  • [00:20:42] The Madhyamaka twist: all of this underlying machinery (the moments, etc.) is only conventionally real, since the Madhyamakas allow nothing ultimately real. Is that still enough to underwrite karmic responsibility and rebirth [00:21:04]?
  • [00:21:10] Nāgārjuna's answer: calling something conventional does not mean we're making it up or can decide what it's like. The recurring metaphor is the world as a magical illusion or a dream [00:21:28]: in a dream you can't choose what you dream, and once inside it you can't manipulate it freely — it follows certain laws. In the Buddhist case, those "laws of the dream" in our waking world are the karmic laws — none of which is ultimately real [00:21:59].
  • [00:22:04] Adamson notes this fits the second (stratified) reading of conventional reality. Westerhoff [00:22:32]: the real question is whether, within Madhyamaka, you want anything like a scientific picture — productive relations between theories. Either you say "the world is just the way it appears, full stop," or you say a theory like physics is in certain ways more useful than the manifest image. The first version takes conventional reality as the way things seem (and empty); the second sees levels of conventional reality [00:23:15].
  • [00:23:29] Labels: the first interpretive position is associated with the commentator Candrakīrti, the second with the commentator Bhāviveka — two streams of reading Madhyamaka that developed an intricate dispute in later India and Tibet [00:23:42].

docs.title: The tetralemma (catuṣkoṭi)
docs.text:
• [00:23:59] Beyond ontology, Nāgārjuna is striking for his attention to methodology — the self-emptiness move was one example; another is his mastery of the tetralemma [00:24:38].
  • [00:24:44] Caveats: in Buddhist literature the tetralemma is complex — its form varies (some have only two alternatives, some four), and authors do different things with it (usually rejecting the four, but occasionally affirming all four). Westerhoff focuses on the dominant form (four alternatives), the dominant handling (reject all four), and the dominant interpretation [00:26:27].
  • [00:26:31] The four alternatives: A, not-A, A and not-A, neither A nor not-A — all rejected. The "A" can be things like the existence of nirvāṇa, the existence of persons, the assertion of emptiness, or the existence of the Buddha after death [00:26:41].
  • [00:26:56] One interpretation: all four positions share an objectionable presupposition, and all four are rejected because the presupposition itself is to be rejected. The example from early Buddhist texts [00:27:18]: blow out a fire and ask "where did it go — north, south, east or west?" You deny all four, because the question falsely assumes the fire goes to some place once extinguished.
  • [00:27:48] A more complex version, from chapter 22 of the kārikās: "empty should not be asserted, non-empty should not be asserted, both or neither should not be asserted, since these are only said for the purpose of designation." Westerhoff unpacks the four [00:28:10]:
  • "Empty should not be asserted" — because emptiness must not be asserted as an ultimately true theory; no theory is, not even emptiness.
  • Nor (conventionally or ultimately) that all things fail to be empty and so have svabhāva — that's exactly what Madhyamaka denies.
  • Nor that some but not other objects are empty — some having svabhāva, some not.
  • Nor that there are objects that both have and lack svabhāva — which seems to violate the law of non-contradiction [00:28:47].
  • [00:28:51] Adamson's objection: wouldn't the fourth limb always violate non-contradiction, so you get it "for free"? Westerhoff [00:29:01]: "another can of worms" — a good objection. The famous handling, due to Bhāviveka, distinguishes two forms of negation used in the tetralemma — one that preserves certain presuppositions of the negated proposition and one that doesn't — and once you see how they interact you can't dispose of the fourth limb so quickly [00:29:31].
  • [00:29:42] A further logical worry: refusing both of two contraries ("everything is empty" / "not everything is empty") looks like violating the law of the excluded middle / bivalence — a meaningful claim should be true or false, so "neither true nor false" seems to break logic [00:30:00].
  • [00:30:16] Westerhoff's reply, again via presupposition failure: ask "is the number three yellow or not?" — three isn't yellow, but if "not yellow" presupposes it has some other colour (green, blue, red), you'd negate that too, since an abstract object has no colour at all [00:30:33]. So you can negate both alternatives of a contradictory pair when the opponent setting them up makes a presupposition behind each that you reject. Given Nāgārjuna's global rejection of svabhāva [00:30:56], there are bad presuppositions behind an enormous number of propositions — perhaps all of them — so you can apply the tetralemma "all over the place," which is pretty much what he does [00:31:13].

docs.title: Reception in India and Tibet
docs.text:
• [00:31:16] A puzzle: Nāgārjuna is highly reactive, spending much of his time criticizing rivals, and such philosophers often don't found living traditions — yet he is one of the most influential Indian thinkers [00:31:39].
  • [00:31:55] The most important split in reading Madhyamaka in India concerns the status of conventional reality — specifically whether some conventions can be better than others given there's no ultimately real reality. Bhāviveka: yes, some conventions are better. Candrakīrti: no — conventional reality is the way it appears, it is deceptive, and there we leave it [00:32:20].
  • [00:32:35] When Buddhism (and Madhyamaka) is translated into Tibet, the tradition continues, and Madhyamaka read according to Candrakīrti — known as Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka — becomes the dominant school in Tibetan Buddhism, in effect the official party line [00:32:57]. Other schools (Yogācāra, Abhidharma) are relegated to propaedeutic steps toward the final correct view [00:33:03].
  • [00:33:22] A key Tibetan debate returns to the opening question: does Madhyamaka ask us to reject the common-sense view of the world? This ties to what the object of negation is — if everything is empty and nothing has svabhāva, what exactly is being rejected [00:33:41]? The Tibetan scholastic tradition sometimes posits a falsely existent object (what Madhyamaka rejects) alongside a conventionally existent object left untouched by the analysis [00:33:56].
  • [00:34:03] This is "two sides of a coin." On one side [00:34:11]: confining the object of negation to a "falsely existent" object risks turning svabhāva into a scholastic epiphenomenon — why care that some false nature is rejected if a conventionally existent true nature is "still flying around"? It would mean a lot of work just to tell us the things we thought were true are true [00:34:31]. If Madhyamaka analysis applies only to "philosophical straw men" and not to "shoes and ships and sealing wax," it's hard to see what the fuss is about [00:34:40].
  • [00:34:47] The other side: defenders say that if Madhyamaka negates common sense / the way things appear, you get a nihilistic theory on which nothing exists. Opponents reply [00:35:04] that it would be very surprising for any philosophical theory to "make the world disappear" — believing the arguments doesn't make things stop appearing. Rather, you're forced into a discrepancy between the theory ("it's all an illusion, it's not there") and the appearance of it as real [00:35:22]. This tradition claims that very tension is what can generate a direct experiential awareness of what the Madhyamakas are trying to show [00:35:40].
  • [00:35:53] Adamson thanks Westerhoff — "one of my favourite Indian philosophy scholars talking about one of my favourite Indian philosophers" [00:35:57] — and promises to continue the series with Jonardon Ganeri next time.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Nāgārjuna — 2nd–3rd-c. CE Buddhist monk, probably of southern India; founder of Madhyamaka, who supplied the arguments behind the perfection-of-wisdom sūtras' claims about emptiness.
  • Mūlamadhyamakakārikā — Nāgārjuna's chief work, 450 verses ("Fundamental Stanzas / Wisdom of the Middle Way"); not a commentary but a philosophical explication of the prajñāpāramitā sūtras.
  • prajñāpāramitā (perfection of wisdom) sūtras — make many philosophical claims without supplying arguments; said (mythologically) to have been guarded by nāgas until Nāgārjuna returned them.
  • nāgas — underwater serpent spirits who, in the legend, safeguarded the perfection-of-wisdom texts; the source of Nāgārjuna's name.
  • śūnyatā (emptiness) — the doctrine that nothing has svabhāva; crucially, emptiness is itself empty.
  • svabhāva — "own being"; substance / essence / intrinsic nature. Has three dimensions: ontological (ground of being), semantic (language mirroring objectively structured reality), and cognitive (a default we project onto experience). Emptiness rejects all three.
  • dharmas — the fundamental phenomena of early Buddhist analysis; Madhyamaka extends no-self from persons to the selflessness of all dharmas.
  • Abhidharma — the metaphysics Madhyamaka also rejects; read here as a trope theory of momentary particulars, and the source of the causal-stream account of personal identity (the candle-flame analogy).
  • conventional reality — what is left after emptiness; not "made up," but law-governed like a dream. Two readings: false-throughout (Candrakīrti) vs. stratified/better-or-worse (Bhāviveka).
  • tetralemma (catuṣkoṭi) — four-cornered scheme (A / not-A / both / neither), here all rejected via presupposition failure (the blown-out fire; the colourless number three); chapter 22 applies it to emptiness itself.
  • Candrakīrti / Prāsaṅgika — commentator holding conventional reality is uniformly deceptive; his Prāsaṅgika reading became dominant in Tibet.
  • Bhāviveka — commentator allowing a stratification of conventions (better/worse); also the source of the two-negations solution to the tetralemma's fourth limb.
  • kāraka theory — Sanskrit grammar's analysis of sentence components; an example of reading language as matching ontological structure (a svabhāva view of semantics).
  • Jan Westerhoff — the guest; Oxford scholar of Madhyamaka who frames Nāgārjuna's philosophy as therapeutic and stresses emptiness as ontological, not merely skeptical.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 48 — "Taking Perspective: The Jain Theory of Standpoints"
docs.text:
← Ep 47

Ep 49 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:13 In brief: The Jains, the "great syncretists" of ancient India, respond to every philosophical question by accepting all the available viewpoints as partial truths — the doctrine of anekāntavāda ("non-one-sidedness"). The episode walks through Umāsvāti's seven nayas or standpoints, shows how each maps onto a rival school, and presents the Jains not as conflict-avoiding pacifists but as relativists who think one-sided theories are flatly false. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannery"; anekāntavāda ≈ "Anacantavada"; naya ≈ "night"; Umāsvāti ≈ "Umazvati"; Kundakunda ≈ "Kunda Kunda"; Siddhasena Divākara ≈ "Siddhasaena/Siddhasena Divakara"; Hemacandra ≈ "Hemachandra"; Śvetāmbara ≈ "Shvetambara"; Āgamas ≈ "Agamas"; pramāṇa ≈ "Pramana"; Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika ≈ "Niaya Vaishika"; Cārvāka ≈ "Chavaka/Charvaca"; Prabhācandra ≈ "Prabachandra"; Advaita Vedānta ≈ "Advaita Vedanta"; Madhyamaka ≈ "Madyamaka/Madyamika"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagarjuna/Nagajuna"; Candrakīrti ≈ "Chandra Kirti/Chandar Kirti"; Bhartṛhari ≈ "Batriari"; Śakra ≈ "chakra"; Frege ≈ "Frege").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Hemacandra — 12th-c. Śvetāmbara Jain thinker; source of the merchant's-wife parable (relayed by modern scholar John Cort) [00:01:25].
  • Mahāvīra — the last of the Fordmakers; his answers to the Buddha's unanswered questions seed the theory of standpoints [00:02:54].
  • Umāsvāti — author of a pioneering sūtra, the first to set out Jain thought in Sanskrit (late 4th c.); systematizer of the seven nayas [00:06:11].
  • Kundakunda and Siddhasena Divākara — the other two early architects of the standpoint theory (Kundakunda probably earliest; Siddhasena around 700 AD) [00:06:24].

docs.title: The merchant's wife and the bull
docs.text:
• [00:00:33] The episode opens with a parable. A merchant's wife, deserted for another woman, obtains a spell guaranteed to put her husband in a state where she could "lead him about with a string." The promise turns out literal, not figurative: he is transformed into a bull. Leading him to pasture, she overhears Śiva mention that an herb growing in the shade of a nearby tree would restore him. Not knowing which plant it is, she gathers every plant beneath the tree and forces the bull to eat them all — and he is restored to human form.
  • [00:01:25] The story comes via the modern Jain-philosophy scholar John Cort, who reports it from the 12th-century Śvetāmbara thinker Hemacandra. The moral: if we want salvation, we should not embrace only one teaching or tradition — we should embrace them all.

docs.title: The Jains as syncretists — anekāntavāda
docs.text:
• [00:01:44] The Jains are "the great syncretists of ancient Indian thought." Where the Vedic schools each defend a single account of the soul and its liberation, and where Buddhists like Nāgārjuna reject all such theories as incoherent, the Jains accept all the available points of view.
  • [00:02:00] Hemacandra's tale might suggest the motive is merely hedging bets — since we cannot know which teaching is right, adopt all at once and trust the correct one is in the pile. But the Jain approach is more sophisticated: a genuine epistemological theory called anekāntavāda, "the teaching of non-one-sidedness," also called the theory of standpoints.
  • [00:02:38] The core conviction: any particular, one-sided answer merely expresses a limited point of view and cannot grasp the manifold nature of things as they really are. To grasp the world aright would be to grasp it from an unlimited number of perspectives — an achievement reserved for the omniscient Fordmakers, the saviors who showed the way to liberation, Mahāvīra being the last of them. The Jain philosopher's job is to approximate that omniscience: appreciate the contribution of each intellectual tradition while seeing that each offers only partial truths.

docs.title: Origins: Mahāvīra versus the Buddha's unanswered questions
docs.text:
• [00:03:20] The theory traces back to Mahāvīra's reaction to early Buddhist doctrine. Early Buddhist tradition lists ten unanswered questions the Buddha refused to resolve: Is the world eternal, or not? Finite, or not? Is the soul identical with the body, or different? And four about the Buddha after death — does he exist, not exist, both, or neither?
  • [00:04:05] The Buddha declined to answer, comparing them to asking "where does a flame go after it is extinguished?" For the Buddhist, the right response is often to expose the faulty presuppositions behind the question.
  • [00:04:16] Mahāvīra responds completely differently. Asked whether the world is infinite, he neither stays silent nor picks one side — he embraces both: the world is finite in size but infinite in time (it never ends), and infinite in properties (limitless color, smell, taste, touch). Asked whether the soul is eternal, he says in a sense yes, in a sense no: eternal because it never ends, non-eternal because it takes different forms across the cycle of reincarnation — first animal, then human, then god.
  • [00:05:05] This is the central illustration of the Jain method. Against Buddhists who say there is no enduring self and Vedic thinkers who make the self eternal and unchanging, the Jains argue both sides are partly right and therefore partly wrong: the Buddhists err because the soul does persist; the Vedic thinkers err in making it unchanging. Just as Madhyamaka systematized themes already in the Buddhist scriptures, the standpoint theory generalizes these reports about Mahāvīra.

docs.title: The early Jain philosophers
docs.text:
• [00:05:53] It has been proposed that Jainism passed through a phase of commentary on its scriptural texts, the Āgamas, with a more logical approach emerging only afterward. In fact things are messier: the two genres overlapped chronologically, and exegesis animated Jain philosophy much as it did the Brahmanical schools.
  • [00:06:07] Chronology is bedevilled by uncertainty over key dates — notably Umāsvāti, whose sūtra "on what is" was the pioneering work, the first to set out Jain thought in Sanskrit; he probably wrote in the late 4th century. Other important early figures: Kundakunda (probably earlier than Umāsvāti) and Siddhasena Divākara (around 700 AD). These three, above all, developed the theory of standpoints as an expression of Mahāvīra's method.

docs.title: Direct versus indirect knowing
docs.text:
• [00:06:40] Mahāvīra himself had not so much a special method as a special insight. The Jains draw a fundamental distinction between indirect and direct ways of knowing, using the standard term for a means of knowledge, pramāṇa. Most of us must make do with the indirect access of perception and scriptural tradition; Mahāvīra enjoyed a direct omniscience of all things, which is why he could see from all points of view at once.
  • [00:07:15] Worse than having a limited perspective is having one without realizing it is limited — the predicament of the Jains' rivals, Vedic and Buddhist alike, who "fetishize a single standpoint as the only valid view."
  • [00:07:32] Though there are infinitely many ways to look at anything, Umāsvāti breaks the possibilities into seven types of standpoint, or naya: (1) the non-distinguished, (2) the general, (3) the practical, (4) the straight thread, (5) the verbal, (6) the subtle, (7) the thus-happened. The first three affirm substance; the remaining four concern the modifications or predicates of substance — already echoing Mahāvīra's two perspectives on the soul (that it endures, and that it changes).

docs.title: Substance versus modification
docs.text:
• [00:08:18] That contrast between the substance point of view and the modification point of view is fundamental to Jainism. Kundakunda holds that substance — sentient and non-sentient alike — is "that which undergoes and endures through all change," and so can be seen from two angles depending on whether we stress its endurance or its change.
  • [00:08:41] Set Advaita Vedānta (which makes a single unchanging brahman the only true reality) against the Buddhist rejection of any enduring independent substance, and the Jain move comes into focus: it convicts both schools of being "nothing but points of view," one-sided because each manages only a partial perspective. But Umāsvāti has something more complex in mind than just two perspectives — hence the full seven.

docs.title: Working through the standpoints — the three substance views
docs.text:
• [00:09:23] (1) The non-distinguished. The least clear of the seven — Siddhasena omitted it from his overview. It seems almost to be the standpoint of refusing to take any standpoint: thinking of a thing without bothering to distinguish whether it is a substance or a property — the attitude of someone merely cataloguing what there is without worrying about kinds. Puzzlingly, the Jains ascribe it to the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosophers, presumably because those schools treated properties as if they were objects in their own right, thus failing to distinguish substance from property. The Jains do not call this illegitimate — all viewpoints are legitimate, "but only so long as they are not taken to have a monopoly on validity."
  • [00:10:28] (2) The general. (And no, Adamson notes, dating makes it unlikely this is a tribute to Buster Keaton's greatest film.) It attends only to the most general commonalities — e.g., that everything shares the property of "being an existent" — ignoring distinguishing features. Adopted dogmatically, it leads to monism, with Advaita Vedānta "unsurprisingly fingered as the leading culprit."
  • [00:11:05] (3) The practical. The complement of the general: it stresses the special distinguishing features of things and how they sort under various headings. From this view a philosopher says every existent is either a substance or a property. Some Jains place the Cārvāka materialists here, probably because they classify both the material body and the spiritual self as substances (rather than properties) and so treat them as the same kind of entity.

docs.title: Naming and shaming — and the non-violence question
docs.text:
• [00:11:42] (4) The straight thread. This attends only to what is presently perceived — the pleasure or pain felt right now. Taken as the uniquely correct standpoint, it reduces enduring substances and persons to the ephemeral deliverances of the senses — the mistake of the Buddhists, or at least some of them.
  • [00:12:05] In explaining these first four standpoints, the Jain writers effectively supply a survey of Indian metaphysics — which is why the Jains are so useful as a source on non-Jain thinkers (it was the Jain Prabhācandra who informed us about the otherwise obscure Cārvāka tradition). But these schools are not merely named — they are shamed, exposed as one-sided.
  • [00:12:35] A tempting reading: the theory of standpoints is an abstract embodiment of the Jain commitment to non-violence — disagreement being a kind of intellectual aggression, so the Jains find a way of agreeing with everyone. But this overlooks that the Jains do not simply congratulate rivals on being partly right; they stress that rivals are partly wrong. Like everyone else, the Jains hold that knowledge leads to liberation — but their knowledge requires seeing things from many viewpoints, whereas the Brahminical or Buddhist thinker adopts just one. The Jains cheerfully assert such one-sided theories are false precisely insofar as they are one-sided, and they saw no breach of non-violence in vigorous debate — hence the story of a Jain who held forth against a Buddhist at such length that "his opponent finally died from exhaustion."

docs.title: The three linguistic standpoints
docs.text:
• [00:13:46] The remaining three show the Jains joining "that most typical of ancient Indian philosophical pursuits," the analysis of language.
  • [00:14:03] (5) The verbal. It takes grammar as a guide to reality — e.g., inferring from past, present, and future verb forms that their subjects differ. On this view, "the mountain existed" and "the mountain will exist" refer to two different mountains. Odd, but akin to a Madhyamaka point: Nāgārjuna (per his commentator Candrakīrti) held we should distinguish "the axe that is seen" from "the axe used for chopping," the distinction marked by grammatical case — object of action versus instrument. Useful, the Jains agree, so long as not applied indiscriminately: it is plausible that the grammatical contrast of subject and predicate often tracks a real contrast of thing and property, but one must not infer metaphysics from every grammatical distinction — else a German would conclude from noun gender that doors are female, houses neuter, and tables masculine.
  • [00:15:21] (6) The subtle. Here we distinguish different words that refer to the same thing but have different etymologies. The lord of the gods is called both Indra (from a verb "to reign") and Śakra (from a verb "to be able"); the names pick out the same god but differ in meaning because of their derivation. Striking, because — etymology aside — it anticipates Frege's sense/reference distinction: "morning star" and "evening star" both refer to Venus yet differ in meaning, as shown by the fact that one might not know they are the same body.
  • [00:16:19] (7) The thus-happened. Many words have functional senses, referring to objects by a capacity they can perform — "cook," "swimmer." On this standpoint such terms should be used only while the object is actually exercising the function: someone is a "swimmer" only while actually swimming. It is a linguistic version of the straight-thread view, reducing everything to the currently present. Taken dogmatically it yields the fallacy of refusing to call a sleeping swimmer a swimmer — echoing Nāgārjuna and Candrakīrti's argument that "the running giraffe is distinct from the seeing giraffe" because of their different actions.

docs.title: The standpoints in practice
docs.text:
• [00:17:18] Siddhasena uses the standpoints to handle the problem of substance. Setting aside the non-distinguished, he starts with the general perspective that sees all substance as one — Advaita monism. The practical standpoint distinguishes substance into types — the attitude of the pluralists among Vedic schools. The straight thread, ignoring all but present reality, yields a theory of constant flux — the Buddhists. Grammarians cannot see past the verbal perspective — think of Bhartṛhari. Other language enthusiasts use the subtle standpoint to classify substances by the etymology of their names. And the thus-happened reduces a substance to its currently performed action.
  • [00:18:17] The summary: broadly, only the general and practical standpoints do justice to the stability and independence of substances, while the rest capture the modifications substances undergo. To adopt one standpoint is to get things partially right; to adopt it narrowly and exclusively is to get them wrong.

docs.title: The Jains as relativists — and what's next
docs.text:
• [00:18:39] The Jains hold an idiosyncratic view of truth. They are not skeptics who deny truth is accessible or who suspend judgment about ever having it. Rather, they are relativists in a special sense: truth is always relative to a point of view or context in which it is uttered or believed. Yet — unlike most modern relativists — they think ultimate truth is possible: the truth attained by embracing an infinity of valid viewpoints all at once.
  • [00:19:13] The Jains realized this theory could not work within the logical system of the Nyāya school, and Nāgārjuna's destructive tetralemma would hardly suit their non-one-sided aims. So they developed a remarkable logic with seven kinds of predication — the topic of the next episode, which will also ask whether, by endorsing the yes-and-no side of every issue, the Jains fall into self-contradiction (the very problem that threatened Madhyamaka).
  • [00:19:46] A closing Jain joke about the podcast's month-long summer break: from a listener's perspective a month may seem long; from the producers' perspective it will be over before they know it. "Taking that point of view, we'll see you next time."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• anekāntavāda — "the teaching of non-one-sidedness"; the Jain theory of standpoints, which holds that every one-sided view captures only a partial truth.
  • naya — a standpoint or perspective; Umāsvāti enumerates seven, the first three affirming substance, the last four its modifications.
  • the seven nayas — non-distinguished, general, practical, straight thread, verbal, subtle, thus-happened — each mapped onto a rival school's one-sided dogma.
  • Mahāvīra — the last Fordmaker (omniscient savior); his "in a sense yes, in a sense no" answers to the Buddha's unanswered questions seeded the standpoint theory.
  • Fordmakers — Jainism's omniscient saviors who showed the way to liberation; only they grasp all perspectives at once.
  • pramāṇa — a means of knowledge; the Jains distinguish indirect knowing (perception, scripture) from Mahāvīra's direct omniscience.
  • substance vs. modification — the fundamental Jain contrast: substance endures through change (Kundakunda), while modifications are its changing predicates.
  • Hemacandra — 12th-c. Śvetāmbara thinker; source of the merchant's-wife parable urging us to embrace all teachings.
  • Umāsvāti — late-4th-c.(?) author of the first Jain sūtra in Sanskrit; systematized the seven standpoints.
  • Kundakunda — early Jain philosopher (probably pre-Umāsvāti); defined substance as that which endures through all change.
  • Siddhasena Divākara — Jain philosopher (~700 AD) who applied the standpoints to the problem of substance and omitted the non-distinguished naya.
  • Āgamas — the Jain scriptural texts, on which a phase of commentary overlapped with the rise of philosophical literature.
  • anekāntavāda vs. non-violence — a tempting but rejected reading: the Jains do not merely agree with everyone; they call one-sided theories false and debated vigorously.
  • relativism (Jain) — truth is relative to a standpoint, yet ultimate truth is attainable by embracing infinitely many valid viewpoints at once.
  • rival schools placed by standpoint — Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika (non-distinguished), Advaita Vedānta (general/monism), Cārvāka (practical), Buddhists (straight thread/flux), Bhartṛhari & grammarians (verbal).

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 49 — "Well Qualified: The Jains on Truth"
docs.text:
← Ep 48

Ep 50 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:17:49 In brief: How the Jains defend their pluralism — the doctrine that rival philosophies are each true only from a standpoint — against the twin charges of self-refutation and self-contradiction, using the qualifier syāt ("in a sense") and the seven-fold scheme of predication (saptabhaṅgī) to be non-one-sided without tolerating real inconsistency. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janarnan Gannery"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagajuna/Nagadren"; syāt ≈ "siat/Seattle"; naya ≈ "Naya's"; Siddhasena ≈ "Siddhasaena"; Vādideva Sūri ≈ "Vadi de Vassuri/Vasuri"; Prabhācandra ≈ "Prabachandra"; Vaiśeṣika ≈ "Vysheeshika"; Mahāvīra ≈ "Mahavira/Mahavida"; brahman ≈ "Brahmann"; Marie-Hélène Gorisse ≈ "Marie Ellen Gouris").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Mahāvīra — last of the Jain ford-makers, source of the conditional-yes answers and the omniscient standpoint [00:02:35].
  • Siddhasena — Jain philosopher quoted on how a manifold thing is fully comprehended only by the omniscient [00:02:47].
  • Vādideva Sūri — 11th-century Jain who lays out the seven-fold predicate theory with particular clarity; quoted at length [00:06:43].
  • Prabhācandra — 10th-century Jain (born 980), offers the "neutrality" reading of the inexpressible [00:13:08].
  • syāt / saptabhaṅgī — the qualifying particle "in a sense" and the seven modes of predication built on it [00:04:27].

docs.title: The test a theory must survive: being applied to itself
docs.text:
• [00:00:31] When you evaluate a philosophical theory there are standard tests: Does it preserve our intuitions? If not, does it give sufficient reason to abandon our previous beliefs? Does it fall prey to counter-examples or leave exceptions unexplained? And one more that must never be omitted — can the theory survive being applied to itself?
  • [00:00:54] We saw the Buddhist Nāgārjuna wrestle with exactly this in his Refutation of My Opponents: the objection that his arguments for the emptiness thesis can be dismissed, since Nāgārjuna himself must admit those very arguments are empty.
  • [00:01:17] The Jain theory of standpoints (naya), examined last episode, looks just as vulnerable. The Jains say philosophical theories are true only from a certain perspective — but is that assertion itself only the expression of a certain standpoint?

docs.title: The Jain reply on universals: standpoints all the way up
docs.text:
• [00:01:35] The Jains can answer readily. Take their approach to the metaphysics of universals. Adopting the theory of nayas, they say there is a perspective that affirms things sharing a universal character, and another that emphasizes the reality of individual particulars.
  • [00:01:52] From the first standpoint, a realist about universals argues that all pots share "potness" in common. From the second, a skeptic about universals says only each individual pot is real.
  • [00:02:05] The Jain says both standpoints are in a sense correct, because each captures something about reality. In saying so, the Jain adopts a third standpoint — the one from which both the universal and the particular ways of looking have contributed something to our understanding.
  • [00:02:22] That third standpoint may itself be partial. But there is also the prospect of a most comprehensive, omniscient point of view that incorporates all standpoints — the point of view of someone like Mahāvīra, the last of the Jain ford-makers. It is the only fully adequate standpoint, precisely because of the complexity of things in the world.
  • [00:02:47] As the Jain philosopher Siddhasena puts it: "since a thing has a manifold character, it is fully comprehended only by the omniscient, but a thing becomes the subject matter of a naya when it is conceived from one particular standpoint." We are not omniscient, yet we can make progress by understanding how each philosophical theory contributes a merely partial truth. So the self-refutation charge fails: the Jain claim isn't one more dogmatic thesis, but a higher-order, partial-but-progressing standpoint.

docs.title: The harder test: do the Jains contradict themselves?
docs.text:
• [00:03:11] There is a simpler, more dangerous test: does the theory involve self-contradiction? This threat also loomed over Nāgārjuna, whose tetralemma has seemed to some to involve entertaining contradictory propositions. Adamson resisted that reading for Nāgārjuna and wants to resist it for the Jains too.
  • [00:03:34] You can see why they get accused. As philosophical pluralists, the Jains answer paired questions like "Is the world infinite?" and "Is the world finite?" with a qualified yes in both cases — each expresses a partial truth.
  • [00:03:52] Many commentators, past and present, have felt that the Jain attempt to reconcile opposite positions amounts to challenging the notion of contradiction — that it tolerates inconsistency. How else could they find something true in both the Buddhist no-self theory and the Advaita theory that all things are really a single self, namely brahman?
  • [00:04:15] No less than Nāgārjuna, the Jains are alive to the threat, and seek to show how one can have impartiality / non-one-sidedness (anekāntavāda) without lapsing into self-contradiction.

docs.title: The little word that does the work: syāt
docs.text:
• [00:04:27] Their answer centers on a single Sanskrit particle, syāt. It is an optative form of the verb "to be," meaning "possibly" or "perhaps" — but in this context it is better rendered "in a sense," or "conditionally," or even "arguably."
  • [00:04:48] Syāt captures the Jain refusal to make categorical assertions: instead they answer questions from one or another perspective, within the framework of a certain metaphysical stance. So rather than asserting flatly that the world is eternal, we say only, conditionally, "the world is infinite" — meaning from a certain standpoint the universe is infinite.
  • [00:05:11] Compare the words modern logicians call modal operators — "possibly," "necessarily." They indicate the way in which a statement is true. "Possibly, the universe is infinite" flags that something might be true; "necessarily…" flags something that must be true. In neither case am I straightforwardly asserting the infinity of the universe. Syāt works the same way: it modulates the assertion rather than baldly making it.

docs.title: Seven modes of predication (saptabhaṅgī) — and where they come from
docs.text:
• [00:05:41] To the syāt qualifier the Jains add a list of seven types of statement, each prefaced by syāt. This is comparable to Nāgārjuna's tetralemma — except the Jains "go him three better," offering seven alternatives where he had only four.
  • [00:05:54] Just as the tetralemma traces back to the Buddha's refusal to answer certain questions, the origins of this remarkable, unprecedented theory lie in reports about Mahāvīra. Confronted with "Is the world infinite?" and "Is the world finite?", Mahāvīra did not fall silent — he said yes to both, but a conditional yes, not an absolute yes.
  • [00:06:18] He was even asked whether a question might have no expressible answer at all. Here the Buddha might finally have said yes — his silence was a rebuke to the question as posed. Mahāvīra likewise admits the right answer may be inexpressible — but even that admission is conditional, the expression of a certain standpoint.
  • [00:06:43] The 11th-century Jain Vādideva Sūri explains the theory with particular clarity. The sevenfold predicate theory uses seven modes of assertion, each preceded by "conditionally" (syāt), all concerning a single object and its properties, composed of attributions and denials — either simultaneously or successively — and without contradiction:
  • Conditionally, an object exists (an attribution).
  • Conditionally, it does not exist (a denial).
  • Conditionally it exists, conditionally it doesn't (successive attribution + denial).
  • Conditionally, it is non-assertable (simultaneous attribution + denial).
  • Conditionally it exists; conditionally it is non-assertable (attribution + the simultaneous pair).
  • Conditionally it doesn't exist; conditionally it is non-assertable (denial + the simultaneous pair).
  • Conditionally it exists, conditionally it doesn't, conditionally it is non-assertable (successive attribution + denial + the simultaneous pair).

docs.title: Getting our heads around the seven options
docs.text:
• [00:08:14] With the tetralemma we had to figure out how Nāgārjuna got away with four possibilities — yes, no, both, neither. The Jain scheme is harder still. One difference: for the Jains there are three basic answers, not just yes and no, but a third — the non-assertable or inexpressible.
  • [00:08:42] Three simple modes get us started: (1) something is the case, (2) something is not the case, (3) something is inexpressible. Example: "there is a pot," "there is no pot," "it is inexpressible whether there is a pot." The theory extends beyond existence to any predicate — "the pot is blue," "the pot is not blue," "it is inexpressible whether the pot is blue."
  • [00:09:13] Then the Jains combine these three into more complex options. "A pot exists" could be (4) both true and false, (5) true yet inexpressible, (6) false yet inexpressible, or (7) all three — true, false, and inexpressible. That is seven in all: three simple cases plus four compound ones.
  • [00:09:37] And remember: all seven are prefaced by syāt, "conditionally." So even the "simple" option where something is said to be the case isn't simple. "Conditionally, there is a pot" / "conditionally, the universe is infinite" holds just in case there is a standpoint from which it is so — and that is compatible with the same thing being false from another point of view.

docs.title: Worked examples: standpoints that flip the verdict
docs.text:
• [00:09:59] We saw last time how this works. The universe has no temporal ending, so from that standpoint it is infinite — yet it is not infinite in size, so there is also a standpoint from which it is finite.
  • [00:10:15] Similarly: from the standpoint that focuses on stable, enduring substances, "there is a pot"; yet from the perspective that focuses only on momentary sensory experiences, there is no pot — only ephemeral experiences of colour, shape, and hardness. (The same realist-vs-momentariness split that divides Vaiśeṣika from Buddhist metaphysics.)
  • [00:10:32] A more banal version: if the pot is in Munich but not in New York, then from a Munich standpoint "there is a pot" is true, but not from a New York standpoint.

docs.title: The trickiest cases: "both true and false," and the inexpressible
docs.text:
• [00:10:47] Trouble starts with saying something is both true and false — dangerously close to a standpoint adopted by people happy to contradict themselves. Yet Vādideva Sūri prefaced the whole account by insisting the seven options involve no self-contradiction.
  • [00:11:11] Why not? Because he says the mixed predicate "true and false" involves the successive attribution and denial of a property. So it is just the standpoint of someone who first notes a perspective from which a claim is true, and then adds another perspective from which it is false. Quite sensible — e.g. a Jain saying "our Vaiśeṣika colleagues believe the pot exists, but the Buddhists deny it." The seven-fold list explains how the theory of standpoints works; but it is the theory of standpoints that explains why the list involves no intentional inconsistency.
  • [00:11:46] Not out of the woods yet: the most puzzling basic option is the inexpressible. Here Vādideva Sūri does seem to court contradiction, because he glosses "inexpressible" as the simultaneous attribution and denial of a property — a standpoint endorsing both a statement and its denial at once. So we seem back among those who contradict themselves. Yet the Jains promised no contradiction. What is going on?

docs.title: Two readings of the inexpressible
docs.text:
• [00:12:33] Explanation one (the simple one): we cannot say both yes and no to a question at the same time, because no one can assert two contradictory ideas at once. So the key Jain insight — that both answers are right, but from different points of view — is inexpressible simply because of the limitations of normal language. This fits Vādideva Sūri's tying the inexpressible to simultaneous attribution and denial.
  • [00:13:03] Explanation two: comes from the 10th-century Jain Prabhācandra — met before as a source for Cārvāka thought, but a brilliant philosopher in his own right, born in 980, the same year as Avicenna, and (incidentally) author of a thought experiment very like Avicenna's "flying man." More than any other Jain, Prabhācandra wrestles with what makes the seven alternatives genuinely distinct from one another while still comprehensive (no option left out).
  • [00:13:42] When Prabhācandra explains "inexpressible," he does not say it involves simultaneous assertion and denial. He ties it instead to neutrality: from the standpoint one occupies, one can neither endorse nor deny a certain claim.
  • [00:14:00] This could be very simple — neutrality from lack of information. In New York, not having been to Munich lately, I just shrug when asked whether there's a pot in Munich.
  • [00:14:17] Or something more interesting. To assert from a standpoint is to adopt a perspective that ratifies some claims and undermines others. Take an example the Jains could never have contemplated — modern physics. From the physicist's standpoint, claims about sub-atomic particles are affirmed while claims about the ancient Greek four elements are denied. But about some propositions a standpoint is simply neutral: physics neither grounds nor undermines claims about morality. You can't work out whether stealing is wrong — or solve the moral dilemmas that perplex the protagonist of the Mahābhārata — by studying physics. Such propositions are neither affirmed nor denied from inside that standpoint. In this sense an answer may be inexpressible.

docs.title: Why this differs from the Buddha's silence
docs.text:
• [00:15:16] If Prabhācandra is right, the Jain "inexpressible" is different from the Buddhist refusal to answer. When the Buddha declined to respond, it was certainly not because he didn't know the answer.
  • [00:15:26] A Buddhist would fiercely resist the idea that Buddhism is just one more standpoint that might lack the resources to answer a given question (the way physics lacks the resources for morality). The Buddhist standpoint claims to be "the whole truth and nothing but the truth." If it fails to answer a question, the question is to blame — it must be ill-formed or rest on false assumptions, like the reality of holes or of enduring selves.
  • [00:15:51] This is why Nāgārjuna's strategy was to expose the incoherence in other views, whereas the Jain strategy is to expose their dogmatic insistence on being the only truth — when in fact there is more to truth than any one school's claim.
  • [00:16:09] So the Jains hold there are ways to answer the questions the Buddha was asked, and point to scriptures where Mahāvīra did answer them. It is just that the right answer requires taking up a standpoint other than the Buddhist one — indeed several different complementary standpoints.

docs.title: Why coherence matters: philosophy in aid of liberation
docs.text:
• [00:16:26] Adamson has insisted on the coherence of Jain epistemology and on its commitment to attaining a true standpoint — not merely because it annoys him when people deny the principle of non-contradiction (it "both annoys us and doesn't").
  • [00:16:43] It is also because Jainism, like its rivals, is a philosophy in aid of a soteriology. No less than other ancient Indian thinkers, the Jains hold out the prospect of liberation, and claim liberation is achieved through knowledge.
  • [00:17:01] This is also why they are willing to say other schools have got things wrong: the partial perspective of a Buddhist or a Vedic thinker is not liberating, because it captures only a fragment of the holistic, comprehensive grasp of things that is nothing other than omniscience.
  • [00:17:17] Adamson admits he hasn't given us that holistic grasp of Jainism — to do so would take many more episodes, "perhaps an infinity of them," which would take up too much storage on the feed.
  • [00:17:37] So one more standpoint on Jain logic and epistemology is promised: next time's guest, Marie-Hélène Gorisse (?), "certainly well qualified" to discuss the Jain theory of conditional truth.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• self-application test — the rule that a theory must survive being applied to itself; the episode's organizing test, passed (the Jains argue) by both their standpoint theory and their seven-fold predication.
  • naya (standpoint) — a perspective from which a claim is conceived; rival theories (realist vs. skeptic about universals, etc.) are each true from some naya.
  • syāt ("in a sense / conditionally") — optative of "to be," used by the Jains as a qualifier (like a modal operator) so that assertions are made from a standpoint, never categorically.
  • anekāntavāda (non-one-sidedness) — the Jain stance of impartiality that finds partial truth in opposed schools without (they claim) tolerating contradiction.
  • saptabhaṅgī (seven-fold predication) — seven syāt-prefaced modes (exists / doesn't / both successively / non-assertable / and their combinations); the Jain answer to Nāgārjuna's four-cornered tetralemma.
  • the inexpressible / non-assertable — the third basic answer beyond yes and no; read either as a limit of language (simultaneous attribution + denial, Vādideva Sūri) or as standpoint-neutrality (Prabhācandra).
  • Mahāvīra — last Jain ford-maker; gave the conditional "yes" to opposed questions and embodies the omniscient, all-incorporating standpoint.
  • Siddhasena — Jain philosopher quoted: a manifold thing is fully comprehended only by the omniscient; conceived from one standpoint it becomes the subject of a naya.
  • Vādideva Sūri — 11th-c. Jain; quoted at length laying out the seven modes "without contradiction," glossing the inexpressible as simultaneous attribution and denial.
  • Prabhācandra — 10th-c. Jain (born 980, same year as Avicenna; has his own "flying man"-like thought experiment); reads the inexpressible as standpoint neutrality.
  • tetralemma (Nāgārjuna) — the Buddhist four-cornered scheme (yes/no/both/neither) against which the seven-fold theory is contrasted; Nāgārjuna's strategy is to expose incoherence in rivals.
  • omniscience & soteriology — Jain liberation is achieved through knowledge; only the comprehensive, all-standpoint (omniscient) grasp liberates, so partial Buddhist/Vedic perspectives fall short.
