docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 50 — "Marie-Hélène Gorisse on Jain Epistemology"
docs.text:
← Ep 49

Ep 51 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Marie-Hélène Gorisse 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Marie-Hélène Gorisse · Runtime: 00:31:50 In brief: An interview on Jaina logic and epistemology: how the Jainas, working inside India's "debating hall," ground inference in epistemology and ultimately in soteriology, defend a dualist soul against Buddhist no-self, and build their signature doctrine of non-one-sidedness (anekāntavāda) — a perspectivism that says rival schools each grasp one true aspect of an irreducibly complex reality, capped by a distinctive theory of inference set against Dignāga and Dharmakīrti. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Marie-Hélène Gorisse ≈ "Marie-Elein-Len-Gorice"; Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannery"; Jaina ≈ "giant/Jain"; anekāntavāda ≈ "Anikauntavada"; nayavāda ≈ "Naya Vada"; Mahāvīra ≈ "Maharevira"; Dignāga ≈ "Dignaga"; Dharmakīrti ≈ "Darmakirti/Dada Makhiote/Dama Kioti"; Tarka; avinābhāva ≈ "Aniata"; Saṅghadāsa ≈ "Sangadasha"; Digambara ≈ "Degombara").

docs.title: Who the Jaina thinkers are, and where they sit
docs.text:
• [00:00:43] Adamson opens by asking Gorisse to place the Jaina logicians: who they are, roughly when they lived (he bets she'll say "we don't know"), and where they sit in India's "broader debating network of schools."
  • [00:01:04] Gorisse first sets the stage. The thinkers she works on contributed to a highly regulated debating hall that was "center stage" in Indian philosophy from roughly the end of the 2nd century CE to the 11th century.
  • [00:01:35] That centrality comes from method: alongside perceptual knowledge and the correct interpretation of sacred texts, the best way to secure a genuine piece of knowledge is inferential reasoning — and her own work characterizes that inference.
  • [00:01:54] A key structural point: logical considerations (necessity, the properties of relations) are directed toward epistemological purposes — clearly defining the means by which we acquire new knowledge. And those epistemological considerations are in turn directed toward soteriological purposes — defining how one should behave in order to "fully realize my own nature." Logic serves epistemology serves liberation.
  • [00:02:39] Three main parties debated in this hall: the Buddhists, the Hindu philosophers of Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā, and the Jainas — her focus.
  • [00:02:56] Jainism, she notes, is pervasively important in Indian culture yet "largely unknown in the West." It is a religious and philosophical tradition whose last great spiritual leader is Mahāvīra, who lived in the 5th century BCE. Like Buddhism, it arose as a reaction against the ritualistic focus of the Vedic corpus, offering instead an "inner fight" grounded in ascetic practices. Jainas today live worldwide but are concentrated in west-central India.

docs.title: The soul as the subject of knowledge
docs.text:
• [00:03:44] Adamson sums up the picture: the Jainas are one school among several debating now-familiar issues, especially with Nyāya — they too have a theory of inference, even "scientific reasoning," as do the Buddhists. But before the epistemology, he asks about the subject of knowledge: the Jainas believe in a soul, so what is it like and how does it relate to matter?
  • [00:04:33] Gorisse: because Jainism is first of all a soteriology, its metaphysics is subordinated to ethics — it must secure human responsibility, which requires a persisting self-identity and an "influential active self."
  • [00:04:58] They get this through a dualism. On one side are souls — single, independent, isolated subjective entities whose very essence is consciousness. On the other is non-soul stuff: objectivity consisting in matter and its organizing principles.
  • [00:05:38] Within the material realm the focus is karma, understood as a kind of matter whose specific property is to develop the consequences of our virtuous or unethical acts. Because our acts witness the self's desire toward external objects, karmic matter takes the form of a given limited mental state.
  • [00:06:06] So the core problem is not to explain but to get rid of the interaction between karmic matter and souls, in order to reach a non-limited state of consciousness. In principle we are all omniscient; only by shedding karmic matter do we realize that omniscient nature.
  • [00:06:35] This matters epistemologically: the Jainas hold their spiritual leaders reached omniscience, so their corpus counts as authoritative. Mahāvīra, for instance, achieved liberation even in this life, while still embodied, by divesting himself of bodily concerns so thoroughly that he recovered the original omniscience we all share.
  • [00:07:12] Adamson confirms; Gorisse adds that the very nature of his omniscience was such that he spontaneously taught what he knew to everyone — "it just flows out of him," Adamson says — by emitting, for some of the Digambara Jainas, a kind of divine sound.

docs.title: Jainism vs. the Buddhists — and a likeness to Sāṃkhya
docs.text:
• [00:07:32] Adamson finds it striking that the subsisting independent soul is so crucial, because people often assume Jaina theories resemble Buddhist ones, since both reject Vedic orthodoxy. Yet on this point they are diametrically opposed to the Buddhists.
  • [00:08:02] Gorisse agrees emphatically. Adamson notes the Jaina view actually sounds more like Sāṃkhya — an independent immaterial soul set against a material subject in which the soul resides. Gorisse: yes, closer to Sāṃkhya, and also to some Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika considerations.

docs.title: Non-one-sidedness (anekāntavāda): everybody is partly right
docs.text:
• [00:08:30] That very feature — Jainism echoing several rival schools at once — goes along with its epistemology, which "in a way seems to be a way of saying that everybody is right." This is the famous theory of non-one-sidedness, a kind of perspectivism; they speak of naya or viewpoints. The thought: whatever anyone knows is always known from a perspective, so I attain truth only from my own standpoint.
  • [00:09:20] Gorisse confirms the doctrine's name — anekāntavāda, the theory of non-one-sidedness, which yields that perspectivism. She grounds it in the claim that Jaina doctrine is a philosophy of synthesis of ancient India's metaphysical theories.
  • [00:09:40] Crucially, the Jainas are realists. They explain the plurality of coexisting yet apparently conflicting valid epistemic stances by the complexity of the knowable itself — the complexity is in the object, not merely in us. This drove them to original semantic approaches: the theory of viewpoints (naya), plus a parallel theory of angles of analysis used in hermeneutics.
  • [00:10:21] That hermeneutic application is especially for interpreting texts — above all monastic rules. Adamson's example: if some monastic orders say you should be naked and others say you shouldn't, you can contextualize both by noting that the recipients differ, so different practices serve the same purpose. Gorisse notes this is one of the main divergences between Mahāvīra and the previous spiritual teacher (a reference to Pārśva, whose name the audio drops).

docs.title: What it means for a claim to be only contextually valid
docs.text:
• [00:11:01] Adamson asks what it means for a claim to be only contextually valid. Gorisse takes her examples from rival epistemological traditions. The Buddhist insistence on momentariness represents a perspective that fixes on the most specific aspect of the knowable — it says something deep and true about the transient character of phenomena.
  • [00:11:44] Human knowledge requires recognizing common features, but we can halt our focus at different levels, from the most specific to the most general. Buddhists stop at the most specific. That is a partially correct but incomplete account — it cannot, for instance, think a persisting self and ethical responsibility.
  • [00:12:12] The Jainas go further: even perspectives that recognize different aspects can fail. They are keen to argue that Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika are wrong to treat a substance (e.g. a table) and its qualities (e.g. its touchable quality) as two distinct entities linked by a relation of inherence.
  • [00:12:39] On the Jaina theory of identity-in-difference, there is one single complex entity that can be grasped either under its substantial or its qualitative aspect — a "fluidity" also manifest in their atomist physics: atoms are all alike, take on specific characteristics, and evolve into the five elements.
  • [00:13:14] Adamson checks his understanding: the Buddhist momentariness thesis is "not completely wrong" because there is something momentary about our existence, but it is not the whole story (Gorisse: exactly). Yet the Jainas don't simply say all theories are correct — when Vaiśeṣika splits an underlying substance from its property, the Jainas say that's wrong, because you're really thinking of the same object two ways. The upshot: there are complex entities understandable only from many perspectives, and rival schools usually manage only one perspective at best. Gorisse agrees.

docs.title: Does non-one-sidedness apply beyond philosophy?
docs.text:
• [00:14:14] Adamson wonders whether the theory is only about philosophical theories or applies more broadly. If we're both sitting in chairs, would they apply non-one-sidedness to that belief — "yeah, you're sitting in a chair, but that's only one perspective on a more complex situation"?
  • [00:14:49] Gorisse: their focus is philosophical theories, especially the permanence or impermanence of metaphysical entities like the soul. But if you can find practical value, there's no problem applying the perspectivism to everyday life.
  • [00:15:08] She cites Saṅghadāsa, a 6th-century commentator on monastic rules, who argued that under-specified statements can be quite useful for adapting rules that are too strict, via a "wise contextual interpretation."
  • [00:15:40] For the chair, she can find no practical use; but in court one might say "I have not been acting as a citizen but as an ethical agent" with another set of underlying rules. Adamson extends it: one set of responsibilities as a father, another as a philosophy teacher — and probably to politics too. He concludes it's "a very powerful idea."

docs.title: The self-refutation objection
docs.text:
• [00:16:18] Adamson raises an objection: the Jainas seem to claim that the theory of non-one-sidedness is correct — not just one perspective among others, but the right epistemology. So aren't they inconsistent, failing to apply their own theory to itself?
  • [00:16:57] Gorisse's reply: non-one-sidedness functions as meta-epistemology. Just as the rules governing the movement of spatial objects don't apply to space itself (as the condition of possibility of motion), the rules of epistemological theories needn't apply to a theory of what makes a good epistemological theory.
  • [00:17:26] She concedes Adamson is right that they do develop a substantive epistemology and conception of the world, and defend it against rivals. Her way to make sense of it: the complex object they aim to know is complex in such a way that the only way to know it is to disregard any particular focus and become aware of the manifold particular-and-universal aspects. So they are "practicing non-one-sidedness even in developing their conception of the world."

docs.title: How they defend non-one-sidedness — by refutation, like Nāgārjuna
docs.text:
• [00:18:12] Adamson adds that they defend non-one-sidedness against one-sided theories by attacking those theories, not by giving an a-priori argument for non-one-sidedness.
  • [00:18:37] Gorisse: yes — and not only on the ground that the rivals are one-sided. They also attack them as incoherent theories that don't hold up.
  • [00:18:54] Adamson draws the parallel: like Nāgārjuna attacking Vedic positions with skeptical arguments, the Jaina skeptical arguments expose the limitations of one-sidedness. Gorisse: there's no positive way to establish non-one-sidedness, but one can refute every one-sided claim — close to Nāgārjuna in that way.
  • [00:19:25] But it's not a skeptical theory, Adamson stresses: they don't say knowledge is impossible; they say knowledge is possible, but only if you adopt a variety of viewpoints. Gorisse: indeed, and humans can even draw up an extensive, exhaustive classification of the types of stance on the knowable — a "deep faith in knowledge."

docs.title: The mango: three theories of inference
docs.text:
• [00:19:54] One sign of that faith is inference, where the Jainas wage a polemic against the Buddhists. Adamson's favorite example (from her papers): from a mango's color I infer its taste — if it looks ripe, it will taste ripe (sweet). Buddhists and Jainas account for this differently.
  • [00:20:37] Gorisse: I'd like to know whether a mango will taste ripe before I taste it (and pay for it). A good way is to reason from the evidence of its ripe color, then ask whether there is a necessary relationship between color and taste.
  • [00:21:11] Dignāga (5th–6th c.) sets three conditions for the color to be good evidence: (1) this mango actually has the ripe color; (2) every ripe mango I've tasted had that color; (3) I've never tasted an unripe mango with that color.
  • [00:21:47] The Jainas — and others — object that these conditions are neither sufficient nor necessary, because such a state of affairs potentially describes an accidental, not a necessary, relation.
  • [00:22:08] For the Jainas, evidence is good only if known to be "impossible otherwise" — avinābhāva — and this is grasped by a separate type of knowledge called Tarka, functioning as a direct discernment of the universal.
  • [00:22:24] The Buddhist Dharmakīrti (6th c.) refutes the need for any such extra knowledge. Evidence is good if one can show an essential or causal relationship between taste and color — giving an ontic foundation to valid reasoning. In the mango case it's a combination of two causal relations: the ripeness causes the color (and is the only explanation of that specific color), and by the same reasoning the ripeness causes the taste.
  • [00:23:20] Here the Jainas disagree with Dharmakīrti. They argue some inferences rest not on essential/causal relations but on relations of co-presence (color and taste) and of succession (e.g. the rising of stars) — these too can ground sound inferences. Accepting such inferences shows the Jainas grant a deeper regularity of worldly phenomena than the Buddhists do.
  • [00:24:03] Adamson reconstructs the three positions: (1) Dignāga — as long as color and taste are always found together, infer one from the other; (2) Dharmakīrti — you need an underlying cause (ripeness) producing both, which guarantees the inference; (3) Jainas — Dharmakīrti is right that Dignāga's mere constant conjunction isn't enough, but you needn't appeal to an underlying nature: past experience suffices, so it's more like inference based on induction. Gorisse: "Yes, it's exactly this."

docs.title: Logical analysis, and Adamson's own verdict
docs.text:
• [00:25:26] This, Gorisse says, is one of many examples of logical analysis in the classical Indian debating hall. After Dharmakīrti it chiefly asks: what are the exact properties between which a necessary relation holds? It's mainly concerned with metaphysical topics — e.g. does "being an effect" necessarily presuppose having a conscious producer? If so, one can build an argument for the pervasive action of a god in the world. "When we speak about logic in India, this is all about the pervasion of one property by another."
  • [00:26:13] Adamson confesses that if we're really talking about necessary inferences, he's "totally on Dharmakīrti's side." Dignāga's critics are right that two properties merely always being found together doesn't make them necessarily connected — they might come apart later, and induction famously doesn't license necessary inference. Dharmakīrti can appeal to an underlying nature or cause that necessitates: whatever has the ripe color has the ripe taste.
  • [00:27:00] Gorisse: so Dharmakīrti goes from universal relations to necessary ones — "if I know there's an oak, I know there's a tree," and even if every tree were destroyed this stays true. Whereas the Jaina who says "one star rises, so the other will rise" faces the worry: what if the second star dies?
  • [00:27:31] Her way to make sense of the Jainas wanting necessity and not merely universality: they grant such a deep regularity of worldly phenomena that, the next time the universe manifests, the nature of the stars is such that one will succeed the other as before. Adamson: so they appeal to the theory of world cycles to explain how an inductive inference could license necessary claims. Gorisse: "Exactly."

docs.title: Tying it back to ethics and liberation
docs.text:
• [00:28:12] To close, Adamson returns to the ethical/soteriological frame: like everyone in ancient India, the Jainas care about liberation and freedom from suffering — but how do these abstract epistemological ideas connect?
  • [00:28:43] Gorisse first names the standard answer, then rejects it. Non-one-sidedness is often called intellectual nonviolence — the intellectual version of not harming other beings, at the core of Jainism and an inspiration to Gandhi. But this is unconvincing: rival theories aren't all merely partially good (Jaina theories are completely good), they're usually dismissed entirely, not just partially — at best assimilated into Jaina theory. That cross-sectarian assimilation, she notes, lets Jainas borrow from rivals to an "impressive" degree.
  • [00:30:01] Adamson: right — if the point were just "I'm non-violent, so I won't argue," why spend so much time refuting other theories? Gorisse: exactly, that's not what they're doing.
  • [00:30:11] Her better account: the three ethical principles of Jainism are non-violence, non-attachment, and non-absolutism. In practicing non-absolutism one acts with special care and realizes that everything is interconnected — and the interpretive techniques tied to non-one-sidedness yield the same recognition of interconnection.
  • [00:30:46] This helps stop the inflow of karmic matter: once we see the interconnected paradigm, we cease desiring external objects. So the practice of perspectivism is genuinely part of ethical behavior.
  • [00:31:08] Adamson restates it: the maxim isn't "don't be violent" but "don't have a limited set of concerns — extend your concern to everything, because everything is interconnected," which goes with seeing the world's complexity from a maximally well-rounded set of viewpoints. Gorisse: "Yes, this is what I meant."
  • [00:31:32] Adamson finds Jaina epistemology "quite attractive" — convinced by the epistemology if not the theory of inference — and thanks Gorisse before signing off to next time.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Marie-Hélène Gorisse — the guest; Senior Teaching Fellow at SOAS (London) and at Ghent University; works on Jaina logic and inferential reasoning.
  • Jainas / Jainism — religious-philosophical tradition reacting against Vedic ritualism via ascetic practice; one of the three main parties (with Buddhists and Hindu Nyāya/Vaiśeṣika/Mīmāṃsā) in India's debating hall.
  • Mahāvīra — last great Jaina spiritual leader (5th c. BCE); attained omniscience and liberation while still embodied, then spontaneously taught what he knew.
  • soteriology — Jaina metaphysics is subordinated to liberation; logic serves epistemology, which serves the realization of one's true (omniscient) nature.
  • soul / non-soul dualism — souls are isolated, independent subjects whose essence is consciousness; non-soul is matter and its organizing principles.
  • karma — for the Jainas a kind of matter that develops the consequences of our acts and produces limited mental states; liberation = shedding it to recover innate omniscience.
  • anekāntavāda (non-one-sidedness) — the signature doctrine: a realist perspectivism holding that rival schools each grasp one true aspect of an irreducibly complex reality.
  • naya / nayavāda (viewpoints) — the semantic theory of perspectives; all knowledge is from a standpoint, fixed at some level from most specific to most general.
  • identity-in-difference — the Jaina view that substance and quality are one complex entity grasped two ways, against the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika split joined by inherence.
  • Saṅghadāsa — 6th-c. commentator on monastic rules; argued under-specified statements help adapt over-strict rules by contextual interpretation.
  • Digambara — Jaina group for whom the omniscient teacher's teaching flows out as a divine sound.
  • Dignāga — Buddhist logician (5th–6th c.); good evidence = three conditions of constant conjunction between mark and target (color/taste).
  • Dharmakīrti — Buddhist logician (6th c.); rejects extra knowledge-types, grounding good evidence in an essential/causal relation, moving from universality to necessity.
  • Tarka / avinābhāva — Jaina "direct discernment of the universal" (Tarka) by which evidence is known to be "impossible otherwise" (avinābhāva), licensing inference from co-presence and succession.
  • non-violence / non-attachment / non-absolutism — the three Jaina ethical principles; practicing non-absolutism realizes universal interconnection and stems the inflow of karma.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 51 — "Change of Mind: Vasubandhu and Yogācāra Buddhism"
docs.text:

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:43 In brief: The two-act career of Vasubandhu (c. 400 CE) used as a tour through the Buddhist schools: first the Abhidharma "presentist" who argues only the present is real, then — converted to Mahāyāna by his half-brother Asaṅga — the co-founder of Yogācāra, the idealist "consciousness-only" school that dissolves even the momentary external dharmas into mind. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannery"; Vasubandhu ≈ "Vasubandu/Vasubando/Vazubandu/Bosubandu/Basubandu"; Yogācāra ≈ "Yoga Chara/Yuga-chata/Yoga-chada"; Asaṅga ≈ "Asanga"; Mahāyāna ≈ "Mahayana"; Abhidharma ≈ "Abidharma/Avidharma/Abidadma"; dharma(s) ≈ "dhams/dhamas/dhattamas/datuma"; Sarvāstivāda ≈ "Sarvasivada/Sarwastivada/Sarastivada"; Vaibhāṣika ≈ "Vypashika"; Sautrāntika ≈ "Sautranta/South Trantica/Sautrantica"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagajuna/Nagadjuna/Nagadren"; Madhyamaka ≈ "Madyamaka"; Vijñānavāda ≈ "Jianna Vada/Vigyana Vada"; cittamātra ≈ "Chitramatra"; citta/manas/vijñāna ≈ "Chita, Manas, Vijnana"; svabhāva ≈ "swabava/svava"; Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra ≈ "Sutra of Profound Secrets"; Bhāviveka ≈ "Baveika/Bavavika"; Dignāga ≈ "Dignaga").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Vasubandhu — Buddhist thinker, c. 400 CE; whose one career "ties together numerous strands of the ancient Buddhist tradition," moving from Abhidharma controversialist to Yogācāra idealist [00:01:06].
  • Asaṅga — Vasubandhu's older half-brother, who converts him to the Mahāyāna; co-founder with him of Yogācāra [00:01:18].
  • Yogācāra (also Vijñānavāda, "the teaching of consciousness") — the idealist branch of Mahāyāna founded by the brothers [00:01:41].
  • Sarvāstivāda / Vaibhāṣika — the Abhidharma school the early Vasubandhu attacks; holds all dharmas (past, present, future) are real [00:04:37].
  • Nāgārjuna and the Madhyamaka — the other wing of Mahāyāna, the comparison-point for placing Yogācāra [00:08:24].

docs.title: Big Brother, and the career of Vasubandhu
docs.text:
• [00:00:36] Today's episode, "Change of Mind: Vasubandhu and Yogācāra Buddhism." Adamson opens with Orwell's 1984 and its sinister repurposing of "Big Brother": the totalitarians play on the fact that big brothers are objects of love and admiration — you fight with your older brother but also look up to him, hoping to benefit from his protection, experience, and know-how.
  • [00:01:06] This may explain something about the intellectual career of Vasubandhu, a Buddhist thinker who lived around 400 CE. By legend he was converted to the Mahāyāna branch of Buddhism through the good offices of his own older half-brother, Asaṅga.
  • [00:01:23] Before that, Vasubandhu had been a controversialist within the Abhidharma branch, attacking rival Abhidharmikas for their views on past and future reality. Once brought around to the Mahāyāna way of seeing things, he joined Asaṅga as co-founder of one branch within Mahāyāna, Yogācāra — often seen as a kind of idealist version of Buddhism that rejects even the minimal concessions to extra-mental reality made by the Abhidharma Buddhists.
  • [00:01:57] So this one man's career ties together numerous strands of the ancient tradition. The welter of schools and sub-schools is confusing — especially since some have more than one name: Yogācāra is also known as the Vijñānavāda, "the teaching of consciousness," for reasons that will become clear.

docs.title: One question to organize the schools: continuity
docs.text:
• [00:02:19] The branches were explained back in episode 43, but Adamson re-frames them around one central philosophical question debated between the schools: how do we account for the apparent continuity of things in the world — inanimate objects, animate beings, or our own selves?
  • [00:02:43] Everyday common sense gives a straightforward answer: these things seem continuously real because they are real. Suppose I see my big brother, the art historian, reading an art-history book. The book in his hand, my brother, and I myself are all substances that persist through time. We also interact — I look over his shoulder; he asks whether I shouldn't have a philosophy book to work through. Such causal interactions even cross time: the next day I remember what he was reading and how many nice pictures it had.
  • [00:03:18] The Buddhists, of course, reject this commonsensical view. Belief in the enduring self is indelibly linked to suffering, so we must give it up to achieve liberation.
  • [00:03:35] More generally, per Abhidharma teaching, continuous substances have only apparent reality. What is really real are atomic, momentary qualities — the so-called dharmas. When we seem to see a book or a brother stably existing from moment to moment, we are assembling fleeting elements into a whole, and that whole has only conventional reality — like the famous chariot that is no more than the sum of its parts.

docs.title: The Sarvāstivāda answer: past and future are real too
docs.text:
• [00:03:59] Yet the Buddhists still need to explain the causal relations between apparent things — especially hard for causation across time. When my only-conventionally-real brother tosses his conventionally-real book onto the conventionally-real table and it bangs (art-history books being impressively large), how do the elemental features I register as his body and its throwing motion produce the noise a second later?
  • [00:04:31] In his early career Vasubandhu sets out to refute a group of Buddhists who gave a surprising answer. To maximize confusion this school also has two names — the Sarvāstivāda, also known as Vaibhāṣika. Like other Abhidharmikas they deny the persistent reality of objects, which are nothing but fictitious combinations of momentary dharmas.
  • [00:04:51] However, for them all the dharmas are real — whether past, present, or future. This guarantees causation across time: if a now-past dharma were non-existent, it could not give rise to a present dharma.
  • [00:05:11] Here Vasubandhu enters: he studied Sarvāstivāda and wrote a treatise setting out its doctrines in verses — then subjected those same teachings to a thorough critique in a commentary on his own verses.

docs.title: Vasubandhu the "presentist": only the present is real
docs.text:
• [00:05:31] Vasubandhu calls his own version of Abhidharma Sautrāntika, meaning that it follows the Buddhist sūtras. Like modern philosophers who call themselves presentists, he insists only present things are real. That sounds like a refreshing concession to common sense in the midst of an intra-Buddhist debate — but he is not merely relying on common sense; he has arguments.
  • [00:06:01] From his point of view the Sarvāstivāda theory ironically sounds like a form of eternalism: if past, present, and future things are all permanently real, that is hardly a suitable doctrine for Buddhists. Besides, if all these things are real, why are only some of them present and currently active? Unless we can explain that, we can't account for the fact that you can only read a history-of-philosophy book presently in your hands — not one still in the future, or already lost to history.
  • [00:06:28] The Sarvāstivādins may reply that past things still have present effects — memories of previous events, or the tossed book that bangs only now when it lands. But Vasubandhu can explain how past things keep having effects even once they stop existing (which, being instantaneous, they always do immediately): there is a causal continuum from one dharma to the next, the throwing-motion causing further motion through the air, the chain culminating in a bang.
  • [00:07:05] Or — a case that interests him more — past actions cause present karmic fruits indirectly, through an unbroken chain of momentary dharmas. He compares this to the way a seed that no longer exists has given rise to a sprout, then a mature plant, then the flower we see now.
  • [00:07:24] The same analysis applies to the apparent self that initiated a previous action and now reaps its karmic reward or punishment. There is no real enduring self, but the elements we falsely take to constitute it are part of a chain of causal influence passing second to second — like a flame being passed from one candle to another.

docs.title: The conversion: from Abhidharma to Mahāyāna
docs.text:
• [00:07:47] Per the traditional story, Vasubandhu wrote this defence of Sautrāntika Abhidharma — attacking Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma — before he came over to Mahāyāna under his brother Asaṅga's influence. (If you're struggling to keep up, don't worry: all these people and schools were merely conventional realities anyway.)
  • [00:08:05] Once converted, Vasubandhu wrote a series of powerfully argumentative works attacking the Abhidharma approach as a whole. This is not our first contact with Mahāyāna: that branch includes the Madhyamaka philosophy, ably if perplexingly represented by Nāgārjuna. Asaṅga and Vasubandhu may have seen themselves as defending something like Nāgārjuna's position, "to the extent that he had a position."
  • [00:08:36] The brothers' approach is prefigured in a text called the Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra (the "Sūtra of Profound Secrets"), which offers a third turning of the wheel of Buddhist doctrine, claiming to bring together the teachings of the first two wheels — Abhidharma and (the earlier) Mahāyāna.

docs.title: Dharmas themselves become mental constructions
docs.text:
• [00:08:59] This later Vasubandhu shares with Nāgārjuna a frankly critical approach to the dharma-theory of Abhidharma. He does to the dharmas exactly what Abhidharma had done to everyday objects: just as they rejected books and brothers as figments of the mind, now Vasubandhu suggests that even the momentary elemental dharmas are mental constructions.
  • [00:09:17] This seems a radical shift from his earlier Sautrāntika doctrine, but it actually retains something of it. Before, he insisted past and future things are unreal — only the present phenomena, both of the world outside us and of mental life, exist. Now he realizes he can do without the external phenomena while retaining the internal, mental ones. Things outside us are merely apparent — comparable to the hair-like images seen by someone with an eye disease. Since everything is a construction of the mind, mental reality is the only reality there is.
  • [00:09:52] How does he justify this breathtaking move? As an application of a principle of philosophical economy already used by other Buddhists: if we can explain our experiences without recognizing something as real, we should eliminate it from our metaphysics. The Abhidharmikas had eliminated chariots, books, and brothers; the earlier Vasubandhu had shown we can do without past and future reality; now the later Vasubandhu contends we don't need present external reality either.

docs.title: Affected by unreal things: the reductionist, not the skeptic
docs.text:
• [00:10:29] He argues mostly by answering objections meant to force him to accept that something is externally existent. His hypothetical opponent complains: if external things are unreal, they could have no effect on us.
  • [00:10:43] Vasubandhu rejoins that people are affected by unreal things — in dreams and hallucinations, or in images the damned see in hell. The point is not that "life is but a dream": dreaming is itself a distinctive mental state, as is being in a faint, so he need not appeal to the idea that we can't tell whether we're awake.
  • [00:11:09] Rather, his point is that our mental experiences can arise without any real external stimulus. His approach is not skeptical but reductionist: mental events are caused, and in fact can only be caused, by other mental events. An external dharma could never be the thing I am perceiving right now, because the dharma is only momentary and would have ceased existing by the time I register awareness of it.
  • [00:11:31] Instead there is a stream of mental experience, which Vasubandhu calls citta, manas, or vijñāna — words for mind or consciousness, for him basically equivalent. Hence Yogācāra's alternative name, the Vijñānavāda: the teaching of consciousness, the doctrine of mind/consciousness only — cittamātra.

docs.title: The storehouse consciousness
docs.text:
• [00:11:55] Vasubandhu still holds his earlier idea of a chain of causality, but now the chain consists only of mental events: everything about our current mental life results from previous mental events. A past event may take time to make itself felt in current awareness — a beautiful botanical metaphor: like dye pulled in through the stem of a growing flower, eventually coloring the petals as they unfold.
  • [00:12:32] At a more technical level he invokes the storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna), already proposed in the Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra. Mental events are like currents coming to the surface of a stream, or seeds planted earlier finally coming to fruit. These metaphors capture how we can direct attention to impressions received in past moments.
  • [00:12:55] Consider a childhood memory — the time your big brother defended you from a bully on the playground. Though not continuously remembered, the memory remains in storage, available as possible content for consciousness.
  • [00:13:13] Vasubandhu is sensitive to the fact that the storehouse-consciousness idea is not found in the Buddhist scriptures — but shrugs it off: plenty written about the Buddha has been lost, and perhaps a reference to this doctrine went missing too.

docs.title: Still a Buddhist: liberation from suffering through non-duality
docs.text:
• [00:13:28] Any doubts about his Buddhist motivation are dispelled by his frequent references to liberation from suffering. The reductionist metaphysics of Buddhism always aimed at eliminating suffering: suffering comes from attachment, and if we dispel belief in the reality of things we can wean ourselves off attachment to them — though this also requires extensive spiritual training, not just following arguments to their conclusion.
  • [00:14:04] These features are alive in Yogācāra, whose very name comes from its emphasis on spiritual practices, or yoga — meditation and mindfulness.
  • [00:14:13] Vasubandhu names the attitude that gives rise to attachment: duality. We suffer because we contrast ourselves as subjects against the objects of perception and desire. In reality this contrast is an illusion. Common sense is wrong to suppose there is a world of persisting objects outside us — and Abhidharma Buddhism does not go far enough, since it still accepts external objects of awareness, namely the dharmas.
  • [00:14:44] Yogācāra takes a further step — or two. First, for Vasubandhu the objects of the mind are internal to the mind, themselves part of mental life. Then comes the still more challenging step: giving up even a mental version of the subject–object contrast. The correct non-dual attitude is one in which the mind no longer treats anything as an object of its awareness. So fundamental is this undermining of everything we take ourselves to know that Vasubandhu calls his teaching of non-duality a "revolution at the basis."

docs.title: The three natures (svabhāva)
docs.text:
• [00:15:19] The revolution of this third wheel has, appropriately, three stages, which Vasubandhu sets out: What is it that appears? A construction of the non-existent. How does it appear? Through dualities. What is its non-existence? A state of non-existent duality. He frames these as the three kinds of independent nature, or svabhāva.
  • [00:15:51] First, an entirely fictive nature — fabricated or constructed by the mind — the natures of the apparent things in our external environment; compared to an elephant conjured out of wooden props by a magician's sleight of hand.
  • [00:16:09] Second, an interdependent nature: subject and object of awareness depending on one another — for example, an act of sight and that which is seen.
  • [00:16:22] Third and finally, an awareness that has given up duality and become perfected or fulfilled — even the mind is not an object for itself. At this stage one is finally liberated from suffering by being liberated from illusion.

docs.title: Where Yogācāra sits: alongside and against Madhyamaka
docs.text:
• [00:16:33] That Vasubandhu sets out his three stages using the familiar word svabhāva is significant: we saw this word in Nāgārjuna, who targeted the very notion in his critique. This raises the question of where Yogācāra sits in the history of Buddhism.
  • [00:16:53] It is grouped with Nāgārjuna's middle way (Madhyamaka) under the broader heading of Mahāyāna, and seems to have much in common with it. Yogācāra too styles itself a middle way, and for the same reason Nāgārjuna gave: it tries to steer between the extremes of nihilism and eternalism (reification) — banishing all things as non-existent, on one side, and taking all things to have stable independent reality, on the other.
  • [00:17:28] Both Mahāyāna traditions express their middle way as an acknowledgement of the emptiness of things. For Nāgārjuna this was the upshot of his skeptical attack on substance, motion, and perception; for Yogācāra it is the upshot of the critique of subject–object duality in consciousness. As Asaṅga puts it: "the non-existence of duality is indeed the existence of non-existence — this is the definition of emptiness."
  • [00:17:52] Nonetheless, the later tradition saw disagreement and even harsh polemic between the two schools. A 6th-century Madhyamaka thinker, Bhāviveka, argues that Yogācāra falls into both extremes on either side of the correct middle way:
  • Where Madhyamaka grants the legitimacy of conventional attitudes toward reality, Yogācāra rejects conventional beliefs entirely — which Bhāviveka counts as a form of nihilism.
  • On the other hand, Yogācāra is reificationist because it accepts the genuine reality of some phenomena — those occurring in the mind.
  • [00:18:37] Bhāviveka has a good point. Vasubandhu does aim to expose the fictionality of everyday objects, so conventional reality seems completely undermined in his philosophy. And even if Yogācāra's mental forms are empty, they constitute a reality that is mental — and Nāgārjuna would presumably not hesitate to attack this mental version of reality as itself empty.

docs.title: Idealism — and beyond it
docs.text:
• [00:19:08] Adamson closes on yet another name modern scholars give Yogācāra: idealism. Vasubandhu makes reality exclusively mental — constituted by nothing but presently-occurrent mental events caused by earlier mental events — so Yogācāra certainly seems to merit the name; it may be one of the earliest forms of idealism in the whole history of philosophy.
  • [00:19:37] But calling Vasubandhu an idealist may underestimate his radicalism. Remember that the third, perfected nature is not just one in which we realize all the objects of our mental activity are themselves mental — it is one in which there is no duality between mind and its objects at all. It is hard, perhaps impossible, to say what lies beyond mental activity structured dualistically; but whatever that reality is, it does not seem to consist of ideas. If Vasubandhu is an idealist, his idealism is "only the last step but one on the path to enlightenment."
  • [00:20:13] Likewise, this is not the last step in the journey through Yogācāra. Next time: another major figure of the school, Dignāga, active in the early 6th century, who continues the "revolution at the basis" with a profound critique of the idea that we have knowledge of external objects. "Remember, Big Brother is watching — or rather listening, and so should you."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Vasubandhu — Buddhist thinker, c. 400 CE; his two-phase career (Abhidharma "presentist" → Yogācāra idealist) frames the whole episode.
  • Asaṅga — Vasubandhu's older half-brother; converts him to Mahāyāna and co-founds Yogācāra with him; coiner of the quoted definition of emptiness as "the existence of non-existence."
  • Yogācāra — the Mahāyāna branch the brothers found; "consciousness-only" idealism; named for its emphasis on yoga (meditation, mindfulness).
  • Vijñānavāda — alternative name for Yogācāra: "the teaching of consciousness."
  • Abhidharma — the broader analytic Buddhist tradition that reduces ordinary objects to momentary dharmas; both Sarvāstivāda and Sautrāntika fall under it.
  • dharmas — the atomic, momentary qualities that are "really real," out of which the merely conventional whole (book, brother, self) is assembled.
  • conventional vs. real — persisting substances (chariot, book, self) have only conventional reality; only the momentary elements are real.
  • Sarvāstivāda / Vaibhāṣika — Abhidharma school the early Vasubandhu refutes; holds all dharmas (past, present, future) are real, to secure causation across time — which Vasubandhu charges sounds like eternalism.
  • Sautrāntika — Vasubandhu's own early "presentist" position: only present things are real; past effects persist via an unbroken causal chain of dharmas (seed → sprout → flower; flame passed candle to candle).
  • karma — past actions cause present karmic fruits indirectly, through the momentary causal chain; no enduring self underlies it.
  • citta / manas / vijñāna — words for mind/consciousness, for Vasubandhu basically equivalent; the stream of mental experience.
  • cittamātra — "consciousness-only / mind-only"; the doctrine that mental reality is the only reality.
  • ālaya-vijñāna (storehouse consciousness) — the repository where past impressions are stored and made available to later awareness; from the Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra; not in the older scriptures.
  • Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra ("Sūtra of Profound Secrets") — text prefiguring Yogācāra; offers a "third turning of the wheel" uniting Abhidharma and earlier Mahāyāna.
  • svabhāva (independent / own nature) — Vasubandhu's "three natures": fictive/constructed (the magician's wooden elephant), interdependent (subject and object of an act of sight), and perfected/non-dual; the same term Nāgārjuna had targeted.
  • non-duality / "revolution at the basis" — the abolition of the subject–object contrast; the perfected stage where the mind treats nothing as its object; the cure for attachment and suffering.
  • emptiness — shared upshot of both Mahāyāna wings: for Nāgārjuna from the critique of substance/motion/perception, for Yogācāra from the critique of subject–object duality.
  • Nāgārjuna / Madhyamaka — the other Mahāyāna wing, a "middle way" between nihilism and eternalism; comparison-point and later polemical rival of Yogācāra.
  • Bhāviveka — 6th-century Madhyamaka critic who charges Yogācāra with falling into both extremes — nihilism (rejecting conventional reality) and reification (granting real mental phenomena).
  • idealism — modern label for Yogācāra; apt, but possibly underselling Vasubandhu, whose perfected non-dual reality lies beyond even ideas.
  • Dignāga — early-6th-century Yogācāra figure, subject of the next episode; critic of our supposed knowledge of external objects.

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:22:47 In brief: Dignāga, one of the most original thinkers in Indian philosophy, argues that the immediate objects of perception cannot be external things (not even atoms), that perception grasps only ineffable particulars while universals are mere mental constructs, and — in his apoha or "exclusion" theory — that words mean not by latching onto real universals but by their position of inclusion and exclusion within a conceptual hierarchy. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannery"; Dignāga ≈ "Degnaga"; Pramāṇa-samuccaya ≈ "Pramana Samu Jaya"; Hetucakra ≈ "Hetu Chakra Damaru"; Ālambana-parīkṣā ≈ "Alambana Parikshya"; Vasubandhu ≈ "Vasubandu"; Yogācāra ≈ "Yoga Chara"; Abhidharma ≈ "Abidharma"; Dharmakīrti ≈ "Dama Kirti / Damakirti"; Asaṅga ≈ "Asanga"; Vātsyāyana ≈ "Vatsyayana"; Uddyotakara ≈ "Odiotakara"; apoha ≈ "apoha").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Dignāga — radically original Buddhist philosopher whose ideas reshaped both Buddhist thought and rival schools; the episode's subject [00:01:48].
  • Pramāṇa-samuccaya ("collected verses on the sources of knowledge") — Dignāga's greatest, mature work [00:02:21].
  • Ālambana-parīkṣā ("examination of the foundations of experience") — an eight-verse treatise rethinking perception, the episode's starting point [00:02:35].
  • Hetucakra(ḍamaru) ("study of the Wheel of Reasons") — his short treatise analysing fallacious argument [00:02:28].
  • Dharmakīrti — Dignāga's great follower who reworks his ideas (and partly compromises their elegance) [00:02:06].
  • The Nyāya school — the direct realists Dignāga argues against [00:03:18].

docs.title: A cloud, a giraffe, and a crocodile — the parable of Liza
docs.text:
• [00:00:36] Jack and Jill, idle and lazy, lie on their backs watching clouds and argue: Jill says one cloud looks like a crocodile, Jack insists it's a dead ringer for a giraffe. A third child, Liza, who has more conscientiously fetched her water, settles the dispute by pointing out that the cloud is simply a cloud — the animals are the work of their imaginations, "superimposed" on the cloud.
  • [00:01:13] Liza pushes further: even the concept of cloud is something we superimpose on our perceptions. So what are we perceiving — just something fluffy and white? No: the object of perception is ineffable, and even "fluffiness" and "whiteness" are themselves mental constructions. With that she departs (and, Jack notes, "there's a hole in her bucket"). Liza, it turns out, has been reading Dignāga.

docs.title: Dignāga and his works
docs.text:
• [00:01:48] Liza's enthusiasm is well placed: Dignāga is "one of the most original thinkers in the whole history of Indian philosophy." His ideas transformed not just Buddhist thought but the theories of rival schools — later thinkers grappled with them and with their reworking in his great follower Dharmakīrti, and even his opponents quietly adjusted their own systems to absorb his approaches and distinctions.
  • [00:02:21] His greatest work is the Pramāṇa-samuccaya, "collected verses on the sources of knowledge." He also wrote two short treatises: the Hetucakra ("study of the Wheel of Reasons"), an innovative analysis of fallacious argumentation, and the Ālambana-parīkṣā ("examination of the foundations of experience"), a work of just eight verses offering a radical rethink of Buddhist ideas about perception. The episode begins with this little treatise.

docs.title: Direct realism and the Nyāya
docs.text:
• [00:02:53] Common sense says we use perception to grasp ordinary objects in our environment — clouds, giraffes, crocodiles. Philosophers rarely leave common sense alone; at the very least they coin a fancy name, here direct realism.
  • [00:03:18] In the Indian tradition direct realism was upheld by the Nyāya school. They were led into some strange claims of their own — that we can also perceive universals and absences — but their basic point was that common sense is right: we really do perceive whole objects, not merely the nearest surface of a thing, or bare flashes of colour, wafting scents and momentary noises.

docs.title: Why external things can't be the objects of perception (the Ālambana-parīkṣā)
docs.text:
• [00:03:43] Dignāga prefers to revise common sense — unsurprising for a Buddhist, but he goes further, criticising earlier Buddhist theories as insufficiently sceptical. He follows in the footsteps of Vasubandhu (who may have been his teacher), developing the Yogācāra approach to perception. He argues that the immediate objects of perception cannot be external things — not even the fleeting atomic dharmas recognised in Abhidharma Buddhism.
  • [00:04:11] The Buddhists call the supposed object "out there" the ālambana — the foundation, ground or objective support of the perceptual experience. Dignāga sets two demands on anything that could be the real object of a perception. First, it must be the cause of the experience: to see a giraffe, the giraffe must cause my visual perception. But causation alone isn't enough — if a mad scientist causes my perception of a giraffe, the scientist is the cause yet I am not seeing the scientist. Second, then, the perception must match the thing perceived — my experience must have "the same form" as that thing. How could I be perceiving a giraffe if the thing I claim to perceive has the shape of a crocodile? Unlike Liza's bucket, this looks watertight.
  • [00:05:22] Dignāga now draws a surprising result: external things can't satisfy both demands. Buddhists hold that clouds, giraffes and crocodiles are made of atoms. Atoms do seem the sort of thing that can cause perception, so they tick the first box — the atoms making up a cloud cause me to see the cloud. But I do not see the atoms; atoms aren't perceptible, and even if observable under special conditions, it isn't atoms I see when my gaze falls on a cloud. So the second requirement fails: the atoms don't match the perception in form.
  • [00:05:56] Maybe we don't see individual atoms but a conglomerate of them — the collection making up a crocodile. That fixes the second condition, since the conglomeration does have the matching form. But sadly the conglomeration is "nothing over and above the atoms," so it can't be a distinct cause, and the first condition fails. Analogy [00:06:17]: from a distance you see a forest — the conglomerate, the wood and not the trees — yet it is the trees that cause your perception, because in reality there are only trees to do the causing.
  • [00:06:34] A third option: perhaps perception is caused not by the atoms or their conglomerate but by some power or shape in the atoms. Consider a rainbow — there's no real arc of colour there; it is composed of water droplets, each helping produce in you the vision of a rainbow. Interesting, but Dignāga makes short work of it: if the perception-causing feature belongs to the atoms intrinsically, the same atoms rearranged should still cause the same perception — yet when the airborne particles shift, you no longer see a rainbow. And consider the more radical recombination when "a crocodile eats and digests a giraffe," the giraffe's atoms going to build the crocodile's body — crocodiles who feast on giraffe meat don't start to look more like giraffes.
  • [00:07:40] Dignāga concludes that what we take to be ordinary objects of perception are really only products of the human mind. What we perceive he calls knowable interior forms — internal forms that both cause our experience and provide its content, something nothing outside us can do.

docs.title: Perception and inference; particulars and universals (the Pramāṇa-samuccaya)
docs.text:
• [00:08:06] For a fuller, somewhat different account, turn to the mature Pramāṇa-samuccaya. Its first chapter distinguishes two ways of apprehending the world: perception and inference (alternatively, experience and reasoning). This isn't original to him — Vasubandhu's brother Asaṅga had defined three sources of knowledge: perception, inference and testimony. Dignāga simply takes over the list and drops the third item.
  • [00:08:41] The two remaining cognitions, perception and inference, correspond respectively to the individual and the general — to particulars and universals. This sounds like common sense: there's the particular white cloud on one hand, and the universal feature of whiteness (appearing in this cloud, that cloud, and an alarming number of the hairs on your head) on the other.
  • [00:09:06] But Dignāga insists universals do not exist in nature, only in our minds. Like the nominalists discussed in the medieval-philosophy podcast, he thinks universals are mere concepts and that everything real is singular or individual. He takes it to be a straightforward contradiction that one universal could be in many instances — a single whiteness in many clouds — so we certainly cannot perceive universals.
  • [00:09:36] As for what we can perceive, you might expect one individual cloud, or the individual white colour of a given cloud — but even to say that is to deploy the very universal concepts ("white," "cloud") that are fantasies of the mind. Instead, the objects of perception are inexpressible / ineffable. The closest we can come to imagining it is something like a perceived flash of colour — better, an entirely unclassified flash of visual awareness. Given the critique of external objects, such a flash is born in the mind, not by any external object: a particular, indefinable, momentary object of experience within our mental life.
  • [00:10:24] So much for perception. What about inference? Precisely because universals are mental constructs, we are able to think about relationships between concepts like colour, whiteness, cloud and giraffe — that white things are coloured, that some clouds look like giraffes, that giraffes are not white. This lets us organise concepts into hierarchies, like genera and species in the logic of Aristotle: giraffe falls under animal, white under colour. (This will prove central to his theory of language.) Human thought is largely the exploration of relationships between mentally constructed concepts; what lies under these constructions is not external objects but particular perceptions.

docs.title: Perception cannot err
docs.text:
• [00:11:08] Note that Dignāga is not a radical sceptic denying all knowledge. On the contrary, he thinks we have immediate knowledge through perception — a direct, undistorted sensory acquaintance uncontaminated by imagination. To secure this he even stipulates that perception can never be in error. Every apparent perceptual error — seeing a rope as a snake, a crocodile as a giraffe — is put down to the distorting intervention of concepts.
  • [00:11:57] For this reason he complains about the Nyāya definition of perception as cognition that "arises from sense objects and is unerring and inexpressible": for Dignāga the definition is not so much wrong as redundant — all true cognition is perception, and it is always unerring and inexpressible already. Error arises only when concepts, which are necessarily general, get superimposed onto perceptual data that is necessarily particular and unique. Pure, unconceptualised perception is therefore invariably error-free.

docs.title: Bracketing the external world — Dignāga vs Dharmakīrti
docs.text:
• [00:12:53] If we saw a rope and correctly classified it under the concept "rope," that too would involve mental construction, not just immediate perception. But Dignāga isn't denying the reality of the rope, or of something out in the world; he simply brackets the question of whether external things exist. Since they can't be the objects of perception (failing to both cause and match the perception), the knowledge we have through perception neither vindicates nor denies external things. Perception is entirely internal to the perceiver.
  • [00:13:29] His follower Dharmakīrti differs on two points. First, where Dignāga might more accurately be called a phenomenalist, Dharmakīrti rejects the reality of external things outright, adopting an explicitly idealist theory. Second, on error: for Dignāga all perceptual experience is free from illusion, but Dharmakīrti insists accurate perception must be not merely free from conceptual structure but also free from illusion — so there can be unconceptualised yet erroneous perception.
  • [00:14:10] Dharmakīrti gives three examples. (1) Jaundice: I see objects with a yellow colour they don't have — a defect of vision, not conceptual construction, since such defects can affect even concept-less small children and animals. (2) The whirling torch: someone spins a torch on a rope and I see only a continuous circle of light — pure visual error, because human vision can't distinguish the torch at each point of its trajectory. (3) Self-motion: when a vehicle begins to move it can look as if we are stationary and the world is moving. Dharmakīrti's example uses a boat; the modern reader may think of sitting in a train when the train on the adjacent platform appears to slide off when in fact yours is moving. (Faithful listeners may recall a similar boat example in a 14th-century medieval debate.)
  • [00:15:39] So Dharmakīrti adds an extra clause to Dignāga's concept of perception — but at a cost: he can no longer locate all error at the conceptual level, and the elegance and explanatory power of Dignāga's theory is compromised, "albeit in the quest for truth."

docs.title: Language without universals — the apoha theory
docs.text:
• [00:16:00] Dignāga's nominalism faces an obvious objection: language is full of references to universals, so if there are no universals, how does language latch onto the world? Before Dignāga, philosophers had thought hard about word meaning. Take "the most Indian of examples," the word cow. We grasp its meaning despite its varied uses: in "the cow is standing" or "bring me the cow" it seems to stand for a particular individual cow; in "a cow is an animal" or "a cow is shorter than a giraffe" for something generic — a generic cow, or the class of all cows; in "he's playing with cows" (of a child playing with toys) or "this is a cow" (pointing to a picture) for anything with the shape of a cow.
  • [00:17:04] The great Nyāya thinker Gautama concluded that the meaning of "cow" is a composite of all three: the individual cow, the cow-shape, and the universal cowhood. Commenting on him, Vātsyāyana seems to read this as "cow" being systematically ambiguous, taking different meanings in different uses. The later Naiyāyikas Uddyotakara and Jayanta read the sūtra differently: an utterance of "cow" refers to an individual cow insofar as it possesses cowhood — the word has a "deep logical form" meaning roughly "that thing being a cow" (a demonstrative plus a predicate), so "the cow is white" is true so long as the thing picked out is both a cow and white.
  • [00:17:55] Dignāga replaces this complicated story with a simple, powerful analysis, given in the fifth chapter of his Pramāṇa-samuccaya, drawing on the conceptual hierarchy discussed earlier. In any hierarchy concepts are organised by containment and exclusion: the concept colour contains white (anything red is also coloured), while white excludes blue (nothing is both white and blue). The old answer was that this conceptual hierarchy mirrors a hierarchy of things in nature — the world is organised a certain way, our classifications reflect it, and individual words refer to things on the basis of the universals those things instantiate (that thing is a cloud because it instances cloudness, not cowness).
  • [00:19:02] Dignāga's alternative is the apoha theory — the theory of exclusion. Words need not correspond to anything external; their meaning is determined merely by their location in the conceptual hierarchy. He compares it to how groups form identity by excluding outsiders: someone may struggle to say what it positively means to be British or American, while being all too ready to exclude others for having the wrong religion, skin colour or accent.
  • [00:19:41] So too with everyday words. What exactly is a cloud? A "rather nebulous idea," hard to define positively — many shapes, colours, made of water or other vapours. Dignāga simply says "cloud" gets its meaning through its relations to other terms: the concept includes cumulus, nimbus and cirrus, is itself included under "meteorological phenomena," and excludes concepts like giraffe (even a giraffe-shaped cloud is not really a giraffe). Exclusion also handles compound expressions: "white cloud" simply excludes more than "cloud" — it excludes both non-clouds and non-white things, whereas "cloud" excludes only non-clouds.
  • [00:20:46] The great advantage: Dignāga does without real universals. Applying "cow," we aren't saying a thing instantiates a general feature in the world; we are just discriminating it from what is dissimilar — from whatever is not a cow. Universals are "concealed double negations": to say something is a cow is to say it is not a non-cow. Language works by positioning concepts relative to one another.
  • [00:21:21] Objection: what about proper names — Bessie, Gina, Hiawatha? Dignāga answers that we never apply such names to individual objects of perception (those can't be expressed in language at all); the proper name of a certain cow or giraffe actually refers to a combination of many individual perceptions. So "Bessie" is just as much a conceptual construction as the universal "cow."
  • [00:21:53] This is another advantage: the theory of language meshes with the account of perception. We never reach a concept so fine-grained that it excludes everything except a single particular — particulars are inexpressible and can only be directly perceived, while concepts and words (even proper names) always work at the level of mental construction. We move internally within that conceptual world when we infer that whatever is a cow is not a giraffe though both are animals, or that a white cloud is a cloud. Such movements are the work of inference and reason — Dignāga's logic, the subject of the next episode.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Dignāga — radically original Buddhist philosopher; argues perception's objects are internal "knowable interior forms," that universals are mind-made, and (via apoha) that words mean by exclusion within a conceptual hierarchy.
  • Pramāṇa-samuccaya — "collected verses on the sources of knowledge," Dignāga's greatest, mature work; chapter 1 distinguishes perception from inference, chapter 5 gives the apoha theory of language.
  • Ālambana-parīkṣā — "examination of the foundations of experience," an eight-verse treatise arguing external things cannot be the objects of perception.
  • Hetucakra(ḍamaru) — "study of the Wheel of Reasons," his short, innovative analysis of fallacious argumentation.
  • ālambana — the supposed external foundation/ground/objective support of a perceptual experience.
  • pramāṇa — a source or means of knowledge; Dignāga keeps two (perception, inference) and drops Asaṅga's third (testimony).
  • pratyakṣa (perception) — grasps the individual/particular; immediate, internal, and (for Dignāga) incapable of error.
  • inference — grasps the general/universal by exploring relations between mentally constructed concepts arranged in hierarchies.
  • svalakṣaṇa (the particular) — the unique, momentary, ineffable object of perception; a bare "unclassified flash of awareness," inexpressible in words.
  • direct realism — the view (held by the Nyāya) that we perceive whole external objects; what Dignāga rejects.
  • Nyāya school / Gautama / Vātsyāyana / Uddyotakara / Jayanta — the direct realists and their competing analyses of the meaning of "cow" (composite of three; systematic ambiguity; "that thing being a cow").
  • dharmas / atoms / Abhidharma — the fleeting atomic constituents external-object accounts appeal to; Dignāga shows they can't both cause and match perception.
  • Vasubandhu / Yogācāra — Dignāga's (possible) teacher and the idealist-leaning Buddhist tradition he develops; Asaṅga is Vasubandhu's brother.
  • apoha (exclusion) — Dignāga's theory that words mean by their place of inclusion/exclusion among concepts, not by corresponding to real universals; universals are "concealed double negations" (a cow = not a non-cow).
  • Dharmakīrti — Dignāga's great follower; turns phenomenalism into outright idealism and adds that accurate perception must be free from illusion as well as concepts, conceding non-conceptual error (jaundice, whirling torch, apparent self-motion).

docs.text:
← Ep 52
