🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:23:29 In brief: Dignāga's theory of inference (anumāna): why he recognizes only perception and inference as means of knowledge and demotes testimony to a kind of inference; his distinction between reasoning-for-oneself and demonstration-for-others; the mountain-smoke-fire schema of pakṣa / sādhya / hetu; the celebrated trairūpya "three conditions" for good evidence; and how his commentator Dharmakīrti reformulated those conditions and tackled the problem of induction by demanding a real causal or essential link between properties. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gennary"; Dignāga ≈ "Dignaga/Dignago"; Nyāya ≈ "Niyaya/Nayaas"; pramāṇa ≈ "pramana"; Brahminical ≈ "brachmanical"; Mīmāṃsā ≈ "Mimamsa"; Yogācāra ≈ "Yoga-Chara"; Uddyotakara ≈ "Ujotakara"; pakṣa ≈ "Paksha/Paxha"; sādhya ≈ "sadya/sadia"; hetu ≈ "hethu"; trairūpya ≈ "Treyrupa/trirupia"; pervasion (vyāpti) ≈ "pervasion"; Gaṅgeśa ≈ "Gangesha"; Dharmakīrti ≈ "Darmakirti/Dama Kirti"; eva ≈ "Eva"; svabhāva-hetu ≈ "swavava hetu"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagadruna"; śiṃśapā ≈ "shimshapha/Shimshapa"; Graham Priest ≈ "Graham Priest").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Dignāga — Buddhist epistemologist; recognizes only perception and inference as pramāṇas, and the first Indian thinker to separate the rules of reasoning from the rules of debate [00:01:24].
  • The Nyāya & Mīmāṃsā schools — the Brahminical opponents who count testimony as an independent source of knowledge [00:01:06].
  • Dignāga's collected verses on the sources of knowledge — where he sets out good vs. bad inference [00:04:29].
  • Dharmakīrti — Dignāga's hugely influential commentator who reformulated the three conditions and addressed induction [00:15:34].
  • Gaṅgeśa — 14th-century thinker who would later review over a dozen accounts of "pervasion" [00:11:17].

docs.title: Testimony on trial: why Dignāga keeps only two pramāṇas
docs.text:
• [00:00:34] A juror is doing "applied epistemology" of unusually high stakes: deciding whether to be persuaded by evidence, often in the form of testimony. Suppose a witness claims to have seen the defendant set a fire. If she's truthful, she knows he's guilty — she saw it with her own eyes. Can she transfer that knowledge to you by giving a convincing account?
  • [00:01:06] The Nyāya school would say yes: testimony is one of the fundamental sources of knowledge and so is designated a pramāṇa (means of knowledge). But as a juror you may doubt the witness's credibility, and as a philosopher you may doubt whether testimony is a knowledge-source at all.
  • [00:01:24] If so, call as your own witness the Buddhist Dignāga. As noted last time, he admits only two means of acquiring knowledge — perception and inference — and refuses to dignify testimony (the assertions of authoritative persons) with the title pramāṇa.
  • [00:01:42] His point is not that testimony never gives knowledge, but that when it does, an inference is required. To get knowledge from the arson witness you must combine her testimony about the fire with the further knowledge that she is reliable; from those two pieces you may infer the defendant's guilt.
  • [00:02:03] This may sound like "pedantic bookkeeping" — a way of trimming the pramāṇas from three to two — but it is really a Buddhist refusing to keep the books venerated in the Brahminical tradition. Prosecuting the case against the vaunted testimony of Vedic texts, Dignāga insists they provide no independent source of knowledge.
  • [00:02:26] His position answers the Nyāya most directly, but it also contrasts vividly with Mīmāṃsā epistemology: testimony is not "innocent until proven guilty" (as Mīmāṃsā held), but must be evaluated for reliability on each occasion.
  • [00:02:39] To this extent Dignāga is a rationalist — every knowledge-claim must rest on evidence directly available to the individual knower. Knowledge by testimony is no counterexample, because each of us must judge the testimony's credibility, and only if it passes muster may we infer that what it asserts is true.

docs.title: Two kinds of inference: reasoning vs. demonstration
docs.text:
• [00:03:09] We saw last time that for Dignāga direct perception grasps unique particulars. Reflection at the general or universal level — e.g. that smoke billows from houses set on fire — is imposed onto perceptual experience, an act of human construction. Inference lives at this general level.
  • [00:03:29] So: "This house is billowing smoke; when houses do that they're on fire; so it's on fire. Good thing it isn't mine." Dignāga calls this inferring to oneself — basically his term for reasoning, deciding whether to be convinced yourself.
  • [00:03:45] He contrasts it with inferring for others: what you do when trying to convince someone else, as when you calmly explain that their house is on fire because smoke is pouring out of it. If inferring-to-oneself is reasoning, inferring-for-others is demonstration — producing an explicit argument.
  • [00:04:08] Here is one of Dignāga's signal achievements: he is the first Indian thinker to distinguish the rules of reasoning (which arguments are formally valid) from the rules of debate (how to persuade people).
  • [00:04:29] A further achievement: in his collected verses on the sources of knowledge, he explains the difference between good and bad inferences — both in reasoning to oneself (reasoning well vs. badly) and in arguing for others (debating fairly vs. unfairly).

docs.title: A neutral theory — adopted even by his opponents
docs.text:
• [00:04:43] So far Dignāga's Yogācāra Buddhism has been the obvious backdrop: the demotion of testimony implies a critique of Vedic tradition, and the claim that general concepts are human constructions places him in the Buddhist tradition of philosophical skepticism.
  • [00:05:04] But when he comes to his theory of inference itself, he seems to aim at neutrality — philosophers of various schools could adopt it, and they did. His analysis was assimilated widely, including the Nyāya school from Uddyotakara onwards.
  • [00:05:28] In honour of this rare instance of Naiyāyikas and Buddhists getting on "like a house on fire," the episode shifts from the arson case to the classic Nyāya example: smoke that reveals the presence of fire on a mountain.

docs.title: The shape of an inference: pakṣa, sādhya, hetu
docs.text:
• [00:05:38] For Dignāga, any inference can be rendered as: "This mountain has fire because it has smoke." First a proposition is stated (the mountain has fire), then a reason is given (smoke).
  • [00:05:52] Note this is the reverse of the deductive pattern in European logicians from Aristotle on, where premises come first and a conclusion follows: "the mountain has smoke, therefore it has fire."
  • [00:06:06] A second contrast with Aristotle: Dignāga's reason is not explanatory. The smoke reveals the fire, or lets us predict it — but there's no asking why there's a fire. Still, Dignāga agrees with Aristotle that the proposition to be proved is something not yet known and not immediately settled by perception. (Aristotle's memorable example: standing on the moon you could just see the cause of an eclipse and need no explanation.)
  • [00:06:40] The inference patterns all share one structure. There is always an object that is the locus or basis of the inference — here the mountain — in Sanskrit the pakṣa.
  • [00:06:53] The inference seeks to show the locus has a certain property — e.g. having fire — called the sādhya (the property-to-be-proved).
  • [00:07:00] We establish this by citing a hetu: another property also possessed by the locus, which is the evidence or sign — here, having smoke.
  • [00:07:17] So every inference has the form: the locus (pakṣa) has the inferred property (sādhya) because it has the evidential property (hetu) — the mountain has fire because it has smoke.

docs.title: When evidence fails — and the need for a rule
docs.text:
• [00:07:28] Many inferences fit this form yet are bad — not compelling moves "in the space of reasons." You shouldn't infer the mountain is covered in grass because it is green: many green things aren't grass (moss, green paint, a St. Patrick's Day parade). Being green is not good evidence for grass; the evidential and inferred properties aren't connected in the right way.
  • [00:08:04] Dignāga's goal is to specify what the right way is — to define the relation among pakṣa, sādhya and hetu. That is to ask: when is evidence sufficient to convince us that one property always comes together with another?

docs.title: The trairūpya: the triple-conditioned sign
docs.text:
• [00:08:17] Dignāga's answer: the evidence must satisfy a set of three conditions — his celebrated trairūpya theory, the theory of the triple-conditioned sign.
  • [00:08:29] First condition: the evidential property must actually occur in the locus. Obvious enough — I can't use smoke as evidence the mountain is on fire unless there really is smoke on the mountain.
  • [00:08:46] The other two are subtler and bring in terminology. Dignāga introduces the similar case (homologue / sapakṣa) and the dissimilar case (heterologue / vipakṣa):
  • A similar case is any object other than the locus that has the inferred property — in our example, something else that is on fire.
  • A dissimilar case is some other object that lacks the inferred property — something not on fire.
  • [00:09:17] This is effectively a method of investigation: to learn whether a thing has a property, notice a second property it has, then check whether other things with that second property also have the first.
  • [00:09:31] So with smoke as the second property: consider a smoky kitchen — there's fire there too (smoke is looking like good evidence). Now consider something dissimilar — your own smoke-free house: no arsonist came, so it lacks smoke, and its lack of smoke coincides with its not being on fire. This confirms smoke really correlates with fire.
  • [00:10:05] These are Dignāga's second and third conditions:
  • Second condition (positive-example): the evidential property must occur together with the inferred property in at least one similar case (like the smoky kitchen).
  • Third condition (no-counterexample): in every known dissimilar case where the evidential property is absent, the inferred property is absent too (like your smoke-free, fire-free house).
  • [00:10:34] Taken together: whatever has the evidential property must have the inferred property. If every locus of smoke is a locus of fire, we can soundly infer fire from smoke in a particular place.

docs.title: Pervasion, generality, and the leaning toward induction
docs.text:
• [00:10:46] Notice Dignāga keeps his promise that inference operates at a general level, with universal concepts. Good inferences are those where a general rule or law connects the properties: "whatever is like this is like that," or in variables, "whatever is X is Y."
  • [00:11:11] Dignāga calls such a connection a relation of pervasion (vyāpti) — a topic of huge importance in later centuries. Gaṅgeśa, in the 14th century, would review more than a dozen accounts of pervasion that emerged after Dignāga.
  • [00:11:29] Could we not just rephrase Dignāga's inference as a pure deduction? Take "the mountain has smoke," add "whatever has smoke has fire," conclude "the mountain has fire." Not quite. Dignāga is primarily interested in inference as a means of acquiring knowledge — the conditions under which an inference's result is a rationally justified belief.
  • [00:12:10] So he's not interested only in form, like a logician noting the validity of "this is an X, every X is a Y, so this is a Y." He is more demanding: a good inference must be not only valid but sound — with true premises. And further still, the premises must be known to be true; only then does the inferrer know the conclusion.
  • [00:12:46] In keeping with this focus on what the reasoner actually knows, Dignāga doesn't quite require the strong "every X is Y." His demand is in one respect weaker: the reasoner must satisfy herself that every known X is known to be Y. She needn't claim all smoky things past, present and future have been or will be on fire — only that every time she has experienced smoke, there was fire.
  • [00:13:19] "The lack of exceptions proves the rule." This shows Dignāga isn't really after pure deduction but something closer to induction: looking to previous experience to justify inferences about the present and future. To that extent his trairūpya can seem familiar and even straightforward.

docs.title: Two worries about the three conditions
docs.text:
• [00:13:43] Worry one — redundancy. Saying "anything with smoke has fire" seems equivalent to "anything lacking smoke lacks fire." So why give the second and third conditions as two distinct criteria rather than one criterion stated positively or negatively?
  • [00:14:13] Perhaps because the second criterion requires us to find at least one actual similar case, whereas the third only tells us to verify that where smoke is absent, fire is absent. The third alone wouldn't guarantee there are any cases (besides the mountain itself) having both smoke and fire; the second adds a positive basis for induction.
  • [00:14:36] Worry two — the locus-exclusion problem. Dignāga always tells us to look at things other than the locus when checking similar/dissimilar cases. Fine for a one-off topic like this mountain. But consider: "Odd numbers are divisible by two because they are integers." If we exclude the class of odd numbers (the locus) from the search, then every remaining integer is divisible by two — so being an integer (evidential property) would count as good evidence for being divisible by two (inferred property). A clearly bad inference passing Dignāga's conditions.
  • [00:15:23] This unwelcome result was pointed out by Jain philosophers, who criticized him and tried to repair it. Criticism and modification also came from within the Buddhist tradition.

docs.title: Dharmakīrti's reformulation
docs.text:
• [00:15:34] By far the most influential critic was Dignāga's commentator Dharmakīrti — so influential his writings effectively replaced Dignāga's among Sanskrit readers. For this reason Dignāga's collected verses (and his own auto-commentary) had until very recently to be read in Tibetan translation, until evidence of the Sanskrit original was uncovered.
  • [00:16:02] Later Buddhist epistemology came mostly as commentaries on Dharmakīrti or manuals digesting his thought. Dharmakīrti had two main complaints: an imprecision in the formulation of the triple condition, and Dignāga's failure to address the problem of induction.
  • [00:16:29] The imprecision. When the locus is a class rather than a single item, Dignāga's first condition — that the evidential property "must be present" — is ambiguous. If a policeman testifies that "arsonists like candles," he might mean all arsonists do, or merely that they tend to, or just that he's met candle-loving arsonists now and again. So when the locus is a class, "the evidential property is present in the locus" could mean it belongs to every member or only some.
  • [00:17:10] The second and third conditions are similarly ambiguous: must I examine all potentially similar and dissimilar cases, or only a few examples? This bears on the redundancy question: if it suffices to find one similar case but I must be exhaustive about counterexamples, the two conditions clearly differ; but if both searches must be exhaustive, they collapse into one and the same search.
  • [00:17:54] Dharmakīrti's fix: introduce the Sanskrit restrictive particle "eva" — meaning only, exactly, really. His reformulated conditions:
  • First (locus condition): the evidential property is present exactly in the locus.
  • Second (agreement) & third (disagreement): the evidential property is observed only in similar cases and is really absent from dissimilar cases.
  • [00:18:28] The "eva" clears each ambiguity: the property is present in the whole locus; present in some (not necessarily all) similar cases; and absent from all dissimilar cases.
  • [00:18:39] On this updated theory it is really the third (last) condition that does the work. Pervasion of one property by another means the evidential property is absent from whatever lacks the inferred property — smoke is absent from whatever lacks fire. This is much stronger than the second condition, which merely asks for one similar case like the smoky kitchen.

docs.title: Dharmakīrti on the problem of induction
docs.text:
• [00:19:08] The second worry strikes at the heart of inductive reasoning — and arises whether we justify positively (finding things with both smoke and fire) or negatively (finding things lacking both). How can we support a universal generalization from a limited number of examples? The 99 smoky things I've seen all had fire — but what of the hundredth, thousandth, millionth?
  • [00:19:39] Dharmakīrti's solution: go beyond merely observing that properties always come together, and demand a link that explains why they do. He identifies different kinds of reason that link properties.
  • [00:19:51] (1) Cause-and-effect reason. The case we've discussed throughout: because smoke is an effect of fire, it never appears without fire. Alternatively, two properties may both be effects of a shared cause — "night follows day" holds not because day causes night, but because both are caused by the rotation of the earth. Another example (cited by some Buddhists): inferring lemon colour from lemon taste, since both are products of the same cause, the lemon itself.
  • [00:20:24] (2) Natural reason (svabhāva-hetu). Dharmakīrti's illustration: being a śiṃśapā tree is a reason for being a tree. Being a śiṃśapā (or a lemon tree) isn't a cause of being a tree, yet the relation isn't accidental either. In the term svabhāva-hetu you recognize svabhāva — the essence or nature of a thing — the very target of Nāgārjuna's critical philosophy. So the nature of the śiṃśapā tree includes or implies the nature of tree.
  • [00:21:09] Puzzlingly, Dharmakīrti says such inferences rest on the relation of identity rather than causality. Perhaps he means the śiṃśapā tree and the tree are the same thing (whereas cause and effect are always distinct); or that the tree has really one property described more and less fine-grainedly — as someone's being "tall" and being "six foot three" are really identical.
  • [00:21:39] (3) Reason based on non-observation. Met in an earlier episode (the Nyāya claim that we can perceive absences): the pattern "there is no pot here because it is not observed." Such inferences rest on a counterfactual: if there were a pot here, it would be observed — assuming normal lighting, working sense faculties, and so on.
  • [00:22:09] Like the first two, this third kind shows not just that two properties do come together in experience, but that they must. A good inference requires a real link or tie: nothing tastes of lemon without smelling of lemon (both caused by lemons); nothing can be a lemon tree without being a tree. "When you don't find that life has given you lemons, you can't make lemonade."
  • [00:22:31] This is Dharmakīrti's solution to the problem of induction: a genuine link between properties explains why we've always seen them together and guarantees they will keep coming together in future.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:22:48] A long episode that, "like someone zesting a lemon," has only scratched the surface. The further development of Buddhist logic is a long story this series won't pursue in full.
  • [00:22:58] But we'll see Buddhist logic's continuing relevance: next time's guest is one of the world's most prominent philosophers of logic, interested in and inspired by Buddhism's logical theories. (A self-referential parting inference: when the locus is an interview featuring Graham Priest, it has the property of being well worth a listen.)

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Dignāga — Buddhist epistemologist who admits only perception and inference as pramāṇas; first Indian thinker to separate the rules of reasoning from the rules of debate.
  • pramāṇa — a means or source of knowledge; Dignāga keeps two (perception, inference), refusing the title to testimony.
  • testimony — for Nyāya an independent pramāṇa; for Dignāga it yields knowledge only via an inference (combining the report with knowledge that the witness is reliable).
  • inferring to oneself / inferring for others — reasoning (deciding whether to be convinced) vs. demonstration (producing an explicit argument to convince others).
  • pakṣa — the locus or basis of an inference (the mountain).
  • sādhya — the inferred property to be proved (having fire).
  • hetu — the evidential property or sign cited as reason (having smoke).
  • trairūpya — the "triple-conditioned sign": Dignāga's three conditions a good piece of evidence must meet.
  • similar / dissimilar case (homologue–sapakṣa / heterologue–vipakṣa) — other objects that respectively have or lack the inferred property; used to test the evidence.
  • pervasion (vyāpti) — the general relation "whatever is X is Y" connecting evidential and inferred properties; later elaborated at length (Gaṅgeśa, 14th c., reviewed a dozen accounts).
  • Nyāya & Mīmāṃsā — Brahminical schools Dignāga argues against (Nyāya counts testimony as a pramāṇa; Mīmāṃsā treats testimony as innocent until proven guilty); Nyāya later adopted Dignāga's inference theory from Uddyotakara on.
  • Dharmakīrti — Dignāga's dominant commentator; reformulated the three conditions using the restrictive particle eva ("only/really") and solved the induction problem by demanding a real link between properties.
  • eva — Sanskrit restrictive particle ("only, exactly, really") with which Dharmakīrti removed the ambiguity in Dignāga's conditions.
  • svabhāva-hetu — Dharmakīrti's "natural reason," where one property's nature implies another's (śiṃśapā ⇒ tree); built on svabhāva (essence), the target of Nāgārjuna's critique.
  • three kinds of reason (Dharmakīrti) — cause-and-effect, natural (essential/identity), and non-observation; each supplies the "must" that mere observed correlation lacks.
  • problem of induction — how a universal generalization can be supported from finitely many cases; Dharmakīrti answers it by requiring an explanatory link, not mere constant conjunction.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 54 — "Graham Priest on Logic and Buddhism"
docs.text:
← Ep 53

Ep 55 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Graham Priest 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Graham Priest · Runtime: 00:46:28 In brief: Graham Priest (Distinguished Professor of Philosophy, City University of New York Graduate Center) explains how the same "non-classical" logics that Western logicians built in the 20th century — many-valued and paraconsistent systems that reject excluded middle or non-contradiction — turn out to capture what the Buddhists' catuṣkoṭi and Nāgārjuna's Madhyamaka were already doing. The real philosophical payload of Buddhist "logic" lies not in its epistemology but in its metaphysics, which can make true contradictions look respectable. Topical order (interview); [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit/proper nouns normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Graham Priest ≈ "Graham Fries"; Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Gannery"/"Janardin"; Jay Garfield ≈ "Jay Garfield"; Nāgārjuna ≈ "Nagajuna"; Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ≈ "Mulamadiamika Karaka"/"Milamadigar character"; Madhyamaka ≈ "Mediamika"/"Mediarmica"; svabhāva ≈ "sphaphava"/"Swabhava"; dharmas ≈ "darmas"; catuṣkoṭi ≈ "Chachashkotty"/"Chachotty"; saptabhaṅgī ≈ "saptabangy"; Dignāga ≈ "Dignaga"; Dharmakīrti ≈ "Dharmakirti"; Frege ≈ "Frager"/"Phrygian"; Brouwer ≈ "Brower"/"Brouz"; Heyting ≈ "Heighting"; Gödel ≈ "Goetle"/"girdle"; Eubulides ≈ "eubilities"; König ≈ "Koenig"; Principia ≈ "Varyngipia"; dialetheism ≈ "dialethism"/"diethism").

docs.title: How Priest came to Buddhist logic
docs.text:
• [00:00:28] Adamson introduces Graham Priest, Distinguished Professor of Philosophy at the City University of New York Graduate Center, famous for his work in contemporary logic, who later "turned his attention to the resources that Buddhism has to offer in logic."
  • [00:01:04] A bit of autobiography: Priest trained as a mathematician (his doctorate is in maths), but by the end of it he'd decided philosophy was "an awful lot more fun." He was hired into a philosophy department knowing "virtually no philosophy," and has spent his career teaching himself the subject.
  • [00:01:31] After ~20 years he'd absorbed a lot of Western philosophy but little Eastern thought — "in the Western academy, no one really knows much about it." The turning point was meeting Jay Garfield, who became a close friend (Garfield then in Tasmania, Priest in Brisbane — far apart, but Australia's philosophical community is small).
  • [00:02:18] Garfield, also trained as a Western analytic philosopher, had moved into the Asian traditions: he taught himself Tibetan and produced one of the best translations of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā — the most important text by Nāgārjuna (1st–2nd century CE; Priest notes the exact dates are unknown), arguably the most important philosophical text in Buddhism. Adamson mentions he'd just read that translation while writing scripts for the series.
  • [00:02:47] Priest had just finished his own book Beyond the Limits of Thought; comparing notes with Garfield, he realised many of Garfield's preoccupations overlapped with his own. Talking to Garfield made him see "I knew at best half the world's philosophy" — he knew nothing of China or India. So he set out to teach himself, partly by teaching ("you can't teach it unless you get your head around it"; Adamson adds that podcasting works the same way), studying in India and Japan.
  • [00:03:58] Adamson probes the motive: was it the technical resonance with his logic, or just filling a gap? Priest: there was a real logical resonance, but it wasn't only that — the views on the nature of reality, the ethics, the political philosophy coming out of China, India, Tibet, Japan and Korea are "just fascinating ideas, even without logic connection." He wasn't "mining" Buddhism for logic material; he was after whatever was interesting.

docs.title: What "non-classical logic" is
docs.text:
• [00:05:35] Before the Buddhist material, Adamson asks Priest to explain non-classical logic. Priest's first provocation: "classical logic is something of a misnomer" — it has nothing to do with the classical civilisations (Egypt, Greece, Rome). It was essentially invented at the end of the 19th century.
  • [00:06:03] The key figure was Gottlob Frege, who initially didn't get the credit he deserved. When the new ideas spread through Europe, North America and Australia, the credit went first to Russell (and sometimes Wittgenstein); only by the mid-1950s did people recognise the debt to Frege — even though Russell had openly drawn on him. Readers went to Russell's Principia (1910) rather than back to Frege, partly because Frege's notation is terrible and Russell's symbolism looked more familiar to mathematicians.
  • [00:07:06] "Classical logic" is therefore "a masterstroke of propaganda" — the name makes it sound ancient when it isn't. Logic has developed in the West for two and a half thousand years; logic, as modern logicians understand it, is "a theory about what follows from what" — given some claims, what can you infer? Many different theories of that have been proposed from ancient Greece, through the great medieval period, to the present.
  • [00:07:48] Priest's gripe: logic today is taught ahistorically — you're handed a logic book, told "this is logic" (usually some classical system), as if it "dropped from the sky," like Moses bringing tablets down from Sinai. It's taught more like physics than ethics — yet even physics students know physics has a history, while most logic students don't know logic has one.
  • [00:08:23] Set the gripe aside: classical logic was "a fantastic advance," so much more powerful than anything before it that within 20–30 years it became orthodox, investigated by brilliant mathematicians — Hilbert (Göttingen, 1910s–20s) and Gödel (Vienna, 1920s–30s, later Princeton). Philosophers then seized it as a tool: roughly 1920–1960, the heyday of analytic philosophy and logical positivism / empiricism, was spent applying logic to the philosophy of science and language.

docs.title: Two ways to deviate: expressive extensions vs. genuine revision
docs.text:
• [00:09:48] But using a tool reveals its limits (here it took 40–50 years). Logicians split: some look for work-arounds within classical logic; others conclude you need to "revamp" logic itself. The result, especially over the last 40 years, is non-classical logics — systems that deviate from classical logic — and they fall into two broad kinds.
  • [00:10:45] Kind one — expressive extensions: thinkers who think classical logic's expressive resources are too limited, so they add machinery. The paradigm is modal logic, which adds tools for possibility and necessity (going back to C. I. Lewis in the 1920s).
  • [00:11:14] Kind two — genuine revision: thinkers who say classical logic is profoundly wrong. This starts early, with the Dutch mathematician Brouwer, working on intuitionist logic around 1910 — roughly contemporary with Principia Mathematica — and developed into a full system by another Dutchman, Heyting, by the 1920s.
  • [00:11:51] The headline casualty in intuitionism is the principle of excluded middle: classically, every statement is either true or false. Intuitionists deny this — there are statements that are neither — and build a logic in which "A or not-A" is not a logical truth. So non-classical logic's origins sit very close to classical logic's; they were just ignored because classical logic worked so well. By the 1960s logicians stopped ignoring them ("like a pair of shoes that bite — you live with it a while, then think maybe I can do better with a new pair").

docs.title: Can a meaningful statement be neither true nor false?
docs.text:
• [00:13:01] Adamson presses: does the classical logician really resist the idea of a statement that is neither true nor false? It seems an obvious observation — they discussed it in the Nāgārjuna episodes under category mistakes: "How heavy is the colour blue?" has no good answer because the question makes a false assumption (that colours have weight). Couldn't a classical logician just say: be precise, factor out category mistakes, and the problem vanishes?
  • [00:13:39] Priest grants it: some logicians do propose a third value ("category mistake") alongside true and false, but most classical logicians simply assume a cleaned-up language with the category mistakes "factored out in the first place." So category mistakes have not been a tough challenge for classical logic. The tougher challenges lie elsewhere.
  • [00:14:15] The earliest serious challenge was intuitionism, driven by the philosophy of mathematics. Brouwer asked: what is truth in mathematics? Truth about the physical world looks fixed by a world "out there" (contentious, but at least defensible). For mathematics, one option is a Platonic mathematical world out there — but to some that's "just a kind of mysticism."
  • [00:15:08] If mathematical truth isn't constituted by an external reality, what constitutes it? Brouwer's answer: provability — "to be true in mathematics is to be provable." But there are statements you can prove neither true nor false; in those cases, said Brouwer, you cannot apply excluded middle, at least until you have a proof one way or the other.
  • [00:15:34] Adamson: can't you sometimes prove that you can't prove either A or its negation? Priest: yes, within a given formal system — that's a standard reading of Gödel's great theorems. But Brouwer meant provability period, not relative to any one system; he had "a very jaundiced view of formal systems," holding that proof is about mental constructions that may not be captured by any single formalism.
  • [00:16:12] So intuitionism is an early challenge resting on a verificationist theory of truth. Classical logic stayed orthodox until about the 1960s, then people began to worry; it's probably still orthodox, especially in philosophy, but "we're not as sure that the orthodox view is right as we were 50 years ago." Logic is in an exciting state.

docs.title: Can a statement be both true and false? Paraconsistency and dialetheism
docs.text:
• [00:23:37] Turning to the third corner — both true and false — Priest gives more history. The issue here is the principle of non-contradiction, which rules out something being both true and false. It has been "high orthodoxy" in Western logic since Aristotle — more entrenched than excluded middle.
  • [00:24:12] Aristotle defends non-contradiction at length in the Metaphysics, but "most modern commentators think these arguments really don't work" — they're unclear and several "beg the question." Still, Aristotle names his targets (Heraclitus, Protagoras), so he thought there was a real fight, and his arguments — good or not — secured the principle a place of high orthodoxy. Hardly anyone has bothered to defend it at length since, because virtually every Western philosopher simply accepted it.
  • [00:25:12] The important exception is Hegel. Interpreting Hegel is "a dangerous business," and there are attempts to "consistentize" him — but read with an open mind, Hegel holds that some contradictions are true. The modern name for that view is dialetheism; a dialetheia is something true and false.
  • [00:25:50] Priest's example from Hegel's Logic: motion. To be in motion is not to be on the right at one time and the left at another, but "to be here and not here, in one and the same place, at one and the same time" — motion itself "realises contradictory states of affairs" (Hegel then draws on Zeno's paradoxes, e.g. the arrow). Hegel is the great exception precisely because he's a major figure; that there are so few others shows how orthodox non-contradiction has been. (Adamson notes the series hasn't reached Hegel "with some trepidation.")
  • [00:26:42] Around the 1960s, contemporary logicians built systems where what fails is not excluded middle but non-contradiction: paraconsistent logics. In classical logic, once you have a single contradiction "all hell breaks loose" — a contradiction implies everything (so one contradiction gives you everything). The defining feature of paraconsistent logic is that this is not the case: a contradiction stays constrained, limited. We now understand these systems well.
  • [00:27:44] If a logic can tolerate contradictions, you start to wonder whether some contradictions are actually true. Priest's promised example: the paradoxes of self-reference, which became central to the foundations of mathematics around 1900 (Russell's paradox "crashed Frege's program" — "we're not playing games here").
  • [00:28:31] The oldest of these is the liar paradox, traced to the 5th century BCE Greek thinker Eubulides. Take "what I am now telling you is false." If it's true, then (since it says it's false) it's false; if it's false, then it's true. So prima facie the liar sentence is both true and false — a candidate dialetheia. Such paradoxes have been argued "ad nauseam" across the three great periods of logic (ancient, medieval, modern), with still no consensus on what, if anything, goes wrong. The dialetheist's gambit: maybe nothing is wrong with the argument — maybe it's a "radical argument for something that's true," and the truth is a contradiction.

docs.title: Did the ancient Buddhists have a "logic"?
docs.text:
• [00:17:36] Adamson asks how fair it is to ascribe a logic to ancient Buddhists, who weren't doing what Russell does in Principia. Priest: they certainly weren't doing anything recognisable as contemporary formal logic — "things are much more complicated and nuanced."
  • [00:18:02] The great Buddhist "logicians," Dignāga and Dharmakīrti, you "wouldn't really want to call logicians in the modern sense." They used the word logic to mean something like epistemology — concerned with the sources of knowledge (perception, testimony, inference). They do engage with inference, and they formulate a formal logic "a bit like Aristotelian syllogistic," but at roughly that level of power or less.
  • [00:18:55] So for Priest the contemporary interest does not lie in Buddhist theories of inference (their epistemology is interesting in its own right, but the inference theories won't excite a modern logician). The interest lies "elsewhere, and a lot further back."
  • [00:19:14] It's hard to draw the line between logic and metaphysics. In the old positivist era, people thought logic was metaphysically neutral — "that is almost certainly false," and most philosophers now agree. (Intuitionist logic is obviously not neutral — it's bound up with the nature of mathematical and physical reality.) Probe almost any system of logic and you find metaphysical underpinnings. The Buddhists and Jains are interesting because they bring very different metaphysical underpinnings — "it's not in the epistemology that you find things interesting for modern logic; it's in the metaphysics."

docs.title: The catuṣkoṭi (tetralemma) — and the Jains' seven
docs.text:
• [00:20:20] In Buddhism you get the catuṣkoṭi, literally "four corners" — four possible answers to a question. Priest's canonical case: someone asks the Buddha what happens to an enlightened person after death — do they exist? not exist? both exist and not exist? neither exist nor not exist? Adamson notes this is what the series earlier called the tetralemma; Priest confirms.
  • [00:21:00] The Buddha refuses to answer yes to any of the four ("that's another story") — but crucially, all four are treated as genuinely "on the cards." Their picture of reality allows these four possibilities. In the West, "at least until recent times," only two are on the cards — yes and no; you can't have both, you can't have neither. (A wrinkle: Aristotle does suggest "neither" about future contingents.)
  • [00:21:48] These thinkers never "worked it up into the rigour of a modern logical system" — but we now know exactly how to, thanks to contemporary non-classical logic, where there are logics with precisely these four possibilities.
  • [00:22:05] "The Jains are even cooler." Where the Buddhists of that period had four possibilities, the Jains have seven — the saptabhaṅgī (seven answers). Why seven? Because it's 2³ − 1. This is bound up with the Jain metaphysics of aspects: reality has many aspects, and a thing can hold one aspect and not another, so you must take all aspects into account — "a long story, but that's how you get seven."

docs.title: Nāgārjuna's use of the four corners
docs.text:
• [00:22:48] Adamson returns to the third corner ("both") as the clearest way to see why this is a different way of doing logic. The "neither" corner is easy to swallow (category mistakes; or, on a provability theory of truth, statements neither provably true nor provably false; or Aristotle's undecided future — "the battle will happen tomorrow"). But why would it ever be useful to call a meaningful proposition both true and false? (Priest answers this with the liar paradox above.)
  • [00:30:25] Adamson observes that the great wielder of the tetralemma is Nāgārjuna, who usually deploys it to lay out four options all of which he refutes — e.g. on motion or causation: self-caused, caused by another, both, neither. Strikingly, when he reaches the third (contradiction) option, he doesn't dismiss it as "obviously silly"; he gives a detailed argument against it.
  • [00:31:22] Why? Because Nāgārjuna is heir to 700 years of Buddhist tradition: the tetralemma is canonical Buddhism, "it's in the sūtras." A good Buddhist won't say "the Buddha was crazy." Just as the Buddha refused to answer the disciple's question rather than dismissing "both exist and not exist" as ruled out by non-contradiction, Nāgārjuna stays faithful to the tradition by taking the contradictory corner seriously.
  • [00:32:11] But Priest pushes back on Adamson's summary: Nāgārjuna deploys the catuṣkoṭi in a novel way. Nāgārjuna is the foundational philosopher of Madhyamaka, one of the two kinds of Indian Mahāyāna Buddhist philosophy, whose central metaphysical idea is that everything is empty.
  • [00:32:56] "Empty" most certainly does not mean non-existent — it's like a glass being empty of beer. Empty of what? Of svabhāva — literally "self-being," translatable as intrinsic nature. Early Buddhism (the first ~500 years) held that ultimate reality is composed of building blocks called dharmas (not atoms in the modern sense), and that these dharmas have intrinsic nature. With Madhyamaka, Nāgārjuna launches a severe attack on that older metaphysics — one of the great turning points in Buddhist philosophy.
  • [00:34:08] How does the catuṣkoṭi feature in the attack? Many chapters of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā perform a reductio on the claim that something has svabhāva. Take the causation chapter (the MMK's first): there's a tacit, unspoken assumption that causation has svabhāva, an intrinsic nature. If it does, there are four possibilities about it (true, false, both, neither) — and Nāgārjuna reduces each of the four to absurdity.
  • [00:35:04] It's "a pretty standard reductio": assume something, show the possible cases, show none works. In the West there'd be only two cases (true, false); because Nāgārjuna works within the catuṣkoṭi, he has four, and must dispose of all of them. The ultimate aim is a reductio on the assumption that something has svabhāva.

docs.title: The fifth possibility: the ineffable and the paradox of expressibility
docs.text:
• [00:35:46] Adamson notes Nāgārjuna at least entertains the "both" option before rejecting it, and asks whether there are places where ancient Buddhists genuinely assert a contradiction, reasoning like dialetheists.
  • [00:36:09] In the MMK's reductios he runs the four cases and rejects all four — but he's rejecting the initial assumption, so that alone doesn't establish a fifth possibility. However, elsewhere in the text Nāgārjuna does suggest a fifth possibility — cases where none of the four applies — and not in a reductio context: he's putting forward a positive view. Here interpretation gets much more contentious among scholars.
  • [00:37:05] Priest's natural reading: it's standard in Buddhism that there are two kinds of reality — an ultimate reality we're normally unaware of, and a conventional reality we are aware of. In the older tradition ultimate reality was composed of dharmas. You might expect Nāgārjuna, having attacked the dharmas, to abolish ultimate reality — but he doesn't, because the sūtras of his time talk about ultimate reality and he must stay faithful to them.
  • [00:37:42] So what is ultimate reality for him? The view that evolves over the next couple of centuries: reality is what remains when you strip away the conceptual overlay. Take a chair and peel off its blueness, its four-leggedness, its chair-ness — all concepts we apply — and what remains, before any conceptual overlay, is ultimate reality.
  • [00:38:21] But then: what is ultimate reality like? You can't say — any answer applies concepts. Can't you at least call it empty? No — "emptiness" is itself a concept. So ultimate reality is ineffable, and that is the fifth possibility: true, false, both, neither — and ineffable.
  • [00:38:50] "Now we're facing real problems." If it's ineffable, aren't you talking about it right now? Yes. Isn't that paradoxical? Yes. Madhyamaka seems to have a genuine paradox, and Buddhist scholars respond to it in different ways — "in exactly the same way that Western logicians have responded to the liar paradox." Priest's own inclination: take the contradiction at face value — accept that some of the things that are ineffable, you can nonetheless talk about.
  • [00:39:39] This is what reconnected Priest with Jay Garfield: Garfield arrived at it via his Nāgārjuna translation, Priest via contemporary logic, and they recognised a shared phenomenon worth working on.
  • [00:40:04] The liar isn't about ineffability, but there are paradoxes in the same family that are — arising with large infinities, where some things are "so large you can't describe them": there are more things in infinity than you can possibly describe, yet you can point to specific such things via a standard set-theoretic construction. This is König's paradox (after Julius König, a Hungarian mathematician/logician, ~1910–20s). So paradoxes of ineffability "look as though they turn up in modern logic as well" — Priest had paradoxes of ineffability, Garfield had what looked like the same, and they began thinking about them together, producing a number of joint papers.

docs.title: Does the influence run both ways?
docs.text:
• [00:40:26] Adamson's last question: is this using the ancient Buddhist tradition to find resources for contemporary logic, or using the tools of non-classical logic to understand Nāgārjuna (which is what Priest's papers — "lots of symbols and mathematical logic" next to svabhāva theory — actually do)?
  • [00:42:07] "It goes both ways." The history of philosophy matters for contemporary philosophy because there have been many great philosophers — "most of them wrong about most things; that's philosophy after all" — yet all had genuine points of insight. We can "mine the history of philosophy for insights to learn anew," just as the West has repeatedly mined Plato, Kant or Hegel — and the same goes for the Asian traditions.
  • [00:42:59] The metaphysical insights of Madhyamaka are "profound," and applying them "you naturally come up with something like a four-valued logic, even a five-valued logic." This shows that when modern logicians built such systems they weren't merely "playing games" / "squiggling symbols like chess." Since every logic has metaphysical underpinnings, the Buddhists and Jains are actually showing us what some of those underpinnings could be — they have "something very important to teach us" about the metaphysics behind modern logical systems.
  • [00:44:11] The influence runs back the other way too. It would be silly to suppose Nāgārjuna (or Plato) had the tools of modern formal logic — but those tools let us articulate their views far more carefully than the thinkers themselves could. It's no criticism: Aristotle lacked a microscope, but would have used one brilliantly; modern logic is "the logical equivalent of the microscope."
  • [00:45:04] So we can return to the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā and reformulate it "with all the clarity and precision of modern logic" — see what it implies, examine its arguments, check how good they are — exactly as we apply modern logic to Anselm's and Descartes' arguments for God, understanding them better than they could because we have the tools. "The Enlightenment goes both ways": Priest loves taking insights from both modern and historical philosophy, East and West, "to help me understand the other better."
  • [00:46:15] Adamson thanks Priest, who calls it a pleasure, and signs off — "join me and Jonardon Ganeri next time" — noting the lesson that the history of Indian philosophy "can be very important for contemporary philosophy, and in its own right."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Graham Priest — Distinguished Professor of Philosophy, City University of New York Graduate Center; logician (a leading defender of dialetheism) who came to Buddhist thought through Jay Garfield.
  • Jay Garfield — Western analytic philosopher turned scholar of the Asian traditions; learned Tibetan, made a leading translation of the Mūlamadhyamakakārikā; Priest's collaborator on the ineffability papers.
  • Nāgārjuna — 1st–2nd c. CE founder of Madhyamaka; attacks the older Buddhist metaphysics of svabhāva-bearing dharmas via reductio arguments structured by the catuṣkoṭi.
  • Mūlamadhyamakakārikā (MMK) — Nāgārjuna's central text; its chapters (e.g. the opening one on causation) reduce to absurdity the assumption that things have svabhāva.
  • Madhyamaka — one of the two Indian Mahāyāna Buddhist schools; its core claim is that everything is "empty."
  • svabhāva — "self-being" / intrinsic nature; what things are empty of in Madhyamaka (emptiness ≠ non-existence — empty "of svabhāva," as a glass is empty of beer).
  • dharmas — for early Buddhism, the intrinsic-nature-bearing building blocks of ultimate reality, which Nāgārjuna attacks.
  • catuṣkoṭi (tetralemma) — the "four corners": four answers on the cards for a question (true / false / both / neither), e.g. about the enlightened person after death, which the Buddha refused to answer.
  • the fifth possibility (ineffable) — Priest's reading of certain MMK passages: beyond true/false/both/neither, ultimate reality (what remains once the conceptual overlay is stripped away) is ineffable — generating a paradox, since one still talks about it.
  • saptabhaṅgī — the Jains' seven answers (2³ − 1), tied to their metaphysics of aspects (reality has many aspects, held under some and not others).
  • Dignāga & Dharmakīrti — the great Buddhist "logicians," better called epistemologists; "logic" for them meant the study of the sources of knowledge (perception, testimony, inference).
  • classical logic — a "misnomer"; invented in the late 19th century (Frege; popularised via Russell's Principia), a theory of "what follows from what," made orthodox by Hilbert and Gödel.
  • non-classical logic — systems deviating from classical logic, of two kinds: expressive extensions (e.g. modal logic, C. I. Lewis) and genuine revisions.
  • intuitionist logic — Brouwer (~1910) and Heyting (1920s); rejects the principle of excluded middle, grounded in a verificationist/provability theory of mathematical truth.
  • paraconsistent logic — 1960s onward; rejects (the explosive form of) the principle of non-contradiction so a contradiction no longer implies everything.
  • dialetheism / dialetheia — the view that some contradictions are true; a dialetheia is a statement both true and false (Hegel on motion; the liar paradox as candidate cases).
  • liar paradox — "what I am now telling you is false"; traced to Eubulides (5th c. BCE); appears both true and false, a stock example for dialetheists.
  • König's paradox — a paradox of ineffability from large infinities (Julius König, ~1910s–20s): there are more things in infinity than can be described, yet specific such things can be picked out.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 55 — "Doors of Perception: Dignāga on Consciousness"
docs.text:
← Ep 54

Ep 56 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:18:06 In brief: Dignāga's theory of self-awareness (svasaṃvedana): for him there is no perception without an awareness built into the perception itself — a "reflexive" view, against the Nyāya "reflective" theory that the mind must perform a separate second-order act to notice it. The episode reconstructs his double-aspect theory of cognition, his memory and regress arguments, weighs their force, and asks how Buddhists who deny the self can put so much weight on self-awareness. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Dignāga ≈ "Dignaga"; Nyāya ≈ "Niaya/Niyaya"; manas ≈ "manas"; Dharmakīrti ≈ "Dama Kirti/Damar Kirti/Damakirti/Dharma Kirti"; Uddyotakara ≈ "Udiotakara"; Yogācāra ≈ "yoga-chara"; Sautrāntika ≈ "South Trantica"; Birgit Kellner ≈ "Birgit-Kerner"; Aśoka ≈ "Ashoka"; Buddhaghosa ≈ "Buda Gosa"; Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Ganari").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Dignāga — the Buddhist epistemologist whose theory of perception was covered in the previous episode; here, his theory of self-awareness [00:00:33].
  • The Nyāya school — his target; holds the rival "reflective" theory of self-awareness via the faculty of mind (manas) [00:02:09].
  • Dharmakīrti — later Buddhist who develops and radicalizes Dignāga's arguments in an idealist direction [00:08:35].
  • Uddyotakara — Nyāya philosopher who reads self-awareness as proof of a real self [00:15:48].

docs.title: Setting the question: is Mick Jagger aware that he is seeing?
docs.text:
• [00:00:33] Adamson picks up the running gag from the perception episode: Mick Jagger still seeing a red door, not yet painted black — fitting, since "you can't always get what you want." The new question: in addition to seeing the red door, is Mick aware that he is seeing a red door?
  • [00:00:56] We are sometimes obviously aware of having an experience — e.g. reflecting on how much we are enjoying a piece of music. But it can seem some experiences come without self-awareness: get immersed enough in music and you may no longer be aware of yourself listening; or, at the other extreme, music plays in a loud coffee shop and you don't notice you're hearing it until someone points it out, then realize a Rolling Stones song has been on the whole time.
  • [00:01:33] Plausible as these examples are, Dignāga would reject the lesson: for him there is no perception without self-awareness. And the awareness he means is one built into the very perception itself — it is just part of seeing a red door to be aware of seeing it, and you can never be oblivious of seeing it while seeing it.

docs.title: The opponent: the Nyāya "reflective" theory
docs.text:
• [00:02:04] These were controversial claims, and Dignāga was not the first Indian thinker interested in self-awareness — he was rejecting a leading theory found in the Nyāya school.
  • [00:02:15] For Nyāya, one reason to postulate a faculty of mind (manas) at all is to explain self-awareness. Mick's vision simply perceives the red door; his mind then has to get involved to give him awareness of that perception. This is a reflective theory: the perceiver must reflect mentally on their perception to become aware of it. The mind performs a function called inner apperception — Mick's mind perceives that he is seeing, much as his seeing perceives the door.
  • [00:02:51] On this view awareness is a second-order phenomenon — like a belief about a belief (I believe that Mick's belief that the door is red is correct), or a desire about a desire (Mick wishing he could stop wanting everything painted black).
  • [00:03:09] Dignāga denies awareness is like that. He grants we can engage in second-order reflection on our perceptions, but that is not what awareness is for him. He adopts a reflexive view: awareness of perceiving is built into the perception already at the first-order level.
  • [00:03:31] The Indian framing of the contrast: other-illumination (reflective) vs. self-illumination (reflexive). Either way, you might still think some perceptions occur without awareness — especially on the reflective view, since if I need a separate second-order act to be aware of a perception, presumably I only do that some of the time. The Nyāya can say the coffee-shop patron is prompted to that active reflection when made aware she'd been hearing the Rolling Stones unnoticed.
  • [00:04:08] Even on a reflexive view one could imagine some perceptions have built-in awareness and some lack it — first an unaware perception of the music, then an aware one once it's pointed out. Dignāga, however, insists awareness is reflexive and always present. Why?

docs.title: The phenomenalist backdrop and the double-aspect theory
docs.text:
• [00:04:33] It has to do with his theory of perception from the earlier episode. Dignāga is a phenomenalist: we do not immediately perceive external objects but at best grasp them indirectly via what he calls knowable interior forms — representations internal to the perceiver. So awareness of such a representation is part of what it is to perceive.
  • [00:04:55] As Dignāga states in his collected verses on the means of knowing (pramāṇa), every thought or experience has two aspects, objective and subjective. The objective aspect is easy: it's in the nature of thought to be directed at some object — even dreams and imaginings have content (a dream of a red door is of the door). But for Dignāga that content is not an external red door; the thought is directed at an internal representation, and he leaves it open whether anything outside corresponds to it.
  • [00:05:44] The subjective aspect is harder to state. Think of it as the way the content presents itself to us. Analogy: photographs and paintings. A photo of a face has the face as its object but also its own qualities — brightness, sharpness, contrast — that depend on how it was taken. Calling a photo overexposed or underdeveloped attends to features of the photograph itself, not what it shows. Likewise many frescoes are all of the Buddha, but what makes one serene, another typically Burmese, are the subjective qualities of the individual paintings.

docs.title: Proving the subjective aspect: second-order reflection
docs.text:
• [00:06:32] To prove perception really has a built-in subjective aspect, Dignāga points to the very phenomenon Nyāya made responsible for awareness — second-order reflection. When I think I am enjoying a piece of music, or tell myself in a dream that I'm only dreaming, I am attending to an experience I must already have been aware of. If the first-order perception had only objective content, this would be impossible.
  • [00:06:55] Take Mick again: if his perception contained nothing but its object (the door), then reflecting on it he could only reflect on the door. But in fact Mick can reflect on the fact that he is seeing the door — attending to his own subjective role, including the way the door looks to him (in foggy London he might think he sees it only through a haze, or that in poor light it almost looks orange).
  • [00:07:27] The painting/photo analogy again: a painting of a painting is not a duplicate of the original; photographing a photograph is not ordering a second set of prints. The second-order image records the way the first image represented its object — photograph an overexposed photo of a face and the object of the second photo is an overexposed photograph, not just the face.

docs.title: The memory argument
docs.text:
• [00:07:53] You might think Dignāga could just invite readers to introspect and see he's right — if you're always aware of your perceptions, you ought to know it. But he does not rest on everyday experience, perhaps because this awareness is often tacit, rarely coming to active attention. (Compare: you spend your whole waking day conscious without explicitly thinking about being conscious — perhaps his self-awareness is like that.)
  • [00:08:28] So he offers a more complex argument from memory, later developed by Buddhists from Dharmakīrti onward. Suppose Mick goes home, cheers up, and now thinks the door's red shade was lovely. Looking back, he does not simply remember a red door — he remembers perceiving the red door while standing in front of it.
  • [00:09:05] This is plausible. You'll recall the Buddhist king Aśoka erected ethical inscriptions across his empire — but unless you're remarkably old you don't remember seeing them erected. Dignāga's double-aspect theory explains the difference: when you remember an event you did not experience, you recall only objective content (a belief that it occurred); when you remember experiencing an event, you are recalling the subjective awareness you had of it.

docs.title: The regress argument
docs.text:
• [00:09:36] The opponent can resist: when we remember an event, maybe we remember two things — the content of the original experience plus a second-order reflection directed at it. So Mick remembers the red door and remembers reflecting that he was seeing a red door.
  • [00:10:05] Against this Dignāga offers a regress argument. How will Mick remember reflecting on his experience? He'd need to have been aware of that reflective act too, to remember it. But the opponent denies cognitions have built-in awareness — so the second-order thought ("ah, here I am seeing a door") will itself need a third-order thought to be noticed ("ah, here I am noticing that I am seeing a door"), and so on indefinitely.
  • [00:10:40] Since for the opponent a cognition is fixed entirely by its objective content and not by subjective awareness, the higher-order thoughts never get awareness into the picture — never include a first-person perspective. We get only: seeing a red door, thinking of seeing a red door, thinking of thinking about seeing a red door, with awareness perpetually deferred.

docs.title: Weighing the argument — does it prove too little?
docs.text:
• [00:11:06] Powerful, but it may achieve less than Dignāga needs. He must show not just that some cognitions include subjective awareness but that they all do — and the regress doesn't show that. The reflective theorist could stop the regress at any stage by saying we've reached a cognition that, unlike simple perception, is self-aware.
  • [00:11:28] Imagine the coffee-shop patron, unaware she's hearing music, who then has it brought to her attention. Isn't it reasonable that in the very act of reflecting on her previously oblivious perception she is aware she is reflecting? ("Ah yes — isn't that sympathy for the devil I hear, and hasn't it been playing for minutes?") Her own mental life is brought to her attention. So the opponent can plausibly say awareness is built into the second-order reflection but not the first-order perception — and that's what she'd remember later.
  • [00:12:08] The same problem hits Dharmakīrti's version, which adds the idea that the original perception is itself somehow in doubt: the perceiver can't be reassured the perception really grasps its object without being aware that it does — "awareness would establish the perception." But add a second-order reflection ("here I am seeing a door") and it seems to need similar ratification. As modern scholar Birgit Kellner notes, Dharmakīrti may be assuming one thing cannot make another known unless it is itself known — fair enough, but it invites the same reply: maybe the second-order reflection is self-ratifying while first-order perception is not.

docs.title: Defending Dignāga and Dharmakīrti
docs.text:
• [00:13:02] In their defence: this reply makes a significant concession — that at least some cognitions are reflexively self-aware. If the regress is aimed at someone who insists cognition never has a subjective aspect and so always needs higher-order reflection to be noticed, then the regress works just fine.
  • [00:13:33] And one who concedes some cognitions are self-aware and others not now owes an explanation of why: why is Mick not actively aware of seeing the door, yet aware once he reflects that he sees it? Dignāga has no such problem, since for him awareness is just part of what it is to perceive or cognize. As Dharmakīrti puts it: someone who does not perceive the awareness of something is not aware of anything at all.

docs.title: How far the theory reaches: idealism vs. realism
docs.text:
• [00:13:55] One reason Dignāga's account was so influential is that it could be accepted across several strands of Buddhism (though some Tibetan Buddhists later rejected it). Dharmakīrti takes it in an idealist direction, denying there are any external objects at all.
  • [00:14:15] Dignāga himself seems to say only that the immediate objects of perception are internal representations and that we are always aware of our perceptions of them — awareness being what gives us access to the internal objects — which is compatible with those representations representing things out in the world. Dharmakīrti, though, felt that if we are only ever aware of internal representations, there's no role left for external objects to play — yielding the full flowering of Yogācāra Buddhist idealism, so influential in Tibet.
  • [00:14:57] Yet Dignāga's basic principle could also be accepted by the non-idealist Sautrāntika tradition, which does accept the reality of external things. The shared principle: we only grasp things as we are representing them, from a first-person perspective. Whether or not we grasp real objects, our grasp is never "objective" in the sense of view-from-nowhere — we always grasp things in a certain way, as a photographic portrait presents only one particular view of a face.

docs.title: The puzzle: why would self-deniers prize self-awareness?
docs.text:
• [00:15:25] It may seem strange this theory arose within Buddhism of all traditions: Buddhists reject the real existence of the self, so why stress self-awareness? Isn't the "first person" in a first-person perspective precisely the self?
  • [00:15:48] This is exactly what Nyāya philosophers like Uddyotakara thought — that introspective self-awareness establishes the reality of the self. Proponents of the self also pointed to memory (the very phenomenon at the centre of Dignāga's proof) as confirming a self that stays identical over time. Indeed some non-Buddhist philosophers after Dignāga borrowed his reflexive account of mind and turned it into a theory of the self, claiming the self just is self-consciousness.
  • [00:16:20] But in denying the self the Buddhists never meant to deny we have a mental life. There are no selves, but there are flowing streams of reflexively self-aware moments of consciousness — streams that include memories of past moments and anticipations of future ones.
  • [00:16:43] The mistake is to allow thoughts of the form "I am happy" or "I am in pain," implying we can draw a firm boundary around one stream of subjectivity and say this and this alone is me. It's like tracking individual waves in the sea and thinking there's a good answer to "is this another wave, or the same wave as before?" — the sort of question the Buddha met with silence. So, despite appearances, the idea that consciousness is reflexive is compatible with there being no self.

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:17:18] That ends the look at Dignāga — but not at Buddhist philosophy. The question just asked was whether there is a single self that comes to awareness whenever we are reflectively or reflexively conscious; the Buddhists say no. But that isn't the only route to an enduring self.
  • [00:17:42] You might think we need a self as a control centre directing our intentions and acts of mind and body. Next time moves to Sri Lanka for a slightly earlier Buddhist who tackled this objection and argued we are like puppets with no one pulling the strings — Buddhaghosa. "So be a doll and join us."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Dignāga — Buddhist epistemologist; holds that perception always carries a built-in, reflexive self-awareness (svasaṃvedana); no perception without awareness of perceiving.
  • svasaṃvedana (self-awareness / self-illumination) — awareness of perceiving built into the perception itself at the first-order level; the reflexive view, opposed to the reflective "other-illumination" view.
  • reflective vs. reflexive — reflective (Nyāya): a separate second-order mental act makes a perception noticed; reflexive (Dignāga): awareness is intrinsic to the first-order perception.
  • Nyāya — rival school; posits the mind-faculty (manas) performing "inner apperception" to explain awareness as a second-order phenomenon.
  • manas — the faculty of mind which, for Nyāya, reflects on a perception to yield awareness of it.
  • double-aspect theory of cognition — Dignāga's claim that every thought has two aspects: objective (its content/object) and subjective (the way that content presents itself).
  • phenomenalism / knowable interior forms — Dignāga's view that we grasp not external objects directly but internal representations; awareness gives access to these.
  • memory argument — remembering an experienced event recalls the subjective awareness one had of it, not just its objective content (contrast: remembering Aśoka's edicts vs. seeing them erected).
  • regress argument — if awareness required ever-higher reflection, the first-person perspective would be deferred forever; so awareness must be intrinsic.
  • Dharmakīrti — later Buddhist who develops Dignāga's arguments and pushes the theory toward full idealism (denying external objects); "one who does not perceive the awareness of something is not aware of anything at all."
  • Uddyotakara — Nyāya philosopher who took introspective self-awareness (and memory) to prove the reality of an enduring self.
  • Yogācāra — Buddhist idealist tradition (Dharmakīrti's direction) denying external objects, influential in Tibet.
  • Sautrāntika — non-idealist Buddhist tradition that accepts external things yet can still adopt Dignāga's first-person-perspective principle.
  • Birgit Kellner — modern scholar noting Dharmakīrti's assumption that one thing cannot make another known unless it is itself known.
  • no-self / stream of consciousness — Buddhists deny a self but affirm a flowing stream of reflexively self-aware moments; "I am happy/in pain" wrongly fences off one stream as "me," like asking whether a wave is the same wave as before.
