docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 56 — "Who's Pulling Your Strings: Buddhaghosa"
docs.text:
← Ep 55

Ep 57 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:19:30 In brief: Buddhaghosa reads the Buddhist doctrine of no-self not as the claim that a person is just a heap of experiences but as a denial of any inner controller — and replaces the "charioteer" model of agency with a marionette, then argues that activity and attention are built into every moment of consciousness, yielding a strikingly modern philosophy of mind that grounds moral responsibility and empathy. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit/Pali terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Gennary"; Buddhaghosa ≈ "Buda Gosa / Budagosa / Buddha Gusa / Budagossa"; Visuddhimagga ≈ "Path of Purification"; Anurādhapura ≈ "Anura-Dapura"; Nikāya ≈ "Nikaya/Nicaea"; abhidhamma ≈ "Abidharma"; Madhusūdana Sarasvatī ≈ "Madhusadana Saras Vati"; Dignāga ≈ "Dignaga"; Theravāda ≈ "Theravada"; Kṛṣṇa ≈ "Krishna").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Buddhaghosa — the Buddhist philosopher whose theory of agency and mind drives the episode; author of the Visuddhimagga ("Path of Purification") [00:01:18].
  • The Visuddhimagga — Buddhaghosa's independent systematic treatise and training manual for the Buddhist path [00:02:49].
  • Kṛṣṇa in the Bhagavad-Gītā — invoked as the rival "divine puppet-master" model of agency, with the later commentator Madhusūdana Sarasvatī [00:04:44].
  • Dignāga — recalled for his idea of perception prior to conceptual construction [00:16:06].

docs.title: Who's pulling your strings? The problem of self-control
docs.text:
• [00:00:28] Nobody likes to be pushed around. We'd like to think that when we do things it's because we chose to, and could have chosen otherwise. If I speed up while walking, it's because I decided to go faster; if I look down, it's because I want to watch my step; and even when I think about a problem without moving at all — even one I'd rather not think about — isn't that also something I am doing myself?
  • [00:00:55] It seems natural, even inevitable, to frame this in terms of control. It's like a flying drone whose movements are directed from the ground by a pilot — except that here the thing doing the controlling and the thing being controlled are both inside one person. On this picture, self-control is just a more intense version of the ordinary causal relationship involved in remote control.

docs.title: Buddhaghosa: no-self as the denial of a controller
docs.text:
• [00:01:18] For the Buddhist philosopher Buddhaghosa, this would be a huge mistake. He thinks the whole point of the Buddha's refusal to acknowledge a self — to allow that there is anything that can be called "I" — is precisely a denial of the controller self.
  • [00:01:34] This is a new perspective within the tradition. Earlier Buddhists understood the theory of no-self to mean that the person is just a stream or heap of individual experiences and feelings. Buddhaghosa instead insists that the doctrine of no-self is about our capacity for agency.

docs.title: A life of will, a doctrine of no will: Buddhaghosa's biography
docs.text:
• [00:01:47] Though born in India and, by all accounts, thoroughly educated in the various Indian philosophical systems, Buddhaghosa decided that the true Buddhist teachings were best preserved on the island of Sri Lanka. There the teachings were still recorded and studied in the actual language of the Buddha, Pali, rather than Sanskrit, the language of elite discourse.
  • [00:02:13] So Buddhaghosa travelled to the great monastery of Anurādhapura and embarked on an enormously thorough study of the Buddhist canon — both the Nikāya and abhidhamma treatises — and all the commentaries written over centuries by a series of talented Sinhala philosophers.
  • [00:02:31] So impressed were the monks that they charged him with writing definitive explanations that would organize and order the teachings. With a team of assistants and apprentices, he did exactly that, in a monumental project of textual production.
  • [00:02:49] For good measure he also composed an independent treatise, the Visuddhimagga ("Path of Purification"), which both presents the doctrine systematically and serves as a training manual for aspirants on the Buddhist path.
  • [00:02:58] So Buddhaghosa was plainly a willful, motivated individual. Yet when it came to describing what it means to be willful and motivated, he had no truck with the idea that each of us is or has a self — an origin of willed directives.

docs.title: Against the charioteer: the marionette metaphor
docs.text:
• [00:03:14] A deeply entrenched model encourages us to think of the self along the lines of a charioteer who controls his horses from the chariot's platform. In this picture of human agency Buddhaghosa finds only "metaphysical magic." Time and again he rejects the idea that there is something inside which controls our bodily movements or our psychological processes. The self of the sectarians, he likes to say, "just does not exist."
  • [00:03:45] The best way to counter the hold a metaphor has on the imagination is to replace it with another. To combat the charioteer, he compares the human being to a mechanical doll / marionette whose limbs, torso and head are held together by strings. He writes: "Just as a mechanical doll is empty, soulless, and undirected, and while it walks and stands merely through the combination of strings and wood, yet it seems as if it had direction and occupation, so too this minded body is empty, soulless, and undirected… yet it seems as if it had direction and occupation."

docs.title: Living dangerously: the divine puppet-master objection
docs.text:
• [00:04:26] Buddhaghosa is living dangerously, since this metaphor can easily work against him. If we are just marionettes, surely someone must be pulling our strings — and who could that be other than a divine agency, a being with its hands on each person's control units?
  • [00:04:44] That is, in fact, exactly the picture of agency encouraged by a thinker already met in this series: Kṛṣṇa in the Bhagavad-Gītā. "Oh, Arjuna," Kṛṣṇa says, "the Lord resides in the heart area of all beings, making every being revolve through his magical power as if they were mounted on a machine."
  • [00:05:05] The later commentator Madhusūdana Sarasvatī identified that machine as precisely "our friend the marionette": the Lord is "just like a magician who causes completely non-independent wooden human forms to revolve, seated on a machine… moved by a rope."

docs.title: Why Buddhaghosa is not committed to automata
docs.text:
• [00:05:26] But it cannot possibly be Buddhaghosa's view that human beings — or "minded bodies," as Buddhists prefer to call us — are automata controlled from the outside. Not just because he doesn't believe in a divine agency (he certainly doesn't), nor only because in the Nikāya the Buddha himself is reported to speak of "self-doing" in the performance of stepping forward or back.
  • [00:05:56] More fundamentally, it is because of the very nature of ethics on the Buddhist view. It is central to Buddhist ethics that the moral value of an action is constrained by the intention with which it is performed. If actions were merely the result of some divine puppet-master, then nobody could be praised or blamed for their intentions, since those intentions would play no causal role in what they do.
  • [00:06:17] So in deploying the risky marionette metaphor, Buddhaghosa simply wants to push back against the insidious grip of the charioteer metaphor, which leads us to think there must be some inner controller.

docs.title: A better simile: the self-driving car
docs.text:
• [00:06:27] If Buddhaghosa lived today, Adamson suggests, he might compare humans to the self-driving cars we're promised will soon fill the streets. Like a self-driving car, the human being is a complex mechanism containing a variety of instruments: some detect what is in the environment, some monitor the functioning of the mechanism itself, others search for objectives or destinations and calculate the best ways of reaching them.
  • [00:06:57] That is the difference between a self-driving car and a remote-controlled drone, whose operator is external — and also the difference between a self-driving car and an ordinary car, or a chariot, "which is like a drone whose operator happens to be on board." The control is internal and distributed, not lodged in an onboard pilot.

docs.title: Turning the old rope metaphor on its head
docs.text:
• [00:07:10] Buddhaghosa develops his alternative by arguing that all consciousness is already active — that every conscious mental state is an expression of agency. He does this by inverting a more ancient Buddhist description of the mind.
  • [00:07:28] In that older description, the flow of mental life was a rope of many interwoven strands: one strand the series of sensory perceptions; another the series of feelings and affective reactions; another habits and dispositions; still another our concepts; all woven together with a final strand of the body's physical states. Together they produce a human being — a rope stretched across time. Within this complex appear "moments of intention and choice," which were said to give the whole rope its agency and direction.
  • [00:08:08] Since this picture was drawn by Buddhists, it gives no place to a unitary inner self — but it still suggests control emanates from discrete elements within the person, namely the volitions woven into it. Instead, Buddhaghosa insists that control and activity are built into every single moment of conscious experience. Our awareness is built up out of many activities which together produce the mindedness of the complex minded-body that is the human being.

docs.title: The blind man and the lame man
docs.text:
• [00:08:38] Buddhaghosa offers a vivid simile: imagine an odd couple — someone blind but able to walk, with a sighted but lame person sitting on the first person's shoulders. Each deliberate action, such as moving in a chosen direction, is the joint product of several capacities working together.
  • [00:09:02] Conscious awareness is therefore no passive response to the environment but "the activity of the mind bending itself onto the world." There is an interplay between mind and body, and between the minded-body and its worldly environment.

docs.title: Attention as a window frame: the components of experience
docs.text:
• [00:09:13] Buddhaghosa identifies several kinds of activity that make up experience. There is awareness, which brings us into touch with our environment in a way we are not when asleep. We can also reach out or direct attention to specific objects — which is what gives thought an object, a goal, an orientation. Once something comes to our attention we can evaluate it, judging it worth pursuing or avoiding, or classifying it under a category.
  • [00:09:39] For Buddhaghosa, being minded is being attentive: we direct ourselves toward certain things and not others. Attention is like a window frame — it sets a boundary to what we see, though we can focus on particular features within that frame. Experience is thus not passive being-affected but active engagement.
  • [00:10:03] And this active engagement is not the job of one part of the mind "in charge." We need no self as a top-down source of motivation, intention, evaluation or awareness. All these features are already present in the various components of mental activity, built in from the ground up.

docs.title: The objection from passivity: noise and pain
docs.text:
• [00:10:28] As often in philosophy, the account works better for some examples than others. It sounds convincing for reading a book: you decide to read up on Buddhism, go to the library, find the volume, sit, and attend to a sentence — a life full of activity.
  • [00:10:51] But aren't there cases where mental life seems passive, at the mercy of the outside world? A loud noise may force itself on your attention — a car backfiring outside the library, making you look up. Or pain: on a meditative walk you step on a thorn. Here active attention seems to come in only secondarily — apparently you involuntarily become aware of the noise or pain, and only then direct your attention, thinking "what was that?" or "boy, that hurt."
  • [00:11:26] Buddhaghosa denies this. He thinks the mind must already be actively involved for us to become aware of the distracting noise or the stabbing pain at all.

docs.title: Three analogies for backstage activity
docs.text:
• [00:11:40] The mango. A man asleep under a mango tree is woken by the sound of a falling mango; he grabs it, squeezes it, smells it, and finally eats it. He sees the mango "only because he heard it first" — awareness often requires coordination between the senses.
  • [00:11:54] The king and the gift. A king sits contentedly inside his palace. There's a knock at the gate; a villager has come bearing a gift. The doorkeeper is deaf and doesn't hear it, but the king's attendant does and instructs the doorkeeper to open the gate, letting the gift reach the king. Consciousness is the king receiving and enjoying the gift; sophisticated mental activity has already unfolded in the background.
  • [00:12:17] The spider. The unperturbed mind is like a spider nestled in the centre of its web. An insect touches the web, sending vibrations to the centre; detecting them, the spider shoots off to suck out its prey's juices. Here the web is "exploited twice" — first to transmit the quiver of the insect's impact, then to transport the spider out to it. So a single sense modality can do double duty: sounding a subliminal alert that a stimulus is present, and then reaching out to it in conscious awareness.

docs.title: Revising the doctrine of the six senses
docs.text:
• [00:13:49] All this helps Buddhaghosa to a major revision of ancient Buddhist theory. Traditionally there were held to be six sense faculties, not five: besides sight, taste, touch, smell and hearing, there is a faculty called mind, whose job is to perceive what goes on in our heads. Since every faculty has its own domain of objects (sight grasps colours), a sixth faculty would require inner mental objects to grasp.
  • [00:14:21] Earlier Buddhists also held that each faculty has its own physical basis — the eye for vision — and so assumed a physical basis for the sixth sense, the "heart base" (a term, Adamson jokes, evoking "the headquarters of a group of militant cardiologists").
  • [00:14:42] Buddhaghosa offers a wholesale revision: the word "mind" cannot be reduced to an additional sense faculty. Rather it names a range of functions associated with sensory perception — four types in all.
  • [00:15:00] Orientation. The first role of mind is like the king's attendant: mental activity is needed to get the senses to orient toward something — as when you turn back from a loud noise to focus on your book, or stop watching television to listen to your spouse (Adamson advises against the reverse). In this role the mind is not a distinct sixth perception but spans all five senses, embedded in their normal functioning.
  • [00:15:54] Bare receiving. The basic reception of a sensory stimulus into perception, "as yet involving no attempt to classify." Here we may recall Dignāga's idea of perceptions that have not yet received the constructions placed on them at the level of concepts.
  • [00:16:10] Classification. "This thing I am seeing is oval in shape," or "is a mango."
  • [00:16:24] Working memory. A further role resembling the modern psychologist's notion of working memory: the mind can "run across" the processed perceptions from the various senses, putting them in order so we can have a unified awareness in consciousness. In this last capacity the mind is more like a workspace than an inner sixth sense.

docs.title: A modern philosopher — but always with an eye on liberation
docs.text:
• [00:16:42] This is a formidably sophisticated account of the mind. Given the proliferation of distinctions, the compelling analogies and examples, and the fierce critique of rivals, Buddhaghosa "wouldn't be out of place in a modern-day analytic philosophy department," and would hold his own there.
  • [00:17:11] Nonetheless, as always in the Indian tradition, such technical theories were advanced with an eye on how to live and how to be liberated. Some account of motivation was needed to preserve our intuitions about moral praise and blame.
  • [00:17:28] There is a further ethical payoff. Buddhaghosa's account could have emerged from reflection on his own mind, but we can also turn our notice to other people. For Buddhaghosa those others have no selves — yet that does not make them unworthy of attention. On the contrary, each human is a unique complex of mental and bodily activities with its own internal interactions and characteristics.
  • [00:17:57] Understanding this should lead to the development of empathy: one conscious creature focuses its attention on another and becomes aware of that other's particular traits and states of mind. Adamson recommends "trying this at home" and in society at large — for what is a flourishing community but humans empathizing with one another, "quite literally keeping each other in mind," as they symbiotically interact with a shared environment?

docs.title: Where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:18:24] This aspect of Buddhaghosa's thought, and his philosophy as a whole, was dispersed widely through the world of Theravāda Buddhism, which today encompasses not just Sri Lanka but much of South and Southeast Asia — shaping ideas about human nature and community across a vast share of the global population. That larger story the series won't try to tell in detail.
  • [00:18:49] In fact the tour through Indian thought is "slowly coming to an end." It will conclude with several broader issues: the philosophy of animals in ancient India, and the possibility of influence between ancient European and ancient Indian thought.
  • [00:19:04] Next time kicks off these general-topic episodes with a theme readily associated with Indian culture, though not necessarily with philosophy: the ritual practices known as Tantra — practices that span the divide between the Vedic schools, Buddhism and Jainism, much as Buddhaghosa's "mind" spans the divide between sight, hearing and the other senses. "So make it your mantra to join us."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Buddhaghosa — India-born Buddhist philosopher who settled at Anurādhapura in Sri Lanka; reinterprets no-self as the denial of an inner controller and treats agency/attention as built into every moment of consciousness.
  • no-self — the Buddhist doctrine that there is no "I"; earlier read as "person = a heap/stream of experiences," but for Buddhaghosa it specifically denies a controlling self that directs our actions.
  • minded body — the Buddhists' preferred term for a human being: "empty, soulless, and undirected," yet seeming to have direction and occupation.
  • Visuddhimagga ("Path of Purification") — Buddhaghosa's independent systematic treatise and training manual for aspirants on the Buddhist path.
  • Pali — the actual language of the Buddha, in which the teachings were preserved in Sri Lanka, contrasted with elite Sanskrit.
  • Anurādhapura — the great Sri Lankan monastery where Buddhaghosa studied the canon and its Sinhala commentaries.
  • Nikāya & abhidhamma — the two bodies of Buddhist canonical treatises Buddhaghosa studied; the Nikāya reports the Buddha speaking of "self-doing."
  • charioteer metaphor — the entrenched (rejected) model of the self as a driver controlling the body's "horses" from within; Buddhaghosa sees in it only "metaphysical magic."
  • marionette / mechanical doll — Buddhaghosa's counter-metaphor: a strung doll that moves with apparent purpose though empty and undirected.
  • Kṛṣṇa / Bhagavad-Gītā / Madhusūdana Sarasvatī — the rival "divine puppet-master" picture, where the Lord makes beings revolve "as if mounted on a machine"; the commentator Madhusūdana glosses that machine as the marionette moved by a rope.
  • intention (and moral responsibility) — Buddhist ethics ties an action's moral worth to its intention, which is why we cannot be mere externally-controlled automata.
  • rope of strands — the older Buddhist image of mental life as interwoven strands (perceptions, feelings, dispositions, concepts, body) with volition supplying agency; Buddhaghosa turns it on its head.
  • attention as a window frame — being minded is being attentive: directing oneself toward some things rather than others, within a bounded but focusable field.
  • the six senses / "heart base" — the traditional doctrine of a sixth "mind" faculty with its own objects and bodily seat; Buddhaghosa rejects this, recasting "mind" as four functions (orientation, bare receiving, classification, working memory) spread across the five senses.
  • Dignāga — recalled for the idea of perception prior to conceptual construction, paralleling Buddhaghosa's stage of "bare receiving."
  • empathy — the ethical upshot: since each selfless human is a unique complex of activities, attending to others should breed empathy and flourishing community ("keeping each other in mind").
  • Theravāda Buddhism — the tradition through which Buddhaghosa's thought spread across South and Southeast Asia.
  • Tantra — the ritual practices spanning Vedic, Buddhist and Jain schools, previewed as the next episode's topic.

docs.text:

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:16 In brief: Stripping the sex-and-black-magic clichés from Tantra to reveal a tradition — cutting across Hindu, Buddhist and Jain lines — in which philosophical ideas were put into practice: mantras, maṇḍalas and ritual that enact, rather than merely symbolize, the unfolding of the whole universe from a single divine consciousness, as theorised by the non-dual Śaivite Abhinavagupta. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Ganari"; Abhinavagupta ≈ "Abinava Gupta/Abhinava"; Śaivism ≈ "Shavism/Shaivism"; Śiva ≈ "Shiva"; Śakti ≈ "Shakti"; śava ≈ "Shava"; Cārvāka ≈ "Chavaka"; Advaita Vedānta ≈ "Adveita Vedanta"; maṇḍala ≈ "mandela"; Oṃ ≈ "Om/Ome/oom"; Chāndogya Upaniṣad ≈ "Chande/Chanda Yoga Upanishad"; Vasubandhu ≈ "Vazubandu"; haṃsa ≈ "Hamza"; André Padoux ≈ "André Padu"; Robert Yelle ≈ "Robert Yell"; Jayaratha ≈ "Jayaratahata/Jayaata"; Bhartṛhari ≈ "Batrihad"; Kuṇḍalinī ≈ "Kundalini"; cakras ≈ "chakras"; Saiddhāntika ≈ "Sidanta"; Kaula ≈ "Kaola"; Dignāga ≈ "Dignago"; Dharmakīrti ≈ "Dharmakirti"; Amber Carpenter ≈ "Amber Carpenter").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Tantra — not sex or black magic but a tradition, akin to yoga, of putting philosophical ideas into ritual practice; spans Hindu, Buddhist and Jain literature [00:00:33].
  • Abhinavagupta — non-dual Kashmir Śaivite, c. 1000 CE; the episode's central theorist of mantra, language and cosmology (and earlier the figure behind the aesthetics of rasa) [00:02:32].
  • Jayaratha — 13th-century commentator on Abhinavagupta, a key further source [00:07:58].
  • Vasubandhu — the Yogācāra Buddhist, here cited as a critic who called mantras meaningless gibberish [00:05:45].

docs.title: What "Tantra" really means — clearing away the clichés
docs.text:
• [00:00:33] The series has already dispelled misconceptions about ancient India: that it offered only mysticism with no philosophy, that yoga is mere gymnastics, that the physical world is real (per Advaita Vedānta) or that only the physical is real (per the Cārvākas). But the word most apt to provoke inaccurate associations is Tantra.
  • [00:01:00] In Western countries the first and last idea people have about Tantra is that "it has something to do with sex." In India itself it is nowadays often equated with black magic, and even better historical knowledge has not spared it disdain and mockery.
  • [00:01:13] A pioneering 20th-century Indian scholar justified studying it in pointedly medical terms: someone should take up "the diagnosis, etiology, pathology, and prognosis of the disease, so that more capable men may take up its treatment and eradication." It would be more helpful, the hosts suggest, to think of Tantra instead as a tradition akin to yoga, in which philosophical ideas were put into practice.
  • [00:01:46] A wide range of rituals could enable the practitioner to achieve liberation from suffering and oneness with the absolute — not to mention feats like seeing buried objects, flying, and turning invisible. As with yoga, the connection to magic recurs, and like yoga, Tantra appeared in many guises across periods.

docs.title: A tradition cutting across schools — and the focus on Śaivism
docs.text:
• [00:02:08] Tantric literature spans the divides between Hindu, Buddhist and Jain traditions; even Hindu Tantra had numerous varieties and schools in the classical period. The episode focuses especially on Tantra within Buddhism and on Śaivism (worship of the god Śiva), and within Śaivism on the non-dual strand represented by Abhinavagupta (c. 1000 CE), familiar from the earlier discussion of the aesthetic theory of rasa.
  • [00:02:42] The more central aspects of Tantra are shared across these schools. At the risk of disappointing the audience, a fascination with ritualistic, spiritualized sex is not one of them. Writings on the topic exist (including by Abhinava), but sexual practices were not the primary focus of classical Tantra — and even when discussed, "there is more, or from a prurient point of view, less, going on than meets the eye." To quote the French scholar André Padoux: Abhinava "is not to be confused with the Marquis de Sade."
  • [00:03:18] What characterizes Tantra instead is its openness to participants of all classes, often both men and women, and a range of concrete ritual practices: meditation, breath control, repetitive chants (mantras), the use of maṇḍalas, and initiation by a guru who serves as spiritual guide.

docs.title: The etymology — Tantra as a teaching that spreads and saves
docs.text: • [00:03:42] If none of that sounds philosophical, that is because it is only the external scaffolding that manifests and assists the practitioner's pursuit of wisdom and liberation. A traditional etymology of Tantra — which originally meant simply "a teaching" or a document setting out a teaching — even encodes this: the syllable TAN means "spreads" and TRA means "saves." Tantra spreads the wisdom that saves us from ignorance and suffering.

docs.title: Ancient roots and the borrowing question
docs.text:
• [00:04:11] Tantric practice reaches deep into the past. The Upaniṣads already discussed mantras, including the central example Oṃ. The Chāndogya Upaniṣad instructs: "one should venerate the high chant as this syllable, for one begins the high chant with Oṃ. A man who utters this syllable with that knowledge enters this very syllable, the sound that is immortal and free from fear." The same text describes initiation with a guru and stresses the notion of breath.
  • [00:04:52] But the first texts classifiable as Tantric in the full sense emerge around the 5th to 7th centuries CE, especially within Śiva-worshipping Hindu belief. The various practices — like reciting mantras — were apparently borrowed from Śaivism by the Buddhists.
  • [00:05:10] Each side spun an alternative history. Buddhist tantric texts, sensitive on this point, ascribe to the Buddha a premonition that rituals he originally prescribed would later be adopted by other schools. Meanwhile a Hindu legend held that Śaivism was a curse to punish those who stopped learning the Vedas properly — so Tantra was "being diagnosed as a kind of illness long before the 20th century." Even as the rituals were adopted across the spectrum of Indian belief, writers across that spectrum dismissed them as preposterous.

docs.title: Are mantras gibberish? Vasubandhu's objection and the answer
docs.text:
• [00:05:45] No less a thinker than Vasubandhu (whom we saw initiating Yogācāra Buddhism) held that mantras are meaningless gibberish — and looking at them, "you may feel that he had a point." Some consist of apparent nonsense syllables, each called a seed (bīja). Others repeat a meaningful but mysterious phrase, like Haṃsa So'ham — "I am that divine haṃsa bird."
  • [00:06:13] Typical of this mantra is that it is a near palindrome, a common structure in the many formulas of Tantra (tradition counted 70 million of them). One standard practice was to begin and end a mantra with Oṃ (or another basic mantra), enveloping the rest. Breath itself is said to be a kind of mantra, as one breathes in and out thousands of times a day.
  • [00:06:40] The symmetrical structure — mimicking the outward and inward movement of breath — is a clue to the underlying philosophical rationale, the theory held to be the key to a mantra's success. Recitation without knowledge is "like casting seed upon barren stone"; that is why initiation with a guru, who reveals the meaning, is needed.
  • [00:07:17] In general terms: as the palindromic structure suggests, mantras evoke the cyclical production of things — in the first instance the going-out and return of the entire universe (recalling the earlier discussion of world cycles). The scholar Robert Yelle wrote that the belief in mantras' efficacy is reinforced by their imitation of the natural order: they should be seen not as gibberish like baby-talk or birdsong, but as poetic language symbolizing the world and even the very origin of the world.

docs.title: Abhinavagupta's cosmology — monism with a complex world
docs.text:
• [00:07:53] The culmination of this thinking comes with Kashmir Śaivism and especially Abhinavagupta; an important further source is the commentary of the 13th-century exegete Jayaratha. Their extensive writings had little impact on actual religious practice in Kashmir, but represent a "high watermark for philosophical reflection about Tantra." Abhinava sets out a sophisticated theory in which the generation of words represents — or is identical with — the generation of the entire universe. Understanding it requires first his cosmology, generated from one principle (singular).
  • [00:08:39] Śaivism had long been monotheistic — among the first Indian systems to endorse a single divine principle. That principle, Śiva, is a pure, ineffable consciousness experiencing permanent bliss; trying to grasp it, says Abhinava, "is like trying to step on the shadow of your own hat while wearing it."
  • [00:09:03] So far this sounds like Advaita Vedānta, and this strand of Śaivism is likewise called non-dual, in distinction from the Saiddhāntika (Śaiva Siddhānta) variety. The Saiddhāntika Śaivas acknowledged the reality of the physical world but regretted it, treating their rites as a means of escaping its suffering. For Abhinava and the non-dual Śaivas, the point is instead to free ourselves of the ignorance that makes us think we are distinct from the divinity of Śiva (also called spirit, consciousness, self).
  • [00:09:39] This is a monism compatible with a complex cosmology. The universe arises from a vibration of self-awareness, expressing itself threefold as consciousness, will (desire), and cognition. This can occur only because Śiva, a male god, is one with the female god Śakti, who represents energy. As the non-dual Śaivas' punning motto has it: without Śakti, Śiva would be a corpse — śava. Thanks to Śakti's energy and self-directed activity, consciousness does not stay inert but goes forth as our multifarious empirical world — yet all things we see are in truth one with the divine. The tantric goal is to realize one's identity with God through rituals that represent (or simply are) the unfolding of all things from Śiva-Śakti.

docs.title: Language as the fabric of the universe
docs.text:
• [00:10:50] This returns us to mantras and language. Śiva is also called the supreme word (parā-vāc), the source of all language but as yet without articulation. This supreme word begins to manifest as the initial vibration of creative energy and self-awareness. As Jayaratha puts it: when the supreme word wishes to appear externally but without yet producing the multiplicity of "what expresses and what is expressed," since pure consciousness still prevails, "she is called the seeing or the visionary" — a form of the subject who sees.
  • [00:11:24] Think of it as the moment a thought is entertained all at once, before being spelled out in words. Abhinava compares it to the flash of understanding posited by the grammarian Bhartṛhari, in which a sentence's meaning is grasped in a single instant. At a further stage, articulated language is rehearsed mentally before being spoken aloud and fully expressed. Abhinava argues there must be such a stage — otherwise children could never learn to speak, nor could mutes comprehend others' words.
  • [00:11:58] Language emerges from the body in stages, through its energy centres, the famous cakras. Within each person the origin is at the base of the spine, where power is coiled like a snake — "coiled" translating the name of the goddess Kuṇḍalinī, who is responsible for the evolution of the phonemes from the simpler, unspoken primordial word. One text says Kuṇḍalinī is made of will, cognition and action; she "creates the garland of letters divided into 42," and dividing into 50 the garland of phonemes, "she brings forth in succession the gods and the other things."

docs.title: The Sanskrit alphabet as a map of cosmic evolution
docs.text:
• [00:12:50] So we have a fusion of cosmology with philosophy of mind and language. Crucially, the production of the world is not merely symbolized by the production of language but actually is linguistic — the universe being "pervaded by sound." Cosmic evolution can therefore be mapped onto the Sanskrit alphabet.
  • [00:13:09] Those three initial moments in Śiva's emergence into self-awareness — consciousness, will, cognition — are connected to the three short vowels a, i, u. Vowels are associated with Śiva, the male principle; consonants are the female analogue — set out even more concretely as vowels = the male seed, consonants = the womb. A single syllable like Oṃ, or any vowel-consonant combination, thus represents the mating and unity of Śiva and Śakti. This may be Abhinava's gloss on another Chāndogya Upaniṣad passage: "as the leaves of a book are bored through by a pen, so all words are bored through by Oṃ."

docs.title: The sexual theme — Kaula, left-handed rites, and twilight language
docs.text:
• [00:13:58] This finally reaches the theme of sexual union — which plays a far more minor role than expected. Sexual rituals are only one aspect of a more general strand called Kaula, which endorsed a range of shocking practices: from adultery, incest and group sex to consuming forbidden things like wine and meat, and even the eating and drinking of urine and excrement.
  • [00:14:33] One passage, aiming to be "as scandalous as possible," advises on liberation: "Inserting his organ into his mother's womb, pressing his sister's breasts, placing his foot upon his guru's head, the practitioner will be reborn no more." It did not take long for some authors to gloss such advice as symbolic and allegorical: incest with the mother as the mind's awareness of the base of the body; pressing the sister's breasts as focus on heart and throat; the foot on the guru's head as meditation on the brain.
  • [00:15:11] How far the shocking "left-handed" practices were actually carried out is much debated; no doubt it varied — some took the advice literally, others symbolically, still others held both levels relevant. To bar a merely symbolic reading, some works spell out the true meaning of coded terminology, sometimes called twilight language.

docs.title: Spiritual aims achieved through the body
docs.text:
• [00:15:41] Either way, there is general agreement across Tantra that we can achieve spiritual aims through the body, correcting what might have looked like an unwarranted asceticism in both Hinduism and Buddhism. One sign: Tantra did not demand renunciation — unlike a Buddhist or Jain monk, a tantric practitioner could remain a householder. Another: many texts frankly aim at worldly advantages — magical feats like invisibility, victory in battle, even alchemy.
  • [00:16:18] And even when sex and other rituals were practiced concretely — for one genuinely recites mantras thousands of times — the aims were always spiritual. The sexual act became a way of realizing one's identity with the union of male and female in Śiva-Śakti, involving long practice of control and often the avoidance of climax. As one scholar notes, the sublimation and self-mastery mean that what is occurring "bears very little resemblance to sex as we generally understand it," since Buddhist tantric assumptions and aims are "virtually indistinguishable" from those of recognizably ascetic traditions.

docs.title: The key philosophical idea — and its parallels abroad
docs.text:
• [00:17:09] It may seem paradoxical that such lofty aims are pursued through bodily powers. But as Abhinava says, the body should be seen as "full of all the paths, composed of all the divinities," and so made an object of contemplation, adoration and ritual fulfillment. This is perhaps the key philosophical idea of Tantra: especially in its non-dual Śaivite version, it privileges pure consciousness as the first principle, taking the empirical, bodily realm to be that principle's outward manifestation. We are told to engage in worldly activities structurally identical to the workings of self-directed consciousness and its production of all things — notably the production of language as mantras — thereby removing the otherwise impermeable veil that screens us from realizing our identity with the absolute.
  • [00:18:04] No wonder that, when Islam came to India, Tantra was seen as congenial to Sufism. There are parallels too with medieval Christian mysticism and especially Kabbalah in Judaism — which offers strong resonances: an alphabet-based cosmology (the ten Sephirot structuring a derivation of all things from an ineffable divine principle), the deployment of erotic language, and, in "prophetic" Kabbalah, even the chanting of apparently meaningless syllables. In none of these cases are we dealing with an irrationalism that competes with rational philosophy, but with attempts to show how philosophical ideas could be put into practice.

docs.title: "Learn by doing" — and where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:18:50] It has been said that while master logicians like Dignāga or Dharmakīrti devised hair-splitting arguments to interpret the world as a void entity, tantric ideas "captured the heart of Buddhism through the back door." But in fact the tantric authors — Buddhist and Hindu alike — had their own philosophical theories and fine distinctions; it is just that, in their view, abstract understanding was not enough. We must marry it to practical action, recognizing that everyday — even supposedly vulgar and despised — things reflect and instantiate the structures of primordial reality. Sometimes you need to learn by doing.
  • [00:19:31] Tantra cut across the intellectual divides of ancient India. Soon the series will turn to the relations between that culture and the world outside India. But first comes another pervasive issue across all the traditions covered — one that leaps to mind when people think of ancient Indian religion: attitudes toward non-human animals. It was widely considered wrong to eat them, which is why eating meat counted among the shocking left-handed tantric practices — perhaps because Indians believed in reincarnation, so that "by tucking into a steak, they might be eating a deceased family member." The next episode is an interview with Amber Carpenter about animals in classical Indian thought.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Tantra — a tradition (like yoga) of putting philosophical ideas into ritual practice; etymology TAN ("spreads") + TRA ("saves") — wisdom that saves from ignorance and suffering. Cuts across Hindu, Buddhist and Jain lines.
  • mantra — repetitive chant; "seed" (bīja) syllables or mysterious phrases like Haṃsa So'ham; often near-palindromes mimicking breath; meaningful only with a guru's revealed knowledge.
  • Oṃ — the central, ancient mantra (from the Upaniṣads); used to envelop other mantras; "all words are bored through by Oṃ."
  • maṇḍala — diagram used in tantric ritual.
  • guru / initiation — the spiritual guide who shares a mantra and reveals its meaning; recitation without this knowledge is "seed cast on barren stone."
  • Abhinavagupta — non-dual Kashmir Śaivite (c. 1000 CE); theorist that producing language is producing the universe; the body as "full of all the paths."
  • Jayaratha — 13th-century commentator on Abhinavagupta; describes the "supreme word" becoming "the visionary."
  • Śiva — for Śaivism the single divine principle: pure, ineffable consciousness in permanent bliss.
  • Śakti — the female god, energy; "without Śakti, Śiva would be a corpse (śava)"; her activity makes consciousness go forth as the world.
  • non-dual Śaivism vs. Saiddhāntika — the non-dual aims to dissolve the ignorance of feeling separate from Śiva; the Saiddhāntika accept the world's reality but seek to escape its suffering.
  • Kuṇḍalinī — "coiled" goddess at the base of the spine; evolves the phonemes (the 42, then 50) and so brings forth gods and things.
  • cakras — the body's energy centres through which language emerges in stages.
  • Bhartṛhari — grammarian; his "flash of understanding" (a sentence grasped at once) is Abhinava's model for the pre-articulate moment of language.
  • vowels / consonants — vowels (a, i, u) = Śiva / male seed; consonants = Śakti / womb; a syllable enacts their union.
  • Kaula — strand endorsing shocking "left-handed" practices (sex, wine, meat, even urine and excrement), often read symbolically via "twilight language."
  • Vasubandhu — Yogācāra Buddhist cited as a critic who dismissed mantras as meaningless gibberish.
  • André Padoux / Robert Yelle — modern scholars of Tantra invoked for, respectively, "Abhinava is not the Marquis de Sade" and mantras as world-symbolizing poetic language.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 58 — "Amber Carpenter on Animals in Indian Philosophy"
docs.text:
← Ep 57

Ep 59 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson with Amber Carpenter 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson with Amber Carpenter · Runtime: 00:25:43 In brief: An interview on animals in classical Indian thought: they saturate the literature (fables, epics, even the divine) yet are rarely thematized as a philosophical question; Sanskrit has no single word for "animal," reincarnation folds animals into the moral economy without individuating a fixed self, and the ethic of ahiṃsā rests on a prior, unrestricted commitment to non-violence rather than on "that pig might be my uncle." Narration order by topic; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janarn Gennary"; Yale-NUS College ≈ "Yale and U.S. College"; Pañcatantra ≈ "Panchatantra"; Hitopadeśa ≈ "Hittipadasha"; Dharmaśāstra ≈ "Dharma Shasta"; Arthaśāstra ≈ "Atta/artist Shasta"; Ṛg Veda ≈ "Rig Veda"; Rāmāyaṇa ≈ "Maramayana"; Hanumān ≈ "Hanaman"; Gaṇeśa ≈ "Ganesha"; Śaṅkara ≈ "Shankra"; Mahāyāna ≈ "Mahayana"; Brahmin/Brahminical ≈ "Romanical/reprimanical"; Jains ≈ "giants/Jane").

docs.title: The guest and the topic
docs.text:
• [00:00:25] Adamson introduces Amber Carpenter, associate professor at Yale-NUS College, for an interview on animals in Indian philosophy — a topic that "leaps to mind" when people think of the Indian tradition, given vegetarianism, reincarnation and so on.
  • [00:00:51] His opening question: what kinds of texts can we look to in order to learn about ancient Indian attitudes towards animals?

docs.title: Where the animals are: a literature saturated with beasts
docs.text:
• [00:01:00] Carpenter: "The astonishing thing about classical Indian literature is that it's absolutely full of animals." Animals are everywhere.
  • [00:01:07] First source — the vast corpus of animal fables: tales of talking animals in social situations, used for didactic purposes. These stories are extremely old, possibly already circulating in the time of the Ṛg Veda, and were reworked constantly across centuries by different religions and circumstances, collected into compilations like the Pañcatantra and later the Hitopadeśa. They depict animals as social, interacting beings — a "background hum" of thinking about animals.
  • [00:02:15] Second source — the works of conduct: the Dharmaśāstras and Arthaśāstras (already covered earlier in the series). As part of right conduct, these give a great deal of information about how one should behave towards other animals.
  • [00:02:34] Third source — epic literature. Carpenter draws a deliberate contrast with the Greek epics, which show little concern with our interaction with animals; the Indian epics are quite different. The Mahābhārata and the Rāmāyaṇa are full of subplots involving animals — e.g. Hanumān, the talking monkey, who is "no ordinary monkey."
  • [00:03:03] A further feature: animals are even incorporated into the divine realm — e.g. Gaṇeśa, the elephant-headed god. Everywhere you look there is some awareness or incorporation of animals.

docs.title: Pervasive in literature, but not a philosophical theme
docs.text:
• [00:03:25] The interesting twist: against that rich background, there is comparatively little active engagement with the question of animals in explicitly philosophical literature. Looking at classical Indian thought, "you might wonder what's the question about animals." Animals are pervasive but not thematized as a specific philosophical issue.
  • [00:03:55] Why? Carpenter argues it is a feature of Sanskrit that there is no word that really corresponds to "animal" the way English uses it to pick out the non-human mobile living things. The Dharmaśāstra and Arthaśāstra have many ways of grouping animals (wild vs. domesticated, etc.), but no single term meaning "all the non-human animals together." So the very question — what makes the non-human animal as a category? — does not arise in the same way.

docs.title: Rational vs. non-rational — a Greek obsession the Indians don't share
docs.text:
• [00:04:42] Adamson contrasts the Greek tradition, where the rational/non-rational divide is pervasive: rational animals (humans) vs. non-rational animals, with debates among Stoics and Aristotelians, and figures like Plutarch and Porphyry arguing non-human animals can think or even use language. Are there debates like that in India — or even the distinction itself?
  • [00:05:14] Carpenter: it is "definitely not as much of an obsessive concern." Where some thinkers do try to say what is distinctively human, they tend to associate it not with rationality but with dharma — the ability to act for the sake of a larger or more distant good, for the sake of liberation or of what is right.
  • [00:05:49] One could connect this to a kind of rationality (and the Greeks do end up linking the notions closely), but in India that is not the keynote. The real question is not "is it rational?" but "are non-human animals different from human animals, and if so how?"
  • [00:06:18] The answer: humans are much better at acting for the sake of a distant goal — at attaining mokṣa and the broadly ethical things. This is where the reincarnation question starts to bite: humans are more likely to achieve these things, but the tradition does not very often draw sharp category distinctions between humans and animals.

docs.title: Animals inside the moral economy of reincarnation
docs.text:
• [00:06:50] Animals are caught up in reincarnation in a way that implies they too fall under dharma: if one can be punished by rebirth as an animal, or an animal rewarded by rebirth as a human — just as men can be reborn as women and vice versa — then animals are part of the same moral economy. (Adamson notes in passing that the idea men are reborn as women, etc., is the texts' view, not his own.)
  • [00:07:37] Carpenter agrees — but stresses what "involvement" means: reincarnation introduces a completely different sense of individuation. You don't get a person simply replaced by an animal. Rather there is a single being whose actions generate consequences that play out in various ways — possibly through the acquisition of an animal-type body with animal-type desires.
  • [00:08:11] A central question: can animals behave morally — act for the sake of a higher good rather than just being driven by desire? Across the board the Buddhists, Jains and Hindus are "not sentimental about animals." An animal life is conceived as disagreeable, a punishment, a life driven by desire and fear, unable to step back and revise one's desires according to what is best. So animal existence is worse off — and arguably less able to be morally responsible. This is acknowledged.

docs.title: The "serve your time as an elephant" problem
docs.text:
• [00:09:03] The worry: if becoming an animal makes you unable to act morally, how do you ever get out? It looks like a story of pure degeneration with no exit.
  • [00:09:15] Two solutions appear in the texts. (1) Just accept it: you arrive as an animal with a stock of karma already built up; you acquire no new karma during the animal life (you can't act morally), but other karma will come into action once the punishment is paid. "Basically you just have to serve your time as an elephant." (2) Alternatively — and this too is in the texts — animals can behave morally, in the sense of acting for a purpose that then acquires good or bad consequences.

docs.title: Is the reincarnating self human, animal, or neither?
docs.text:
• [00:09:48] Adamson presses the metaphysics: if the same being is human, then animal, then human again, that suggests the self being reborn is neither human nor animal. Compare the episode on women in Indian thought, where sometimes the self seems really male (even when reborn as a woman) and other times genderless. Is it a human trapped in an animal body, or a self that is neither?
  • [00:10:35] Carpenter: there is no unanimity — different texts and philosophers disagree. Śaṅkara is famous (or infamous) for holding that something special about the male Brahmin body is necessary before one achieves mokṣa; but plenty of others denied this, and there are even stories of animals going straight to liberation without an intervening human rebirth. The dominant view, she thinks, is of a being that is in itself neither human nor any other animal.
  • [00:11:20] And of course, when you come to the Buddhists, they challenge the very idea that we should be looking for something "in itself" at all — so they are well placed to say there is no real answer to "but what is it really?"

docs.title: Vegetarianism and ahiṃsā — the line doesn't run the way you'd think
docs.text:
• [00:11:41] Adamson raises vegetarianism and the broader ethic of ahiṃsā (non-violence). The natural thought: I shouldn't eat animals because one might be a reincarnated human — maybe even my grandfather. Is that the moral logic the tradition actually uses?
  • [00:12:05] Carpenter: "Not as often as you would expect" — and in fact it works the other way around. "I mustn't eat it because it's my uncle" can only piggyback on a prior conviction that one doesn't eat one's uncle." And even then it doesn't go through: if the pig's life is so disagreeable, why not liberate your poor uncle and do him a favour?
  • [00:12:44] So there is no straight line from reincarnation to non-violent behaviour. What you actually need is a prior commitment to non-violence. Combine that with a metaphysics of reincarnation that doesn't individuate beings, and the principle of non-violence comes out unrestricted in scope: there is no presumption that it applies only to humans and then gets extended to animals. One is simply to be non-violent — towards whatever could be a recipient of violence or harm.
  • [00:13:27] Adamson reframes it: animals and humans have in common that they are potential victims of violence, and that is why they fall under the rule.

docs.title: How far does the boundary stretch — plants, even stones?
docs.text:
• [00:13:33] Adamson notes that non-violence literature sometimes extends to plants, and even to stones. Is there a global ethic of avoiding violence to anything, or does it matter whether the victim is an animal versus a plant or rock?
  • [00:14:08] Carpenter: the answer is both. There are two distinct things ahiṃsā means, held together with different emphases:
  • (1) Don't harm that which is capable of being harmed. How far this extends depends on the school: for a Jain it extends very far; for a Buddhist fairly far, but not quite to plants.
  • (2) Violence is a mindset — an ill-will — and that is simply bad in itself. Even toward a stone you don't think can be harmed, adopting a violent, ill-willed attitude is an expression of confusion that is "not good for you or for anybody around you."

docs.title: For the animal's sake, or for mine?
docs.text:
• [00:15:18] This connects to Adamson's next question: is benevolence toward animals for the animal's sake (it has a right not to be harmed) or for the moral agent's sake (I don't want a violent mindset; it might block my own liberation)? It sounds like Carpenter thinks both are at work.
  • [00:16:07] Carpenter: to an extent, yes — both, in different emphases in different places. The Buddhists are keen on exercises that recognize every living being suffers and wants not to suffer and wants to be happy; this is crucial to developing compassion, and enlightenment just is the perfection of compassion together with the perfection of wisdom.
  • [00:16:43] One caveat: Indian moral thought is not rights-based. The notion of an animal having a right I must respect is "not the kind of language you ever see." So it is not framed as just vs. unjust, but as appropriate/inappropriate, or as dharma — what is or isn't according to dharma. Making that case, one might appeal to a rule, or to what conduces to one's own liberation, or to the nature of the animal and its suffering.

docs.title: Different schools, different proportions of the same arguments
docs.text:
• [00:17:35] Adamson asks whether this holds across Jains, Buddhists and Vedic thinkers, or is truer of one group. Carpenter: you find strands of all of these in all of them, but in different proportions.
  • [00:17:48] Within the Brahminical tradition — with the Vedas and the Arthaśāstra-type texts to refer to — you are more likely to get appeals to rules ("here's what you do and don't do"). With the Buddhists you find a preponderance of texts emphasizing the suffering of the creature.
  • [00:18:16] Part of the reason: the Buddhists have a polemic against Brahminical animal sacrifice. Even after the Brahminical tradition largely stopped sacrificing animals, it remained committed to the idea that it's okay to do — and the Buddhists and Jains came back hard at that.

docs.title: Two fun facts about the Buddhists
docs.text:
• [00:18:49] Carpenter offers two: (1) Buddhists aren't always vegetarian, and (2) Buddhists hold that plants aren't alive (they're not unique in this).
  • [00:19:03] On plants: if you mustn't be violent toward anything capable of harm, and you think plants can be harmed, then you can't eat plants. The Jains were strict and clear about exactly this — you couldn't eat plants in any way that damages or kills them; for Jains to eat is to engage in violence, which is why being alive at all is to be compromised by the necessity of violence.
  • [00:19:38] The Buddhists, following the middle way, are more pragmatic: one can eat plants, and this is not a bad thing. But because they too hold the no-harm principle, they are forced to conclude that plants aren't capable of being harmed — they can't feel pleasure and pain, which in the Indian context is the very criterion for being alive. So, in effect, plants aren't alive.
  • [00:20:21] Nobody is very explicit about this; it grows up gradually as a worried sideline. And the Buddhists aren't alone — to the objection "plants grow, so they must be alive," others answered: crystals grow and reproduce too, yet you wouldn't call them alive. A genuine philosophical question lurking around the edges.
  • [00:20:53] On meat: the Buddhists agree there are degrees of harmfulness — harming a mosquito isn't as bad as harming a human. The original monastic criterion for what you could eat: you couldn't kill it yourself, couldn't have it killed for you, couldn't hear it being killed, couldn't know it was killed for you — but if someone's leftovers are placed in your bowl, you eat it. If those leftovers are meat, then whether that person ought to have been eating it "is their affair" — you eat what you're given.
  • [00:21:47] Only with the Mahāyāna movement, several centuries later, do arguments arise that if you are striving for enlightenment and really trying to be compassionate, you don't eat animals at all — even leftovers.
  • [00:22:03] This becomes a point of Jain–Buddhist polemic: the Jains taunt the Buddhists as "meat-eating supposed ascetics," insisting they are the hardcore ones.
  • [00:22:13] A favourite Buddhist argument against eating meat (once they do oppose it): when you eat meat you smell different — you stink — not because humans will be put off (our sense of smell is poor), but because prey animals (rabbits, mice) have an acute sense of smell. Walking around stinking like a carnivore strikes fear into every little furry creature you pass — and inducing that fear is a cruel, alarming thing to do.

docs.title: Ending with the fables: no distance between human and non-human
docs.text:
• [00:22:55] Adamson proposes closing on the fables. Beyond Hanumān, the literature teems with "precocious" animals; like Aesop, India has talking-animal tales, but it is, if anything, an even more striking feature. What do the fables tell us about philosophical attitudes toward animals?
  • [00:23:33] Carpenter: the most striking thing is what they express — "the lack of distance between the human and the non-human." Animals appear in a wide variety of guises: they can be wicked or good, crafty, tricky, lazy — but also charitable, generous, thoughtful. They express the full range of moral qualities.
  • [00:24:11] Crucially, they are social. One might think sociability is distinctive of the human realm, but the fables depict animals as social — and not merely as a convenient proxy for humans (though they can function that way too). They show a receptivity and perceptiveness about genuine non-human animal interaction: animals take stances toward one another and engage with each other. The world is not a human one with a colourful animal backdrop, but "an extremely rich one in which all kinds of creatures are going about living their lives."
  • [00:25:00] This is reinforced by the fact that the fables are constantly shared, reworked and spread as part of everyday discourse.
  • [00:25:09] Adamson's closing thought: the fables both express and reinforce the idea of a continuum of living, conscious beings from humans to animals — because a child raised on stories of talking animals is "less likely to think what the Stoics thought about animals." Carpenter: "Exactly — and that can only be a good thing."
  • [00:25:38] Adamson thanks Carpenter and previews the next episode: whether Greek philosophy was influenced by Indian philosophy.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Amber Carpenter — the guest; associate professor at Yale-NUS College, who has worked extensively on Buddhism.
  • animal fables — ancient, constantly-reworked didactic tales of talking, social animals; a "background hum" of Indian thought about animals.
  • Pañcatantra / Hitopadeśa — major collections into which the fable tradition was gathered.
  • Dharmaśāstra / Arthaśāstra — works of conduct that prescribe right behaviour, including toward animals.
  • Mahābhārata / Rāmāyaṇa — the epics, full of animal subplots (e.g. Hanumān the talking monkey).
  • Hanumān — the talking monkey of the Rāmāyaṇa; "no ordinary monkey."
  • Gaṇeśa — the elephant-headed god; example of animals incorporated into the divine.
  • dharma — duty / what is right; for the Indians, what distinguishes humans is the capacity to act for dharma and a distant good, more than "rationality."
  • karma — accumulated moral consequence of action; explains how one can serve out an animal rebirth yet later exit it.
  • mokṣa — liberation; humans are far better placed to attain it, though some texts allow animals to reach it directly.
  • reincarnation / individuation — rebirth across human, animal and divine; introduces a self that is in itself neither human nor animal, and doesn't individuate beings.
  • Śaṅkara — held (infamously) that a male Brahmin body is needed before achieving mokṣa.
  • ahiṃsā — non-violence; rests on a prior, unrestricted commitment, not on "that animal might be my relative."
  • two senses of non-violence — (1) don't harm what can be harmed; (2) violence as an ill-willed mindset that is bad in itself, even toward a stone.
  • Jains — strictest on harm: to eat is to do violence, so all life is compromised; the "hardcore" ascetics who taunt the Buddhists.
  • Buddhists — middle-way pragmatists: not always vegetarian (original rule allowed leftover meat); hold plants aren't alive because they can't feel pleasure and pain (the Indian criterion for being alive).
  • Mahāyāna — later Buddhist movement that argued the truly compassionate eat no animals at all, even leftovers.
  • compassion / suffering — for Buddhists, recognizing that every being suffers and wants happiness is central; enlightenment is the perfection of compassion plus wisdom.
  • not rights-based — Indian ethics frames the issue as appropriate/inappropriate or according to dharma, never as the animal "having a right."
