docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 59 — "Looking East: Indian Influence on Greek Thought"
docs.text:
← Ep 58

Ep 60 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:22:35 In brief: The series' one episode on India's possible influence on Greece — surveying the real channels of contact (trade, the Persian court, Alexander), Thomas McEvilley's catalogue of parallels, the formidable obstacles to transmission, and the two best test cases (Pyrrho and Plotinus), reaching the measured verdict that some Indian ideas probably did filter west, but only intermittently and incidentally, never as the detailed, well-informed engagement seen in the Greek-Arabic-Latin translation movements. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit/Greek terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Gannery"; Pyrrho of Elis ≈ "Pyro of Ellis"; Sextus Empiricus ≈ "Sexus Empiricus"; Thomas McEvilley ≈ "McEvely/McEvilly"; Megasthenes ≈ "Magasthenes/Megastanis"; Seleucus ≈ "Seljukos"; Strabo ≈ "Strebo"; Diogenes Laertius ≈ "Diogenes Laersius"; gymnosophists ≈ "naked sawfists"; Taxila ≈ "Tuxina"; ataraxia ≈ "Atadaxia"; Everard Flintoff ≈ "Flintov"; Anaximenes ≈ "anacymines"; Parmenides ≈ "Permanides"; Madhyamaka ≈ "Madyamika"; Iamblichus ≈ "Iamblicus"; adiaphora ≈ "a-diaphora"; anātman ≈ "un-Otmahn"; svabhāva ≈ "Svavava"; Porphyry ≈ "Porfrey"; Hecataeus ≈ "Hecateus").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Thomas McEvilley — author of the massive The Shape of Ancient Greek Thought, which detects echoes of Indian ideas in nearly every Greek philosopher [00:05:31].
  • Megasthenes — Hellenistic ambassador to the Mauryan court; our best eyewitness on Indian culture, surviving only in quotations [00:04:21].
  • Pyrrho of Elis — founder of Hellenistic skepticism; said to have travelled with Alexander to India and met its sages [00:11:35].
  • Plotinus — 3rd-c. AD founder of Neoplatonism; joined an expedition east hoping to learn Persian and Indian philosophy [00:16:54].

docs.title: The most common question — and why it's the wrong reason to care
docs.text:
• [00:00:31] If you give public lectures on ancient philosophy, you are "almost guaranteed" to be asked whether Greek thought was influenced by ancient Indian culture — perhaps the single most common question from general audiences. It's understandable: what could be more intriguing than that Plato, Aristotle, or Plotinus drew on the Upaniṣads, early Buddhism, or Vedānta?
  • [00:01:07] Taking the possibility seriously threatens to undermine the very contrast between "Eastern" and "Western" philosophy — which is fine by the hosts, a contrast that deserves undermining anyway.
  • [00:01:15] What they find more problematic is the unspoken assumption behind the question: that if Indian thought really did influence Greece, that would secure India a rightful place in the history of philosophy. If this series has been even halfway successful, you should already be convinced Indian thought deserves that place in its own right.
  • [00:01:35] The same distortion afflicts philosophy in the Islamic world: Avicenna and Averroes have drawn attention chiefly because they influenced Latin Christendom, not as thinkers worth studying for themselves — and the vast number of Muslim philosophers after the 12th century are omitted from most histories simply because they came too late for the Arabic-Latin translation movement and were unknown in Europe.
  • [00:02:08] So as we examine influence, remember that the real importance of Indian philosophy is its intrinsic fascination. And if we were going to justify interest by influence, we'd do far better to stress India's massive impact on China and other parts of Asia, which on any reckoning dwarfs whatever it contributed to ancient Europe.

docs.title: Was there any contact at all? — trade and the Persian meeting place
docs.text:
• [00:02:41] The obvious first question: was there any contact and cultural exchange between ancient Greek and Indian cultures at all? The answer "can only be a resounding yes." Trade routes between Europe and India were open well before Presocratic philosophy even emerged.
  • [00:02:58] Scattered literary testimonies survive: the Hippocratic corpus mentions pepper, Sophocles Indian gold, Xenophon Indian hunting dogs. The Persian Empire would have offered a meeting place — the army Xerxes led against the Greeks apparently included Indian soldiers, and Greek and Indian scholars would have met at the Persian court.
  • [00:03:28] Still, during classical antiquity — the era of the Presocratics, Plato, and Aristotle — knowledge of India was limited and indirect. The most valuable information sat in ethnographic writings now lost, notably by the "fabulously named" Skylax, who in the 6th century BC joined a military expedition to India under the Persian king Darius. Herodotus mentions that expedition and draws on another ethnographer, Hecataeus.

docs.title: Alexander, Megasthenes, and the śramaṇa movements
docs.text:
• [00:04:02] The key moment comes around the time of Aristotle, with the conquests of Alexander the Great. Reaching Bactria and India in about 330 BC, he brought Greek culture, founded Hellenistic cities, and created the conditions for deeper engagement with Indian society.
  • [00:04:21] That engagement is most palpable in Megasthenes, an ambassador to the Mauryan court sent by Seleucus, the Hellenistic king who succeeded Alexander in the conquered eastern lands. Megasthenes dealt with the mighty emperor Chandragupta and may have visited the great city of Pāṭaliputra, so he could describe Indian culture as a direct witness — though using the tropes of Greek ethnography and making "perplexingly basic errors," for instance denying that slavery existed in ancient India.
  • [00:04:51] Megasthenes' work too is lost, except in quotations by later authors, notably the historian Strabo. Thanks to him we know Megasthenes was aware of the śramaṇa ascetic movements, even contrasting two kinds of renouncers: those who stayed in the city working as healers, and those who withdrew to the forest.
  • [00:05:14] All of this makes it "eminently plausible" that Indian philosophical ideas could have reached Greek intellectuals — and anyone who reads in both traditions will hit on striking parallels.

docs.title: McEvilley's catalogue of resonances
docs.text:
• [00:05:25] Someone who has done far more than read around a bit is Thomas McEvilley, whose massive The Shape of Ancient Greek Thought detects echoes of Indian ideas in pretty much every Greek philosopher, from the Presocratics down to the late Neoplatonists. A sampling:
  • Matching lists of fundamental elements — air, earth, fire, water — in both cultures.
  • Both Heraclitus and the Viṣṇu Purāṇa saying divine forces play "like a child."
  • The Ṛg Veda making ocean the source of all things, as Thales made water his primary principle; the Upaniṣads identifying air as primary, agreeing with Anaximenes.
  • The Pythagorean doctrines of vegetarianism and reincarnation sounding "rather Indian."
  • The monist trend in Vedic thought culminating in Advaita Vedānta echoed in Parmenides — and the Chāndogya Upaniṣad sounding like Parmenides when it denies anything can come to be from nothing.
  • [00:06:33] For later philosophy, McEvilley remarks it is hard to identify any significant difference between the methods or stated purposes of Pyrrhonist and Madhyamaka dialectic — a strong parallel between ancient skepticism and Buddhism — and compares the philosophically motivated rituals of Tantra to theurgy in Neoplatonists like Iamblichus.

docs.title: Three explanations: influence, coincidence, deep shared roots
docs.text:
• [00:06:56] McEvilley is largely content to flag the echoes without committing to one explanation. Alongside more-or-less direct influence from India, he admits two other possibilities.
  • [00:07:08] Coincidence. We have two enormous bodies of writing; if we trawled the thousands of pages of Pāli and Sanskrit philosophy and found nothing reminiscent of anything Greek, that would be extraordinary — especially since philosophical reflection is bound to throw up certain fundamental ideas independently (atomism in physics, skepticism in epistemology, monism in metaphysics). A skeptic could see McEvilley's resume of resonances as just similar ideas reached independently.
  • [00:07:49] Deep shared roots. McEvilley seems attracted to the idea of obscure common origins behind both traditions — shared mythic tendencies also found in Near Eastern and Egyptian religion, pointing to cultural connections from before historical records. That might explain the urge to trace all things back to one physical element. But it is "unsatisfyingly vague," and not really enough to account for the more exact parallels, where the resonance is so strong one suspects direct textual appropriation.
  • [00:08:25] Tellingly, in his many hundreds of pages McEvilley offers few parallels of that exact sort. The one he treats as something close to genuine proof: a testimony that Heraclitus explained night and day by two exhalations, one bright and one dark — the same idea found in the Chāndogya and Bṛhadāraṇyaka ("Great Forest") Upaniṣads.
  • [00:09:03] Anticipating readers who think a shared element-list is just obvious, McEvilley notes that China had a different list — water, fire, wood, metal, earth. (Adamson adds that 1970s disco culture got it down to three: "Earth, Wind & Fire.")

docs.title: The obstacles in the way of transmission
docs.text:
• [00:09:24] To decide whether there was real historical influence, it helps to think harder about how it could have happened — and there were formidable obstacles.
  • [00:09:40] Distance. The two civilizations were separated by thousands of miles; it is not obvious that complex philosophical ideas could travel that far alongside pepper and luxury goods.
  • [00:09:53] Language. Profound cultural exchange in the history of philosophy typically involved a deliberate translation effort — rich Muslims commissioning Arabic versions of Greek science in the 8th–9th centuries AD, Latin Christians translating from Arabic and Greek in the 12th. Nothing like that happened here: there was no Sanskrit-Greek translation movement, indeed not a single case of a philosophical work from India being translated into Greek or Latin in antiquity.
  • [00:10:29] Elite exclusivity. The ancient Indian elite excluded almost all other Indians from their intellectual activities, never mind distrusted foreign "barbarians." It is more plausible that the less-exclusivist śramaṇa philosophers — Buddhists, Jains, and Ājīvikas — were open to sharing ideas with outsiders. And any ideas that did fight past these obstacles would likely have been greatly oversimplified or distorted in transmission.

docs.title: What would convince a skeptic — and enter Pyrrho
docs.text:
• [00:11:00] To persuade cautious historians of profound, direct engagement, they'll want an "intrepid traveler" — in practice a Greek who reached India, since no Indian thinker seems to have gone to Europe. They'll need not just evocative parallels but historical evidence that the thinker was genuinely inspired by Indian ideas — and, given the exclusivity point, the ideas should likely be śramaṇa, not Brahminical.
  • [00:11:35] "Step forward, Pyrrho of Elis" — putative founder of Hellenistic skepticism and namesake of the radical Pyrrhonian skepticism later adopted by the 2nd-c. AD author Sextus Empiricus. Excitingly, Diogenes Laertius gives a detailed ancient life reporting that Pyrrho accompanied Alexander's expedition to India, where he met "naked sophists" — the gymnosophists, ascetic philosophers said elsewhere to have been encountered by Alexander's entourage near Taxila.
  • [00:12:11] Diogenes says it was a direct result of meeting these sages that Pyrrho adopted his signature policy of suspending judgment — since our beliefs are only matters of custom, and in themselves things are "no more one thing than another." On this basis scholars like Everard Flintoff and, more recently, Christopher Beckwith have argued Pyrrho's introduction of skepticism to Greek philosophy was a more-or-less direct borrowing from early Indian skepticism. Flintoff leaves open which ascetic movement Pyrrho met; Beckwith wrote an entire book arguing the Pyrrho stories are crucial evidence for the nature of early Buddhism.
  • [00:12:58] The hypothesis is attractive because Pyrrho was renowned for achieving ataraxia — freedom from disturbance, impervious to physical and mental pain, just as a liberated Buddhist is free from all suffering. And he reached it precisely by suspending judgment about all things, using techniques to puncture the pretensions of "dogmatists." Among them was an argument resembling the tetralemma, the fourfold menu of options used so effectively by Nāgārjuna — found in early reports of the Buddha himself, in a testimony about Pyrrho, and across Sextus (even though such forms appear already in Plato and Aristotle).

docs.title: Why the Buddha is not a Pyrrhonian
docs.text:
• [00:13:53] There is "one small problem": Buddhists are very far from being Pyrrhonian skeptics. The Buddha did sometimes refuse to answer philosophical questions, but typically because the questions made misleading presuppositions — e.g. assuming the existence of the self — not because he suspended judgment.
  • [00:14:15] Indeed Buddhism's most signature commitment, the doctrine of no-self, would count as a negative dogmatic belief to any self-respecting (or "no-self-respecting") Pyrrhonian, who would suspend judgment about whether there is a self. Likewise each of the four noble truths is a straightforward assertion a Pyrrhonist would decline to endorse.
  • [00:14:46] Beckwith "rather cheats" by trying to make the Buddha a universal skeptic like Pyrrho — suggesting that when Pyrrho called all things adiaphora (undifferentiated, not distinct) he meant the same as the Buddha's anātman (lack of self or independent reality). But the notions are very different: Pyrrho meant we can never judge anything to be more one thing than another (no action more good than bad), whereas the Buddha was rejecting a specific metaphysical idea — far from suspending judgment about ātman, he forthrightly denied it, and the skeptical consequences were never meant to undermine Buddhism's positive doctrines like the four noble truths.

docs.title: Sextus versus Nāgārjuna
docs.text:
• [00:15:34] Jumping ahead to the 2nd-c. AD successors — Sextus and Nāgārjuna — yields the same conclusion. Nāgārjuna's dialectical subtlety in undermining rivals is comparable to Sextus's, but Sextus would unhesitatingly classify him as a negative dogmatist, not a true skeptic, because Nāgārjuna was committed to the principle that all things are empty and dependently arising.
  • [00:16:04] Whatever exactly he meant by that (much disputed), Sextus would want to suspend judgment about whether all things are empty: there are, he'd say, good arguments on both sides of the debate between upholders of svabhāva (intrinsic reality) and adherents of emptiness.
  • [00:16:23] The upshot is not that we can rule out Buddhist influence on Pyrrho. The likelier conclusion satisfies "neither the skeptic nor the enthusiast": Pyrrho may have encountered and been inspired by Indian philosophers on campaign with Alexander, but — given the cultural and linguistic barriers — he failed to understand what they were saying, or at best borrowed from them very selectively.

docs.title: Plotinus and the lure of Vedānta
docs.text:
• [00:16:54] Several centuries on, another, even more influential Greek has often been tied to Indian thought: Plotinus, the 3rd-c. AD founder of Neoplatonism. As with Pyrrho, we have evidence of both interest and eastern travel: his student, editor, and biographer Porphyry reports that in 242 AD Plotinus joined the expedition of the emperor Gordian III precisely hoping to learn about the philosophy of the Persians and Indians.
  • [00:17:28] Unfortunately the expedition was an abortive one, so it can't really prove Plotinus had the encounter he hoped for. He never mentions India in his own writings — but Porphyry does: his work on vegetarianism has a reasonably well-informed section on Indian practices, and Augustine tells us that in another (now lost) work Porphyry set out to compare Neoplatonic philosophy with "the practices and teachings of the Indians." So Plotinus had both the motive and the means to access Indian ideas, if only indirectly.
  • [00:18:08] Are there signs of influence? Positive answers compare his Neoplatonism with Vedānta, especially the Advaita variety. This is chronologically awkward — Śaṅkara lived about half a millennium after Plotinus — but perhaps Plotinus was picking up the same older Indian ideas that would later inspire Advaita, notably the Upaniṣadic concept of brahman. In apparent agreement with that strand, Plotinus identifies the paradigmatic source of being as a single universal mind and urges us to realize our unity with it, making the physical universe nothing but an image or outward manifestation of intellect — the seat of knowledge and (we might venture) consciousness or selfhood. He also carries forward earlier Greek themes that recall India, such as reincarnation.

docs.title: The case against — and a methodological conundrum
docs.text:
• [00:19:08] The main argument against Indian inspiration is that Plotinus "could, and quite evidently did," develop all these ideas through engagement with earlier Platonism. His universal mind is also the realm of Platonic Forms — not a new idea so much as a modification of Middle Platonism, the tradition of reflection on Plato's dialogues in the generations before him. Some contemporaries even accused Plotinus of stealing his whole system from the Middle Platonist Numenius — surely exaggerated, but "with a grain of truth."
  • [00:19:45] Hence a methodological conundrum: should we accept claims of intercultural influence only when developments cannot be explained as internal to a tradition? That seems unduly demanding — nothing prevents Plotinus from being inspired both by his Platonist predecessors and by Indian ideas, especially if he saw them as agreeing.
  • [00:20:13] The Plotinus-Vedānta comparison is further complicated by the fact that Plotinus posits a higher principle above the universal mind — a pure unity that is explicitly not a mind and does not think about anything, even itself. And if we wanted to locate a self or seat of consciousness in Plotinus, it fits the individual soul better than the universal mind. As with Pyrrho, initially striking parallels look less exact once we attend to the details.
  • [00:20:43] Then again, that is just what we should expect: where access to Indian thought was bound to be very imperfect, why expect perfect parallels? In that spirit even sympathetic scholars reach half-hearted conclusions — McEvilley writes that although it was "virtually certain" Plotinus had some contact with Indian ideas, that contact "probably didn't amount to much," and the similarities may stem from the longer-standing presence of Indian themes already in Greek thought. Another recent assessment guesses Greco-Roman authors had more information than sources survive, "though probably in a very general and distorted way."

docs.title: The overall verdict
docs.text:
• [00:21:36] Such moderate conclusions are salutary, because by the standards of the history of philosophy this question evokes unusually strong feelings: many want to believe the influence was real and deeply significant; others — not least scholars of Greek philosophy who'd rather not have to learn Indian philosophy — are equally determined to exclude it entirely.
  • [00:21:57] The honest verdict: we should almost certainly admit that ideas did filter into the ancient European world from Indian culture. But in stark contrast to the tremendous, determinative impact of Greek ideas on the Islamic world, and of Islamic-world works on Latin Christendom, the Indian contribution to ancient Greek thought was intermittent and rather incidental — rarely if ever a detailed, well-informed engagement with Indian philosophy by Greek or Roman intellectuals.
  • [00:22:27] For that kind of engagement we must wait for later moments of cultural exchange — the topic of the next episode of the history of philosophy in India.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Thomas McEvilley — author of The Shape of Ancient Greek Thought, cataloguing echoes of Indian ideas across Greek philosophy; flags three explanations (influence, coincidence, deep shared roots) without firmly choosing.
  • Megasthenes — Seleucus's ambassador to Chandragupta's Mauryan court; eyewitness on India (and on the śramaṇa renouncers), surviving only in quotations by Strabo.
  • śramaṇa — the non-Brahminical ascetic/renouncer movements (Buddhists, Jains, Ājīvikas); less exclusivist, so likelier than Brahmins to share ideas with foreigners.
  • gymnosophists — the "naked sophists" / ascetic philosophers Alexander's entourage met near Taxila; the sages Pyrrho is said to have encountered.
  • Pyrrho of Elis — founder of Hellenistic (Pyrrhonian) skepticism; reportedly took his policy of suspending judgment from meeting Indian sages on Alexander's campaign.
  • ataraxia — Greek "freedom from disturbance"; Pyrrho's goal, compared to a liberated Buddhist's freedom from suffering.
  • tetralemma — the fourfold argument-menu used by Nāgārjuna, with parallels in reports of the Buddha, Pyrrho, and Sextus.
  • Sextus Empiricus — 2nd-c. AD Pyrrhonist who would class both the Buddha and Nāgārjuna as negative dogmatists, not true skeptics.
  • Nāgārjuna — 2nd-c. AD Madhyamaka Buddhist committed to the thesis that all things are empty and dependently arising (hence dogmatic to a Pyrrhonist).
  • anātman / svabhāva — Buddhist denial of a self vs. the intrinsic, independent reality (svabhāva) that emptiness denies; the Buddha rejects the self rather than suspending judgment about it.
  • four noble truths — straightforward Buddhist assertions a Pyrrhonist would refuse to endorse — proof the Buddha was no skeptic.
  • Plotinus — 3rd-c. AD founder of Neoplatonism; joined Gordian III's expedition (242 AD) hoping to learn Indian/Persian philosophy; his "universal mind" invites comparison with Advaita Vedānta's brahman.
  • Porphyry — Plotinus's biographer; wrote on Indian practices and (per Augustine) compared Neoplatonism with Indian teachings.
  • Advaita Vedānta / brahman — the monist Upaniṣadic strand (later systematized by Śaṅkara, half a millennium after Plotinus) whose ultimate reality is likened to Plotinus's universal mind.
  • Middle Platonism / Numenius — the internal Greek tradition that can fully explain Plotinus's system, the chief argument against needing Indian influence to account for it.

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:20:37 In brief: A survey of how Indian ideas travelled west — first into the Islamic world (al-Bīrūnī's pioneering, if homogenizing, comparative study of India), then into early-modern and modern Europe (Locke, Leibniz, Hume, Hegel, Schopenhauer, down to 20th-c. Oxford) — with the recurring flaw that Western readers flattened India's diversity into one "monolithic teaching" and saw it through what they expected rather than what it said. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit/Arabic terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Gernardin Gannery"; al-Bīrūnī ≈ "Al-Biruni/Arbiruni/Al-Beruni"; Barmakids ≈ "Barma kids/Badma kids/Bodhma kids"; Ibn al-Nadīm ≈ "Ibn Nadim/Imnanadi Dim"; al-Kindī ≈ "Arkindi"; śramaṇa/Shamaniyya ≈ "shramana/Shamania"; Jahm ibn Ṣafwān ≈ "Jahm Im Safwan"; Maḥmūd of Ghazna ≈ "Mahmoud O'Hazna"; Gauḍapāda ≈ "Gaurapada"; Suśruta ≈ "Sushuta"; Pañcatantra ≈ "Pachatantra"; al-Shahrastānī ≈ "Ashah Hastani"; Rashīd al-Dīn ≈ "Rashid Adin"; Suhrawardī ≈ "Suhavardi"; Dārā Shukoh ≈ "Dada Shikou/Dadaashikou"; Charles Dolu ≈ "Charles Dolou"; Pierre Bayle ≈ "Pierre Bélle/Bale"; Francis Bernier ≈ "Vanieres/Banyé"; Colebrooke ≈ "Colbrook"; Bṛhaspati ≈ "Brihaspati"; Schopenhauer ≈ "Schovenhauer"; Radhakrishnan ≈ "Sarvepaly Radha Krishnan"; Matilal ≈ "Bimal-Khrishnan Matilal"; Strawson ≈ "Strasson"; Dummett ≈ "Dummit").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• al-Bīrūnī — medieval scientist whose Treatise on India (completed 1030) was the first ambitious comparative study of Indian thought for an Arabic readership [00:00:50].
  • The Barmakids — wealthy Bactrian-descended clan in the late-8th-c. caliphate who actively sponsored the transmission of Indian science [00:02:23].
  • Dārā Shukoh — 17th-c. Mughal prince who translated the Upaniṣads into Persian and wrote Confluence of the Oceans [00:08:30].
  • Hume, Hegel, Schopenhauer — the three European moderns through whom Indian (especially Buddhist) ideas are traced, and who repeatedly misread India [00:10:01].

docs.title: al-Bīrūnī: the first great comparativist
docs.text:
• [00:00:32] Last time covered modern scholars who noticed parallels between ancient Indian and ancient Greek thought. But searching for such resonances is not distinctively modern — it was already the project of the medieval scientist al-Bīrūnī, whose treatise on India was completed in 1030.
  • [00:00:56] The treatise was aimed at an Arabic-speaking readership who would thereby be equipped for encounters with Indian culture. His approach is comparative: he systematically juxtaposes Indian ideas with those of Greek philosophy and science, and even flags some of the same parallels noted by contemporary historians — such as the transmigration of souls. Indeed al-Bīrūnī identifies belief in reincarnation as the distinctive marker of "the Indian creed," much as the Trinity marks Christianity or the Sabbath marks the Jews.

docs.title: Why a Greek-savvy readership existed: the translation movements
docs.text:
• [00:01:34] al-Bīrūnī could presume his readers knew Greek ideas because a prodigious Greek-to-Arabic translation movement had already made them available, in the 8th–10th centuries AD.
  • [00:01:44] At around the same time some Indian texts were translated too, focused on scientific works: Arabic versions of medical texts like the Suśruta, and in the mid-8th century an astronomical handbook called in Arabic the Sindhind, produced at the behest of the caliph al-Manṣūr. Indian astronomy and astrology were an important source for those disciplines in the Islamic world.
  • [00:02:14] Beyond the sciences there was the Kalīla wa-Dimna, a literary work derived (via a Persian translation) from the Indian book of animal fables, the Pañcatantra.

docs.title: The Barmakids and the earliest awareness of Indian ideas
docs.text:
• [00:02:23] Readers of Arabic could especially thank one family, the Barmakids, who were influential in the late-8th-c. caliphate. They hailed from Ṭukhāristān in Bactria — the only area under Arab rule where Buddhism and Sanskrit literature were still actively studied.
  • [00:02:45] The wealthy and powerful Barmakids took an active interest in Indian science: they summoned Indian doctors and philosophers and even dispatched a fact-finding mission to India. A document on Indian culture written for one of them is lost, but the 10th-c. bibliophile Ibn al-Nadīm claimed to have seen a copy written out by none other than al-Kindī — the first Muslim thinker to make explicit use of Greek philosophical sources.
  • [00:03:15] The same Ibn al-Nadīm knew of the Buddhists in Transoxiana, calling them the Shamaniyya — a term traceable to the Indian word for the renouncer movement, śramaṇa.
  • [00:03:28] Particularly intriguing are reports of a debate between the early-8th-c. theologian Jahm ibn Ṣafwān and a group of Buddhists, who argued that his belief in the god of Islam could not be substantiated on empirical evidence. So a full century before al-Kindī — usually credited with initiating philosophy in the Islamic world — there was at least fleeting awareness of Indian ideas about the sources of knowledge (pramāṇas).

docs.title: al-Bīrūnī's small-scale translation movement
docs.text:
• [00:04:01] al-Bīrūnī went far beyond his predecessors, made possible because he was attached to the court of the warlord Maḥmūd of Ghazna, who made destructive incursions into India. al-Bīrūnī is frank about the enmity Indians bore toward Muslims as a result; he worked with scholars who had presumably been brought to Maḥmūd's court under duress.
  • [00:04:27] The result was a small-scale Sanskrit–Arabic translation movement. With his Indian advisors he prepared translations of Patañjali's Yoga-Sūtra and the Sāṃkhya-kārikā, drew on Gauḍapāda's commentary on the latter, and used an Arabic Bhagavad-Gītā (which, by his quotations, often diverged from the version we know). They also translated the other way, from Arabic into Sanskrit — Euclid, Ptolemy, and al-Bīrūnī's own works.
  • [00:05:05] So his treatise is a remarkably well-informed document with extensive Sanskrit quotation, relating its sources not only to Greek thought but to Christianity, Judaism, and Manichaeism. Islam is implicitly exempted from the comparison and given special status — though he does note an affinity between Indian philosophy and Sufism.

docs.title: al-Bīrūnī's flaw: India as a single doctrine
docs.text:
• [00:05:36] What al-Bīrūnī does not do well is convey the diversity of Indian thought. He treats the ideas of the Indian elite as a single body of doctrine, which he contrasts with "vulgar popular beliefs" he openly disdains. But he is an "equal-opportunity elitist": he says the Greeks too were idolaters, and that ordinary Muslims would venerate images of the Prophet or Mecca given half a chance.
  • [00:06:09] al-Bīrūnī is impressed by tendencies toward monotheism in Indian philosophy — the first thing he reports of the Indian religion reads like a statement of Islamic monotheism (God eternal, free, omnipotent, resembled by none of his creatures). Taking Patañjali as his key, he presents Indian thought as a single harmonious teaching aimed at liberating the soul from ignorance and attachment to matter so as to attain union with God.
  • [00:06:38] This may remind us of Vedānta — yet that tradition goes unmentioned by al-Bīrūnī. His focus is the soul's relation to a single all-powerful God, achieved by detaching action from desire, as the Bhagavad-Gītā instructs. His tendency to lump everything together and see it echoing other cultures set the tone for all subsequent engagement with Indian thought.

docs.title: Later Islamic engagement, down to Dārā Shukoh
docs.text:
• [00:07:13] In the Islamic world it was a while before another such engagement. The 12th-c. theologian-philosopher al-Shahrastānī wrote a survey of religious doctrines and did discuss India, but his treatment is disappointingly sketchy and seems not to draw on al-Bīrūnī. Better informed is the historian Rashīd al-Dīn (writing around 1300), aided by new information from a Buddhist scholar.
  • [00:07:38] There was also interest in India's mystical traditions: the 12th-c. Illuminationist philosopher Suhrawardī insisted his own teachings accorded with the sages of India, and yogic meditation reached Arabic readers through translations of a work called the Pool of Nectar — though a study concludes it offered only a narrow window, barely distinguishable from the standard occult and mystical practices already current in Islamicate society.
  • [00:08:12] It was really the Islamic invasions of India that recreated the conditions for renewing al-Bīrūnī's project. His hunch that Sufism matched Indian belief was borne out by the success of Islamic mysticism in the subcontinent. The syncretic trend climaxed with Dārā Shukoh, a 17th-c. prince who translated some of the Upaniṣads into Persian and wrote Confluence of the Oceans — the title pointing to the agreement between Indian and Islamic culture, the latter understood mainly as philosophical Sufism (covered in Ep 189 of the main HoP podcast).

docs.title: India reaches Europe — Locke and Leibniz
docs.text:
• [00:08:58] By this time information about Indian philosophy was reaching Europe too — and the results were "not always edifying." Dārā Shukoh's younger contemporary John Locke mocked the notion of a mysterious underlying substance by comparing it to a "poor Indian philosopher" who imagined the earth needed something to bear it up and so rested it on an elephant, supported in turn by a tortoise.
  • [00:09:28] Leibniz rose to India's defense, chastising Locke: this Indian conception of substance, "for all its apparent thinness, is less empty and sterile than it is thought to be," with consequences of the greatest importance that could give philosophy "an entirely new face." Neither passage suggests deep knowledge — but opportunities to learn more were increasing.

docs.title: Hume and the Buddhist back-channel
docs.text:
• [00:10:01] Alison Gopnik has raised the possibility that David Hume was acquainted with Buddhist philosophy. While writing his Treatise of Human Nature, Hume was in residence at the Jesuit academy of La Flèche, where he could have met the much older Charles Dolu, who had been on a trip to Siam in the 1680s.
  • [00:10:22] Dolu in turn knew Ippolito Desideri, who had done missionary work in Tibet. Both were well informed about Buddhism; Desideri even wrote a treatise on "a false and peculiar religion observed in Tibet," urging (like al-Bīrūnī before him) that people should know more of it in order to contest it, and highlighting its "Pythagoreanism" — presumably its commitment to reincarnation. Gopnik: in 1735 Hume, rusticating in a small French town, was "only one remove away" from ideas thousands of miles distant in Siam and Tibet. Perhaps it is no coincidence that Hume's empiricism and skepticism about the self strikingly recall Buddhism.
  • [00:11:22] Hume's Treatise was also influenced by Nicolas Malebranche and Pierre Bayle, who in turn knew something of Chinese philosophy. Malebranche wrote a Conversation Between a Christian Philosopher and a Chinese Philosopher (1708); Bayle's Historical and Critical Dictionary (1703) described Chinese philosophy essentially via the Buddha's life and thought. Again a skeptical attitude toward the soul comes to the fore — another conduit for the Buddhist no-self doctrine into Europe.

docs.title: Francis Bernier and the spider
docs.text:
• [00:11:58] Yet another source was the well-travelled Francis Bernier, who had been to India and served as court physician to the Mughal prince Dārā Shukoh. Bernier exchanged ideas with one of the court intellectuals who had helped translate the Upaniṣads.
  • [00:12:17] Writing from Shiraz in 1667, Bernier said his three-year collaboration with a pandit — facilitated by his own Persian translations of Gassendi and Descartes — let him report many things from Sanskrit books though he knew no Sanskrit.
  • [00:12:41] Here too a link to Hume: Bernier publicized the Indian metaphor comparing God to a spider that extends filaments from itself and then withdraws them, so that creation will ultimately collapse back into God. In his Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion Hume cites this analogy and ascribes it to "the Brahmins" — but is dismissive, calling it a cosmogony that "appears to us ridiculous, because a spider is a little contemptible animal" whose operations we'd never take as a model for the universe.

docs.title: 19th-c. Indology: Colebrooke, the Mills, the Schlegels
docs.text:
• [00:13:17] In the 19th century Europeans finally caught up with al-Bīrūnī by making Indology a serious enterprise. A key figure was Henry T. Colebrooke, who translated mathematical and philosophical works from India into English.
  • [00:13:35] A tantalizing connection runs from Colebrooke to John Stuart Mill. One might expect Mill to know much about India — his father James Mill was an East India Company administrator and author of the colonial-minded History of British India. Yet the younger Mill's philosophy makes no explicit use of Indian thought. He would, though, probably have known Colebrooke's 1827 lecture on the materialist theory of mind of the Cārvāka school.
  • [00:14:05] This Cārvāka theory is comparable to emergentism in philosophy of mind — and Mill sounds rather like a follower of Bṛhaspati, the school's founder, when he writes in his System of Logic that "all organized bodies are composed of parts similar to those composing inorganic nature… the phenomena of life result from the juxtaposition of those parts in a certain manner."
  • [00:14:42] Indology was also emerging in Germany with the Schlegel brothers: Friedrich Schlegel learned Persian and Sanskrit and published On the Language and Wisdom of the Indians, while his brother August Wilhelm Schlegel took up the first German chair of Indology in Bonn, 1818.

docs.title: Hegel: extravagant praise, casual dismissal
docs.text:
• [00:14:58] The Indologists' impact shows in Hegel, who knew Colebrooke's essays (published in the Royal Asiatic Society's transactions, 1824) and reviewed August Wilhelm Schlegel's work on the Bhagavad-Gītā — putting him in a position (or at least the impression of one) to assess India's philosophical contribution.
  • [00:15:25] For Hegel the Indians had reached only a primitive stage in the development of spirit (Geist): a "completely abstract notion of substance as a single underlying principle," identified with an "equally abstract and empty subjecthood." Once again Indian philosophy is reduced to a monolith, with all weight placed on the monist strand of Brahminical thought.
  • [00:15:50] His verdict combines extravagant praise with casual dismissal: in the Oriental world "we do find philosophizing too, indeed the most profound philosophizing — but insofar as it remains the most profound, it remains also abstract. For us, the real philosophy begins only in Greece."

docs.title: Schopenhauer: "The Buddha, Eckhart, and I"
docs.text:
• [00:16:13] A more positive assessment comes from Schopenhauer, who on occasion called himself a Buddhist and was hugely impressed by the Upaniṣads — which he read in an 1801 Latin translation based on the Persian version of (you guessed it) Dārā Shukoh. Of this text he said it was "the most profitable and sublime reading that is possible in the world… the consolation of my life and will be that of my death."
  • [00:16:45] Whether admiration meant real influence is hard to say. He claimed agreement with Buddhism and with the medieval mystic Meister Eckhart, writing: "The Buddha, Eckhart, and I all teach essentially the same" — Eckhart bound by Christian mythology, Buddhism clearer for lacking it, and "complete clarity lies with me." Yet he insisted that when he began The World as Will and Representation he was as yet unacquainted with the Buddhist philosophy that resonated with his system.
  • [00:17:34] Like the others, Schopenhauer still lumped Indian traditions together as one doctrine. Our own tour, by contrast, has shown a stark opposition between Vedānta's monism of consciousness and Buddhist skepticism about the self. Schopenhauer saw little difference between union with the Upaniṣadic brahman and the Buddhist liberation through abandonment of will: for him brahman was simply the will of his own philosophy — a self or subject able to view things as a whole, sub specie aeternitatis.

docs.title: Wittgenstein, and the abiding distortion
docs.text:
• [00:18:07] That idea was later taken over by Wittgenstein, who writes in the Tractatus: "The view of the world sub specie aeternitatis is the view of it as a limited whole. The feeling of the world as a limited whole is the mystical feeling."
  • [00:18:32] But this does not do justice to Schopenhauer's Indian sources. As the earlier Upaniṣad episodes argued, the Upaniṣadic brahman concerns the phenomenology of consciousness — the underlying subject of thought and perception, not a principle of agency or willing.
  • [00:18:50] This is typical of the European reception. By Schopenhauer's day vastly more was known about Indian philosophy than the Greeks could ever have known — the Sanskrit translations missing in antiquity were now available, and scholars like Colebrooke and the Schlegels gave India sustained, careful attention. Yet with Hume, Hegel, and Schopenhauer we still see Europeans influenced as much by what they assumed Indian philosophy should say as by what it really said.

docs.title: Into the 20th century — and where we go next
docs.text:
• [00:19:18] There is much more to the engagement between Europe and ancient India; only a few famous names have been touched, and the story has not reached the 20th century, when two holders of Oxford's Spalding Professorship — Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan and Bimal Krishna Matilal — worked to win British philosophers' attention for India.
  • [00:19:45] Radhakrishnan's effort to showcase India's tradition of philosophical idealism was mistimed — British idealism was already falling out of favour. Matilal had greater success introducing his Oxford colleagues to Indian epistemology: Peter Strawson, Derek Parfit, and Michael Dummett all paid tribute to his brilliance and to the Indian ideas he brought them — for Parfit the Buddhist analysis of persons, for Strawson the descriptive metaphysics of Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika.
  • [00:20:24] In the 21st century there is "really no excuse" to imagine, with Hegel, that real philosophy began only with the Greeks. In that spirit, next time the series draws to a close: a quick review of philosophical developments in India since antiquity, and final thoughts on the contemporary relevance of the history of philosophy in India.

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• al-Bīrūnī — medieval scientist at Maḥmūd of Ghazna's court; his Treatise on India (1030) was the first richly informed comparative study of Indian thought for Arabic readers, but flattened India into one doctrine.
  • Suśruta / Sindhind / Kalīla wa-Dimna — early Indian works that reached Arabic: a medical text, an astronomical handbook (commissioned by caliph al-Manṣūr), and animal fables derived from the Pañcatantra.
  • Barmakids — late-8th-c. caliphal family from Bactria's Ṭukhāristān (where Buddhism and Sanskrit still flourished) who sponsored the transmission of Indian science.
  • Ibn al-Nadīm — 10th-c. bibliophile; recorded al-Kindī copying an Indian document and called the Buddhists Shamaniyya (from śramaṇa, "renouncer").
  • pramāṇas — Indian "sources/means of knowledge"; awareness of them shows in the Buddhist demand that Jahm ibn Ṣafwān ground belief in God empirically.
  • Yoga-Sūtra / Sāṃkhya-kārikā / Bhagavad-Gītā — Sanskrit texts al-Bīrūnī translated or used (with Gauḍapāda's commentary), reading them as one teaching of union with God.
  • Dārā Shukoh — 17th-c. Mughal prince; translated the Upaniṣads into Persian and wrote Confluence of the Oceans on Indian–Islamic (Sufi) agreement; his version seeded the Latin text Schopenhauer read.
  • Locke vs. Leibniz — Locke mocked Indian "substance" via the earth-on-elephant-on-tortoise image; Leibniz defended it as fertile for philosophy.
  • David Hume — possibly exposed to Buddhism via La Flèche (Dolu, Desideri); his no-self skepticism and empiricism recall Buddhism; cites and dismisses the Indian "God as spider" analogy.
  • Francis Bernier — physician to Dārā Shukoh; relayed Sanskrit ideas (via a pandit) to Europe, including the spider cosmogony.
  • Cārvāka / Bṛhaspati — Indian materialist school (its founder Bṛhaspati); its theory of mind, publicized by Colebrooke (1827), is comparable to emergentism and echoed by J. S. Mill.
  • Hegel — judged India only a "primitive stage" of Geist; "real philosophy begins only in Greece"; praise mixed with dismissal.
  • Schopenhauer — called himself a Buddhist; revered the Upaniṣads; "The Buddha, Eckhart, and I teach essentially the same"; wrongly equated brahman with his will (the self viewed sub specie aeternitatis).
  • Wittgenstein — inherited the sub specie aeternitatis "world as a limited whole = mystical feeling" idea in the Tractatus.
  • Radhakrishnan & Matilal — 20th-c. Oxford Spalding Professors who pressed India on British philosophy; Matilal's Indian epistemology influenced Strawson (Nyāya/Vaiśeṣika), Parfit (Buddhist persons), and Dummett.

docs.title: HoPWaG India · Ep 61 — "What Happened Next: Indian Philosophy After Dignāga"
docs.text:
← Ep 60

Ep 62 →

🎧 Listen: official page · 👤 Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri 📄 Read the full transcript

Speakers: Peter Adamson & Jonardon Ganeri · Runtime: 00:23:24 In brief: The last scripted episode of the India series: a recap of the first millennium-and-a-half it has covered (Vedas to Dignāga), then a lightning sketch of the next millennium-and-a-half — Dharmakīrti, Śrīharṣa's skepticism, Gaṅgeśa's Navya-Nyāya revolution, the early-modern Sanskrit and Islamic flowering, the colonial turn to political philosophy, and the contemporary present — ending with the areas where Adamson thinks Indian thought is most promising for philosophy today. Narration order; [hh:mm:ss] = audio jump point. Sanskrit terms normalized to standard transliteration; obvious speech-to-text slips fixed against context (Jonardon Ganeri ≈ "Janardin Canary/Ganari"; Dignāga ≈ "Dignaga"; svabhāva ≈ "Swavava"; Madhyamaka ≈ "Madyamaka"; Vasubandhu ≈ "Vasubandu"; Yogācāra ≈ "Yoga Chara"; Umāsvāti ≈ "Omasvati"; Dharmakīrti ≈ "Darmakirti / Dama Kirti"; Lawrence McCrea ≈ "Lawrence McCrae"; Abhinavagupta ≈ "Abidava Gupta / Avinava Gupta"; Utpaladeva ≈ "Utpala Deva"; Jayanta Bhaṭṭa ≈ "Jayanta Bhata"; Jayarāśi ≈ "Jayorashi"; Śrīharṣa ≈ "Shrihasa / Srihasa / Shrihasha"; pramāṇa ≈ "Pramana"; Mīmāṃsā ≈ "Mehamsa"; Advaita ≈ "Advaita"; Gaṅgeśa ≈ "Gangesha"; Navya-Nyāya ≈ "Navia Niaya"; Raghunātha Śiromaṇi ≈ "Raghunata Shiromani / Raganatha"; Navadvīpa ≈ "Navadvipa"; Madhusūdana Sarasvatī ≈ "Madhusudana Saraswati"; Appaya Dīkṣita ≈ "Apaya Dixita"; Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara ≈ "Nilakanta Chaturdara"; Dārā Shikoh ≈ "Dadaashiko"; Muḥibbullāh Ilāhābādī ≈ "Mujbala El Ahabadi"; Maḥmūd Jaunpūrī ≈ "Mahmoud Jan Puri"; Muḥibb Allāh al-Bihārī ≈ "Muhibbala al-Biharis"; Sullam al-ʿUlūm ≈ "Sulaam al-Ollum"; Battle of Plassey ≈ "Battle of Placie"; ahiṃsā ≈ "Ahimsa"; Michael Dummett ≈ "Michael Dummet"; Chike Jeffers ≈ "Chi K. Jeffers").

docs.title: Thinkers & texts introduced
docs.text:
• Dharmakīrti — Dignāga's brilliant disciple, whose work became the canon later philosophy argued with for centuries, even as Dignāga's own texts faded [00:06:05].
  • Śrīharṣa — 12th-century skeptic whose Khaṇḍana-khaṇḍa-khādya ("morsels of refutation") demolished definition-based philosophy [00:07:25].
  • Gaṅgeśa — 14th-century author of a single book, who founded Navya-Nyāya (the New Nyāya), the second great revolution after Dignāga [00:09:31].
  • Raghunātha Śiromaṇi — 16th-century figure of Navadvīpa in Bengal who reignited a self-conscious, exploratory phase of philosophy [00:10:51].
  • The colonial-era thinkers — Gandhi, Nehru, Ambedkar, Tagore, who made political and social philosophy central [00:14:18].

docs.title: Recap: what the series covered — from before the pre-Socratics to Dignāga
docs.text:
• [00:00:31] The series tried to follow the "Without Any Gaps" approach, but India's tradition is so vast that many "barely known figures and movements" had to be skipped, and even those included could not be done full justice. It began with texts older than the pre-Socratics of ancient Greece and worked forward as far as Dignāga and his contemporaries, around 600 AD.
  • [00:01:00] In the earliest phase, philosophy appeared above all as a reflection on how one lives — a path to a desirable final state, whether mokṣa (ultimate freedom) or nirvāṇa (release from all human suffering). These philosophies of path and purpose included the ancient ritual wisdom of the Vedas, brought (it seems) by Aryan settlers, and the Upaniṣads, poetic visions of the unity of humanity, ritual and cosmos. Under this heading came the original teachings of the Buddha and Mahāvīra, and the vast Hindu epic the Mahābhārata — which contains within it the Bhagavad-Gītā — as another thread woven into "the rope of thought through time" that was early Indian philosophy.
  • [00:01:49] Keeping the weaving metaphor, the series then turned to the Age of the Sūtra (sūtra literally means "thread"). These texts were so compressed and aphoristic that they were "extremely hard to figure out" without an interpretive gloss — so the series also met the great commentators, who really brought systematicity into Indian debate and drove the evolution of the schools: Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Mīmāṃsā, Cārvāka, and Vedānta.
  • [00:02:22] Buddhist and Jain philosophers were not left out. Their switch to Sanskrit fundamentally transformed Indian philosophy until the end of the first millennium. Among the keenest Buddhists was Nāgārjuna, whose assault on the metaphysical notion of svabhāva (self-nature) inspired the Madhyamaka, the "Middle Way" philosophy. Another was Vasubandhu, who both standardized Abhidharma in Sanskrit and laid the foundations for Yogācāra. The series also looked at the early Jains, including Umāsvāti, and their perspectival approach to epistemology.

docs.title: Dignāga: a genius, and a new way of writing philosophy
docs.text:
• [00:03:08] After "meandering through all this early history," the series finally reached Dignāga — a "philosophical genius of the highest order," a figure who would make it onto even the most conservative "top of the pops" list of greatest philosophers. His work was decisive in shaping the next period: a cosmopolitan Age of Dialogue in Sanskrit that lasted until the collapse of Buddhism in India — a collapse "usually, but not entirely uncontentiously, blamed on invasion from the Islamic world."
  • [00:03:39] Adamson and Ganeri are not alone in seeing Dignāga as inaugurating an entirely new epoch, though scholars differ on why he was so influential. The podcast emphasized his theoretical innovations — new ways of defining terms, new formalizations of sound argumentation — but others stress that he invented a new way of writing philosophy, a "transformation of discursive practice."
  • [00:04:13] Lawrence McCrea is quoted: Dignāga "initiated a sudden, widespread, and radical transformation in the reading, citational, and discursive practices of Sanskrit philosophers" — perhaps even more dramatic in effect than his specifically philosophical contributions. He made the systematic investigation of, and response to, the texts of rival traditions a basic organizing principle of his own work. These new ways of arguing and writing were immediately taken up and "rapidly became the hallmark of philosophical activity in a broad Sanskrit cosmopolis" that endured for centuries and spread well beyond the subcontinent.

docs.title: End of the survey — and a promise of the briefest of hints
docs.text:
• [00:05:00] That brings the series to its end. It occasionally glimpsed further ahead (e.g. Abhinavagupta, 11th century), later figures came up via interview guests, and special themes got attention — non-violence, the role of women, animals, karma, time, even tantra. In effect, the series covered "the first millennium and a half of Indian philosophy" — "not too bad in 60 episodes."
  • [00:05:26] But things "really picked up speed in the next millennium and a half, between Dignāga and the present day." A huge amount of great philosophy happened in that time; perhaps a future series will treat it properly. For now, Adamson offers "the briefest of hints" at the history of philosophy in India from Dignāga onward.

docs.title: Dharmakīrti eclipses his own master
docs.text:
• [00:05:52] It is an irony that, despite his enormous impact, Dignāga's Sanskrit works were lost for a long time — because he was "blessed, or possibly cursed," with an extremely brilliant disciple, Dharmakīrti. It was Dharmakīrti's work that provided the canon for later authors: widely disseminated, commented on, and attacked, even as Dignāga's own writings faded into the background.
  • [00:06:21] For at least three centuries, most serious Indian philosophy took Dharmakīrti as its principal point of reference. As all the schools the series reviewed developed, they took Dharmakīrti as their foil — and in doing so achieved great progress, articulating their core beliefs and supplying arguments "of a higher caliber than had ever been necessary before."

docs.title: Kashmir, and the persistence of skepticism
docs.text:
• [00:06:50] Many important figures came from Kashmir, including Śaiva thinkers like Utpaladeva and the aforementioned Abhinavagupta, as well as the Nyāya genius Jayanta Bhaṭṭa.
  • [00:07:01] Skepticism, which had played a major role in Indian thought from an early period (and may even have helped trigger ancient Greek skepticism), continued in later times. In the 9th century, Jayarāśi described himself as "a lion who had come to upturn every philosophical cart."
  • [00:07:19] Matters came to a head with Śrīharṣa's revolutionary critique of the fundamentals of pramāṇa epistemology. His 12th-century classic — "amassed morsels of refutation" (the Khaṇḍana-khaṇḍa-khādya) — is a brilliant destructive analysis of the "definition-mongering" activity of past thinkers. Śrīharṣa argued that a philosophical method based on the search for definitions is misguided, indeed incoherent, and developed a rival method of refutation to expose as vacuous the very way of doing philosophy that Dignāga had made so influential. Remarkably, his method required him first to reconstruct the best possible version of any definition — not merely the best anyone had actually formulated — articulating opponents' positions "with greater insight, accuracy, and acuity than their own proponents."

docs.title: Two more lines of critique: Mīmāṃsā on inquiry, Advaita on common sense
docs.text:
• [00:08:21] Other critiques gathered momentum. One came from new developments in Mīmāṃsā theory about the nature of inquiry, still within its traditional framework of defending the legitimacy and authority of Vedic knowledge. To suppose the Vedas authoritative is to accept their teachings as unquestionable: if the Veda teaches something, there is "no need to engage in verification." This pushed Brahmanical thinkers to reflect on methodology and the nature of knowledge, contesting the notion that truth must be the outcome of discovery and confirmation.
  • [00:08:59] Another critique was a growing challenge to the metaphysics of common sense: increasingly sophisticated Advaita philosophers sought to undermine the principle that appearance is trustworthy — in particular, that there is a world of everyday objects known to a plurality of distinct cognizers.

docs.title: Gaṅgeśa and the second great revolution: Navya-Nyāya
docs.text:
• [00:09:14] In the 14th century, in response to all these pressures, a philosopher emerged who transformed the landscape as brilliantly and decisively as Dignāga had in the 6th — "a second great revolution." His name was Gaṅgeśa.
  • [00:09:33] He wrote only one book, one that "styles itself as the jewel that fulfils the wish for truth" (the Tattvacintāmaṇi). His new conceptual methodologies — his answer to Śrīharṣa's general skepticism and to the specific challenges from Mīmāṃsā and Advaita — rapidly gained currency across the Sanskrit world.
  • [00:09:51] His new method was called Navya-Nyāya, the "New Nyāya." It spread to all intellectual disciplines and proved especially influential in law and jurisprudence. Its heart was a "meticulous technique for the disambiguation of terms and assertions," so that an opponent's thesis could be carefully separated into a variety of possible readings, each then individually refuted.

docs.title: The early-modern flowering: Raghunātha, Navadvīpa, and Varanasi
docs.text:
• [00:10:21] The 16th and 17th centuries were "an extraordinary period for philosophy in India" — partly, but only partly, the result of new encounters with Islamic culture. Exposure to new paradigms led Sanskrit philosophers to innovate self-consciously: "to think with the old structures, but not defer to them." An "astonishingly vast" number of Sanskrit works survive from this time.
  • [00:10:51] In the writings of those who followed Raghunātha Śiromaṇi — from about the middle of the 16th century until the middle of the 18th — there is a metamorphosis in epistemology, metaphysics, semantics, and philosophical logic. Many of these philosophers lived in Raghunātha's hometown of Navadvīpa in Bengal, and their works are full of phrases of "a newly open and exploratory attitude" — "this should be considered further," "this needs to be reflected on." What drove the work was not fresh exegesis of ancient texts but inquiry into the problems themselves, with a sense of an ongoing project.
  • [00:11:25] A second group, based in Varanasi and again profoundly influenced by Raghunātha, used his work to reinterpret ancient metaphysics, sometimes with the support of the Islamic rulers of Mughal India.
  • [00:11:43] At the same time — in opposition to Raghunātha's "new reasoners," while co-opting his methods — thinkers like Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Appaya Dīkṣita, and Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara brought a distinctive renewal to Vedānta, amid "complex negotiations with Mughal patronage and power, and with their own pasts."

docs.title: Islamic philosophy in India, in parallel
docs.text:
• [00:12:08] Alongside these Sanskrit developments, Muslim philosophers were producing important and innovative work in parallel centers of Islamic learning. Three Islamic trends emerged in the 17th and 18th centuries.
  • [00:12:24] First, the bilingual project of Dārā Shikoh and others, who translated philosophy from Sanskrit into Persian. Second, the Sufi philosophy of Muḥibbullāh Ilāhābādī, a prolific author in Persian and Arabic and a defender of the Andalusian mystic Ibn ʿArabī. Third, a debate between Avicennan thinkers — such as the influential Maḥmūd Jaunpūrī — and Illuminationists.
  • [00:12:51] Meanwhile, Muḥibb Allāh al-Bihārī's Sullam al-ʿUlūm is "a milestone 17th-century Indian textbook in Arab-Islamic logic." Some of this was discussed in the series on philosophy in the Islamic world (Episode 189). But, Adamson concedes, "we still have only the most rudimentary understanding" of the intersections between Sanskrit, Persian, and Arabic scholarship in early-modern India, and little insight into philosophy in Indian vernacular languages of the period.

docs.title: Colonial occupation and the turn to political philosophy
docs.text:
• [00:13:27] The series next "moved to the era of British colonial occupation" — which, Adamson stresses, "was not quite the total disaster for indigenous philosophy" that it was in many other colonized parts of the world. One effect it did have was to foreground new philosophical priorities, especially the need to respond to an incompatibility at the heart of the colonial project: European claims about liberty, tolerance, equality, and secularism on one hand, and the "manifest illiberalities, intolerances, and inequalities of colonial rule" on the other.
  • [00:14:00] That rule began with the East India Company's exploitative governance from the Battle of Plassey (1757) until the failed war of independence in 1857, then continued under direct British crown rule until independence in 1947.
  • [00:14:18] Brilliant thinkers like Gandhi, Nehru, Ambedkar, and Tagore — now often writing in English — made political and social philosophy the center of Indian philosophical activity, where earlier it had been mind, language, epistemology, and metaphysics. Others reflected deeply on the subject — its freedom, agency, and identity — in an effort to formulate the grounds of an intellectual decolonization. In the struggle for freedom, "the whole of India's philosophical past became an immense resource," its perceived spirit of negotiated pluralism and non-coercive cosmopolitanism made central to the design of a post-independence nation.

docs.title: From the 1950s to the present
docs.text:
• [00:15:05] Philosophy has continued to progress from the 1950s to today — though sometimes struggling to find a voice inside "Victorian-era universities" and understandably taking a backseat to the urgent task of rebuilding an economy ravaged by extractive colonial governance. There are positive signs that, as India enters a period of economic prosperity, philosophy will reassume "its traditional place at the very heart of Indian society and culture."
  • [00:15:35] Thanks both to new perspectives from the South Asian diaspora and to a new generation of Western philosophers with a more global and cosmopolitan view, the study of Indian philosophy in universities worldwide is enjoying "a period of unprecedented growth." Adamson hopes the podcast will help push insights from Indian thought into philosophy as taught and researched outside India.

docs.title: Where Indian thought looks most promising today
docs.text:
• [00:16:13] Adamson closes by naming areas where the Indian contribution seems "distinctive and promising" from a contemporary point of view.
  • Ethics — non-violence [00:16:24]: returning to Amber Carpenter's interview on the Indian ethic of non-violence toward animals. The Indian rationale was very different from today's. Peter Singer uses utilitarian principles (animals can suffer and get something positive from life); other ethicists take a rights-based approach (animals have as much claim to liberty and welfare as we do, potentially justifying total animal liberation). By contrast, ancient Indian ahiṃsā was "a holistic way of life," with avoidance of animal suffering only one of its many aspects. To live by ahiṃsā is to take a certain attitude toward all living things, including plants, toward oneself, and even toward inanimate objects — "kicking a stone in anger could be a violation," though a stone has no rights and cannot suffer. As the Mahābhārata puts it, "ahiṃsā is the dharma … the highest truth from which all dharma proceeds." It would be interesting to see a modern philosopher revive this — putting avoidance of violence at the center of ethics rather than extracting non-violence from some other notion like utility or duty. The recent revival of Aristotelian virtue ethics, with its similar holism, gives "some cause for optimism."
  • Metaphysics — Nāgārjuna [00:18:27]: Sāṃkhya's category theory or Vedānta monism seem unlikely to appeal to the average philosopher today, but Nāgārjuna might be a more plausible source of inspiration. As heard in the Graham Priest interview, Nāgārjuna's reasoning can be compared to non-classical logic, and his ideas about emptiness and dependent origination are worth revisiting. If "to say things are empty is to claim they have no fixed intrinsic essence" — that the being of things is "purely relational" — this could excite a modern metaphysician: rather than a world of discrete objects bearing relations, what if relations were the fundamental building blocks? Some philosophers already admit relations are ineliminable, and some think a relational view fits modern physics better than one based on intrinsic natures. Nāgārjuna "could be a formidable ally."
  • Epistemology & philosophy of language [00:20:08]: a long-standing concern of the ancient Indians, with both constructive work (the theory of pramāṇas) and rich skeptical traditions. Śrīharṣa's critique is attracting contemporary epistemologists, as is Sanskrit work in philosophy of language, especially its highly developed accounts of metaphor and literary significance.
  • Philosophy of mind [00:20:39]: perhaps the area with most cross-cultural activity. Classical Indian theories of mind have fed into cognitive science and new understandings of consciousness, attention, and self-representation. The Oxford philosopher Michael Dummett thought philosophy of mind was the area that would "profit most from philosophers working in divergent traditions coming together" — and there does seem to be truth in that.

docs.title: Conclusion, and what comes next
docs.text:
• [00:21:12] The series ends "on an emphatic note": ancient Indian thought "has everything a historian of philosophy could want" — rich with interpretive challenges, full of subtle texts that respond to one another and are intriguing in literary form. It was historically influential (somewhat on European ideas, but "above all in cultures across Asia"), it addressed core questions in every department of philosophy, and it advanced novel ideas — some ripe for contemporary uptake. No philosopher is obliged to study Indian intellectual history (there is too much other great philosophy elsewhere for that), but "any philosopher could benefit greatly from doing so."
  • [00:22:18] So the podcast will keep exploring non-European traditions. These will eventually include China and other East Asian cultures (a chance to learn about the influence of Indian thought) — but the next stop is Africa. In a further series of comparable length, Chike Jeffers will join Adamson to explore philosophy in Africana culture, from ancient Egypt down to the diaspora of the late 20th century, appearing on the same feed.
  • [00:23:06] Before that, there will be "one last look at Indian culture" — a finale with "a very special secret interview guest." Since this was the last scripted episode, Adamson finishes by thanking Jonardon Ganeri for lending his expertise and helping tell "the history of philosophy in India."

docs.title: Key thinkers, texts & terms
docs.text:
• Dignāga — c. 600 AD genius whose theoretical innovations and new "discursive practice" (systematic engagement with rivals' texts, per Lawrence McCrea) inaugurated the Sanskrit "Age of Dialogue."
  • Dharmakīrti — Dignāga's disciple whose work became the canon; for three centuries the chief foil against which every school sharpened its arguments, eclipsing Dignāga's own (lost) texts.
  • Jayarāśi — 9th-century skeptic, "a lion come to upturn every philosophical cart."
  • Śrīharṣa — 12th-century skeptic; his "morsels of refutation" (Khaṇḍana-khaṇḍa-khādya) argued that definition-based philosophy is incoherent, replacing it with a method of refutation.
  • pramāṇa — means/instrument of knowledge; the epistemology Śrīharṣa attacked and the Nyāya tradition defended.
  • Gaṅgeśa — 14th-century author of one book ("the jewel that fulfils the wish for truth," the Tattvacintāmaṇi); founder of the second great revolution.
  • Navya-Nyāya — Gaṅgeśa's "New Nyāya"; a meticulous technique for disambiguating terms so a thesis can be split into readings and each refuted; spread to all disciplines, especially law.
  • Mīmāṃsā — school defending the unquestionable authority of Vedic knowledge; its later theory of inquiry contested that truth must come from discovery and confirmation.
  • Advaita — non-dualist Vedānta; its philosophers challenged common-sense metaphysics and the trustworthiness of appearance.
  • Raghunātha Śiromaṇi — 16th-century philosopher of Navadvīpa (Bengal); sparked a self-conscious, problem-driven phase of "new reasoners."
  • Madhusūdana Sarasvatī / Appaya Dīkṣita / Nīlakaṇṭha Caturdhara — early-modern thinkers who renewed Vedānta while negotiating Mughal patronage.
  • Dārā Shikoh — Mughal prince behind the bilingual project translating Sanskrit philosophy into Persian.
  • Muḥibbullāh Ilāhābādī — Sufi philosopher in Persian and Arabic, defender of Ibn ʿArabī; Maḥmūd Jaunpūrī — Avicennan thinker; Sullam al-ʿUlūm (Muḥibb Allāh al-Bihārī) — milestone 17th-c. Indian textbook of Arab-Islamic logic.
  • ahiṃsā — non-violence as a holistic way of life (toward all beings, plants, oneself, even objects); "the highest truth from which all dharma proceeds" (Mahābhārata).
  • emptiness / dependent origination — Nāgārjuna's view that things have no fixed intrinsic nature but are "purely relational" — proposed as inspiration for a relational metaphysics.
  • Chike Jeffers — scholar who will co-present the next series, on Africana philosophy.
